How to describe this game in my words?  Start off it's a turn based rpg (older rpgs like Final Fantasy are an example), has a squad and sort of base mechanic that of XCOM, random look and dungeon crawling that of Diablo, Torchlight, and Binding of Isaac, and either in your opinion a very strong, or very light pinch of a hard game (example the Souls Series and Bloodbourne).  What I meant to say by this, is that the game is supposed to be a hard turned based rpg.  How did they make it hard you might ask?
So from my understandings that resources are limited for each run of a dungeon, so with your money you hav to carefully spend i9t with the items that you are offered to make the most out of it.  Another thing that is implemented into the game is perma-death.  Which means that if your character that you just got, or had for some times finally dies.  You won’t get him back because once he or she is gone, they are gone.  Another mechanic to make it more harder, and probably the key aspect of this game.  Is that of the stress mechanic.  The stress mechanic gives each and every hero or adventurer their own stress bar.  During dungeon runs some actions, or during fighting the stress bar will fill up.  When it fills up completely it will put the hero into a resolve test, where if he or she goes through with it they will resolve and will become heroic, but if he or she fails they will have a melt down.  Which will resolve into having more problems his his teammates, pass turns, make the enemy attack him or her, or move into different positions to make it much more troublesome.  If it fills up again, the hero will have a heart attack and send him straight into deaths door, which can once again result into killing the said hero.  Once dungeons are done, the heroes will still have stress from what they took from the dungeon, and to fix this you can have them taken to either the church or the tavern to reduce or remove their stress they were given.  Sometimes they will not be available for future missions because of their stress, or if their level is at a certain point will not do the easier missions.
Each adventurer and hero you get will have different abilities.  Examples will be a Crusader with his damaging attacks towards the front line against the unholy (undead), The hard but Enjoyable Jester with his bleed stacks, buffs, and a finishing move to kill off his enemies, blight and damage over time plague doctor with its minor healing and powerful blight attacks, to the houndmaster with his trusty dog and extra damage against beasts.  You can switch, mix, and match the sixteen classes to form a party for a dungeon, some to counter the dungeon, for bosses, or just straight for loot.  The maximum you can have with classes is twenty five, so you either have to ditch some that aren’t a viable to you, or isn’t worth keeping anymore and get fresh new blood from the stables.
Speaking of the stables.  You have a town that you can upgrade to give it better benefits, from having the ability to get better weapons and armors for your classes, to upgrading their abilities and buying buff items called trinkets.  Which gives some strong buffs, but can have some minimal side effects to the class from slower speed, or lower damage.
So my final thoughts on the game.  I think in my point of view it was worth my money, and I high recommend the game.

So, Trove is a voxel-based adventure and building game where you go out adventuring into realms to gather treasure and resources to build... And of course, build.
Think of it as the freedom of Minecraft (with a kajillion mods, but without the over-complexity of crafting) mashed with the world of Ace of Spades and the adventuring from Cube World.
Is this going to be the next Minecraft, or Cube World? Nope - Because Trion Worlds, like always have screwed over their entire playerbase. Other than their MMO Rift, every Trion World game seem to follow this formula:
The only problem is how locked or grindy everything is.
Want to craft a mount? Be prepared to run around killing the same creature for their drops for 10 hours.
Want better gear? You need Magic Find to get decent gear. Not enough Magic Find? You need to buy magic find.
Want new classes? You can't earn them anymore. You must buy them.
Want to expand your world? Be prepared to grind like crazy to find Infinium. Enjoy your next 10 hours hopping between worlds to get enough for a decent plot worth of land expanders.
Whatever happens, even if a bug or a glitch kills you, even if the game crashes, it's all your fault. Git gud.

This game has a really gorgeous storybook aesthetic to it, Lovecraftian themes and a cool narration style that immediately sold me on it way back in the dark days of early early access.  As it's progressed toward release, though, it's become apparent that underneath that cool appearance and neat sound design is also a pretty deep, rewarding and interesting game!  So, that's good.
Basically, you recruit a party of adventurers from random classes as they come to your ancestral home.  You use those people (and you will go through them like tissue paper at first) to explore the ruins of that home, which is overrun by all kinds of awful eldritch horrors, tendrils clinging limpid to the ancient stone like the tenebrous tentacles of.... wait, sorry, what was I talking about?
Your adventurers will freak the hell out and get stressed by darkness and monsters and horrible things, and will eventually start to crack.  You have to manage their stress levels, their quirks and paranoias and such that they pick up over the course of their adventures, and rotate through several different crews of people.  You'll go on quests, and by completing them, level up each of the game's areas, making them harder and giving you access to longer quests.  I thought the camping mechanic was a nice touch, as each class has both a customizable loadout of battle skills as well as a loadout of camp skills.  When you camp, you get some neat dialogue between party members as you use skills on each other, helping to heal or decrease stress or other such things.
Positioning is key in the combat, as almost all attacks have positions they can and cannot be used from, as well as enemy positions they can and cannot hit.  Enemies will sometimes use attacks that shuffle you around, and you can do the same to them, with sometimes-devastating effect.  Enemies also leave corpses behind that can impede your positioning and targeting efforts, and some classes you can recruit (there are a WIDE variety) have skills for handling these corpses and disposing of them.
It's an uphill climb, a hard battle of attrition against the inevitable victory of all-devouring darkness, and it's a hell of a good time.

So you're thinking about buying this game, huh? Well, let me put this simply: Go the whole 9 yards. Get it, and the DLC too.
This section is for those new to the series. If you've played a Souls game before, you should skip past this (unless you want some juicy insight). The Dark Souls series is based around action rpgs that take place in medieval fantasy lands, which have you embark on a quest for a mantle of extreme power and influence, which requires you to first become an immensely powerful being. You become more powerful both by leveling up your weapons via various forms of the upgrade material known as Titanite (and Dragon Scales!), and your character by leveling up via Souls, which is a currency that is used for just about everything. You will gain souls by either killing various enemies and/or using/bartering items you find along your journey. However, you will not automatically level up wherever you are; you will need to head back to a 'home base' of sorts, and speak to a lady who "tends" to it (unless you're playing Dark Souls 1, in which case it's at any bonfire). However, the catch is that if you drop your souls basically wherever you died (if you fell off of a cliff, it'll still be retrievable at the cliff); and if you are either human or 'embered' (which in this game it's the latter), you will lose this status as well, and need to use another item to gain this status once again. When you die, you will be returned to a checkpoint of sorts, known as a Bonfire. You light bonfires and rest at them in order to regain healing potions (of which you have a limited amount, that can both have the amount of HP healed increased via bringing a specific item to a certain kind of person/bonfire, or the amount of uses increased via either kindling bonfires for Dark Souls 1, or retrieving estus shards and bringing them to someone who can make use of them- such as Blacksmith Andre in Dark Souls 3) known as Estus (and also in Dark Souls 3, Ashen Estus), as well as replenish your current HP. Bonfires are immensely useful, as they not only serve as places of a brief respite, but also provide a place to fast travel to (save for Dark Souls 1, where you must get through half of the game to access this, and it only works on certain bonfires). They normally can't be rested at if enemies are too close, but also when other players are alive in your world, and/or when you are going into someone else's world. The aforementioned human/embered status allows for you to engage in about half of the online play (being able to be invaded, as well as and summon other friendly players), saving the rest for various items you will be able to procure throughout your journey- some being easier to obtain than others. While PvE (player vs. enemy) is nice in the series, PvP (player vs. player) is a high point for it. Try not to shy away from it much, because it's usually quite fun if you can manage to have a fair (or generally interesting) fight.
This iteration of the Souls franchise is less like Dark Souls as we're used to, and more like Bloodborne; as you'll barely ever rely on a shield (unless you wish to die), and there's
only
semblance of poise. Though, to be fair, this is closer to what the head developer (Miyazaki) had in mind when he originally created the series (apparently).
Even though Dark Souls 3 leaves all of us Souls vets vying for a simpler time, it has an undeniably addictive nature. For every time you might be discouraged, and/or wishing to quit, you will come to realize that both Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3 fill a niche of gaming that apparently can't be filled with other games. The fluidity of its combat is far greater than its predecessors, and although it may leave a bit to be desired (I still want ye olde poise!), it makes me realize that it creates an itch that I just can't seem to scratch no matter how hard I try to by playing other games.
It's quite fair (for the most part), and an overall enjoyable experience- even if you're not having your hand held through the game. The PvE is, of course, somewhat repetitive if you've beaten the game before at least once or twice; but the PvP- that's where a lot of the excitement is. You just can't compare fighting AI to fighting against other players. As I mentioned before, it can be quite fair; however, be warned: minmaxing and twinking (getting the most bang for your buck out of a lower leveled character, and getting better gear from a better character to a worse one, respectively) are two aspects of the game that will heavily influence a majority of your time engaging in PvP. Some builds are far more powerful and effective against others, so be mindful of your playstyle and what kind of weapons/spells/miracles you use.
I can only end this by saying I wish that there was more to it. Not more to learn, but content to play with. Not to say that this lacks replayability, or will age poorly- I have roughly 400 hours of playtime at the time of writing this, and I still feel like picking up my controller and playing it. It's immensely entertaining, and will no doubt be enjoyed for years to come. I only wish that there was more to do, or that the community could pick up where From Software left off, and create our own content to play- but it would be impossible to do so, with how the game is regulated. Though this may be the end of the Dark Souls series, Souls-Like games (such as Bloodborne) will hopefully be able to fill the Dark Souls-sized hole in my heart.

Your first experience in this game if you like adventure/action/platformer genres will probably be similar to mine.
It fills those 3 extremely well. I do believe playing with friends highly improves the experience also. If not while adventuring, definitely while building. The building is quite a bit faster than games like MC or Terraria, but it's also more limited shape-wise. It does however compensate with some neat decorations.
After close to 10hours of playtime, all I can say is that I don't see how the microtransactions are necessary, and unlike the company's previous title; Archeage; you do not need to be a patron to enjoy the game. Some things will take a bit of getting used to due to a lot of people enjoying solo-play every now and then, but the game makes sure you aren't penalized for having someone you don't know near you.
Everybody in the nearby area gets the same materials, exp from mobs, chests from bosses, loot chests from digging etc. As long as you're close enough, you get it.
I also absolutely love how free the movements are. With my playtime, I already have crazy movement speed with about 15 additional jumps. I rarely hit the ground before I'm at my destination. :P
The mounts are quite unique but also pretty interesting. While not all of them are obtainable through F2P, you can buy quite a few and craft some others while being a completely F2P player.
My personal opinion of this game; 9/10. And it's pretty much brand new.
I do hope for new stuff, new classes, new looks, new building blocks, new decorations, new biomes etc.
Oh and did I say that you can quite literally traverse Candy Land, be knocked out of it into the Treasure Isles where pirates might push you away into the Peaceful Gardens? :P Every single bosses are themed as far as I know, so are the mobs, tons of unique dungeons, quite a decent tutorial etc.
However, a few people do mention a lack of  content. If you do like the MMORPG vibe where you level up classes, beat dungeons, mess around with friends etc, with a building twist, I'd say you'll be enjoying your time in Trove.
I must've been extremely lucky, because I have yet to have even the slightest problem with logging onto the game. No queue, no DC, no nothing. The game runs extremely smoothly even though my computer has been pretty crappy lately... I believe people who put those comments in their reviews, mainly because they are too common not to be true, but I personally haven't dealt with any issues like that. Pretty happy about that and it does show on my rating.
TL;DR
9/10
The game doesn't need to improve much gameplay-wise, and what it -could- improve is not quite necessary seeing as their game is already quite solid.
It's almost brand new, their lack of content shouldn't make or break the game quite yet. It does however change my personal rating a bit.
They do need to protect the game. Whether it be server issues, toxic community, etc. They need to protect it. Or make it manageable somehow. I've seen too many "CAN ANYONE GIVE ME FREE WINGS PLEASE" spammed for about 5minutes in the world chat to then be followed up with "ANYBODY GIVING FREE WINGS??!??!?!?!?!". That is a problem. But I review the game and the game only. Not the community nor the connection issues that people have. Which is why I put the 9. The game is fun and good. Movements are quick, responsive and neat-looking. I do wish people had an experience as pleasant as the one I seemingly had. :P And I was in a call with 3 other people. It does help the experience, whether or not you grind for materials.

How to describe this game in my words?  Start off it's a turn based rpg (older rpgs like Final Fantasy are an example), has a squad and sort of base mechanic that of XCOM, random look and dungeon crawling that of Diablo, Torchlight, and Binding of Isaac, and either in your opinion a very strong, or very light pinch of a hard game (example the Souls Series and Bloodbourne).  What I meant to say by this, is that the game is supposed to be a hard turned based rpg.  How did they make it hard you might ask?
So from my understandings that resources are limited for each run of a dungeon, so with your money you hav to carefully spend i9t with the items that you are offered to make the most out of it.  Another thing that is implemented into the game is perma-death.  Which means that if your character that you just got, or had for some times finally dies.  You won’t get him back because once he or she is gone, they are gone.  Another mechanic to make it more harder, and probably the key aspect of this game.  Is that of the stress mechanic.  The stress mechanic gives each and every hero or adventurer their own stress bar.  During dungeon runs some actions, or during fighting the stress bar will fill up.  When it fills up completely it will put the hero into a resolve test, where if he or she goes through with it they will resolve and will become heroic, but if he or she fails they will have a melt down.  Which will resolve into having more problems his his teammates, pass turns, make the enemy attack him or her, or move into different positions to make it much more troublesome.  If it fills up again, the hero will have a heart attack and send him straight into deaths door, which can once again result into killing the said hero.  Once dungeons are done, the heroes will still have stress from what they took from the dungeon, and to fix this you can have them taken to either the church or the tavern to reduce or remove their stress they were given.  Sometimes they will not be available for future missions because of their stress, or if their level is at a certain point will not do the easier missions.
Each adventurer and hero you get will have different abilities.  Examples will be a Crusader with his damaging attacks towards the front line against the unholy (undead), The hard but Enjoyable Jester with his bleed stacks, buffs, and a finishing move to kill off his enemies, blight and damage over time plague doctor with its minor healing and powerful blight attacks, to the houndmaster with his trusty dog and extra damage against beasts.  You can switch, mix, and match the sixteen classes to form a party for a dungeon, some to counter the dungeon, for bosses, or just straight for loot.  The maximum you can have with classes is twenty five, so you either have to ditch some that aren’t a viable to you, or isn’t worth keeping anymore and get fresh new blood from the stables.
Speaking of the stables.  You have a town that you can upgrade to give it better benefits, from having the ability to get better weapons and armors for your classes, to upgrading their abilities and buying buff items called trinkets.  Which gives some strong buffs, but can have some minimal side effects to the class from slower speed, or lower damage.
So my final thoughts on the game.  I think in my point of view it was worth my money, and I high recommend the game.

40 weeks into my first game and it no longer feels insanely hard. Its actually a nice blend of very unforgiving yet very patient.
My graveyard is stuffed full of dead and failed heroes. I ran out of money several times. I lost whole parties of my favourites. I invested in new weapons and skills only for them to die on the next mission. Sometimes missions go well only to deliver so many diseases and flaws randomly at the end that financial diastser arrives anyway. Thats the unforgiving bit.
Once you embrace the idea that things are going to go badly, heroes are going to die, money is going to run out regularly, the patient bit of the game starts to become clear: there is no crushing difficulty curve ramping up in the background. A disastrous mission or even three or four in a row does not kill the game... your town upgrades remain, new adventurers arrive every week and you can always train and equip another team. And you can (almost) always retreat.
Dont overcommit to a mission or any one character. Dont pressure yourself into thinking every mission has to succeed and it starts to make sense and the game becomes hugely addictive fun.

Darkest Dungeon is the first review for a game i've done since I started on Steam 11 years ago.   I've played 35 hours, and I feel like i could invest 100 more.   It's brutal but fair.   Unforgiving at times but rewarding.   When you manage to get through a difficult dungeon victoriously, it really gives you a great sense of achievement.
Starting out initially can be a little overwhelming, but once you get through the early stages, and start leveling up your building's/heros and collect a few items, it is very very possible to get through dungeons with little to no difficulty if you are careful and make good decisions.
After 35 hours i'm just beginning to get into some of the tier 2 bosses, and have my village leveled up quite a bit.   There were certainly times during my playtime where i slammed my mouse down and felt like the odds were stacked against me, but the best part about this game is the fact that you always have a way out if needed.
Up against the wall and about to lose an important party member?  --Run from the fight and live to fight another day.  Leave the dungeon/forfeit the loot, but SAVE that important party member.
All in all, this is easily one of the top 10 strategy games i've ever played.   It's fun and absolutely addicting as #ll.
If you are into really well designed/fair but challenging strategy games, i'd say don't hesitate another second... this will be a game worth your hard earned $$.

How to describe this game in my words?  Start off it's a turn based rpg (older rpgs like Final Fantasy are an example), has a squad and sort of base mechanic that of XCOM, random look and dungeon crawling that of Diablo, Torchlight, and Binding of Isaac, and either in your opinion a very strong, or very light pinch of a hard game (example the Souls Series and Bloodbourne).  What I meant to say by this, is that the game is supposed to be a hard turned based rpg.  How did they make it hard you might ask?
So from my understandings that resources are limited for each run of a dungeon, so with your money you hav to carefully spend i9t with the items that you are offered to make the most out of it.  Another thing that is implemented into the game is perma-death.  Which means that if your character that you just got, or had for some times finally dies.  You won’t get him back because once he or she is gone, they are gone.  Another mechanic to make it more harder, and probably the key aspect of this game.  Is that of the stress mechanic.  The stress mechanic gives each and every hero or adventurer their own stress bar.  During dungeon runs some actions, or during fighting the stress bar will fill up.  When it fills up completely it will put the hero into a resolve test, where if he or she goes through with it they will resolve and will become heroic, but if he or she fails they will have a melt down.  Which will resolve into having more problems his his teammates, pass turns, make the enemy attack him or her, or move into different positions to make it much more troublesome.  If it fills up again, the hero will have a heart attack and send him straight into deaths door, which can once again result into killing the said hero.  Once dungeons are done, the heroes will still have stress from what they took from the dungeon, and to fix this you can have them taken to either the church or the tavern to reduce or remove their stress they were given.  Sometimes they will not be available for future missions because of their stress, or if their level is at a certain point will not do the easier missions.
Each adventurer and hero you get will have different abilities.  Examples will be a Crusader with his damaging attacks towards the front line against the unholy (undead), The hard but Enjoyable Jester with his bleed stacks, buffs, and a finishing move to kill off his enemies, blight and damage over time plague doctor with its minor healing and powerful blight attacks, to the houndmaster with his trusty dog and extra damage against beasts.  You can switch, mix, and match the sixteen classes to form a party for a dungeon, some to counter the dungeon, for bosses, or just straight for loot.  The maximum you can have with classes is twenty five, so you either have to ditch some that aren’t a viable to you, or isn’t worth keeping anymore and get fresh new blood from the stables.
Speaking of the stables.  You have a town that you can upgrade to give it better benefits, from having the ability to get better weapons and armors for your classes, to upgrading their abilities and buying buff items called trinkets.  Which gives some strong buffs, but can have some minimal side effects to the class from slower speed, or lower damage.
So my final thoughts on the game.  I think in my point of view it was worth my money, and I high recommend the game.

For your average gamer, I may not recommend this title, at this time. Considering the game is still in 'beta' development stages, there are new updates and content added, extremely often. With Character and World wipes coming, this will make it difficult for most players to do anything that they may get attached to, such as, developing a home world, or collecting rare, high tier items/weapons/armor.
That being said, for a gamer who may like to experience the raw nature of an early access title, this one is right there. Nearly as many things broken as working, and a flood of new items/monster behaviours/events to experiment with at any given time. Being able to have your input considered, during these crucial development stages, is one of the nice things available to players at this point.
While it keeps the traditional feel of the mining/crafting genre, it adds a few fairly straigtforward sets of goals to accomplish in order to progress in the game, allowing players who could not get into the driveless feel of games like minecraft, to get into this genre and still have a sense of actual progression.
When Starbound emerges from beta, and into full development, it is a game that will be hard to match in terms of shear explorability, and potential replayability.
All in all, another highly recommended title.

40 weeks into my first game and it no longer feels insanely hard. Its actually a nice blend of very unforgiving yet very patient.
My graveyard is stuffed full of dead and failed heroes. I ran out of money several times. I lost whole parties of my favourites. I invested in new weapons and skills only for them to die on the next mission. Sometimes missions go well only to deliver so many diseases and flaws randomly at the end that financial diastser arrives anyway. Thats the unforgiving bit.
Once you embrace the idea that things are going to go badly, heroes are going to die, money is going to run out regularly, the patient bit of the game starts to become clear: there is no crushing difficulty curve ramping up in the background. A disastrous mission or even three or four in a row does not kill the game... your town upgrades remain, new adventurers arrive every week and you can always train and equip another team. And you can (almost) always retreat.
Dont overcommit to a mission or any one character. Dont pressure yourself into thinking every mission has to succeed and it starts to make sense and the game becomes hugely addictive fun.

Darkest Dungeon is the first review for a game i've done since I started on Steam 11 years ago.   I've played 35 hours, and I feel like i could invest 100 more.   It's brutal but fair.   Unforgiving at times but rewarding.   When you manage to get through a difficult dungeon victoriously, it really gives you a great sense of achievement.
Starting out initially can be a little overwhelming, but once you get through the early stages, and start leveling up your building's/heros and collect a few items, it is very very possible to get through dungeons with little to no difficulty if you are careful and make good decisions.
After 35 hours i'm just beginning to get into some of the tier 2 bosses, and have my village leveled up quite a bit.   There were certainly times during my playtime where i slammed my mouse down and felt like the odds were stacked against me, but the best part about this game is the fact that you always have a way out if needed.
Up against the wall and about to lose an important party member?  --Run from the fight and live to fight another day.  Leave the dungeon/forfeit the loot, but SAVE that important party member.
All in all, this is easily one of the top 10 strategy games i've ever played.   It's fun and absolutely addicting as #ll.
If you are into really well designed/fair but challenging strategy games, i'd say don't hesitate another second... this will be a game worth your hard earned $$.

What can be said about Fallout 4 that already hasn't been said? Simply put, I believe it to be like this: if you have never played another Fallout game, or did not enjoy the others then this game will be the one for you. The gunplay and VATS system are fast paced and superior to the previous games, adding in a sense of urgency to firefights as well as less reliance on the VATS system. The world itself is beautiful, expansive, and full of little secrets and side-missions that will keep you entertained for hours. There are a few things in the game that irk myself and others who are familiar with the series. Crafting and base building are extremely important to the game, which is fun at first, but after a few times of realizing almost all of your inventory is nothing but garbage and adhesive it can be a little annoying. There are also the 4 main factions, as you play the game you will most likely gravitate towards one or the other until you realize that they are all more or less unlikeable, and unlike Fallout New Vegas there is no option to be in it for yourself. There has also been some debate regarding the DLCs, but aside from their pricing I find them all to be interesting and enjoyable. All in all, Falout 4 is a game worth playing, but if youre new to the series I would recommend trying out New Vegas first.

I've only played the game a few hours and yes, it's an incredibly challenging game that requires you spending time to think about every move you make and properly planning out your steps, the game then will do it's best to ruin your attempts but you have to hold fast. In all, I most certainly say that you should play this game, but there's a few things that may turn away the casual player if they aren't willing to invest too much or take too many risks.

This game is a creepy, morbid delight, dang. The art style is gorgeous -- I love the heavy lines and deep shadows, and the character designs are great. The narration was written by somebody who clearly had a lot of fun with the eldritch purple prose, and the narrator reads it with gusto. It's having a lot of ♥♥♥♥ing fun rolling around in its premise.
And I am too, frankly. The combat is, as the saying goes, "easy to learn and difficult to master" -- it's a turn-based system and it's quick to pick up the basics of positioning your party members to best use their skills, but there are enough classes & enough variations on skill loadout that you have a lot of potential for tinkering. Managing your party's physical and mental health as they go through the dungeon is stressful in the best way; my favorite moment for that so far was in the last fight of a dungeon crawl, when my Jester had already succumbed to the Hopeless affliction and then wound up on Death's Door but because of the affliction
. The affliction mechanics in general are great, especially in the way that the behaviors they produce then add to the stress levels of the rest of the party. (The reverse is also neat to watch, the way a character who pulls off a critical hit boosts not only her own morale but her allies', too.) It makes for a lot of drama and emotional tension with a group of technically "generic" characters traversing procedurally generated dungeons.
The part that seems most frustrating to me about the early game is managing resources. While you CAN flee a dungeon at any time and keep whatever loot you've picked up so far, and doing so is a good idea if you're in deep trouble, a few runs like that in a row and you start to run low on cash to outfit the next party with food and torches. Still, I think this is a problem that resolves itself as you get a little further on; once you're able to get a few characters to Resolve Level 2 and unlock some skill upgrades, the odds of needing to flee a low-level mission drop drastically.
Because you can lose a character on very short notice, there's a certain amount of grinding the early levels that will be necessary to replace (or preemptively work up alternates of) favorite classes. I can see that becoming a drag eventually and probably for a very grind-averse player it wouldn't be a good choice of game. But again, the individual stress mechanics and reactions do a lot to make the grind less predictable and more interesting.

This game reminds me of Diablo, Frank Frazetta, Conan The Barbarian, HP Lovecraft, Edgar Allen Poe, and old medieval woodcuts. It's like they all got smashed together by Cthulhu into one amazing video game masterpiece.

I'm glad I took the time to play this game because it's unbelievably addictive. The added mechanics can be disabled for the most part, but they add extra depth to the combat strategy in this game, so you'll probably prefer to keep them on.
The game itself is a perfect example of graphic design and art direction done right. The game is dripping with the oppressive atmosphere of the eldritch terrors that were released from the darkest dungeon. The combat mechanics are significantly more involved than I expected. The only other game I would compare them to right now is the much more lighthearted Renowned Explorers which is another game I also recomment.
The narrator is amazing, but he can get a little repetitive if you're into long game sessions. The game can also be a grind, especially if you spend your gold poorly.
That said, it's one of those games that sucks you right in. You forget all about your real world problems for a few hours, and you feel like a kid all over again.
It takes a special game to make you feel like that when you're a jaded adult.

It also has some more variety amongst the crafting options and offers more building options.  There is also a larger modding crowd around the Starbound game as opposed to Terraria. There are some flaws, however, which make Starbound a lesser experience.  For starters, Starbound has an annoying webpage-like start screen.  Second, there is a decidedly higher system requirements mark for Starbound, meaning Terraria is more likely to run on your low-end laptop, albeit poorly.  Finally, Starbound's visuals are less retro and do not offer the same kind of charm as Terraria.
I love both games.  I think they are both worth spending some time with.  I no longer play Terraria, because I've had my fill of it for a long while.  While Starbound is fresh and interesting, I intend to wait until the game is more feature-complete before delving very far into it.

Though recent changes to the gameplay have been the matter of controversy, for me this is still the same game I paid for, and still extremely enjoyable. Before I explain my thoughts on this, I'll address the other aspects of the game, which are very well done. Aesthetically,  the game is remarkable. The artwork is unique, dark, and has a very distinct style. The soundtrack and narration keep the same ominous tone. The different elements blend together perfectly into a coherent and memorable experience that delivers on the promise of dread and suspense. The game offers a large variety of skills, classes, items and enemies, scattered across (eventually five) unique locations. The gameplay consists of pretty short dungeon raids, and between them the player can upgrade and manage the party, as well as the hamlet- which is the base of operations for the game. The turn-based fights are affected heavily by the positioning of both your party members and the enemy, which can be manipulated by various skills. This gives depth to the fight system and helps set apart the various classes and enemies. The inability to save is necessary to create the sense of risk and the proper fear of failure, while the progression between missions and the large roster helps mitigate losses and limits the damage to progress after a catastrophic raid. This is the exact experience I came looking for when I bought the game. As a fan of the genre, Darkest Dungeon fully met my fairly high expectations, and even exceeded them at some points. If after hearing about the game you find yourself interested, I recommend you get it. It delivers fully on it's promises and is well worth the price tag. But for those reading this who are worried because of the recent controversy, this is my take on it:
There have been many complaints over the last months about the game becoming too difficult, after the devs attempted to rebalance it and reduce the effectiveness of strategies that some users saw as "broken". I can certainly see why more casual players reacted poorly to these changes, and are now blaming the devs for pandering to a small but vocal group of min-maxers. I understand- but completely disagree. I admit that after the game was retooled, and the difficulty suddenly spiked, it did take me a while to get used to the changes and I lost several missions which was very frustrating. But a short-lasting frustration while adapting to changes does not make a valid argument against a game and is of no use to new players. When I bought the game, I expected it to be ruthless and, at times, frustrating. A string of unfortunate events can, and eventually will, cause you to fail quests and lose members of your party,  hurting your progress. That has been true since the early-access release, and is a staple of the genre. Still, with a little bit of care and risk management, which the game allows for, such events will be few and far between and will not set you back too much. As I can attest to- you do not have to "min-max" in order to succeed in this game. A pretty minimal amount of care is needed to properly equip your party, come up with a reasonable party composition and buy provisions. Once you understand the risks and the basic strategies against the various enemies, this is enough to win 90%+ of raids without losing any characters. Some more advanced team building strategies can bring this closer to 100%, but a decent amount of effort will allow you to progress and succeed, and do so in your own "sub-optimal" way. The game is not easy and it requires some thought. You can't really breeze through most encounters. But, this has been true since the game's release on early access and it was to be expected from the way the game was presented. If the game would've been release to EA in it's current difficulty, I truly think most of the players who decided to change their recommendations would have recommended it. Also, the devs added the possibility to toggle off some of the most hardship-inducing and controversial features, so players can enjoy a more casual game which will be more similar to the original form. This last addition renders most of the new arguments against buying the game completely invalid. In any way, if you are looking for a decent, reasonable challenge- Darkest Dungeon provides just that.

I was eyeing with this game for some time, honestly I am not a huge fan of such turn based RPGs.
But did a litle diggind and found out from many sources that this is in fact quite a Lovecraftian game.
It is not based on any novel of Lovecraft but the symbols, some monsters are giving homage to him. So this made me buy it.
But.
The game itself is as you see turn based rpg, but also includes town management, micro management of mercenaries, buying skills, upgrading weapons, etc. It is not an easy game as you can read in many reviews. It is not terribly hard, but you will learn soon not to take anything granted. From your best stance your group can easily be rendered into a pile of bloody pulp or helpless lunatics.
Combat and encounters can be very punishing (such as in any Lovecraftian game where the odds are never in your favor) but also because of this, it can be veryvery rewarding, which makes you want more. Yes it is typically the game where you go one more run, one more, and again.
If you are looking for easy grinding, move along. But nevertheless it is a fun game with tremendous replayibility.
The only thing I am missing at the moment (but I guess it will be implemented once the game hits release) is the story.

Contrary to other gamers I did not experience crashes and severe FPS drops but I can hear my computer on a heavy workload as if it were some high-end FPS game. Seriously, this game desperately needs some optimisation.
And I get it: As a resistance you have to operate on a time limit but the constant turn timers force you into a certain play style. Gone are the days when you could position your soldiers for maximum effect. Snipers almost are a redundant class. Streamlining is one thing in a game. It is another matter entirely to artificially inject a sense of urgency with game play mechanics limiting your range of tactical choices. Thanks to some quick modders you can now set up longer timers or remove them entirely from the game which basically is a bloody cop out. The devs simply included too many of those timer missions early in the game which is rather unfortunate because that's when your squads are at their weakest compared to the alien opposition. Any mistake in keeping up concealment is punished mercilessly by this game. So you find yourself inching forward with the waypoint movement system. Even worse, this whole system of forcing you into quick movement tactics is counterproductive when you reach later stages of the game. The key story missions don't have timers and you'd be well advised to dust of your old EU skills of slowly advancing your front line.
So what's the bottom line? Well, XCom 2 is a good game at least in theory. The enemies are varied and each species presents their own specific challenge. The timers are bloody annoying but you can get used to them. The real problems come from the bugs in this game. When you see your squad go to hell in an ironman game because one of those snake creatures can pull your soldier through a door and two floors, then you feel your frustration level rising because you were not defeated by a bad move but by a bad game engine. Sure, with some experience you learn to expect certain bugs and work around them but a truely excellent game would not force me to reserve some head space in order to avoid problems which shouldn't be in the game to begin with.
pros:
- interesting and varied enemies
- a real tactical challenge
- a good UI
- a competent AI
- tons of customization options
- compared to XCom 1 a greater choice in missions
- steep learning curve as the game is brutally unforgiving (if you want a challenge)
cons:
- still some performance issues
- still some glitches especially with the detection and line-of-sight system
- the game forces you to adopt a certain playstyle in order to succeed (at least early in the game)
- melee enemies have unbelievable range
- steep learning curve as the game is brutally unforgiving (if you are new to the game)

Right from the start, everything in XCOM2 is familiar. While all the assets have been reworked, the core of the game is nearly unchanged. And then you should absolutely get it, because this game gets the point. I don't mind that they didn't change the gameplay, because it was already nearly perfect. The emphasis this time is in customisation and diversity, which was precisely what XCOM was lacking. Soldiers and equipment are now much more precious and unique, which makes you all the more invested in developing them and keeping them alive. Not only that, but you can keep your character designs across playthoughs, which seems so obvious now, and yet I've never seen it before.
With the foundations that this game has layed on customisation and the support for Workshop, I believe that this game will be interesting for a very long time.
Criticisms aside (wahh, this isn't pure fallout), this game is kind of amazing.

Trove is a great little MMO that takes what was great about Minecraft and Terraria and expands on it. Trove is a some-what sandbox/dungeon crawler game that does not have any kind of story but encourages exploration. I spent hours on the beta before it hit Steam. Trove let's you build your own home/base with a ton of options in a nice sudo-8bit voxel style. You can explore dungeons, go on mini raids, sail on the ocean and fight pirates, fly, and much more. It is a free game with an in game store, but nothing in there utterly breaks the game experience. The store has some cosmetics with the same stats as anything in the game. There is a nice selection of classes in Trove with more being added fairly often that shake up the playing experince from something like Minecraft. Each class has it's own skills and more are unlocked as you level that class up. The classes can be swapped on the fly all on the same character, so if you don't like the feel of a certain class you can always swap with no harm! The combat system is simple but smooth and fun. There is something for the more casual players in this game of making a nice home, and having some fun exploring with friends, and then some nice end game dungeons for a little more devoted player, along with rare mounts to craft/collect. The game also encourages playing with others as you share loot and "glim" or gold income. A very funny game to play with some friends. With a development team that is very social with it's community I can only highly recommend this little gem. 9/10.

But for those reading this who are worried because of the recent controversy, this is my take on it:
There have been many complaints over the last months about the game becoming too difficult, after the devs attempted to rebalance it and reduce the effectiveness of strategies that some users saw as "broken". I can certainly see why more casual players reacted poorly to these changes, and are now blaming the devs for pandering to a small but vocal group of min-maxers. I understand- but completely disagree. I admit that after the game was retooled, and the difficulty suddenly spiked, it did take me a while to get used to the changes and I lost several missions which was very frustrating. But a short-lasting frustration while adapting to changes does not make a valid argument against a game and is of no use to new players. When I bought the game, I expected it to be ruthless and, at times, frustrating. A string of unfortunate events can, and eventually will, cause you to fail quests and lose members of your party,  hurting your progress. That has been true since the early-access release, and is a staple of the genre. Still, with a little bit of care and risk management, which the game allows for, such events will be few and far between and will not set you back too much. As I can attest to- you do not have to "min-max" in order to succeed in this game. A pretty minimal amount of care is needed to properly equip your party, come up with a reasonable party composition and buy provisions. Once you understand the risks and the basic strategies against the various enemies, this is enough to win 90%+ of raids without losing any characters. Some more advanced team building strategies can bring this closer to 100%, but a decent amount of effort will allow you to progress and succeed, and do so in your own "sub-optimal" way. The game is not easy and it requires some thought. You can't really breeze through most encounters. But, this has been true since the game's release on early access and it was to be expected from the way the game was presented. If the game would've been release to EA in it's current difficulty, I truly think most of the players who decided to change their recommendations would have recommended it. Also, the devs added the possibility to toggle off some of the most hardship-inducing and controversial features, so players can enjoy a more casual game which will be more similar to the original form. This last addition renders most of the new arguments against buying the game completely invalid. In any way, if you are looking for a decent, reasonable challenge- Darkest Dungeon provides just that.

Spoiler alert: I love this game. <3
People like to complain about it a lot, so let me get my few complaints out of the way:
1. It doesn't give you as many role-playing options as you might be used to in previous Fallout games. You don't have the Karma system anymore, and you can't be a truly bad guy. You are limited to going along with a certain faction's storyline.
2. SPECIAL skills have changed a lot. Leveling up is no longer putting points into things and improving across the board, instead, you choose 1 Perk per level, or can level up a SPECIAL skill by one point. This system isn't terrible, it's just different. My characters felt a lot more focused in one area than I'm used to having, and, with hundreds of hours into one game, I still haven't leveled up enough to get all of the perks.
3. Making caps is not as easy as it was in other games. It's not about finding valuable guns and armor and selling them to shopkeeps (at least that's not as profitable for me), instead, I found that selling purified water from settlements is much better.
4. Crafting is not super intuitive at first. Many people, for example, were complaining about how hard it is to find screws to build weapon mods. It took me ages to realize that if you drop armor and weapons in settlements, you can "scrap" them (obtaining screws from guns, leather from armor, etc. along the way).
That's honestly about all I have to complain about, because like I said, I really enjoy this game.
It is very obvious when playing this and other Fallout games that they were thought about intensely, and that someone is really putting a lot of love into it all. I am always amazed at finding things I've never seen even after hundreds and hundreds of hours of exploring. When I talk about the game with people who don't game, they don't understand how a game can be this deep and have this much content. How you can play the same game every weekend for a year and still not be done with it.
Playing through the game, I would recommend to not try to blast through and finish the main quest as fast as you can - that's not finishing the game, not really. If you allow yourself to be immersed in the world, complete quests, explore, go into buildings even if they're not part of the main questline - you will find all those secret places and all the love that went into the game.
Don't just play the main questline and say you've played it. Take off running in any direction and see where it leads.
Once you and the game are thoroughly acquainted, survival mode is definitely worth a try. By removing the option of fast travel and introducing elements like hunger and the need for sleep, the game becomes so much more immersive.
I definitely recommend this game and plan to continue thoroughly savoring it until we're blessed with another.

At first, I wasn't going to make a review, but after seeing so many people give it thumbs down recently I feel like I should throw my two cents in.
Personally, I loved the game. The combat was fun, it had a pretty nice amount of variety, and...well, honestly, the combat may be what sold me. From a strict gameplay perspective, I had a lot of fun with the weapons and building myself up to be a tank and single handedly wipe out groups of raiders. To put into perspective how much fun I had with this game, I had to play it at the absolute LOWEST graphics settings, in windowed mode, at 640x480 (or something close. Definitely a small window though) in order to get 45+fps, and I found myself getting lost in this world over and over again. I'd play for hours without even realizing that this wasn't even close to the full experience that this game had to offer. It was honestly super fun. I'm a little bummed that the Karma system was taken out, as well as weapon repair (although weapon modding is fantastic), but I managed to get over that by the end of the game.
Now, the story: I see why people were upset. This game only has 4 major endings (I think you can play it in a way that it lets you have a sort of "fifth" ending, but there are really only 4 endings) and it makes a pretty clear definition of who is bad and who is good. Or, rather, that each faction has bad and good in it. For example, the Brotherhood of Steel wants to help keep the wasteland safe, but they do so with a very strict code of honor and human supremacy, refusing to compromise on anything. The only real "good" faction I can think of is the one you create, and even then you can skip on creating them almost entirely and just focus on the other 3 factions. The plot is ultimately a giant game of hide and seek for your son, and then once you find him it's either help him or destroy him. Don't get me wrong, it had some very nice moments, and if you play as a woman, the female voice actor is 10/10. I haven't played the DLC, so the DLC story may be great or awful, but most people seemed to like Far Harbor. The plot was basically nice moments tied together by weak transitions. The overall tone of this game seemed to be a LOT more optimistic than the other games. I remember playing 3 and getting very creepy feelings or feelings of despair, but with 4 I just got tense in some combat areas and overall hopeful toward the future. I personally didn't mind that tone change, but it may throw a lot of people off, especially veterans.
If you were like me and jumped into the series with Fallout 3 and have only played games following that, you will probably like Fallout 4 pretty well. However, if you have been playing this series since its beginning, and had issues with the newer games before 4, I can see why you might not like it. Objectively, I think it's a good game, but subjectively, I can see where it sometimes fails to live up to Fallout standards.
Combat: 8/10 (sometimes repetitive, especially after main campaign)
Story: 5/10 overall, 8-9/10 when it gets good.
Graphics: 10/10 (based on the videos and screenshots I see of it running maxed out. I didn't get that luxury but I was never bothered)
tl;dr issa good game if you accept that it isn't like the older Fallouts.

Long ago. 3 years ago, on Aug 27, 2011. I was but a young lad. young, naive, perhaps innocent. In the new world of Spiral Knights.
Spiraling down a chasm of confusion and curiosity, I was finally brought up with a recommendation to Spiral Knights. Filled with swords, pistols, shields, parties, dungeons, and list of items
The game Spiral knights(SK) from recollection memories during my first journey through it's dungeons and game-play nearly three years ago. Was enjoyable to say the least.
If you for one second can imagine an down graphics to appeal to the ages of 7-13 then probably this game is for you. If your into friendship and co-op through dungeons facing monsters with your trusty pistol or sword and shield, then perhaps this game is for you.
However, I digress. S.K. proved to be something that is beyond the average you normally see. Imagine yourself a kid, after the game boy era, the ps1 era, the xbox era, and you have an era of mmo games. Granted, mmo's have existed since probably before the age of 2001 with WoW at its center.
The mmo S.K. is to be honest short lived game, pulling your slightest attention for the smallest of seconds through promotions with Team Fortress 2. Such was the case for me when I ashamedly downloaded this game for another TF2 hat promo from S.K.
Enjoyable in the sense, that I alone played by myself seeking for riches and glory. I didn't expect much, and that is proven by my hours spent on this game. Later on, I played with my friends together in a typical fashion of dungeon crawling and killing bosses. I'd compare SK to Torchlight, however both games are entirely different and this review isn't about a comparison.

The Gist -
Darkest Dungeon is 2D Based Dungeon Crawler/Hero Manager with RogueLite Elements like PermaDeath and Procedurally Generated Dungeons. It relies heavily on Dice-Based Mechanics and Number Rolls for a lot of what happens in the game.
Darkest Dungeon basically is Betrayal at the House on the Hill with more combat, less exploration, and more eldritch horrors. If you're a big fan of Dice-Based Tabletop Games and now the fickleness of Nuffle and RNJesus you'll feel right at home with this game.
On Presentation -
Darkest Dungeon has great presentation, nearly everything about it is oozing with little touches here and there, if you're a big fan of Mike Mignola of Hellboy Fame, you'll probably like the game's aesthetics a lot. Not only that, but the script writing for the Narrator is top-notch too. Music is great too, and subtly changes to carry the atmosphere as your party's lights get dimmer, slowly becoming more and more tense and horrifiying as your party loses their sanity (Basically, their's a torch system, and once that starts losing its lights, the music changes accordingly) .  couple that in with how dynamic the battle animation flows and how often than not battles go awry, his voice and the game's aesthetic will have you by the edge of your seat.
On Gameplay -
Darkest Dungeon's main gameplay is managing your heroes, believe me on this one but actually completing quests is not that important. What is but a few more extra gold to the ones you've managed to haul if your heroes are just gonna die doing so? What is some paltry amount of stress to the possibility of death? You already have your inventory filled with gold, do you really need that more gold? Darkest Dungeon is a game where you must know when to quit, It's a game about risks. Even the most well laid plans can fall apart, even the most bravest of heroes can die (And will die).
The other, big part of the game is well, the combat. It's pretty basic 4v4 Linear 2 Dimensional Combat. You arrange your heroes from front to back and depending on their skills, they can either hit from that position or can't, and they can't all reliably hit your enemies, their skills most of the time can only hit certain enemy positions too so there's often a lot of planning involved when choosing who to bring. This is even greatly stressed by how different each of the 4 dungeons are from each other, from their general layout, to the common enemies you find in each one. What is a viable party in one dungeon may not work for the other.
Just a reminder, the game heavily relies on RNG mechanics so just remember that if your attack misses 3 times, you probably did something to anger Nuffle or Random Number Jesus somewhere in your life.
On Heroes -
There's not much control on which heroes you get and what they specialize in, and there isnt much customization in the way either other than locking certain quirks in and equipping special items. Coming from experience, there are more times your heroes will be characterized by their flaws than their abilities when thinking of who to bring in certain dungeons (Not that it's a bad thing). It's less about erasing these flaws and more about learning how to live with them.
On Replayability -
This game has tons  of replayability, from experimenting party compositions, to doing self imposed challenges, to just mucking about. Something the Developers seem to have not realized when they decided to stretch the content of the game 3 sizes too thin by chopping the number of quests into three different difficulty categories. It's incredibly grindy, with each level of difficulty being waaaay more difficult than the last one.
Conclusion -
Darkest Dungeon is a "fun" game where losing is part of the enjoyment. The game heavily relies on random number generation for a lot of its mechanics so take that in mind. It's not really for everyone but as someone who doesn't classify themselves as a hardcore gamer and still managed to find some enjoyment in it, I say give it a try.

This is an excellent game. The amount of thought and strategy you need to put into it is so surprising.
The game is brutally unforgiving. It autosaves after every move or action you make. Your characters have permadeath. AND, if they are carrying any items on them, you don't get them back when they die. The game warns you when you launch it that you WILL lose champions and you WILL need to retreat, and it is very true.
The game doesn't make it impossible. There are ways for you to make money so you can keep your characters' health in order. This isn't like XCOM where you can take one of your soldiers, and just slam this one completely full of upgrades and promotions. In Darkest Dungeon, you need to diversify and plan ahead. The diseases, quirks and mental disabilities make it physically impossible to use one character to carry the whole party. You need to think tactfully and you need to build an appropriate team.
There are moments where the game seems as if it is stacking the deck against you, but a lot of the time, the error and losses are on you and you alone. Either you got cocky, impatient or simply underestimated what you may need.
This game is highly recommended if you want a challenge. And the fact that it is in early access means that there is only more to be added (assuming the devs haven't abandoned the game or don't plan to abandon it). But seriously, this game is relentless. It walks you through a tutorial, then it begins hammering you down, and yet you still go back for more. I've lost maybe 29 characters in the time I've played (not really proud of that number), and I am willing to lose more for the cause.

To start, I want to say that Fallout is my favourite game series of all time, with Fallout 2 being my favourite closely followed by New Vegas.
This review is subjective, of course, because there is no such thing as an objective review. It's just my opinion.
Short story:
Pros: Lots to do, great attention to detail, superb character facial editor and solid combat, if a bit repetetive.
Cons: Fallout 4 is a game for Far Cry fans, not Fallout fans. If you want an immersive story, an rpg where you can tailor your character, or deeply meaningful choices, go elsewhere. You'll have better luck with Piranha Bytes' Risen.
Long story:
If you want to play Far Cry, Post Apocalyptic Edition, then this is the game for you. The combat is solid, if repetitive. Every single quest is "go here, shoot this, return". Ironic that there is an item in the game which sums up the entire plot. Some of the super mutants drop random notes with the following orders. "Kill. Loot. Return."
This sums up my Fallout 4 experience. Unfortunately Bethesda is going the way of EA, alienating their hardcore fans in order to appeal to a bigger market.
While I can't fault this business decision, I will be looking at lot more closely at Bethesda reviews before I purchase their games in future, if I purchase them.
A good example is the base building minigame. CMostly meaningless and with little lasting appeal, yet it took up a huge amount of their resources to develop. Resources better spent elsewhere, making this a more memorable experience. Not a bad thing, but not really important in a Fallout game if you're sacrificing depth to spend resources on building this feature. This feature should have been added as a last resort if they had time.
They are losing depth for the sake of mass market appeal. Truth is, a game that makes you think is infinitely more immersive than one that holds your hand the entire way. And boy does Fallout 4 hold your hand.
In the original Fallout, you could approach quests in so many ways. There is a quest to eliminate Roger Westin in Fallout 2. You can sneak into the compound, talk your way in, shoot your way in or just kill the guy who gave you the quest. Once inside you can fight your way out, or poison Westin quietly, or load him up with so many super stimpacks that he overdoses. Or you can convince him to pay you more to go kill the original contract giver. You can try and lie about killing him even if you haven't. Not to mention you can, at any point, say the wrong thing and get yourself shot. Not so in fallout 4. No matter what dialogue choice you pick, the result is pretty much always the same. You end up at the same ending and the only solution to most problems is to shoot your way out. The dialogue has lost most of its wit and nuance that the previous games had too.
I spent a hundred hours waiting for the game to get good, and though it appeared deep at first, it eventually opened up like the husk of a plasma blasted ghoul to reveal its rotting interior.
A giant marker points you to everything you need to do, and not once did the game ask me to figure something out for myself. While the mods available for Fallout 4 may one day give this game the kind of replayability that Skyrim's modding community did, they are not quite there yet.
I sincerely hope that Bethesda realizes that Fallout 4 is their most successful game because it rides the hype train hard, not because it's the shining jewel of all their creation. If they continue compromising on depth and quality for ease of access and simplicity, they will go the way of Assassins Creed, with a rapidly flagging fanbase. And though it may be a savvy business decision to beat a dead horse, so to speak, by milking every last drop from an IP until it can make you no more money because everyone hates it... Well... That's not what game development should be about. It should be about making something because you love it, and want others to as well. That's what separates a good game from a 'go down in history' game.
Level design: The detail in the world is incredible, and there are many amazing details in the level design - the level designers should be promoted they are creative geniuses.
Writing: (Spoiler alert) Bring Chris Avelone back. This game has the literary depth of a steamrolled teaspoon. The plot doesn't really resolve - the institue literally does not have any motive (finish their questline; they never give a reason for any of their savage murder/replacing people. They never have an actual  plan to better the common wealth other than some vague "we're smarter, so we can justifiably kill poeple" logic.) Bethesda are master physical world builders. Their sense of humour is on the level of a dehydrated swiss gaurdsman at a turkish borderpost. "Ha, ha. Mein hond haff no nose! How then dous he smell? Terrible! Ha. ha."
Pricing model: DLC prices are inexcusable. Just because you CAN make more money, doesn't mean you should if it's wrong. I know we live in a free market yadayada but there is a serious division between people who make games because they enjoy them and companies who kill games by hiring a bunch of people, overworking them under tight scrutiny on a tiny timeline, and pushing out ♥♥♥♥♥♥ products. Bethesda please please PLEASE don't become EA/Konami. We trusted you. I hope Fallout 4 isn't the last quality open world game you realease.
To sum up: Good game, serious flaws (Tod howard had the grace to admit this). Might have killed the series for me. And made me hesitate before buying any other Bethesda game.
The only reason I play this game a lot is because I don't own far cry, or any other open world shooters. So it fills that niche nicely. It does not fill my fallout niche. If I ever buy a far cry or GTA game this entire series will suddenly become redundant. See Bethesda? Keep your unique depth ya dummies. Divinity 2 got 10/10 for a reason.
Go play Fallout 2. But don't waste your hard earned cash on Fallout 4's ridiculously priced dlc until it goes on a hefty, hefty sale. Just compare Bethesda's prices to that of CD Projekt Red's The Witcher 3 and you will see the greedy path they are following.
We are living in a post Witcher 3 world people. Let's release our RPG's with some higher standards.

CONS;

I don't usually review games, but for Fallout 4 I'll make an exception.
I came into Fallout with Fallout: New Vegas. It is my favorite video game of all time. Coming into Fallout 4 it's impossible not to draw the comparison. And while I do ultimately think this is a fun game to play, I need the comparison to illustrate what could've been and what I feel is missing from Fallout 4 that makes it so disappointing.
First, things I feel that Fallout 4 improved:
- Graphics. Anyone can tell you this, it's a waste of time for me to. It's a very pretty game. The SoSu looks much more like a Human than the LW or Courier
- Companions. I love the companions in this game. Their individual likes and dislikes make them feel a lot more fleshed out than previous companions and the addition of romance is nice. My main complaints here are the lack of women you can travel with (only 3 to the 9 - or 11 with the DLC - men) and a lack of any kind of character progression after romancing a companion.
- Crafting. I didn't usually bother with mods in FNV because I didn't like the crafting system. Most junk items were just that. Here, everything has a use and I really like that aspect of it personally. I know that's not to everyone's taste.
- Building Settlements. Here's the thing. The last thing I should want to spend all my time on in a Fallout game is building towns like it's the wasteland Sims but that's sure what I spend countless hours of my first playthrough doing. It's really fun even if the options are limited. However, once you build it, there's nothing really to do with it, I'd love if there was more to actually do in the settlements.
- Nuka-World. I just love Nuka-World. That's the whole point. Nuka-World is the reason I finally bought the game.
That's where my good points end, however. Here are the things that feel like a step backwards from Fallout: New Vegas:
- The Story. This has been talked to death at this point. There's no real choice. The only choice you have is the faction you eventually side with. Nothing else has any impact on anything. It's boring. In Fallout: New Vegas there are so many options and different ways to handle different factions and story branches but here you get one (1) choice. Everything else is predetermined. Not only that, but you can constantly feel the pressure that you're Meant to be playing as Nate and you're Meant to side with the BoS (despite how awful they are in this game). FNV has no such pressure to play some kind of True Ending.
- The SPECIAL and Perk System. By eliminating stats in favor of leveling up your SPECIAL directly and just generally simplifying the whole perk system, it changed it from a fun way to build a character to just simply leveling up, powering yourself up, etc. There's no real thought in it. You can get all the stats and only one is moderated by lack of another stat. Gone is the chance to balance a character by having them be Bad At Some Things. (For example, one of my Couriers, Julep, had high luck and perception at the cost of intelligence, which made for a much different playthrough than my other Courier Finley who had high intelligence but perception and endurance. Throwing perks into that mix, Julep use light armor throughout the game because he had a combination of perks that made it viable, though it required planning to get to that point. However, it made sense for a sneak and lucked based character to have light armor. No such specialization is possible in FO4.) Overall, it just makes for a blander experience.
- The Radiant System. Again, talked to death, added as a cheap way to keep the game going but it just makes things feel unsatisfying.
- The DLC. While Far Harbor and Nuka-World are great, the Vault 88 DLC feels lacking and the other DLCs simply aren't worth it at all. The price tag is far too high for what you get out of any of the DLC.
That being said: I did enjoy playing this game. I can't not recommend the game because, yes, I did enjoy playing it. But I enjoyed it in spite of it's story, not because of it. That shouldn't be how you have to play a game. Overall, I think this game has so much wasted potential. I hope Bethesda can clean up their act for the next Fallout title. Listen to feedback from fans and pay attention to what made Fallout: New Vegas such an excellent game.
My recommendation comes with this warning: only play this game if you've run out of stuff to do in Fallout: New Vegas.

Watching a hero die before I even get to make any choices or actions is really frustrating, and ruins a whole game week- because 3 heroes is a massive handicap and you're doomed to retreat or die soon into the dungeon. Another thing that was frustrating is finally getting to camp, and then being attacked for it so you lose all the health, stress reduction, and other benefits of camping. I really like what I see from the devs of this game, I've gone back and read a lot of the updates and such- so I'm sure they'll iron it out they seem very committed but honestly, at the moment, I don't recommend this game.

Full Disclosure: The Fallout series is one of my favourites of all time. The first and third will always have very special places in my heart. The first started my love affair with the world and the options--never before had I played an RPG so open with so many possibilities for completion (one ending only takes an hour). The third because it, like Super Mario 64, it so well captured the 'are cars are broke but our spirt isn't' world of the first game, but cracked it open and allowed you to explore it in 3D. NV took that template and properly fleshed it out, but albeit leaning harder into the absurb black humour and ridiculouness in the periphery that Black Isle of the days of old was so fond of injecting into their games. Fallout 4 is an extension, or iteration on the third. I'm not a power gamer or min-maxer by any means so all the streamlining they introduced was welcome. The factions that were introduced were well balanced and there were some good storeis there. The 'radiant' quests introduced in an earlier Elder Scrolls game finally clicked for me. Long after completing the main game, I was tasked with defending a settlemetn from an invading force, and one of the inhabitants rallied everyone together for a pep talk. It was unexpected and perfect. The negatives of this game are the same with all of Bethesdas'--the quality of the animations and wiriting in some areas. They're improving in the areas I think they can due tot the limitations of the engine or size of game they are making, but man, it'd be nice to see more realistic people in the game. Writing, voice acting, animations, everything.

Not the greatest. There are aspects that are really good and are really huge improvements over 3/NV, like the weapon modding, base building, power armor, gunplay, etc. Most of the core game mechanics and gameplay elements are really good and enjoyable. I don't like the new perk-based advancement, but it's not terrible, it's just not my preference. That's not the problem with this game; they did a good job of making the actual game portion of FO4 fun.
The problem is that nothing else about the game is compelling. 3 and NV both did a much better job of making compelling characters and reasons for you to advance. NV especially had a much more believable world that really drew you in. The story and characters in this one are painfully bad and are mainly just there to get you from one end of the map to the other. The main quest in particular is just awful; the faction quests and side quests are more of a mixed bag, but most aren't particularly great either.
If you just want something to screw around with modding weapons and armor and building bases in, then maybe pick this up on a discount. If you want a compelling Fallout game, I'd suggest New Vegas instead.

My darkest thoughts go out to negative reviewers seem to whine primarily about the difficulty. No pain - No gain! I picked this game up less than one week ago. I am hopelessly hooked. I started and abandoned at least a dozen campaigns before I learned the ropes (and I am still learning). One game went on for 24 weeks (in game weeks) before I started over. In the last dungeon run, which I thought should be fairly easy, I lost two of my best heroes. They were only mercenaries and I was their Lord, but I felt at that moment that I had not  managed wisely enough all the factors from the start of the campaign, so the monsters were becoming too powerful for my troops. After a couple more false starts, where I got a really poor mix of heroes dropped off by the stagecoach, I started yet another game. At Week 10 I feel like my troops are nearly as powerful as they were in week 24 of the previous game.
I can see room for improvements. For instance the game leads you to believe your graveyard will be full of fallen heroes. My experience is that losing a hero, particularity a veteran is a very bad thing. You spend 1000's upon 1000's of gold to maintain a hero. When they die all that money goes down the toilet. Furthermore your chances of mission failure go up severely if you lose one of your four. If you fail too many missions you are perennially broke. Meanwhile the dungeons are not getting any easier. I think it would be good to have more low level mission options -veterans of a certain level could be banned (the game already does that), so that I can level up new troops and restore my gold. That way heroes could be more expendable as the developers seem to have originally intended.
