So after a long discussion with myself, whether or not I should buy Dark Souls 3, since I didn't played the first games then, I decided to give the Dark Souls Series a try.
In this review I am trying to give people, which are as unsure as I was, a good impression on the game without spoilering to much about the story, since (in my opinion) the story/the lore behind the whole Dark Souls Series is one of the most beautiful things to discover in this games.
Let me start with the pro arguments for buying Dark Souls 3. (Remember that this is my personal opinion!)
-Dark Souls 3 yet the third Game in the Dark Souls Universe, builds a perfect introduction for newer players.
It guides the player in his first steps without losing its difficulty
-Like the other Souls Games, Dark Souls 3 manages it to be difficult but not that frustrating to stop playing and wanting to kill yourself
-The Dark Souls Series delivers a Story which is so deep that it might consume you and make you wish that there isn't an end of the weekend and you just could continue to explore the world and watch youtube videos about the lore of each boss and place you are in the game.
Just to cover arguments, which might lead you to not buy Dark Souls 3.
-Some players and long fans of the series claim Dark Souls 3 to be more beginner-friendly or easier then the previous games, a often used example for that claim are the bonfires within Dark Souls 3. Not only that some Areas are overloaded with bonfires but also that bonfires are used to teleport towards every location you want to.
-The most important thing to mark is that Dark Souls might not be your game if you can't bring up the dedication which is needed to come through any Dark Souls Game, if you are the kind of player who gives up on a game after a few deaths, that might not be the right game for you my friend!

A very good game plagued by questionable design decisions. The most obvious culprit is the mission turn limits. Apparentely this was done because overwatch was too strong and they wanted more fast paced/tense gameplay.
Unfortunately it's not well implemented, I don't know if its better on other difficulties but on Ironman/commander you barely have enough time to get from point A to B. This makes lots of abilities and even the sharpshooter class quite useless. Why would I carefuly place my sniper on a roof top to flank the enemy if I know I won't have enough time to get her to the evac point in time? Combine this with some extremely powerful enemies like sectoids that appear early and often and you got yourself a major headache.
On the other end of the spectrum the Ranger and Specialist are much stronger for the pace of the game, the specialist being especially crucial in the hacking missions.
There are also lots of reports of bad performance, I've been lucky enough not to get any but I also turned down certain performance killing options. But from a game that is supposed to be a pc exclusive and was delayed to make sure it's flawless, it's very dissapointing.
On the bright side the graphics and sound are great. Executing a perfect ambush against a group of enemies is extremely satisfying (unfortunately you rarely get the chance to do this because you have to hurry so much.
I have no doubt that with a few patches/modding this game will shine and I will have no problem recommending it, but right now (especially with the price tag) I can't do so.
TLDR version :
+ Great sound and graphics
+ Ambushes are very satisfying
+ I love the new revamped classes, especially the specialist.
+ Still the same heartpumping X-com action.
-Mission timers for almost EVERY mission
-some very powerful enemies early on with little way to counter them
-Performance problems
P.S. I chose the "not recommended" option but I would choose a "neutral" option if there were one. It is not a bad game by any stretch and I feel I might update this to positive if a performance patch comes out soon.

It runs on almost max settings on the top of the line iMac 5k Retina at 1440P 25FPS. Performace is a little disapointting but it is more then playable. THe game is beautiful.
I recently got the game to run on my Early 2015 13" Retina MacBook Pro with just a Iris 6100 graphics adapter. The frame rate was low and it was on minimum graphics detail but it runs and is playable. I'd like to not have to see the game is unsupported on this machine everytime. I'm just glad my MacBook can play the game on the road now. That is super sweet.
On the PC side of things the game isn't using SLI. I have SLI enabled and using hardware monitor I found that the second GPU was at 7% utilizaion. I found that if you set go into the nVidia control panel and in the graphics settings add a profile for this game and set to force SLI in mode 2 the frame rate is much improved.
I had some issues with the game locking up and the save feature not working but it appears that the developer has worked the issues out because I haven't seen the issues since.
The game itself is fun. It feels like a worthy X-Com sucessor. There are new mechanics to contend with like fire. Unlike the first X-Com nw bullets can be modified to set enemies on fire. The mechanic is similar to bleeding. The sword for the ranger is well done for close combat. If units close in or you want to take out someone with near 100% chance the swords work a lot like combat knifes.
Overall I really like this game and I am glad that the developer has supported this game. This is a good buy if you liked Xcom Enemy Unknown and/or Enemy Within or pretty much any other strategy game of this nature.

- The game uses known concepts of dungeon games in a very original new way
- Varied styles of play
- Aesthetic design is extremely fitting and striking
- Great sound, music and narration adds to the moody tone
Though I do think this game has very few downsides, there are 2 things:
- I don't like that it's in early access, though this game is very playable since februari 2015 (but not finished yet)
- The game gets easier as you play more, instead of harder. This could probably be fixed by releasing an über hard "Darkest Dungeon", as a final challenge. I think the devs are already working on that.
A very enjoyable game, especially if you like to be challenged. The feedback you get from crits or cool moves your heroes have is awesome, the dread you feel when you run into a hard fight when your team is low on health and high on stress, it all adds up to a very exciting mix which I learned to love and hate. (though the good kind of hate)
9,5/10
--------------
EDIT: I see a lot of negative reviews mentioning the difficulty of the game, especially after certain nerfs to some really OP strategies. They say the game punishes you in unfair ways with some crazy RNG or random quirks and diseases. There are ways to counteract these things.
Like any challenge in this game, it can certainly be overcome with persistance and time. If one or more of your heroes die, there are always new heroes to level up again to take their place. You need a reserve team for even the reserve team in case heroes fall. Like NASA, you need to plan for everything. If it doesn't work out, you need to think on the fly and try to make it through.
While I can agree the setbacks can be frustrating to get through with this game, it also makes it more rewarding when you win.

After not playing it for a few days and looking at how the game is structured, I realize that it honestly is just a 'find loot' kind of game. There is no story or purpose other than collect blocks, build structures, find loot, gain power/mastery levels. Their real attempt at making a story for it was sending me an e-mail of a post they made talking about the 'in the beginning' of the world of Trove. Maybe thats a hint at something coming, but to be frank that should of already been included. You don't just publish a book, have all the action scenes in it and then release the actual story months later. Ontop of this I then came to realize that the game advertises their products every time you log-in, with no option to even disable for a week (at least I didn't see one). I get the appeal of the game, and I did like it for a second, but with no story, no end-game to grind for (the shadow arena aside), and the consistent advertisement: Trove isn't entirely structured for me. Not a bad game mind you, just not one I would recommend for players who want depth on why they are grinding, whether its part of progression in a storyline or to top the scoreboards.
If you like grinding for the sake of grinding then play Trove. Move along if you need anything else to give purpose to grinding.
*original review*
Verdict at the bottom to those who hate walls of text or reading.
So as of this review I've obtained about 8 hours of defined gameplay time. To be frank maybe 5 of it was actual game time. The other 1 hour was downloading the game (not that large, I just have bad internet) and the other 2 was waiting in a line of over one-thousand players to get in their servers. Knowing games from glyph... well only archeage, queues are to be expected, and this was just because of server issues, not experiencing any queues as of right now but if they come back it's only expected, games a popular f2p being developed by dedicated people who look to make this a great sandbox-mmorpg.
So, now that the fine-print is out of the way: time for the entire review.
Trove is simple.. Trove is complicating. This is one of those games that's easy to pick-up but difficult to master due to the amount of content and many classes that they are adding to the game. One important thing to remember is that this game is about the creativity of the Trovian community. All items in the game were designed by players. I assume the worlds were too but I didn't do much homework on 'who did what' for this game. But if you look at each item you pick up, you will see that it was submitted by a player and the team behind Trove liked it enough to put it in the game. ANYONE CAN SUBMIT. There are no restrictions on who can submit what, only what can be submitted (for obvious reasons).
One of the game's mechanics, and basically what 'defines' your profile is your 'Mastery Level.' As you play the game you will find you are taking on more items than you need and will have to break them down into raw materials used for crafting (most of the time its Flux or sometimes rarely the materials needed to upgrade your items). You do this at a 'Loot Collector.' Introduced early in the game, this is the main source of breaking down loot you don't need. The perk of the LC is that as you deposit items into it and gain the materials, you are also collecting that item in your collection, allowing you to go back and use that as a skin (free of charge with no restrictions). Each item you deposit into the loot collector that yields an original, first time deposit will grant 1 mastery point. You need 100 to level each time. Early on you will find the Mastery Level is easy to rank up, but you will see that later on as you find copies of items, you will have to do other things in order to gain the mastery points. Learning recipies, leveling classes, obtaining badges, there are many different ways to obtain Mastery Levels. And each level grants a new perk (in the form of money, items, and sometimes additional stats).
The gameplay is very hack-and-slash. You could say cubeworld (style + fighting) mixed with minecraft (building) mixed with Diablo (the HUD and loot) mixed with Borderlands (loot and how much there is). You begin by selecting your class, currently all but 2 are available for free to select. The restriction here is you can only choose one and there are no additional character slots. In order to play the other classes you have to buy them using ingame money or real money. After the super brief tutorial, you will spend most of your time going from dungeon to dungeon, traversing many biomes, hunting down better, rarer loot to try to upgrade your arsenal or blocks to build new things with. There is never a shortage of dungeons due to frequently created worlds for players to participate in. Most likely you will find yourself spawning into a completly new world around many players and tons of fun around you.
May be asking yourself the options of building now that I mentioned worlds are always being created and deleted. Players have, free of charge and can place down as often as they like in designated areas, a Cornerstone. This is basically  a 'mobile plot' that you can establish at any spot marked with a ' ? ' sign. This allows you to always have a base to go to and you never have to travel all over the world to get to it. You can place anything on it that you can craft or loot. Players can even create their own portals to teleport to different difficulty worlds.
Ontop of the Cornerstone, there is one world players can build on that will never be reset or deleted: Club Worlds. Clubs (Guilds) offer a group of friends the option to establish themselves in their own world that they created. This, again, is free for anyone to participate in. Players can create their own world that represents who they are. Again this is built with anything looted or crafted by the players. One of the many perks is how this can replace the hub world (the center of the universe for players to trade, meet people, and teleport to different difficulty worlds) by offering everything in their own private island.
The last topic is the f2p/p2w (free to play / pay to win) aspect of the game.
Bottom-line: there is none. You can gladdly spend money on this game and buy all the classes, but for those who don't have the means to access funds like this they can unlock everything completly free with dedication. Mounts are mostly cosmetic, with some being wonderful to buy, but you can buy them using ingame money or even craft some of them. The game is really balanced between the concept of paying money to play and just wanting to participate for free.
So verdict in numbers:
Gameplay: 9 / 10 (its fun but repetitive and currently [7/25/2015] there are no skilltrees)
Style: 8.5/10 (nostalgia is nice but can be rough on the eyes)
Loot System: 9/10 (fun to find new gear, currently [7/25/2015] no quests to obtain 'fixed' gear, however.)
Pay-to-Win Factor: 9/10 (there is no 'extreme' p2w, but because classes can be purchased there can still be an arguement for one)
Creativity: 10/10 (entire game is based on player creations, can't say this game restricts people)
Character customization: 7/10 (although not talked about: the only real modifiable pieces are hat, mask, and weapon. You can unlock costumes for classes by leveling up or purchasing them from the ingame store. The character creation is pretty well developed, however)
Verdict: 8.75 / 10
The game is still very good and worth picking up for free. The only true evil about the game is using another launcher to play and update it with. If you are a fan of hack-and-slash, cube world looking, diablo loot droppin, minecraft block placing sandbox mmorpgs, then give Trove a shot.

Engrossing, excellent Turn Based Strategy! The stress level for you and your heroes is off the charts! Darkest Dungeon is a simple game with a good deal of dark humor, but the strategic possibilities are endless.
My darkest thoughts go out to negative reviewers seem to whine primarily about the difficulty. No pain - No gain! I picked this game up less than one week ago. I am hopelessly hooked. Admittedly I have not finished a campaign, but I think I can safely say that if I prudently manage my troops and their quirks...If  I spend  gold and resources  wisely...if I craft my teams of 4 carefully and use their skills opportunistically...And most importantly manage their STRESS! ...Then I believe I will ultimately succeed!
I started and abandoned at least a dozen campaigns before I learned the ropes (and I am still learning). One game went on for 24 weeks (in game weeks) before I started over. In the last dungeon run, which I thought should be fairly easy, I lost two of my best heroes. They were only mercenaries and I was their Lord, but I felt at that moment that I had not  managed wisely enough all the factors from the start of the campaign, so the monsters were becoming too powerful for my troops. After a couple more false starts, where I got a really poor mix of heroes dropped off by the stagecoach, I started yet another game. At Week 10 I feel like my troops are nearly as powerful as they were in week 24 of the previous game.
I can see room for improvements. For instance the game leads you to believe your graveyard will be full of fallen heroes. My experience is that losing a hero, particularity a veteran is a very bad thing. You spend 1000's upon 1000's of gold to maintain a hero. When they die all that money goes down the toilet. Furthermore your chances of mission failure go up severely if you lose one of your four. If you fail too many missions you are perennially broke. Meanwhile the dungeons are not getting any easier. I think it would be good to have more low level mission options -veterans of a certain level could be banned (the game already does that), so that I can level up new troops and restore my gold. That way heroes could be more expendable as the developers seem to have originally intended.

As much as I complain about the game, my hours played betray how good a game this when seprated from its predecessors.
The good:
-Much smoother and more fluid UI navigation and Combat than previous games.
-A fun (if repetative) system for building settlements. If you love building houses in the sims, or decorating housing in mmo's, there's a lot here for you to play with.
-Great voice actors and companions that can draw you in, see Nick Valentine, Hancock, etc.
-Modifying guns and being able to name them makes your weapons feel super personal.
-Mods mods mods
The Bad:
-Dialogue choice is very limited, and in some cases non-existent. A quick repeat of the different choices you can choose from in most conversations will show you how little effect you have on the world. However in some areas, like the main story quest for Far Harbor they did manage to give the player a feeling of impactful decisions with real consequences.
-I mentioned modifying guns as a good point, but as a result there are very few actually unique feeling weapons in the game unlike the previous titles, and eventually most loot-which is procedurally generated, of course- becomes worthless to you very shortly.
The Ugly:
-"Radiant Quests" or procedurally generated quests. They bring you no worthwhile rewards, they serve very little purpose towards the advancement of most factions, and they are EXTREMELY repetative. They only seem to exisit in the game as "filler" content. ANOTHER SETTLEMENT NEEDS YOUR HELP!
Summary:
-Progress in gameplay, regress in role-playing elements, unfortunate rise of procedural generation. Still a good game.

For me, this is simply one of the best games out of 2015. Despite it seeming simplicity, it is actually a surprisingly deep and characterful game. A couple of it's main strengths are:
- Challenging and rewarding gameplay
- The game uses known concepts of dungeon games in a very original new way
- Varied styles of play
- Aesthetic design is extremely fitting and striking
- Great sound, music and narration adds to the moody tone
Though I do think this game has very few downsides, there are 2 things:
- I don't like that it's in early access, though this game is very playable since februari 2015 (but not finished yet)
- The game gets easier as you play more, instead of harder. This could probably be fixed by releasing an über hard "Darkest Dungeon", as a final challenge. I think the devs are already working on that.
A very enjoyable game, especially if you like to be challenged. The feedback you get from crits or cool moves your heroes have is awesome, the dread you feel when you run into a hard fight when your team is low on health and high on stress, it all adds up to a very exciting mix which I learned to love and hate. (though the good kind of hate)
9,5/10
--------------
EDIT: I see a lot of negative reviews mentioning the difficulty of the game, especially after certain nerfs to some really OP strategies. They say the game punishes you in unfair ways with some crazy RNG or random quirks and diseases. There are ways to counteract these things.
Like any challenge in this game, it can certainly be overcome with persistance and time. If one or more of your heroes die, there are always new heroes to level up again to take their place. You need a reserve team for even the reserve team in case heroes fall. Like NASA, you need to plan for everything. If it doesn't work out, you need to think on the fly and try to make it through.
While I can agree the setbacks can be frustrating to get through with this game, it also makes it more rewarding when you win.

Darkest Dungeon is really an enjoyable game. Hardcore and unforgiving, but with it's own unique aspects and vibe. Pro's: great vibe(!), I can't stress this enough, it really has a unique feel to it. Diversity! The different dungeons, opponent and bosses are well thought of, and although things won't always go as planned, you will still get the feeling that you'll slowly but gradually grow in the process. The flawedness of ur heroes: Mania's, phobias, traits or sicknesses will all influence the game in its own way, and gives a kind of realistic feel to it. Another thing is decision-making/tactics. What parties will you send, which classes do synergize well with eachother? Are you going to spend ur priced money on stress-reduction, enhancing traits or stack so you can pay for better weapons and armor? Many choices... many effects.
That being said, this game truly gets either the best or the worst out of me: it really is a unique thing in itself. The damned/gothic vibe that is characteristic to this game is awesome, and the suprises, frustrations and failures are well worthy of happening when contrasted with the kick of a succesful expedition. To clarify this, this is one of the few games that makes me say "YES!" feeling fulfilled when i've succesfully finished an expedition when things weren't looking so good.
If you like rocket on rocket action this games for you.

Duels are the only fun online as invaders are 9 out of 10 times ganked or stuck with a host that turtles and hides behind other players. Blue phantoms are useless or never get summoned. Healing is too fast for PvP and throws off the balance of finding a good opportunity to chug estus. Unless you're running a marathon you don't need to manage stamina, poise is a meme now, and you can only respec 5 times per NG which seems dumb but at least you can change your character's look now. I cannot recommend this game.
It's not because it's the battle system, the skill system, or the fact that somehow it feels like you're always taking one step forward and two steps back (between gear upgrades, skill upgrades, removing stress, removing disease, trying to afford locking in quirks, trying to afford removing quirks, trying to afford trinkets, and always having to prioritize your heroes depending on what situation they work best in - which changes each map, thanks to negative and positive quirks). That's all got nothing to do with why I can't recommend this game. Good luck with managing even HALF of that, by the way. You can't do it.
I can't recommend this game because of one simple fact: Your star hero, the one who should never die because you've taken all the proper precautions with him, ends up dying in one round of combat due to crappy RNG. And the game autosaves after EVERY MOVE. Automatically. There is literally no way you cannot undo the damage that has been done.
Permadeath kills this game. For people with tons of time on their hands, this game could be a lot of fun. And I do mean tons of time - you can dump HOURS into a character, literal hours, only to have them die in one round of combat like mine did. (For those who are wondering, my Crusader died - in the CHEAPEST WAY POSSIBLE - to three spiders. They ALL dodged FOUR ATTACKS. Statistically speaking I have a better chance of being hit my lightning while typing this.)
So RNG and permadeath has killed this game for me simply because every now and then you have a cheap death that will literally destroy hours of time that you put into this game. That's not fun for me because there's no advancement - I'm not going to spend even MORE time getting back to where I was, only to have RNG+Permadeath trollkill me again.
Don't buy this game. Not now. If they fix permadeath or, you know, make it so that cheap RNG deaths are taken out of the equation, then I can suggest this game.
Until then, much like my now dead Crusader, this has been sent to the grave with no possibility of return. I'm not a masochist, but if you play this game, you better be one.

This is a classic example of a games company taking a really great product and applying the 'not broken, don't fix it' rule. The game is absolutely the same basic concept with the core gameplay absolutely intact. No-one's tried to reinvent the wheel because there was no need, and that's kind of refreshing. How many times has someone taken something great and stuffed it up by adding wider wheels, go-faster stripes and a fugly great spoiler on the back?
But here, there's none of that so far. Instead every aspect of the game has been thought about and either refined or tweaked. You can do a bit of looting, the environments feel a lot more involving, the AI seems a good bit smarter, the graphics are excellent, skill trees are more involved, you can customise skillsets and weapons and on and on. So far they don't seem to have done anything that doesn't work. It's just a really, really good game.
Anyway, enough waffling. World won't save itself you know.

So after a long discussion with myself, whether or not I should buy Dark Souls 3, since I didn't played the first games then, I decided to give the Dark Souls Series a try.
In this review I am trying to give people, which are as unsure as I was, a good impression on the game without spoilering to much about the story, since (in my opinion) the story/the lore behind the whole Dark Souls Series is one of the most beautiful things to discover in this games.
Let me start with the pro arguments for buying Dark Souls 3. (Remember that this is my personal opinion!)
-Dark Souls 3 yet the third Game in the Dark Souls Universe, builds a perfect introduction for newer players.
It guides the player in his first steps without losing its difficulty
-Like the other Souls Games, Dark Souls 3 manages it to be difficult but not that frustrating to stop playing and wanting to kill yourself
-The Dark Souls Series delivers a Story which is so deep that it might consume you and make you wish that there isn't an end of the weekend and you just could continue to explore the world and watch youtube videos about the lore of each boss and place you are in the game.
Just to cover arguments, which might lead you to not buy Dark Souls 3.
-Some players and long fans of the series claim Dark Souls 3 to be more beginner-friendly or easier then the previous games, a often used example for that claim are the bonfires within Dark Souls 3. Not only that some Areas are overloaded with bonfires but also that bonfires are used to teleport towards every location you want to.
-The most important thing to mark is that Dark Souls might not be your game if you can't bring up the dedication which is needed to come through any Dark Souls Game, if you are the kind of player who gives up on a game after a few deaths, that might not be the right game for you my friend!

I was a little hesitant getting this game, just because the cell shaded graphics aren't my thing. However, once you get into the game there's nothing to be concerned about. The cell shading turns dark and grungy, just like you'd expect from going into a dungeon for a while.
The game takes place as you roll into an abandoned hampton, and you are thrown into the combat tutorial. It is merciless, and depending on the rng for attacks and damage, you may not make it out the first time. Once there, you'll see what you'll call your home base. As you progress through the game, new areas become opened and you can upgrade your equipment and character skills in this area. You'll also recruit new characters from here, and deal with stresses of the old characters.
The core of the game is to complete the check list held by the hampton's grounds keeper (assuming? I haven't finished the game yet). You do this by going spelunking and cave diving. You have several options to go "dungeoning" in, and each area has specific mobs that you fight. Some have unholy, some have bandits, and some have beasts. After completeing a few, you'll get to bosses. The bosses are on the check list for the gounds keeper.
The grueling and merciless part of the game is while you're actually in the dungeons. This is also one of the most interesting aspects in my opinion. You'll be in the dungeons, and you're characters will become stressed from combat and the darkness (just like a real person would!). As your stress bars fill, you'll get detrements (like refusing to be healed!). If the stress bar fills up twice, they die! Death in this game is permanent, so although you can just recruit another class without difficulty, you do tend to be attached to characters that you have leveled up.
All in all, the game is not for the faint of heart. You can drop in and out after clearing a section of the dungeon, without any questions like "I wonder what happens next". The merciless and unforgiving permadeath is something that makes you pull your hair out. Discovering the mechanics on how to make the game work for you, instead of against you is what keeps you going.
I'd give this a solid 8/10 stars. Worth picking up regularly, definitely pick it up on a sale.

I cannot recommend this game.
It's not because it's the battle system, the skill system, or the fact that somehow it feels like you're always taking one step forward and two steps back (between gear upgrades, skill upgrades, removing stress, removing disease, trying to afford locking in quirks, trying to afford removing quirks, trying to afford trinkets, and always having to prioritize your heroes depending on what situation they work best in - which changes each map, thanks to negative and positive quirks). That's all got nothing to do with why I can't recommend this game. Good luck with managing even HALF of that, by the way. You can't do it.
I can't recommend this game because of one simple fact: Your star hero, the one who should never die because you've taken all the proper precautions with him, ends up dying in one round of combat due to crappy RNG. And the game autosaves after EVERY MOVE. Automatically. There is literally no way you cannot undo the damage that has been done.
Permadeath kills this game. For people with tons of time on their hands, this game could be a lot of fun. And I do mean tons of time - you can dump HOURS into a character, literal hours, only to have them die in one round of combat like mine did. (For those who are wondering, my Crusader died - in the CHEAPEST WAY POSSIBLE - to three spiders. They ALL dodged FOUR ATTACKS. Statistically speaking I have a better chance of being hit my lightning while typing this.)
So RNG and permadeath has killed this game for me simply because every now and then you have a cheap death that will literally destroy hours of time that you put into this game. That's not fun for me because there's no advancement - I'm not going to spend even MORE time getting back to where I was, only to have RNG+Permadeath trollkill me again.
Don't buy this game. Not now. If they fix permadeath or, you know, make it so that cheap RNG deaths are taken out of the equation, then I can suggest this game.
Until then, much like my now dead Crusader, this has been sent to the grave with no possibility of return. I'm not a masochist, but if you play this game, you better be one.

At first, I wasn't going to make a review, but after seeing so many people give it thumbs down recently I feel like I should throw my two cents in.
Personally, I loved the game. The combat was fun, it had a pretty nice amount of variety, and...well, honestly, the combat may be what sold me. From a strict gameplay perspective, I had a lot of fun with the weapons and building myself up to be a tank and single handedly wipe out groups of raiders. To put into perspective how much fun I had with this game, I had to play it at the absolute LOWEST graphics settings, in windowed mode, at 640x480 (or something close. Definitely a small window though) in order to get 45+fps, and I found myself getting lost in this world over and over again. I'd play for hours without even realizing that this wasn't even close to the full experience that this game had to offer. It was honestly super fun. I'm a little bummed that the Karma system was taken out, as well as weapon repair (although weapon modding is fantastic), but I managed to get over that by the end of the game.
Now, the story: I see why people were upset. This game only has 4 major endings (I think you can play it in a way that it lets you have a sort of "fifth" ending, but there are really only 4 endings) and it makes a pretty clear definition of who is bad and who is good. Or, rather, that each faction has bad and good in it. For example, the Brotherhood of Steel wants to help keep the wasteland safe, but they do so with a very strict code of honor and human supremacy, refusing to compromise on anything. The only real "good" faction I can think of is the one you create, and even then you can skip on creating them almost entirely and just focus on the other 3 factions. The plot is ultimately a giant game of hide and seek for your son, and then once you find him it's either help him or destroy him. Don't get me wrong, it had some very nice moments, and if you play as a woman, the female voice actor is 10/10. I haven't played the DLC, so the DLC story may be great or awful, but most people seemed to like Far Harbor. The plot was basically nice moments tied together by weak transitions. The overall tone of this game seemed to be a LOT more optimistic than the other games. I remember playing 3 and getting very creepy feelings or feelings of despair, but with 4 I just got tense in some combat areas and overall hopeful toward the future. I personally didn't mind that tone change, but it may throw a lot of people off, especially veterans.
If you were like me and jumped into the series with Fallout 3 and have only played games following that, you will probably like Fallout 4 pretty well. However, if you have been playing this series since its beginning, and had issues with the newer games before 4, I can see why you might not like it. Objectively, I think it's a good game, but subjectively, I can see where it sometimes fails to live up to Fallout standards.
Combat: 8/10 (sometimes repetitive, especially after main campaign)
Story: 5/10 overall, 8-9/10 when it gets good.
Graphics: 10/10 (based on the videos and screenshots I see of it running maxed out. I didn't get that luxury but I was never bothered)
tl;dr issa good game if you accept that it isn't like the older Fallouts.

You can do a bit of looting, the environments feel a lot more involving, the AI seems a good bit smarter, the graphics are excellent, skill trees are more involved, you can customise skillsets and weapons and on and on. Excellent game in my opinion. For an indie game the narration is superb, and has a dark, gothic art style with lovecraftian themes. In that sense, you can "sort of" compare the art style to Bloodborne. That being said, it is a turn-based RPG that has heavy emphasis on resource management and preparation. Heed whatever warnings the game gives you and prepare accordingly, because you won't necessarily be able to complete a dungeon every single attempt. It is difficult, yes, but I personally found the game to let you have a reasonable amount of mess ups before something actually bad happens to you (based on my time with the game anyways). I would personally call it more "hard but fair" opposed to what seems to recently be common, "unfair difficulty". Speaking of which...
Apparently, many of the negative comments that came after early December's patches are due to people getting butthurt over nerfing exploits and making the game more difficult. Basically, people could set up their parties so that they could basically kill an entire enemy party without resistence and never net stress (stress is a flavor mechanic of the game which builds up due to being crit, being in the dark, etc. and eventually incurs debuffs and even heart attacks), therefore trivializing much of the game. It was also rumored that people partook in mass account creation to downvote any positive comments at the time and to upvote negative ones, so keep that in mind when reading other reviews.
Darkest Dungeon is kind of niche and will require some patience in order to progress in. I can't garuntee you'll love it, but I really like it for what it is - a unique turn-based RPG with heavy emphasis on decision making and resource management. Hopefully this review was helpful in some way.

The good:
-Much smoother and more fluid UI navigation and Combat than previous games.
-A fun (if repetative) system for building settlements. If you love building houses in the sims, or decorating housing in mmo's, there's a lot here for you to play with.

The Bad:
-Dialogue choice is very limited, and in some cases non-existent. A quick repeat of the different choices you can choose from in most conversations will show you how little effect you have on the world. However in some areas, like the main story quest for Far Harbor they did manage to give the player a feeling of impactful decisions with real consequences.
-I mentioned modifying guns as a good point, but as a result there are very few actually unique feeling weapons in the game unlike the previous titles, and eventually most loot-which is procedurally generated, of course- becomes worthless to you very shortly.
The Ugly:
-"Radiant Quests" or procedurally generated quests. They bring you no worthwhile rewards, they serve very little purpose towards the advancement of most factions, and they are EXTREMELY repetative. They only seem to exisit in the game as "filler" content. ANOTHER SETTLEMENT NEEDS YOUR HELP!
Summary:
-Progress in gameplay, regress in role-playing elements, unfortunate rise of procedural generation. Still a good game.

This review is not meant for veteran Fallout players. If you read other reviews, many are from people who've played dozens of hours. Some are Fallout veterans who dislike the game because it isn't the true Fallout sequel they wanted. These are completely justified gripes, some of which I personally agree with.
But, I'm going for an objective review for first-time players or casual past Fallout players.
Now, on to the game. I enjoy the base game quite a bit and 100 percent suggest it.
The actual game mechanics are a solid 8/10- shooting is satisfying, movement is reactive - the smoothest Bethesda game. Survival Mode is great - best thing in a base, non-isometric Fallout yet. It gives the game more stakes in a way, so it's not just spam the quick save button.
Plus, mods. You can turn the game into a straight survival shooter - a couple hits and you die. A couple hits, the bad guy dies. Monsters are actually scary. Enemies scale properly. Perks aren't overpowered. This, in my eyes, are the best part of mods. They literally change the base game at its core.
My game is almost more STALKER than Fallout through basic weather mods, weapon and armor aditions and various filters and overlays.
Now, RPG elements. Level up, basic back story, etc. The RPG elements are much simplified from all prior Fallouts and take A LOT from Skyrim. It uses perks entirely, no more leveling stats up to 100. Personally, I like seeing these direct and immediate effects of a perk rather than the rather subtle changes in numbers. These, again, are subjective and a turn off for veteran Fallout-ers, and rightly so.
Back story is laid out pretty well solid and you can't escape that. Lines are voiced, but that's not really a negative. Just makes it more difficult for full role-players. But again mods are here to save the day. Several of mine completely eliminate the backstory and even change dialogue to completely ignore rather core parts of the story.
Now, quests and main story. Depends on the quest. There are some gems in here for sure, just gonna throw out Silver Shroud and U.S.S. Constitution. Think those are universally liked. Also, the DLC Far Harbor has a great story all around. Other quests, not so much, including the main quest. Basic options and four factions are offered, so there are basic choices. Mostly though, they're hit or miss for sure. However, you can ignore those and get to the absolute best part of the game...
Exploration.
I'm a much bigger fan of Fallout 3 over New Vegas because the world felt so much more alive in Fallout 3. At the very basic level, it comes down to exploration and world vs. story writing and choices. New Vegas was more on rails. All enemies were in the same place every playthrough. No real variation.
I despised this. But Fallout 3...the random encounters, the expected quests coming out of nowhere...exploring our nation's capital...it was great. Coming out of the vault was the single greatest game experience I've had, maybe surpassed by giraffes in Last of Us.
They stepped it up in Fallout 4. Tons of places to explore. Random encounters everywhere. Distince biomes. Very unique, memorable locations, moreso than any other Fallout. Of course, many enemy types are the same at locations, but they still vary to an extent.
So, this game is less RPG than previous Fallout titles, for better...or worse. It was "simplified" in a sense.
It's in the fantastic Fallout universe and has the Fallout feeling while keeping Bethesda's fantastic exploration and player choice top and center. Is it a great standalone game? Yes. However, veteran Fallout fans might be put off, rightly so.
Have fun, Vault-dweller.

I don't know, something about the game feels wrong. Maybe it's the performance issues, maybe it's the 'slower paced' gameplay, or maybe it's the lack of Micheal McCann. I just don't get the same feeling like I do with EU/EW.
Even Long War feels more satisfying, and that♥♥♥♥♥♥is brutal.
I wanted to be excited for this sequel, and I was for sometime... It feels like it was partially for nothing.
--- Pros so far ---
- Customization is great. Customize guns/people to a higher extent versus EU/EW.
- Graphics are nice. I care more for gameplay though.
- Mod support right outta the box.
- New terrain/landscapes are nice.
- New enemies.
--- Cons so far ---
- No Micheal McCann. His music was the one thing that made me excited going on missions, made me care for Earth's survival, and made me care even more about the soldiers under my command.
- Gameplay feels slower versus EU/EW. It feels like I'm forced to watch a soldier finish his/her 3 second animation before I can call my next move. Makes the game feel slower to me. Or maybe that's the performance issues? We'll see by next patch.
- Story is pretty lame. I won't go into it, do to spoilers.... Hopefully it gets better.
- Performance issues. Random stuttering, even on high-end rigs.
- Base building is overally simplified.
- Get to this ♥♥♥♥ing spot in x amount of turns. It's like you don't want me to plan things.
- Some enemies need balancing.
I will never thumbs this up, even if they fixed the performance issues. This is not the xcom I wanted, nor is it the xcom I was told it was.
--- Edit ---
I'm happy there were people who shared my concerns and have decided to 'fix' some of the problem areas of the game. Reminds me of the Skyrim/Fallout modders. At least with mods, I think this game is a bit more playable.

Excellent game in my opinion. For an indie game the narration is superb, and has a dark, gothic art style with lovecraftian themes. In that sense, you can "sort of" compare the art style to Bloodborne. That being said, it is a turn-based RPG that has heavy emphasis on resource management and preparation. Heed whatever warnings the game gives you and prepare accordingly, because you won't necessarily be able to complete a dungeon every single attempt. It is difficult, yes, but I personally found the game to let you have a reasonable amount of mess ups before something actually bad happens to you (based on my time with the game anyways). I would personally call it more "hard but fair" opposed to what seems to recently be common, "unfair difficulty". Speaking of which...
Apparently, many of the negative comments that came after early December's patches are due to people getting butthurt over nerfing exploits and making the game more difficult. Basically, people could set up their parties so that they could basically kill an entire enemy party without resistence and never net stress (stress is a flavor mechanic of the game which builds up due to being crit, being in the dark, etc. and eventually incurs debuffs and even heart attacks), therefore trivializing much of the game. It was also rumored that people partook in mass account creation to downvote any positive comments at the time and to upvote negative ones, so keep that in mind when reading other reviews.
Darkest Dungeon is kind of niche and will require some patience in order to progress in. I can't garuntee you'll love it, but I really like it for what it is - a unique turn-based RPG with heavy emphasis on decision making and resource management. Hopefully this review was helpful in some way.

So, Xcom 2 is here and people are asking "How is it?"
Overall it is a great game and a really nice improvement over the last Xcom game, but it is not perfect. Let's start off with the Negatives shall we?
The game is not optimized very well and has some bugs, this seems to vary from person to person but there is no denying Firaxis needs to get to work on some performance fixes. I also had a few graphics bugs when my character goes to pick up his teammates when they are down and a few times the game has gone below 50 fps. No gamebreaking bugs and the performance issues have not been disasterous but they are there and should def be mentioned.
With all that said, shall we get to the positives now? There is alot of them so let's get started. First off there are some wonderful additions that really add to the gameplay and overall enjoyment of the game. The animations and graphics are also better, not drastically huge improvement but without a doubt things are smoother and tighter as far as how the game looks. There is a bunch of other new features that add to the game and make it feel like a well thought out sequel instead of just more of pretty much exactly the same as before ala AC or FC series. Voice acting is good and the game also controls very well. I can see myself playing this game for many, many hours. Alot of hours have gone into the old Xcom games and Enemy Unknown for me and this one will be no different, it is very addicting.
Overall the good far outweigh the bad for me personally (and by a good amount) but some might want to hold off until a patch or two come out for the performance issues and small bugs. These are my thoughts after 16 hours on the game so far (I will post more after 50 hours, this right now is just a first impressions), if you love Xcom as a series this is a no brainer, I liked the last Xcom but it wasn't as good as the older xcom games, this game here though takes that the last game did well and adds a bunch of great features and improvements, while unfortunately suffering from the odd nagging issue. Xcom is back and it is back in a big way, once the kinks get ironed out this will be even better. Already a game of very high quality but at the same time one that can improve and get better in a few aspects. There are so many aspects to games, from graphics, to ai, writing, voice work, to gameplay,  performance, controls and much more. Normally, I have a rule not to review early access titles until they have been officially released as a finished product, but I decided to make an exception for Darkest Dungeon (DD) because of the great feedback the game (and developers) have received. I received a review copy and was extremely interested to try DD because I love dungeon crawling and rogue-likes, and the title had already received massive acclaim for being true to both genres.
The aesthetics are fantastic - the amount of detail in the character models and environment is very high. Each character's skills are flashy and cool to see. The sound effects and music are great at maintaining a dark, intense vibe - enhancing the rogue-like atmosphere and reminding you that you can die (forever!) at any moment. The story is unfinished, but what currently exists is fairly basic - you must travel through different dungeons, eventually reaching the main one. Many have tried, many more have failed. You will also fail. Many times.
Controls are easy to learn and the tutorial helps explain every mechanic in the game. The learning curve is moderate to extreme depending on your experience with rogue-likes and turn-based strategy. The developers have done an exemplary job of communicating with the gaming community, going as far as adding an option to remove a newer feature - corpses (killing enemies would leave behind a corpse that had to first be destroyed before the lineup of enemies moves forward - many people found this annoying) and heart attacks (your characters could instantly die if their stress reached high levels). The tutorial is good at getting you ready for the madness that is the Darkest Dungeon. There are a lot of mechanics to keep up with (in particular, player stress), but there are always tooltips for everything, be it while you are inside or outside of combat. Furthermore, new elements - usually reflected by new buildings being available in your main camp - are introduced slowly, so you have time to get used to things before a new feature is added. The most challenging parts of DD will be managing your party stress and maintaining a balanced party structure (ex: you don't want to go into battle with 4 healers lacking any offensive abilities).
Gameplay consists of you traversing through a dungeon, exploring rooms and the passageways between them. You must complete a main mission - like exploring 90% of the rooms or completing 90% of the room battles - before you can receive a reward and leave the dungeon. If you retreat early, your party will accumulate significant stress. Stress can be disastrous, as it will sometimes cause heart attacks (if the feature is turned on) and can cause people to panic (granting either a buff/debuff for the duration of the dungeon).
Combat is intense and can be very, very challenging. Replayability is high because you can construct your 4-member party from a large pool of characters, randomized whenever you return to the main hub. You can build a roster, which is highly advised because you need to alternate between healing/recovering stress party members - this takes a game day (or longer) - and using them in battle. Perks and disabilities can become extremely annoying, as these are also randomized, and debilitating conditions (ex: kleptomania will cause a character to sometimes open items and keep them - preventing the items from going into your inventory) can only be removed if you spend a considerable amount of gold.
During battle, you will take turns attacking your opponent, healing/buffing your allies, or using items. One of my favorite characters can transform into a werewolf, but it will cause stress to the other party members. If a party member reaches 0, they are downed and can be revived by others, however, if they are continually attacked, they will permanently die.
Overall, the gameplay is rapid, unforgiving, and a lot of fun. I must admit, for an early access project, there is a lot of content to enjoy even if you were to buy DD as is (with no future updates). If you are a lover of rogue-likes, dungeon crawling, and turn-based strategy, then you must try this game.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

Yes, this game is ridiculously difficult, and yes, much of it is tied to RNG. However, the RNG in Darkest Dungeon reminds me of something similar to XCOM. An attack with 95% chance to hit can still miss and its infuriating when it does. Has that stopped people from loving XCOM? No. So the only cause I can find for all the negative reviews from long time early access players is failure to adapt to the changes that have been made.
Darkest Dungeon is made to be punishing, and it's void of guarantees. The design of a game like this is intended to force the player overcome impossible odds on a mission through careful thought in combat, and managing your party members well in town (in this case by properly budgeting treatments, upgrades, provisions, etc.) and if the player can successfully do these things then they will be successful to some degree.
Failures come as often as these successes though. Party members will die, and you will be forced to abandon quests in order to save others. But some of the greatest satisfaction comes from salvaging your roster after losing one or two in a dungeon, and then using that roster to clear a dungeon or defeat a boss, then collect the fruits of your labor. The sense of accomplishment is tremendous, and the rewards are worthwhile.
So please give this game a shot if you're looking for a punishing challenge with appropriate rewards and satisfying and intricate gameplay.

Fallout 4...
Just like any Bethesda games, you either love it or hate it. Personally, this is probably the one I've spent most time on (aside from New Vegas and Elder Scroll IV). First off, let me just say thank you Bethesda for no more ugly character faces. No matter how long I spent fixing my character's faces in the past game...they look apocalyptic. Not in a good way. Even ghouls looks better than what you were able to customize. The latest installment has a good aray of customization options. I may not stare at my characters straight in the face, but at least I know what they look like.
The game also implemented a ''settlement'' building option. Which is similar to a sim game in building your own city and maintaining your inhabitants. The only downside is that building the shops doesn't allow you to make big money. In fact, the way how it works is still very obscure.
Storyline: I did not hate it. In fact, this game has one of the better storyline next to New Vegas, I find. There's also a lot of ''shoutouts'' to current events happening in the real world. There are also some interesting characters companions (not spoiling it). As with every Bethesda games, there will be some wonky characters. It is expected.
Modes: There are a few different difficulties you can change whenever you want in the game--veterans of the game will be pleased that there is the ''survival mode'' available. But you will have to deliberately select when playing.
File size: If you have limited bandwidth--this game will be a nightmare to download. It's 26gb, give or take.
Overall? A fun, addictive game. Is it worth playing? Yes.

Finally, a game that Trion currently hasn't attempted to turn into a cash cow. Trove, as you'd guess is a hybrid of Minecraft meeting WoW with the building and voxel based buildng from Minecraft and the loot and dungeons from WoW. There's loads of reviews saying how great this game is but, all the while this game does have its fair share of flaws including the ungodly waiting time. No matter where you are, trying to join Trove at around 3pm-ish is almost impossible due to the low server count. It takes around thirty minutes to load into the game but can vary from entering the game instantly with no wait time to essentially leaving the game open, tabbing out and watching a video or something.
Trion have said that they've attempted to fix this but that in turn caused huge server down times and only slightly helping the problem. Why reccomend this game you might be asking? well, it's because if you manage to sit through those loading screens and get into the game, you'll see that Trove has become everything that Cube World failed to be. We're seing activity from Trion with updates and articles coming out every so often unlike Cube World which last had an update on July 23rd 2013 and only recieved a video on "how it's going to have quests" but a video saying something will be added isn't anything like actually having it in.
As you'd guess, the main point of Trove is to focus on the whole RPG aspect with a tiered loot system which can be turned into base matterials to enchan weapons to be even stronger. As forv the classes, there's a huge selection of play styles from the knights tanking to the gunslingers "♥♥♥♥ing jump and shoot" style, it's diverse. What Trove also does well is its different activities which all help with the main role of the game. By leveling up your skills, you gain mastery points which give you buffs, items or ingame currency which can purchase classes or other things. The skills which can be improved are the following: Gardening, Ringcrafting and runecrafting which all help you in some way. Runes give you recipies for blocks and the ring crafting provides bonus stats on top of how gardening gives the player the ability to craft stronger boats and other things.
Do I recommend this game?
Yes, IF you can sit through the insane queueing time

5. Weapons in the left hand were a staple of Dark Souls 2, and many of them were designed specifically to be used like this, whereas there’s only about 2 in DS3 to my knowledge (Rapier and Handmaid’s Dagger) which gave you and extremely high amount of variety and versatility to any build.

So, Xcom 2 is here and people are asking "How is it?"
Overall it is a great game and a really nice improvement over the last Xcom game, but it is not perfect. Let's start off with the Negatives shall we?
The game is not optimized very well and has some bugs, this seems to vary from person to person but there is no denying Firaxis needs to get to work on some performance fixes. I also had a few graphics bugs when my character goes to pick up his teammates when they are down and a few times the game has gone below 50 fps. No gamebreaking bugs and the performance issues have not been disasterous but they are there and should def be mentioned.
With all that said, shall we get to the positives now? There is alot of them so let's get started. First off there are some wonderful additions that really add to the gameplay and overall enjoyment of the game. The animations and graphics are also better, not drastically huge improvement but without a doubt things are smoother and tighter as far as how the game looks. There is a bunch of other new features that add to the game and make it feel like a well thought out sequel instead of just more of pretty much exactly the same as before ala AC or FC series. Voice acting is good and the game also controls very well. I can see myself playing this game for many, many hours. Alot of hours have gone into the old Xcom games and Enemy Unknown for me and this one will be no different, it is very addicting.
Overall the good far outweigh the bad for me personally (and by a good amount) but some might want to hold off until a patch or two come out for the performance issues and small bugs. These are my thoughts after 16 hours on the game so far (I will post more after 50 hours, this right now is just a first impressions), if you love Xcom as a series this is a no brainer, I liked the last Xcom but it wasn't as good as the older xcom games, this game here though takes that the last game did well and adds a bunch of great features and improvements, while unfortunately suffering from the odd nagging issue. Xcom is back and it is back in a big way, once the kinks get ironed out this will be even better. Already a game of very high quality but at the same time one that can improve and get better in a few aspects. There are so many aspects to games, from graphics, to ai, writing, voice work, to gameplay,  performance, controls and much more. This game nails 90% of these things with near perfection, but struggles with that one issue, optimization.
So many mods for this game! Played a ton of hours on it now and I am blown away by how many cool mods there is already. New Classes, New Voice packs, new helmets/hats/tattoos,etc.. for customization your troops. While, of course, the difficulty may make this series slightly inaccessible to some players, I believe that anyone that decides against at least once playing through any of the Miyazaki-led Soulsborne titles is missing out on something amazing. Dark Souls was an amazing game as it was, but III has improved in almost every way. The combat is a lot more fluid, while still maintaining a sense of weight to it. Playing with friends is a lot easier to do than in previous installments, taking the password system from Bloodborne to allow semi-private playthroughs. The bosses, again taking more from Bloodborne, are much more in depth than in previous titles, with each boss having at least 2 stages, and with quite a few of them having awe-inspiring moments that leave you sat there with a wide grin across your face, involuntarily muttering the words "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥". The characters on the other hand, are a part of the game I think could have been improved on. Don't get me wrong the characters are all fine, but in Dark Souls I, almost every character's story arc was tragic, and could bring a tear to your eye. The story and lore in III as a whole though, especially now that the dlc has all been released, was all amazing, and rounded off the series almost perfectly, answering some questions that fans have been asking since the first game, while still leaving us to interpret a lot of the lore ourselves, which I believe has been a major strong point to the souls series since the beginning. All in all, Dark Souls III is a nigh perfect video game, and I would highly recommend this game to both Souls-veterans and newcomers alike.

That one word can sum up one of the most honest truths of Darkest Dungeon.
It doesn't hold your hand and coddle you through your journey. Instead it forces you to work with what you have.
You aren't going to get a magical drop that will make the world instantly a better place. Your people will deal with stress, and you will have to deal with them. They are flawed, some more than others. They don't always listen and they aren't
the most courageous people you will ever see in a game but this is what makes them worth while.
Will you treat them like cannon fodder, will you take car of them? CAN you take care of them? They are after all your heros. Your chosen refugees used to put your plan in motion.
Perma Death, is by far the biggest excitement. When you have that core group or maybe just one charactor you really are trying to keep alive. You have upgraded them and kept them in good health, both mental and physical, but then... you come across something powerful, something you where not expecting to find.... And you can not run. I am aware that the game is difficult, and at some times, immaculate odds are pinned against the player, sometimes beyond his/her own means. (Things such as stress, disease, debuffs, you name it.)
However, that is not to say there isn't any form of strategy. If anything, that plays the biggest part. And it just so happens that this game is more slow with it, with each decision on and off the dungeons being impactful to your chances of success or failure. Whether to bring someone who has a crippling disease, or a party containing one half-stressed person, there are loads of variables. Ideally, you want to keep you strongest members alive. But they can die, the same as you weaker members, and be lost to the dreaded perma-death. (Though at least in this case, there is the death's door status, which stops you from outright dying, but debuffs you for the expedition.)
This WILL turn off a lot of casual strategy players. However, I find this game rather enjoyable, and I praise the game for keeping its challenge. And you have the ability to tailor the challenge if you find the game too hard and want to ease in.
The aesthetics are appealing and the chilling narrator speaks of lines that make the atmosphere of the game all the more effective.
And despite the game being in a considerably long beta, it has certainly come a long way. It's well on its way to becoming a pretty solid game, if it isn't there already.

This isn't like a normal RPG where you keep your main character throughout the game. I had just completed a "more difficult" mission to kill a named boss enemy, and suffered no losses. While waiting for my main crew to chillax and recover, I figured I'd take a few characters that needed to level up on an "easy" mission - whoops! Lost one, and two others are now masochistic and obsessed with torturing people, and won't let me heal them... figures! This game keeps you guessing. Don't get attached to any characters! The beauty of this game is figuring out how to roll with the punches and maintain forward momentum! Also, just enjoying the artwork, environment, and neat interactions that can happen is very rewarding.

This is going to be hopefully a short review.
So I was a little sceptical about the game due to it's Minecraft-like graphics. Read some of the reviews and decided that I will give it a shot, since there were a lot of positive ones. I had nothing to lose, but I was still sceptical after all the positive reviews. So with my first log-in there was like... I can't even describe it. There were a lot of colors, it looked awesome. It looked so simple, you have about 4 spells ( excluding your basic attacks ) which are so simple made. There is no class advance and stuff ( even though you can change your class whenever you like, as long as you charge some real life money)  Once I entered combat, the gameplay seemed so smooth, I couldn't believe my eyes. I feel that the live action combat system is very well made, and I might compare it to TERA's combat system, and even say that it feels a little smoother. The community is very, very friendly, so far. Whenever I asked any questions in the Global chat, they always answered me. After some time spent in the game, I found out that the game is not as simple as it seems. There are a lot of instances, and the end-game content seems to be quite good as well. There are a lot of different item grades, for different levels, there are item upgrades. Though there is a different side of the game. The even more minecraft-like. You can farm almost every color material that you see in the world. The world is completely destroyable. There are a lot of dungeons with different type of colored blocks. You can make your dream house, castle, hell you can even create a whole forrest! So far, so good. The only issues I've encountered are the from-time-to-time long server log-ins. Though it says exactly how much time you are supposed to wait, so it's not really a problem for me. The most time I've waited was about 30 min. Usually it is around 10 min, if there is any waiting. Overall the game seems to be very fun.

I hope I helped :)
PS. The Cash Shop is not an issue with the game, people who are using it don't have some kind of strong advantage in the game, so chill your tatas!

This game is not about playing to win, or even developing characters. It is about setting you up for a frustrating exercise in futility and leaving you with absolutely no hope. The items that bestow stat boosts also carry penalties. The money and resources spent developing your hamlet will leave you without resources to purchase items for quests. You will experience random deaths and afflictions of characters, which you will be unable to cure because you lack money needed from finishing dungeons. In other words, this game has been overweighted to such an extent that it is designed to cause you to fail at every turn. And not matter how careful you are, you will lose.
The worst part is that you will be unable to level any characters up high enough to advance in the game, because they will likely gain so much stress and affliction they will die of a heart attack before reaching level 2.
I appreciate the lovecraftian elements of this game. However, the developers have weighted the game to such an extent against the player, that it isn't even enjoyable to play.
That said, if you simply want to play to see how long you can go before all your characters die, then this game will provide at the least a lot of entertainment value because of the narrator commentary and creepy graphics. To be fair, I think the developers have a decent basis for what could be a very versatile game to the broader gaming community. But at this point, it is purely designed for graphic visual value, because it isn't even challenging - it's hopeless.
If anyone in the company or development actually reads this review, I would urge you to consider programming some variability into the in terms of challenge levels. It would probably have a broader appeal to the larger gaming community. As it stands now, I think it is likely a very small niche group of folks that would actually enjoy the gameplay.
Examples of in-game issues: Want to heal outside of combat? Nope. Healer skils are only available during combat. And food only heals one lifepoint at a time outside of combat - while penalties like bleeding and plague continue to linger outside of combat. You can cure them with items, but if you don't have the money, you don't have the items. You can only camp to restore life in certain dungeons, so if it's a single-shot playthrough dungeon with no camping option, you have no heal ability outside of combat. Treasure drops in the dungeons are so random and rare as to be not worth it. And healing abilities in combat are somewhat random in the amount they restore. The game is designed to kill your heroes. Period.
You can leave a dungeon at any time. But if you do, it may disappear, which means you lose out on the item rewards for completion. Further, you don't get to keep provisions purchased but not used for the next dungeon. And the costs to remove and heal heros who are likely crapping themselves when they return to the hamlet means you have little resources for provisions in the next dungeon.
I like the concepts in the game. And I appreciate the developers really aren't going for a game that's playable to win - it's more about sacrifice and how far you will push to complete. The problem is, if you do push then your heroes will likely die and you won't finish the dungeon anyway - and you can't advance in the game if your characters don't have higher levels, which require money and resources gained from dungeons, which cycles back to the basic problem.
Psychologically, there's very little positive reinforcement in this game, and a whole lot of discouragement and negative reinforcement such that if you are attached to your characters or advancing in the game, you are in for an excercise in frustration. This type of psychological situation doesn't affect everyone negatively, so if that isn't a consideration for you, you may very well enjoy this game.
I don't recommend this game to the broader gaming community. However, if you are the kind of gamer that appreciates the dark, twisted, and impossible to win kind of game that leaves you breathless and frustrated (and I know there are gamers out there like this), then you are in for a treat. This game won't disappoint.
Improvements that could help this game are healing abilities being active outside of combat, or having food restore far more health. But then, I suppose that would mean your heroes might not die as quickly, which would defeat the whole purpose of the game probably. At the least, it would be good to have variable levels of challenge settings in the game in order to help players at all levels truly enjoy and appreciate the dark storyline and potentially awesome gameplay. Right now, however, it just isn't there outside of a niche group.
On another note - I spent hours investing time carefully cultivating characters to be able to take on the first boss (the hag). The turn system in this game is so random, that the hag ended up having multiple turns before I even got a shot off, and she wiped out my whole party with her pot (which she puts your heros into to cook them). The whole battle was a joke. To say that I think the game developers have a tremendous amount of work to do on this game is an understatement. The part that upsets me the most is that I cannot get my money back. But certainly, it is the last time I will ever buy a game from this company.

Not only myself, but the majority of Fallout fans have given this game a load of criticism. It's only until now that I realize how much I love this game.

The world entered this game with extremely high expectations and expected something far better than Fallout: New Vegas, which was already a masterpiece. People gave it an unfair chance and expected too much, these people indeed included myself when the game first came out.

The game's sidequests are great honestly, there are lots and they don't lack content and reward.

The game's main story is alright, not nearly as good as FO3, but similar to FNV in my opinion, simple kinda get revenge for something then choose and fight for a faction. The game can continue a lot after the main story, which to me is a very, very important touch that FNV and F03 (W/O Broken steel) did not have.

Another thing I really enjoyed was building a strong relationship with a companion, was a grind, but gets you emotionally attached to a character and is highly rewarding.

The Gun, Armor, Power Armor, and Chem modifications are great, gives a nice variety of things and makes basic weapons and such reborn. The settlement mode is something I always wanted, loved this.

I cannot speak for the DLC, as I have yet to buy them / play them completely through.

A reasonable game in terms of performance, I cannot speak for lower end cards as I have a GTX 1080 and an i7, but the game is beautiful and smashes it's predecessors in the series.

Overall this game is a blast for me, if it isn't better than FNV, a game i absolutely adore, then it is a close second. Bought this game Day 1 on the Xbox and then bought it when I built my PC, I have absolutely no regrets.

After revisiting this game i've come to the conclusion that this game has earned its praise. Bethesda built an immersive open world with original characters, and a wealth of content. Not to mention the game's fantastic soundtrack. This all put together makes a game that you can just lose yourself in. But... I have some complaints.
We all know about the ancient, worn out engine that bethesda used to make fallout 4, and at this point its being drug on far past its prime. The sometimes ugly graphics, terrible load times and annoying bugs can all be credited to bethesda's relunctancy to ditch this old engine and redesign their game. I feel like this game deserved a redesigned engine, and the next RPG bethesda releases needs to have a new engine
Another thing I didn't like was the main questline. I feel like having such an urgent, dire plot like trying to find your lost son doesnt fit well with this game, as players like to explore the world and tackle side quests while playing through the main story-line. In this instance it feels kind of unnatural and wierd to put aside finding your kidnapped son to explore the world, which is what most players end up doing. And for the sake of the plot, and overall immersion, I feel like the story is just a bad choice. I much prefer the storyline for New Vegas, where you're left with little regarding the main quest and are left to explore the wasteland at your own pace. Another complaint about the main story is the endings, I'm not going to spoil the ending for new players, but you're basically left with a choice, and what I think the writers had in mind was that each choice could be "the right choice" but it turned out, for me at least, that both endings were the wrong choice. I finished the game with a bad feeling about my decision no matter which side I chose, so I ended up loading the game before I had to choose and just leaving it at that. Not making a decision at all. Which sucks for the flow of the story.
That being said there are plenty of side quests and questlines with interesting stories and a wealth of unique characters that give the game heart and immersion. I could just lose myself in the world, doing side quests and building up settlements. The diversity, and freedom this game offers players still impresses me, and makes me want to keep revisiting this game. Overall, i'd give it an 8/10, and i'd say its a must have for PC gamers (can't forget mods of course).

While, of course, the difficulty may make this series slightly inaccessible to some players, I believe that anyone that decides against at least once playing through any of the Miyazaki-led Soulsborne titles is missing out on something amazing. Dark Souls was an amazing game as it was, but III has improved in almost every way. The combat is a lot more fluid, while still maintaining a sense of weight to it. Playing with friends is a lot easier to do than in previous installments, taking the password system from Bloodborne to allow semi-private playthroughs. The bosses, again taking more from Bloodborne, are much more in depth than in previous titles, with each boss having at least 2 stages, and with quite a few of them having awe-inspiring moments that leave you sat there with a wide grin across your face, involuntarily muttering the words "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥". The characters on the other hand, are a part of the game I think could have been improved on. Don't get me wrong the characters are all fine, but in Dark Souls I, almost every character's story arc was tragic, and could bring a tear to your eye. The story and lore in III as a whole though, especially now that the dlc has all been released, was all amazing, and rounded off the series almost perfectly, answering some questions that fans have been asking since the first game, while still leaving us to interpret a lot of the lore ourselves, which I believe has been a major strong point to the souls series since the beginning. All in all, Dark Souls III is a nigh perfect video game, and I would highly recommend this game to both Souls-veterans and newcomers alike.
