Darkest Dungeon is hard, mean, upsetting and unforgiving. If your heroes die, they are dead permanently. Therefore every mission is tense, every time you fear for your group and you have good reason to do so.
(I recommend to NOT play drunk! ;-))
Gameplay:
You have your town with some buildings where you can basically upgrade your heroes. For example you have the blacksmith to improve their armor and weapons or you send the heroes into the sanatorium to remove phobias and quirks they developed when they had to go fight the gruesome monsters. When your heroes are very stressed because of the horrors they saw in the Warrens or the Ruins they had to explore, you can send them to the abbey or the brothrel to make them unstressed again, Also you can hire new heroes here, buy and sell trinkets and so on. Of course, all of this costs money and money you only get when you send out your brave heroes.
Apart from money you need other stuff from down there, like deeds or busts which are used to upgrade the town buildings.
In the dungeon you have a group of four people which fight monsters in a turn based combat. It is important to learn which enemies have what effects on your party (some stress your people out, others simply attack and reduce your health, others debuff your heroes or weaken them by giving them deseases or make them bleed).
Is the health at zero, your hero is not dead but at death's door. This means every following hit has a certain chance to kill your hero. There are much more factors that are influencing the outcome of your mission like traps or how stressed your heroes become.
When your heroes are about to die, you can always abort the mission to save your heroes' life.
(Maybe that is what this game is about: To decide when to retreat and when to go on)
Positive:
- gloomy but beautiful 2D grafics
- sound, music and voice acting!
- interesting and tense turnbased combat (tense because dead heroes stay dead forever!)
- 14 different hero classes with individual strengths and weaknesses
- numerous trinkets to upgrade you character
- Positive and negative consequences for your heroes after missions (Quirks and deseases)
- interesting character and enemy design
- no sexist depiction of female characters
- you can individualise your heroes by naming them and giving them one out of four pre-made colour schemes
- Red Hook is a great developer, they react to emails quickly and include the gamers in the development of the game
Negative:
- sometimes unfair chain of events that end up killing your hero
- not enough different healing classes which results in similar team combinations
- Some boss battles still too easy which makes them feel unrewarding
- still some balancing to do for some hero classes that have useless skills
First of all you have to note that this game is still in Beta and will release at 19th January 2016.
Even though it is an early access game, It worked from the start and I never regretted buying it.
If you like turn based combat and rogue like games, this might be something for you.

I wrote a long review, but it didn't get posted for some reason, so I'll be brief.
I love this game.  It's a very challenging, gothic horror-themed, turn-based RPG.  I love the fact that you have to consider the physical and mental condition of all of your characters.  I love all of the different character classes, and figuring out how to combine them and use them effectively in different situations.  They're all fun to use, and they all have plenty of individual skills that you have to decide when (or if) to upgrade, and how to use them in tandem with the skills of other group members.  I love the balance in tone.  It's funny, dark and violent, but nothing too extreme in either direction.
This game finally taught me to take negative reviews with a huge grain of salt.  I watched a couple of gameplay videos and quickly realized that most of the negative reviews that had previously given me pause were not to be taken seriously.  It's a great game that works well, and will force you to make sacrifices and hard choices, and maybe even to bounce back from defeat.  You have to prepare yourself, manage your resources, and choose which characters to invest in, and which ones to replace.  I rarely buy early access games, but I made an exception for this one, and I'm glad I did.
I highly recommended it for anyone who's not very easily frustrated.

I want to start by saying I had already played this game in the past, before there were even secondary bosses or a Cove area, and I did so for very, very long. it was an intensely fun and rewarding experience, and it absolutely made me think it would be money well spent to acquire it for myself when it was finished. Hell, I'd have payed twice its price tag, to get a completed game which was that enjoyable.
I received it as a gift from a friend recently and was positively overjoyed, I could not wait to come back and see all that was added in this past half year. I created a new save file, started playing... and despaired. But I decided to keep playing, and to not stop playing until I had seen all the changes and could properly grasp what the game presently had to offer.
So it is now, after over 30 hours of gameplay time, that I want to write this review and say that I do NOT, in any way or form, recommend this game as it currently is. It is no longer the game I played back then. It has changed into something that is barely recognizable; it -is- technically the same game, but it most definitely does not feel the same. And it comes nowhere near what it once was in terms of enjoyment.
I've read many bits and pieces of (sometimes conflicting) information as to why this happened, namely:
-A highly-vocal group of "fans" steering this game into its sad current state
-Developers which have a very particular vision for this game, and scour strategy guides and topics for things to nerf in order to take away any and all slight advantages a player could afford
So before I get into any details, I want to make this clear: I am not familiar to any such forum drama, I do not know who holds the blame, and I have no idea whatsoever as to why the game changed into what it is today. The one thing I know for certain is: it did change. Badly.
This game is now unquestionably an anti-fun game. By "anti-fun" I don't mean overly hard, I don't mean overly grindy, I don't mean overly complex. I mean it is a game that seems carefully tailored to remove all sense of fun from playing it. Practically all enjoyment is gone, all progression feels meaningless for the most part, all achievements help you in basically no way whatsoever.
Chief among the worst offenders are two mechanics: corpses and heart attacks. And yes, I know you can turn corpses off, but then we are not playing the game "the way it's meant to be played", we are not experiencing all it has to offer. And so, to elaborate:
Heart attacks - having a hero reach the 100 stress threshold was already a terrible thing to happen before, in a GOOD way. It was a challenge to be overcome, it was an entertaining encumbrance. That lone hero would bring the entire party down the path of stress soon enough, and you'd usually end up with a group of raving lunatics cutting themselves, refusing heals, shuffling about, acting on their own... and a lone hero who passed the Virtue check going strong and carrying the expedition. It was a predicament, it was not a situation you wanted to be in at all, but it was FUN.
This is not the case anymore. Stress accumulation is now roughly 2-3x higher than it once was, everything stresses out our heroes greatly and continuously. And it doesn't stop at 100 with a potentially compromising situation which would force you to seriously consider withdrawal, while still having a chance to go forth in case other conditions were favorable. No, now it NEVER stops, and it is guaranteed to erase hours of game time and tens of thousands of gold that you spent treating, training, and equipping the heroes that WILL inevitably die from it at some point. You used to be able to bring a mildly-stressed hero on an expedition; doing so now is signing a death sentence for that hero and possibly the others as well, and a virtual guarantee that the expedition will fail
I will not even touch with a 10-foot pole how unrealistic it is for everyone to be getting heart attacks left and right, and will simply leave it at: This is not fun. This is not acceptable, even. It is not enjoyable to have to constantly be worried because stress, something you can't effectively heal from, is an ever-present threat of almost instant death, which, thanks to this game's unforgiving RNG and mechanics, is VERY usually the same as instant death. Heart attacks could maybe, -maybe- be acceptable if they happened at 300 stress. And this is still a VERY big maybe. But as it is, it is undeniably an anti-fun mechanic that serves only to aggravate players for things we are unable to control.
-------------------
Corpses - This is by far the worst offender of the two, and that's without even touching how stupidly unrealistic it is for a lone, butchered body to be effectively keeping an enemy out of our reach. This mechanic kills the utility of certain classes, artificially inflates the usefulness of certain skills which, for the most part, are otherwise generally useless, and perhaps most importantly it can cause catastrophic situations for essentially no logical reason. Enemies are -never- inconvenienced by corpses unless we use a move skill on them, and even then, most enemies will quickly return to their preferred position since every other skill of theirs causes them to move in their preferred direction. It is simply and legitimately a mechanic meant to drain the enjoyment and sense of accomplishment from the game, causing us to need more turns to take out a priority target that's out of reach, thus taking more damage and stress for, again, -no reason whatsoever-.
But I want you to fully appreciate the actual stupidity of this mechanic. Corpses appear when the enemy is killed with regular damage that isn't a critical hit, which is like 90% of all killing blows, give or take. If the enemy is killed by a critical hit, bleed damage, or blight damage, there won't be a corpse. BUT:
-If the enemy is bleeding/blighted, and is killed with a regular attack, there will still be a corpse!... that is bleeding/blighted. For some eldritch reason, if the enemy doesn't have those last 2 HP taken by bleed or blight damage, it suddenly turns into a corpse that CAN take a load more bleed and blight damage. Absolutely fantastic.
-If the enemy is killed by a critical hit that does 2 damage, there won't be a corpse. If the enemy is killed by a regular attack that does 30 damage, there will be a full HP corpse. Being labelled a critical hit apparently means more than what makes critical hits important, which is their damage.
Both of the above points happen for a very simple reason: artificial difficulty. Forcing you to not attack an enemy and kill him instantly this turn, and instead have him bleed out over 2 turns so that you won't be wasting a turn dealing with its corpse. Taking the ability to avoid corpses away from your hands and into the RNG's by making it so the blow has to be a critical hit, and not just a powerful hit. Because attacking bleeding/blighted enemies, or hitting near-death enemies with powerful skills, so that they wouldn't leave corpses behind? Those would be things the player could control, and we wouldn't want that, now would we?
In order to make corpses borderline bearable, at -least- the following changes would be needed:
-Any enemy that dies while bleeding/blighted would leave no corpse
-Any damage beyond what is needed to kill the enemy would be subtracted from the corpse's HP. For example, if you deal a 5 damage blow to an enemy with 2 HP, the corpse would lose 3 HP right as it spawned
And again, this is so corpses would be more bearable. It is no substitute for the fact that, much like heart attacks, they shouldn't exist at -all-.

I never write reviews, because I cannot write. However, the people at Red Hook have created such a unique experience that I am compelled to voice my opinions on this truly once in a lifetime experience. Games like this come once in a blue moon. A blue, horrible, haunted moon.
Where do I even start?
Every moment in the Darkest Dungeon is perfectly crafted to force you to make hard decisions that not only affect you, but people you are responsible for. It's a roguelike, personnel management, dungeon crawler, graphic novel, horror game. That is a lot of Genres to try and nail, but Red Hook stuns that baby, pulls it to the front row, then lands a critical strike.
Do I kill that deadly enemy fighter to keep my delve into the ruins going? Or, do I kill that cultist priest who is about to force my healer to examine her life choices, possibly driving her mad, but maybe forcing her to finally overcome her fear of the undead and take a stand against evil? Then again, that stupid skeleton with the sword always seems to land critical strikes. Oh, wonderful. The gargolye just stunned my ranged fighter. I guess that limits my options.
The combat is so perfect in this game, I could write this whole review on it. But the best way to describe it is "stressful". The fights are turn based, with things like speed, health, damage, critical strikes, dots. The difference here is how significant every action is. Everything you do has consequences. Enemies are not fodder in this game. One group could wipe out your whole party. Attacks are animated like the action scenes of a graphic novel, with bold lunges and sweeping strikes animated beautifully. Combat never drags out, and actually stresses out your fighters. Every enemy attack carries weight and dangerous side effects. Picking apart the enemy party based on what monsters enhance others is a game in of itself. Careful management of your party is crucial to your success. Each of your fighters have different skills which supplement your other fighters. Maximizing your party efficiency is a game in of itself.
Then, there is the stress. Not just the game mechanic, but YOUR stress.
Getting too technical would ruin the magic of this masterfully implemented mechanic. You have to experience it to fully appriciate it. So I will keep it vague. The hardships you put your party through, forcing them to fight the undead, demon possessed swine corpses, and a canabalistic hag, cause them to act against your wishes, hurt themselves, or refuse to fight entirely. When your fighters become stressed they act without orders. They attack the wrong monsters. They touch the wrong things in the dangerous dungeon. In a game that hinges on every action being potentially dangerous and life threatening, this mechanic forces you to make hard choices.
What's really interesting is how this marriage of danger and fear management, and how your fighters respond to it, totally subvert the usual dungeon crawler tropes and expectations. Your party members are eager at first, to quote the game "foolishly seeking fame and fortune." However, if one fight goes bad, or someone gets sick from touching a dirty cart, the 'heroes' start to waver. They develop fears, strengths, and personalities. Sure, that healer was the lifeblood of your party in the warrens, but now we need to go into the cove, and she's afraid of fish monsters. That knight gets a bonus in damage against undead, but fighting undead stresses him out. Your backup healer is still passed out drunk in the bar after nearly dying to a rabid dog, and the your backup BACKUP healer doesn't have good enough armor to go on this quest, and you can't afford to upgrade him right now.
There are times when you have to send an unprepared party against a vastly superior enemy, hoping that they just survive, dragging enough treasure back to fund your failing expedition. There's a real sense of regret after some delves. You're always left feeling like you could have done more. You always feel like you just barely survived, not entirely sure at the human cost of your quest for knowledge.
And this is where the story comes into play.
The game's narrative is a flawlessly crafted love letter to Lovecraftian fiction and lore. If you are not familiar with Lovecraft, the primary theme being realized in this game is that humanity in general is fleeting and pointless, and that the sins of the father ALWAYS come back to haunt the children. You play the role of a nameless, faceless protagonist who is trying to find out what happened to one of his reletives, and the family house where he lived. The story is told through a series of letters and notes left by your ancestor, and by your costly expeditions into the remains of your family estate. There is a beautiful, ironic echo throughout the entire game as you send wave after wave of hapless adventurers to their doom, all while reading about your ancestor's similar actions. There is a real sense of helplessness to your curiousity, and ancestoral destiny. You regret your actions. You're getting people killed. But, the next delve into the forrest may unearth the secret of why the villagers became fungal zombies. You HAVE to kill the possessed heap of discarded swine gore, but none of your heroes will do it.
Well, they'll do it. You just have to pay them more. Hopefully one or two will die. Their minds were slipping anyway. It's okay. The stagecoach is always bringing new adventurers to your estate.
If you like horror games, this is for you. If you like roguelikes, this is for you. If you like graphic novels, this is for you. If you want to see what kind of person you are; if you want to know how much of a monster your quest for answers will make you become, this is for you. Your ancestor's estate is waiting.

Darkest Dungeon is a 2D RPG dungeon crawler with a grim premise promising hardship and challenge to anyone who enters.
The good:
+Fantastic artstyle, narrator and music! The atmosphere of Darkest Dungeon is simply amazing.
+The characters the player can recruit are all different and have fun quips and personalities.
+Addictive dungeon crawling that will make you go for "just one more quest."
+The UI is elegant and superbly done.
+The devs have added options to remove/toggle corpses, nerf enemy crits and more small tweaks.
+Certain heroes now bring items with them when embarking, for example the crusader will bring holy water.
The bad:
-The difficulty isn't a curve, but a wall, a wall that has been known to be hit even in the tutorial. The game wants to be hard and that's a fine selling point. However, this is not elegant design like Dark Souls, but rather by arbitrarily stacking the odds against you.
-You have to juggle gold, experience points and resources for buildings in order to progress, which is fine in theory, but gold will quickly become the least of your worries as you grind away at resources and while doing that you have to avoid overleveling heroes as this makes it impossible for them to participate in missions they will then deem to easy, yes you read that right, your heroes will actually go against your orders.
-With a huge variety in heroes imbalance is sure to arise, but the issue is how obvious it is. For example, the plague doctor has been one of the weakest hero types throughout this entire Early Access, and they still are because they simply can't match the healing of the Vestal or the damage of the Arbalist.
-Most trinkets are useless. Almost all of them come with one or two bonuses, but also one or two negatives. A select few artifacts only have bonuses, but they usually aren't too great and they are hard to find.
-The quirk system is currently stacked against the player, just like everything else. Negative quirks can fester and become extremely expensive to get rid off. Positive quirks don't have this option, so sometimes after leveling you'll lose valuable quirks because your hero leveled up. Furthermore, diseases are now their own seperate thing, but they don't disappear over time and have to be removed as well, once again, it's just tedium for tedium's sake, because now you have to spend even longer on grinding them away too.
-Red Hook has so far with every update and without fail nerfed heroes and strategies into oblivion, which is fine, afterall the game should be balanced. However, they have crossed the line where it has now become mandatory to use a walkthrough on how to min-max. Gone are the days where 4 jesters could enter a dungeon and while they wouldn't be a great team they could pull through.
-After nearly 50 hours it has become clear to me that one of the biggest issues is the pacing. Upgrading your town takes way too many resources and you never gain the ability to hire heroes higher than level 0. You never truly lose, you're just doing the same thing over and over, always making the same heroes and dismissing them after they become too expensive to make viable.
Bottom line:
Darkest Dungeon has so much potential and back when I first bought it I was absolutely hooked by the atmosphere and surface gameply, but once you get deeper you realize just how poor the execution truly is. One misstep feels like it can ruin your entire game; forcing you to start over.
The game still has immense potential, but the goal of making a hard game has grown and taken over the core design and it's killing the experience. I vehemently hope that I can change this to a recommendation once the next promised update hits.

Darkest Dungeon is hard, mean, upsetting and unforgiving. If your heroes die, they are dead permanently. Therefore every mission is tense, every time you fear for your group and you have good reason to do so.
(I recommend to NOT play drunk! ;-))
Gameplay:
You have your town with some buildings where you can basically upgrade your heroes. For example you have the blacksmith to improve their armor and weapons or you send the heroes into the sanatorium to remove phobias and quirks they developed when they had to go fight the gruesome monsters. When your heroes are very stressed because of the horrors they saw in the Warrens or the Ruins they had to explore, you can send them to the abbey or the brothrel to make them unstressed again, Also you can hire new heroes here, buy and sell trinkets and so on. Of course, all of this costs money and money you only get when you send out your brave heroes.
Apart from money you need other stuff from down there, like deeds or busts which are used to upgrade the town buildings.
In the dungeon you have a group of four people which fight monsters in a turn based combat. It is important to learn which enemies have what effects on your party (some stress your people out, others simply attack and reduce your health, others debuff your heroes or weaken them by giving them deseases or make them bleed).
Is the health at zero, your hero is not dead but at death's door. This means every following hit has a certain chance to kill your hero. There are much more factors that are influencing the outcome of your mission like traps or how stressed your heroes become.
When your heroes are about to die, you can always abort the mission to save your heroes' life.
(Maybe that is what this game is about: To decide when to retreat and when to go on)
Positive:
- gloomy but beautiful 2D grafics
- sound, music and voice acting!
- interesting and tense turnbased combat (tense because dead heroes stay dead forever!)
- 14 different hero classes with individual strengths and weaknesses
- numerous trinkets to upgrade you character
- Positive and negative consequences for your heroes after missions (Quirks and deseases)
- interesting character and enemy design
- no sexist depiction of female characters
- you can individualise your heroes by naming them and giving them one out of four pre-made colour schemes
- Red Hook is a great developer, they react to emails quickly and include the gamers in the development of the game
Negative:
- sometimes unfair chain of events that end up killing your hero
- not enough different healing classes which results in similar team combinations
- Some boss battles still too easy which makes them feel unrewarding
- still some balancing to do for some hero classes that have useless skills

Spiral Knights turned a new leaf a year or two ago and it wasn't so much a moneysink, as of now you don't have mist energy, lifts are free, and crafting costs aren't ♥♥♥♥ing insane like they used to be. Everything is cute, so in contrast to other hack-n-slash games this is great if you're a squeamish person. I, personally am not and I prefer to have my enemies twitching with blood gushing out is a reward by itself. Combat is a bit slow, but incredibly fun, especially with a party because the game attempts to swarm you with enemies, and it's cool to personally smack each and every one of them with your sword, bomb or gun.
The thing that got on my nerves the most in this game are overspecialization of weapons. Each enemy does different types of damage, Elemental, Piercing, and shadow, and you can find yourself screwed if you show up to a level full of shadow damage dealing enemies with elemental Armour, and you're much more vulnerable. The weapon damage system is similar, enemies can either be very good at resisting a damage type or very weak to it; making weapons tremendously more situational and will cause you to grind more just so you can be the jack of all trades. The game as it is now has basically turned into Team Fortess 2 in the dress-up aspect except the game's content and enjoyment comes to a stop in a certain point because the development team doesn't feel like making actual new content and resorts to making Spiral Knights endgame a big dress up.
A good multiplayer hack-n-slash that's being held back by major flaws.

***TEXT ONLY REVIEW***
The games of the Souls Series are RPGs of their own kind. With an on-point combat system you fight through well-placed and unique enemies and as in every other RPG seek to become stronger. But unlike in most others of these games, in Dark Souls death is a firm part of the game. One you will very likely encounter soon enough. While you may think it would be off-putting for you to die and die repeatedly in the same boss-fight, you might very well be wrong. The game quickly captures you in its almost daring way to try once more every time you die. Especially for new players it can be a stony road, but the better you get to know certain enemies, their attacks and the timings you need to dodge them, the farther you will get. The satisfaction of finally being one step further after failing so many times is not only satisfying, it also teaches you that failure is the best part of your learning process.
But not only should you learn to know your enemies, but also yourself. After choosing one of many different starting classes, you can freely allocate stat points to any attributes you like, all of which give you different strenghts in combat and help you build the character you want to play.
Should the challenge of the game itself start to fade at some point you can always compete with other playes in PvP combat of different kinds.
And should the challenge of the game be too much, you can summon help from a friend or a kind stranger, to assist you in beating a certain boss or accompany you through an area.
Dark Souls III is the perfect closure for the whole of Dark Souls, especially with the Ringed City DLC and it is also a great entrance for new players to the series. While, in my opinion, not as difficult as Dark Souls 1, it really draws every last drop out of the combat system and design.
While Dark Souls really shines with its combat system, that's not the only thing it has to offer. Although you really have to search for the actual story, once you find it you will discover an unexpectedly deep lore, which stretches over centuries and not only gives you an impression of whom you are going against on your way, but also about the world in which you do it.
Should you consider getting Dark Souls III, I can tell you as much: It will not always be easy. In fact it will probably never be easy. But nevertheless it will be very fun.

I am proud to say that I've lost twice. I have had to reduce the difficulty level from what I'm used to playing in most games, inclucing Xcom: Enemy Unknown. This game is harder but so much fun! You may still see some reviews complaining about bugs and there may be a few but the recent hotfix has fixed so much for me. I used to see graphical bugs somewhat frequently but I haven't seen any since the patch. Additionally, performance has significantly improved on my machine. My framerate has been great and everything is just smooth and more amazing than ever.
Now that that's out of the way let's talk about the actual game.
I absolutely love this game. It feels like a badass intense board game between humans and aliens. There is always something interesting to do and there is a lot to balance between research, engineering, moving The Avanger, and killing aliens.
The procedurally generated battlefields are very well done. I always feel like I'm playing a new map and there is little repetition. I would love to see more variety in the locations in the future.
The combat is smooth (especially post hotfix) and engaging. Every bad decision could kill one of your favorite soldiers that you have worked so hard to rank up. Every good decision is so satisfying and nothing feels more accomplishing than finishing a mission with a screen that says "FLAWLESS" on it.
The story is full of heart and has it's share of twists and turns. It is very well written and makes you want the humans to succeed. I love that you are the underdogs in this game and constantly playing catchup. The enemy is always interesting and hard to read.
Dark Events - Oh Dark Events, how you constantly scare the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. These Dark Events suck to deal with. You don't ever want any of them to happen, but you can only stop one of them at a time.
Concealment - I love the concealment feature in Xcom 2. You can move your soldiers quickly into optimal locations for an ambush which, when executed correctly, are so satisfying to watch! Be careful though. Even bumping into a civilian will break concealment so never wander into an area where you don't have line of sight. You should always know where you are going and what is within sight before you move forward.
TLDR: This game is fun, intense, and exciting. The majority of the bugs and performance issues have been resolved with more patches on the way. The game has a good balance (when playing on an appropriate difficulty for you) of tragic losses, epic wins and close calls. Play this game. It is worth every penny. It is a game that I see myself playing years down the road.

Fallout 4 is a FPS with light RPG elements. Have you ever throught, "What would it look like if Bethesda played through New Vegas, and then decided to make FO4 a completely opposite experience?" This would pretty much be it. S.P.E.C.I.A.L attributes, skills, and perks have all been dumbed down into a much simpler system. V.A.T.S. changed from a tactical pause to bullet time. Conversations with NPCs now use the awful Mass Effect-styled radial menu (though I must admit not being locked in spacetime during dialog is a great change, and there are mods that bring back the classic dialog windows). Personally for me the worst part is the half-baked survival mode which clearly feels out of place in the game. Not even included at release, it's clear that the map, the quests, and various game merchanics are just not designed to mesh well with a survival-style difficulty mode.
Fallout 4 is very obviously a step back from the direction Obsidian took the franchise. When you play through this game, and you see what Bethesda is trying to do with VR, it's clear that whatever company Bethesda was before Skyrim no longer exists. Learn from my extensive mistakes, and avoid this game.

I never write reviews, because I cannot write. However, the people at Red Hook have created such a unique experience that I am compelled to voice my opinions on this truly once in a lifetime experience. Games like this come once in a blue moon. A blue, horrible, haunted moon.
Where do I even start?
Every moment in the Darkest Dungeon is perfectly crafted to force you to make hard decisions that not only affect you, but people you are responsible for. It's a roguelike, personnel management, dungeon crawler, graphic novel, horror game. That is a lot of Genres to try and nail, but Red Hook stuns that baby, pulls it to the front row, then lands a critical strike.
Do I kill that deadly enemy fighter to keep my delve into the ruins going? Or, do I kill that cultist priest who is about to force my healer to examine her life choices, possibly driving her mad, but maybe forcing her to finally overcome her fear of the undead and take a stand against evil? Then again, that stupid skeleton with the sword always seems to land critical strikes. Oh, wonderful. The gargolye just stunned my ranged fighter. I guess that limits my options.
The combat is so perfect in this game, I could write this whole review on it. But the best way to describe it is "stressful". The fights are turn based, with things like speed, health, damage, critical strikes, dots. The difference here is how significant every action is. Everything you do has consequences. Enemies are not fodder in this game. One group could wipe out your whole party. Attacks are animated like the action scenes of a graphic novel, with bold lunges and sweeping strikes animated beautifully. Combat never drags out, and actually stresses out your fighters. Every enemy attack carries weight and dangerous side effects. Picking apart the enemy party based on what monsters enhance others is a game in of itself. Careful management of your party is crucial to your success. Each of your fighters have different skills which supplement your other fighters. Maximizing your party efficiency is a game in of itself.
Then, there is the stress. Not just the game mechanic, but YOUR stress.
Getting too technical would ruin the magic of this masterfully implemented mechanic. You have to experience it to fully appriciate it. So I will keep it vague. The hardships you put your party through, forcing them to fight the undead, demon possessed swine corpses, and a canabalistic hag, cause them to act against your wishes, hurt themselves, or refuse to fight entirely. When your fighters become stressed they act without orders. They attack the wrong monsters. They touch the wrong things in the dangerous dungeon. In a game that hinges on every action being potentially dangerous and life threatening, this mechanic forces you to make hard choices.
What's really interesting is how this marriage of danger and fear management, and how your fighters respond to it, totally subvert the usual dungeon crawler tropes and expectations. Your party members are eager at first, to quote the game "foolishly seeking fame and fortune." However, if one fight goes bad, or someone gets sick from touching a dirty cart, the 'heroes' start to waver. They develop fears, strengths, and personalities. Sure, that healer was the lifeblood of your party in the warrens, but now we need to go into the cove, and she's afraid of fish monsters. That knight gets a bonus in damage against undead, but fighting undead stresses him out. Your backup healer is still passed out drunk in the bar after nearly dying to a rabid dog, and the your backup BACKUP healer doesn't have good enough armor to go on this quest, and you can't afford to upgrade him right now.
There are times when you have to send an unprepared party against a vastly superior enemy, hoping that they just survive, dragging enough treasure back to fund your failing expedition. There's a real sense of regret after some delves. You're always left feeling like you could have done more. You always feel like you just barely survived, not entirely sure at the human cost of your quest for knowledge.
And this is where the story comes into play.
The game's narrative is a flawlessly crafted love letter to Lovecraftian fiction and lore. If you are not familiar with Lovecraft, the primary theme being realized in this game is that humanity in general is fleeting and pointless, and that the sins of the father ALWAYS come back to haunt the children. You play the role of a nameless, faceless protagonist who is trying to find out what happened to one of his reletives, and the family house where he lived. The story is told through a series of letters and notes left by your ancestor, and by your costly expeditions into the remains of your family estate. There is a beautiful, ironic echo throughout the entire game as you send wave after wave of hapless adventurers to their doom, all while reading about your ancestor's similar actions. There is a real sense of helplessness to your curiousity, and ancestoral destiny. You regret your actions. You're getting people killed. But, the next delve into the forrest may unearth the secret of why the villagers became fungal zombies. You HAVE to kill the possessed heap of discarded swine gore, but none of your heroes will do it.
Well, they'll do it. You just have to pay them more. Hopefully one or two will die. Their minds were slipping anyway. It's okay. The stagecoach is always bringing new adventurers to your estate.
If you like horror games, this is for you. If you like roguelikes, this is for you. If you like graphic novels, this is for you. If you want to see what kind of person you are; if you want to know how much of a monster your quest for answers will make you become, this is for you. Your ancestor's estate is waiting.
Don't waste your time.

Dark Souls 3 is different than the original Dark Souls in that it sacrifices an interweaving world for a more centralized hub area similar to Demon Souls. The story isn't given to the player through cutscenes but instead snippets of NPC dialog, item descriptions and details found in the environments and enemy design. Its combat system is simple yet can be challenging and rewarding. All attacks go through 3 stages, the wind up frames, the action frames and the cool down frames. It's through managing these features of the attacks in combination with limited stamina consumption that create the unique and fun combat that is now a staple of FromSoftware games. Dark Souls 3 adds to this combat system through something known as weapon arts which help diversify the combat further and add more rewarding combat capabilities to those who can take full advantage of the weapon arts. I truly recommend this game for all who can afford the time to play it but beware, after completing the Dark Souls franchise it may leave a void in you that may never be filled by any other game. Good luck and have fun.

This game barely - BARELY - gets a recommendation from me. I like this game. I want to like it a lot. Here's why I don't.
For starters, you should know - if it isn't already obvious to you - that this game prides itself on being extremely difficult. If that's not for you, don't buy it. Just don't. Save yourself some stress and blood pressure, because this game isn't just extremely difficult, it's freaking sadistic. And when I say sadistic, I don't mean in the, "Oh, wow! That was so challenging! I feel so accomplished after completing that!" kind of way. I mean in the, "Are you F*CKING kidding me?!" kind of way.
This game is like X-COM if X-COM was a 2D sidescroller set in a fantasy worl that was inspired by - sorry - ripped wholesale out of the mythos of H.P. Lovecraft. This game has everything that X-COM fans love - the challenge, the overwhelming odds, the permadeath, the tactics - but very little of its finesse. Where X-COM knows exactly how much butt f*ckery to inflict upon your person, this game gives not one single sh*t about whether you stroke out in your chair. I'll 'splain.
This game has an intricate tactics system based around positioning: you have four positions available in your party, and the likewise the enemies you fight have a potential maximum of four positions to occupy. This is important, because most skills can only hit certain positions FROM certain positions - e.g. Skill X can only be used from position 1-2 on enemy position 3-4, etc. Great. Cool. Sounds good. Sounds like it'll make me think, and force me to actually use my brain instead of following the shiny trail of bread crumbs to the finish line like so many modern games.
And it does. Except it only does that half the time, and it spends the other half of the time mercilessly destroying everything you've worked so hard to achieve. You'll start off a dungeon - a level ONE dungeon - by walking into a hallway battle in which your party is magically "surprised" - meaning they get totally shuffled around, and f*ck you very much, now two of your guys are dead or close to it on Round 2. Why? Because half of your party can no longer use their skills, and the other half are forced to used non-combat skills or skills that add debuffs, but do no damage. Meanwhile, your melee only character gets force all the way to the back of your party and can only move toward the front one space at a time. Wait, what? Why can my ranged characters move two spaces, but the people who absolutely cannot be where they now can only shuffle like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ zombies back toward the fight? Why are 90% of the enemies in this game faster than 90% of my party members, allowing them to b*tch-slap my guys to death before they can even reposition? Why does every strike do a quarter to a half of each of my characters' health bar in damage in ADDITION to filling up a quarter of the stress bar?
I get it - I get that the game is supposed to be difficult. I get that characters are going to die, and that's unavoidable. Fine. Whatever. Do your thing. I played through X-COM a bazillion times and lost tons of guys and got over it. But this? Losing people to the stupidest sh*t possible at the beginning of a dungeon? Ridiculous. And again, this doesn't happen all the time - but it happens enough that it makes me want to stop playing, which is really a damned shame because when this game works, it works really well. Playing a fight out just right so that you're able to feel like you've actually accomplished something is a wonderful feeling. Getting buttf*cked in a dungeon's first hallway by a group of regular goons is absolutely, positively not.
But enough about the bad - let's talk about the good and the meh. I already touched on combat, so I won't get too into that here except to say that when it works, it's awesome. Many of the characters have a really cool synergy with each other, and if you're able to figure it out it's a very rewarding system. The skillsets are many and varied, and very few of them are what I'd call useless. There are a few duds, but not many.
The art, which has been touched on by many people, is indeed beautiful in a very dark and terrible kind of way. I tend not to play indie games too much because they're often very ugly, and aesthetics is a big deal to me. I haven't played Undertale despite the urging of many of my friends simply because I can't get past the sh*tty 2D pixel graphics, and I know that that's a silly, petty outlook to have, but I can't change what I like. So when a hand-drawn 2D sidescroller manages to keep my attention, it should give you some idea as to the quality of the art.
The music, which to my ear seems to be comprised of about three tracks played on loop, gets the job done. That's it. It's dark and dreary and depressing, and it does an outstanding job of making lending the game a feeling of hopelessness (especially when coupled with the aforementioned butt*fckery). Other than that it's unremarkable and not tremendously memorable.
The story - or what story there is at the time of this review - is interesting when it shows up, but nothing groundbreaking. I'm looking forward to this game getting out of Early Access so that we can get the whole product. Stories about C'thulhu and madness are always fun, and this one is no different.
The rest of the gameplay - meaning when you're back at base and not dungeon crawling or massacreing monsters/getting your a*s kicked - is passable, but nothing terribly special. You can spend resources - which are often ridiculously few and far between, with no really reliable way of collecting more - to upgrade your hamlet (the town that acts as your base of operations) and, subsequently, your characters. This is a long, painful, and sigh-inducing process as you constantly end each dungeon crawl with only a handful of the resources your need.
The characters themselves are, perhaps, my favorite part of the game. There are a total of fourteen different classes (currently, though I think more are incoming) and they are all distinct. Of particular note in my opinion are the Aboimination, the Hound Master, and the Jester. The Abomination is the most different from the others, and is effectively two classes in one. Unlike the others, it starts out with every possible skill in its set unlocked and ready to go; it starts in human form - which acts sort of like a caster - and can turn into a werebeasty thing that functions as a tank with mega DPS. The trade-off for such a powerful unit is that it can't be in a party with holy characters, and every time it turns into a beast it induces stress in your other party members (ran out of room to talk about stress - sorry). The stress thing is a little silly mainly because it also induces stress in other Abominations (wat).
The Hound Master - my personal favorite - is a guy and a dog. In addition to having a cool character model - and a dog - it acts as a backline sniper that can also make the entire enemy team take bleed damage (a DoT effect). It cures stress, can do an incredible amount of damage, and can mark targets for your team so that the rest of your guys can hit harder. All around very solid, very reliable, and very fun. The last guy, the Jester, is a stand-out character mainly because he's...well, kind of weird. He's a pretty standard glass cannon, but his most interesting feature is that he has a couple of moves that make him move forward or backward in your hero lineup. Neat, and they are often very useful, but the fun peters out a bit when you realize that your hero lineup is often a finely-tuned thing that can't stand a whole lot of d*ckery. For that reason, a hero that is insanely fun and highly effective no matter where he is in your lineup gets relegated to "meh" status because he can really only fit in a couple of hero lineups without screwing up the works. Maybe I just haven't figured out how to use him yet. *Shrug'
All in all a good, but not perfect, game.

For being an early release, I think it's safe to say this game is definetly worth the money. There are some minor mechanics and aspects that have yet to be added, but the current state of the game is very fun. Yes, it is similar to terraria, but it expands upon this survival crafting genre. Space exploration, mining, and boss battles are extremely satisfying and totally enjoyable. I've only played solo, but the co-op is just an improvement of the solo game. Teaming up to take on a boss or gather materials is as fun as it is in terraria or minecraft (just to give a comparisson, not that it's the same). In it's early state, there are character wipes and the occasional bug, but the game is still solid. If you see it as an early look of things to come, this game has tons of potential. For the money, it is absolutely worth it. I regret not one second of the near 30 hours I poured into this game, and I highly suggest you buy it now.

I will preface this with saying that I bloody love Fallout 4. Its a hoot and a holler and a joy forever, but there are, of course, things I really hate about it. Anyway, here's my awkward♥♥♥♥♥having a swing at a review.
Fallout 4, its a brilliant game just not the best "Fallout" game. If you're a veteran of the series from 1 up to New Vegas and are expecting a purebred, wholesomely "Fallout" experiance; I'd say this might not be for you.
The writing is there, the charm is there the gameplay is there but Fallout 4 leaves so much to be desired when compaired to the other games in this series! The elements just dont fit together like the other games. At times the gameplay feels amazing but the experiance feels dry, cold and the writing is horrible then out of the blue a mission appears with striking charaters being downright funny in classic fallout absurditiy, but the AI bugs out and leaves everyone standing around like they've all forgotten they're supposed to be killing one another and you get taken right out of the immersion.
It doesnt have that clumsy, yet welcoming feeling of adventure until around 20 hours or so into the main game, sure you CAN run about causing havok at level one but the missions hold you by the hand so badly at first. I wont say any spoilers here but when you first use power armor, by god its the worst shoehorning I've ever take a part of! It doesnt feel nautral, it doesnt feel..Fallout you know? (Okay, I lied a little, the game CAN be clucky and janky as balls on occasion but its pretty well optimised so when it does happen it aint a big deal. Adds to the charm I suppose.)
In Fallout 3 you worked your face off to get to the level of wasteland debauchery and hijinx where you can finally use power armour, its also in a perfect part of the storyline and makes you feel like &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥yes! I've earned this godly ability to be a damn mech!". Fallout 4 hasnt got that. Fallout 4 holds your hand as you recieve the most overpowered item in the the fallout lore then makes sure you have your lunch before sending you off into the padded schoolyard that is the minutemen missions.
Look, this game has divided fans across the board. Yes it's probably the weakest one in the series because it sticks out like a sore thumb but remember, mistakes make progress and if the devs take the core of Fo4 and fix everything thats wrong, praise be to atom.
I love it, I cant stop playing it despite all its flaws. Grab a copy and give it some time, once you get into it it eats up days like they're sweetrolls and the robot ruined the cake. In that regard, it is, to me, a bloody great experiance.
For a more well arctulated review that isnt the scrawlings of a lunatic, check out Lazy Game Review's video on Fallout 4. Clint sums it up perfectly and if you're undecided now, he'll set you straight.

Darkest Dungeon is a good game and I can recommend it after a few hours of playthrough.
However, I should mention that it isn't necessarily a "fun" game.  When I say that, I mean its not a game you should play when you're tired or stressed out; it's a game that is interesting because it utilizes a stress mechanic for both the characters and the player themselves.
If you're going to go into this and treat it as a typical hack & slash roguelike, you're going to be disappointed.  The purpose of this game isn't to dominate, its to scrap by by whatever means necessary.
You can either play it on the tips of your toes or you can take the safer route and grind out the lower levels a bit.
The game does, imo, lack some variety, but I imagine the developers are working on this.
Don't get me wrong, this is a very good game.  Well polished, great sound, great visuals.  The gameplay mechanic does what the developer wants it to do and if you want to embrace that, go for it.

Written the 1st Jan 2016 - First time reviewing a game, in response to unfair negative reviews.
Don't look at my little hours played, I've played a lot of the game in a cracked version before buying it (because it is worth it).
The game is meant to be hard.
But the game is good, and addicting.
Here's my rating :
10/10 would die again to progress.
For more details about my review :
The game is about you trying to patch up the errors of a Lord (you are one of his relative) who entirely f*cked up his domain when he investigated some dark magic (called here "eldritch").
For that, you recruit some ppl (in a team of 4 ppl) to fight the eldritch horrors off the domain.
You may lose characters, have bad RNG, but that's part of the game.
It's called CHALLENGE.
The thrill comes from you overcoming those problems.
I lost many Lv 5/6 squads trying to fight bosses or exploring the game, so what ? I got new ones. And I built them considering the "current flow" and what works the best.
If you go by "hmm yeah I'll go with the same kind of party as usual because I'm used to it, even if I can see that my style of fighting isn't good anymore to progress" you'll get frustrated.
You're allowed to care for the characters, heck that's what your supposed to do if you want to be at the best condition to SURVIVE.
That was my review.
Because the negative reviews were unfair : they didn't even look in the options to see that they could disable the things they disliked in the game.
But hey, only peasants go for an easier experience than the original proposed by the game developper, right ?

A voxelcrafting mmorpg.
As far as FTP games go this is in my opinion one of the best.
Cons
*Personal chest space cost real money to expand, this in the end doesnt matter club world chests can be used as more storage.
*Qeue times, Not to much of an issue for me with priority log in after waiting out a qeue. This im sure wont be a issue for long.
Pros
*Its a voxelcrafting game so a comparison can be made to minecraft, get blocks build stuff and get crafting materials around the world by exploring different biomes.
*its also an MMORPG, Explore the world, in the case of this game the randomized biomes. Find people to play with or play solo. Trade items with other players, buy and sell.
*Progression, something that a lot of ftp mmorpg dont have is a rewarding leveling system, Trove rewards you left and right with the mastery system, From cubits that can be used in the games store to stats that apply to all your classes.
* Crafting, The crafting system is simple but thats why i like it. The crafting benches tell you what to you need to craft the item.
*The future, Trove has become so big since it went up on steam the servers couldnt handle it and weve been having 30 minute log in qeues while they try to fix the issue. This in my opinion is a good sign that this game has a future. After its all fixed i hope to see more content added to trove.
Some things id like to see in troves future.
*PVP something like an arena, CTF, Capture point, the basics are all we need really but something new and creative would be even better.
*A pretty HUB world, as it is its plain and with all the blocks in the game it can be re done no problem.
*Class progression routes, The game as it is is fairly simple with 4 abilitys including your normal attacks and i really like that. Id like to see the option to pick from a pool of abilitys rather than just unlocking them makeing the game more in depth while keeping it simple at the same time.

Also you apparently can't hit wrong enemies by accident. Corpse reanimation via psi powers is an instant action and seemingly requires noi 'maintenance' by the the one doing the resurrection. Also all reinforcement actions are poorly 'translated' into turn based environments. At times when you look all the things that happen you can safely say your team is having a nap while the enemies do strange chains of actions.
So in essence this game pretty much has all the flaws I expected it to have and for now I haven't seen that many improvements over the last version. There are some small tweaks in functionality but for now I have completed only a couple of missions so there are still plenty of things to discover.
Is the game currently worth the full price? No, not really. I suppose some issues may get an official fix and mods will probably fix some others so this game has a fair potential. Even as it is the game seems to be reasonably enjoyable but the actual game mechanics seem to be on par with the most simple board games ever created.
Edit: Started out with a recommendation but now that I have played more the game just feels so unbelievably scripted. Ammo clips also don't last very long as these 'soldiers' spray and pray all the time. There are no single shots for most weapons, meaning that even your more senior officers will act like total rookies to the end of time. Also movement rate for everything is far too great compared with the other things you can do. Also firing a weapon ends the turn for that soldier. You can run before moving if you like but you can't do it the other way around. This game getting over 90 points is just ridiculous and 80 would be a far more accurate.

Fallout 4 is a FPS with light RPG elements. Have you ever throught, "What would it look like if Bethesda played through New Vegas, and then decided to make FO4 a completely opposite experience?" This would pretty much be it. S.P.E.C.I.A.L attributes, skills, and perks have all been dumbed down into a much simpler system. V.A.T.S. changed from a tactical pause to bullet time. Conversations with NPCs now use the awful Mass Effect-styled radial menu (though I must admit not being locked in spacetime during dialog is a great change, and there are mods that bring back the classic dialog windows). Personally for me the worst part is the half-baked survival mode which clearly feels out of place in the game. Not even included at release, it's clear that the map, the quests, and various game merchanics are just not designed to mesh well with a survival-style difficulty mode.
Fallout 4 is very obviously a step back from the direction Obsidian took the franchise. When you play through this game, and you see what Bethesda is trying to do with VR, it's clear that whatever company Bethesda was before Skyrim no longer exists. Learn from my extensive mistakes, and avoid this game.

Absolutely fantastic. One of the best games I've ever played, with phenominal atmosphere and intense gameplay. It's rough, for sure, and a bad turn of luck can ruin a run, but the game is surprisingly forgiving once you learn when to bail and how to adapt. The blend of Rougelike and RPG elements often leaves the RNG a pivotal factor, but hardly one that can't usually be subdued by decent strategy and preparation, and even my harshest losses were always brought about by hubris rather than poor luck.
I'd also like to clarify and state that I'm not a 'hardcore' gamer. I'm no masochistic challenge-junkie who thrives on adversity or anything. I'm honestly pretty bad at most games, I'm just persistant and know to learn from my defeats. Did this game tear me a new one for the first while? Absolutely. Did I find myself ragequitting when my favourite hero died? You bet. Did I grumble and whine when a good string of luck turned sour? Of course I did, but did it ever turn me off from the game? Not for more than a few days, then I was right back in it, all the more prepared for the next time things started getting rough.
I've been playing this game for nearly a year, and have seen the game continuously improve, with the devs actively playing off community feedback. Even when an update introduces some new mechanic that unbalances things, they're patched pretty readily within a few days to restore order. I would recommend this game in a heartbeat to anyone interested.

I haven't played DD since the Corpses and Hound update. After almost 6 months, I have to say that DD is a completely different game compared to what it was.
One thing I really appreciate is that now the game forces you to plan ahead what your strategy will be (skill combos, provisions, monsters weaknesses) before entering a Dungeon. This means the game is harder (yes!) but also more interesting and less repetitive (just destroying everything with aoe damage is not that fun, at least for me). Corpse’s mechanics have been tuned and are now less annoying (actually they can help you in some situations). Also the new class, the Abomination, is pretty nice and has some interesting mechanics. In the other hand, I understand those who find it frustrating and hard. I think that the solution is to add an easy, mid, hard mode and let the players choose.
To sum up, I think DD is a great game, better than it was before, and worth its price. Can't wait for the final release!

So, lets get the obvious "lol servers suck 30 minute queue this is lame." MMO's almost always have a generally shaky startup. Out of the 13 hours I've played, I was in a queue for 6 at least. So sure, it's lame you have to wait. But let's cut to the chase:
I've played many an MMO like this, and some I've very much enjoyed. My main problem with this game is summed up in one question: WHY am I doing what I'm doing?
Trove drops you into a world with extremeley little context and a severe lack of understanding of what all there is to do. In the first hour, I was asking "Where are these obsidian guys coming from? Is there a greater evil antagonist I don't know about? What is a club? What are these non-weapon items used for? Is this NPC in the main Hub the only trader in the game?"
At the end of the day, Trove's only entertaining activity - and I use "entertaining" in the relative sense that it's more entertaining than, say, watching paint dry - is grinding for better equipment, so that it becomes easier to grind more for even better equipment, and so on, for hours, to the point where I imagine the best player in the game finally says, "Yay! I've obtained the best armor and weapons in the game... what now?"
I can tolerate bugs and glitchy fighting in games, I can tolerate queue lines, and I can tolerate weak story line - not that Trove is guilty of all these, just saying in general. But a lack of purpose or any actual obtainable goal leaves me feeling empty and unsatisfied.
But the developers may be adding new content soon, so maybe it will be a little more organized and we can actually grasp some understanding of our role in the game. I'll keep an eye on this title; to say the least its visually stimulating. And it made for a few good laughs while playing friends.
But until then: 3/10, uninstalled and probably will never play again.

I got this game after briefly watching the folks over on Vinesauce play it. I was enchanted by the art style and the narration almost immediately, and the feeling of enchantment quickly turned into full-on romance.
This game is hard. Harder than anything else I've played in years. And I wouldn't want it any other way. Every time I complete a mission there's a feeling of elation, of  magnificent accomplishment. I wish I could award the poor little sods who delve these depths for me medals.
If you, like me, have an easy time getting attached to units in games just becuase they landed that crucial critical hit, or because they managed to survive that gutwrenching blow, this will be a heartbreaking experience for you.
You get to watch these little people snap. At each other, at the enemies, at themselves, at shadows. They are all doomed, in a wonderful way, and the heartbreak is perfect.
If you like turn based games, if you like psychologically-tinted attacks and effects, if you like vaguely cthonian monstrosities and dimly lit corridors painstakingly decorated in ruin, You should immediately get Darkest Dungeon.

Darkest Dungeon is a good game and I can recommend it after a few hours of playthrough.
However, I should mention that it isn't necessarily a "fun" game.  When I say that, I mean its not a game you should play when you're tired or stressed out; it's a game that is interesting because it utilizes a stress mechanic for both the characters and the player themselves.
If you're going to go into this and treat it as a typical hack & slash roguelike, you're going to be disappointed.  The purpose of this game isn't to dominate, its to scrap by by whatever means necessary.
You can either play it on the tips of your toes or you can take the safer route and grind out the lower levels a bit.
The game does, imo, lack some variety, but I imagine the developers are working on this.
Don't get me wrong, this is a very good game.  Well polished, great sound, great visuals.  The gameplay mechanic does what the developer wants it to do and if you want to embrace that, go for it.

Don't look at my little hours played, I've played a lot of the game in a cracked version before buying it (because it is worth it).
The game is meant to be hard.
But the game is good, and addicting.
Here's my rating :
10/10 would die again to progress.
For more details about my review :
The game is about you trying to patch up the errors of a Lord (you are one of his relative) who entirely f*cked up his domain when he investigated some dark magic (called here "eldritch").
For that, you recruit some ppl (in a team of 4 ppl) to fight the eldritch horrors off the domain.
You may lose characters, have bad RNG, but that's part of the game.
It's called CHALLENGE.
The thrill comes from you overcoming those problems.
I lost many Lv 5/6 squads trying to fight bosses or exploring the game, so what ? I got new ones. And I built them considering the "current flow" and what works the best.
If you go by "hmm yeah I'll go with the same kind of party as usual because I'm used to it, even if I can see that my style of fighting isn't good anymore to progress" you'll get frustrated.
You're allowed to care for the characters, heck that's what your supposed to do if you want to be at the best condition to SURVIVE.
That was my review.
Because the negative reviews were unfair : they didn't even look in the options to see that they could disable the things they disliked in the game.
But hey, only peasants go for an easier experience than the original proposed by the game developper, right ?

>Start game
>Get in queue with 1000+ people

>Get in game
>Play for a little while
>Go to a different world or back to the Hub

>Start game

I am a die-hard fan of Fallout games. I am so much of a fan that I was already Level 64 when the first Fallout game came out in 1997.
When the franchise virtually collapsed after Fallout: Tactics I missed it so much that I placed empty re-badged Nuka Cola bottles and BOS armor pieces all around the country, just to make it more wasteland-ish. I knew it was a long process but someone had to do something.
Then, when the franchise resurrected a couple of years later I was so happy that I did not care that Fallout3 was Elder Scrolls: Oblivion with VATS. I did not know what to suspect anyway. So, I was happy.
By the time I got bored after spending 6581 hours in the GOTY version of Fallout3, Bethesda gave the engine to Obsidian for a facelift. New Vegas stole an another 8580 hours off my lifetime. I was still happy.
I also played Skyrim that was developed from New Vegas with a weaker storyline and no VATS. I imagined that the dragons are vertibirds, the trolls are supermutants and ebony bows are anti-matter guns. I spent 38911 hours there dreaming that I play Fallout: Primal. I was moderately happy.
It was a long enough wait to create a list of my realistic expectations of Fallout 4:
- game free of charge for me as I already own Morrowind GOTY, Oblivion GOTY, New Vegas Ultimate and Skyrim Legendary. Some discount, at least.
- after installation, the developer renting two callgirls who are working on my jackhammer during gameplay, one of them a ghoul with a dosen of extra holes
- movie graphics, 320256 x 201064 yottaHD resolution with 2000 FPS
- cure for both cancer and hypergamy
- world peace
- no bugs
- infinite real life
- after game freezes and framedrops, $1000 appearing with "we so madly, deeply sorry, we send the ghoul girls again for free" notes on my bank account
- stopping of global warming
- eternal summer weather, around my place
- instant nag breaker app for the wife
- a 500 BHP sportscar shipped by the developer after me finishing the main story line
What happened? Fallout 4 implemented NONE of these!!!
I am so deeply peased off. I am so seriously disappointed! Now that I had a plan of what I expect, it became such a bad game without satisfying my personal expectations. I was sure that they incude at least some of these. Is it so much? It is not! Damn it's 2015! Developers should have known my expectations, that's why they are the developers, and they failed so miserably!
Even Donald Trump lost the election!
That's all the developers' fault! Fawck you developers, you completely forgot how to make me happy! I'll never buy an another game from any developer until y'all go fawckin' bankrupt and can make no games until I'll have nothing to play with! That time you will realise that you were wrong and you should have consider that you satisfy the personal expectations of every player and make everyone happy! This is my opinion and my opinion is the truth!
***
The bottom line: Matter of fact, I enjoyed this game despite that it can be a bug and freezefest at times (just like the predecessors). I had been completely happy already if Bethesda guys just grabbed the Skyrim engine, added VATS and a new wasteland storyline. Instead, Fallout 4 took a bold move to expand its own boundaries that I personally appreciate. Sure it failed here and there but it still has a great wins vs failures ratio and it's not nearly as a bad game as many folks suggest. So what? It is not perfect. Neither you are, nor the previous Fallout RPGs were. Do you remember the instability of Fallout 1, the car save bug that totally trashed your progress in Fallout 2, the compatibility issues of Fallout 3 or the bugfest of New Vegas? I do. None were perfect but all of them worked. Just like this latest 4th episode. Nothing changed there really. The general public arrogance did.
Everyone seems to hate something. I hate deceiving reviews that suggests a distorted picture of the reality, be that overly positive or negative.
The game: is just a game. An imperfect balance of numerous elements of high complexity. Time and effort, a lot of trials and errors, some effort of evolution and development, much effort to aim the product to certain audience. Also, of course, there are business decisions. No one makes AAA+++ games for candies and compliments. They are products just like your paper towels and condoms.
The gamer: is just a gamer. An imperfect balance of habits and sometimes unrealistically high expectations and distorted subjective perception of the reality that everyone believes that his opinion is that close to objective truth that it's a fact.
The reviews: public projections of the unbalanced, misguided subjective perception above. There are four main categories of them:
- positive neutral /the "playboy"/: reviewers who are not overwhelmed with the game but enjoyed that after all
- negative neutral /the "beta tester"/: they tend to point out the weaker points of the game without making it personal
- positive affected /the "fanboy"/: almost as useless review as of the one below as there is some serious distortion of facts in here
- negative affected /the "hater"/: no matters what, they grab the opportunity to be personally offended and will find a way to hate the subject and destroy their own fun and try to picture their opinion as objective truth.
So, none of these will give you the info you need. It is all useless bullsheet. The reviews, the voting, all the damn hubble-bubble. So, now that I'm writing a review, I admit that aside some fun while making, it is completely pointless. Go caress pvssies instead.
Games are like pvssies. Wether they are furry, purring, fuzzy or juicy, if 100 guys caress the very same pvssy, it will be a completely different personal experience for all of them.
And please don't give a fawck on what anyone tells you. Including me.

So this game is interesting, there are a few areas that need a little work but at the same time its incredibly addictive (at least for me).
Pros:
-Very tough gameplay on the same level as dark souls and such. The harsh gameplay and game mechanics can be very similar to the souls series. Where the difficulty of the game has successes feel very satisfying.
-Ambience: This game does the setting and general dark fantasy feel very nicely. The narrator is excellent, the artwork and fiction is very nicely set up. There are touches of a few different mythos sprinkled around and it really does feel like a gothic horror environment which i love.
-Town set up: the idea of slowing re-building and upgrading your hamlet is really cool and has me wanting to play just to get those building to look nice again. Knowing that investment now will pay off later making your life much easier as a whole.
-Characters: the different characters in the game are rather nice. With each class representing nifty little D&D tropes that work well in the game environmen. It does feel like you are a guy who just kinda points at 4 people in a little hellhole town and says "were ganna go kill some stuff and see what we find, cmon." it appeals to the city/people manager in me.
Cons:
-Some of the characters aren't quite balanced correctly it seems with some of the others. I feel like the jester for instance just doesnt have the same utility and strength as some of the other classes. Also the abomination, whose general design i love, feels a little too strong in places.
-Some of the items need some better balancing, there are some that feel like "why should i ever NOT have this equipped?!?" while others seem...lackluster.
-Some of the mechanics need to be tweaked and balanced a little bit more, the cove for instance would drive me up the wall and seemed harder than the others. The warrens could also be rediculous with disease and suddenly you get back to town and wonder if its worth curing all of them or just replacing the toon (recruiting new people is free btw).
-New mechanics with bosses (not having any clues regarding how the fights work) and having toon death also forfeit the trinkets they carry. In the souls series the deaths, while frustrating, arent debilitating because you dont loose anything usually you cant get back by grinding. Loosing some of your best trinkets because you didnt know how a fight works and something two shots a toon because you dont know? just feels incredibly harsh and will turn people off.
Closing statement:
I like the game, even with its current flaws. But i have suggestions for the developers:
1. Give more fluff for some of the background people. I would love to hear about who the caretaker is and why hes there (i might just be missing something but i havent seen it), who is the innkeeper, priest, nurse, blacksmith and guildmasters? there are people in the hamlet now and honestly i dont know why they are there except for you being there. Even just a biography blurb somewhere would be nice. Its worldbuilding and fleshes out the peripheral aspects of your environment just a bit better. Even better, have the ability for them to comment on things. Like the caretaker, your heroes, the bosses you slay, ect.
2. Balance out some of the classes a bit more. Some of them feel more relevant than others which is unfortunate.
3. Balance out some of the trinkets, same as 2 really but since the game is still early release i suppose this is to be expected that more work is required.
4. Put some ability to acquire information about monsters/bosses in the game. Have a pickup or something (writing on a wall/ bookshelf/ tree carvings ect) that allows you to flesh out monster profiles that a scribe in town would compile for you. Like a librarian who looks over his glasses at you as if hes saying " Now what? WTF did you run into this time?!?" You could even have a bonus being concept art or other game art get added to the profiles as they get more complete. Once again worldbuilding.
5. Have a tutorial for the retreat mechanic, Its pretty important early on when you get in over your head and need to cut your losses but the game only gives you a text prompt/explanation regarding it.
Anyway My $.02. Its worth the money in my opinion if you like a challenge and are mildly masochistic in your gaming.

I too, was reluctant to purchase this game because of a number of rather vocal negative reviews. When it went on sale, I decided to chance it. Well, to make a long story short, I think this is a really good solid game and add to that, the developers keep working on it to make it better. Just make sure you read all the reviews, not just the negative ones so that you get a good idea of what you are looking at.
The game is not easy, nor is it disappointingly hard. You will lose adventurers and get your butt kicked, however you will do a fair share of kicking the bad guys butts as well. A big problem for a large number of people is that the game can not be saved manually, which disallows the ability to restart again and again until you get the outcome you wished for, but that is also one of the things that make this game fun. You need to live with your choices and weather the loss of your beloved adventurers who succumb to the monsters of the catacombs.  I have had no crashes, no apparent bugs and the game runs smoothly. Managing your team and building your small army of dungeon adventurers is only half the fun, the other half is seeing a well planned and coordinated dungeon quest succeed. And while losing your best team to a boss can be maddening and frustrating, it only makes the immersion deeper.
Pros:
-Great Artwork
-Good Narration
-Cool Animations
-Managing, Equipping and Guiding your team
-Fun stuff like: potions, magic items, traps and treasure (all the requisite stuff for a dungeon adventure)
-Character Development (leveling them up, picking new or improving abilities and weapons)
-Pretty much bug free (I haven't seen any yet...(50+ hours)
-Appropriate music scores
-Actually has a backstory
-Developers are working hard
-You can step away from the game if you have to (turn based)
Cons:
-Still Early Access (looking forward to the complete product)
-Whining on the forums because some purchasers didn't get everything wanted (too hard, too easy, unbalanced, etc...)
-Makes you play for longer than you realize (you look at the clock and find out it is 2am, darn, I gotta go to work in 5 hours)
-Doesn't have the esperanto language option.....:)
Anyway, I am very happy with my purchase and at 50+ hours have gotten more than my money's worth. If you don't like games that make you live with your choices or might kill off your favorite character because it makes you cry, then this isn't for you. But if you like an exciting dungeon delving game with elements of party management and careful recruitment choices, by all means get it.
Remember, read more than just the unhappy reviews.
