This game is awesome!
DD is a difficult game.  It is not like most RPGs where your heroes wade through hordes of monsters, chug a couple of potions, and keep on smiting.  It's designed to be a struggle where your heroes are pushed to their physical and emotional boundaries and frequently don't survive the test.  If you enjoy the challenge, however, the wide variety of classes and skills make for a really enjoyable range of tactical possibilities which need to be tailored to match the dungeon and your specific party composition.  Not to mention that the art is fantastic which makes watching your heroes descend into madness (or syphilis) very enjoyable.
A note on recent surge of negative reviews:  these started to appear after Red Hook made some changes to up the difficulty of higher level dungeons and to mix up the meta.  Up to that point, the best way to approach dungeons was to just stack damage and crit and go around one-shotting everything.  Patches made this approach less viable and some people didn't try and adapt to the new changes (using armor-ignoring damage over time or corpse removal skills).  I believe a lot of the frustration with old strategies not working fueled these negative reviews.
:  This tactical RPG game is really great if you're okay with the fact that it does not pull punches.  You really need to pay attention to what your heroes can do and what they're up against to succeed.  The feeling of success when you pull your ragged squad through almost impossible odds is what it's all about.

First off. Saying Fallout 4 is a
improvement to the previous Fallout games would be a huge understatement. VATS aren't the only way to kill people any longer! Scavenging and looting is way more seamless and quick, gunplay is playable now, and overall navigation of the variouse UIs and HUDs is a great improvement aswell.  And the exploration part of this game is probably the best I've ever seen in a game recently. They've remapped lots of keys to better places. That said, the combat isn't really to special. Sure, it's playable now, but it's not very exciting and it also falls very short on any type of strategy that isn't just going in guns blazing. Movement can feel kind of clunky at times, especially when in power armor. And the exploration part of this game is probably the best I've ever seen in a game recently. Although if that's what you're going for, it'll be a blast.
The story is very interesting at first, but after you reach Diamond City, around an two or three hours in, it just feels like a drag. You're just following other people the entire time and being told the whole story instead of really being a part of it. You're not really given a choice to be a villain, it's just what you think is the best moral choice. There isn't any option to be a raider or bad guy until Nuka-World, which you have to pay extra for. There are countless plotholes throughout, and especially with the institute. Unlike other Fallout games and various RPGs, you cant ask too many questions about the situation and the story is very linear up until you have to make 3 different choices on whole dont
wanna blow up. You can't find a way to keep peace, you cant kill everyone, and going against the Minutemen isn't even a choice. It reaqlly doesn't let you create your own story, and you can see it from the beginning. Early on you find out about your backstory, your character has already lived years of their life in a normal society. They can have a different personality than you may want to give them. And that's an issue.
While the graphics arent on Witcher level and the performance isnt on Counter-Strike level, the game actually runs fine for a AAA title and looks better than it needs to be. It doesnt constantly crash and have a landfill of bugs, and thats very pleasing to hear from a Bethesda title. In fact outside of heavily modded plkaythroughs, I had not one crash and only one corrupted save file. People also complained bout the graphics not looking real, THEY DONT NEED TO BE! They look sharp and are actually colorful. The landscaped are great and have stories behind them, while that starts to lack towards the endgame areas, it still holds true.
Any RPG elemts in this game are pretty much nonexistent. Just like I said in the paragraph above, you can't make your character the way you want to from scratch. In New Vegas, I could be a superhero, a cowbay, a supervillain, a loner, or a ladykiller, and unlimited other personalities. In Fallout 4, if you're a dude, you're a soldier that looks for his son, if you're a women, you're a lawyer who can somehow become a mega soldier thats looking for her son. Lots of personalities don't fit. What evil maniac spends his time in a lawless wasteland looking for their baby the whole time? There arent many consiquences if you kill a person essential to the story, or in other cases, you flat out cant kill them. Yeah sure, their faction might hate you, but killing an entire army alone has no affect on anyone else. You can't maker your own conversations or relationships with people. Everything is pre determined. Leveling is so simple now. Just chose one perk and you're finished. No other skill trees, just various perks with no downsides and little descision making.
While on launch, building your own settlement is kind of clunky and limited, with some extra mods and even the DLCs it becomes loads of fun. You create your own towns or fortresses and it's really one of the only things that makes you feel like you actually make a difference in this world. It could've been more polished and expansive, but Bethesda is new to it and, consiodering you're a PC player, mods can fix a lot of that.
The AI in Fallout 4 is much better but also SO much worse than the previous games. It actually acts like it doesnt want to die and tries to put of a good fight. But MY GOD are all the characters and AI in this game boring. Each character has absolutely no personality. And if they do, it's a lazy steriotype of whoever they are. The only 2 characters I actually formed a bond with and cared about were Dogmeat, because it's a pupper, and Nick Valentine, because it seems like his personality had care put into it and his backstory is interesting. But I feel like a 5 year old wrote the scripts and characters for this game. It doesnt make you feel connected.
With how negative the RPG part of this game is it's hard to give this part a good review. But my god is this game's world fun to play around in. It doesn't add that much to the Fallout lore and universe except for the various factions and Synths, but you can find stories and lore all around the world. It really will feel like your living  after the apocolypse.

I too, was reluctant to purchase this game because of a number of rather vocal negative reviews. When it went on sale, I decided to chance it. Well, to make a long story short, I think this is a really good solid game and add to that, the developers keep working on it to make it better. Just make sure you read all the reviews, not just the negative ones so that you get a good idea of what you are looking at.
The game is not easy, nor is it disappointingly hard. You will lose adventurers and get your butt kicked, however you will do a fair share of kicking the bad guys butts as well. A big problem for a large number of people is that the game can not be saved manually, which disallows the ability to restart again and again until you get the outcome you wished for, but that is also one of the things that make this game fun. You need to live with your choices and weather the loss of your beloved adventurers who succumb to the monsters of the catacombs.  I have had no crashes, no apparent bugs and the game runs smoothly. Managing your team and building your small army of dungeon adventurers is only half the fun, the other half is seeing a well planned and coordinated dungeon quest succeed. And while losing your best team to a boss can be maddening and frustrating, it only makes the immersion deeper.
Pros:
-Great Artwork
-Good Narration
-Cool Animations
-Managing, Equipping and Guiding your team
-Fun stuff like: potions, magic items, traps and treasure (all the requisite stuff for a dungeon adventure)
-Character Development (leveling them up, picking new or improving abilities and weapons)
-Pretty much bug free (I haven't seen any yet...(50+ hours)
-Appropriate music scores
-Actually has a backstory
-Developers are working hard
-You can step away from the game if you have to (turn based)
Cons:
-Still Early Access (looking forward to the complete product)
-Whining on the forums because some purchasers didn't get everything wanted (too hard, too easy, unbalanced, etc...)
-Makes you play for longer than you realize (you look at the clock and find out it is 2am, darn, I gotta go to work in 5 hours)
-Doesn't have the esperanto language option.....:)
Anyway, I am very happy with my purchase and at 50+ hours have gotten more than my money's worth. If you don't like games that make you live with your choices or might kill off your favorite character because it makes you cry, then this isn't for you. But if you like an exciting dungeon delving game with elements of party management and careful recruitment choices, by all means get it.
Remember, read more than just the unhappy reviews.

This game is awesome!
DD is a difficult game.  It is not like most RPGs where your heroes wade through hordes of monsters, chug a couple of potions, and keep on smiting.  It's designed to be a struggle where your heroes are pushed to their physical and emotional boundaries and frequently don't survive the test.  If you enjoy the challenge, however, the wide variety of classes and skills make for a really enjoyable range of tactical possibilities which need to be tailored to match the dungeon and your specific party composition.  Not to mention that the art is fantastic which makes watching your heroes descend into madness (or syphilis) very enjoyable.
A note on recent surge of negative reviews:  these started to appear after Red Hook made some changes to up the difficulty of higher level dungeons and to mix up the meta.  Up to that point, the best way to approach dungeons was to just stack damage and crit and go around one-shotting everything.  Patches made this approach less viable and some people didn't try and adapt to the new changes (using armor-ignoring damage over time or corpse removal skills).  I believe a lot of the frustration with old strategies not working fueled these negative reviews.
:  This tactical RPG game is really great if you're okay with the fact that it does not pull punches.  You really need to pay attention to what your heroes can do and what they're up against to succeed.  The feeling of success when you pull your ragged squad through almost impossible odds is what it's all about.

Thought I'd make a quick edit to the review now that the game has come out of Early Access.
Darkest Dungeon lets you assemble a roster of dungeon adventurers and send them into dungeons in order to defeat pestilent creatures that have plagued the land in order to fully restore a hamlet back to its former glory. The game is not so much a pure dungeon crawler, but more of a dungeon crawl management simulator (for lack of a better word). You do not only navigate the heroes through a dungeon. You also take full responsibility for their wellbeing. As heroes go through dungeons, they accumulate stress and could even get diseases, and you have to make sure you bring them back to top shape in between your dungeon runs. You do not just control a single party of heroes. You have to rotate several different heroes around and pick the ones most suitable for the job at hand.
There are 4 areas where you can take your expedition: Ruins, Warrens, Weald, and Cove, and each one has its own dangers and challenges, what means that you need to prepare your team accordingly. The dungeons also come in different lengths (Short, Medium, and Long) and of different difficulty (Apprentice, Veteran, and Champion). As of the final release, the final dungeon has been added too (have not yet had the bravery to try it out).
The combat is really fun and in my opinion has a lot of tactical depth to it. It's not just a simple turn-based battle system, but each position within your party setup is important. Some hero classes prefer frontal positions in the squad (like the melee tanks), others prefer to hang back (like healers or ranged attackers).
The game has been balanced around loads during Early Access, and though some aspects of it might feel unfair still, overall the gameplay feels pretty solid and requires a lot of strategising and adjusting to the situation when bad things start to happen. The game can be pretty punishing towards those who do not take caution. And even if you do everything right, things can still go wrong at times, and part of the gameplay is also having to deal with that. The game encourages tip-top preparation and contingency planning. That means that the game is easily not for everyone, but those who do enjoy that sort of thing will be up for a real treat.
Art, music, and voice acting are also superb. Easily a cherry on an already delicious cake.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes a good challenge and doesn't mind it when a game occasionally throws them some curve balls. I can't remember the last time a game has kept me interested for 70 hours and counting.

I've been replaying this game recently (yes replaying it) and realized I haven't written a review yet, so here it goes.
Fallout 4 is one of the best games I have ever played. This is coming from someone who has played Skyrim, Witcher 3, and tried to get into New Vegas, which I'll probably like eventually. Let's break it down.
Story: Overall the story isn't great, and let's be honest if you haven't heard it yet then what is wrong with you? Ok, so who actually cares about Shaun? The experience most people probably had was they went through some of the story, banged Piper, then slaughetered the other factions, mainly for the sweet loot. Not once did anyone ever care about Shaun. Bethesda don't seem to do well with main stories BUT, they definitely do well with side quests. There are SO many side quests, and most of them are fantastic. For instance, there is one where you put on an old TV show costume and become a radio show hero who guns down bad guys in dark alleyways. Sure the quest doesn't last forever, but it's definitely not something you'll forget when you look back on the best moments of this game.
Character Creation: Ok so this is probably the worst part of Fallout 4. Each conversation you have gives you 4 dialouge option per response, Friendly, Understanding, Curious, and Raging ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. If you play the game twice you'll most likely respond to situations in the same way, considering being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ most of the time just denies you side quests.
Exploration: This is where Bethesda truly shines. They are artists when it comes to creating immersive, detailed, beautiful worlds filled with things to do and see. You can't walk 50 feet without stumbling upon something interesting, whether it be a disgustingly amazing super mutant camp or just a prewar skeleton arranged in a certain way, it's hard to find empty wasteland.
Combat: A lot of people like to call this game a first person shooter, acknowleding the fact that this game lacked in rpg elements. They were definitely right about one thing, because the combat is great. The V.A.T.S system is smooth, the gun play is satisfying (A lot more than New Vegas) and it feels great to kill everything around you and then collect the spoils of war. Granted by the end of the game it kinda becomes a walk in the park, even the most feared creatures can be killed in seconds with the right equipment, but towards the end of a game that's what you want. If you spent the entire game fighting for your life it wouldn't be as satisfying because there would be no end. It would just be a constant struggle, rather than gradually progressing throughout the game.
Settlement Building: The settlement building in this game is both great and horrible. On one hand building your own base and creating a network of towns in an effort to make the Commonwealth a better place is extremely rewarding. It feels great to be able to go home to a house you made and decorated, and sleep in a room with stuff that reminds you of all your adventures in the wasteland. On the other hand building anything in this game is a huge pain due to how glitchy the building system is. Of course this can be fixed with a huge selection of mods, but the base game could've done a better job with the actually building mechanic. Another plus to this is that it's actually worth it to collect scrap. Rather than having a million useless things scattered about a building that the game allows you to pick up, it actually gives you useful resources that are a necessity to building your empire. Of course if you're skipping on the settlement building, you can always just focus on the crafting components of weapons and armor in order to keep your inventory light.
DLC: This aspect of the game is both good and bad. Unless you really like settlement building, it really isn't worth getting the workshop DLCs. The contraptions DLC is pretty good because of the interesting machinery and structures it gives you, but the Vault-Tec Workshop DLC isn't worth it. It sounds cool to build your own vault, but clearing out the space is a pain and building the vault itself is a nightmare. You're better off just sticking to the surface of the wasteland. When it comes to the other DLCs, it's up to you. I definitely reccomend Nuka World and Far Harbor as they actually give you entirely new locations to explore, new quest lines, and TONS of new stuff, but Automatron is different. Automatron is a short but sweet quest that involves creating your own killer robots and using them to destroy other robots. I would definitely reccomend it if you can get it on sale.
Mods: This game's modding community is amazing. There are some creators out there who are completely changing the game to what they want and Bethesda has supported it. The controversy behind Creation Club is still a bit tense, but it could be a great feature to the modding community if done right.
Overally I definitely reccomend this game. What it lacks in story and character, it makes up for in world design and exploration. Far Harbor and Nuka World are worth buying, as well as automatron if you can get it on sale. The modding community is huge and continues to grow, and just adds more to an already amazing game.

This is not a review sayings it's a complete waste of money. It's not. This is a decent game. But compared to the other Fallout games? This is so disappointing, and it depresses me because this game could have been so much more.
The things this game does better than previous Fallouts:
Aiming and shooting feels 100 times better than in 3 or NV.
Settlement building and crafting weapons and armor is very neat, adds use to a lot of otherwise "wasted" items.
Graphics (obviously not a surprise considering it's way newer).
What this game does worse:
No skill system.
Voiced dialogue. While the voice acting isn't bad, it kind of detracts from the classic Fallout experience of your character
having lots of choices but no "voice". In this game you have a voice but no choices.
No skill checks.
Legendary loot makes it feel like Diablo/Borderlands and not Fallout.
No damage threshold system, meaning that somehow a .38 calibre pistol is still damaging you (however weakly) whilst in power armor that weighs hundreds of pounds and can brush off any other high calibre round.
No ammo crafting (it exists in a dlc, but only through a building you make and its super janky and limited).
Weak weapon design. No real world assault rifles.
Bad weapon balance. A .45 calibre two shot sniper rifle (pistol round) does more damage than a .50 calibre sniper rifle. And somehow making a weapon have an automatic reciever reduces the damage by like 45%.
Retconning established lore, such as plasma rifles using microfusion cells and having power armor's power supply last indefinitely (in terms of practical use.
Overall, not a "completely terrible game", but as a die hard Fallout fanboy this was a massive disappointment. I'd say I got my moneys worth out of this game, however disappointing, but I won't promise you will.

Your ancestor has messed up big time. His place is now host to a huge monster that has unleashed its dark and twisted venom across the land, leaving only one terrified Hamlet untouched, most likely out of amusement at their futile attempts to keep its clutches at bay.
All kinds of foul creatures and rogue men now plague the estate, a letter your ancestor has sent you pleads for you to come back and use the Hamlet as a starting ground to build a last stand against unholy horrors. Your enemy has almost all the land, resources and a fantastic army at their disposal to snuff any attempts.
You have a kleptomanic Crusader and a cheat of a Highwayman, both bribed by your coin to try and survive guiding you through the roads to even GET to the shattered Hamlet in one piece.
You look over the terrain. The Hamlet is in shambles, you rely on whatever crazy mercenaries make their way here on promise of glory, money and adventure. No super-human heroes in divine armour, no immense power or tricks. Pure fate and your expertise on monster killing (psst, you don't have any!).
This isn't going to be easy.
Darkest Dungeon is a pretty amazing turn based dungeon crawler and micro management game where you have to be more focused on surviving than winning. Everything is stacked against you pretty much the whole way along and you need to know when to call it quits and bring heroes back alive.
The art style is something I love immensely. It's gritty, dramatic and pretty grim, everything that the game is about. This isn't a vacation, things are going to get a whole lot worse before they get better.
People will die, sometimes things will seem to be unfair, but it's down to you to make the most of what you have. Push back against the darkness, take what you've learned from each plunge into the depths and don't let the sacrifices of the many be in vain.
This game has recently had extra options for difficulty adjustments (turning off gradual stress, turning off heart attacks etc.) so you can either play with some of the features on at a time and then include additional ones when you feel you've gotten comfortable, or just not use them, up to you. On a personal level I find the game is playable with all the features on (currently week 10+ on a new save and no deaths so far, that's not gonna last long though haha) but some players may find it's a bit much at once so it's nice to have the options.
A lot of the bad stuff can be mitigated by prepping and cutting your losses, fleeing a dungeon with at least one person alive (though you should really be trying to leave the second you think things are going south) will have them carry back whatever they've found back to the Hamlet, so it's not a complete loss.
The stress mechanic is pretty neat, a lot of the time stress will be the killer rather than health. Again, all down to management. Prioritise taking down monsters that will give you the hardest time. Figure out what items to bring. Learn what heroes work best together as they come to the Hamlet, soon you'll be making trips with a dedicated taskforce in mind. Nothing feels greater than going into a dungeon that kicked your butt before and coming out on top because your monster knowledge and team planning paid off.
If you love a strong challenge and the feeling of being a lone rebellion against a great threat, then I can't recommend this game enough, get it and start that love-hate relationship with stress inducing monsters today!

My friends and I play nearly every survival game that drops. I tried this game 3 years ago and it was ok, It was like dayz/survival lite at the time and i only played it for maybe a couple hours. Fast Forward to full release and WoW has it come along way, Nelson, great job man.
As i mentioned before my friends and i play a ton of survival games and decided to try Unturned on full release. Jumping into the game many might be turned off by the graphics, but thats never really bothered me if the game play is fun (to many ppl♥♥♥♥♥♥on Minecraft for graphics but fail to realise how much that game really ofters, its not a kids game but an All Ages game). We loved Dayz mod - and all the other similar mods for arma2 and 3 like Epoch etc. so there was some benchmarks we put this game up against (not to mention all the other Dayz survival clones we have played, Rust, Hurtworld, Miscreated, Ark, the list goes on... and on... and on....).
We started with playing on the offical maps starting with Germany and then moving onto Russia. We enjoyed Russia for the quest system (need more of this) and large map, but still felt like the map was a bit small so after looking around we found The Driftless map and Wow was that perfect size map (i love the detail the creater put into the map). The insane size map (not offical but should be) feels every bit as big as any arma map, plenty of space to get "lost".
As we ran around and started to learn the ins and out of Unturned, my friends and I would make comments along the lines of "Man it sure would be cool if you could do "X" " ... and nearly everytime... you Could.

- "Man, i wish these cars had an inventory to store my junk" - well why not build a safe and slap it onto the truck, Very cool although i wish there was some restrictions as to how crazy you can build on cars :) (maybe a weight limit).
- "Damn, if wish this game had LIft and Tow like arma mod" - well maybe not tow but why not find yourself the Skycane chopper.
I mean this game offers a ton of things that the "big boys" do:
- Multiple weapons - from shovels, pocket knives, to pistols, SMG, and rocket launchers AND attachments - scopes, silencers, Mag/drums, grips.
- Multiple vehicles - cars, trucks, apcs, choppers, jets - and you can craft your own.
- Robust Crafting - you can craft a ton of stuff, from cooking and bandages and basic survial stuff to base building.
- Base building - it can hold its own - you can build a basic shake all the way to a mega base with laser turrets, farms, and your very own oil rig to get you that sweet gasoline.
- zombies/Boss - the zombies are tough at first until you learn how they work, but once you quickly catch on they are on par with most other zombie AI in other games. The boss zombies are a nice addition.
- Easter eggs and more - There are plenty of things to find, neat areas to explore like underground subways systems that you need a light or nightvision.
- WORKSHOP - this is a big one in my book. Games can get old and stale after a bit, or sometimes the devs just dont have the time to work on all the cool idea, but when you open your game up to mods from the community you not only added content but longevity to your game. Now you go from 1 dev to thousands of potental content creators. Its the same reason Minecraft was so successful (a ton offical content first came from the modding community) or that Dayz was even a thing (let alone why arma is where it is now). I applaud Nelson and his commitment to the modding community.
- Level Editor - piggybacking off the workshop - the in game editor is great. I started working on my own map (using an insane template) and the editor is great fun. I have not used the DevEdit much as its not quite as intuitive as the basic editor (need to watch more videos on it) but the base editor was great, and i can publish to the workshop to easily share my content.
There are still some things i would love to see, like roaming AI (im much more a fan of Bandit AI then Zombies), Tow Trucks, And Multiplayer Level Editor etc., but i have no doubt that Nelson, if not already working on it, will give thought to any ideas tossed his way. And if he cant make it due to the amount of dev time it may take, im sure he will put some basic hooks in there for the modders to make it happen.
All in All i fully recommend this game to anyone that loves survival games like Dayz, and would tell them to not♥♥♥♥♥♥on it before you play it just because of the graphic style. Its free, and it does basically the same as that $20-$40 game does.

There seems to be a fair amount of backlash regarding this game, as people like to criticize the new update for making it "unplayable".
That's really odd, because I find it to be a fun, enjoyable--albeit stressful--experience. If it is so unplayable, then why am I able to play it? A lot of people seem to complain about the game's difficulty and the fact that the game tends to throw a monkey wrench in your best-laid plans (a random trap attacks your Plague Doctor, enemies land a few critical blows in a row, etc.). I'd like to start out by saying, rather flatly, that this game is a roguelike, gothic, dungeon crawler. It is not Candyland.
The game does a great job of playing out the difficulties and trials associated with exploring haunted or possessed dungeons and labyrinths, infested with creatures and abominations created by your own ancestor who leaves you to clean up his grievous mess. Your team of heroes will get stressed and they may go crazy or pull through and save your team from utter ruin. This makes sense from a regular person's perspective. You're going through creepy dungeons with a bunch of strangers, armed only with the best gear a nameless heir can provide you (or is willing to), only to hope that you can survive fighting disgusting, fleshy pig creatures, skeletons, fish monsters, zombie mushroom creatures and more. How would you, as a normal person or even as a hero, not end up stressed out by this?
Of COURSE the game is supposed to be stressful and arbitrary in design to an extent--that's the point. Do you remember a roguelike game where you remember the layout of every dungeon and the item drop rates and enemy spawn rates were overly-consistent? That wouldn't be a very roguelike game if this were the case. So, if you were traversing through the halls of these places, you would be stressed out too, fighting such monsters. This would lead up to the point when you would fear for your own life from dealing with such insufferable creatures, or pull through and refuse to take this kind of treatment lying down. Sure, the game is quite spontaneous with some of the situations that occur. I once interacted with a curio incorrectly, only for my Vestal to end up with Syphillis. Needless to say, she wasn't welcomed to the Brothel any longer.
This game sets out to do what a roguelike does best: throws spontaneous game mechanics out at you while you do your best to fight them off. The object in the game is not to expect what happens next, but to survive whatever that next thing is. If your characters can't survive the onslaught, then I hope you've upgraded your Stagecoach.
tl;dr This game is great, but a lot of people complain about the difficulty, claiming it to be unfair or "unplayable". The game does get frustrating, but it is understandably so. It is a great purchase, especially for the $10 it is on sale for at the moment. I highly recommend it if you like gritty, dark, challenging roguelike games with turn-based elements.

Xcom 2 retains most of the same formula as its previous game except this time they added more, The enemies are stronger, tougher, and smarter and made missions much more faster paced. Humanity
has new ways to fight from new technology to even strategy on the field. Xcom is even more bad♥♥♥♥♥than before and adds so much more. It starts off a bit hard, gets harder and then pisses you off if you've made the wrong choices or just bad but still a good game.
The graphics is improved in this version of the game while still using the same engine and a beefier pc is needed to run it although it isn't drop dead gorgeous it still looks very good. At the same time there are some performance issues for the game even for me running a Titan and higher end processor but it is minuscule and the situation seems like it can be fixed via patches.
The environment is more detailed and come in many different varieties all over the world towns, cities, snow, rain, sand etc.
New alien sounds and voice acting in the game along with some returning familiar voices. The guns sounds great and new alien devices just blows your eardrums with its creative sci fi fx along with thier speeches. Accompanying this are also some great voice acting which goes does a really great job for the story. The music pieces for this game is phenomenal and gets your adrenaline going.
The story is much more action packed this time around and explosive along with time sensative missions. Most of the game is accompanied by cut-scenes but there are also in game chatter between characters to let players understand the lore and situation of what has has been happening to the world in the past years. There are also archives and logs players can go through
to discover and read to obtain more insights. The aliens are up to something but what exactly play it and fondle thier plans.
The game pretty much follows the same formula from the previous Xcom game except the r.n.g the game (Random number generator) during shots seems alot more improved (Sorta LOL)_. You can still of course miss shots at 40% or even 50% but it doesn't happen ALL THE DAMN TIME! Although 80% chance to shoot in the face can still miss lol.
Along with the returning gameplay there is more strategy and the action is faster paced since there are many missions which are turn sensative (many of them). The new concealment system helps player plan ambushes on the battlefield and also strategize ambush attacks
on the aliens before they can react along with new devices to scout, technology to upgrade, guns, armors and even environment hacking  to buff your units or debuff enemies  for a better chance to fight back.
There are also plenty of new class promotions, skills and load out for characters. The enemies this time are tougher, harder and even more annoying. They will bind you, poison you, shoot lasers at you, mind control you,teleport around you, aoe you, blow you up and kick your teeth in, thankfully you can retaliate.

Your ancestor has messed up big time. His place is now host to a huge monster that has unleashed its dark and twisted venom across the land, leaving only one terrified Hamlet untouched, most likely out of amusement at their futile attempts to keep its clutches at bay.
All kinds of foul creatures and rogue men now plague the estate, a letter your ancestor has sent you pleads for you to come back and use the Hamlet as a starting ground to build a last stand against unholy horrors. Your enemy has almost all the land, resources and a fantastic army at their disposal to snuff any attempts.
You have a kleptomanic Crusader and a cheat of a Highwayman, both bribed by your coin to try and survive guiding you through the roads to even GET to the shattered Hamlet in one piece.
You look over the terrain. The Hamlet is in shambles, you rely on whatever crazy mercenaries make their way here on promise of glory, money and adventure. No super-human heroes in divine armour, no immense power or tricks. Pure fate and your expertise on monster killing (psst, you don't have any!).
This isn't going to be easy.
Darkest Dungeon is a pretty amazing turn based dungeon crawler and micro management game where you have to be more focused on surviving than winning. Everything is stacked against you pretty much the whole way along and you need to know when to call it quits and bring heroes back alive.
The art style is something I love immensely. It's gritty, dramatic and pretty grim, everything that the game is about. This isn't a vacation, things are going to get a whole lot worse before they get better.
People will die, sometimes things will seem to be unfair, but it's down to you to make the most of what you have. Push back against the darkness, take what you've learned from each plunge into the depths and don't let the sacrifices of the many be in vain.
This game has recently had extra options for difficulty adjustments (turning off gradual stress, turning off heart attacks etc.) so you can either play with some of the features on at a time and then include additional ones when you feel you've gotten comfortable, or just not use them, up to you. On a personal level I find the game is playable with all the features on (currently week 10+ on a new save and no deaths so far, that's not gonna last long though haha) but some players may find it's a bit much at once so it's nice to have the options.
A lot of the bad stuff can be mitigated by prepping and cutting your losses, fleeing a dungeon with at least one person alive (though you should really be trying to leave the second you think things are going south) will have them carry back whatever they've found back to the Hamlet, so it's not a complete loss.
The stress mechanic is pretty neat, a lot of the time stress will be the killer rather than health. Again, all down to management. Prioritise taking down monsters that will give you the hardest time. Figure out what items to bring. Learn what heroes work best together as they come to the Hamlet, soon you'll be making trips with a dedicated taskforce in mind. Nothing feels greater than going into a dungeon that kicked your butt before and coming out on top because your monster knowledge and team planning paid off.
If you love a strong challenge and the feeling of being a lone rebellion against a great threat, then I can't recommend this game enough, get it and start that love-hate relationship with stress inducing monsters today!

Personally to me, in RPG's, I do not like to redo one simply cause I have already lived the story how I wanted to live it; if I play again it won't be the same.
Cons: Since the beginning of the game you learn about "settlements". Settlements are bases in the game that you will track down and protect. You can also find scrap and junk and make building and equipment for the settlements. Every settlement requires food, water, shelter, and defense. The reason why it is a con is because I feel like it takes you away from the actual game. So many times I be doing a quest and the game tells me, "a settlement is in trouble go help them!". Man that is like laying in bed and finally get super comfortable then you forgot to turn off the lights. I just think the settlements are out of place in the game; it feels like a crossover game more than Fallout. I am not here to worry about other people, I am here to do quest and get awesome loot! Also another thing as I spent time in the game, it feels a lot like skyrim in a way. How the animals and mechanics react just makes me feel like I am in skyrim again. This isn't really a con but just something to thing about if you play.
I have played 3 through 4 and still say that Fallout 3 is the best in the series, but all things said this game is definitely worth the time cause the side quests are pretty good.

EDIT: So, I'm leaving my initial thoughts up, because the game does have some pretty glaring issues going from console to PC. These aren't really things I think the player should have to deal with, however, once they're are dealt with.... Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I see what what fans of the series are on about. This is an example of difficult gameplay done so ♥♥♥♥ing right. After I had plugged in a controller and set it from full-screen to windowed mode (As it crashes like a mother ♥♥♥♥er in full screen) this game really started to shine. The oppressive atmosphere is so well done, you really feel like an insignificant speck in an uncaring and dying world. And having probable death around every corner has me playing in a way I haven't done since I was a kid. Peeking around corners, hesitating to go forward. You taste failure often, but never because of something you can't do something about. And because of that, your successes become the result of real improvement, which gives one hell of a sense of accomplishment when you finally win. So, yeah, it lives up to the hype, it's a game that actually gives players a challenge, which is getting harder and harder to find. It's absolutely worth your time and money, BUT FIRST, get a controller, switch to windowed, and maybe play around with your graphics card settings, otherwise your first taste of this piece of fried gold will be a hell of a lot like what I've got written below.
Gotta say, I hate this game. I'll try to stay away from complaints about difficulty, as this is a Dark Souls game, and I knew what I was getting into. The difficulty is the point.
So, I understand that the previous installments were somewhat infamous for this, however it bears mentioning. This game is not made to be played with a mouse and keyboard. So much so that the tutorial messages are given to you for an xbox contoller "Power attack with right bumper", that sort of thing. And this definitely carries into gameplay, menu navigation has never been more headache inducing. You can get into and out of your menu by pressing escape, but the shop menu has to be navigated with E and Q. Or by clicking to bring up a second menu with the option to go back. Equipping items is terribly unintuitive. Instead of going to your inventory and selecting it, you have to go into "Equipment" which is different from your inventory for some reason, then add the item to a list of things you can equip, exit that menu, then use shift and the mouse scroll button to select it.
Secondly, there's no way to pause the game for....some reason. I guess because people are supposed to be able to enter your game, and entering a paused players world is a bit problimatic. But if you're just playing the game for the single player, this is an annoyance on a massive scale. At the very least there should be an option for going offline to enable you to pause the game.
Thirdly, this game crashes constatly. It crashed within a minute of starting a new game. Over the two hour period I was playing, it crashed four times. All in different places, which makes it hard as hell to fix the problem since what casues it appears to be random chance. This game is crashing more than my modded to oblivion Fallout 4, and it doesn't help that every time you start the game back up it scolds you for not exiting the game properly. The crashing is bad enough, you don't need to rub it in.
So, here's where I stand. I've done some research, played around with my nvidia driver settings, I'll use my xbox controller, and I'll see how things go from there. I payed 30 bucks for it, I might as well try to get my money's worth. But as it is, this game is an obtuse, broken, and unbalanced mess, and you probably should avoid it like the plague.

Your ancestor has messed up big time. His place is now host to a huge monster that has unleashed its dark and twisted venom across the land, leaving only one terrified Hamlet untouched, most likely out of amusement at their futile attempts to keep its clutches at bay.
All kinds of foul creatures and rogue men now plague the estate, a letter your ancestor has sent you pleads for you to come back and use the Hamlet as a starting ground to build a last stand against unholy horrors. Your enemy has almost all the land, resources and a fantastic army at their disposal to snuff any attempts.
You have a kleptomanic Crusader and a cheat of a Highwayman, both bribed by your coin to try and survive guiding you through the roads to even GET to the shattered Hamlet in one piece.
You look over the terrain. The Hamlet is in shambles, you rely on whatever crazy mercenaries make their way here on promise of glory, money and adventure. No super-human heroes in divine armour, no immense power or tricks. Pure fate and your expertise on monster killing (psst, you don't have any!).
This isn't going to be easy.
Darkest Dungeon is a pretty amazing turn based dungeon crawler and micro management game where you have to be more focused on surviving than winning. Everything is stacked against you pretty much the whole way along and you need to know when to call it quits and bring heroes back alive.
The art style is something I love immensely. It's gritty, dramatic and pretty grim, everything that the game is about. This isn't a vacation, things are going to get a whole lot worse before they get better.
People will die, sometimes things will seem to be unfair, but it's down to you to make the most of what you have. Push back against the darkness, take what you've learned from each plunge into the depths and don't let the sacrifices of the many be in vain.
This game has recently had extra options for difficulty adjustments (turning off gradual stress, turning off heart attacks etc.) so you can either play with some of the features on at a time and then include additional ones when you feel you've gotten comfortable, or just not use them, up to you. On a personal level I find the game is playable with all the features on (currently week 10+ on a new save and no deaths so far, that's not gonna last long though haha) but some players may find it's a bit much at once so it's nice to have the options.
A lot of the bad stuff can be mitigated by prepping and cutting your losses, fleeing a dungeon with at least one person alive (though you should really be trying to leave the second you think things are going south) will have them carry back whatever they've found back to the Hamlet, so it's not a complete loss.
The stress mechanic is pretty neat, a lot of the time stress will be the killer rather than health. Again, all down to management. Prioritise taking down monsters that will give you the hardest time. Figure out what items to bring. Learn what heroes work best together as they come to the Hamlet, soon you'll be making trips with a dedicated taskforce in mind. Nothing feels greater than going into a dungeon that kicked your butt before and coming out on top because your monster knowledge and team planning paid off.
If you love a strong challenge and the feeling of being a lone rebellion against a great threat, then I can't recommend this game enough, get it and start that love-hate relationship with stress inducing monsters today!

For a free-to-play game, it was great.  I enjoyed most of my time playing with friends, and the large quantity of weapons and armors seemed very enjoyable.  However, the game has numerous difficulty spikes, along with areas that (thanks to newer updates) almost force you to pay to get the best type of armor you want.  However, thanks to the varying damages and damage resistances, as well as status effects, newer players are basically punished for not paying.  Although they have made quite a few changes to the game since it began, some of which making it much easier for newer players (such as doing away with elevator costs, and removing "Mist energy", they replace those things with more difficulty spikes.
Also, while the game is nice when you begin, and harder later on (forcing you to play with others, and hopefully good players at that), the other portions of the game (PvP, and the DLC's) are extremely lacking.  PvP is a mashup of horrible pings, buttmad children, and people using the game's auto-aim feature.  The DLC's offer you two things: A useless couple costumes, along with extra lives and such, or an extremely annoying (and difficulty spike filled) raid on a Gremlin base.  However, at the end you get an overpowered weapon, decent bomb, and the ability to make a decent gunner mask.
The story of the game is also lacking.  It seems almost like they aren't sure what to do with the game.  They have plenty of lore, whether it be about the Spiral Knight Order, or any of their enemies, however they seem to have nowhere to take the game's story from here.  The "end" of the game was supposed to be getting to the core to find an energy source and leave.  Instead, you get to the core, find out its locked, and have an option (if you save up a lot of in-game money, or pay roughly $7.50) to re-play any of the four boss levels, only more satanic, leading you to believe that you're in that world's version of hell, perhaps.  However, the game stops there.  It leaves so many questions that I'm sure everyone wants answered.  What happened to the recon unit, what happened to the Shadow Lairs, what happens to Warmaster Seerus, what is in the core, or even if you will escape?
Sadly, i've been playing this game for around two years, and in my time they havn't added much in story progression since then.  I'll reccomend the game now, but I feel they're losing players, and if they don't finish the story in a good way, or at least expand more, the game will kinda get empty, and eventually die.

There seems to be a fair amount of backlash regarding this game, as people like to criticize the new update for making it "unplayable".
That's really odd, because I find it to be a fun, enjoyable--albeit stressful--experience. If it is so unplayable, then why am I able to play it? A lot of people seem to complain about the game's difficulty and the fact that the game tends to throw a monkey wrench in your best-laid plans (a random trap attacks your Plague Doctor, enemies land a few critical blows in a row, etc.). I'd like to start out by saying, rather flatly, that this game is a roguelike, gothic, dungeon crawler. It is not Candyland.
The game does a great job of playing out the difficulties and trials associated with exploring haunted or possessed dungeons and labyrinths, infested with creatures and abominations created by your own ancestor who leaves you to clean up his grievous mess. Your team of heroes will get stressed and they may go crazy or pull through and save your team from utter ruin. This makes sense from a regular person's perspective. You're going through creepy dungeons with a bunch of strangers, armed only with the best gear a nameless heir can provide you (or is willing to), only to hope that you can survive fighting disgusting, fleshy pig creatures, skeletons, fish monsters, zombie mushroom creatures and more. How would you, as a normal person or even as a hero, not end up stressed out by this?
Of COURSE the game is supposed to be stressful and arbitrary in design to an extent--that's the point. Do you remember a roguelike game where you remember the layout of every dungeon and the item drop rates and enemy spawn rates were overly-consistent? That wouldn't be a very roguelike game if this were the case. So, if you were traversing through the halls of these places, you would be stressed out too, fighting such monsters. This would lead up to the point when you would fear for your own life from dealing with such insufferable creatures, or pull through and refuse to take this kind of treatment lying down. Sure, the game is quite spontaneous with some of the situations that occur. I once interacted with a curio incorrectly, only for my Vestal to end up with Syphillis. Needless to say, she wasn't welcomed to the Brothel any longer.
This game sets out to do what a roguelike does best: throws spontaneous game mechanics out at you while you do your best to fight them off. The object in the game is not to expect what happens next, but to survive whatever that next thing is. If your characters can't survive the onslaught, then I hope you've upgraded your Stagecoach.
tl;dr This game is great, but a lot of people complain about the difficulty, claiming it to be unfair or "unplayable". The game does get frustrating, but it is understandably so. It is a great purchase, especially for the $10 it is on sale for at the moment. I highly recommend it if you like gritty, dark, challenging roguelike games with turn-based elements.

Will update this once I get home from work, review mostly written for old xcom players.
+ The combat has been improved a lot because of small things that makes the game have a much better pacing. As an example they've added the ability to actually see if you have a line of sight on the enemies so that you wont have to worry about it when moving around.
+ The new system in which you spawn invisible to the enemies makes the first part of every map more enjoyable because it means you're setting up ambushes instead of hoping for good rng with the pod openings.
+ I for one like the new base building system even if it at first glance might look dumbed down. It feels like you wont have to play a certain way IE follow a certain building line that was always the same no matter what.
+ So far the enemies have been fun and rewarding to face, and I'm eager to see what they will throw at me for the rest of the game.
* Some graphical glitches like weapons or enemies clipping trough walls, pretty much the same as the previous game. It doesn't affect game play unless you really care about graphics.
* Difficulty has been scaled down and it feels like if you would play on a difficulty level under commander(classic) it would probably be really easy compared to the previous game.
- The AI has a habit of some times running into really stupid positions. As an example I've had two occasions now where AI ran into cars that exploded the next round, instantly killing them. Not sure if intented but I doubt it.
- Terrible optimization makes the menu, cutscenes and base almost unplayable. I don't know if this is a common issue but my rig should easily be able to handle this on even the highest graphics. Luckily since it's a turn based game it doesn't affect game play that much.
Easily recommend the game for now!

Darkest Dungeon is a really great game that pulls of the rare trick of being both aesthetically beautiful, atmospheric, mechanically deep, and having those mechanics service and support the story and atmosphere.
The general flow of the game is remiscent of a dark fantasy XCOM - you assemble 4-man squads of heroes and attempt missions for gold and experience. Your characters acquire debilitating conditions or die outright on these missions, so there is a real sense of risk and danger. As your heroes gain levels, they are able to attempt longer and more dangerous missions, until they are able to attempt the (currently unimplemented, as of the time of this review) endgame dungeon, The Darkest Dungeon.
Fundamentally, the game can be quite punishing and hostile. That's not to say it's not fun, or it's for masochists only, but you need to be the sort of person that can shrug off losing. At the end of the day, it's only a video-game. This game is not a rogue-like, but it tends to have a reputation for being one I think because you need the sort of personality that can accept losing as part of the game to play this. The game is built around the assumption that some level of death and losing is inevitable. Unlike XCOM, where an entire high-difficulty attempt can be ruined because your squad died, it's much easier to move on after a party wipe in Darkest Dungeon.

Not much has changed for XCOM in this second incarnation of the classic turn based strategy game. The graphics are slightly improved but still very low polygon and low texture quality. The performance for a turn based strategy game is atrocious. Even with a GTX970 the game keeps stuttering.
There are slight improvements in the training, equipment and base building but nothing dramatic. We now have loot drops that have to be picked up within 3 turns or they disapear.
The horrible forced camera movement that follows every soldier and moves automatically to everything that does even the most basic action is extremely annoying.
The game has no smooth flow and feels jerky and forced throughout the whole experience. Every action takes 2-3 seconds to complete and sometimes the camera just stays at a dead enemy for a couple of seconds doing nothing.
You can't give commands while your soldiers move, you have to wait for the animations and camera movement to finish before you can give a command.
Movement can be a challenge due to the very laggy and jerky interface. It is sometimes hard to get your soldier where you want him to go and involves a lot of rotating and scrolling to actually be able to click somewhere. It can be frustrating.
The game still features the infuriating: "Aliens get an extra turn when you detect them." Why exactly do enemies get a full turn when i am the one that detects them even when it's my turn still?
Buy only if you are an extreme fan and loved the first one.

CON:

Don't be fooled. This game might have a cute and coloful look but what makes it a true gem is that it requires skill to master and plenty to keep the challange going while the COOP aspect adds infinite replayability.
This is a true action game with one of the best combat systems I've come across. It feels balanced with enough variety to keep it interesting and engaging, but with enough simplicity to keep it from being unnecessarly bloated like many other games with weapon/armor upgrades end up feeling. Every enemy is fought differently and certain weapons work best against them. With all the different specialization routes like buffing up on armor, gunning, bombing, slow swords, fast swords, knockback techniques, precise shielding and dozens of different enemies on screen, it is truly rewarding to master.
Although this game can be played exclusivly solo, the thing that really makes this game never-ending is the COOP. Technically it is a MMO but parties are limited to 4 players that must work together with different strategies to complete levels.
Like any other game, it does have shortcomings, most notably the steep learning curve pertaning to making and using the variety of gear that is available, However, if you enjoy challanging action games with plenty of upgrading and COOP, you should absolutely must give this a try.

Let me Preface my review by saying that my playtime is misleading, since I've played Darkest Dungeon far more and far earlier than this latest iteration (today's date being december 29th) and I would like to do more than yack on about how the people who are upset are idiots who expected a mamby pamby walking simulator, but I'm not going to jump on the other fence and say that red hook is doing the best job possible either. Let's look at both sides of the argument.
the people who are angry at red-hook:
the game is too RNG based
there are more technical flaws that should be addressed
patches are removing different styles of play, mainly, the sucessful ones
trinkets are barely useful at best and downright harmful at worst
the large amount of different types of debuffs
the above, combined with the natural difficulty of the game, has made it less and less about player interaction having negative or positive consequences, but instead making it more and more dependent upon elements outside the player's control.
the people who aren't angry with red hook
There are options to minimize the difficulty of the game
it was always advertized as a difficult game, they are just keeping in with the tradition (I'm hearing a bit of people throw around Dark souls, I'll talk about this later)
you aren't supposed to metagame.
balance takes precident over new content and other fixes
Now, that's a lot of main points, let's try to address some.
first and foremost, it is in my personal opinion that the technical aspects of the game, such as bugfixing, should take a higher priority than new content, or balances and fixes. People may disagree, but I pay money to have my game work, I'd appreciate it if that request was fulfilled.
RNG: RNG should not be the decisive factor of the game. The player accounting for variables is a part of roguelikes, but ultimately it should be in the player's control whether or not they receive most of the damage given to them. In a battle where you're torch lit, there is a chance for you to be surprisd, have all the enemies land crits on you, have all four of your people go to death's door, or go insane, and die the next turn. The chance of that happening is very low, but it can still happen. There's also a chance that your hellion, who has 40 stress, gets hit by a trap, now it's 60 stress, she gains another 5 stress from the room even though it's perfectly lit, she goes into a room, get's surprised, is knocked to the back. Gets targeted by a stress dealer, now it's 80, get's critically shot by the crossbow skele, she goes insane the next round. Was that 60 stress mitigatable at all? no. No scouting rolls even though I keep my torch well lit, no way to protect a surprised character with low stress resist. Player choice should be the crux of a rougelike, not an afterthought.
Difficulty: as said above in RNG, I believe there should be more player control. In Dark Souls, There is no RNG, the only random element is the human element in PvP, if you fail, it's your own fault because you did something wrong. There is little "difficult, but fair" in DD, only the former.
removed different styles of play and metagaming: videogames are always going to have a metagame, dark souls has a meta, Diablo 2 has a meta, pokemon has a meta. When you remove the viability of a playstyle, you are removing another facet of player control, feeding into the above mentioned issues. When you find a system that works, the best way to combat that isn't by nerfing that ability necessarily, but by doing something that matches that. I actually think corpses work well in this way (especially current patch corpses that disappear after a while) they don't turn front-heavy teams useless, they make it so that you have to figure out creative ways to deal with back row harassers, or you just remove the corpses in an extra turn of combat, oh well. Oh, and a lot of people still don't use grave robber for some reason, Huh.
Trinkets: they need a rebalance, the "give and take" nature of a majority of trinkets usually work to a disadvantage, due to the nature of how enemies target, how abilities work, etc. As they are, I can't really think of a way to use a -20 bleed resist, -20 blight resist, +20 heal receive charm because they'll never be healed enough to make up for the increased damage because Red hook made healers poor as a design choice. And with the amount of debuffs given freely by base attacks (which there is no answer to, no mitigation against, and no reciprocation from your guys. Your moves are gimmicks, they don't do a debuff unless the move gimmick is based around that) there's nothing gained from it, there aren't any buffs, it just serves to take more out of your hands.
Options: I think that this is a very good thing that should have been treated more as a difficulty selection, as opposed to an "option", but I still do appreciate it very much. You still can't roll back to when the man at arms and dog guy were the best characters, but steam disabled version rollbacks a while ago so I can't fault Red hook for that.
Do I think it's worth it? meh, If you enjoy the artstyle, the narration, the obvious dediction the team has for the project, than I think it is. You'll most likely be able to grind you pay's worth of time out of it, whether you enjoy it or not isn't my concern. I just wish there was more room for experimentation and direct player choice.

Update:
tl;dr: Enjoying the game, but when I first started playing I had major technical issues.
It seems as of the day after I posted this the servers have improved massively, I just didn't get around to updating the review.
Although I can't speak for everyone, my personal experience for the first 4 hours or so of dealing with trove was very poor. The signup for 'glyph' would repeatedly refuse my passwords, and would take quite a long time to send the emails. After near-on an hour messing around with the signing up I managed to get in game, only to be greeted with huge wait times to even connect.
This only proceeded to annoy me further as you can't change settings (fullscreen, sound options, resolution, ect) until you have SUCCESSFULLY JOINED the game.
I personally was annoyed by this to no ends because despite the horrendous state of the servers (when I originally posted), yet they had a working micro-transaction store.
After getting in-game I was repeated encountering my computer completely crashing (which happened on no other games), but this seems to have stopped now. (This was likely a problem on my side, but as I said, it happened only on Trove).
BUT.
After all this, I managed to finally be able to play the game, and I am actually really enjoying it. I still don't like the fact it has the availability of micro-transactions but I have yet to feel like they actually influence the game, since the game contains no PvP (that I can see), and I am really not feeling any pay-walls or 'pay2win' at all.
I usually don't defend the mindless comments like 'itz nut pay2wen itz pay 3 shurtcut' but I can safely say that it does feel like one of those rare occasions when the only people paying will be those who have too much money to play the game properly.
There are a lot of bugs still in-game, and the servers still like to die a lot randomly though, but they seem to be being resolved over time.
Also loot in dungeons drops per person, so there will be no loot stealing or similar, and that I really like.
Overall the gameplay itsself is really solid, but only if you can see through the major flaws it has covering it.

It's a good game with a great Fallout feel. I welcome the addition of crafting settlements and think it is well done. I'm coming into this game in 2017, so I may have missed the earlier bugs and kinks but it comes off as well polished to me. I think there could be more "scripted" RPG elements like we're used to from other Bethesda games of late (this was not always the case if you date back to Daggerfall like me), but then again I really enjoy taking the least likely settlement and building it up into something. It's fun to have the settlers you armed fight side by side with you, and there are plenty of quests to go around. If anything negative is to be said its that some places feel like they were rushed or not fleshed out enough and the opportunity to add more characters with interesting personalities was missed in some spots.  Some locations just have no one and nothing but your imagination to fill them out - not even roaming enemies, which makes the game feel more empty than it should. Overall it is enjoyable and since I'm an old school gamer who doesn't really like riding cut scenes on rails (like famous JRPGs) it's up my alley at the end of the day and worth the sale price I got it for certainly.

Changes up the formula of the Dark Souls series in a few minor ways, with a lot of clear influence from Bloodborne. I really wanted to like this game. I love roguelikes, and I'm not averse to a challenge. The sales pitch sounded great, but the implementation is clumsy at best and outright cruel at worst.
Playing Darkest Dungeon is like signing up for one of those military-style fitness training programs—you know, the ones with the cool obstacle courses—and being taken into the woods with a bag over your head, stabbed twice, given a compass, and told to find your way home. Is it technically what it says it is? I guess. Is it something most rational people would enjoy? Meh.
The core of a good game is there. The core mechanics—classes, itemization, skills, etc.—are strong, and the production values, although cringe-inducingly campy (and not necessarily on purpose), are solid. But the game fails to find the distinction between challenging and frustrating. Every character upgrade costs money, and that's only after you amass enough tokens to unlock it. Almost all loot has penalties in addition to stat boosts. You buy supplies at the beginning of each quest, and get refunded pennies on the dollar for anything you don't use. Your party randomly gets hungry and demands food, and it's not clear what causes this or when it will trigger. It's almost impossible to heal outside of combat. Combat animations are slow and repetitive, and there's no way to skip them. Most treasure chests are trapped, or just empty. Most shrines take an item from you and then do nothing. This has the effect of making almost every type of scenery feel bland and indistinct. Characters level up and then suddenly refuse to participate in quests below their level.
It's also really macabre, but not in any gritty or realistic way. It's just mostly splashed with blood, emo pronouncements and a really unsettling narrator with a severe case of Asperger's. ("Monstrous size has no intrinsic merit, unless inordinate exsanguination be considered a virtue!" Seriously, someone says this. Out loud. More than once.)
Essentially, Darkest Dungeon cooks up situations so dire as to require constant inventiveness from the player, but offers little of its own cleverness in return. I get what they were trying to do, and maybe there are people out there that will enjoy it. But if you ask me, games are supposed to be one of the few areas of life that aren't frequently and arbitrarily frustrating.

Personally to me, in RPG's, I do not like to redo one simply cause I have already lived the story how I wanted to live it; if I play again it won't be the same.
Cons: Since the beginning of the game you learn about "settlements". Settlements are bases in the game that you will track down and protect. You can also find scrap and junk and make building and equipment for the settlements. Every settlement requires food, water, shelter, and defense. The reason why it is a con is because I feel like it takes you away from the actual game. So many times I be doing a quest and the game tells me, "a settlement is in trouble go help them!". Man that is like laying in bed and finally get super comfortable then you forgot to turn off the lights. I just think the settlements are out of place in the game; it feels like a crossover game more than Fallout. I am not here to worry about other people, I am here to do quest and get awesome loot! Also another thing as I spent time in the game, it feels a lot like skyrim in a way. How the animals and mechanics react just makes me feel like I am in skyrim again. This isn't really a con but just something to thing about if you play.

I think I need to say this first, the game is awesome, but its optimization not. I press the "automatically detect hardware recommendation" the game set all the options on ultra... but the menus run with an important lag (10-15fps), when the "action camera" join the scene the fps experience a considerable decrease, about 20fps (but for example explosions or smoke looks perfectly during the game at 60 fps) so the game is poorly optimized at this point. I can run Wild Hunt for example on ultra on 60fps so... Think about it.
This is XCOM Enemy Unknown ultra enhanced edition. This is more and better. This is pure XCOM turn-based strategy.
XCOM 2 is all the good things the original had (as well as the bad things too) with a lot of new stuff.
Now you are behind the enemies lines, XCOM becomes the underdog, acting furtively, in the shadows, they are now an organization declared criminal by the new order...  The time has come to reclaim our world. Now they are not fighting an invasion force, the XCOM project are now against a greater more organised force, with power and resources. And they are really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with you.
The new concepts, guerrilla tactics, the implementation of stealth, new enemies, a good variety of mission types, the customization of the weapons (you can add ons like scopes, lanterns, silencers,  enhanced ammunition... modify many aspects), of your soldiers (now you'll miss 'em when they die, if the moment comes... and trust me, surely come), can modify their aspect in a very deep way (but all the male faces are ugly as hell) there's a high level of customization. Your headquarter is really badass now.
The maps are open now, you can move about the map freely, until you either stumble into range of an enemy or decide open fire on them, so, this is the guerrilla aspect of the game, you can now prepare an ambush, seek for the better positions before a gunfire or even almost end a fight before the enemies can react at your presence. but the situations can become in a different, very bad for you, scenario in a heartbeat, so you need a plan B, always.
The combat feel so agil and natural. The game is very more dynamic this time. Fights are brutal, raw and complex. The game is really challenging and tough, doesn't forgive a mistake.
The environments are procedural battlefields, high-quality procedurally generated maps, there is slums, city centres, forest, suburban spaces, all interesting, richly detailed, destroyable (explosions can start fires that propagate, for example), interactives... (at this point maybe you got your suspicions... the game is amazing in every aspect!)
XCOM has a real evocative history now for the first time, with cutscenes, and remarkable characters with a backstory and its own opinions. People you want to save.
There are now Dark Events, and will change the game in unpredictable ways. Dark events are "counter-operations" undertaken by Advent against XCOM.
It's the more exciting turn-based tactical game ever made.
Of course it has its minor flaws, soldiers firing the same enemy during overwatch, missing high chance shots with an average of 87.3%... but we're here to suffer, weapons through walls, some glitches, "weird walls" when you enter in a building... but nothing really remarkable.
The graphics aren't spectacular neither the animations.
It's true that the game needs much better optimization, quite. I can run The Division beta or The Witcher 3 on ultra and 60fps but XCOM barely runs, on menus (yeah weird), about 20fps, in battle runs fine.
About mods and steam workshop. XCOM 2 has Steam Workshop support, this will improve the game in many ways and make it probably endless. Long War Studios (the team behind XCOM: Enemy Unknown's Long War overhaul) has already produced three mods for XCOM 2, all of which are playable from launch, highly welcome move! This feels like a free DLC because Long War Studios teamed up with developer Firaxis Games, and they've been working together!! so this mods perfectly fit with the core of the game, without problems or complications.

WELCOME BACK TO XCOM BABY!!
--------EDITS&ADDONS----------
20hrs of XCOM BABY later, and I've just dismissed my "Sharpshooter" for several other ragequit misses, including no less than a 97%. I heard he has since been employed on an Imperial Star Destroyer as a Stormtrooper.
To make this review "more helpful", I feel I should add that this IS a game worth buying, though missing often (and often you will) can become a real frustration - you find yourself grinning in sweet revenge when the same RNG happens to the Aliens and they miss you from from point blank range.
Shooting mechanics aside, the only other issues I've come across since playing are:-
*Mission timers (which mods can fix already). Plus, this is a personal preference, it's not a fact that this makes the game worse. I actually enjoyed some of the missions when realising I had 3 turns remaining to act out the impossible. You really think about what skills you have remaining and use every resource possible to inflict the greatest amount of damage while moving forward as fast as you can. All normally works out well... Assuming you hit the target, that is! *ahem*
*The occasional bug / framerate drop (which will no doubt be patched very soon). Again, this is computer specific and really, I hardly noticed it once I tweaked my settings. I had to lower a few things, but no biggie!
That's it. I see no real reason not to buy this game, especially if you liked Enemy Unknown/Within. I'm currently finding myself pinned down at times on Normal. Yes, NORMAL, and I have no Ironman, and I still finish some missions thinking "Wow... How did I get outta that one?!" I can't wait to (hopefully) survive this playthrough and crank up the difficulty to make it even more of a challenge.
Good luck fellow Commanders! May your aim be true.
And if you miss, channel all that anger, know it happens to the best of us, and tell yourself "That's XCOM BABY!"

I'll be blunt; this is a good game just not a very good Fallout game.  Fallout has always had a system of RPG aesthetics; diplomacy, skill checks, good creative dialogue and lore intensive story element.  Falllout 4 gameplay wise is superior to all the other previous titles; gun mechanics are a huge improvement from earlier.  I'll even go as far as the FPS system seems to be a much better system than the old top down system.  That being said not EVERYTHING is perfect;
The dialogue system is disgusting and borderline abhorrent.  It's basically a very watered down version of the Mass Effect system to a degree that dialogue is just a poor joke.  RPG elements are pratically non-existent; diplomatic avenues and open ended circumstances would have been interesting but instead it seems to be patterned on a method of, "Kill em all, let god sort em out," mentality that in my honest opinion does NOT help the franchise, in fact its detrimental.  There's no avenue for creativity, there's an inherant lack of imagination and seems less like an RPG and more like a Borderlands clone with substantially less weapons available in comparison.  Now some may say they like that system however they cannot represent the entire playerbase that love the Fallout franchise.
With that I'll say this; is Fallout 4 a good game?  YES IT IS!!!!  It's beautifully crafted and I give the development team a lot of credit for getting its atmosphere spot on.  Is it superior to the other games?  YES Gameplay wise.  Is it the superior RPG?  NO IT IS NOT.  By itself its a great game but far from being an RPG.  Do I still recommend it?  Of course I do.  If you're new the Fallout franchise then you'll love this game.  If you're an old RPG veteran looking to make a comeback you might disappointed but will stil love the eye-candy.  I would suggest getting a couple of the Nexus favorite mods (Full Dialogue Interface to replace the horrible default Dialog system) and DEF_UI would be a good idea as well if you want it to be more immersive.
Other than that its a beautiful game.
UPDATE:  I'll be blunt; the Creation Club feature is not only unsettling but downright exploitive at times.  I'll freely admit that I did purchase the Horse Armor, Gauss Rifle and Modular Backpack.  That sadly will be the limit because everything else is cosmetic and is on many fronts free from the Nexus.  On occasion Nexus mods are superior (the Chinese Stealth armor for example).  I will not downvote Fallout 4, but neither will I give it high praise from what looks like Bethesda starting to take advice from Activision and EA Games on how to exploit their customers.
