A computer mouse is a pointing device (hand control) that detects two-dimensional motion relative to a surface. This motion is typically translated into the motion of a pointer on a display, which allows a smooth control of the graphical user interface.
Physically, a mouse consists of an object held in one's hand, with one or more buttons. Mice often also feature other elements, such as touch surfaces and "wheels", which enable additional control and dimensional input.
A mouse typically controls the motion of a pointer in two dimensions in a graphical user interface (GUI). The mouse turns movements of the hand backward and forward, left and right into equivalent electronic signals that in turn are used to move the pointer.
The relative movements of the mouse on the surface are applied to the position of the pointer on the screen, which signals the point where actions of the user take place, so hand movements are replicated by the pointer. Clicking or hovering (stopping movement while the cursor is within the bounds of an area) can select files, programs or actions from a list of names, or (in graphical interfaces) through small images called "icons" and other elements. For example, a text file might be represented by a picture of a paper notebook and clicking while the cursor hovers this icon might cause a text editing program to open the file in a window.
Different ways of operating the mouse cause specific things to happen in the GUI:[36]
Click: pressing and releasing a button.
(left) Single-click: clicking the main button.
(left) Double-click: clicking the button two times in quick succession counts as a different gesture than two separate single clicks.
(left) Triple-click: clicking the button three times in quick succession counts as a different gesture than three separate single clicks. Triple clicks are far less common in traditional navigation.
Right-click: clicking the secondary button, or clicking with two fingers. (This brings a menu with different options depending on the software)
Middle-click: clicking the tertiary button.
Drag and drop: pressing and holding a button, then moving the mouse without releasing. (Using the command "drag with the right mouse button" instead of just "drag" when one instructs a user to drag an object while holding the right mouse button down instead of the more commonly used left mouse button.)
Mouse button chording (a.k.a. Rocker navigation).
Combination of right-click then left-click.
Combination of left-click then right-click or keyboard letter.
Combination of left or right-click and the mouse wheel.
Clicking while holding down a modifier key.
Moving the pointer a long distance: When a practical limit of mouse movement is reached, one lifts up the mouse, brings it to the opposite edge of the working area while it is held above the surface, and then replaces it down onto the working surface. This is often not necessary, because acceleration software detects fast movement, and moves the pointer significantly faster in proportion than for slow mouse motion.
Multi-touch: this method is similar to a multi-touch trackpad on a laptop with support for tap input for multiple fingers, the most famous example being the Apple Magic Mouse.
Mouse gestures
Main article: Pointing device gesture
Users can also employ mice gesturally; meaning that a stylized motion of the mouse cursor itself, called a "gesture", can issue a command or map to a specific action. For example, in a drawing program, moving the mouse in a rapid "x" motion over a shape might delete the shape.
Gestural interfaces occur more rarely than plain pointing-and-clicking; and people often find them more difficult to use, because they require finer motor control from the user. However, a few gestural conventions have become widespread, including the drag and drop gesture, in which:
The user presses the mouse button while the mouse cursor hovers over an interface object
The user moves the cursor to a different location while holding the button down
The user releases the mouse button
For example, a user might drag-and-drop a picture representing a file onto a picture of a trash can, thus instructing the system to delete the file.
Standard semantic gestures include:
Crossing-based goal
Drag and drop
Menu traversal
Pointing
Rollover (Mouseover)
Selection

This is XCOM Enemy Unknown ultra enhanced edition. This is more and better. This is pure XCOM turn-based strategy.
XCOM 2 is all the good things the original had (as well as the bad things too) with a lot of new stuff.
Now you are behind the enemies lines, XCOM becomes the underdog, acting furtively, in the shadows, they are now an organization declared criminal by the new order...  The time has come to reclaim our world. Now they are not fighting an invasion force, the XCOM project are now against a greater more organised force, with power and resources. And they are really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with you.
The new concepts, guerrilla tactics, the implementation of stealth, new enemies, a good variety of mission types, the customization of the weapons (you can add ons like scopes, lanterns, silencers,  enhanced ammunition... modify many aspects), of your soldiers (now you'll miss 'em when they die, if the moment comes... and trust me, surely come), can modify their aspect in a very deep way (but all the male faces are ugly as hell) there's a high level of customization. Your headquarter is really badass now.
The maps are open now, you can move about the map freely, until you either stumble into range of an enemy or decide open fire on them, so, this is the guerrilla aspect of the game, you can now prepare an ambush, seek for the better positions before a gunfire or even almost end a fight before the enemies can react at your presence. but the situations can become in a different, very bad for you, scenario in a heartbeat, so you need a plan B, always.
The combat feel so agil and natural. The game is very more dynamic this time. Fights are brutal, raw and complex. The game is really challenging and tough, doesn't forgive a mistake.
The environments are procedural battlefields, high-quality procedurally generated maps, there is slums, city centres, forest, suburban spaces, all interesting, richly detailed, destroyable (explosions can start fires that propagate, for example), interactives... (at this point maybe you got your suspicions... the game is amazing in every aspect!)
XCOM has a real evocative history now for the first time, with cutscenes, and remarkable characters with a backstory and its own opinions. People you want to save.
There are now Dark Events, and will change the game in unpredictable ways. Dark events are "counter-operations" undertaken by Advent against XCOM.
It's the more exciting turn-based tactical game ever made.
Of course it has its minor flaws, soldiers firing the same enemy during overwatch, missing high chance shots with an average of 87.3%... but we're here to suffer, weapons through walls, some glitches, "weird walls" when you enter in a building... but nothing really remarkable.
The graphics aren't spectacular neither the animations.
It's true that the game needs much better optimization, quite. I can run The Division beta or The Witcher 3 on ultra and 60fps but XCOM barely runs, on menus (yeah weird), about 20fps, in battle runs fine.
About mods and steam workshop. XCOM 2 has Steam Workshop support, this will improve the game in many ways and make it probably endless. Long War Studios (the team behind XCOM: Enemy Unknown's Long War overhaul) has already produced three mods for XCOM 2, all of which are playable from launch, highly welcome move! This feels like a free DLC because Long War Studios teamed up with developer Firaxis Games, and they've been working together!! so this mods perfectly fit with the core of the game, without problems or complications.

Tl;dr: Very linear game, with variety little variety of ways to actually (as in viable ways to) playthrough the game. If you enjoy playing through the souls games once or twice you'll like it. if you like to play games co-op you'll also have a lot of fun with friends. If you expect hundreds of hours and tons of playthroughs you will not like it.
Because I don't recommend this from my standpoint, this will be more of a critique than a review, explaining what makes me not recommend it rather than reviewing its good sides too.
Since you aren't obsessive over the souls games and haven't put over a thousand hours into each of them other than 3, like I have, you'll probably enjoy this game.
What matters to me in a souls game isn't the story or lore. I really don't care about those things. I have played each other to insane degrees because playing through each of the other ones other than 3 is really fun and varied.
There are a ton of fun ways to play through Demons Souls. The floodgates are loose the second you're done with 1-1. Go rush Firelurker and make a meat cleaver, hyper mode with the white bow, kill Ostrava and get Demon Brandt, then later go kill every boss with broken magic, drain another player of a soul level, and break someones equipment completely.
Every playthrough you could go about in a million different ways, go through whichever order you liked, and use pretty much anything you wanted to and it'd be viable. Everything in that game was pretty much broken and really highly damaging, and there was always a way to playthrough a game with a specific weapon even if it wasn't already great.
The same thing holds true in Dark Souls, although you can't go and do anything from the beginning, you can still do a lot. Get a weapon to +15 before killing Taurus demon, power within and red tearstone existed and you could pick them up immediately at the start, you could also get great heal and WotG before even ringing a bell, get a chaos weapon before ringing your second bell, get your pyromancy flame ascended, and get a great early start by going straight to the catacombs and making a fire infused weapon, or even break the game by getting a lucky drop with a black knight.
I can't praise Ds2 as much as those two because of well... a lot of things that I'd rather not get into at the moment, but it still had multiple ways to start and finish the games, wasn't incredibly linear and most weapons felt fun and viable.
What I love about those games is that you can do so many different playthroughs, with so many different weapons, and its still fun. Theres so many options right from the start and not tooo much is locked till the end.
That's why I don't enjoy Dark Souls 3 that much and I personally can't reccommend it if you're like me.
You can do dex, you can do some strength, but most of the game only feels good if you're using fast, refined infused weapons on a quality build. The game has a speed similar to bloodborne, so playing slow weapons just honestly feels bad, and in the later half of the game the nice feeling of being able to destroy enemies with charge attacks from a slow weapon goes away, and its faster and easier to kill them with a straight sword or katana, which it almost always is in this game. Fast weapons are king, and quality builds are what is what I'd say to be the only good feeling way to playthrough this game. 40/40 and a straight sword.
Armor and defense barely matters. Vitality feels like a dead stat because of this.
Pure Magic and Faith playthroughs essentially don't exist, either.
You have to put at least 60 into your stat, designate 3 of your ring slots for boosts of your magic type, and use a specific hat and offhand weapon in magics case, all while pumping attunement, and assigning estus that you could be using to heal to ashen estus, all for you to be able to the same damage as going up and hitting an enemy with two r1's.
And because of the speed of enemies hitting enemies with the actual good spells and miracles, is really, really hard.
Basically every enemy has huge closing-the-gap lunge attacks that make it really hard to keep a safe distance from them, and even when you are, hitting them becomes harder. It feels almost like you DO have to stay close to them to hit while basically playing like you're a melee character. Whatever made magic fun in the other games definitely isn't here, and its more trouble that its worth. And on a side note, offensive miracles are even worse at doing damage than sorcery.
While speaking of miracles its interesting to point out that the starting heals are of worse fp usage than just using estus. You can't really become a healer until you get great heal, when the ashen estus outweighs the regular estus healing (as long as you can cast it twice and your estus can replinish all your fp), but by that point you're basically halfway through the game, which is about how all of the spells' placements feel. Obviously the best offensive spells should be toward the end of the game but they put bad stuff there too. Would it really be hard to place a 15 faith requirement buff thats actually bad not at the last area of the game? The only way to playthrough with magic is to either play most of the game with a raw astora sword, and finish with your real build, or to use a strength/dex/quality build with magic on the side for buffs. Actually relying on pure magic and offensive miracles throughout the game feels really bad with how all the good stuff is closer to the end than the beginning.
It feels that way with a lot of armor and weapons as well, and the real reason for that is that the whole game is too linear. Every start to the playthrough goes in the exact same orders, and finishes in about the same order too. There is little to no branching off in this game. It's tiring to start a playthrough to just kill the same enemies in the same order and pickup the same items, more than like 3 times, and maybe feel like you have a real build towards the end. You can decide to go to one area early two times in the game, with an additional area being fully optional. It just doesn't interest me. You can't go to 4-1 and grab the falchion, jump in the well and kill the rotten twice for an insanely powerful weapon, or kill the 4 Kings Immidiately and become a Darkwraith way too early. You CAN kill the dancer early, which can get you neat stuff early on but you get walled off from the actual unique and good items found in the archives, but that just isn't enough freedom for me.
I can't really recommend the game from my standpoint because it feels like playing through the game feels exactly the same every time, and it just isn't meant to be played without a quality melee build and a straight sword, which just goes against what I find fun in these games. I know a lot of this sounded like specific whining, and it was specific whining, but thats what made me not like this as much as the others. It's just not interesting to playthrough more than once.

MEDIOCRE OPEN-WORLD SHOOTER. TERRIBLE FALLOUT GAME.
The Good:
+ Power Armor: Some people might not like that it's more of a vehicle now rather than a suit of armor you put on, but I really enjoyed feeling like a walking tank. I always modded my Fallout 3/NV games to give me a similar experience. I also enjoy all the customization of Power Armor.
+ Settlement Building: It was fun for the most part, though totally lacking in practicality. If there was an actual need to defend and build settlements, it would have been a great addition to the gameplay (larger settlements more at risk of large raids, but larger rewards etc.). However, the execution was lacking. Only listing this as a positive because it was a welcomed addition, but completely half baked.
+ Weapon Customization: Not much to say. It's nice that weapon customization was a feature in the base game instead of having to rely on mods. A step in the right direction. However, a general lack of unique weapons and ammunition (for instance all energy weapons use the same ammo except for the gatling laser).
The Bad:
- Power Armor: Yes, I know I listed it as a positive, but the implementation of Power Armor in terms of character progression/story is HORRIBLE. You get a full suit, which is usually reserved for endgame, in the first 30 minutes after you leave the vault. Any kind of achievement you may have as a player of actually getting a highend item like Power Armor is lost when it's just handed to you from the start.
- Removal of Skills, Traits, and Conversation Skill Checks: Skills being merged with perks, removal of special traits, and a super high level cap means that all your characters will eventually become superpowered "jack of all trades". You'll have difficulty creating unique characters for a second playthrough because they'll all feel and play the same. There's also no point in trying to make a science character and having the option of using your knowledge in dialogue choices, or pumping up strength to intimidate people, because dialogue is only affected by charisma. This is a complete step backwards from previous titles.
- Removal of Item Condition and Alternative Ammo: I think item condition is something that made Fallout feel more like you're fighting for survival. You had to make sure your weapons and armor were in good condition before heading out. It also had a huge impact on the economy, where you could make caps repairing damaged weapons or armor you find. As a player, you had to make the choice if the weight was worth the condition and value of the item. Now, you can just pick up anything you find with complete disregard, or use your weapon as freely as you want without having to worry about anything but ammo. You can't even change ammo types to use higher damage ammo types, but with the trade-off of weapon degradation. This wasn't "streamlining" the current system, it was removing gameplay. Bethesda thought Power Armor was important enough for the player to need to repair, but nothing else. Why?
- Damage Resist instead of Damage Threshold: DT is a much better system than DR. It made for more interesting gameplay and firefights. So, now instead of having to use high damage, low ROF weapons to kill heavily armored opponents, just shoot them repeatedly with whatever you have until they die.
- Lack of Choice: You only get 4 dialogue options and they are all rather bland and essentially lead to the same outcome. No branching dialogue paths or different way to approach conversations with NPCs.
- Boring Story: The story is subpar and uninspired. This seems to be a trend with Bethesda's Fallout games. Fallout 3 find your dad. Fallout 4 find your son. Yeah... really original premise right there Bethesda. What's worse is that the writing ties you into a single character and doesn't leave you many options to roleplay as a different character. In fact, a lot of NPC dialogue is tied to the main story and finding your son that any alternate start mods are difficult to create without major changes in dialogue.
- Voiced Protagonist: Nice try, but again, total failure of execution. You'd think with all the money Bethesda makes that they could hire more than just 1 male protagonist voice actor and 1 female protagonist voice actor. You give us an elaborate character creator but only 1 voice per gender. If you're going to use a voiced protagonist, do it right and give us options. Why does my character that looks like Vin Diesel sound like the most generic white dude from Irvine? At least give us a built in option to disable it and go back to the original style of dialogue; you did it with the "cinematic" camera. We shouldn't have to rely on mods to fix this.
- Cinematic Camera: As I said previously, you can turn it off, but the implementation of it is horrible. It always freaks out during dialogue, either whipping around violently or focusing on places other than the character that's speaking (I don't need to see my character's crotch while he's speaking, thanks).
- Lack of Depth, Interesting Quests, overuse of Radiant Quests: If I have to do another goddamn Minuteman Radiant Quest I'm going to lose my mind. If my character is a general, why am I doing the grunt work while all the people under my command stand around and do nothing? You can't take soldiers with you or send them to defend or attack places for you. I always avoid Minutemen quests because of this. What makes this even worse is that most quests, not just radiant quests, are solved by going from point A to point B and killing everyone. There's rarely different ways to approach a quest and if there is, it's usually not worth it for the rewards/effort.
- Uninteresting World: I'll admit, I wasn't a huge fan of the New Vegas map, but I still found myself excited to explore and see a lot of unique locations. Personally, I think Fallout 3 had the best world to explore with how dense it was and all the unique landmarks, plus the metro. Fallout 4's map is beautiful and densely populated with locations, but nothing very unique that stands out. I still have fond memories of the Brotherhood fighting entrenched Super Mutants in the Capital Mall, all the museums, Temple of the Union, Underworld, Old Olney and it's population of Deathclaws, Tenpenny Tower, Rivet City etc.. The most interesting and unique location of Fallout 4 is the Glowing Sea and the Third Rail and that's about it.
- Subpar Graphics, Poor Optimization, and Old Engine: Bethesda seriously needs to update to a new engine instead of cutting corner. The Creation Engine cannot handle the world they're trying to create. I have a very high-end PC and I still get dips into the 20s sometimes when I'm in downtown Boston. This is completely unacceptable when there are more and more open-world games on the market. Maybe Bethesda could have gotten away with this several years ago, but not anymore. While I'm not usually a stickler for graphics, they're not up to snuff for what other developers are doing. Bethesda actually used to produce huge open-world games like Oblivion that still had very good graphics for the time. I'm not expecting a miracle, but if a smaller developer like CDProjekt Red can create a beautiful open-world game, then there's no excuse for Bethesda.
- Game Balance: The game is incredibly easy on normal settings. On the most difficult settings, Bethesda's idea of a challenge is to turn enemies into bullet sponges while you take more damage. All this accomplishes is just prolonging fights, but doesn't actually add a huge amount of challenge. I wish the "survival" difficulty was more of a glass cannon approach, similar to the Metro or STALKER games, where you'll die in 1-5 hits but so will a lot of enemies (except for Super Mutants, Robots, Yao Guai, or Deathclaws).

A computer mouse is a pointing device (hand control) that detects two-dimensional motion relative to a surface. This motion is typically translated into the motion of a pointer on a display, which allows a smooth control of the graphical user interface.
Physically, a mouse consists of an object held in one's hand, with one or more buttons. Mice often also feature other elements, such as touch surfaces and "wheels", which enable additional control and dimensional input.
A mouse typically controls the motion of a pointer in two dimensions in a graphical user interface (GUI). The mouse turns movements of the hand backward and forward, left and right into equivalent electronic signals that in turn are used to move the pointer.
The relative movements of the mouse on the surface are applied to the position of the pointer on the screen, which signals the point where actions of the user take place, so hand movements are replicated by the pointer. Clicking or hovering (stopping movement while the cursor is within the bounds of an area) can select files, programs or actions from a list of names, or (in graphical interfaces) through small images called "icons" and other elements. For example, a text file might be represented by a picture of a paper notebook and clicking while the cursor hovers this icon might cause a text editing program to open the file in a window.
Different ways of operating the mouse cause specific things to happen in the GUI:[36]
Click: pressing and releasing a button.
(left) Single-click: clicking the main button.
(left) Double-click: clicking the button two times in quick succession counts as a different gesture than two separate single clicks.
(left) Triple-click: clicking the button three times in quick succession counts as a different gesture than three separate single clicks. Triple clicks are far less common in traditional navigation.
Right-click: clicking the secondary button, or clicking with two fingers. (This brings a menu with different options depending on the software)
Middle-click: clicking the tertiary button.
Drag and drop: pressing and holding a button, then moving the mouse without releasing. (Using the command "drag with the right mouse button" instead of just "drag" when one instructs a user to drag an object while holding the right mouse button down instead of the more commonly used left mouse button.)
Mouse button chording (a.k.a. Rocker navigation).
Combination of right-click then left-click.
Combination of left-click then right-click or keyboard letter.
Combination of left or right-click and the mouse wheel.
Clicking while holding down a modifier key.
Moving the pointer a long distance: When a practical limit of mouse movement is reached, one lifts up the mouse, brings it to the opposite edge of the working area while it is held above the surface, and then replaces it down onto the working surface. This is often not necessary, because acceleration software detects fast movement, and moves the pointer significantly faster in proportion than for slow mouse motion.
Multi-touch: this method is similar to a multi-touch trackpad on a laptop with support for tap input for multiple fingers, the most famous example being the Apple Magic Mouse.
Mouse gestures
Main article: Pointing device gesture
Users can also employ mice gesturally; meaning that a stylized motion of the mouse cursor itself, called a "gesture", can issue a command or map to a specific action. For example, in a drawing program, moving the mouse in a rapid "x" motion over a shape might delete the shape.
Gestural interfaces occur more rarely than plain pointing-and-clicking; and people often find them more difficult to use, because they require finer motor control from the user. However, a few gestural conventions have become widespread, including the drag and drop gesture, in which:
The user presses the mouse button while the mouse cursor hovers over an interface object
The user moves the cursor to a different location while holding the button down
The user releases the mouse button
For example, a user might drag-and-drop a picture representing a file onto a picture of a trash can, thus instructing the system to delete the file.
Standard semantic gestures include:
Crossing-based goal
Drag and drop
Menu traversal
Pointing
Rollover (Mouseover)
Selection

It's fun to have the settlers you armed fight side by side with you, and there are plenty of quests to go around. Tl;dr: Very linear game, with variety little variety of ways to actually (as in viable ways to) playthrough the game. If you enjoy playing through the souls games once or twice you'll like it. if you like to play games co-op you'll also have a lot of fun with friends. If you expect hundreds of hours and tons of playthroughs you will not like it.
Because I don't recommend this from my standpoint, this will be more of a critique than a review, explaining what makes me not recommend it rather than reviewing its good sides too.
Since you aren't obsessive over the souls games and haven't put over a thousand hours into each of them other than 3, like I have, you'll probably enjoy this game.
What matters to me in a souls game isn't the story or lore. I really don't care about those things. I have played each other to insane degrees because playing through each of the other ones other than 3 is really fun and varied.
There are a ton of fun ways to play through Demons Souls. The floodgates are loose the second you're done with 1-1. Go rush Firelurker and make a meat cleaver, hyper mode with the white bow, kill Ostrava and get Demon Brandt, then later go kill every boss with broken magic, drain another player of a soul level, and break someones equipment completely.
Every playthrough you could go about in a million different ways, go through whichever order you liked, and use pretty much anything you wanted to and it'd be viable. Everything in that game was pretty much broken and really highly damaging, and there was always a way to playthrough a game with a specific weapon even if it wasn't already great.
The same thing holds true in Dark Souls, although you can't go and do anything from the beginning, you can still do a lot. Get a weapon to +15 before killing Taurus demon, power within and red tearstone existed and you could pick them up immediately at the start, you could also get great heal and WotG before even ringing a bell, get a chaos weapon before ringing your second bell, get your pyromancy flame ascended, and get a great early start by going straight to the catacombs and making a fire infused weapon, or even break the game by getting a lucky drop with a black knight.
I can't praise Ds2 as much as those two because of well... a lot of things that I'd rather not get into at the moment, but it still had multiple ways to start and finish the games, wasn't incredibly linear and most weapons felt fun and viable.
What I love about those games is that you can do so many different playthroughs, with so many different weapons, and its still fun. Theres so many options right from the start and not tooo much is locked till the end.
That's why I don't enjoy Dark Souls 3 that much and I personally can't reccommend it if you're like me.
You can do dex, you can do some strength, but most of the game only feels good if you're using fast, refined infused weapons on a quality build. The game has a speed similar to bloodborne, so playing slow weapons just honestly feels bad, and in the later half of the game the nice feeling of being able to destroy enemies with charge attacks from a slow weapon goes away, and its faster and easier to kill them with a straight sword or katana, which it almost always is in this game. Fast weapons are king, and quality builds are what is what I'd say to be the only good feeling way to playthrough this game. 40/40 and a straight sword.
Armor and defense barely matters. Vitality feels like a dead stat because of this.
Pure Magic and Faith playthroughs essentially don't exist, either.
You have to put at least 60 into your stat, designate 3 of your ring slots for boosts of your magic type, and use a specific hat and offhand weapon in magics case, all while pumping attunement, and assigning estus that you could be using to heal to ashen estus, all for you to be able to the same damage as going up and hitting an enemy with two r1's.
And because of the speed of enemies hitting enemies with the actual good spells and miracles, is really, really hard.
Basically every enemy has huge closing-the-gap lunge attacks that make it really hard to keep a safe distance from them, and even when you are, hitting them becomes harder. It feels almost like you DO have to stay close to them to hit while basically playing like you're a melee character. Whatever made magic fun in the other games definitely isn't here, and its more trouble that its worth. And on a side note, offensive miracles are even worse at doing damage than sorcery.
While speaking of miracles its interesting to point out that the starting heals are of worse fp usage than just using estus. You can't really become a healer until you get great heal, when the ashen estus outweighs the regular estus healing (as long as you can cast it twice and your estus can replinish all your fp), but by that point you're basically halfway through the game, which is about how all of the spells' placements feel. Obviously the best offensive spells should be toward the end of the game but they put bad stuff there too. Would it really be hard to place a 15 faith requirement buff thats actually bad not at the last area of the game? The only way to playthrough with magic is to either play most of the game with a raw astora sword, and finish with your real build, or to use a strength/dex/quality build with magic on the side for buffs. Actually relying on pure magic and offensive miracles throughout the game feels really bad with how all the good stuff is closer to the end than the beginning.
It feels that way with a lot of armor and weapons as well, and the real reason for that is that the whole game is too linear. Every start to the playthrough goes in the exact same orders, and finishes in about the same order too. There is little to no branching off in this game. It's tiring to start a playthrough to just kill the same enemies in the same order and pickup the same items, more than like 3 times, and maybe feel like you have a real build towards the end. You can decide to go to one area early two times in the game, with an additional area being fully optional. It just doesn't interest me. You can't go to 4-1 and grab the falchion, jump in the well and kill the rotten twice for an insanely powerful weapon, or kill the 4 Kings Immidiately and become a Darkwraith way too early. You CAN kill the dancer early, which can get you neat stuff early on but you get walled off from the actual unique and good items found in the archives, but that just isn't enough freedom for me.
I can't really recommend the game from my standpoint because it feels like playing through the game feels exactly the same every time, and it just isn't meant to be played without a quality melee build and a straight sword, which just goes against what I find fun in these games. I know a lot of this sounded like specific whining, and it was specific whining, but thats what made me not like this as much as the others. It's just not interesting to playthrough more than once.

I am a huge and I repeat huge fan of the fallout series, I have an ungodly amount of hours in 3 and NV on the Xbox 360 and over 130 hrs from when I had fallout 4 on the Xbox one. So obviously i really like fallout, but is this one worth your time both hardcore fallout fans and new players? Let's find out.
Story: The story is actually in my opinion pretty good, you play as a create a character known as the sole survivor. The world goes to crap, so you go to your vault for safety only to find out you're part of an experiment, only to wake up 200 years later with your son kidnapped and your wife dead. So you go out on an adventure to rescue him where you'll run into various factions who will test your morals. The story goes deeper and does twist here and there and is a bit more ambitious then the stories of 3 or NV. However a change to gameplay does affect the story in a way that can't match the previous two games but we'll get to that later. This game doesn't look half bad, ran 1080p 30FPS on the Xbox one on my 1050ti superclocked with an I3 4170 60 is no problem. Overall the story is actually really good and an actual main reason to play the game.
Gameplay: Now this is where fallout 4 changes pretty significantly, fallout is no longer an open world RPG with some first person shooter elements, but now an open world first person shooter with some RPG elements. First let's talk about the first person shooting, yes it is vastly improved over the mediocre shooting of both NV and 3. You actually don't need to depend on the V.A.T.S. system to accurately line up a shot. While the RPG elements have been reduced the fallout style framework is still there. This is still a massive world with goof characters that you can get yourself lost in for hours upon hours. The side quests are pretty good except for a certain type of side quests that we will discuss later. Overall the gameplay is still as fun as it's ever been, but there are some drawbacks to this particular fallout game.
Bad stuff: Now this stuff is pretty subjective, but as a big fallout fan I have to criticize this stuff. The RPG elements have been reduced significantly. The karma system that influenced how people see you through your actions, gone. Weapon and armor repair system  (not including power armor), gone. Faction reputations are there in a sense, but it has been streamlined compared to NV. The skill system is gone (which has been there since fallout 1) and is now instead replaced with a simplified perk chart. Now one could make the argument that obsidian made new Vegas so not all the awesome RPG elements from there will be in a Bethesda made game. But many of these were in 3 which was made by Bethesda so it's weird that they would remove them. The dialogue tree is also simplified, while a good amount of choices will matter there will also be a good amount that don't. Again I don't see why they made an unnecessary change to it. Now let's talk about something else that's a hit or miss and that's the settlement system. The option is given you to rebuild the wasteland by establishing settlements which does tie into a faction. Now if you're the creative type you may enjoy it alot, however this will give you an endless stream of repetitive quests like an MMO so be cautious.
Final verdict: I know it sounds like I was very critical of 4 But truth be told the main reason I loved fallout was for its Lore and characters. Which thankfully in this game is still very good. That being said I have two recommendations, If you're new to the series or you're a fan who can look past these RPG reductions, do pick this up at full price it is a great game. If you're a hardcore fan i can understand your reservations, while RPG wise it's not as good as 3 or NV it is still worth playing through at some point, but more like when it's on sale.

MEDIOCRE OPEN-WORLD SHOOTER. TERRIBLE FALLOUT GAME.
The Good:
+ Power Armor: Some people might not like that it's more of a vehicle now rather than a suit of armor you put on, but I really enjoyed feeling like a walking tank. I always modded my Fallout 3/NV games to give me a similar experience. I also enjoy all the customization of Power Armor.
+ Settlement Building: It was fun for the most part, though totally lacking in practicality. If there was an actual need to defend and build settlements, it would have been a great addition to the gameplay (larger settlements more at risk of large raids, but larger rewards etc.). However, the execution was lacking. Only listing this as a positive because it was a welcomed addition, but completely half baked.
+ Weapon Customization: Not much to say. It's nice that weapon customization was a feature in the base game instead of having to rely on mods. A step in the right direction. However, a general lack of unique weapons and ammunition (for instance all energy weapons use the same ammo except for the gatling laser).
The Bad:
- Power Armor: Yes, I know I listed it as a positive, but the implementation of Power Armor in terms of character progression/story is HORRIBLE. You get a full suit, which is usually reserved for endgame, in the first 30 minutes after you leave the vault. Any kind of achievement you may have as a player of actually getting a highend item like Power Armor is lost when it's just handed to you from the start.
- Removal of Skills, Traits, and Conversation Skill Checks: Skills being merged with perks, removal of special traits, and a super high level cap means that all your characters will eventually become superpowered "jack of all trades". You'll have difficulty creating unique characters for a second playthrough because they'll all feel and play the same. There's also no point in trying to make a science character and having the option of using your knowledge in dialogue choices, or pumping up strength to intimidate people, because dialogue is only affected by charisma. This is a complete step backwards from previous titles.
- Removal of Item Condition and Alternative Ammo: I think item condition is something that made Fallout feel more like you're fighting for survival. You had to make sure your weapons and armor were in good condition before heading out. It also had a huge impact on the economy, where you could make caps repairing damaged weapons or armor you find. As a player, you had to make the choice if the weight was worth the condition and value of the item. Now, you can just pick up anything you find with complete disregard, or use your weapon as freely as you want without having to worry about anything but ammo. You can't even change ammo types to use higher damage ammo types, but with the trade-off of weapon degradation. This wasn't "streamlining" the current system, it was removing gameplay. Bethesda thought Power Armor was important enough for the player to need to repair, but nothing else. Why?
- Damage Resist instead of Damage Threshold: DT is a much better system than DR. It made for more interesting gameplay and firefights. So, now instead of having to use high damage, low ROF weapons to kill heavily armored opponents, just shoot them repeatedly with whatever you have until they die.
- Lack of Choice: You only get 4 dialogue options and they are all rather bland and essentially lead to the same outcome. No branching dialogue paths or different way to approach conversations with NPCs.
- Boring Story: The story is subpar and uninspired. This seems to be a trend with Bethesda's Fallout games. Fallout 3 find your dad. Fallout 4 find your son. Yeah... really original premise right there Bethesda. What's worse is that the writing ties you into a single character and doesn't leave you many options to roleplay as a different character. In fact, a lot of NPC dialogue is tied to the main story and finding your son that any alternate start mods are difficult to create without major changes in dialogue.
- Voiced Protagonist: Nice try, but again, total failure of execution. You'd think with all the money Bethesda makes that they could hire more than just 1 male protagonist voice actor and 1 female protagonist voice actor. You give us an elaborate character creator but only 1 voice per gender. If you're going to use a voiced protagonist, do it right and give us options. Why does my character that looks like Vin Diesel sound like the most generic white dude from Irvine? At least give us a built in option to disable it and go back to the original style of dialogue; you did it with the "cinematic" camera. We shouldn't have to rely on mods to fix this.
- Cinematic Camera: As I said previously, you can turn it off, but the implementation of it is horrible. It always freaks out during dialogue, either whipping around violently or focusing on places other than the character that's speaking (I don't need to see my character's crotch while he's speaking, thanks).
- Lack of Depth, Interesting Quests, overuse of Radiant Quests: If I have to do another goddamn Minuteman Radiant Quest I'm going to lose my mind. If my character is a general, why am I doing the grunt work while all the people under my command stand around and do nothing? You can't take soldiers with you or send them to defend or attack places for you. I always avoid Minutemen quests because of this. What makes this even worse is that most quests, not just radiant quests, are solved by going from point A to point B and killing everyone. There's rarely different ways to approach a quest and if there is, it's usually not worth it for the rewards/effort.
- Uninteresting World: I'll admit, I wasn't a huge fan of the New Vegas map, but I still found myself excited to explore and see a lot of unique locations. Personally, I think Fallout 3 had the best world to explore with how dense it was and all the unique landmarks, plus the metro. Fallout 4's map is beautiful and densely populated with locations, but nothing very unique that stands out. I still have fond memories of the Brotherhood fighting entrenched Super Mutants in the Capital Mall, all the museums, Temple of the Union, Underworld, Old Olney and it's population of Deathclaws, Tenpenny Tower, Rivet City etc.. The most interesting and unique location of Fallout 4 is the Glowing Sea and the Third Rail and that's about it.
- Subpar Graphics, Poor Optimization, and Old Engine: Bethesda seriously needs to update to a new engine instead of cutting corner. The Creation Engine cannot handle the world they're trying to create. I have a very high-end PC and I still get dips into the 20s sometimes when I'm in downtown Boston. This is completely unacceptable when there are more and more open-world games on the market. Maybe Bethesda could have gotten away with this several years ago, but not anymore. While I'm not usually a stickler for graphics, they're not up to snuff for what other developers are doing. Bethesda actually used to produce huge open-world games like Oblivion that still had very good graphics for the time. I'm not expecting a miracle, but if a smaller developer like CDProjekt Red can create a beautiful open-world game, then there's no excuse for Bethesda.
- Game Balance: The game is incredibly easy on normal settings. On the most difficult settings, Bethesda's idea of a challenge is to turn enemies into bullet sponges while you take more damage. All this accomplishes is just prolonging fights, but doesn't actually add a huge amount of challenge. I wish the "survival" difficulty was more of a glass cannon approach, similar to the Metro or STALKER games, where you'll die in 1-5 hits but so will a lot of enemies (except for Super Mutants, Robots, Yao Guai, or Deathclaws).

Tl;dr: Very linear game, with variety little variety of ways to actually (as in viable ways to) playthrough the game. If you enjoy playing through the souls games once or twice you'll like it. if you like to play games co-op you'll also have a lot of fun with friends. If you expect hundreds of hours and tons of playthroughs you will not like it.
Because I don't recommend this from my standpoint, this will be more of a critique than a review, explaining what makes me not recommend it rather than reviewing its good sides too.
Since you aren't obsessive over the souls games and haven't put over a thousand hours into each of them other than 3, like I have, you'll probably enjoy this game.
What matters to me in a souls game isn't the story or lore. I really don't care about those things. I have played each other to insane degrees because playing through each of the other ones other than 3 is really fun and varied.
There are a ton of fun ways to play through Demons Souls. The floodgates are loose the second you're done with 1-1. Go rush Firelurker and make a meat cleaver, hyper mode with the white bow, kill Ostrava and get Demon Brandt, then later go kill every boss with broken magic, drain another player of a soul level, and break someones equipment completely.
Every playthrough you could go about in a million different ways, go through whichever order you liked, and use pretty much anything you wanted to and it'd be viable. Everything in that game was pretty much broken and really highly damaging, and there was always a way to playthrough a game with a specific weapon even if it wasn't already great.
The same thing holds true in Dark Souls, although you can't go and do anything from the beginning, you can still do a lot. Get a weapon to +15 before killing Taurus demon, power within and red tearstone existed and you could pick them up immediately at the start, you could also get great heal and WotG before even ringing a bell, get a chaos weapon before ringing your second bell, get your pyromancy flame ascended, and get a great early start by going straight to the catacombs and making a fire infused weapon, or even break the game by getting a lucky drop with a black knight.
I can't praise Ds2 as much as those two because of well... a lot of things that I'd rather not get into at the moment, but it still had multiple ways to start and finish the games, wasn't incredibly linear and most weapons felt fun and viable.
What I love about those games is that you can do so many different playthroughs, with so many different weapons, and its still fun. Theres so many options right from the start and not tooo much is locked till the end.
That's why I don't enjoy Dark Souls 3 that much and I personally can't reccommend it if you're like me.
You can do dex, you can do some strength, but most of the game only feels good if you're using fast, refined infused weapons on a quality build. The game has a speed similar to bloodborne, so playing slow weapons just honestly feels bad, and in the later half of the game the nice feeling of being able to destroy enemies with charge attacks from a slow weapon goes away, and its faster and easier to kill them with a straight sword or katana, which it almost always is in this game. Fast weapons are king, and quality builds are what is what I'd say to be the only good feeling way to playthrough this game. 40/40 and a straight sword.
Armor and defense barely matters. Vitality feels like a dead stat because of this.
Pure Magic and Faith playthroughs essentially don't exist, either.
You have to put at least 60 into your stat, designate 3 of your ring slots for boosts of your magic type, and use a specific hat and offhand weapon in magics case, all while pumping attunement, and assigning estus that you could be using to heal to ashen estus, all for you to be able to the same damage as going up and hitting an enemy with two r1's.
And because of the speed of enemies hitting enemies with the actual good spells and miracles, is really, really hard.
Basically every enemy has huge closing-the-gap lunge attacks that make it really hard to keep a safe distance from them, and even when you are, hitting them becomes harder. It feels almost like you DO have to stay close to them to hit while basically playing like you're a melee character. Whatever made magic fun in the other games definitely isn't here, and its more trouble that its worth. And on a side note, offensive miracles are even worse at doing damage than sorcery.
While speaking of miracles its interesting to point out that the starting heals are of worse fp usage than just using estus. You can't really become a healer until you get great heal, when the ashen estus outweighs the regular estus healing (as long as you can cast it twice and your estus can replinish all your fp), but by that point you're basically halfway through the game, which is about how all of the spells' placements feel. Obviously the best offensive spells should be toward the end of the game but they put bad stuff there too. Would it really be hard to place a 15 faith requirement buff thats actually bad not at the last area of the game? The only way to playthrough with magic is to either play most of the game with a raw astora sword, and finish with your real build, or to use a strength/dex/quality build with magic on the side for buffs. Actually relying on pure magic and offensive miracles throughout the game feels really bad with how all the good stuff is closer to the end than the beginning.
It feels that way with a lot of armor and weapons as well, and the real reason for that is that the whole game is too linear. Every start to the playthrough goes in the exact same orders, and finishes in about the same order too. There is little to no branching off in this game. It's tiring to start a playthrough to just kill the same enemies in the same order and pickup the same items, more than like 3 times, and maybe feel like you have a real build towards the end. You can decide to go to one area early two times in the game, with an additional area being fully optional. It just doesn't interest me. You can't go to 4-1 and grab the falchion, jump in the well and kill the rotten twice for an insanely powerful weapon, or kill the 4 Kings Immidiately and become a Darkwraith way too early. You CAN kill the dancer early, which can get you neat stuff early on but you get walled off from the actual unique and good items found in the archives, but that just isn't enough freedom for me.
I can't really recommend the game from my standpoint because it feels like playing through the game feels exactly the same every time, and it just isn't meant to be played without a quality melee build and a straight sword, which just goes against what I find fun in these games. I know a lot of this sounded like specific whining, and it was specific whining, but thats what made me not like this as much as the others. It's just not interesting to playthrough more than once.

So it was around Fall when I started this game during its beta, initially writing it off as some other MMO that tried to spice up the genre by making it look "aeshetically different" as does almost every F2P. However, my friend ranted for a long while about how awesome this game was and how much fun we could have if played with a big group of our buddies, so I decided to give it a shot.
Whew.
Glad I did.
Do note, the beginning may be a little boring. You start off with only a single class and simply kill stuff while mining for minerals and crafting materials along the way. This can feel tedious at first if not accompanied by a friend, as you will feel insignificant in such an endless open world with nothing but one job; level up. You do get the ability to create and customize your own cornerstone though, which is essentially your "home". This can be transported to any unoccupied cornerstone plot that you can easily find anywhere in the world. Some of these cornerstones can be extremely intricate and detailed, even massive at times, despite only being given a small square border to build within. This is only the tip of creativity in Trove, as it gets even bigger once you start a club.
It was like starting a very thick adventure novel. The exposition was slightly drawn out and showed the most uninteresting section of the book; but once it began, it really began. The whole world opened up after playing for about 8 hours, after finally hitting level 10 and starting a club. The prospect of building and construction had always been my incentive to keep playing a game on a long-term basis, so it easily blew my mind when I realized that these creations could be shared with the world as if you were making the game.
On top of that, the grinding is incredibly satisfying. Every major upgrade that you make to your equipment FEELS like a real upgrade, allowing you to progress further and further until you are eventually hailed upon as a god by anyone that sees you do damage on your own, especially at high levels.
Pros:
- Excellent art design (some of it player-made)
- Totally worth your time as a F2P
- Friendly community (for the most part)
- Hours upon hours can be poured into this game with still more to do
- Devs actually have a good sense of humour
- Progression feels good
- Trading is easily accessible
- ♥♥♥♥ING CLUB WORLDS!!!
- Not pay to win
- You can orchestrate an entire song with just blocks
- Mounts are really cool
Cons:
- Limited inventory space
- Slow start
- Can be confusing as to what you can do in the game as a newcomer
- Interesting soundtrack but will get slightly repetitive if you play for a while
- Servers have been slow due to overload since its official release (hopefully those will be fixed soon)
- Dragons take forever to get
All in all, these cons are minor nuisances when playing the actual game as it is a blast to play in the long run. Also, at the time of this review, PvP is apparently going to happen some time soon so yeah hype.

This is the worst Fallout game I've ever played.
That's not to say it's a bad game, because it's not. It stands on its own merits, but it wasn't what I went looking for at first.
The main story failed to grab me. It felt more like a chore than a story, the further I got. That's kinda to be expected, since it's a Bethesda open world RPG, but what saddens me about it is that they seemingly wanted the story to be good. It was obviously a big focus, with the voiced protagonist and so on, but it just falls flat. Atleast there are side quests to keep me happy, right?
No, actually. There are only a few interesting side quests in the whole game. Most of them feel the same, are tied to factions and therefore softlocked behind the main questline, or are part of the radiant quests system. There are a few highlight here and there, but it feels like they are unwilling to go far enough to feel great. There's a feeling of "something is missing".
Character building is a shadow of what it was previously. I don't feel like I'm playing a character with strenghts and weaknesses. I don't have to make choices regarding my characters stats and perks. The new system is more fluid and forgiving, but at the same time takes away uniqueness from every playthrough and player character.
On the other hand combat has gotten a much needed facelift. Now guns actually feel like guns and are less clunky. I have to say that this is something I would've expected from a game released in this day and age, but credit where credit is due. Bethesda managed to make combat enjoyable and feel less like "Oblivion with guns".
Speaking of combat, enemies are also way more interesting to fight against. They are less stupid (still not the brightest bunch) and they've managed to make different enemies also feel different. They act and attack in various ways. Ghouls, for example, have the habbit of playing dead and getting up to gut you once you are close enough. It feels very organic and less gamey than what I'd have expected. There's also a greater enemy variety, with some neat surprises here and there.
Fallout 4 also introduces a new mechanic, settlement building and managment, into the series and it's a blast, even if a bit shallow. You get a set of building blocks to make your own towns and settlements with, which ties in very well with the scavenging aspect of the series. Now everything from ceramic cups to metal buckets has some value as building materials. I've spend countles hours just building, trying to create the perfect base for myself. You can also fill settlements with NPCs, indroducing a "the Sims-lite" type gameplay. It's relatively barebones, but makes you care about what type of conditions you leave your settlements in. Using mods and DLCs to expand the items available makes a big diffrence and makes this way more entertaining than it propably should be.
All in all, Fallout 4 disapointed me, but I've started to like it for different reasons than those that I came to love Fallout for. It manages to create a feeling of survival of the fittests that previous 3D entries in the series haven't offerred yet, but at the expense of roleplaying and interesting story, people and locations. Even with all of its faults, I recommend giving it a shot.

This game is simply amazing. I reviewed this in early access stage, but everything I said stands.
In the end, Darkest Dungeon is about resource management, as you delve into the dungeon and must make the best use of your items and party skills. Each dungeon has its own properties and some of your men are better suited for one specific dungeon type, so knowing your resources and using them well is crucial. But as you delve, your heroes gain stress and permanent quirks that make them vulnerable or even dangerous to the party in some situations, and it's up to cure or replace them.
As we're speaking, the game is still under Early Access and some tweaks are being applied to stats here and there. However, I consider it to be perfect at the current stage, for the time I've been playing it.
It's all I love about dungeon crawling. Combat is turn based, which is great because I prefer to ponder and choose my moves rather than rely on reflexes.
Oh and did I mention that the graphics are beyond gorgeous? Because they really are. Absolutely recommended.

It boasts better graphics, more things coming down the pipeline, and that it would be a fun, adventurous little title where you were a space explorer!... Buy the game, click play, cue the space opera music that makes you sound like you're the last of your species in a desolate wasteland of a universe.
Where Terraria, the game it based many of it's gimicks on, had a happy, adventurous feel that made you want to dig for hours, too much of this game's sullen, moody, if not outright depressing music will make you want to turn the game off and never play again. Nevermind the fact the game has very little to truly set out and do, beyond fighting a handful of the same enemies over and over again.
For instance. The coordinate system will take you straight to the exact same planet from someone else's game. Universes are not randomly generated, meaning you can, in fact, have the exact same maps and experiences as everyone else, the only difference is the fact you can start off on different planets. Worse yet, if you're like me, you start on a toxic planet where everything is trying to kill you, even the water itself. Not to mention you have to eat food in-game to survive.
Don't waste your time, it's hype and nothing more. Get Terraria if you want something upbeat, happy, truly random, and driven by exploration. Get this game if you want to be depressed the entire time, and fight to even have any sort of decent enjoyment in exploring.

So, after seeing this game released and finished, I can finally say it. It's nice to see the early access state to finished barely changed anything, except add in more fake difficulty.
Pros:
-REALLY, REALLY good artwork and style, some animations could be a tad better, but they're mostly 99% good most of the time.
-An interesting gimmick of stress and the psychological horrors that adventuring could have.
-Unique quirks system making every hero feel slightly different.
-Interesting classes, all with unique dialogue.
-Pretty simple game to grasp.
-More game options to get rid of... unwanted gameplay aspects.
-Super easy to mod, the devs even encourage modding (In case anyone wants to know, just make a comment in the review asking how, and I will be glad to share on how to mod the game).
-Death's door to prevent complete and utter insta-kills/give a fighting chance.
-Wayne June does an AMAZING job as the ancestor. Honestly, I would say it's the best thing about this game.
Cons:
-The gimmick of stress is just one huge annoyance, the chances of actually getting into 100+ is by doing a dark run or getting gimmicked by stress attacks.
-Heart attacks, 1. Stress takes many years to actually start having health issues, you don't have a heart attack instantly. 2. If you get hit by it once, you now go to insta-death's door, a second time? Bye bye, hero.
-Quirk system, most are just annoyances that, once again, are just gimmicks.
-Disease system, most are, again, annoyances, however, it needs more balancing (i.e. hero gets Black Plague, throw hero away or cure it because they literally can't help now. Hero get rabies, leave it, it's more of a buff than anything. Hero gets Griping in the Guts, annoying, but it's easy to get around.)
-Afflictions and virtue chances, virtue chances are so low, I think it might be possible for someone to have 100+ hours into the game and never get a virtue. Afflictions are major gimmicks, reducing nearly every stat for the hero and making them do random things. You can generally keep going with an affliction, but if the player has more than about 2 rooms, you will have to cut off the run short, only to do... nothing.
-Above, why does it do nothing? It's mainly a farm and grind game, any gold you need can easily be obtained just by slamming heroes into dungeons, with or without supplies. The upgrades to the town make it to were you need less gold. Everything is an infinite amount of gold and heirlooms.
-Because everything is an infinite supply, including heroes, it makes it more smart to upgrade your town first rather than try and play normally.
-Heroes are on infinite supply, no matter what, this game will never truly be hard if there's no true way to "lose" since gold and heirlooms can be farmed. If you lost all heroes without upgrading the stagecoach, what happens? 4 fresh heroes right there.
-Champion dungeons become a long, slow, tedious grind to the boss. It also requires some serious number crunching and near perfect min max team comp, leaving barely any room for expirements.
-...The only way you can figure out this game is legitimately rolling low numbers on purpose is modding. How? Perfect example, as a joke, I made the Jester (funny stats for a funny character) do 0-9999 damage with a modifier of 100+% damage increase... he would constantly hit from 2000-4000. You start off with 67% of a death resist, I even increased it to about a 75%... they still have a good chance of dying from 1 hit.
-The numbers ROUND DOWN. A double edged blade, to an extent, since it also applies to the enemies. Need an example? A vestal can heal for 7-8. Adding a trinket that gives a 33% heal buff, lowest heal she can get is 9 (9.31, to be precise). Highest would be 10 (10.64, precisely). Instead of rounding up when it hits a .5 and above, it rounds down. This effects the player mostly though because even if they still get rounded down, the enemies can outdamage any negative things that happen.
-Class balance is fine for the most part, except the classes that outperform the others, outperform them HEAVILY. A vestal can NEVER outheal any damage, only prolong them from death. An occultist? He can not only have the best debuff in the game, but outheal the damage to a character. Hellions? Best meleer in the game. Why? She's the only class in the game that can hit ranks 2-3 while in rank 1-3 and 4 in rank 1. Lepers cry because once they get pushed to rank 3, they literally can't do anything worthwhile. When they're in ranks 1-2? They can only hit enemy ranks 1-2. Does he have the damage to make up for it? For a normal class? Sorta. Hellion though? She's barely a few points off of leper damage except she can add a bleed DoT.
-DoTs... bleed is pretty much the only good DoT. Blight upon hit does 0 damage and at max rank does a DoT of a whopping... 7. Yay. A hellion could basically hit for that along with a bleed that does about 3 damage. I don't understand Red Hook's obsession with blight doing no damage.
-However, you need some DoTs because of prot and champion dungeons. With all these recent patches, they added prot which was a means of prolonging the fight to make it "harder" meaning use some more DoTs just for them. Also, there is no possible way you can get up to the jacked prot the enemies have. The best you will get will probably be 15%, using both trinket slots.
-These devs constantly buff enemies while nerfing heroes. Matter of fact, the entire every team is viable has been bogus since the release of the game and has only be stomped more into the ground with these stupid nerfs.
-Final level is filled with nothing but stress gimmicks and enemies that tank (granted, they can do a lot of damage, esp. with crits + DoTs) that wants you to min max a team.
-There's a slight more, but I won't touch on them except... the crazy, annoying doomsayer. ♥♥♥♥ him. I hope they remove him. His yelling sounds like some bad, cheesey, low budget porno that doesn't make any goddamn sense.
TL;DR version: The game is good if you're gonna play a small amount and then move on. If you plan to spend a lot of hours in it, pass or wait for about a... 75% sale, at least............. Also ♥♥♥♥ the doomsayer, ♥♥♥♥ing remove him already.
Side note: Before I get♥♥♥♥♥♥stormed by I'm bad, casual, not helpfuls, etc. I have played enough "hard" games and even relatively obscure games, Dark Souls (not really obscure, but "hard, but fair" which a I call bull and beaten it), Legend of Grimrock 1&2, Pillars of Eternity, a few Ys games, and more. I can say, this game would be good for a mobile, up until champions, which can take up to an hour from the tankiness of enemies. I am very far from bad, casual, etc., it's just the way the game plays, it's just meat grind simulator till you can use heroes leveled etc. (specific heroes too) and then it becomes 95% of the time, the house wins game. Huge time sink to even START in the higher level dungeons. Honestly, veteran is the most fun that can be had, and that was ruined by the crit focus every battle.
Side Side Note: I have feeling the people upvoting this generally agree with what I have to say, but if you have read this far, please tell others to not just mindlessly upvote bad and/or good reviews. It doesn't help anyone, and it can possibly even mix opinions and facts. For example, if one says x game is bad because it requires too much number crunching whereas another one says x game is bad because it seems like the devs wanted you to be a 2 year old to play, then... yeah, kinda hard to truly tell where opinions and facts start and end. So, please try to spread the word of don't upvote/downvote till you know where this review is coming from. Also, don't upvote memes and joke reviews, it, once again, hurts to see where facts and opinions mix. Just... vote funny and move on.

A lot of people complain about the new updates but I've found it just means you need to be more cautious.  I used to not buy torches and just rely on getting critical hits to stay sane in the darkness but that is no longer possible now, at least not for long.  Even then, when you are fully prepared for a dungeon bad luck can happen that will ruin things.  Sometimes you need to retreat or abandon a quest, sometimes people die.  The game and the challenge comes from dealing with and mitigating your chances of failure.  Nothing is a sure fire solution to preventing it and really that is what keeps it fun and interesting.  Beyond that, there are more options now that let you adjust the difficulty of the game to keep or remove things that add to the games difficulty.
At of the time of this writing, build #12231 I have to say I've very happy with things, the game is polished enough it doesn't feel like a beta at all.  I'm looking forward to the general release coming in January to see if the developers have anything else in store.   Hopefully a tweak here or there to things that don't get much love like some of the more irrelevant camping skills.

An interesting spin on the MMO Genre Spiral Knights takes instance raiding and builds an entire game around it.
The large majority of levels that can be found within the 'Clockworks' (as the dungeons are referred to in game) are selected randomly based on a level type and 'element' that is known before entry. This combination also determines the enemies that will be found, allowing for some pre-planning. This means that no two runs into the same section of the clockworks will be the same.
The art direction for the game is very interesting, with the playable characters rendered as a cross between medieval knights and clockwork soldiers; the only part of a Knights face that is visible is their eyes which match the players colour and can be one of a selection of shapes.
The story for the game sets the player as one of a force of Knights who were in the midst of an interstellar journey when they encounter Cradle: a seemingly clockwork planet. When their ship flies too close a strange force pulls it into the atmosphere of the planet, forcing an emergency evacuation, scattering escape pods all over a small portion of the surface.
Through a series of storyline missions and optional end-game bosses the story is slowly revealed, with hints of much more to come.
Overall I would recommend this game, however without spending real money on the energy market it can be slow to gain access to a wider arsenal of armours and weapons that may be required to enjoy the game more.

It boasts better graphics, more things coming down the pipeline, and that it would be a fun, adventurous little title where you were a space explorer!... Buy the game, click play, cue the space opera music that makes you sound like you're the last of your species in a desolate wasteland of a universe.
Where Terraria, the game it based many of it's gimicks on, had a happy, adventurous feel that made you want to dig for hours, too much of this game's sullen, moody, if not outright depressing music will make you want to turn the game off and never play again. Nevermind the fact the game has very little to truly set out and do, beyond fighting a handful of the same enemies over and over again.
For instance. The coordinate system will take you straight to the exact same planet from someone else's game. Universes are not randomly generated, meaning you can, in fact, have the exact same maps and experiences as everyone else, the only difference is the fact you can start off on different planets. Worse yet, if you're like me, you start on a toxic planet where everything is trying to kill you, even the water itself. Not to mention you have to eat food in-game to survive.
Don't waste your time, it's hype and nothing more. Get Terraria if you want something upbeat, happy, truly random, and driven by exploration. Get this game if you want to be depressed the entire time, and fight to even have any sort of decent enjoyment in exploring.

This game is simply amazing. I reviewed this in early access stage, but everything I said stands.
In the end, Darkest Dungeon is about resource management, as you delve into the dungeon and must make the best use of your items and party skills. Each dungeon has its own properties and some of your men are better suited for one specific dungeon type, so knowing your resources and using them well is crucial. But as you delve, your heroes gain stress and permanent quirks that make them vulnerable or even dangerous to the party in some situations, and it's up to cure or replace them.
As we're speaking, the game is still under Early Access and some tweaks are being applied to stats here and there. However, I consider it to be perfect at the current stage, for the time I've been playing it.
It's all I love about dungeon crawling. Combat is turn based, which is great because I prefer to ponder and choose my moves rather than rely on reflexes.
Oh and did I mention that the graphics are beyond gorgeous? Because they really are. Absolutely recommended.

This is the worst Fallout game I've ever played.
That's not to say it's a bad game, because it's not. It stands on its own merits, but it wasn't what I went looking for at first.
The main story failed to grab me. It felt more like a chore than a story, the further I got. That's kinda to be expected, since it's a Bethesda open world RPG, but what saddens me about it is that they seemingly wanted the story to be good. It was obviously a big focus, with the voiced protagonist and so on, but it just falls flat. Atleast there are side quests to keep me happy, right?
No, actually. There are only a few interesting side quests in the whole game. Most of them feel the same, are tied to factions and therefore softlocked behind the main questline, or are part of the radiant quests system. There are a few highlight here and there, but it feels like they are unwilling to go far enough to feel great. There's a feeling of "something is missing".
Character building is a shadow of what it was previously. I don't feel like I'm playing a character with strenghts and weaknesses. I don't have to make choices regarding my characters stats and perks. The new system is more fluid and forgiving, but at the same time takes away uniqueness from every playthrough and player character.
On the other hand combat has gotten a much needed facelift. Now guns actually feel like guns and are less clunky. I have to say that this is something I would've expected from a game released in this day and age, but credit where credit is due. Bethesda managed to make combat enjoyable and feel less like "Oblivion with guns".
Speaking of combat, enemies are also way more interesting to fight against. They are less stupid (still not the brightest bunch) and they've managed to make different enemies also feel different. They act and attack in various ways. Ghouls, for example, have the habbit of playing dead and getting up to gut you once you are close enough. It feels very organic and less gamey than what I'd have expected. There's also a greater enemy variety, with some neat surprises here and there.
Fallout 4 also introduces a new mechanic, settlement building and managment, into the series and it's a blast, even if a bit shallow. You get a set of building blocks to make your own towns and settlements with, which ties in very well with the scavenging aspect of the series. Now everything from ceramic cups to metal buckets has some value as building materials. I've spend countles hours just building, trying to create the perfect base for myself. You can also fill settlements with NPCs, indroducing a "the Sims-lite" type gameplay. It's relatively barebones, but makes you care about what type of conditions you leave your settlements in. Using mods and DLCs to expand the items available makes a big diffrence and makes this way more entertaining than it propably should be.
All in all, Fallout 4 disapointed me, but I've started to like it for different reasons than those that I came to love Fallout for. It manages to create a feeling of survival of the fittests that previous 3D entries in the series haven't offerred yet, but at the expense of roleplaying and interesting story, people and locations. Even with all of its faults, I recommend giving it a shot.
