-Pretty simple game to grasp.
-More game options to get rid of... unwanted gameplay aspects.
-Super easy to mod, the devs even encourage modding (In case anyone wants to know, just make a comment in the review asking how, and I will be glad to share on how to mod the game).
-Death's door to prevent complete and utter insta-kills/give a fighting chance.
-Wayne June does an AMAZING job as the ancestor. Honestly, I would say it's the best thing about this game.
Cons:
-The gimmick of stress is just one huge annoyance, the chances of actually getting into 100+ is by doing a dark run or getting gimmicked by stress attacks.
-Heart attacks, 1. Stress takes many years to actually start having health issues, you don't have a heart attack instantly. 2. If you get hit by it once, you now go to insta-death's door, a second time? Bye bye, hero.
-Quirk system, most are just annoyances that, once again, are just gimmicks.
-Disease system, most are, again, annoyances, however, it needs more balancing (i.e. hero gets Black Plague, throw hero away or cure it because they literally can't help now. Hero get rabies, leave it, it's more of a buff than anything. Hero gets Griping in the Guts, annoying, but it's easy to get around.)
-Afflictions and virtue chances, virtue chances are so low, I think it might be possible for someone to have 100+ hours into the game and never get a virtue. Afflictions are major gimmicks, reducing nearly every stat for the hero and making them do random things. You can generally keep going with an affliction, but if the player has more than about 2 rooms, you will have to cut off the run short, only to do... nothing.
-Above, why does it do nothing? It's mainly a farm and grind game, any gold you need can easily be obtained just by slamming heroes into dungeons, with or without supplies. The upgrades to the town make it to were you need less gold. Everything is an infinite amount of gold and heirlooms.
-Because everything is an infinite supply, including heroes, it makes it more smart to upgrade your town first rather than try and play normally.
-Heroes are on infinite supply, no matter what, this game will never truly be hard if there's no true way to "lose" since gold and heirlooms can be farmed. If you lost all heroes without upgrading the stagecoach, what happens? 4 fresh heroes right there.
-Champion dungeons become a long, slow, tedious grind to the boss. It also requires some serious number crunching and near perfect min max team comp, leaving barely any room for expirements.
-...The only way you can figure out this game is legitimately rolling low numbers on purpose is modding. How? Perfect example, as a joke, I made the Jester (funny stats for a funny character) do 0-9999 damage with a modifier of 100+% damage increase... he would constantly hit from 2000-4000. You start off with 67% of a death resist, I even increased it to about a 75%... they still have a good chance of dying from 1 hit.
-The numbers ROUND DOWN. A double edged blade, to an extent, since it also applies to the enemies. Need an example? A vestal can heal for 7-8. Adding a trinket that gives a 33% heal buff, lowest heal she can get is 9 (9.31, to be precise). Highest would be 10 (10.64, precisely). Instead of rounding up when it hits a .5 and above, it rounds down. This effects the player mostly though because even if they still get rounded down, the enemies can outdamage any negative things that happen.
-Class balance is fine for the most part, except the classes that outperform the others, outperform them HEAVILY. A vestal can NEVER outheal any damage, only prolong them from death. An occultist? He can not only have the best debuff in the game, but outheal the damage to a character. Hellions? Best meleer in the game. Why? She's the only class in the game that can hit ranks 2-3 while in rank 1-3 and 4 in rank 1. Lepers cry because once they get pushed to rank 3, they literally can't do anything worthwhile. When they're in ranks 1-2? They can only hit enemy ranks 1-2. Does he have the damage to make up for it? For a normal class? Sorta. Hellion though? She's barely a few points off of leper damage except she can add a bleed DoT.
-DoTs... bleed is pretty much the only good DoT. Blight upon hit does 0 damage and at max rank does a DoT of a whopping... 7. Yay. A hellion could basically hit for that along with a bleed that does about 3 damage. I don't understand Red Hook's obsession with blight doing no damage.
-However, you need some DoTs because of prot and champion dungeons. With all these recent patches, they added prot which was a means of prolonging the fight to make it "harder" meaning use some more DoTs just for them. Also, there is no possible way you can get up to the jacked prot the enemies have. The best you will get will probably be 15%, using both trinket slots.
-These devs constantly buff enemies while nerfing heroes. Matter of fact, the entire every team is viable has been bogus since the release of the game and has only be stomped more into the ground with these stupid nerfs.
-Final level is filled with nothing but stress gimmicks and enemies that tank (granted, they can do a lot of damage, esp. with crits + DoTs) that wants you to min max a team.
-There's a slight more, but I won't touch on them except... the crazy, annoying doomsayer. ♥♥♥♥ him. I hope they remove him. His yelling sounds like some bad, cheesey, low budget porno that doesn't make any goddamn sense.
TL;DR version: The game is good if you're gonna play a small amount and then move on. If you plan to spend a lot of hours in it, pass or wait for about a... 75% sale, at least............. Also ♥♥♥♥ the doomsayer, ♥♥♥♥ing remove him already.
Side note: Before I get♥♥♥♥♥♥stormed by I'm bad, casual, not helpfuls, etc. I have played enough "hard" games and even relatively obscure games, Dark Souls (not really obscure, but "hard, but fair" which a I call bull and beaten it), Legend of Grimrock 1&2, Pillars of Eternity, a few Ys games, and more. I can say, this game would be good for a mobile, up until champions, which can take up to an hour from the tankiness of enemies. I am very far from bad, casual, etc., it's just the way the game plays, it's just meat grind simulator till you can use heroes leveled etc. (specific heroes too) and then it becomes 95% of the time, the house wins game. Huge time sink to even START in the higher level dungeons. Honestly, veteran is the most fun that can be had, and that was ruined by the crit focus every battle.
Side Side Note: I have feeling the people upvoting this generally agree with what I have to say, but if you have read this far, please tell others to not just mindlessly upvote bad and/or good reviews. It doesn't help anyone, and it can possibly even mix opinions and facts. For example, if one says x game is bad because it requires too much number crunching whereas another one says x game is bad because it seems like the devs wanted you to be a 2 year old to play, then... yeah, kinda hard to truly tell where opinions and facts start and end. So, please try to spread the word of don't upvote/downvote till you know where this review is coming from. Also, don't upvote memes and joke reviews, it, once again, hurts to see where facts and opinions mix. Just... vote funny and move on.

Great game !  Lots of fun with a unique art style.
Game balance is much improved over the earlier builds.  It's challenging but without the frustrating party wipes due to bad luck and poor design.
While you can start multiple campaigns, each campaign has only one save that the game auto-updates.  Characters can and will die and there's no bringing them back.  With that said, once you know the game mechanics, you have to be overconfident or unlucky to get a character killed.   What's more likely is that they will become so riddled with afflictions and phobias that you start wondering if it's worth the time and money to cure them.
"Alas, poor Dismas.  He grew un-well."
The game mechanics appear simple at first, but the more you play, the deeper you realize the strategy elements go.
With multiple classes, quirks, afflictions, equipment levels, learned skills, trinkets, and character position, there are a lot of things to consider when putting together a party.  There's also a limited amount of supplies you can carry, so you have to consider carefully what to bring. Supplies and loot occupy the same space. Bring too many supplies, and there's no room for loot.  Bring too few supplies, and you starve in the dark.
Visually, characters of the same class look the same.  Crusader Bill looks just like crusader Bob. You can change their name and choose an overall color scheme, but they look the same.  You'd think this would make the characters feel generic, but it doesn't.   Over the course of a campaign - for however long they survive - each character will develop differently.  Bill is smitten by a worker in the brothel and that is the only place he will go to de-stress.  Bob finds religion and will only de-stress in the abbey.  Bill becomes paranoid and mutters constantly when in a party. Bob becomes vigorous and regenerates a bit of health.  Visually the same, but in character totally different.
Is Darkest Dungeon a perfect game? Hard to answer. I think it is a game that is perfectly itself - and that self is very engaging.
If you're looking for a turn-based, dungeon experience with a unique art style, challenging game play, and a lengthy campaign ( broken into manageable bites ),  give Darkest Dungeon a try .

Everyone says that the new update has ruined the game.
Simply not true. I've lost heroes because of my own mistakes, underestimating opponents (♥♥♥♥ing Ancient Webbers), and (rarely) RNGesus, but it's never been because the game was too stacked against me.
To earn gold, you HAVE to budget. In early stages, when you're upgrading your Hamlet, you have to learn when Heroes are more trouble than they're worth and to let them go (i.e. their stress reduction cost total > the gold you're taking in, too many diseases, bad quicks that are locked in, etc). Everyone in the beginning is expendable. The overall goal is to accumulate wealth and upgrade that Hamlet.
Simply said, you're not going to get to level 6 on your Heroes from the very beginning.
After a while, gold and upgrading become less of an issue. Gold farming is incredibly easy to the Champion level dungeon runs (presuming you survive), with 15K gold as a reward for completing it, and it cost me about 4K to get more than enough supplies to survive. Adding in all the loot that I got (around 14k on my last run), the difference is real. Putting in about 6K in stress reduction, and 4K in quick-removal/disease removal, I still came out on top.
Even with the ease of gold farming in later stages of the game, your Heroes can AND WILL die. I lost nearly an entire party of level 6 Heroes to Webbers because I had gotten into a "click, kill" mentality, and thought that the blight damage would be under control. Wrong.
You have to think about each move you make, because every encounter has the possibilty of going south.
Update (Jan 5 2016): I'm very pleased that the featured reviews are all recommended like this game deserves, instead of the people who raged when updates happened and couldn't think critically about it.

TLDR: If you're a fan of roguelikes, you'll probably like this game; if you approach it like an RPG, where you can just force your way through any problem if you try enough times, you probably won't. I don't write many reviews. I feel as though I have to give my own piece like so many others do already. I played A LOT of Fallout 4, for a while I did enjoy it but as time went on I realized I actually didn't like it. I liked the mods. I likedwhat the community was doing to fix it. Fallout 4 is possibly the WORST RPG I have ever played, it's a decent game overall but compared to the RPG mechanics of so many other games outside of previous entries it just rots.
The map is a fairly large size and can provide a lot of content but the quality of said content such the quests drastically varies in quality.  You'll have many quests that are straight up copied or quests that refresh on the spot and never really resolved. The gameplay is solid, specifically the combat, especially when compared to previous FPS fallouts. The ability to mod weapons in the vanilla game gives enough to really change your weapons. You could turn a pistol into a submachine gun or even into a sniper rifle or shotgun.
The game has had the skills RIPPED out and there are no perks. Perks have just been overly simplified into a terrible skill tree that requires pumping points into your S.P.E.C.I.A.L in order to unlock more. If you had rank 10 of every S.P.E.C.I.A.L and were level 50 you wouldn't be able to pick what you want till you pic apart the skill and work your way down. There is a mod that fixes this and provided you have the requirments you can skip some skills to get what you want but this is just an aid, not a fix.
That isn't the only thing torn out that further simplifies the gane, karma is gone. You can shoot someone in the head and as long as no one sees it to go hostile you're all good with no downside....that reminds me, good luck killing anyone. The game has a nasty habit of not wanting you to miss ANYTHING so there are plenty of NPCs whom you will try to kill and they'll fall on their♥♥♥♥♥and then get back up and say "that wasn't very nice"
-My following statments will be SPOILERS TO THE MAIN QUEST.-
-Labeling a video game as an RPG that provides freedom to do whatever you want but then goes against that is frusterating. You play as either a mother or father who make it to one of the many Vaults in the Fallout universe right as the bombs are falling, your put into statis and your wife/husband (depending which sex you chose) is killed and your son is stolen. Time passes and your pod opens and releases you, your quest now is to find your son and avenge your dead wife....and the game will never stop reminding you.
-Nearly every dialogue is your character whinning about his son or how his wife is dead. Which brings me to dialogue, when your game has "sarcastic" as a reply in your mass effect dialogue wheel you know you've failed as a writer. Rarely do your stats have ANY impact or meaning in your dialogue. You'd get the occasional "lady killer" perk check but that should be expected.
-When you need to decide to pick between the brotherhood of Steel, The Railroad, the Institute there is so little of a difference bedies which final 2 factions you wipe out and in what order. The minutemen are the only ones who seem different but they're the most bland.
-Going to back to the main character briefly. Your whole quest is to find your son, a plot thread you're suppose to care about....but you really shouldn't. The character cares but you don't. The issue being that it isn't YOU'RE character because you're being forced to follow a forced relationship like in Fallout 3. In Fallout original, 2 and New Vegas you were a blank slate and were able to be who you wanted to be you only had a vague objective. If Fallout 4 had started with you waking up in the vault and finding a gun, hacking a computer and picking a lock before deciding on your character THAT would be so much better.
Do yourself a favour and played Fallout 1, 2, and New Vegas for a much better RPG experience.

It's not always a good idea to buy a game before it's actually completed. Darkest Dungeon is a fitting exception to the rule.
The game is set in a gloomy world where you answered the summons of an unnamed ancestor. Said ancestor was the master of a sprawling estate. Unstatisfied with what he had, he began to delve into the dark arts. As the kin that answered the call, you're tasked to bring redemption to the land your ancestor cursed with his endeavours. You start when you enter the dismal hamlet at the edge of the property...
Gameplay is quite simple but engaging - explore procedural dungeons by bringing enough supplies for the run. Supplies support basic needs (light, food) as well as unlock obstacles encountered (Shovels to dig through obstacles, keys to unlock chests).
Encounters happen randomly in runs, and combat harks back to initiative-based RPG battles. Party members come in different classes. Their skills are based on where they stand in the party formation, and what/where they are targeting. Party members have 2 key stats - health and stress. Members die when health flatlines for too long, and their performance can suffer greatly if their stress overfills (they can also die if it goes way beyond the threshold). Complete the run by achieving goals or retreating once you'd have your fill.
The game is designed to vary greatly depending on RNG - so easy battles can turn hard very quickly (reverse is less often true). Supplies, and especially support in town (ammenities like training, therapy, armaments, and their upgrades), are expensive to encourage management. With the only 'free' resource being adventurers offering to sign up with you, you'll find yourself throwing them to their doom to advance your cause... which begs the question how much of better a person you actually are compared to your ancestor.
The game doesn't leave you dead when you fail - adventurers will keep coming and the runs available are adjusted based on the level of available adventurers. Your main task is to upgrade facilties and stockpile stats-boosting inventory to support your cycle of adventurers. The trick is to not be attached to your party members, and expect death. The main challenge is the punishing RNG. In the worst cases, retreat is an option...
(unless of course that Maria the Vestal's stress levels are beyond high and she dies of heart attack after gaining even more stress from running away... and you regret not sending her to the brothel before the dungeon run to be with her lover for some stress therapy because you're cheap - but then again better losing her than wiping the whole party, which included Mark the Highwayman you've equipped with the best weapons and invested thousands training... )
+ Good challenge, with enough options that make it interesting.
+ Art is fitting of the theme and well made.
+ Narration / Voice-acting is limited but also fitting to the theme.
+ Variation in play due to different enemy types and adventuring classes you decide to bring - e.g. you can rely one the basic trinity of tank/dps/heal, but also mix in various hybrids that stun, debuff, reposition the enemy for greater effect.
+ UI has gotten better over time, and now complements the gameplay.
+ Post-Release, the game is now better balanced against flukes (Game's still punishing but the fairer challenge enhances the experience)
- Dungeons get repetitve, though the constant threat of death keeps one on edge. Combine this with the emotionally-scarring RNG makes this game an ill fit for those who find themselves getting anxious easily.
- Equipment levels don't scale well - higher level equipment can include high tradeoffs, so sometimes you're better off with lower level equipment. This in turn makes dungeon runs at higher levels a matter of diminishing returns (since the equipment drops may not be as useful for party despite them risking their necks for it)

Great game !  Lots of fun with a unique art style.
Game balance is much improved over the earlier builds.  It's challenging but without the frustrating party wipes due to bad luck and poor design.
While you can start multiple campaigns, each campaign has only one save that the game auto-updates.  Characters can and will die and there's no bringing them back.  With that said, once you know the game mechanics, you have to be overconfident or unlucky to get a character killed.   What's more likely is that they will become so riddled with afflictions and phobias that you start wondering if it's worth the time and money to cure them.
"Alas, poor Dismas.  He grew un-well."
The game mechanics appear simple at first, but the more you play, the deeper you realize the strategy elements go.
With multiple classes, quirks, afflictions, equipment levels, learned skills, trinkets, and character position, there are a lot of things to consider when putting together a party.  There's also a limited amount of supplies you can carry, so you have to consider carefully what to bring. Supplies and loot occupy the same space. Bring too many supplies, and there's no room for loot.  Bring too few supplies, and you starve in the dark.
Visually, characters of the same class look the same.  Crusader Bill looks just like crusader Bob. You can change their name and choose an overall color scheme, but they look the same.  You'd think this would make the characters feel generic, but it doesn't.   Over the course of a campaign - for however long they survive - each character will develop differently.  Bill is smitten by a worker in the brothel and that is the only place he will go to de-stress.  Bob finds religion and will only de-stress in the abbey.  Bill becomes paranoid and mutters constantly when in a party. Bob becomes vigorous and regenerates a bit of health.  Visually the same, but in character totally different.
Is Darkest Dungeon a perfect game? Hard to answer. I think it is a game that is perfectly itself - and that self is very engaging.
If you're looking for a turn-based, dungeon experience with a unique art style, challenging game play, and a lengthy campaign ( broken into manageable bites ),  give Darkest Dungeon a try .

Main story is very poor. Your choices of endings are all unsatisfactory. If you came intothis game expecting an RPG like New Vegas, you will be disappointed.
In New Vegas you could talk, scheme or murder your way to the top of various factions and influence who was left standing in the end. You could fight for a faction or bring it down from the inside. You could usurp a faction and use them to take New Vegas for yourself. You could drive every faction out and leave the wasteland in anarchy. You could start a new independant vegas to stand against the world, and you could rule it or leave it to rule itself.
In Fallout 4, Team A wants to nuke Boston and Team B also wants to nuke Boston. You nuke Boston with the help of Team A or Team B. Your choice. Don't want to nuke Boston? That's fine, all you have to do is never complete the story.
Most of the side stories are interesting.

Fallout 4 is a 6/10 RPG, a 4/10 shooter, and a 6/10 town building/tower defense game. Deeply regrettable.

The game can be a lot of fun, particularly once you gain a grasp of the combat basics and stress management. That being said, buyer beware: this is a very punishing game. Part of the reason is that if the RNG doesn't like you, it will crush you like a bug. Being prepared can mitigate the crushing, but on occasion even with prep you will lose a hero (or more). And that is a feature, not a bug.
Another reason which makes the game punishing is that it turns certain RPG conventions upside down. Clearest example: if you try to interact with all interactive dungeon elements (called "Curios"), you will get hurt. So you need to learn how to safely navigate dungeons.
All in all, it is a lot of fun, as long as you are OK with the terms the games imposes on you

Someone asked 'What's hard about Trove / What's the game in a nutshell' and this is my summary, I'm a level 32 TR with 3 other classes above 15 and have around 75 hours at time of writing this.
Right now its a 50 hour playsink with some wallet warriors ruling the marketplace but its potential is undeniable, I know it's commonly said about MMO's but this game has uniqueness, it's just bland right now. This is my TL:DR of the game
learn the game levels 1-10,
spend your time in uber1-uber5 levels 11-20 getting enough gear level/mastery ranks to enter u6
enter uber-6 and make profit - but the game really ends progressively here
The monsters you kill dont even change in size nor color, it's the same dungeons thousands and thousands of times over. There's masteries and professions and a 'collection' system thats designed to make you feel like therer's infinite progression until you max out but in my small opinion the core gameplay is whats more important, and once youve gotten over the 'holy crap this game is something new and unique', it really starts to feel like youre stuck in a loop until you can afford to financially upgrade your gear.
The game is built on a structure that isnt at all desgined to be hard (Unless you picked Gunslinger or Neon Ninja, and for the sake of time im not going into class balance but holy fk), but only time consuming. The only thing to do is go find materials to create 'x' or to upgrade shadow levels of your gear. Once youre past using the earlier upgrade materials it's expensive as hell to progress and takes 5 hours+ for ONE tier upgrade (even if you make 3K flux/ hr reliably)
what keeps me playing is the club im in is full of ~200 nice/mature/experienced MMO people that make repeating dungeons / repeating mining / repeating shadow arenas at least a bit dynamic and fast, without a group to run with I would have quit already.
I recommend it because the developers are in touch with the community and the promise for the game is there. Club member restrictions need expansion, along with all the other side-aspects of the game. The core is just boring in my humble opinion.

Main story is very poor. Your choices of endings are all unsatisfactory. If you came intothis game expecting an RPG like New Vegas, you will be disappointed.
In New Vegas you could talk, scheme or murder your way to the top of various factions and influence who was left standing in the end. You could fight for a faction or bring it down from the inside. You could usurp a faction and use them to take New Vegas for yourself. You could drive every faction out and leave the wasteland in anarchy. You could start a new independant vegas to stand against the world, and you could rule it or leave it to rule itself.
In Fallout 4, Team A wants to nuke Boston and Team B also wants to nuke Boston. You nuke Boston with the help of Team A or Team B. Your choice. Don't want to nuke Boston? That's fine, all you have to do is never complete the story.
Most of the side stories are interesting.
Graphics not up to 2015 standards. Bad, hacky Bethesda lighting. Invisible spotlights follow each character around, making them look out of place in any environment. Some of the worst hair I've ever seen rendered.
Building settlements quickly becomes a chore. Repetitive NPC dialogue is extremely grating.
Shooting was promised to "feel great"; it feels bad, man. It feels a lot more like Fallout 3's barely playable shooting than anything with actually good shooting - DOOM for example.
Fallout 4 is a 6/10 RPG, a 4/10 shooter, and a 6/10 town building/tower defense game. Deeply regrettable.

The game can be a lot of fun, particularly once you gain a grasp of the combat basics and stress management. That being said, buyer beware: this is a very punishing game. Part of the reason is that if the RNG doesn't like you, it will crush you like a bug. Being prepared can mitigate the crushing, but on occasion even with prep you will lose a hero (or more). And that is a feature, not a bug.
Another reason which makes the game punishing is that it turns certain RPG conventions upside down. Clearest example: if you try to interact with all interactive dungeon elements (called "Curios"), you will get hurt. So you need to learn how to safely navigate dungeons.
All in all, it is a lot of fun, as long as you are OK with the terms the games imposes on you

The server sometimes had this kind or rubberbanding effect : when you breaka cube it sometimes reappear right in front of you.
There are a lot of dungeons scattered all over the map and clearing them get you some reward at the end.
The character evolution is based on a mastery system : the more actions you do, the more achievements, the stronger you get.
It's a fun game to play with friends, still fun alone though.

as a HUGE fan of the souls series and an avid gamer... dark souls 1 2 and 3 are all in my top 6 games, and now with most patches and all dlc released i feel its a good time to give my opinion of the game. its souls, so already you know its a well made game. bosses are fantastic and sometimes frustrating, some brutally hard others a cakewalk. weapons and armor feel and look amazing. weapon arts add more dynamics to any fight. all in all dark souls 3 is an amazing game experience from the closed beta to now i have enjoyed the game immensely.
but alas even good games have flaws, invading is annoying as hosts just gank you or already have a summon and, well gank you, if they have way of blue they can summon 2 blues to save them, and they can use a seed of the giants tree to make mobs turn against you (recent patch made it only last 45 seconds thank god).. you also get unembered health while invading making it super hard without a proper invasion based build.  pvp is also consumed by a "meta" aka what are the "best" weapons and spells in the game. combo that with people who parry to much, people who only r1, and then the rare run and chuggers. pvp is definitely not the best in this game, but it is still super enjoyable when you git gud and destroy a 6 v 1 gank.
when the pvp is good damn is it fun, i reccomend the arena for the best pvp experience, but do as you like.
other annoying bits of the game could be getting certain covenant items (looking at you darkmoonblade), or even farming for certain drops but that is such a minute part of the game unless you actively search for said things.
all in all should you buy dark souls 3? yes, however if you dont have it by this point wait and get the fire fades edition with all dlc and such included.
dark souls 3 is an amazing game and a good way to end the series, i would have loved more from this game but it is still one of the best games on steam.

Darkest Dungeon isn't a game for everyone, that is true.
It's a roguelike turn-based RPG that will push your ability and luck for the limit.
(on my last review i said that the balance of the game was kinda screwed up, which is still true, but the Devs fixed a part of it and they added some difficulty options to make your life easier, disable the Death Door one and enable the critical one, it will make your life A LOT easier)
You will basically have 2 layers of gameplay:
The Administration and the Dungeon Crawling
The Administration part is self explanatory, you will have to administrate which facility you will upgrade, what and who you will bring to the missions, the heroes' stress and of course, the trinkets and of course, your most important resource, your money.
The Dungeon Crawling is the main part of the game:You will choose what map you want to go, then get you resources the adventure on. Your will be modified by a great variety of factors:your resources, your heroes' level of stress, your luck, the death door and the torch.
The Battles work the following way: You will have four heroes with 4 abilities and the option to use items and change their poisitions, but you can only execute one of these options. After you use your heroes' turn the next NPC or hero will act. A Hero can attack(this attack can be a critical), buff and debuff as the enemy. While fighting there are a great variety of factor that will decide the victorious party, including the one of the most important mechanics of the game:The Stress
A Better Explanation Of The Game Mechanics
The Stress:Stress is the factor that can drive your hero either mad or to be virtuous>
Stress is modified by a variety of factors;
You can gain stress by the lack of light, critical hits, death of characters, a mad character, traps and other enemies attacks;
You can lose stress by camping, skills, in the city or by random events.
The RNG:
RNG(Random Number Generator) Is what will determine your damage, your chance of hitting, your loot etc.
The Torch:
Influenced by the RNG, the torch will determine a variety of factors like the stress, the chances of surprising monster and to be surpised, the criticals and the loot(the lower the torch the better the loot).
General
Positive:
-Now Challenging Gameplay
-Artstyle
-Good amount of content
-Dozens and dozens of party combinations to suit your playstyle
-Replaiabilty
-The Narrator
Negative:
-Can be pretty frustrating
-Some bosses are pretty unfair
-It punishs you really hard when you make a mistake.
Score: 85/100

Spiral Knights claims to be a dungeon-crawler similar to The Legend of Zelda: The Four Sword/Four Swords Adventure. While the feel is the same, Spiral Knights stands on its own without needing the comparison. The randomized paths make it so players won't have the same experience twice, and it adds a new level of strategy as you descend deeper towards the Core. Players have access to three different weapons: Swords, for those who like to take on enemies head-on; Guns, for those who rather pick them off from a safe distance; and Bombs, for those who like making their friends question their sanity as they chase enemies around with them. The game is taliored for co-op play, but you can play it alone if you wish, making it one of the few MMOs that allow for such a thing. It also has gamepad support for those not liking to use a keyboard and mouse. Some people claim Spiral Knights is Pay-To-Win, and yes, spending money does make things a bit easier later on, but it isn't necessary, and you can play through the game fine without spending a dime.
I recommend Spiral Knights, and I recommend you bring a friend along.

DS3 provides a streamlined and updated game within the Dark Souls universe. It retains its signature challenging but fair standards while leaving some of the more aggravating features behind. For example, hit boxes, the areas where attacks are happening and can hit your player, are far better in DS3 compared to 1 and 2. When you dodge a strike it is much easier to be reliable, and reinforces Dark Souls' learn-to-improve gameplay scheme.
It is visually and audially stunning, and if you enjoy these types of action games I cannot recommend it more highly, with the DLCs being excellent content in my mind as well.

Many people call this a grindfest, and they are kinda right. After finding a good team composition for every dungeon and getting the hang of things, the game is basically over. And the "amazing" and unique stress mechanic in this game consists of following procedure:
Enemy stresses hero, hero goes to 100 stress, RNG gets activate, if you are lucky you get some stat boosts, and if you're unlucky the hero will sometimes damage themselves and others, stress the time or pass some rounds. Wow. Mindblowing. Absolutely terrific. I have never seen such a thrilling game mechanic in my entire life.

Main story is very poor. Your choices of endings are all unsatisfactory. If you came intothis game expecting an RPG like New Vegas, you will be disappointed.
In New Vegas you could talk, scheme or murder your way to the top of various factions and influence who was left standing in the end. You could fight for a faction or bring it down from the inside. You could usurp a faction and use them to take New Vegas for yourself. You could drive every faction out and leave the wasteland in anarchy. You could start a new independant vegas to stand against the world, and you could rule it or leave it to rule itself.
In Fallout 4, Team A wants to nuke Boston and Team B also wants to nuke Boston. You nuke Boston with the help of Team A or Team B. Your choice. Don't want to nuke Boston? That's fine, all you have to do is never complete the story.
Most of the side stories are interesting.
Graphics not up to 2015 standards. Bad, hacky Bethesda lighting. Invisible spotlights follow each character around, making them look out of place in any environment. Some of the worst hair I've ever seen rendered.
Building settlements quickly becomes a chore. Repetitive NPC dialogue is extremely grating.
Shooting was promised to "feel great"; it feels bad, man. It feels a lot more like Fallout 3's barely playable shooting than anything with actually good shooting - DOOM for example.
Fallout 4 is a 6/10 RPG, a 4/10 shooter, and a 6/10 town building/tower defense game. Deeply regrettable.

Earlier this year, i reviewed this game much like a stereotypical teenage girl at One Direction, E.g "OMG OMG OMG. THIS IS THE BEST!". I am happy to say that twelve months on, that is still my reaction.
Starbound, in-case you can't read, have the worst google skills on the planet or have been living in a not-funhouse for the last 2 years (btw, go see Guardians of the Galaxy), is a charming little 2D sidescroller set in space. Thats right, this little gem lets you live out all those Star Trek/Wars/Firefly/pretty much every other "space fantasy" out there. With 6 races to choose from out of the gate, and a nice collection of adorable options to trick out your 8-bit virtual you. Once you pick a race, name, idle animation (refered to as "personality") and some sweet digs, you're dropped into your very own, cosy (that means small) little spaceship. From there, you can pretty much do whatever your inner J.T. Kirk desires, but there is a tutorial. Once you've done the first few tutorial missions,(or not, your choice) is about when you might deduce that your ship needs fuel to go places, who would have thought. Fuel is represented by a bunch of things, most commonly though is Coal,(wood, technically, but meh)wich you are able to collect because you were a good boy, and finished the tutorial. Once you have fuel in your ship, you are ready to explore what, in my opinion, makes thiis game.
The Space Exploration in Starbound is simple, yet fantasticly diverse. While you don't actually fly your ship from planet-to-planet yourself, instead picking out a destination on a starmap from your "Captains Chair" followed by a sweet jump-to-hyperspace animation; space travel is still a wonderful experience. The planets are not "randomly generated", meaning you wont have a different universe every time you start anew (though you do orbit a different planet each time), but there are loads of different planets. Conviniently, each planet is given a set of co-ordinates, which can be entered in the starmap in the respectice areas. Even more convenient, is the random planet button, who's function I shall leave a mystery. Even more convenient, is that the wonderful community involved with this game, has taken the time to stockpile a collective database of co-ordinates for planets of interest. See for yourself
. While it only contains some planets, it still shows the extent of the(freakin' awesome) exploration in this game, let alone the community associated with it. As awesome, helpful, cheerful and downright delightful the community is though, it's not the greatest.
When a game developer gives you early access to their game, they are trusting you to constructivley critsize their game, mention any and all bugs and/or tell your friends about their game. Personally, I am known(or not known) for doing only one of these things(Hint: It's not the first two things). I mean, this is my first review of anything, ever. But what broke my otherwise indefinite vow of internet silence, is my love of Starbound. I love this game, so i'm more than a little bit biased when i say that the communty backlash regarding the lack of an update, is a little bit unjust. True, it has been an awful long time since the last update, and the Nightly Builds have been less that pleasing so far, but the sudden disapproval of this game is a little silly. As into Starbound as i am, i am also a little annoyed, and I get why people are doing/saying what they are doing/saying. But the idea of Early access is to let you in on the developmental process, and play the game as it's being made, and somtimes along the way, bad things happen. When a video game is delayed, some might think of the delay as bad news. Most of the time, not so. when this happens, it usually means that the developer is unhappy with the end product, and would like to improve upon the would be final product. If less games were delayed, we would have few good ones. But the video games i'm reffering to, aren't early access titles, meaning they have no community input whatsoever. Some of those games turn out great, while some could have used more of a delay. If only they had the community opinion, they could have made the changes necessary to better their title. Which is the great thing about early access; we are there, every step of the way.
In conclusion, Starbound is an immense game, with not all that much to do. Relying heavily on it's community in it's current state, with mods filling in for it's  missing features, it still manages to feel empty. In multiplayer though, this game becomes a colorful adventure, that highlights it's biggest strength; It's Community. I highly recommend this game to those looking to take the plunge, and urge those who have wavered, to stick with it. We are what Starbound is riding on, it can't fail.

I have never written a review on Steam before but felt it was necessary for this game. In no way am I possibly going to be able to cover every aspect of the game, but hopefully this is helpful.
Firstly, this game is early-access. It doesn't feel like it, other than the last, locked area and the updates being fairly frequent.
When I was considering buying this game, I checked the reviews. Ratings were highly positive, so I figured checking reviews would just give me a more exact idea of what's great about the game. Boy, was I wrong. Apparently, there was an update that came out fairly recently and prior to my purchase that nerfed many of the top "strategies" (quoted as I believe these relied on unbalanced skills/classes) and introduced mechanics that, frankly, didn't make it harder or easier - just slightly DIFFERENT. My message to you: IGNORE THEM. This game is fantastic.
I'll start with the non-controverisal parts.
The setting is awesome. If you are a fan of HP Lovecraft or maybe even just general, occultish and gothic settings, you will love this aspect of the game (if you do love the setting, go read Lovecraft, btw). The setting is dark, desparate, and unnerving. Your Ancestor's narration is fitting and meticulous - perfectly representing the setting.
The music is great, as well. There isn't a lot of variation, but what is there is good. The tempo and other aspects of the music will change with the light level - essentially the same music, but more epic. Thus far, I have tried to keep my torch well-lit (basic explanation is the game is easier with higher light levels, but you get more/better loot when it is darker), but I did accidentaly experience the music change and was impressed.
The art is endearing and well-made. This isn't a crazy-graphics game, and they embraced that. I really like the artwork - you can check it out for yourself so I'm not going to try to put it into words...
Now, for the more controversial aspects.
The varied classes are great. There are a ton of classes - 12 or so, I believe. They all have their niches, their semi-preferred adventuring locations, their synergies with other classes, their synergies with non-class specific trinkets that you can bring to increase (as well as decrease) certain stats. I haven't come across a class that feels redundant, and I think that says a lot given the variety.
GAMEPLAY! I have never, ever, been a big fan of turn-based RPGs. I'm not sure why. But this game has totally changed my opinion to the point that it has probably opened up an entire sub-genre of RPGs to my interest that I had never considered (assuming I stop playing this game). I doubt it is too different from other turn-based RPGs, though based on some of the criticisms I may have had an advantage coming into this game without preconceptions about turn-based strategy - particularly when it comes to healing.
To wrap this up, I'm going to try to directly address some of the criticisms that almost stopped me from buying this fantastic game.
Yes, it can be difficult. There are plateaus of difficulty. There are 3 "difficulties" of missions: 0, 3, and 5. Heroes will not adventure if the mission is more than 2 ranks below them. This means that the beginning of the game can be a little tough - though nothing like what I was expecting after reading those reviews. It gets fairly easy, new boss mechanics notwithstanding, as your characters enter levels 1 and 2 while adventuring at tier 0 zones. Then you have to start doing the rank 3 missions, and it gets a little tough again since you're doing it with rank 3 heroes. And so on and so forth. All I recommend is that you make sure your weapons, armor, and skills are ranked up to 3 before you send a group to a rank 3 mission. This balances the game A LOT.
Healing. I feel like a lot of the criticism is centered on healing not being particularly strong enough. This may be true for the genre, but it doesn't matter for this game. Healing in this game is about keeping your character BARELY alive. Your characters essentially need to be killed at least twice as bringing them to 0 or lower HP in one hit will bring them to "Death's Door". Your hero can then RESIST DEATH on subsequent hits, staying on death's door. Otherwise, healing can be pretty useful for longer dungeons - have the last enemy DOT'd and stunned? Do the math - oftentimes they will die over their next two turns, and the DOTs process prior to their move and stuns force them to skip the turn. So you can use healers to bring a lot of life into everyone over the next 1-2 rounds, knowing that that enemy is going to die without being able to process another turn. You can also just eat food, though inventory space is often limited to stock up enough to do this reliably. It can happen, though.
RNG. Lots of hate about the RNG. That criticism is why I wanted to play this game a ton before writing a review. They have added an option to cap enemy crit damage - basically setting it to max normal-damage rather than a multiplied value of the rolled damage. I haven't enabled this feature yet, but I imagine this probably goes a long way in calming people down. But my general experience has been pretty balaced - yeah, sometimes the enemies chain 2-3 crits in a row and murder one of my heroes. But this ABSOLUTELY operates in the other direction, too. Seeing all the criticism of RNG made me hyper-aware of it in my gameplay, rather than me forgetting all the good things that happen to me while focusing only on the bad. This game can give you a lot of love through RNG.
This game is awesome. Don't pay too much attention to the negative reviews here. The game is meant to be hard and your heroes will die occasionally. Learn the game as you play and do your best, and you'll be fine. The difficulty is extremely manageable and makes your accomplishments feel that much beter. I highly recommend buying this game.

I owned the Xbox One version of the game and easily sunk around 1000 hours into it. After all the hype I've gathered from the reveal trailer, and buying it day one, it was everything I had hoped for. Usually disappointment kicks in after the usual novelty of playing a game, but Fallout 4 is exactly how I imagined it in my head, and every bit as fun. So what's the best summary I can give for this installment?
It's nowhere near perfect. And this isn't exactly a vocal minority, but Fallout 4 is probably the worst fallout in the series...and that doesn't have to be a bad thing. Just, if you go in expecting New Vegas or F3, you'll likely be very bummed. Judging from the trailers, I knew almost right away that F4 would stand out, and I was right. Fallout 4 feels like a completely different title, but still manages to be Fallout and retain the overall vibe. I feel as if people would have complained alot more if F4 more closely resembled NV or F4, because while they're great, they both play and feel almost a little too similarly. Same engine and everything, albeit some minor tweaks.
Then you have Fallout 4. If you can play it with an open mind, you'll likely have a great time. Because it's an awesome game overall...there's always something fun to do. But a terrible portrayal of an actual fallout game. I hope I've articulated that enough to make sense. It's no Skyrim, but for me personally, it comes close.
Now for some of the glaring flaws that most will notice right away. First off, quests. Some are noteworthy and memorable, some are just filler and lackluster. F4 also relies too heavily on radiant quests as a crutch, to make up for the lack of creativity and quantity found in Skyrim. While fun and always offer the player tasks to accomplish, they become repetitive and monotonous. If you haven't played F4 yet, I'm willing to bet you've seen the Preston Garvey memes on facebook. Yes, Preston is just as annoying as they say he is. As with the rest of the radiant quest givers. Quests are just lacking quality and quantity overall. And about 80% of them are lazy shoot to kill objectives. It is what it is. Doesn't detract from the mindless fun that I have regardless, but I do miss the creativity and writing of previous fallouts and skyrim.
RPG elements are almost nonexistent here. They've revamped the perks, and depending on how you view it, could be the bane of your existence or a welcome feature. Fans of the series hate it because alot of their favorite elements, like speech checks, have been either removed or reworked. Fallout 4 feels less of an RPG compared to its predecessors, but there's still plenty of character builds to be had. Replayability may be irrelevant since if you play the game long enough, you have access to every perk in the game. But hey, freedom of choice.
Alot of reviews complain about the factions, but I like them. Siding with a faction will determine the ending of your playthrough. Again I feel like laziness creeps its ugly head out with the endings, but they're fine. At least by Bethesda's standards, with the elder scrolls and fallout series. Every faction makes you second guess yourself about gray areas and morality. Neither are wholly good or evil, but cling and abide by their beliefs until the bitter end. However, the minutemen are pretty straightforward and aren't difficult to figure out at all. They just have one goal in mind: to restore the commonwealth back to its former glory, or at least maintain the peace.
The rest is pretty self explanatory. If you like what you've seen in gameplay videos, there's no reason to not give this a go. The addictive gameplay, combat, and exploration makes up for the cons, and the add ons and mods will only further enhance your experience, especially on PC.

I had fun trying this out during the free weekend awhile back and afterwards I dived back into Fallout: New Vegas. 4 is pretty and uses a lot more color compared to previous titles. I'm not fully sold on the voice acting for the main character and while the intro provides an interesting look at the world before the Nuclear War it does also kill a lot of the potential role playing. I'm not also sure I like how they have the perk/skill tree revamped and I have a feeling I ultimately would have wanted to restart once I had a better handle on what to go for. The changes to V.A.T.S also found me using it a lot less even once I rebound the keys to be more manageable.
The settlement system is a neat addition though it does mean you're going to be gathering loads of junk if you want to spend any decent amount of time in it. I couldn't quite get the power management and building a home from scratch but it looks like if you go full blown sims with it you could easily spend as much time with the settlements as you do the rest of the game. Although I had a vague idea where to go after Concord and the first settlement at Sanctuary 4 feels far more  "go where you want and the main story will be here waiting no matter how much you neglect looking for what was taken from you" compared to New Vegas which mostly funneled you in a suggested direction that introduced you to a lot of things in the game. I like the weapon and armor crafting system but between it and the settlement crafting I found only a single merchant through a Minutemen mission and all she sold was food.
For the time I had with Fallout 4 I ultimately think I like New Vegas a little more in terms of setting and that the world feels like it has found ways to continue but that doesn't mean I didn't enjoy my time with 4. I can whole heartedly recommend it and I'll probably pick it up during a sale as I work through some of my wishlist.

My friend Kickstarted this a year or two ago. I remembered him describing it as "Torchbearer: The Video Game" (if you're into pen-&-paper RPG's, you might get that reference). I picked it up for $12 when it went on sale, unaware it was still in Early Access.
My first impression was absolute adoration. The art style is dark, cartoon cut-outs with 4-frame animations; the best way I can think to describe it is an Edward Gorey Colorforms set. The game is narrated by the most melodramatic ham since Orson Welles chewing through a pompous, overwrought Lovecraft-inspired script ("These winding caverns teem with pelagic nightmares")... and it's glorious. It's absolutely amazing that you can come away from a game impressed by the sound design, but apparently you can.
The game itself is you as a sort of dungeon-delve overlord, building parties of adventurers with different skills, sending them into deathtraps like the Weald and the Ruins, and trying to keep them sane and breathing while they collect treasure for you.
But the game is HARD. Hard to the point of infuriation. And it's a "roguelike", so you're not going back to a saved game when a new enemy or a random critical ♥♥♥♥s you over completely.
My biggest issue with games like this is that they don't tell you how to play correctly, but they punish you to the point of flat-out failure if you play incorrectly, which means you are doomed to have to start over again and again and again until you learn to do things the right way. After a while, I got so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥I wasn't sure I wanted to continue playing it.
But I kept getting these nagging desires to come back to it, and eventually, I made peace with what the game IS, rather than what I've gotten used to in video games over the years. This is a callback to old school gaming, before the internet. A time when you had to memorize a boss's pattern or a trash mob's attacks because that information isn't on a mouseover tab. A time when you had to just grit your teeth and smash your face into the unknown to find out what was in it. A time when you earned your wins with piles upon piles upon piles of losses.
As I've gotten older, it's been exceedingly rare for these game to be FUN enough for me to want to pour the failure-time into it enough to achieve success-time. I'm more interested in "experience" games (games that simulate something or tell a story, and don't really need to offer a challenge, just an interesting concept), or competitive games that involve a static rule set and competing against another player. It's been a really long time since I had that "Contra" feeling. The feeling of dying over and over and over and over again, and still wanting to press Start, because now I know how to get past THIS screen and what's on the next one?
It's a special kind of nostalgic entertainment, and it means I can't really recommend it to everyone, but if that sounds like something that you'd dig, I would HIGHLY recommend you try Darkest Dungeon.
And that godd@mn narrator is a treat by any metric.

Dark Souls III review ‘base game’                                                                 configuration test: i5 6600 / gtx1060
Dark souls III is the third chapter of the series: the Age of Fire is running out, the First Flame is dying and you are The Ashen One, an Undead who has the duty to bring Lords of Cinder back on their thrones in the Firelink Shrine in order to link the flame and save the world once again, or not. . .; as well as the other souls games, trama will be hidden and must be reconstructed by the entire lore of the game, reading the descriptions of the objects and speaking to npcs in the game
The game takes all goods seen in Bloodborne but it inherits lot of defects from previous installments
GAMEPLAY 8,5/10
The gameplay is the main focus of the game series, solid, beautiful, complex to master: one precision must be done primarly, it is not the hardest game of the three, but, speaking of Bloodborne elements, it is clear you can’t just go straight against the enemy, sometimes shield yourself it is not a valid option, you must learn to dodge enemies.
About the defects, main concerns are the hitbox; they aren't perfect, the main problem of the previous games is present, so, enemies can hit you through the walls, a problem we would like to see fixed in a 2016 game
Level design is mostly like Dark Souls 1, there are lot of shortcuts and the entire game develops itself a lot in vertical; also present some macro areas as we have seen in Dark Souls 2; The only thing that clashes with the level design is the placement of the bonefires, in fact, it is not difficult to find two, or even three different bonefires very close to each other, according to the pattern: area closure, area start, central bonefire for shortcuts
New element of the series, taken from Bloodborne, is the ability of bosses to change appearance, acquire new abilities and consequently be much more dangerous; Additionally, there is also the presence of bosses ‘Zelda-like’, against which the brute force is not enough, but you must first devise a careful strategy to understand well how to act
Another element that could be included among the defects is the camera; in some situation, especially in narrow zones or against certain bosses, it is not perfect: let's say, during the whole run, we have encountered this problem in five or six situations, certainly not a large number, but that causes many problems in a punitive game like Dark Soul, it will lead you to certain death.
One of the concern of the community was the poise, the ability to sustain hits by enemies before you can be staggered out; It seemed to be broken or it did not work as expected, but as Dark Souls 3 reports:
‘The value was 'off' by default. It was later discovered by other people that this value was only turned on during what was thought to be hyperarmor frames at the time, and that poise damage is constantly being calculated at all times but you are only able to resist stagger during attacks or actions with hyperarmor frames’ (source:
Another problem encountered during the run is that the game sometimes freezes for few seconds, or completely, which seems to be related in a bug with nvidia drivers; in fact, rolling back drivers and changing some option in control panel helped to reduce a lot this problem
it is always present the possibility to play co op or pvp by placing signs with dedicated stones or using red eye orbs for the invasions
GRAPHICS 8/10
The game is a big step ahead; it looks very beautiful, even if the particle details aren’t the best out there Some game zones will make you keep your breath and will be easy to get screenshot for your desktop
Some assets are taken from Bloodborne, for the player, this time, is a good thing
It is also well optimized: with the configuration test we have a solid 1080p@60fps
SOUNDS 9/10
Sound is almost perfect in every situation, in particular during boss fight where every appearance change is accompanied by sounds change.
The sound of the environment is well recreated while some sounds of the undead will freeze your blood in veins
PROS
-	Gameplay
-	Graphics
-	Sounds
CONS
-      Atavistic defects of the series
-      Camera in certain situations
FINAL VOTE: 8,5/10

I've seen a lot of reviews that blast Darkest Dungeon for its RNG.  For the way a single enemy crit can spiral into death, madness, or a total party wipe.  They say the game mocks their planning, their skill, and their pain.
Darkest Dungeon is punishingly hard, which in this case is a selling point.  It's a game about fear and suffering and loss, and so it gives those to the player... along with the moments where your Crusader becomes Courageous instead of Abusive, or where your Jester survives five Deathblows in a row and finishes the boss with a Finale.
It isn't the kind of game you breeze through in a weekend.  (Well, maybe on Radiant difficulty...)  It's the kind where your A-Team gets eaten by unspeakble monsters from beyond the stars, so you send your B-Team to fight a mutant crow for their trinkets, then send your C-Team against fishmen to finance B-Team's
therapy.
Then you send B-Team into the gaping jaws of Hell, and maybe they avenge A-Team.  Or maybe they die screaming in the dark.
If you like XCOM's eagerness to kick you when you're down, and Dark Souls' atmosphere, this is the game for you.

INGREDIENTS
1 cup water
2 cups raisins
1 cup shortening
1-3/4 cups sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
3-1/2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/2 cup chopped walnuts
===
DIRECTIONS
Combine water and raisins in a small saucepan; bring to a boil. Cook for 3 minutes; remove from the heat and let cool (do not drain).
Preheat oven to 350°. In a large bowl, cream shortening and sugar until light and fluffy. Beat in eggs and vanilla. Combine flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt and spices; gradually add to creamed mixture and mix well. Stir in nuts and raisins.
Drop by teaspoonfuls 2 in. apart onto greased baking sheets. Bake 12-14 minutes or until golden brown. Remove to wire racks to cool. Yield: 6 dozen.

I've seen a lot of reviews that blast Darkest Dungeon for its RNG.  For the way a single enemy crit can spiral into death, madness, or a total party wipe.  They say the game mocks their planning, their skill, and their pain.
Darkest Dungeon is punishingly hard, which in this case is a selling point.  It's a game about fear and suffering and loss, and so it gives those to the player... along with the moments where your Crusader becomes Courageous instead of Abusive, or where your Jester survives five Deathblows in a row and finishes the boss with a Finale.
It isn't the kind of game you breeze through in a weekend.  (Well, maybe on Radiant difficulty...)  It's the kind where your A-Team gets eaten by unspeakble monsters from beyond the stars, so you send your B-Team to fight a mutant crow for their trinkets, then send your C-Team against fishmen to finance B-Team's
therapy.
Then you send B-Team into the gaping jaws of Hell, and maybe they avenge A-Team.  Or maybe they die screaming in the dark.
If you like XCOM's eagerness to kick you when you're down, and Dark Souls' atmosphere, this is the game for you.

I really hail this game. It is ferocious and uncompromising. It really makes you struggle against odds. Not Leaning against odds, or Pushing against odds, or Walking By odds. Struggle against odds.
It also has a sadistic kind of touch, and makes me believe that several features are there to sharpen the pain of failure. Assigning names to your heroes seems to be the most devilish one, when you end up seeing the beloved ones in the graveyard.
Yet it feels fair, never hard for the sake of it, thus never frustrating. Failure is usually a logic consequence of bad choices. Thinking and planning are paramount and at no point you can hope to steam roll through the dungeons, grabbing riches and paying no toll.
I also love that there is no 'free ride' for the veteran explorers, and each level has its own, deadly, challenges.
To sum up, Darkest Dungeons is a very solid and carefully crafted game, a real gem of thought and intention. And it already is, as I am playing the Early Access. You really would not tell. Au contraire, the frequent fixes and updates come as boons on top of an already polished and enjoyable game.

I owned the Xbox One version of the game and easily sunk around 1000 hours into it. After all the hype I've gathered from the reveal trailer, and buying it day one, it was everything I had hoped for. Usually disappointment kicks in after the usual novelty of playing a game, but Fallout 4 is exactly how I imagined it in my head, and every bit as fun. So what's the best summary I can give for this installment?
It's nowhere near perfect. And this isn't exactly a vocal minority, but Fallout 4 is probably the worst fallout in the series...and that doesn't have to be a bad thing. Just, if you go in expecting New Vegas or F3, you'll likely be very bummed. Judging from the trailers, I knew almost right away that F4 would stand out, and I was right. Fallout 4 feels like a completely different title, but still manages to be Fallout and retain the overall vibe. I feel as if people would have complained alot more if F4 more closely resembled NV or F4, because while they're great, they both play and feel almost a little too similarly. Same engine and everything, albeit some minor tweaks.
Then you have Fallout 4. If you can play it with an open mind, you'll likely have a great time. Because it's an awesome game overall...there's always something fun to do. But a terrible portrayal of an actual fallout game. I hope I've articulated that enough to make sense. It's no Skyrim, but for me personally, it comes close.
Now for some of the glaring flaws that most will notice right away. First off, quests. Some are noteworthy and memorable, some are just filler and lackluster. F4 also relies too heavily on radiant quests as a crutch, to make up for the lack of creativity and quantity found in Skyrim. While fun and always offer the player tasks to accomplish, they become repetitive and monotonous. If you haven't played F4 yet, I'm willing to bet you've seen the Preston Garvey memes on facebook. Yes, Preston is just as annoying as they say he is. As with the rest of the radiant quest givers. Quests are just lacking quality and quantity overall. And about 80% of them are lazy shoot to kill objectives. It is what it is. Doesn't detract from the mindless fun that I have regardless, but I do miss the creativity and writing of previous fallouts and skyrim.
RPG elements are almost nonexistent here. They've revamped the perks, and depending on how you view it, could be the bane of your existence or a welcome feature. Fans of the series hate it because alot of their favorite elements, like speech checks, have been either removed or reworked. Fallout 4 feels less of an RPG compared to its predecessors, but there's still plenty of character builds to be had. Replayability may be irrelevant since if you play the game long enough, you have access to every perk in the game. But hey, freedom of choice.
Alot of reviews complain about the factions, but I like them. Siding with a faction will determine the ending of your playthrough. Again I feel like laziness creeps its ugly head out with the endings, but they're fine. At least by Bethesda's standards, with the elder scrolls and fallout series. Every faction makes you second guess yourself about gray areas and morality. Neither are wholly good or evil, but cling and abide by their beliefs until the bitter end. However, the minutemen are pretty straightforward and aren't difficult to figure out at all. They just have one goal in mind: to restore the commonwealth back to its former glory, or at least maintain the peace.
The rest is pretty self explanatory. If you like what you've seen in gameplay videos, there's no reason to not give this a go. The addictive gameplay, combat, and exploration makes up for the cons, and the add ons and mods will only further enhance your experience, especially on PC.

INGREDIENTS
1 cup water
2 cups raisins
1 cup shortening
1-3/4 cups sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
3-1/2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/2 cup chopped walnuts
===
DIRECTIONS
Combine water and raisins in a small saucepan; bring to a boil. Cook for 3 minutes; remove from the heat and let cool (do not drain).
Preheat oven to 350°. In a large bowl, cream shortening and sugar until light and fluffy. Beat in eggs and vanilla. Combine flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt and spices; gradually add to creamed mixture and mix well. Stir in nuts and raisins.
Drop by teaspoonfuls 2 in. apart onto greased baking sheets. Bake 12-14 minutes or until golden brown. Remove to wire racks to cool. Yield: 6 dozen.

Let me start off by saying this, this is one of those games that i wish there was a neutral recommendation. Im going to upvote this game since I enjoy it more the dislike it, but keep in mind I have my reservations.
+The amazing visuals and audio really set a mood for the game. Also, whoever they have as the narrator is spot on.
+Simple turn based combat, this ♥♥♥♥♥ not complicated in a good way.
+Many different classes allows for interesting strategy diversity
+This is a difficult game, Its a good game to boot up when you want to play something challenging.
=The scarcity of resources is relevant to the atmosphere of the game, but makes your victories feel pretty empty.
=RNG plays a heavy hand in this game, I dont feel like this is a negative thing, but if its something that pisses you off this might be something to consider before purchasing the game.
-This is advertised as a roguelike, and like many roguelikes, its hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Despite this it has no loss condition so theoretically you can game the system by sending new recruits with no resources on missions with no intention of keeping them after. Then retreat the last one or two and keep what you have gotten so far. This actually seems to be a necessity to be honest since resources are so scarce.
-Combined with the above negative, your not really going to be attached to too many of your adventurers, and if one of the one you care about dies, it is really annoying, but in the end all it means you are just going to have to grind a different one up. This is in stark contrast to almost all other roguelikes whereas you get rather attached to your charactes because the loss of them means you either lose the game or are going to have an increasingly difficult chance for succeeding. When losing someone is only a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and thats it, the game turns into just a grind. Additionally when the core of the game is the adventurers you send out, there is little to care about in the game, making it feel shallow despite the obvious effort put into it.
Directed more toward the developers:
Just because my main complaints are directed at no loss condition or general irrelevance of losing characters, there needs to be balance changes to resources or strength of the adventurers if added due to the game would become impossible otherwise. Also, I realise these were intended mechanics but in my opinion, while interesting ideas, there is no redeeming quality to the mechanic. I am confident that the obvious creative minds that you have you can remedy this without making the game a cakewalk.
I want to make some observations in response to some of the negative review as well:
An incredible amount of reviews scorn the addition of corpses. There isnt really an intelligible reason to argue they shouldnt exist. As well they arent exclusively negative an equal amount of skills can only target things in the back and many enemy attacks are worse farther back in the line. In fact, without them it drastically reduces position manipulating abilities usefullness.
Many people are pissy about the difficulty of the game...I really dont feel as if any complaint should be targetted for difficulty in a game that advertises as "roguelike" unless its directed at it being too easy.

I like roguelike elements in games, but this game punishes you not by needing to start over a 8 hour game, but by setting back your existing 8 hour game by 4 hours of playtime. Allow me to explain: Your characters level when you take them into the dungeon, but around level 4 your higher level characters will refuse to go to the lower level dungeons to help escort and level your lower-level characters. It's more or less suicide/disaster when you bring your lower level characters to higher level dungeons. This took me several hours to discover, otherwise I would have continued escorting all my low-level characters up to a decent level. It requires careful planning to make sure the exp gets spread out so no one char gets too high and becomes unusable until the rest of your team catches up(or fails to catch up because an A-lister can't go in your dungeons anymore). The problem occurs when some of your A-team chars die or are out of commision for awhile and your B-team can't compete in the current dungeons. Painstakingly raising rookies to even B-team status will literally take hours, assuming all goes well.
It gets to a point where instead of "oh crap, a char died, I'll just start over my 2-8 hour game" you go "oh crap, a char died, I can either trash my 8-12 hour game, or try to get back into it by investing 3 hours into a rookie and try to salvage all the time I put in". It becomes quite tedious.
ALLLLLL this could be alleviated if you could buy higher level characters(for a higher price, or not even characters that rival your high level chars, maybe just level 2 so you don't need to spend 2-3 hours grinding a few levels for your rookies).
All in all, I think this game needs work. I like a roguelike, but I want punishment to be DEATH not limbo.

Overall great game, if you want challenge and uniqueness to your classic turn based rpg hit this up.

Trove:
The first thing you may wonder is "Is it a Pay to Win?" I will gladly say that its not, you can get almost everything by just playing there is only a couple of things to buy but they do not affect gameplay at all!! You don't get any advantages for paying money for mounts and packs.
Trove is an open world MMO RPG it is great to play with friends also big groups of people. Solo however is great aswell you can have just as much fun without friends. The building aspect of the game is great, you start with a small plot where "you" and only you can build and you can find empty plots to place your building anywhere in the world, there is also Club Worlds that you can make invite friends and build whatever you want! (Club Worlds are much bigger than the plots)
There is a wide variety of weapons, masks and hats (Still adding more each patch) there is a variety of monsters and bosses you find across each individual biome. Dungeons do not end you can do as many as you like!
There are different levels of "Adventure Worlds" each one gets harder and harder but set for a certain level so you cant acess a really high level without being "say" level 12 for Uber-2
Overall you may ask this is a rip off of Cube World, in my eyes there both great games but lets say remember Cube World is still pre - Alpha, There is not as many things to do in Cube World as there is in Trove.
All up Trove is a great game and anyone can enjoy it!  10/10 :-)

It is not easy to boil this game down into a brief review but I will try.  Let's say it's a dungeon themed survival game that invovles a great many horror elements.  It reminds me of the works of Hellboy and BPRD creator Mike Mignola with it's shadowed art style and dark themes.
First thing to know? This game is devistatingly difficult, which fits perfectly with the theme of insurmountable horror.    The art style, narration, and gameplay all serve to remind you that you and your heroes are in a world of darkness and depravity with little hope of making it out of this alive.
Does this sound grim?  It is, but hopefully this will not dissuade you if you are fond of fantasy horror rife with themes of great hopelessness and unimaginable evil.
There a few game mechanics that don't make sense (IE - why don't I keep the items I bought from my last dungeon crawl if I didn't use them) and the narration is sometime overwraught.  That said, this game is exactly what it sels itself as...a challenging and engaging dive into one of the darkest dungeons you'll ever tread.

I need to give this game two reviews: one for gameplay, and one for its story.
Gameplay:
Dark Souls 3 is the best looking game of the series. It has the most refined and fluid gameplay of the series. For a few months after release, I still believed DS2 had better PVP. The PVP in DS3 has since grown on me tremendously, however, and I now prefer Dark Souls 3's PVP to everything else in the series. The game is fun, challenging, and beautiful. Play it.
Story:
Hidetaka Miyazaki doesn't like writing sequels, and it shows. The game itself is fantastic, but its ties to Dark Souls are obviously forced. Bandai/Namco wanted another game in their new cashcow series (and no one can blame them), and Miyazaki agreed to make one more game to put the series to bed. I honestly wish this had been a Souls game in spirit only, and that he'd not reused any characters, locations, armor, etc. from the previous games. After playing through the game and both DLCs, I'm left feeling the way a lot of people felt after watching the final season of Lost. "You didn't answer my questions. I wanted a satisfying ending, but I realized a while ago that I wasn't getting one. Still, I'm glad it's over." Don't go into DS3 looking for answers or resolution, aside from the one very big and satisfying reveal in an optional area of the vanilla release. Just enjoy the gameplay.

This game really feels like it SHOULD be good, but it's just too grindy and there just is not enough real content. Once you play for about a half-hour you have played the entire game.
It's got some really cool ideas that I haven't seen before, don't get me wrong, but it really needs just more to it. For example, there's spots in all the worlds where you can claim them as your home. Basically you build your home and take it with you into worlds. It can't be widened, but you can build it up extremely high or extremely low.
The game is also really easily accessible which is nice. It's about a GB in size and there's no party system. You just teleport to your friends and everyone auto shares loot and everything you pick up, even with other randoms that are roaming around.
That's about all the good parts tho. The combat is just too overly simple to really enjoy after a while. I'd say it's a bit more involved than most MMOs honestly, but with only 3 abilities there's only so much you can do.
The game really just needs to be less of a grind and give me more reason to have fun and build. I noticed there are "community-dungeons" but there's no way for someone like me to make one. In a game like this, everyone should be able to. Have people rate your dungeon and the better the rating the more chance it has to show up.
Anyway, tldr; game is almost good but not enough it needs more to do and more fun to be had. Also the music is really boring and uninspired. It's decent for a free to play game though
