So after 3 play throughs and being just short of 400 hours in to this game, I honestly can't reccomend it as a great Fallout game that I was anticipating. They ripped out the RPG elements and delivered a Settlement Builder scavenger hunt.
So first off your character's backstory is decided for you which really kills the ability to create multiple characters with unique play styles and backstory because that is really what feeds RPGs replayibiity. You're forced to gon this questline in search of your son which makes it really hard to play an sort of evil or villianous character. The lack of Karma system really bummed me out as I felt I was forced into the good guy role for every single character I played. They further dumbed down the RPG elements by ripping out skills for your character and instead replaced it with "perks" and unlimited leveling. This kills the replay value and depth to characters because these new "perks" are shallow and some amount to damage percent increases or crafting ability instead of unqiue gameplay changes like they were in previous titles. Leveling feels far less rewarding, character development is also less rewarding as each character now has to take the same perks in order to have any sort of advancement in game.  The dialogue is atrocious with only 4 options ever, some of which are just the same reply with different words which adds redundancy to the game. They don't even give you an accurate representation of what your character will say and instead limit you to "yes, yep, saracasm, no" in many instances. It's honestly one of the worst things they could've done to this game and kills the replay value immensely because the depth of each conversation amounts to a puddles worth of experience.
The new focus of the game is the crafting system and settlement building which you can tell righ off the bat is what they wanted to focus on instead of building a fleshed out world. There are too many locations that are just empty of any depth and are avalible for you to build settlement after settlement. The world feels dull and repetitve when instead of finding new sidequests you just find a new place to build your 15th home for a bunch of nameless and souless NPCs. Crafting is unavoidable unless you want to use the garbage weapons that spawn on every enemy. You end up spending more time scavenging ruins than questing, looking for salvage to build your settlements or guns and armor with than actually rolepalying. The weapon variety is lacking and really kills new play throughs for me as there are only like 50 guns total with the ability to modify them slightly. No enemies really feel unique or special either as when you progress through the game, they just get reskinned and renamed with a bigger health bar. I will say combat is more satisfying than previous Fallout titles as the enemy AI has improved quite a bit and the enemies will resort to different tactics to attack you with but this is on of the only parts that has shined through for me in this game.  Combat itself is probably the best part of this game which is sad since IMO, Fallout was meant to be an RPG, not an FPS with extremely minor rpg elements and a crafting system.
Questing has been outright killed when Bethesda decided it would be worth implementing radiant quests which consist of go kill these monsters/raiders, fetch this worthless item, etc. instead of actual stories with different choices and endings. The 4 factions all give you the same stuff to do with a different name and the rewards are so worthless that it doesn't make you want to continue the effort to complete them over and over and over again. Each of the 4 factions felt really shallow and didn't have much to offer in new ways of playing the game, each felt kind of like a reskin of the other when it came to the tasks they asked you to complete for them.  The few unique side quests I can remember pertained mostly to companions which I will say were improved upon compared to previous titles but still fall flat and leave you with repitition. Companions did have more personality and even an affinity rating system but this could be achieved by basic tasks of getting in and out of power armor or taking drugs over and over.  The main story itself only has 2 endings and is pretty boring IMO.
The DLC for Fallout 4 isn't something I can honestly give a proper review as I may have paid for it, but because of the mod breaking changes they made when they added them (Far Harbor and Nuka World) to the game, I lost previous save files and couldn't bring myself to replay this game. But it's rather insulting when they delivered great expansions to Fallout 3 for all their DLC's then and instead choose to add more crafting systems and extra settlement content which should've been added to the base game as a free update. It adds nothing to the experience of the game and is an insult to the players.
Overall if you're looking for a post apocalyptic Far Cry esque game, Fallout 4 can deliver that much to you. But this isn't a great RPG and lacks so many proper elements to give your more than a playthrough or two to enjoy. It really has the width of an ocean but the depth of a puddle and I can only hope that the next installment in the series will look at the things they did wrong here.

This game really feels like it SHOULD be good, but it's just too grindy and there just is not enough real content. Once you play for about a half-hour you have played the entire game.
It's got some really cool ideas that I haven't seen before, don't get me wrong, but it really needs just more to it. For example, there's spots in all the worlds where you can claim them as your home. Basically you build your home and take it with you into worlds. It can't be widened, but you can build it up extremely high or extremely low.
The game is also really easily accessible which is nice. It's about a GB in size and there's no party system. You just teleport to your friends and everyone auto shares loot and everything you pick up, even with other randoms that are roaming around.
That's about all the good parts tho. The combat is just too overly simple to really enjoy after a while. I'd say it's a bit more involved than most MMOs honestly, but with only 3 abilities there's only so much you can do.
The game really just needs to be less of a grind and give me more reason to have fun and build. I noticed there are "community-dungeons" but there's no way for someone like me to make one. In a game like this, everyone should be able to. Have people rate your dungeon and the better the rating the more chance it has to show up.
Anyway, tldr; game is almost good but not enough it needs more to do and more fun to be had. Also the music is really boring and uninspired. It's decent for a free to play game though

I finally finished this game, and at the end of it all....I just can't recommend it if you're a casual gamer like me.
The learning curve for a casual player is pretty steep.  the controls aren't intuitive and the in-game tutorial messages are useless, seeing as they're still showing controls for gamepads rather than PC, and there are no clear directions as to what you're supposed to do or where you're to go.  You just figure it out as you go.  This can be good or bad depending on who you are.
I quit the game in disgust after dying for the millionth time against the 3rd or 4th boss, and still didn't feel like I had a good grasp of the game.  Since gaming is a smaller part of my life, I didn't have the same reaction other reviewers had under these circumstances.  I felt no obsession with winning or anger that drove me to boot the game up again.  I just felt frustrated, annoyed, and regret over the purchase, as I had spent so much time on it with no progression.  By this point I was just over the refund time cap, so I couldn't return it, which was just salt in the wound.
After a few months I tried again and was successful, but I didn't feel "exhilerated" or anywhere near as euphoric as others seem to feel.  I just felt relief that I could finally continue, that an annoying barrier was finally behind me.  From that point, the game grew on me, and by the final boss, I had become pretty good at it.  But I didn't feel fulfilled at the end.
This may be because the story isn't really there.  It's buried in item descriptions and vague dialoges with npcs.  You can find out what's going on around you, but the easiest way to do this is to look online for explanations that have been cobbled together overtime.  That's just not something that says "good story" to me.  It's vague and ambiguous, which is fine, but as a result, I felt far less connected to the world.  Not once did I care about any character in the game.  To me, it was always just a hack-and-slash.
So, that's why, after the final boss was dead, I decided to write this.  If you're a casual gamer, I would advise you to stay away from this one.  Unless you have the extra time to find out all the additional information and play strategies on the internet to learn about every single bit of how this game works, I don't think you'll enjoy yourself very much.
That's not to say there aren't good things.  Sometimes the combat can truly be fun.  The graphics are great.  You get some amazing views.  The character builds are very involved and rewarding.  If you aren't turned off by the brutally unforgiving nature of the game, then you may find something to like under the surface.
Otherwise, I would ultimately advise you to save your money.  There are games that are far more enjoyable overall, with better story as well.

I feel like this game has a ton of potential, and I enjoy using up heroes then discarding them as they slowly become useless.
Except it's not slowly. Your units will miss a large portion of the time when striking, their stress increases incredibly fast and will break after only a few rounds of combat and your healing is so useless your units die constantly.
Funding upgrades for any of your units is pretty much useless because they'll most likely die before you can even upgrade them, leaving you with a handful of level 1 new recruits to fight a level 3 dungeon.
It feels a lot like FTL where you're supposed to lose a lot and die a lot, except the game becomes so frustrating it sucks a lot of the fun out.
Maybe the final product will be better, but as of right now I don't recommend the early access version.

Bear in mind, yes, this game is still in playtest, so things are going to change. New content keeps rolling out, and I can't wait until the final Darkest Dungeon level is released. It's definitely a game for people who like strategy mixed with luck, and it helps significantly if you have a certain love for things that are inspired by Lovecraftian mythos, because attachment to the heroes generally ends poorly. If you like winning all the time, min-maxing, or just power gaming in general, you're going to have a bad time. If you like playing the long game, losing a battle to win a war, live for risk, and can graciously accept when fate deals you a bad hand, you're going to have a better time. End of story.

Ever since they removed the energy requirement for the elevators, this game has been a lot more enjoyable.  The massive overhaul they did to the alchemy (item crafting) system, the elevators, and even pets, has greatly improved a game that I had already enjoyed.  This is a game however that is much more fun to play with a group of friends, since the later levels can get quite challenging.  Anyone who has ever liked dungeon crawlers should deffinately play this.
It is constantly evolving due to the times, and they do listen to their fanbase.  I remember the largest complaint being the elevators costing energy to use, and now they don't.  They always have holiday items and events, some of which I regret missing because of the items, and are always looking for more things to add.
The large variety of combat styles makes the game a solid 9/10 in my opinion.  One can go full bore hack and slash, Mr McShooty, or Mr KaBoomy.  You can hybridize them, or focus them like being a speed sword, a heavy damage sword wielder, speed/damage gunner, and so on, depending on your loadout.  I personally use a sword and a gun and swordsman armor (Currently vog armor, and working on skolver).  Players will need to learn to adjust these based on where they go in the game.  Sometimes guns-blazing works better than hack and slashing, and vice-versa.
The mission system now provides players with almost everything they need to get their first set of 5-star armor, which is a big plus for new players.  The basic armor they give is actually pretty good, and will work in nearly all situations, allowing players to work more on skill than simply being prepared.
On a final note: I still hate howlitzers (undead turrets).  I have more deaths caused by them than anything. (Well... Maybe Kat swarms, but those are easy to avoid for the most part.)

I feel like this game has a ton of potential, and I enjoy using up heroes then discarding them as they slowly become useless.
Except it's not slowly. Your units will miss a large portion of the time when striking, their stress increases incredibly fast and will break after only a few rounds of combat and your healing is so useless your units die constantly.
Funding upgrades for any of your units is pretty much useless because they'll most likely die before you can even upgrade them, leaving you with a handful of level 1 new recruits to fight a level 3 dungeon.
It feels a lot like FTL where you're supposed to lose a lot and die a lot, except the game becomes so frustrating it sucks a lot of the fun out.
Maybe the final product will be better, but as of right now I don't recommend the early access version.

After having not played this game for months since it was first released on early access and picking it up again for the 'inhuman bondage' update, I had to stop playing and ask "what have they done with the difficulty?"
When i started playing i hardly had anyone die and the difficulty was fine, it was trying but doable. I was able to mix and match my team compositions and steadily build up my characters which was a lot of fun.
Now with the newest update i've had 8 deaths in the last 4 hours, enemies are noticably hitting harder, dodging more and having more turns to act than my own party members. A enemy even had 0 dodge listed in its status and still managed to dodge my party member's attack which had a 85 to hit, twice.*
My party members are also stressing out much more often and dieing to heart attacks since there is a very good chance they will be at death doors when their stress meters hit 200 which was something that didn't happen nearly as much when i played the vanilla version.
From what i could read of other people's reviews, it seems I'm not the only one who is experiencing this lash back from the game with mention of majority of trinkets now being useless, only certain party compositions being optimal, significant debuff issues and certain battle system changes being frustrating rather than challenging being some of the key issues.
In its current iteration i feel like it's more a issue of luck than skill that decides whether or not you will succeed completing a quest or whether you will abandon it with 2-3 party members dead. This forces you to get some new recruits and grind up those characters again resulting in even more hours being used in a game that is already a heavy grind.
More frustration with RNG than skill and tactical thinking, i find the current iteration of the game needing some significant tweaks before it can be called enjoyable. I like these type of rough-like games when they challenge me but not when they feel like they're going out of their way to stop me playing with random dice rolls.
----------------------------------------------------------------
*Edit: Found out that accuracy is calculated by (base accuracy - dodge) so if your skill is anything less than 100, you have a chance to miss. Review tweaked to reflect this.
If you want a second opinion I suggest giving this article a read which does a pretty good job of describing the current state of the game (even with latest update):

Ultimately, I recommend the game. The art style, the variety of party arrangements, and the stress and quirk systems lend the game a fantastic, varied, and harrowing play. I do love a good challenge where the stakes feel significant. That said, unbalanced elements do not a fair challenge make. I usually mitigate this with overprovisioning. I use the retreat function when things get hairy.

Just bought this game and after a short spin-up to learn the mechanics of the game, began to make some forays into the dungeons.  It was immediately apparent that the difficulty threshold was quite high-- which is good thing to me, being an old EQ guy who liked it when you suffered horribly for mistakes (for those of you who never played EQ in the early days, think of it like Dark Souls in a MMORPG setting with no institutional knowledge base to draw on for help).  But from the beginning it was clear that if you dawdled and held back from finishing off a monster to give a toon a well deserved heal or buff, the game inexplicably punishes you for it by heaping stress on the toon who passes on his turn.  Furthermore, if you choose to push onward after meeting your objective, you meet increased resistance to your group with mobs that dish out massive crits and hits-- something which a previous heal would have been very beneficial to have gotten.
But no!  For some reason holding off to heal increases stress!  No, it makes no cognitive sense that your group would suffer for doing something for which any character would obviously welcome when they are near death.
"Oooh, that gunshot wound is bleeding you out!  Want a heal?"
"Naaah.  I'm too stressed as it is.  Having you make me feel better would only make me worry about getting hooked on those Oxycontins you're offering me."
"Oh.  Umm, ok then."
<death ensues>
See what I mean?  The internal logic of the game makes no sense at all.

I also haven't gotten any quests since about 4 hours which has me slightly concerned - however, I assume that that will fix itself when I visit the next planet/moon/space-rock.

Although it becomes repetitive at some point, I still greatly enjoy this game. The artstyle is very attractive and novel.  The game design itself stands out as imaginative and unusual, this is terrific as the designers certainly did not attempt anything old and tired as the majority of reskinned game clones out there.  There is a good bit of dark humor as well.  The game does a very good job punishing you for mistakes, which generates a healthy sense of anxiety while exploring and managing your party - this is at the core of the charm and attraction that this game has.  So, of course, as any game with a challenge it's a bit masochistic.
The downside to the game is that the it is pretty grindy and, while initially there is enough diversity and challenge, after a time it starts feeling quite repetitive.  There is no true story to the game, just some background setting that lets you know where you are and what you are trying to accomplish but it stops there and does not evolve.  The narrator is excellent though and to a degree serves well to compensate for lack of an actual story.  If you belive that a good RPG should have a decent story based 'RP', this game may feel incomplete to you.
Now to the basics of the game to explain how it works and give you an idea if this is something you may want to pick up and try:
- basically you have a roster of heros/mercenaries that fight and very often die for your cause.  The dead ones are replaced by new arrivals that you find at a stage coach and you may choose to add these rookies to your roster if you wish.
- there are many classes, although some appear much better equiped to deal with challenges than others.
- you take a party of 4 into a randomly generated dungeon where they explore, fight, eat and camp OR starve and suffer stress and negative quirks that permanently weaken them.
- At the Hamlet in between dungeon runs, you manage an economy expanding various services that your heroes will require, including places to heal them, cure their quirks and upgrade them.
- the combat is turn based with point and ckick mechanics.
- your heroes progress from lower level dungeous to harder ones if they are lucky to live long enough and level up.
That's it.

Just bought this game and after a short spin-up to learn the mechanics of the game, began to make some forays into the dungeons.  It was immediately apparent that the difficulty threshold was quite high-- which is good thing to me, being an old EQ guy who liked it when you suffered horribly for mistakes (for those of you who never played EQ in the early days, think of it like Dark Souls in a MMORPG setting with no institutional knowledge base to draw on for help).  But from the beginning it was clear that if you dawdled and held back from finishing off a monster to give a toon a well deserved heal or buff, the game inexplicably punishes you for it by heaping stress on the toon who passes on his turn.  Furthermore, if you choose to push onward after meeting your objective, you meet increased resistance to your group with mobs that dish out massive crits and hits-- something which a previous heal would have been very beneficial to have gotten.
But no!  For some reason holding off to heal increases stress!  No, it makes no cognitive sense that your group would suffer for doing something for which any character would obviously welcome when they are near death.
"Oooh, that gunshot wound is bleeding you out!  Want a heal?"
"Naaah.  I'm too stressed as it is.  Having you make me feel better would only make me worry about getting hooked on those Oxycontins you're offering me."
"Oh.  Umm, ok then."
<death ensues>
See what I mean?  The internal logic of the game makes no sense at all.

Play it for the challenging PvE, as the PvP is extremely unbalanced due to fromsoft's lack of competence. Although dark souls still has the best level design, dark souls 3 has the best pve overall. One of the highlights for this game is how polished it is in comparison to other dark souls games and the weapon arts which are a very direct yet enjoyable way to make each weapon more unique or interesting. The DLC for this game is especially good, the 2nd DLC being the best one and some of my favorite dark souls content ever. Sadly the overworld isn't as free and interconnected as dark souls 1's but it does give you a decent amount of choice. The best areas of the game though have to be in the DLC though, i heavily recommend getting them, it's worth the price if you do enjoy dark souls. For one you get 2 giant♥♥♥♥♥swords that you can duel weild, and you also get a shield that is quite literally a giant set of doors. You also get a covenant that allows you to be summoned as a boss. Sadly invasions suck in this game and fighting others in this game still is a lagfest. Overall a great dark souls game, a lot better of a souls game than 2. Just don't expect anything very different from it compared to the first dark souls, but saying it's just meant to jerk off dark souls 1 fans is a bit exaggerated. It has it's own concepts, it's own overworld, and it's really just the sequel that dark souls 2 didn't end up being even if it flew too close to the original at moments.
TL;DR - This is the best dark souls for PvE, it may not have an overworld on the level of ds1 and has the worst PvP in the series, but it's still a very solid souls game, being one of the most polished games in the series. Just don't expect balanced PvP, as again, this is the dark souls for mainly PvE whether fromsoft wanted that or not. Just make sure you get the DLC though if you enjoy it, the DLC is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.

This game's taking a lot of flack. Originally it was too easy... Now it's too hard... So many mixed reviews... I think the reason for this boils down to a couple things.
A) This is an early access title that has seen a lot of success and (based on what I've read) has changed quite a bit since the original release, and not just content specific changes, but mechanically as well.
I think a lot of people got into this game early, liked what they were playing, envisioned a certain evolutionary path, and are disappointed the developers went a different route. I get that, but, y'know, early access. You're always risking falling in love with something and watching it grow into something very different.
B) This game isn't being recognized as the rogue-like that it is. I know it says rogue-like in the description, but note that "rogue-like" is not one of the top four tags. This is a shame, because, in my opinion, this game brings a lot to the table as a rogue-like. It takes elements from more traditional rogue-likes such as Rogue Legacy and blends it with the dungeon crawling elements of games like Diablo, the character development and permadeath of games such as XCOM, the horror elements of games like Call of Cthulu (very Lovecraftian in nature), the narration of games such as Bastion,  stirs in some nice tactics based around team composition, resource management, and easy to understand stat modifiers, and leaves it up to you to figure it all out. All of this combines to make this game feel like an original, atmospheric, and fun adventure. What more can you really ask for out of a rogue-like?
Despite the flack, as a lover of rogue-likes, I'm really enjoying this game. It offer's risk, reward, and the agonizing pain of failure. It has a lot of untapped potential, but, based on previous actions, I believe this developer will exploit much of it before they're done here. It is early access, but the way they release content holds well in the early access platform. It is a bit grindy, but remember: rogue-like.
I love the concept of trying to make up for the failures of an old man who reached his sanity's end. I love the atmosphere of horror, madness, and the looming fear of the fact that you will likely fail just as those before you did. I love the characters and the many team composition options presented. I love the enemies, their corpses, and the randomness of their difficulty. I love the art. I love the music. Most of all, I love that every single decision you make, you have to pay for.
If you want an indie turn-based RPG, play Divinity, Wasteland, Shadowrun, or the plethora of other titles that have come out in the last couple of years with the CRPG revival. If you want a rogue-like indie turn-based RPG, this just might be your game. Darkest Dungeon is a game of risk and consequence, not just a loot hoarding dungeon crawler.

This game's taking a lot of flack. Originally it was too easy... Now it's too hard... So many mixed reviews... I think the reason for this boils down to a couple things.
A) This is an early access title that has seen a lot of success and (based on what I've read) has changed quite a bit since the original release, and not just content specific changes, but mechanically as well.
I think a lot of people got into this game early, liked what they were playing, envisioned a certain evolutionary path, and are disappointed the developers went a different route. I get that, but, y'know, early access. You're always risking falling in love with something and watching it grow into something very different.
B) This game isn't being recognized as the rogue-like that it is. I know it says rogue-like in the description, but note that "rogue-like" is not one of the top four tags. This is a shame, because, in my opinion, this game brings a lot to the table as a rogue-like. It takes elements from more traditional rogue-likes such as Rogue Legacy and blends it with the dungeon crawling elements of games like Diablo, the character development and permadeath of games such as XCOM, the horror elements of games like Call of Cthulu (very Lovecraftian in nature), the narration of games such as Bastion,  stirs in some nice tactics based around team composition, resource management, and easy to understand stat modifiers, and leaves it up to you to figure it all out. All of this combines to make this game feel like an original, atmospheric, and fun adventure. What more can you really ask for out of a rogue-like?
Despite the flack, as a lover of rogue-likes, I'm really enjoying this game. It offer's risk, reward, and the agonizing pain of failure. It has a lot of untapped potential, but, based on previous actions, I believe this developer will exploit much of it before they're done here. It is early access, but the way they release content holds well in the early access platform. It is a bit grindy, but remember: rogue-like.
I love the concept of trying to make up for the failures of an old man who reached his sanity's end. I love the atmosphere of horror, madness, and the looming fear of the fact that you will likely fail just as those before you did. I love the characters and the many team composition options presented. I love the enemies, their corpses, and the randomness of their difficulty. I love the art. I love the music. Most of all, I love that every single decision you make, you have to pay for.
If you want an indie turn-based RPG, play Divinity, Wasteland, Shadowrun, or the plethora of other titles that have come out in the last couple of years with the CRPG revival. If you want a rogue-like indie turn-based RPG, this just might be your game. Darkest Dungeon is a game of risk and consequence, not just a loot hoarding dungeon crawler.

If pressed to give a final opinion on Fallout 4, I would probably respond by saying that - while it has excellent production values - it was a game I ultimately did not enjoy playing very much. But this statement is very much at odds with my reported play-time on Steam: I invested over 100 hours into the game. It's an unusual discrepancy that I have struggled to understand myself.
Certainly Fallout 4 is not without is merits. Its large, open world is beautifully detailed and Bethesda has well-utilized the updated Creation (nee Gamebryo) engine to crank out some of their best renderings to date. The texture detail in some areas is simply stunning. The game-world is far more open than Bethesda's earlier titles; while you still encounter a load-screen when entering the larger dungeons, many smaller areas that once would have been separate maps are now part of the overland map, giving the whole game a much more cohesive feel. The world is stuffed full of things to discover, and - like all Bethesda's games - the biggest thrill is walking across the world and discovering a new area to explore. Like a jackdaw to a shiny object, I was constantly distracted by the lure of some new dungeon or ruin to discover, and rare was it that I'd cross the Wastelands on some quest without numerous detours because some new "unexplored area" icon appeared on my mini-map.
Unfortunately, this was the only real joy I received while playing the game. The individual quests - always a weak point of Bethesda's games - I found uninteresting, with particular disdain for the main quest. The procedurally generated "Radiant" quests were exceptionally poor, especially when they were auto-assigned ("Rescue the town from imminent attack") and saddled with a time-limit. The latter was an especially egregious sin as it took me away from the free-form wandering that was game's strength. The franchise's newest mechanic - the base-building - was tedious and fatiguing, with  limited build options and fiddly controls. After establishing a few homes for my braindead followers (the AI doesn't lift a finger to help themselves, requiring the player to not only build their homes but assign them to specific tasks) I largely ignored the base-building feature in favor of the more interesting exploration. Many of the older mechanics - unfulfilling combat, dry dialogue options, uninspired AI, and cumbersome crafting - still suffered from rough spots that have haunted Bethesda's games since the start. Individually these issues didn't harm the game too much, but the continued lack of improvement in this area was disheartening
I think that if I had to put my finger on Fallout 4's biggest problem, it would be that it was such an unadventurous sequel; except for the addition of the base-building, it added very little new to the franchise.  Most disappointingly, it took absolutely no chances with the setting. In many ways the game felt little more than a re-skin of Fallout 3, both in terms of gameplay and setting. Once again I took the role of a bad♥♥♥♥♥(albeit easily diverted) vault-dweller facing off against the same bunch of mutants and wasteland factions I've battled against since the original game in 1997. Oddly enough, the increased level of graphical detail - while pleasant to look at - made the game actually much less immersive, since its increased realism only brought into contrast many of the inconsistencies of the game's world (like, if the war was over 200 years ago then why are there still-fresh corpses from the war all over?).
It was the lure of discovery that kept me playing for as long as I did, but the payout was rarely worth the effort. Like an addict, I kept scouring the wastes - adding tens of hours to my overall play-time - in hopes of finding some redeeming and exciting set-piece but instead was reward with an unending sense of ennui. When I finally did come to the end of the main quest, I found I had little desire to keep playing beyond that point. This is a distinct divergence from my experience with other Bethesda titles, where I would happily play and re-play the game ad infinitum. With Fallout 4, I was happy to have finally come to a concluding moment so that I could abandon it without guilt or worry I might be missing something. significant. I'd seen enough to realize that even were I to play another hundred hours I still wouldn't discover anything that would make that investment worthwhile.
That said, I can't dismiss the fact that I /did/ play the game for more than 100 hours.  Flawed and chary as the game-play may have been, the production values were competent and the game definitely delivered on quantity - if not  overwhelming quality - of content. So I will grudgingly give it a recommendation, especially to newcomers who have not already played this game when it was entitiled Fallout 3.

I have never seen such an amazing game so ruthlessly attacked with negative reviews simply because the player base disagrees with how the devs have attempted to balance gameplay. To anyone out there who is interested in purchasing Darkest Dungeon let me say that this is in my opinion a fantastic, albeit challenging, turn-based RPG which I would highly recommend to anyone with even a passing interest in the genre. It is easily in my top 5 games of this year and it is quite simply THE best example of early access done right, period. Red Hook Studios should be commended for the beautifully polished experience they have produced and the continued negative criticism they receive for their ongoing attempts to support the game is absolutely awful. Such unconstructive criticism will only succeed in discouraging other game devs out there from trying to follow in Red Hook's footsteps.
Let me make this clear, it is perfectly alright to disagree with the changes that are making to the gameplay formula and express such discontent on forums, in videos, and other constructive ways of critiquing the changes and calling into question how they disrupt the current gameplay paradigm. But to post increasing negative and entirely unjustified reviews as a means to punish the Devs is entirely uncalled for and I sincerely hope newcomers interested in this game will look past such fraudulent "reviews".
Darkest Dungeon is a tactical turn based RPG with an intriguing infusion of lovecraftian horror. Your heroes are not the noble exemplars you may expect. They are anxious and rapacious, easily driven to madness by the foul miscreants and monsters they face on their adventure. And when they return from their ghastly quest where else should they turn for relief but the sins of the flesh. Cure hopelessness with a drunken bender or better yet the brothels, assuming of course our hero hasn't yet developed strange enough fetishes as to forbidden from returning. If such is the case then perhaps they had best spend a week in the Sanitarium for social reconditioning.
We cannot fault our heroes for their numerous vices and failings however, not when so many before them have fallen to the unspeakable horrors lying in wait. Whether it be shambling undead and vicious iron or eldritch abominations with their accursed blight, heroes will fall in battle all the same. A mercy perhaps, considering the circumstances of their condition. But all this cruelty is not without prior machination. An ancestor seemingly forgotten has charged our heroes with returning to their familial estate and cleansing its darkest dungeons of the monstrosities brought forth through foul experimentation. Will you atone for his sins or surrender to the pit of despair as your ancestor did before you? Finding solace only in death... by his own hand.
Needless to say I am quite the fan of this hidden gem. Whether it be the art style, sound effects, gameplay decisions, or eerie narrator, Darkest Dungeon is not another game with a classic case of cognitive dissonance in how it acts and how it plays; from start to finish the dark and twisted presentation is flawless and omnipresent. The gameplay is a difficult and oftentimes hopeless affair which only serves to make success all the more rewarding. I find it to be extremely deep with an addicting level of challenge. Heroes will die and quests will be failed; ever will you be teetering just on the edge of madness. But injury and despondency set the stage for heroism... or cowardice.
I highly recommend this game and hope you will consider purchasing it. It is still in early access and as such many of the gameplay elements are being refined and may be subject to change. If you find that certain elements are not to your liking then let the developer know! But be civil and constructive when discussing the changes you want and understand that the gameplay is highly nuanced and Red Hook will need time to balance certain changes. They have been listening to community feedback and do seem to be genuinely committed to crafting the best possible game they can, a trait which in my opinion is lacking in most other studios these days. I support Darkest Dungeon and hope you will as well.

I recommended this game awhile back.  And I still would for certain people.  I had very high hopes for this game and to certain degree I still do.  The devs seem to make patch fixes fairly consistently but they seem to be ignoring the overall issue with this game.
It is an RPG, meaning you make decisions and develop your characters to suit your personal needs.  But what makes an RPG truly great is being able to witness how your decisions affect the gameplay, either through the interactions with te NPCs or with the flow of combat.
This game is no exception, your development of the town and characters DOES reduce the risks of losing said characters.  However, this game has been proving to me more and more that success in this game has become less about skill, less about decisions and more about luck.  It all comes down to a roll of the dice, one bad encounter, a few badly timed criticals and misses and those character you've been polishing for hours and hours are either dead or scarred beyond repair.
Don't get me wrong, a game being sadistically difficult is one thing, Dark Souls fans will agree that a challenging game is often the most rewarding.  However, a game that is this dependent on luck, and will consistently punish you no matter how much you play leaves me thoroughly unsatisfied.  It doesn't reward progress or character development, the combat remains just as luck-based late game as it does early game.
I won't say this game isn't still fun to a degree.  I still love the art style and the intent of the combat.  But for a game to be fun it must reward the player's efforts somehow.  Make them feel like their struggles were worth something and that there's a possibility of them succeeding.  This game doesn't do that, it is truly a bad sign when you use strategies that got you success in one playthrough that are then crushed in the next.
Hopefully the devs will see these and make some slight tweaks, which I truly believe is all this game needs to be enjoyable.  But really as it is, the only people i can see enjoying this game are masochists, even the souls games on their hardest settings weren't as ruthless as this game.

Hardcore fans will express their undying love for the first Dark Souls. It's easy to see why - there's a lot that Dark Souls gets right in execution. It's one of those games that many should aspire to be. Dark Souls II was less well-received but I still maintain that it was a decent addition to the series.
Now, among hardcore fans, Dark Souls III looks a bit polarizing. I see a lot of folks who praise its changes in gameplay mechanics, I see others criticizing its overall quality and seemingly lower difficulty.
The thing is, Dark Souls is not a game that's difficult. Dark Souls is a game that's all about improvement and repetition. As you improve, you get better at the game. As you get better, it gets easier. By the time Dark Souls III came out, veteran Dark Souls players have been through the ringer more than a few times to the point where one of them can just dodge-roll through the entire game and still beat it. Hell, a guy even beat all three games plus their DLCs with just a Broken Straight Sword.
The point is, Dark Souls is a game about skill. Levels don't matter. Armor doesn't matter. What matters is how well you're able to use those weapons and abilities at your disposal. They (happily) did away with armor improving to give each equipment set a minimal amount of functionality while giving players leeway to make their characters look however they want - there's a reason Dark Souls III can sometimes be referred to "Fashion Souls" (I think this actually applies to all of the games, but I'm not sure).
It looks intimidating because it's done a good job of fooling you into believing it is. Everything in Dark Souls is absolutely killable. If you die, you're the one that made a mistake. There's probably only one or two situations in the entire game that feels genuinely "cheap" to players, but all in all Dark Souls III is a fair experience that's easy to pick up and learn for anyone new to the series.
Definitely giving it a whole-hearted recommendation.

... but then, i found something in it as i got into playing, something... that felt great. I was actually enjoying the whole thing. So much, actually, that i didn't stop when i finally got the hat... which was, by the way, hundreds and hundreds of hours as well as thousands of monsters slain ago.
+Pros
-The gameplay is quite solid, fun and enjoyable third person hack-and-slash/shooter action in this Role-Playing, multiplayer title, and that gameplay certainly makes it stand out in the sea of MMOs being launched today.
-The excentric, anime-like art style by the staff member who one in-game would know as "cherub" is quite the compelling work; with bright, abstract colorations and chibi-like figures all drawn out to flow throughout it's world that breathe an interesting life into the work.
-The community is mostly good, and there are some quite friendly people and guilds out there plenty welcoming to new members... but i'd advise steering away from the PvP segment of the community.
-The possibilities for how to play are quite expansive
-Armor is customizable with accesories and a selection of starter faces (more can be purchased as well)
-The market system allows you to buy premium currency at a player controlled rate, and nowadays, item crafting can even be entirely free; allowing everyone to experience every aspect of the game for free
-Enter the clockworks: an ever-shifting and entirely random maze of catacombs. Running 29 levels and cycling between up to 8 different maps per area, with those areas coming from a long list divided up among different themes, and with 3 of those themes per gate, the gameplay is exspansive here and it adds much replay value. The levels you travel one time may not be the same the next, and no 2 (of 4 at any given time) gates are alike
-Core missions provide a supplementary story arc that is built on by the DLC Operation: Crimson Hammer. It is piecemeal at times, but it is present enough for one to begin to get it
-Challenge missions and shadow lairs give a challenge to people who are brave and think they've seen it all
-Compatible with Steam trade, allowing you to trade items from other games for items in this one or vice versa
-Cons
-The PvP system is awful: the standard PvP (lockdown) is overrun with horrible balancing issues that allow certain combos to dominate, and people who pay their way to victory; and the one properly balanced and skill-based multiplayer (Blast Network) is a repackege and remodel of bomberman that noone really plays. If you were hoping to get a place to face up and see who is best, might as well just turn around. PvP is better most anywhere else.
-Lag will iron out the experience in this game: If you haven't gone out of map once and found yourself dead and mobbed the next second, you have not truly played Spiral Knights
-The balancing team is about as great as EA's testing department
-The market mentioned above can be fairly unpredictable, spiking at unexpected times when events come up. This could easily make or break anyone financially
-Updates, for whatever reason and regardless of size, never cease to stretch on for ungodly lengths of time
Overall, it is a really nice, really solid game... but with a few issues that could be hammered out to really make it better. It is a standout in the bunch, and any real RPG, Hack-And-Slash, or TPS fanatic should have this somewhere on their hard drive... and that somewhere best not be the trash bin.

Whether or not you appreciate this game will probably come down to whether or not you enjoy the settlement-building system. Through building up your settlements you'll have great motivation to go out and explore the world in search of more salvage, run down side quests as a means to find new spots to strip, and grind your way up in levels making great use of that now-removed-level-cap that drove me so crazy in the last game.
If you don't explore the settlement building system you may end up just rushing through the main quests. Even with the Brotherhood of Steel and all the alterantive quest lines that's not much more than twenty hours of game play, making for a dissapointing open-world RPG.
However that's true of Fallout 3, which didn't even have a settlement-building system. So I'm not sure this complaint is really relevent--it is an open-world RPG after all, so naturally the game relies on a player willing to get off the beaten track.
I think the only valid complaints about this game are the graphics and the sound. There's a lot to like about the graphics actually, but the highest setting textures are so low resolution you can spot it from a dozen feet away from any object. The sound effects are simply lacking, and the voice actors aren't great. To put it politely.

Yeah. It's good. If you've played a Bethesda game you know what you are getting. The things that are supposedly dumbing down the experience like the 4-way dialogue options instead of chosing the written sentences don't bother me too much. It happened to me before that I read a sentence and then my game character interpreted it in a totally different way than I expected so it's not too bad that you basically select the emotion and let the character do the talking.
It's a big worldmap although not as big as I expected after playing Skyrim. It feels slight smaller to me.
It's open. It looks good. It has all the weird quirks that an open world game in the size of Fallout has that just come with the technology.
There's a lot of attention to detail (like that the light from you pip-boy actually shines in the color of your screen, adjusted in the options menu). A lot of things are interconnected in a very complex way so that it sometimes is a miracle the game logic doesn't break after a few hours of gametime. You can see the amount of work that went into it.
This is why I don't understand some of the flaws that aren't even really connected to the game world itself ... What I can't forgive is the way the inventory system is still handeled to this day. It's like in all the old games -  wall of text. Yeha, it's the pip-boy. Sure it fits the mood. But with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of stuff being carried around all the time this manual sifting through the inventory takes time away from the actual game that isn't fun. And it's even worse if you accidently store or grab all items from a box by accident. Have fun going through the list piece by piece again.
In the same way there's the building aspect of the game. Actually a really cool feature but in practice the shortcuts feel super clunky. Buttons are double- or triple-assigned to behave the same on keyboard as on gamepad. And it shows. The system is pretty complex for an RPG game so it's rather sad that as soon as things become more complex the building shifts from fun to enraging. Say you just built a complete house (it's possible) and want to add furniture to it, yet the button that would confirm the furniture menue also moves the wall, generator, switch or whatever is underneath your cursor. So you always HAVE to look into the nothing to keep on building. And there's tons of these little things that start adding up in the building system.
Assigning people to specific tasks is also very annoying because you have to actually look for them, then assign them to their task. So it's not like you have a list of tasks and know who does what and how to shift it. Want to find that someone who does nothing? Good luck running around your town or settlement finding him or her.
Maybe there are systems to make these tasks easier later on in the game but if that's the case I haven't found it.
Why is it that we STILL can't place reminder markers on the Map? Even Zelda:BotW got this right and it's the first true open world iteration of the series ever. It really is the minor things that let the players down. Things that don't feel smooth even though they should by now.
Also if I have to listen to that goddamn fiddeling in the Minutemen's stronghold (that can be heared nearly everywhere and plays OVER the regular game music) I swear I'm gonna fly to Bethesda and punch somone in the arm. repeatedly. Very hard.
That's the mixed bag you get with Fallout 4. A super complex open world game with very good graphics considering the amount of things to find on the map. A lot of gemplay time. A mini management simulation within. And some frustrating things that the designers should have known better than to leave like this.
All in all it's a very cool and addictive game when it does what does best - let you explore the world. It falls short to the point that things become annoying in the details. I know I like it and I don't regret buying it but it's sad to have a game that takes so many work to create fall short on things that aren't even related so closely to gameplay breaking features.

An outtake to sum up my review:
Here is what I expected when I purchased Darkest Dungeon: a modern take on roguelikes with interesting attrition-based mechanics that require clever tactics to overcome, a variety of hero classes which can be combined into parties that capitalize on different ways of playing the game, and a challenge which was meaningful and fulfilling to overcome.
I did not get these things. What I got was a sub-standard dungeon crawler with masochistic tendencies and a design philosophy that discourages strategic and tactical thinking. Alongside this is a meaningless progression grind that would make any mobile tower defense game proud.
It's an exercise in rolling dice that requires a large investment of time for little to no satisfaction.You will grind for hours to kit out a team to take on the end bosses but your victory rarely feels earned - careful planning and team structure will not win the day, lucky crits and blasting everything with all the♥♥♥♥♥♥you can muster will.

"So Grimault, I hear you've inherited some property."
"Yeah. I couldn't believe it when I got the letter! The place is really sweet. I mean, it's a bit beat up and has a vermin problem, but it's got atmosphere."
"Wow. I guess you could fix it up. What sort of vermin?"
"Uldrich terrors, undead, that sort of thing. It's actually pretty bad... but I'm willing to overlook a lot for a place containing an infinite supply of gold."
Bentham splutters her ale over the side of the caravan. "An infinite supply of gold?"
"It just seems to show up randomly. Actually the whole place seems to change randomly whenever you enter it. We've been collecting it for - " A loud knock interrupts Grumault. "Hold on. It's probably another adventurer."
Grimault walks to the front of the caravan and can be heard talking to someone.
"Sure! Yeah, okay you can go in with... uh... those three guys. Naw, don't mind the corpses. Oh him? Yeah, he's just afraid of light... and darkness... and people.... and he's paranoid... and has the boubonic plague... and stress-related - Look, it's just best if you don't hang out with him. Yes, off you go! Bring me back whatever gold you find. Have fun!"
Grimault walks back.
"Who was that?"
"Oh, an adventurer. They seem to show up in caravans every week. We send them off in groups of four to go explore the mansion."
"Is that safe?"
"Not even remotely. Most of them don't come back, and the ones that do are total wrecks. They usually can't even tie their own shoes. I've been using the loot they come back with to upgrade this place. Check out my sweet blacksmith's shop!"
"Sounds dangerous. Don't they ever want to keep the loot for themselves?"
"You know what, that's never come up. Seems weird, now that you mention it..."
"Grimault, has anyone ever told you that you're a psychopath?"
"All the time. So want to check out the mansion?"
"Yeah!"
"Cool! Just head on over there with... uh... those three guys."

So to start out Darkest Dungeon is still in Early Access, that said it's perfectly playable as is, but it does still have the occasional kinks.
The gameplay is suprisingly engaging for a turn based game, mostly due to the high risk levels that keep you on your toes. The game is unforgiving as I'm sure many have said it is a challenge. Some people have said it is too hard, and I disagree it simply requires you to redefine sucess. For me I restart anytime things go badly I simply can't help t, but it certainly is a game you can bounce back from defeat in.
The story isn't really flushed out, and its in need of more real continuity, and roleplay aspects, but the lore in the game is really well thought out. If your a fan of lovecraftian horror you'll love the subtle, disturbing, and suggestive vib of the game.
I'm generally not a fan of turn based games, but this one is well worth that downside can't wait for the full release, but if it was released as is it would still be a great game.

Anyway, I expected more. Yes, I know the git gud stuff and all but the thing about the combat is nothing special really to keep you motivated. It's actually annoying.
Only interesting thing is that the weapons come with unique skills which unfortunately you won't be using unless for yolo. Instead you will spam your light attacks all day long.
You will also fail until you learn your enemies and you will be repeating the process whole game. Die-Learn-Kill-Die-Learn-Kill
You will most likely never beat any boss at first run. It's not necessarily a bad thing but you won't progress until you learn bosses moveset which is usually several times of getting smashed.
The camera is horrible and it will often be the cause of your deth.
Coop experience is utter garbage. People can invade and kill you while you're playing PVE with a friend. It's also complicated and clunky to set it all up. Youtube is your friend again and it will be for the most part of the game.
It's just the marketing. The game is really not even close to it's hype. Maybe past souls games were better but this one is just meh.
I've also had black screens on 144hz monitor on exit and alt tab. I searched a bit and this is pretty known issue. It overall loks like a bad port to pc.

This game has great atmosphere and mood. It includes eldritch and rather dark themes. You really do feel hopeless, caught in a land of despair and ruin, trying to restore your family's manor to its former glory. In this game, you recruit adventurers to achieve that by going through dungeons to collect gold, items, and valuable resources to build up your manor.
This is where the difficulty kicks in. You will realize how human the adventurers you recruit are. They have their limits, and react differently when pushed to it. While the concept of the game isn't hard to grasp, trying to complete a mission and keep all your adventurers alive is a challenge. It pushes you to make decisions whether to keep going for loot at the risk of one of your comrads or abandoning the mission in order to save their lives. With varied missions and bosses, you will find yourself at the edge of your seat when things get tough. You will feel the terrible dread of failure, and you will feel the surge of excitement coming from every close call and win. The game requires you to learn from your mistakes and keep your cool in every moment of despair.
This game definitely requires patience. I feel like this game will turn off people who don't enjoy the challenge it offers. For those who can handle it, I feel like they will really like this.

And Fallout strayed almost entirely away from the rpg aspect, you are usually supposed to get a certain perk with something else about it to keep it from being too good, but you are now able to get every single perk, which basically has no repercussions whatsoever. And the dialogue isn't the best, there are sometimes when you can say funny things, but that's like 0.01% of all of the other garbage dialogue, in other words... you're forced to be a good-ish guy if you so choose. The dlc does allow you to be more evil if you want but still, if you play the previous games and enjoyed the off-the-wall dialogue, you won't find it in Fallout 4. And there was a great amount of memorable bosses in the previous Fallout games like John Henry Eden (if you can count him as one), Caesar, and Master and there were even memorable enemies like the Khans, Nightkin, Cazadors, and the Enclave (all of which are better than the Gunners and Desciples, Pack, Operators, Forged, Rust Devils, and other nameless groups of Raiders) I understand that they might be trying to go a different direction but what they are doing is mangling the only good parts that made Fallout good to me. When i say "sadist" i´m talking about the difficulty. It´s not the hardest in the saga, that´s for sure. But it probably is a very close second. The problem with this game and i´ts difficulty is rather simple, it´s core mechanics are conflictive with themselves. Rolling costs almost no stamina (i see this as a flaw on it´s own, since it does not punish panicking) and has a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of i-frames, so most of the time, blocking is almost useless if not completely useless. But then, the very few shields that are good at blocking, are just absurdly overpowered at it (silver knight). And since most of the good shields are not compatible with the "brand new, game selling weapon arts" i found very little incentive to use them for any other thing than parrying, and that can be done with a simple caestus, which, for some reason is better for parrying than a shield.
But those are just very minor, complains and if you are not someone that plays a lot and does challenge runs/PVP you shouldn´t feel that way.
The meat on the masochism comes in the form of a very common complain from old Souls fans. See, Dark souls and Dark Souls II were set in the same universe, but in a time and space so distant from each other that you could only see the mangled bones of lordran in Drangleic. I really liked this idea, it did fit with the whole "time and space is convoluted" thing, finding reincarnations of old lords and all that stuff. Even the main plot point was different, and it had a decent plot twist, even with all its flaws (i mean, there were a lot, don´t get me wrong) the game tried to innovate. But then came the third game.
I mean, from the very first moment Lothric was introduced i felt kind of awkward because it sounded so similar to Lordran that i was expecting it to recycle places from the first one.
I have no issue with calling the hub world "firelink shrine" but i have issues with it being a separate part of the game when they could have made it connect with lothric castle very easily. I have a lot more of issues regarding the lack of interconectedness as i had in dark souls 2, there are a lot of missed oportunities and it really leads me to believe that what they did in dark souls 1 was an accident, because the only game out of the following three that had some semblance of interconectedness was bloodborne, and it is like 2 areas that are pretty worthless to connect. Of course this is fixed with the teleporting mechanic, but it grinds my gears because i expected so much more of the last game and it´s level design.
Talking about level design, Anor Londo, for me at least, was more of a "why would Anor londo be perfectly fine after all this time has passed?" than a "Wow so much memories" i mean, we don´t know exactly how much time has it been since the first dark souls, but a few cyclest at least (note: the game emphathises how important the rekindling of the flame is and how fast the world goes into a deplorable state when it´s fading), but it felt quite like an attempt for a nostalgia trip rather than a logical placement for the building, i mean, it´s not bad that it´s there, but it´s not good either, it wasn´t necessary, but it does not damage the game either. It´s a very small portion of the game and the renewed archer section was very enjoyable.
A few other levels that i think need some critique are the profaned capital, which was a very poorly executed idea, with Yhorms fight being a gimmicky one, and a bad one since they hype him up and it ends up being trivial and silly.
The swamp which is pretty meh, just wading around in poision for 15 minutes straight.
And well, i have an issue with Tower of la... Irithyll Dungeon.
I´d say the rest of them are fine (i intentionally forgot about ash lake, not even going to explain why it´s bland)
It repeats the same exact events that happened in dark souls but with very small twists.
The flame is fading so they resurrect 4 lords of cinder that linked the flame in past ages, the problem is, linking the flame is not an enjoyable experience so they run away and start doing their things like constantly killing themselves (Abyss watchers) or eating people alive. Y´know, regular stuff. And there you come in, an unkindled, basically someone that was meant to link the flame but failed for some reason (probably wasn´t strong enough to handle the first flame?) and was turned to ash.
Well since those lords wont link the flame they send 4 unkindled ones to hunt every single lord, but you end up hunting them all or helping the rest of them doing their jobs. Then you do the classic "put their heads here and there" and you arrive at a distant age where the world is already destroyed, you fight the soul of cinder, which is a good boss only it lacked a sense of finality for me and there you go you do whatever you want with the firrst flame, link it, leave it to finally fade away, or the edgy ending in which you consume it and linkin park sounds faintly in the background.
Thats the main plot, now, the interesting part of the lore is elsewhere. Gwynn had more daughters than we thought and his son allied with the dragons and is a tough boss.
There is a way to remove the humanity from the hollows and turn it into human dregs and it turns out that the pygmies are not small at all and ringed knights are scarier than black knights.
The curse ends up being some sort of powerfull atribute of the humans and a lot more interesting plot points. I really liked the lore in this one, even if it was a continuation of the first, it clarified a lot of things.
No complains, the bosses have memorable soundtracks that fit very well with their character and fights and it has some of the best music i´ve heard in gaming history. Shovel knight takes the 1st prize im sorry guys. The sound on the other hand has a very weighty feeling to it that dark souls II lacked, and it´s refreshing to feel the blows of your weapons and being able to sense when an enemy is moving or not. It almost feels like you are in those places sometimes, as some other reviewers have pointed out "you can almost smell it".
A necessary introduction the way the paintings work, but a very rushed, low quality addition to the game.Only has two bosses, one being a highly praised fight that i don´t enjoy at all and the other being a guy wearing assless chaps and reused armor from the game who´s wielding a new dlc weapon (a pretty popular one) and randomly summons small wolves. there is also a not so small wolf in that fight but he has less hp than Vordt and by the time he comes out you have already fought him 1-2 times in the rest of the dlc.
Now, the "good fight"
I don´t like it, and it´s not because of its difficulty. I just dont enjoy how friede seems to have hyper armor frames on her dashes and can get away from big weapon hits with such ease. Whenever i have to fight this boss i just take out any Straight Sword or Curved Sword and just steamroll her out of my sight. The third phase would have been something impressive if it hadn´t been obvious from the beggining, i mean, till the end of the second phase the fight is pretty easy, especially if you have played the other 2 games with multiple enemy encounters like O&S or the Sentinels. The music is of course good and the characters are fine, i just dont like the way the handled her dashing in the fight.

Just play it (again), it´s brilliant.

Hardcore fans will express their undying love for the first Dark Souls. It's easy to see why - there's a lot that Dark Souls gets right in execution. It's one of those games that many should aspire to be. Dark Souls II was less well-received but I still maintain that it was a decent addition to the series.
Now, among hardcore fans, Dark Souls III looks a bit polarizing. I see a lot of folks who praise its changes in gameplay mechanics, I see others criticizing its overall quality and seemingly lower difficulty.
The thing is, Dark Souls is not a game that's difficult. Dark Souls is a game that's all about improvement and repetition. As you improve, you get better at the game. As you get better, it gets easier. By the time Dark Souls III came out, veteran Dark Souls players have been through the ringer more than a few times to the point where one of them can just dodge-roll through the entire game and still beat it. Hell, a guy even beat all three games plus their DLCs with just a Broken Straight Sword.
The point is, Dark Souls is a game about skill. Levels don't matter. Armor doesn't matter. What matters is how well you're able to use those weapons and abilities at your disposal. They (happily) did away with armor improving to give each equipment set a minimal amount of functionality while giving players leeway to make their characters look however they want - there's a reason Dark Souls III can sometimes be referred to "Fashion Souls" (I think this actually applies to all of the games, but I'm not sure).
It looks intimidating because it's done a good job of fooling you into believing it is. Everything in Dark Souls is absolutely killable. If you die, you're the one that made a mistake. There's probably only one or two situations in the entire game that feels genuinely "cheap" to players, but all in all Dark Souls III is a fair experience that's easy to pick up and learn for anyone new to the series.
Definitely giving it a whole-hearted recommendation.

I really can't say enough good things about this game. The art-style, gameplay, game mechanics and sound design are all top-notch and pretty innovative. The replayability is constant and I find myself starting seperate playthroughs over and over while continuing my original playthroughs just to see the different aspects and synergies of the characters. Yes this game is highly addicting but like most games it comes with a few issues. First off, the Light/Dark and Stress Mechanic is pretty innovative but can become pretty frustrating for you especially early on in the game when first getting started. It can make or break a playthrough in the early stages of the levels and on top of that the difficulty spike in the beginning just adds to your characters stress level and yours. Why the early stages are made so tough and so challenging and why your characters stress meters go up so fast to the point of killing your first few characters  in a sometimes unfair way is beyond me and as you build your characters they do get stronger and before you know it you'll be doing all-dark/no light runs if you stick with it but it does take time. Also, you build/level your characters through money. You need money to build a blacksmith for better weapons and armor, a guild to unlock new perks for your characters, a campfire to unlock your characters camping perks(on longer missions you'll be able to camp and reduce your stress, buff your characters and heal injuries), and an Abbey andTavern to reduce your characters stress off mission. There's also a Sanitarium to help get rid of bad character traits and you will have characters who end up with some pretty bad traits that you need to get rid of asap but like I said, it all costs money and the trait-removal is very expensive and you will find yourself farming for gold early on and this can become tedious and you can actually hinder or kill some of your characters but the game does get easier as you go on.The devs have said they fixed a lot of these issues however these things can still happen and often do. I suggest to any newcomer to take our time and find charatcers asap that can heal other characters and that can stress relieve as well. Stick with it because it really is  a fantastic and innovative gem that deserves credit for being bold and trying something new. With addictive gameplay and intense battles you'll find yourself dreaming about the dark halls of "Darkest Dungeon". 9/10

The first 15 hours or so of the game were alot of fun, the atmosphere/setting is incredible and the gameplay reminded me alot of playing XCOM on ironman. But unfortunately when you scratch the surface you see some pretty deep flaws in the basic design of the game.
While the game is very difficult, it is not truly challenging in terms of strategy or tactics. This is because there is no time limit on your campaign. No matter how badly you play will never need to start over as you would in XCOM, and eventually given enough time put into the game you will acquire enough resources to upgrade all your buildings to the max. Which is basically required in order to progress at all.
So in reality the game is just incredibly grindy. Its not about making the right decisions and starting over if you make the wrong ones. It is only about investing enough time (ALOT!), until you acquire enough resources to be able to beat the game. Which is not a rewarding form of difficulty.
Despite all my complaints the game is probably worth the low cost simply for the fun initial experience. As mentioned the setting/art/narration is great, so I suppose I would still recommend the game even tho it was pretty dam disappointing in the end.

After reading mixed positive and negative reviews on the latest patches and updates I had to play now even though I planned to play only at lunch.
I've tried this game on the early patches long time ago and was really thrilled to play this game. Now lot of people are complaining about corpses, increased difficulty and even cheating enemies.
Well I don't know what are these people talking about. I didn't feel that the game is much more difficult than it used to be and it's fair as well. Sure, you can have a very bad run when you miss lot of attacks and receive crits, but that can happen in any RPG as you have all actions regarded in a percentage and the same goes for enemies. On the other side you can have a very good run when you destroy everything. Maybe the randomness is little bit more than in other games but not that much and when you stack enough trinkets you take away part of that randomness (you can increase your hit and crit chance and many other stats by progressing through the game).
As far as corpses are concerned I feel they add a new strategic element to the game and positioning is even more important. Beside, if you really don't like them you can just turn them off in the options menu (making the game much easier, with less strategy involved).
So really the only way I can see people having problems with difficulty is not playing it correctly (not being very good at games that require strategy and planning - in that case this game is not for you) or they are simply making a mistake of treating all heroes from stress level. That should be done only with good heroes, the useless ones should be dismissed and hired new ones for free, that way you can't run out of resources as some people complained.
I definitely recommend this title as a highly enjoyable, dark, grim, strategic and rewarding experience.
Perhaps sometimes your party will get destroyed or stressed too much so you will have to dismiss them but there are always new heroes eager to join your cause.

My review for this game when it first came out was a not recommended because of frequent crashes, and 50 minute queue times. I changed this to positive because of lots of bugs patched and queue times vanishing. This game had amazing gameplay and at the time was not grindy, it was fun and held your hand through just about everything. I noticed that more and more microtransactions were added, and things like dragon coins and souls were more and more expensive to the point where everything was so grindy it wasn't worth even trying-- just buy Flux from them or a third-party vendor (basically gold farmers from WoW but on trove) and get whatever you want through the market! Nope. Now everything is non-tradeable, super rare, random dropping, and more expensive. The gem update made all the gear you paid $70 for absolutely useless (WHICH I FOUND OUT THE HARD WAY) and made everything even more of a grindfest.
Now, I believe in games that make you work for the good loot you want but this game's boring, repetitive dungeons that you get sick of after 50 hours and the low drop rates and loot rewards just makes this game soul-suckingly bland. At this point now the game is what I would say "stale". Boring gameplay and un-fun after you uncover the paywall and the un-entertaining grindfest that the game really is.
Please, save yourself the hundreds of hours other people wasted having fun to get divided between two roads-- spend a thousand hours getting your gear to be on par with people spending hundreds of dollars, or waste your money to get up there.

While the game is very difficult, it is not truly challenging in terms of strategy or tactics. This is because there is no time limit on your campaign. So in reality the game is just incredibly grindy. Its not about making the right decisions and starting over if you make the wrong ones. It is only about investing enough time (ALOT!), until you acquire enough resources to be able to beat the game. Which is not a rewarding form of difficulty.
Despite all my complaints the game is probably worth the low cost simply for the fun initial experience. As mentioned the setting/art/narration is great, so I suppose I would still recommend the game even tho it was pretty dam disappointing in the end.

So let's get the elephant in the room out of the way: I understand why FO4 gets the flack that it does.
The storyline is a bit too railroad-y, there's no karma system, so everyone basically treats you the same, and without mods installed, the dialogue options are obscure (though I kind of like the Sole Survivor having spoken lines - though it sadly means we miss out on beautiful 1 INT dialogue.)
It also does a few things that have the effect of feeling odd in-universe, like Power Armor requiring fusion cores that have extremely short operating lifespans.
As a roleplaying game, it's weak.
So why the thumbs-up review?
The game looks, feels, and runs great. I personally love the settlement building addition, and it fits into how I've made roleplaying decisions in previous FO titles. It makes all the junk you feel like you should want to scavenge suddenly worth scavenging.
Power Armor *FEELS* like Power Armor. The fusion core mechanic makes deciding when to take your Power Armor out feel like a meaningful choice.
The weapon and armor modding takes the FO3 & FONV crafting and modding systems ands makes them feel absolutely terrific and makes me want to use them.
Enemies act in ways that are believable and exciting (fighting a FO4 feral ghoul for the first time was exhilarating coming from FO3/NV). Most enemies are actually fun to fight, and require you to take different approaches in order to be successful.
The changes to the perk system are nice and streamlined; they remind me of a blend of FO3 and Skyrim, and it's the best iteration in the series, in my opinion.
And for me, personally, the main storyline was always deeply secondary to me getting out and exploring everything, which had this far been extremely satisfying.
My opinion may change, but it's unlikely to at this point, I don't think. I already feel I've gotten my money's worth, and I still have a lot left to explore.
Before playing, consult your oncologist to see if Dark Souls is right for you.

Spiral Knights is a massively multiplayer online role-playing game created by Three Rings Design and published by Sega. The free-to-play, Java-based game was released to advance testers on November 12, 2009[2] and to the general public on April 4, 2011.[3] The game was released through the Steam software distribution system on June 14 of that year,[4][5] and through Kongregate on September 22.
In the game, the player controls a knight of the Spiral Knights order, which has crash-landed on the mysterious planet Cradle. Knights collectively explore the Clockworks, the mechanized, constantly reorganizing dungeon that fills the planet's interior. The knights equip armor and weapons to aid them in their battles against the monsters inhabiting the Clockworks. When they are not exploring, knights trade with each other and with vendors, in order to improve their equipment.
