Just gonna start by saying; I love this game. I recommend this game. If you want a game that will make you feel incredible after beating it, get this game.
What's Good;
The Stats; in most RPGs, there is always that one stat that simply isn't worth a point. I'm not talking like a magic stat for a knight class; I'm talking a stat that is generally not worth investing in across most builds (resistance in the first DS, for example). There are no stats like that in this game. Every stat is used for something, even luck (a stat usually thrown to the wayside in many of the RPGs I've played). This means you can get really creative with your builds, and the PvE is made in such a way that any build with the least bit of thought behind it can work so long as you have the skill to pull it off.
The Enemies; Most enemies (note the usage of the word most) are pretty balanced. Aside from a few enemies (the Jailers come to mind) there are no enemies that seem overly cheap or rely on a gimmick to kill you. This balance gives the game a very fair difficulty; any death is usually due to player error. Which is good; because that means the player can learn, adapt, and get better at the game. Gimmicks only teach players to get around the gimmicks; a truly challenging opponent teaches the player how to get better at the game.
The Bosses; I love the bosses in this game. The arenas, the scores, the uniqueness to all of them, I just love them. I wish there was a boss rush mode or something where you can fight each one in a gauntlet-style type of game and see how far you can get. Seriously, the only reason I go through NG+ over and over again is to fight these bosses. And they carry the same great traits from the regular enemies; they all seemed to me to be fair challenges. There are a few pushover bosses, and there are more than a few that railed me again and again; but every time I died it was because I messed up. And there is nothing that beats the rush you get when you kill a boss you've been stuck on for a while, absolutely nothing.
The Weapons (in PvE); There are so many freaking weapons in this game. In the base game alone, there are 191 weapons from 24 different categories to choose from, each with different move sets and stat scalings. Throw in 15 different infusions, and the amount of variance in the combat system is staggering. There is a weapon for every build you can think of, and Fromsoft made sure not to leave us wanting for weaponry.
The Areas; For the most part, the areas in DS3 are incredibly beautiful and easy to navigate. There were only a few moments when I found myself lost, despite the lack of any sort of map. The only issue I have with this ease of navigation is that it also makes the secrets rather obvious. The hidden walls usually stick out like a sore thumb, and if you get into the habit of looking over the side of any cliff or rafter you find yourself on the secrets won't stay hidden for long. This is just a minor gripe, however, as the secret areas should not take priority over general ease of navigation.
What's Meh;
NG+; This one is subjective. The argument for NG+ is that it makes the game harder, giving you another challenge to overcome. You beat the game? Cool. Now beat it again, but it's harder this time. That is enough for me to start it up, as I'm a knight through and through. I simply don't enjoy any other playstyle as much as I do the sword and shield wielding knight, so the lack of difference there doesn’t bother me. The argument against NG+ is valid as well; lack of character progression, absurd enemy damage at later levels, and the general feeling of powerlessness as your once gigantic health bar can now only take two or three hits from a boss. Again, I enjoy that sort of challenge from NG+, but I can see why others would only see it as an annoyance.
The Item Drops; Again, this one is subjective. I have notoriously terrible luck with anything and everything RNG, so some may not have this problem. But, in my experience, the drops just seem to hate me. This was especially prevalent when farming for the covenant items, which took days to complete. Proper farming gear and a solid route make it bearable in most cases, but expect a heck of a time commitment if you want those gauntlets you love to drop.
What's Bad;
The PvP; This was my major problem with the first game, and it's my major problem with this game. The PvP takes most everything good about the game and throws it out the window. For the sake of organization, I'm gonna split it up into the two main styles of PvP; Invasions and Duels
Invasions; They're just annoying for all involved. Gank squads run rampant online, with an invader possibly facing a 3v1 situation, which just isn't fun. Sure, it's great if you win, but if the host and their phantoms are the least bit competent the invader won't stand a chance. And if you don't find that host fast, expect more phantoms to come, 'cuz a host can summon help after they've been invaded. Of course, this isn't to make the host out to be the a**hole. Why wouldn't you use any tools at your disposal to take down an invader? After all, they invaded your world against your will, and are actively trying to kill you. This encouragement of cheap gank tactics and stally gameplay throws away what is most fun about the game IMO, and only serves as an annoyance rather than an engaging facet of gameplay.
The Duels; I don't have as big a problem with these, as they're usually voluntary. Of course, remember what I said about varied weapons? remove that from the equation, as there are many weapons that just don't deal enough damage, or whose move set or range lets them down. Sure, against a computer you can learn to compensate for this, but against a human player with more refined tactics, using a bad weapon becomes much less possible. And Most offensive magic is completely useless, as the projectiles are easily dodgeable and have tons of startup lag, making you an easy target. Supplementary magic is useable, but many will opt to put their stats into HP or raw attack power instead of the stats required to make them worthwhile. Note that these problems are most obvious against two players of equal skill, as a comparison between two players of unequal skill makes all kinds of cheese possible. One positive note about duels is that there aren't really any OP weapons (so far). Every weapon has a weakness, and with the proper experience that knowledge lets you fight against an "OP" weapon with confidence.
In short; buy this game. The PvE is excellent, and while I don't like the PvP at all, there are those who enjoy it. And, if you find you don't enjoy it either, just go into online settings and set it to "play offline" (NPC invasions still occur as normal). It is a great entryway for any newcomers to the DS series, and is a fitting conclusion for any veterans out there. I love this game, sixty bucks and two-hundred plus hours well spent.

NOTE: For you lazy guys, there's a TL:DR at the bottom of the review. Thank me later.
Alright, alright, look. Most reviews now say this game is awful, that it isn't a Fallout game, that it isn't an RPG, that it lacks an interesting story, etc.
Now, I've played Fallout 3 and New Vegas before. They're both good games. Whenever people review Fallout 4, they always compare it with those two - always. However, I actually played this game before F3 and FNV, and I thought it was the best thing ever.
You get to mod the crap out of weapons, recruit Minutemen, defend settlements, shoot EVERYTHING, save your child, and so on. You get to be a part of the wasteland, and I was in love with that. Sure, the choices are limited and you have little control over things, but that's just the main story. Even at the very beginning you get to either shoot a drug dealer in the head and save a diner owner or join in on the fun and murder the diner owner's family, or just kill them both! While the choices are few, you can still define who you want your character to be, and that's what makes an RPG.
Now, I personally love the characters in the game, specifically Piper and Nick Valentine. The "noir" story behind F4 really sucks you into the atmosphere, and I honestly don't know why there's so much hate for the story.
While I don't have it on here (as of today), I do own all the DLC on my Xbox, and I've got to say, on sale, the DLC is a sandbox dream. Automatron is great, and actually throws a plot twist and a big decision at the end. The Workshop DLC is okay, with Vault-Tec on top thanks to the short story. Also, while I haven't gotten much into Far Harbor or Nuka World, most people - on Steam too - say that they're great.
TL:DR - Fallout 4 is a great game on its own, especially for people new to Bethesda games. The DLC is optional, but I do recommend Automatron, Far Harbor, and Nuka World while they're on sale. Also, modding through the Nexus makes this game a roller coaster of opportunities. Despite all the hate, I, having played this game for over 400 hours (on PC and on my Xbox), call this one of my favorite games. From the sandbox settlement system to the characters to the mass destruction, I give Fallout 4 a good 8.5/10.

A chilling atmosphere of hopelessness, famine and doom. I started the game with rather neutral feelings, but after a beautiful intro that bombarded me with amazing voice acting, a captivating artstyle and a soundtrack to die for, I immediately got into the vibe of this great game. However, if you are expecting a fun dungeon crawler where you kill enemies and spend your time being OP, you might want to just walk on by. Because this game is DIFFICULT. Death is permanent (and believe me; there'll be a lot of it) and that does not just apply to the increasingly terrifying creatures this game will force you to face. There will be few victories, and even when a quest is marked as a success, it won't always feel as one when you later visit the graveyard to see the many fallen Heroes that fought so bravely before they finally fell victim to the enemy... or their own insanity.
Darkest Dungeon is a game about trying to push on despite all the death and despair surrounding you and your party and I highly recommend it to anyone who's looking for a challenge doused in a big layer of eerie.
Stress levels are to outweigh even that of Dark Souls, a game famous for its difficulty, so be warned.

To be entirely fair, i have not played this game for even remotely as long as i should before judging it, but this is, after playing Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim and Fallout 3 by far the worst Bethesda game i have ever touched.
For me rpgs are all about immersion, shutting out all light and sound aside from my screen and headset and let myself fall into the world. This is pretty impossible in a game which crashes 2-3 times a session, regularly freezes in one of the ten billion loading screens, looks awesome and garbage in the same screen, since some textures are flat out 20 years outdated (why can i count the pixels on a speed limit sign?). And that is just the technical side.
Enemies as well as allies have a ridiculously bad pathfinding, actively pathing toward the next object they can get stuck on, so they can teleport to you later, while you are running down an empty street. Dialogue options are sometimes impossible to guess right, we are reaching mass effect levels of misunderstanding. Enemies teleport right into your face, because they were stuck in the middle of an animation. I guess the only way of enjoying this game is to avoid any contact with npcs. Although i wonder what to do then.
You know a game is failing, when you cant even judge an rpg by its characters of story, because you cant even bring yourself to play it for long enough to even know anything about it. Remember that this game was released 19 months ago and is on a technical level most games have surpassed in early beta.
As a bonus, being forced to google half of the controls because they are not listed in the menu under "controls" is not a design decision, it is an obvious mistake that should not survive ANY quality control.
If this game was not developed by Bethesda, who have a strong fanbase, it would have been utterly crushed by critics and the public. Was there any quality control at all?

My biggest regret is that I actually spent over two hours in game so I cant get my money back, definitelly dont recommend if you dont like getting frustrated over cheap tricks the developers used to make the game harder than it really is.

This game is actually really good and extremely addicting. The only things I feel are off about it is as follows.
#1 - The Combat could be a little more fleshed out.
The combat is basically like every other online third-person combat game, and here and there it feels more like a "Mash to Slash to Win" game. Only once or twice have I really resorted to tactically using my character's moves (currently playing Ninja), and that's only when it got to the "Oh crap, my health is low" moments.
#2 - The music could stand to be a LOT... A LOT more diverse.
Bum-bum buuum, bum-bum buuuum~
I think I've heard that same line of notes about four hundred times while playing the game. It's okay as -opening- music, but you can literally find it in any Biome. The only biome which introduces different music is the "Haunted" Biome as far as I can tell.
Just as well, the music is hardly memorable... That is when it's not being drilled into your brain. I can remember Minecraft's music just fine. It was calm, creepy in places, but still set the mood. Trove's music- don't do that. Especially when they only have one memorable track that I can notice. Either all the tracks for every biome are the same, or they're so bloody similar that I can't notice a difference. I know yer new to the game, Trove, but you gotta liven it up a bit.
#3 - I really wish this game wasn't focused so much on the <16 year old demographic.
This seems a bit too much like a kiddy game, and coming from a 21 year old gamer who was really hoping this would be like a Minecraft/Adventure RPG mashup it's really dissapointing that the only people I can co-op with are at best 14 years old. :| Not a comfortable thought. Maybe try and offer an appeal to the older demographic as well as the younger. Don't ask me how to do that, I ain't a marketing guy, just don't hire an analyst to figure it out, frikken ask somebody.
And by the way, Trove, no, you're never going to stop being compaired to Minecraft. You're too simmilar, even with RPG elements. Might as well embrace it.

This is not an easy review to write.  Am I enjoying myself with Fallout 4?  Yes.  Are mods absolutely necessary in order to do so?  In my opinion- yes.  Do I wish the next Fallout game to be like this one?  Absolutely not.  I think this game would have been better off divorcing itself from the Fallout Franchise and Universe and instead making itself an FPS with base-building and RPG elements unrelated to the Fallout brand.  The reasons for this-  Fallout 1 was amazing because of the freedom it gave you.... Fallout 2 expanded on this- giving you a larger area and even more choice.  Get married?  Star in an... *ahem* adult movie?  Sell your wife into slavery?  Kill a weapons dealer to get an early head start on having good equipment?  Absolutely.  Join the Slaver's Guild even though it means having a brand permenantly burned into your forehead?  Sure!!  Your decisions, big and small, rippled throughout the world and at the conclusion of the game you would get a breakdown as to how every location changed in the future due to your actions.  It was amazing and liberating- the replay value was so high because you could play through the game several times and have wildly different experiences based on your gender, morals, which skills you chose.... I do playthroughs even now, many years after Fallouts 1 and 2 came out, and I still discover new things.  This is why, while I am enjoying Fallout 4- I hope that Fallout 5 or New Vegas 2 leans more towards the RPG side of thing.  I don't see why Fallout 4 could not have increased the gunplay/FPS aspects of the game AND kept the RPG-elements of Fallouts 1, 2, and New Vegas.
That's not to say Fallout 4 does not have RPG elements.... there are 10 perks per attribute and there are 7 attributes- a total of 70 perks of which you select one per level.... and most perks have multiple levels.  Thus there are several hundred "Perk" levels.  This is fine and all- it leans more towards the Skyrim model of character delelopment.  I prefer the SPECIAL system combined with skill-points, using Perks as traits that give individuality and specialization to a given character.  I feel there is more freedom to character development in this way- but this isn't my biggest complaint with Fallout 4- it is the writing and the lack of "free agency" that you have.
Fallout 1 and 2 would have been successful even if they were drastically different games.... the writing was THAT good.  You could examine everything in the environment and get a witty description.  The writing added flavor and even with the dark subject matter it managed to stay somewhat light-hearted.  Fallout 3's writing was rather dissapointing and it lacked the soul that the earlier Fallouts had.  That is why New Vegas is so popular with so many people- the writing was akin to Fallouts 1 and 2 and it had that Fallout "Soul".  It also gave you your "Free Agency" back.  Without spoiling anything- you could choose what mark on the world, if any, that you wanted to make.  You could kill anyone, from some bum in a back alley to world leaders and politicians.... and the game would respond to your actions.  Fallout 3 felt like it was shoehorning you in a certain direction- and while you could have some freedom- you were basically going the same direction no matter what your choices.  I'm only 50 hours into Fallout 4 but one of the big complaints I read was that it was similar to Fallout 3 in a lot of the ways that Fallout 1 and 2 fans were not as big on.  That's not to say Fallout 3 was bad- but in the same way I'm enjoying Fallout 4 while wishing that it had that Fallout "Soul"- it reminds me of the mixed feeling I had about Fallout 3.
Yeah- I recommend playing Fallout 4.  I REALLY REALLY hope Obsidian gets another crack at a Fallout game and that there will be another Fallout game that reminds me of 1, 2, and New Vegas- but as an FPS with RPG and base-building elements I'm having a good time with Fallout 4.  I'm torn because I don't like that my thumbs-up will be seen as a "Do More of the Same Please" to Bethesda- but I can't give a game that I'm enjoying a thumbs-down.  I've seen lots of comments echoing my sentiments so I'm fairly sure that if Bethesda spends any time at all doing research they'll realize that there is a sizable group that wishes for the Fallout series to return to it's roots.  I'd be thrilled with a New Vegas 2 with the enhanced combat mechanics of Fallout 4- I don't see why improved combat and old-school-sensible RPG elements should be mutually exclusive.  Steam really needs a choice between thumbs up and thumbs down.... I'm not sure that I'd necessarily use it in this instance but I don't like the binary "Either I loved it or hated it" mechanic in place now.

Great game, great series, hands down one of the best gaming experiences of my life.
Dark Souls is ruthlessly fair. It takes many hours, many mistakes and many deaths to "git gud". Patience, young padawan.
A few pieces of advice:
1. I DO play alongside a checklist because I hate missing large chunks of content and DS games are non-linear so it's very easy for that to happen otherwise. (Encounter new areas fresh and be as thorough as is reasonable, but then double check to see if you missed anything big.)
2. I DON'T play online because my framerate is terrible and it's too tempting to let other people beat the game for me.
3. I DO actively avoid video walkthroughs and "how to beat boss x" because it just gives too much away and I like the pants scared off me when I encounter a new boss for the first time.

I recently purchased Darkest Dungeon and I haven't been able to stop playing it.
Before I write my review I wish to state that there are far too many negative reviews that are completely unjustified. Yes, the game is unforgiving however it is nothing like what the other reviewers have stated.
A lot of the people complaining are the same crowd as the 'casuals' you find in other games suggesting changes to allow them to 'win more often'. For example, "“Some traps for example are not visible and will just hit you without any counter option (but luck as in dodge)”. The traps become visible if you have 'scouted' the map. I have 112 hours at the moment and I do not lose any heroes  at all (your heroes have permanent death) and I have a full roster of heroes of every class. I can only imagine that the people who are finding the game incredibly difficult are struggling to understand the mechanics of the game. You will see below as to why it is identical to the 'casuals' you often find in other games.
People are a complaining about balance changes. For example, "“The developers … seem to be haphazardly throwing illogical and badly though-out game altering patches (sometimes game breaking in terms of fun)”. People were just AoE'ing enemy characters to death, removing any skill from the game as players could kill the enemy characters before they could even react. This was changed so you couldn't just 'no skill' AoE mobs down and people are complaining about this. People were double and triple stacking classes because of this and just mindlessly using the same AoE abilities (You can see this in YouTube videos before the changes). Know the abilities, choose classes that compliment each other and play smartly; this is how the game should be, right?
The other complaints is that everything is too expensive. For example, "Players who came into this new update with their towns half finished and their parties mostly set up will be fine, but if you're just starting out, the unforgiving gold deficit will keep you in crippling poverty and grind progress to such a slow and repetitive crawl".
I started after the patch and although I dont have a huge amount of gold, my whole roster is upgraded to the max levels. Previously it was absolutely ridiculous and you never had to worry about how to spend your gold. It was just an unnecessary resource as you made an insane amount of gold and it cost nothing to upgrade skills/abilities, armour/weapons or use 'stress recovery' options for your heroes. Gold must be a reward for completing a dungeon and you should have to spend it wisely, not sit with it in thousands and never have to make a decision on how to spend it.
People in the Steam reviews have used the cliched "it is not polished enough" which is the complete opposite of the truth. I do not think you will find many games as polished as this where the passion of the developers shine in their work.
----------
Review:
Darkest Dungeon to me has been a refreshing experience. It features the narration of Wayne June in the most unique way I've ever encountered in a game. The narrator will essentially comment on the combat pushing the sound design from Darkest Dungeon to a new level. When you land a critical hit, Mr June will make you feel it.
Graphics:
The game has a very dark art style to it. Everything is very well drawn. The creatures are hideous (in a good way) which adds to the dark theme of the game.
Sound:
There has been no cost spared in sound design. As someone with a degree in Music Production, Sound Design and Music Business, I really have a lot of appreciation for what they have done here. As mentioned there is the narration of your combat, but the amount of sounds they have created for the skills, which sound really good, is unbelievable. They all sound like the ability should. They have even gone as far to make unique sounds for when the abilities fail. Monster sounds are just as scary as the monsters are gruesome, making it easy to immerse oneself.
Gameplay:
I see the Steam reviews are saying the game is unbalanced and too difficult. I find the game to be almost perfectly balanced, if not too easy. I have 2 final bosses to finish and I have not wiped or died on any of the final bosses so far. I find the AI is a bit too forgiving where it could have got a kill it instead attacked a hero with more health.
The game uses a unique system that when you get to 0 hp, you reach the status of 'Deaths Door'. You then do resist checks against attacks and if it fails, you receive a 'Deathblow' and that hero dies permanently. This is unforgiving however you have the option to retreat from combat and the dungeon if it is not going your way, which you should be as doing.
Overall:
One of the most unique games I've ever played and I only hope the developers look past the negative Steam reviews because this game is absolutely a diamond in the rough; a complete winner in my eyes.

All armors and helmets can be customized with accessories earned throughout the game.

Before this review starts, I know I screwed up the Dark Souls II review, so I apologized for that one.
Dark Souls III is a RPG game created by From Software and published by Bandai Namco Entertainment (formerly Bandai Namco Games). The game sets in interconnected world of Lothric. The whole throughout of the playthrough, you will find similar area from the predecessors, the enemies, the NPC, weapons and armor for long time Dark Souls fan. The lore is still cryptic as usual and you will find the lore understandable if you know what is going on during cutscenes and dialogs. The game is running with Bloodborne engine, which is a great thing. So, let's talk about the changes in this game.
The changes for Dark Souls III is somewhat accessible. Accessible as in - upgrading armor is removed, so pretty much you can wear whatever you like (Fashion Souls III). Combat system is great, but power stancing from Dark Souls II is gone. The poise, ugh it's completely obsolete, no matter what you wear. Covenant system seems to have a nice change, where you can change at any time without losing the Covenant.
Okay, I am going to do a positive side. I am not sure if it is a fixed difficulty where for the first 11 hours, I feel like this game is easy. Fast forward, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ it can be friggin hard and take 20+ tries to take down the boss. The enemies and bosses do have their own unique attack patterns as usual, so it is not the best to play agressive. I have not played the Sorcerer or Pyromancer yet, but I am assuming they are still powerful but not as overpowered from the predecessors. The item system is improved. The official soundtrack of Dark Souls III, it's a 10 out of 10.  The combat system is extensive, you can change variety of weapons (my favorite weapons so far is Great Scythe and any twinblades). The multiplayer is now better than ever. I can't tell you how much I love the matchmaking options system, where you can put the password so one of your friends don't get summoned by randoms and play offline system. This is the best Dark Souls multiplayer yet. I am done with positive side, now I am going to talk about the negative side.
Everytime I beat any boss fight, the bonfire spawns at the boss fight area (how many friggin bonfires are there in total?). I feel like Dark Souls III is being generous to players because it doesn't feel like an actual difficult game from predecessors. I really do understand that people who never played Dark Souls before. I found New Game Plus to be more, easier than playing on your first playthrough. It's disappointing and I wish they could've done something to New Game Plus, like damage modifiers, enemy health pool and usual stuff to make the game difficult. The poise in this game like I said feels nothing to me. The performance issues seems to be minor at times, even hard froze, FPS spikes, that's it. The items in this game can be worthless. The PvP, it's really annoying how people play - as in chasing the invader but getting baited by PvE enemies, the meta can be broken. Newcomers will find it difficult when getting invaded by seasoned players, so it's best to play offline on Matchmaking Options. Forgot to say that the PvP is riddled with cheaters and modders.
Man, I got to say that I am still sad that I finished the trilogy (need to get the Season Pass to play the Ashes of Ariandel and The Ringed City). The combat system, lore, bosses and items are great. But performance issues are minor, boss fight area bonfires are unnecessary and poise system is obsolete. This game made me want to come back and sink more hours into the game for builds, PvP and pretty much s h i tposting memes for me (Hail yung maestro). The conclusion was satisfying and I am glad that I finished the Souls series. I will give this game a 9 out of 10, a great solid recommendation for newcomers and veterans alike.

When you're playing this game, you really feel like you're fighting an uphill battle. You can't stroll around the dungeon. You have to get in and get out as fast as you can before your provisions run out, and your heals are like plugging a dam: you're frantically trying to fix them as best you can before more show up. Spiral Knights is a MMORPG game, with new components, chapters to the storyline, and holiday events featured from time to time. The basic premise is you crash-landed on an unknown planet and you collect and buy various supplies within the planet to upgrade your gear, while unraveling the mysteries of the planet and the missing Alpha team.
Since it's inauguration a few years back, the game has gone through several major changes, especially in late July 2013, where the game is now primarily free-to-play. While it is no longer limited by elevator and reviving energy costs, it does get tedious to perform typical tasks such as leveling up equipment (requiring several fire crystals, minerals, materials and energy) which requires going through levels often with the same layout more consistently--sometimes hoping to get lucky.
That all said, Spiral Knights is a good game, but preferably played less extensively to avoid getting bored from it entirely. My biggest takeaways include its addictive, ambient soundtrack by Harry Mack; a Spiral Knights wiki detailing a lot about the game; and several supplies obtained in the game are tradable via Steam.

Do you enjoy pressure?
Because this game hefts the burden of adventure squarely on your back and doesn't think twice about applying further weight. It is about risking the lesser evil lash against your favorite sword-at-arms that just might save the entire party, or forcing the heavy hand of loss---the gear acquired, the coin spent, the time given and heroics witnessed---against the whole. This is a game about choices, the worst of choices, and their dark punitive glee. If you look to negative reviews complaining about difficulty, this fact will be confirmed.
Make no mistake; this game is excellent and does precisely what it intends to do, from the artwork to the slow, bone grinding of the mechanics. Only ask if this game is for you.

DISCLAIMER - This was my first experience with the Fallout series.
Shortly after witnessing my husband murder and my sons kidnapping, I, a lawyer from (roughly) 200 years in the past, was blasting fools with a 10mm pistol with no other motivation than: "hey, those guys look meaner then the other ones their shooting at."
Fallout 4, AKA The Hunt for Ductape, does many things right: Piper, world design, immersion, Piper, interesting characters, etc., but it also
short of many things  as well: Dogmeat, character motivation, Preston Garvey's idea of splitting work evenly, Dogmeat, variety (in missions, enemies, gameplay).
Most of the time in this game was this:
While this experience certainly is fun at first, mostly due to gunplay, it can get very boring, very quickly.
Another major problem is that character motivation, or rather, lack thereof. When you start this open-world, RPG game you are immediatly given a sense of urgency: "oh no, i need to find my son quickly, because i love him and stuff." And it creates this weird 'atmosphere' wherein, you pass a building and you look at it and think "oh, there could be ductape in that building" and so you check. Then you find enemies, whether it be Super Mutants or Raiders or anything else, so you begin killing them all and clear out the building of enemies. Maybe you find someone that gives you a quest so you go and do that. Then you move and find another building and do the same. Soon, you almost forget about finding Shaun and it begins to feel like a handicap on your experience. The character motivation do to anything except find Shaun doesn't exist until you join a faction. It just seems so forced. Maybe some people like it this way, but I would've preferred to see the main story be of the dichotomy between The Brotherhood of Steel, The Railroad, and The Institute.
Speaking of the factions (I'm forgoing The Minutemen because they don't play a role in the Synth debate much), why is it so obvious who is the objectively morally-superior faction? You either support genocide with The Brotherhood, slavery with The Insititute, or freedom with The Railroad, I feel that this could've been done better. Bethesda, make me think about who I wish to align myself with. This determines
of the game you get, this shouldn't be a no-brainer.
One thing this game did well (at least in my opinion with limited RPG experience) is really allowing me to play how I want. In my first run I played as a stealth-based, charasmatic V.A.T.S. ♥♥♥♥♥. I don't usually write reviews, but I enjoy this game and it's developers so much I thought I might give it a go.
As a player returning to this game from the beta and has logged 45 hours since, I can whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys hack 'n' slash, dungeon crawlers, or any other game where you collect gear, kill stuff, craft stuff and freeroam with ad-hoc parties of both friends and other random players.
I've noticed a couple of people complaining about server lag in the game, but this lag is non existent. I and many others have no lag at all. The only time I have seen lag was when the server was under a sudden heavy load (which was very rare and is occuring less and less)
Pros:
- Good optimisation: runs well on my mid-range PC on max settings @1920x1080 60fps
- Interactive, Friendly Devs: I have frequently seen the devs communicating and interacting with players. They are very friendly and constantly on the ball fixing issues with the game.
- Active Development: Tying in with the last point, the game is constantly having patches and hotfixes to fix issues. The devs are regularly adding new content (and even have a subreddit for the community to submit their own creations to be added)
- Lots of re-playability: Even after going through the entire game with one class, you can then switch to another class and have even more adventures while not having to do most of the grinding before.
- Any Play Duration - If you have only a small amount of time to play, this is a good game for you. If you want to play for a long period, this is also a good game. I've played for just 5-10 minutes at a time doing a few dungeons quickly before logging off, and, more recently, I have been playing long sessions (pretty much all day) for the last 2 days.
- Is NOT pay to win
Cons:
- Long queue times: Since it's release, the game has sky-rocketed to 3rd most popular F2P game on steam. As a result of this, there are sometimes long queues lasting up to 30 mins. However, the devs have been keeping on top of this, and I'm noticing queues less and less due to increased server capacity.

This game has A LOT of potential, but falls very short of the mark. Let me give a quick synopsis of it.
You are trying to reclaim your family's estate from dark forces. You recruit adventurers from the town to perform various quests, all involving adventuring in dungeons. You will have the ability to upgrade your party's skills and equipment, in addition to equip them with trinkets that can help or hinder them. There is a very diverse spectrum of character classes and builds that you can recruit, along with both positive and negative traits.
Building a party of 4 adventurers whose skills benefit and support each other is key to adventuring successfully. While you adventure you will find treasure, trinkets, and "heirlooms". The latter of which you can use to upgrade the resources in the town to better support your adventurers. During your adventures your characters will not only take health damage, they will also gain STRESS. Varying factors can cause stress, everything from taking a lot of damage, enemy attacks, insufficient equipment, traps, other character's actions, your character's quirks, and even not enough lit torches. Having too much stress will cause your character to acquire quirks as they slip deeper into insanity, most of the ones you acquire will be detrimental, and hurt your character's performance, rarely will the quirk actually help them. In addition to quirks the characters can become diseased, further hurting (very very rarely helping) them. To remove the Stress, quirks, and diseases, you need to make use of the facilities in the town where the character will recover for 1 week in game (the time it takes to  perform 1 quest). Due to needing to recover from stress, diseases, or quirks you need to have multiple effective parties while the others recover.
- In the dungeon there is no way to heal outside of combat other than a dubious "Camping" which is not always present and subject to the characters skill sets and quirks. You can eat food for 1 HP each, until the character gets full (3 or 4 HP total). This is next to useless as most enemies will eliminate that in one hit.
- Negative Quirks and Diseases are acquired faster than they can be healed. Paying to reduce stress, and cure quirks and diseases can get VERY expensive, there is no way to keep up with it, you have to become resigned to having patchwork characters with annoying negatives.
- Farming is disallowed. Finally have a party of decent heroes? Think you can run some low level dungeons to get some gold so that you can actually pay to cure and outfit them? No, too bad. There is a level cap, your heroes will utterly refuse to go on quests that are "beneath them". I can understand this, so that you don't farm until you are unbeatable. But one Levelled hero should be able to join a low level party.
Basically if you don't mind completely random events trashing characters that you've put time into and become attached to, then this is the game for you!

Ok, let's get the obvious out of the way first. It's not an RPG per se anymore. It's more like a First Person Open World Action Game with minor RPG elements. And to me that's fine. Sure, I was suprised when I first realized how the SPECIAL point system worked on this game, but not a huge deal. It is what it is.
This time your character is voiced. Ok, nice I guess. But the reactions of the chacter to different situations is all over the place. On the same conversation he might suddenly be very angry and the next sentence he is perfectly calm. And sometimes you just wonder why your character reacted like that at all. And the voice acting also defines too much what kind of character you are. You cannot have a blank slate charater and then play how you like.
Bethesda is STILL using this same crappy Game Bryo engine that they have been using for years. It's been improved. polisihed and the game does look nice outdoors (nice lighting) when you don't look too closely, and not too distant. But climb on top of some building in the city and you see all the low poly objects in the distant and they look outright ugly and terrible.
Gameworld feels artificial, like a playarea for a game. Not a believable enviroment where people used to live. This has always been a problem in Bethesda's games. Illusion of scale is not there. Let's take GTA 5 for example. GTA gives excellend illuision of a big city and massive rural area around it even though the map is relatively small, if you compare it to real life. Fallout 4 on the other hand does not. Go to the edge of the city and at first it feels like there's a big city on the distance. Go into the streets of said city and you see how unbelivable it is. Too small and cramped streets. Cars would hardly fit to drive on so small streets. Diamond "City" is a perfect example. It should be this big settlement where the survivors have gathered and prospered since the war, but actually is just a couple of huts and shops (and a noodle stand) that is more like a really, really small village. I mean it used to be this big city baseball stadium and it looks more like someones back yard. Illusion of scale, that is a huge deal in Bethesda's game and that continues to be a problem in this one too.
The game feels like a Fallout 3.5 rather than Fallout 4. It's been improved on most areas, combat is better, voice acting is better, it looks better (though new engine is desperatly needed) but still lacks on so many areas like Bethesda's game have always been lacking. And the game should decide if it want's to be a Open World FPS or RPG. Nothing wrong with FPS, I would welcome it gladly, but just decide which.
Now, the trouble is that no-one else is making games like these (ok Borderlands is kind of in the same category but still completely different). How to review this if it is the best example of these kind of game's there is? To me this game has alot of things that pulls me to play it but when I start playing it I start to wonder why I am playing it. Everything is so skin deep and ultimately becomes boring. Ultimately though I cannot recommend this.

I don't usually write reviews, but I enjoy this game and it's developers so much I thought I might give it a go.
As a player returning to this game from the beta and has logged 45 hours since, I can whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys hack 'n' slash, dungeon crawlers, or any other game where you collect gear, kill stuff, craft stuff and freeroam with ad-hoc parties of both friends and other random players.
I've noticed a couple of people complaining about server lag in the game, but this lag is non existent. I and many others have no lag at all. The only time I have seen lag was when the server was under a sudden heavy load (which was very rare and is occuring less and less)
Pros:
- Good optimisation: runs well on my mid-range PC on max settings @1920x1080 60fps
- Interactive, Friendly Devs: I have frequently seen the devs communicating and interacting with players. They are very friendly and constantly on the ball fixing issues with the game.
- Active Development: Tying in with the last point, the game is constantly having patches and hotfixes to fix issues. The devs are regularly adding new content (and even have a subreddit for the community to submit their own creations to be added)
- Lots of re-playability: Even after going through the entire game with one class, you can then switch to another class and have even more adventures while not having to do most of the grinding before.
- Any Play Duration - If you have only a small amount of time to play, this is a good game for you. If you want to play for a long period, this is also a good game. I've played for just 5-10 minutes at a time doing a few dungeons quickly before logging off, and, more recently, I have been playing long sessions (pretty much all day) for the last 2 days.
- Is NOT pay to win
Cons:
- Long queue times: Since it's release, the game has sky-rocketed to 3rd most popular F2P game on steam. As a result of this, there are sometimes long queues lasting up to 30 mins. However, the devs have been keeping on top of this, and I'm noticing queues less and less due to increased server capacity.

This game has A LOT of potential, but falls very short of the mark. Let me give a quick synopsis of it.
You are trying to reclaim your family's estate from dark forces. You recruit adventurers from the town to perform various quests, all involving adventuring in dungeons. You will have the ability to upgrade your party's skills and equipment, in addition to equip them with trinkets that can help or hinder them. There is a very diverse spectrum of character classes and builds that you can recruit, along with both positive and negative traits.
Building a party of 4 adventurers whose skills benefit and support each other is key to adventuring successfully. While you adventure you will find treasure, trinkets, and "heirlooms". The latter of which you can use to upgrade the resources in the town to better support your adventurers. During your adventures your characters will not only take health damage, they will also gain STRESS. Varying factors can cause stress, everything from taking a lot of damage, enemy attacks, insufficient equipment, traps, other character's actions, your character's quirks, and even not enough lit torches. Having too much stress will cause your character to acquire quirks as they slip deeper into insanity, most of the ones you acquire will be detrimental, and hurt your character's performance, rarely will the quirk actually help them. In addition to quirks the characters can become diseased, further hurting (very very rarely helping) them. To remove the Stress, quirks, and diseases, you need to make use of the facilities in the town where the character will recover for 1 week in game (the time it takes to  perform 1 quest). Due to needing to recover from stress, diseases, or quirks you need to have multiple effective parties while the others recover.
- In the dungeon there is no way to heal outside of combat other than a dubious "Camping" which is not always present and subject to the characters skill sets and quirks. You can eat food for 1 HP each, until the character gets full (3 or 4 HP total). This is next to useless as most enemies will eliminate that in one hit.
- Negative Quirks and Diseases are acquired faster than they can be healed. Paying to reduce stress, and cure quirks and diseases can get VERY expensive, there is no way to keep up with it, you have to become resigned to having patchwork characters with annoying negatives.
- Farming is disallowed. Finally have a party of decent heroes? Think you can run some low level dungeons to get some gold so that you can actually pay to cure and outfit them? No, too bad. There is a level cap, your heroes will utterly refuse to go on quests that are "beneath them". I can understand this, so that you don't farm until you are unbeatable. But one Levelled hero should be able to join a low level party.
Basically if you don't mind completely random events trashing characters that you've put time into and become attached to, then this is the game for you!

Remember back in the day when you were playing a game that was somewhat challenging, and you were learning all of the games's quirks so you could exploit them and do well? That's what Spiral Knights feels like. The game has a lot of quirks, and mastering them will ensure your survival in Spiral Knights' deep deep dungeons. But by all means, they don't make it a bad game. If anything I think they make the game much more fun, Spiral Knights is definitely one of the most enjoyable F2P games I've ever played. Since they removed the fee for going down to the next dungeon floor, you can play as much as you like too!
The only flaw, like most F2P games out there, is that eventually you'll come to a grind wall. You won't be grinding for experience, you'll be grinding for alchemy orbs, the key ingredients used in crafting the equipment you'll need to advance in rank and go through the story missions. If you're someone who enjoys blazing through the story missions of games, Spiral Knights will defintely disappoint once you reach around rank 4. But if you just enjoy going through dungeons with friends or strangers, and looking for a game with an old-school feel to it, Spiral Knights might be the game for you.

Ok, let's get the obvious out of the way first. It's not an RPG per se anymore. It's more like a First Person Open World Action Game with minor RPG elements. And to me that's fine. Sure, I was suprised when I first realized how the SPECIAL point system worked on this game, but not a huge deal. It is what it is.
This time your character is voiced. Ok, nice I guess. But the reactions of the chacter to different situations is all over the place. On the same conversation he might suddenly be very angry and the next sentence he is perfectly calm. And sometimes you just wonder why your character reacted like that at all. And the voice acting also defines too much what kind of character you are. You cannot have a blank slate charater and then play how you like.
Bethesda is STILL using this same crappy Game Bryo engine that they have been using for years. It's been improved. polisihed and the game does look nice outdoors (nice lighting) when you don't look too closely, and not too distant. But climb on top of some building in the city and you see all the low poly objects in the distant and they look outright ugly and terrible.
Gameworld feels artificial, like a playarea for a game. Not a believable enviroment where people used to live. This has always been a problem in Bethesda's games. Illusion of scale is not there. Let's take GTA 5 for example. GTA gives excellend illuision of a big city and massive rural area around it even though the map is relatively small, if you compare it to real life. Fallout 4 on the other hand does not. Go to the edge of the city and at first it feels like there's a big city on the distance. Go into the streets of said city and you see how unbelivable it is. Too small and cramped streets. Cars would hardly fit to drive on so small streets. Diamond "City" is a perfect example. It should be this big settlement where the survivors have gathered and prospered since the war, but actually is just a couple of huts and shops (and a noodle stand) that is more like a really, really small village. I mean it used to be this big city baseball stadium and it looks more like someones back yard. Illusion of scale, that is a huge deal in Bethesda's game and that continues to be a problem in this one too.
The game feels like a Fallout 3.5 rather than Fallout 4. It's been improved on most areas, combat is better, voice acting is better, it looks better (though new engine is desperatly needed) but still lacks on so many areas like Bethesda's game have always been lacking. And the game should decide if it want's to be a Open World FPS or RPG. Nothing wrong with FPS, I would welcome it gladly, but just decide which.
Now, the trouble is that no-one else is making games like these (ok Borderlands is kind of in the same category but still completely different). How to review this if it is the best example of these kind of game's there is? To me this game has alot of things that pulls me to play it but when I start playing it I start to wonder why I am playing it. Everything is so skin deep and ultimately becomes boring. Ultimately though I cannot recommend this.

As a Lovecraftian fan, this game is pure excellence. It's unbridled focus on Necromancy, Cosmic Horrors, Weird Fiction Tropes and recently on an Innsmouth-centric revolt allows an atmosphere of insidious dread to prevail through such terrible game mechanics. Yes, I said it. Reveling in the diverse rogue gallery of lore-centric enemies is awesome. You'll feel like you got lost inbetween Algernon Blackwood and Lovecraft while crawling through catacombs as Wayne June proclaims your inevitable failure, and the masked Leper leading your party suddenly cracks.
But I feel a unique, separate kind of dread when all four of my level 5's miss the basic skeletals and get wrecked. Or when Cup of Annoyance is cast 37 times in a row by their back line without giving me a turn, stressing my entire party to Hell itself. DD's combat engine is dicerolls from D&D, home brewed, without much semblance of balance.
Darkest Dungeon is a sidescrolling click-n-crawl much like Grimrock, with a tiered party of 4 classes taking different depth charts. Positioning is important, as archers can't shoot from the front, and your crusader can't swing from the back. Following? You crawl down hallways, which are littered with procedurally generated loot, into rooms, filled usually with bad guys. That's all it is, besides for a feature creep styled town where heirlooms acquired can upgrade it to provide cheaper upgrades. No town events, invasions, 1-day missions, or anything resembling variation. Objectives range from scouting all the rooms, killing all the bad guys, or collecting 3 pieces of unique loot. All 3's results do not effect your party any differently, leading me to realize DD is a monotonous descent into the uniquely terrifiyng realm of boredom, and boredom that punishes you for being alive.

I have to say that this game is one of my favorites. 9.3/10
You will face hard♥♥♥♥♥enemies, you will fail probably even more than win, you will get frustrated because you let your higher level, well-equiped and fully upgraded hero die. But in the end, when you complete a dungeon alive a smile will pop in you face.
The game is all about grinding. The more dungeons you complete, the more gold you have to spend in upgrades and trinkets (equipments for your heroes). Each dungeon has a reward, and there are three kinds of dungeons: you have a short dungeon - it has fewer rooms - and its easier to complete, you also have medium dungeons - it has an considerable amount of rooms - and you get a campfire, with you can set a camp and rest/buff you heroes mid-quest, and last but no least you have long dungeons - it has a lot of rooms - you will have to go through a huge amount of rooms in order to complete those kind of dungeons.
You also have to set a strategy before going into an adventure. In certain areas of the game, monster will be more resistent as certain kind of DoT (damage over time) than others. Keep it in mind when you`re think in bring a Plague Doctor to the Weald, or remember to have a Crusader in you party when you`re going to the cursed Ruins.
You will also have to manage resources before going to an adventure. You can buy torches, food, antivenom, bandages etc. Everything to raise the chances of your crew to return alive to the town. I`d say that is still possible to complete a dungeon without bringing anything, but you`ll have to retreat 99% of the time.
Well, if world isn`t perfect, why should this game be?
After about 100 hours I`ve reached the max level with every class in the game, killed all the bosses, collected all the ancestral items and my town was fully upgraded. Well, there was anything more to do. You still have dungeons to complete, but as I said the fun part is the grinding, and when you finish grinding you don`t have much to do. You definitely can still have fun, challenging yourself to do a dark run (without torches) and so on, but that`s up to you.
I`d highly recommend this game for everyone who enjoy play RPG, turn-based like games. This game is totally worth the $15 you have to pay.

Bought this game for 20 bucks, installed a few mods, played. Enjoying it so far.
In my opinion anyone who gives it a bad view because it's not a true fallout game or a true rpg shpuld have done research. If you like games like borderlands with expanded open world options, and a nice character creator and decent voice actors, this is something you'll enjoy. If you want a focus on rpg gameplay, pass on this one.
As a standalone game it's actually really good. The level design is to die for, the fluidity of the 3rd person movement is lovely, although a little too heavy for my taste (the delay in your character to get moving from a full stop is realistic but puts an inherent disadvantage to using 3rd person over 1rst. Not a big deal, but it could cost you a hit if your character is being sluggish). Do note tho that if you have your weapon drawn the 3rd person movement because about as responsive as 1rst, so combat should be nice. With a few ini tweaks you can adjust the over the shoulder camera to give you a better view while shooting, and give you a better holstered cam. Survival is very fun, but could do with some tweaking (I recommend horizon). Gun play feels really nice, grenades are fleshed out and the modibility of armor and weapons is really nice. The gore system is as good as ever. Characters have unique voice actors for once, so each person feels like an individual. Voiced protagonists.
I could go on, but I've sucked off the game enough already.
There's plenty of room for improvement, and bugs are apparent, but I'd say pick it up on sale, and maybe find other ways of acquiring dlc that doesn't include hashing out more chow to Bethesda. I've played probably over a hundred hours on this game on ps4 as well, and that's without any real mod support, and I enjoyed it.

In 2011, my journey began. And in 2017, that journey ended. The original Dark Souls (2011) kindled a relationship with a video game that I had never experienced before. That relationship is stronger than ever, having morphed and strengthened over time across the series’ three iterations. The first game caught my attention, enthralling me in an imaginary universe I had never experienced before, but also tested my metal. The second game continued on the first game’s strengths, but never captivated me like DS1. And now we have the third.
In all honesty, I had my reservations about the latest, and final Souls game. Before the game’s release I felt that From Software, the developer of the Soulbourne series, had exhausted their creativity and originality with the first and second games, and thus the third would end up a mere imitation of the series previous outings. But alas, my cynicism was proven wrong. Spoilers aside, this third outing in the series sees players take control of the ‘Ashen One’, a being tasked with bringing a bunch of ‘Lords of Cinder’ to task, thus ending, or beginning anew, the age of fire – a daunting task, as in DS1 & DS2, you yourself became a Lord of Cinder at each game’s conclusion. The game functions and plays exactly as the previous two games. “If the formula aint broke, then no point trying to fix it!” Over +-35 hours you will explore a wide array of environments, defeat enemies, collect souls, consume said souls, and kit out your character with increasingly more powerful items, outfits and weapons, so that you can go and explore more dangerous locales,  defeat even bigger enemies and consume more plentiful souls. This formula is repetitive, but maintains the player’s attention through continuously presenting him/her with increasingly more challenging encounters that require skill, learning, knowledge and, for me at least, pure dumb luck.
For some, the Souls games may prove difficult, but I believe the better term is ‘challenging’. Once you have learned the ins and outs of the game’s combat and rpg mechanics you should be good to go. Of the three souls games DS3 does a good job of presenting the player with challenging encounters that never enter the realm of feeling impossible. The only boss that disproves this is Midir, an optional DLC encounter who functions much like other bosses, but has a ridiculous amount of health that can take what feels like eons to whittle down. Moreover, the challenges the bosses present are, arguably, made easier by offering the player options to summon npc characters to help fight most of the games many bosses. On the other hand, your journey is complicated by numerous invasions, whereby npc characters will invade your world and try their damndest to end your life. However, the AI of these invaders leaves a lot to be desired. Most can be easily defeated by stepping backwards after the invader attacks, then darting back in to deliver some damage; rinse and repeat and you’ll destroy any invader. Overall, the choreographed invasions are pretty poor in comparison to what would occur in previous Souls games. Boss fights are the highlight of this game, and they rise to the high expectations set by both DS1 and DS2. DS3 provides a plethora of diverse bosses that range from humanoid warriors to hulking behemoth tree-giants. Each have their own style and atmosphere that never come too close to seeming akin to each other. A major boon for DS3 is that every boss has at least two different phases which force players to often alter their strategy mid-fight in order to compensate for a new phase of attacks or even environment. However, DS3 is quite conservative with regards to the kind of bosses it presents to the player. DS3 does not provide anything close to the alien and strange creatures that can be found in DS1 or Bloodborne; rather most bosses stick to having a humanoid form whilst wielding a large sword- or club-like weapon.
To fight these big badass bosses, one needs good equipment. DS3 does a great job at providing a magnificent array of armor sets, weapons and spells. Importantly, the game plays on the nostalgia factor by providing items from past souls games. At one point I was able to kit out my character almost exactly as once done in DS1, as well as DS2. One complaint that I do have with regards to weapons is that the game has a tendency to force the straight and great sword options on the player due to them being so common, prevalent and effective. Both DLCs added much variety to the weapons arsenal, as well as special attacks that can be quite mesmerizing on first sight. Moreover, if arcane warfare is your thing, then DS3 has it covered. Faith, pyromancy and mage builds are supported by a multitude of spells for each school of magic, and are devastating in both PvE and PvP.
An integral component of the Souls games is exploration. The DS3 adventure occurs across many well designed environments, each having their very own particular atmosphere and context-specific encounters. From dark dungeons to sky-high castles, putrefying swamps to forgotten caverns, the games does a great job at proving a wide array of areas to explore. Apart from the challenging enemy encounters, the player will interact with several npc characters, some of which will help you out, while others will attempt to hinder your progress. These npc’s are far more expressive than those in previous Souls iterations, with many doing more than just standing around looking glum as in past Souls games. Some of these encounters reveal lengthy questlines, that once completed, have major influence on the overall main story line as well as on a variety of events. This is a welcome advent to the Souls series.
Leading from this, we have the lore of the game. Like previous Souls games, little of the game’s overarching narrative is told through direct story telling methods. Rather, the bulk of interesting and enigmatic lore and story comes from item descriptions and thorough inspection and observations within the game world. By just paying extra attention to one’s surroundings, major plot points and supporting content can be uncovered. For those gamers that prefer story flung into their faces through lengthy cut scenes and detailed in-game codex’s, be aware! DS3, as well as all other Souls games, takes a more active rather than passive approach to storytelling.
With regards to presentation, DS3 is a beautiful game that successfully brings life to a dark fantasy world. Characters models are well designed and textures are good enough to seem realistic. However, some areas lack the intricate details afforded to others, making for an uneven experience from region to region. Adding to the aesthetic of the game, is the music and sound. DS3 sticks much to what has been done in past Souls games. Adventuring across the game’s world is mostly done in absence of any music score. This and the environmental noise and sound do well to capture the feelings of isolation, loss and entropy. Once a major encounter begins then only does the typical Souls score commence.
Overall, Dark Souls 3 is a fantastic entry and end to the Souls series. It may not experiment or adjust the Souls formula as much as some may have hoped for, but it does present a daunting adventure that will challenge anyone willing to take the chance. Personally, I find Dark Souls 3 to be a great Souls game; not quite as good as its older brother Dark Souls 1, or even its demented cousin Bloodborne. But it is a damn fine game in its own right.

This game is easily the best game of 2016. It is a great ending to the souls series. Dark Souls 3 is my first souls game. From what I've heard it is the hardest. After 4 playthroughs, I think I have played enough of the game to give a good review. ( I have not yet played any of the DLC). I am going to be revealing minor spoilers so be wary. Lets start with a list of the features I liked and disliked.
+Difficulty Level
This is the first game that I have ever played that really challenged me. My first playthrough was basically an abusive relationship. The game would hit me, I would cry about it and quit, but eventually came back to it after an hour. The first few areas had me thinking, "This isn't so bad". Then came the Abyss Watchers my favorite boss in the game. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥that was a hard fight for me. And that is my favorite thing about this game. The fact that is excrutiatingly difficult.
+Music
I am a sucker for instrumental music, and this game extremly delivered. Walking into my first Gundyr fight, when the music kicked in, it was a moment that I would remember for a long time. When I was fighting the Abyss Watchers, and they combined together to put up one last fight, the violin solo made me feel pity for the curse of the Watchers. The music is really amazing in this game.
+/- Level Design
The level design for this game is really unique, and it really does not hold your hand. It is highly possible for you to miss entire areas of the game, and exploration is key. I do not know how I feel about this. I like the style the game is going for, but it sometimes is annoying to miss an item. The side quest are somewhat hidden, and it is best to double back on an area to make sure you did not miss something. On my first playthrough of the game, I missed a lot of the items, and ended up looking up some of the locations. Having to do that took some fun out of the game, and it was annoying. The world it self is highly detailed and looks amazing. The locations do make the game world seem a little small though.
+/- Story
It is possible to play through this game and not know anything about the story, other than you have to keep a fire from going out. It is sad that the game does not tell you more, because the story for the game is really intresting. Most of the story is hidden in item descriptions, and vague npc dialouge. I would suggest looking up a video explaining the lore for the game if you plan on playing it, though be wary of spoilers.
+/- Enemies and Bosses
The games Enemies and Bosses are pretty unique. Each area has a specific set of enemies that the player has to learn to defeat. They are designed well. The Bosses are really awesome. In the begining cutscence, the Lord of Cinder are displayed as these unique and badass super people who you have to kill. Almost all of their fights are challenging (ahem Yhorm) and are entertaining. I wish there was a feature that allowed you to fight the bosses again individually, but the closest thing we get is a new game plus system. I played a playthrough of new game plus on my strength build, and it was a joke. Having end game gear against enemies who are slightly buffed makes the game downright easy. It may just be easier with a strength build, but I would stay away from it.
+/- Weapon and Estus System
The game changed the system which Estus flask and weapon upgrading works. For Estus, you find shards which can grant you additional flask, and undead bone shards, which make your Estus heal more health. I really like this system. Your Estus flask sort of "level" with you. I like the weapon upgrading system. I like how there is different types of titanite for boos weapons and normal weapons, and also how you have to devote a titanite slab to get a weapon to +10, which there are only 8 of in the game.  My only gripe with the weapons are the weapon arts. I think they are a cool way to make every weapon feel unique, but some weapons have seriously underpowered weapon arts.
Meh -The Invasion system
The pvp in this game is okay. I personally found that it was an annoyance to be invaded while clearing areas that are hard enough without another player making things more difficult. Though it was really entertaining to be right at the bonfire and then a deadly duo including Aberdolf Lincler ruins your day. I do like the summon system. I used it to help other players defeat bosses that I really liked to play against and that they might be having a hard time with.
I have really enjoyed this game, and I feel that it has ended the series in the best way it could. It gave intresting enemies and bosses, beautiful levels, an intriguing but somewhat hidden story, and a good weapon and estus sytstem. I would highly reccommend getting this game, as it will be well worth your $60.

This game will probably be fun for you for the first 40 or so hours, but after that, it just gets very repetitive.
Effective strategies that clever players devise for success are ultimately nerfed in the patches.  To me, the pleasure of a game is figuring out strategies to overcome challenging situations, rather than relying on luck from a random number generator.
Even with the nerfs to your characters and the power boosts to the enemies, the game is still manageable and is not nearly as difficult as you might be lead to believe based on the reviews of other gamers on here.
However, the game gets boring because of the lack of customization for the characters.  There aren't any special armors or weapons to find.  You simply have generic upgrades, so when going on your quests/missions, there isn't really anything too exciting that you will ever find.  It just the the same old gold, and items that help you unlock generic upgrades.  There are "trinkets," but these are nothing to write home about, and are also generic.  You will get multiple copies of the same useless trinkets.
The bosses can be cool, but it seems like the developers got lazy.  Rather than making new bosses, they just re-used the old bosses, but made them tougher.  So you have to fight necromancer level 1, level 2, and level 3.  This just adds to the lack of excitement.
I guess I get a certain level of satisfaction successfully going through this game while having only minimal causalties when I read how so many others are frustrated and can't seem to figure how to achieve consistent success.  However, this minor joy is not enough to keep me coming back for more.
In summary, the game a lot more content (far more than it will ever have) in order for this game to be noteworthy.  Will you enjoy the game for the first 40 hours or so?  Probably.  Then you will realize that you are tired of going through the same process over and over again without any hope of a unique reward.  I am hopeful that someone out there will create a mod which makes the game a lot better.

This game will probably be fun for you for the first 40 or so hours, but after that, it just gets very repetitive.
Effective strategies that clever players devise for success are ultimately nerfed in the patches.  To me, the pleasure of a game is figuring out strategies to overcome challenging situations, rather than relying on luck from a random number generator.
Even with the nerfs to your characters and the power boosts to the enemies, the game is still manageable and is not nearly as difficult as you might be lead to believe based on the reviews of other gamers on here.
However, the game gets boring because of the lack of customization for the characters.  There aren't any special armors or weapons to find.  You simply have generic upgrades, so when going on your quests/missions, there isn't really anything too exciting that you will ever find.  It just the the same old gold, and items that help you unlock generic upgrades.  There are "trinkets," but these are nothing to write home about, and are also generic.  You will get multiple copies of the same useless trinkets.
The bosses can be cool, but it seems like the developers got lazy.  Rather than making new bosses, they just re-used the old bosses, but made them tougher.  So you have to fight necromancer level 1, level 2, and level 3.  This just adds to the lack of excitement.
I guess I get a certain level of satisfaction successfully going through this game while having only minimal causalties when I read how so many others are frustrated and can't seem to figure how to achieve consistent success.  However, this minor joy is not enough to keep me coming back for more.
In summary, the game a lot more content (far more than it will ever have) in order for this game to be noteworthy.  Will you enjoy the game for the first 40 hours or so?  Probably.  Then you will realize that you are tired of going through the same process over and over again without any hope of a unique reward.  I am hopeful that someone out there will create a mod which makes the game a lot better.

Starbound is very interesting, and nostalgic. It brings memories of old space-exploration tales with crazy aliens, spacecraft technology of the 80's, pretty 16bit-like graphics, and a ton of customization and construction materials - with even more yet to come.
Just because you've played terraria or Minecraft or Cube World, doesn't mean you've played all there is to voxel sandboxing games. Give Starbound a try, but keep in mind it is still beta/early access. There's a lot of things to do already, and soon quests will be added.
And of course. Mods. Never forget mods - the game is made from the ground up to allow easy modding, and there are already a number of alterations rolling around online [specially on the Nexus website].
Believe me, you won't be disappointed - and if you're still not sold, just wait for the full version and regret missing being part of the development :)

Starbound is a fantastic side scrolling plat-former. The game is still in early Beta stage and is one of my favorite games already.
Overview: Starbound is a game where you are leaving your home planet and run out of fuel. You are abandoned in space and have to beam down to the local planet full of hostile and some passive life forms. You have to create an escape from the planet by finding fuel, surviving and fueling your ship to find the next boss to explore further reaches of the Galaxy.  It has that nice 8-Bit style that makes he game feel like it's running on an old school system to give you that real nostalgic feel. The developers are some of the most dedicated devs when it comes to their fans. From constantly tweeting fans back to adding mods that the community made in to the actual game and on top of that giving credit to the person who made the mods.
Exploration: Starbound has one of the most large maps I have seen when it comes to an exploration stand point. It has 5 different Sectors of the Galaxy, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta and X. In each of the Sectors there are probably over 1000 planets easily. The higher up you go the better loot you find, along with the harder enemies.
Combat: The combat system is a very simple yet efficient combat system when it comes to DPS  and Attack Speed. The Weapons are also cleverly named even though it's random name generation for weapons.
Lighting: One of the things that drew me into Starbound was the beautiful lighting system. It's hard to explain it's really just easier to experience. Point being they really showed their strong point in this lighting system.
Community: Starbound is in Beta still which is fantastic, because the community is so strong for a Beta from Starbound Steam groups to Starbound sub Reddits to even just a twitter community. The community so far is ever expanding.
Starbound 10/10 would space again.
