This is a good-looking (though obviously low-budget) game with a cool atmosphere. It knows that it wants to be a difficult dungeon crawler, and delivers very well. I finished all currently available content and really enjoyed it.
Combat is very well done - despite the simple basic idea (reminds me of Disciples 2). 4 guys stand off VS 4 enemies and take turns hitting each other. What makes this interesting is:
The difficulty is almost spot on (some parts are a bit easy). There are people who say that they got screwed by RNG and died. In my 90 hours of playing, a character died (without me obviously making a mistake) ... maybe 5 times? Keep in mind, you can have 25 characters active at once, and the game tells you at the start some will die. This game is in Ironman mode (no save-load) - overcoming RNG is the whole point of it.
You can flee from battle (may take a few turns) and you can flee from dungeons (instant and 100% success). If you get many deaths, it's because you took unnecessary risks, simple as that.
The game is quite difficult, but it is fair. You can't outright lose the game at all, most of your progress will stay even if you lose your best group (which you shouldn't like I said above). DD does teach you to be patient. :) "Be wary, triumphant pride precipitates a dizzying fall" and "Beware, overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer", you hear those a lot from the narrator, and that's the best way to describe your number 1 cause of character death. If you go into a dungeon unprepared expecting to get through on pure skill, you will die. :)
Apart from being unfinished in some areas (e.g. the last dungeon is still in development) and having a few balance issues (and exploits), the game's main flaw is the lack of diversity in dungeons and monsters. Most of the replayability comes from having things happen to your guys and having to modify your group. Once you have seen a few e.g. Ruins dungeons, you really won't see anything new there for the rest of the game, barring bosses (8 unique ones). You will see less than 10 types of monsters in any given dungeon.
After playing through the whole game once, I doubt I will do so again in the near future - though considering how good the game is, I will likely come back once it is released and has more things added.
DD is good in Early Access and hopefully will be even better once it is finished. If you enjoy good-looking, difficult dungeon crawling with interesting combat, this could very well be the game for you. Especially if you like discovering things and keeping notes - a very good idea in this game.
Most of the negative reviews are "this game is too difficult and unfair". I don't know how you can get any more fair than your mistakes leading to your characters dying.

What I enjoyed personally:
- The world is simply beautiful. Looking at the Commonwealth from a top of a high building is awe-inspiring.
- Melee is possible outside of VATS and its very cinematic
- Fights in a ruined city: this is a single thing that I really enjoyed in F3 and something that Bethesda did better than Obsidian's FNV. Lonesome Road FNV DLC brought a bit of it to NV and it was great.
- Very smooth gameplay
- Interactive and diverse environment: cars and vertibirds going boom feel really great and bring some life to the Commonwealth. Jetpacks just add an entire new layer to the game
- Bethesda's subtle way of telling stories - something underappreciated in F3 as well. Careful reading of notes and examination of the surroundings often reveal a new depth to visited locations.
- Survival is interesting. At survival level there is plenty motivation to use all available resources - including the interesting environment.
Negatives:
- This is not New Vegas 2
- There are literally no choices to be made in the game. It's a single-player MMORPG in this respect.
- Radio is nonexistent. Music is bad.
- Plot and characters are not involving.
- There is no great mystery or overarching story to be discovered, the way there is in FNV. All events that can be glimpsed from the notes and dialogues are very local. They do not link with each other.
- Crafting makes exploration redundant. With the right perks you can make an impenetrable bathrobe by adding scrap metal to generic cloth.
- People praise gunplay, but nothing quite compares to the first cowboy repeater I found in NV. The new guns don't necessarily have the oomph that many claim they do.
- Colour palette is grey and more generic postapocalypse rather than Fallout
Overall:
Ultimately dull and boring virtual playground. Spent over a day in the game and it just made me want to go back to Mojave.

Ah, Dark Souls III... What can I say about you that hasn't been said a hundred times already? Well, I might as well give it a shot.
This is honestly one of my favorite games of all time. I first played through the game on PS4 at launch, because my computer was in dire need of an upgrade, but I picked it up here later to sit snugly with the other two games. Plus, the free online features and sale prices don't hurt one bit. So, despite my hours not reflecting it, I've played this game a ton, so I can safely say that I consider Dark Souls III the best game in the trilogy. I know that's something of a controversial opinion in the Dark Souls community right now, but what can I say? It contains all the spit and polish that the original Dark Souls deserves and more.
I like to call it a "greatest hits" game. It's most reminiscent of the original Dark Souls, but it has little splashes of Demon's Souls, Dark Souls II, and even Bloodborne thrown in for flavor. Tons of gameplay mechanics, story references, and old content have been dusted off to breathe more life into an already great game. I know the word "streamlined" is a bit of a red flag for some people, and trust me, I understand why, but I promise that it is nothing but a good thing in this case. The level design is back to form compared to Dark Souls II, the challenge is at its best with no artificial difficulty in sight, the enemies and bosses are varied and fun to fight, and it still has that Dark Souls writing, world building, and atmosphere that we all know and love.
I like to think PvP is improved, too. Yeah, Poise isn't "working as intended", to get that dumb joke out of the way, and a handful of weapons are overpowered to a degree, but by and large, you can get by all of the "cheap" stuff in PvP by simply playing better (to get another stale joke out of the way). Some Covenants are a little wonky, too, but at least you can switch between them on the fly now. I personally prefer it this way, so you don't get actual cheap stuff like Giantdads, or various other troll builds, and everyone's on a much more even playing field. That said, I mostly play for the PvE stuff, so I wouldn't really call myself an expert. All I do know is that this game's PvP experience has been the most fun for me.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. Regardless of if you're a veteran of the series or just someone who wants to see what all the fuss is about, it's one of the few triple A games on the market that's actually worth the $60 pricetag.

You wont find random weapon drops in this game, instead what you will uncover is a fairly well balanced experience that allows you to grow steadily as you buy or build a vast array of different weapon and armor types that will help you along your way. A player expecting Diablo-esq or even your typical MMO experience will be sorely disappointed, or maybe even pleasantly surprised at just how different Spiral Knights handles itself.
There is no grand world to explore in Spiral Knights, but thats not to say that you wont find a certain kind of beauty and charm to some of the locations you will visit. What it focuses on instead is the core gameplay element: Fighting monsters. At heart SK is primarily a PvE game set inside smaller 5-10 minute zones, the order of which are selected by a slightly randomized mechanic and have a constantly shifting nature. This does not mean that the levels themselves are randomized, but there is often enough variety to them that you wont notice repeats until you are many, many hours in unless you decide to play the same static missions over and over. If you hit a standstill in the missions you can opt to play daily prestige missions, some of which can be both extremely challenging, and quite rewarding once you learn how to complete them with your friends, or if a good challenge does not compel you, you have the option to fall back to the clockworks. Thats the name of the ever-changing level system which slowly progresses in difficulty as you delve deeper in an attempt to reach the core.
SK is a free to play game which has done away with the typical limitations of such titles. It no longer employs an energy system which limits how often you can play, no the game is truly free. All items in the game are purchased with one of two in-game currencies and even the game's expansion pack has now been made available for purchase with in-game currency. You may opt to purchase some of this currency with real money but it is by no means necessary in order to enjoy your time with the game. Doing so may give you a boost once you reach a certain stage of the game, but because the focus of the game is not PvP this does not feel like misplaced feature. There are two different PvP modes however: a capture and hold style game called Lockdown, and a heavily bomberman-inspired mode called Blast Network.
The main objective when playing Spiral Knights is to level your gear and collect crafting ingredients so that you may build bigger and better versions of your preferred weapons. Along the way they will increase in power and gain some semi-unique forms of charged attack which may inflict status effects, knockback, give ranged attacks to melee weapons, and have other special uses. You will need to actively dodge and shield against enemy attacks as well as position your strikes, shots, and bombs so that they hit their mark. This is not to say that there is a ton of depth to the weapon combat, but you have a few different moves which help to make things more interesting while you use your selected variety of guns, bombs, or swords; In addition to your 1-2-3 hit combo you have things like a charged attack, shield bump, shield bash, dodge, and a small variety of consumable items which may inflict various effects on enemies or offer heals and temporary buffs to your character or even summon a companion to help you fight. A recent addition even included pets which may be leveled up and that give your character minor buffs and offer a few special attacks/utility of their own.
In the end Spiral Knights is not an Everquest, its not WoW. Its a smaller and much more accessible action-rpg whose main focus is on the action element of fighting monsters from a 3/4 overhead view. Its a game which you may play solo, or bring a few friends. You can even team up with a couple of randoms and still enjoy fighting a variety of different monsters that have their own styles of attack and movement as you earn the money to upgrade your gear and find the ingredients to craft something new that will surely help you continue the fight in harder areas. If you've grown tired of walking up to monsters, standing still, and pressing '1, 2, 1' then you owe it to yourself to look at Spiral Knights. Its something just a little bit different.

Every time I boot up this game, I wonder if I'll have a pleasant stroll through the Ruins, or if I'll get absolutely wrecked.
This game's difficulty balances on the edge of a knife; you could get lucky and have almost no trouble in one mission, or get half your party wiped out 2 hallways from where you started (Curse you, Shambler!).
Fairly recently, the game has been given options to make the game slightly less tricky (or just change some mechanics that I'm POSITIVE are probably pointed out in previous reviews): Heart Attacks and Corpses. While I don't see any real difficulty bonus to corpses (as long as you keep corpses in mind for party compositions), some people are pretty annoyed by the concept. That feauture, as well as heart attacks (your characters getting so stressed they DIE), have a toggle option. While I would recommend playing with both on, if you are having serious trouble, it can help a little (though the game is still hard enough even without them).
This game is hard. Upgrading your town and keeping your party members alive is incredibly challenging. I can't describe to you how miserable you feel to have your whole party wiped, all their equipment taken away forever, and forcing you to try another mission afterwards with B-tier equipment on a party with almost no cash to give them provisions, crossing your fingers and praying that they'll live long enough to get you SOMETHING to start the ball rolling again.
But that elation when you beat the odds and somehow manage to make everything work out, and you actually recover from that crippling blow to your morale? Priceless.

This is something of a sad thing to say, but I can't really recommend this game at it's current Price, or it's DLCs, not unless they're less than $30 at least.
I'll try to describe in Detail why this game isn't very good, from both a PvP and a PvE aspect as best I can, so let's start with PvE.
In Dark Souls 3 PvE, the game at first, doesn't seem too different from many other games of an RPG Genre, very basic enemies staggered by your weapon, they don't have very powerful weapons or tools to defeat you with but you have to play careful or be overwhelmed, very fair and basic stuff, so it's not very much so worth getting into, what's really worth getting into is later-game, wherein enemies actually deal fair damage to you. In mid-game  enemies still try to overwhelm you, though now they move much faster and their weapon strikes are almost always faster than yours, this can lead to unfair fights wherein if you begin to get over-tasked, you may not be able to get away before getting killed in combat because you simply can't move or the enemies lash out at you far too quickly for you to heal, this can be frustrating to deal with at first if you're going through the game alone, however this problem can be solved if you simply bait them out one at a time. In late-game, though there is a mix of a few newer enemies, for some reason they simply re-use the exact same enemies you fought earlier, only harder hitting and maybe a new technique or 2, but otherwise pretty well the same, any tactic you used on the enemies at the beginning of the game, which makes it ridiculously easy to simply walk up to them and smash your Light-attack button because your swings will almost always knock them out of any of their attacks, the only reason you'd have to stop is to regain Stamina so you can repeatedly swing your weapon again. This truly baffles me, as in previous games, from the Souls Series, I have never seen re-use of enemies on this scale, and likely for good reason, so as to make you learn new tactics for each area and make them more memorable. It is also very apparent that the tactic you use to beat Beginning level enemies can also be used to beat almost every enemy up until Mid-Game where they begin to get faster than you.
TL/DR: Enemies are somewhat poorly made
The very coveted Dark Souls Bosses. The bosses for Dark Souls 3 are mostly well made, save for some exceptions, which can be quite the annoyance or completely disappointing. This shor bit is going to list off some poorly made Bosses, so skip reading this if you don't want to be spoiled, but know that it's roughly 45/55 on how I personally feel about Bosses.
This is just something of a detailed list of bosses that were poorly done but were mandatory, if they weren't mandatory they wouldn't be worth mentioning in my opinion.
TL/DR: 1/4 of bosses are bad

Discussing the bosses also makes it apparent there are less bosses than the previous two Souls series games, With Dark Souls 2 having a bare minimum of 20-16 bosses if you use Shortcuts and skips and Dark souls 1 having 14 bosses if you use every shortcut and skip device available to you. This is another point Dark Souls 3 has against it, considering 4 of it's 13 are unimpressionable bosses, which isn't neccesarily something I can say about about the others in the previous games. This can also considerably reduce the time to beat the game.
TL/DR: Less Bosses than previous games, thus making game quicker to beat
Another thing worth mentioning is that many weapons in PvE are unviable, the only things you'll usually every need are a Dark Sword or an Ultra-Great weapon, using anything else is usually more of a challenge, and you'll often see this is usually what people are using when playing Co-Operativley or during Invasions. This removes a lot of personality from characters, because not many people will sacrifice personal taste for damage, though every weapon should be reasonably good.
TL/DR: No good reason for PvE weapon variety
Lastly, Co-Operative play and Host Bonus's in Dark Souls 3 makes it ridiculously easy. In regards to summoning: Now, don't get me wrong, this is true in every Souls-Game, however in this one, every enemy except for some bosses can be VERY easily staggered, meaning that if you bring 2 or 3 extra players into your game, you can usually just carelessly swing your weapon with abandon, as any enemy that comes into contact with a hit will be unable to move until they recieve a second hit, letting your and your friends keep whacking it in an infinite cycle. If you haven't somehow managed to kill it and your summons haven't taken the aggresion from the enemy, you have a large plethora of Estus and lots of Rolls to be able to survive almost anything, along with a 25% health increase to help you survive more lethal attacks. This in totallity means you can simply mow down enemies with your pals and never think about attacking Human-Sized foes and makes you sloppy at fighting bosses because all you've likely had to do is spam light-attack and you'll likely beat most bosses by summoning too.
TL/DR: Summoning+Being a Host makes game no challenge at all

Dark Souls 3 Re-uses a LOT of Assets from previous games.
For some reason a some magics were added from previous games and others were not at all.
In Dark Souls, there is a mechanic unique to it that you likely won't find in many other games, the ability to invade and combat people during their PvE experience. This being said, Dark Souls 3 has pretty well ruined this mechanic, with the previously mentioned Host Benefits and Co-Operative play and the ability to also stagger Invading players like regular enemies, this allows the Host and his phantoms to have an overwhelming advantage against invaders unless an invader uses only combat builds designed to kill other players in a single hit (Also known as Glass Cannons). Also in Dark Souls 3 was the inclusion of moving while using the healing item Estus, making it nearly impossible to punish another player who has run away and is currently healing because they can just walk out of punishments. With all this, there is no good reason to Invade in Dark Souls 3, it's literally been ruined to an almost unrecognizable degree, especially if you've played the previous Dark Souls games.
TL/DR: They've Soiled It
:
Duels in Dark Souls 3 are okay, though there's clear superiority in what weapons you should use, and Heavy armor is absolutely pointless.
Now, I know there are some people who might be wondering what some above average things are about this game, so let me give you a brief summary of those:
By Jove, the Soundtrack is amazing, even for some of the lesser Bosses, it really gives you a feel for what you're fighting and puts you in the moment.
This one is a bit generalized, but I mean things like the armors, the Backgrounds and some areas, which clearly have a goodly bit of detail put into them, some of these clearly have had a lot of work put into them.
Now I spent a good paragraph listing off how I dislike some of the bosses in Dark Souls 3, but there are some VERY good bosses in this game, that will no doubt enamour you (Make sure to do hidden Bosses if you do get this game)
I'd love to go into more detail about some of these things but reviews can only be so long, so I'll just tell you my final score for Dark Souls 3 is a 5/10 and with it's DLC it's a 6/10. Again, I recommend buying it when it's cheap on price, or if you just wanna say you beat Dark Souls

I can't stop playing this game!
After 60 hours, I still find new combinations of powers/characters to try out, or I find new monsters in the level 5+ dungeons, or I go back down to the lower level characters and level up and find out how to use a new class to its fullest...The challenge of the game is such that, if you prepare really well and are cautious, you are mostly going to be okay going through the dungeons - and feel like you're Indiana Jones on steroids - but you are never entirely safe from sudden disaster, and that adds an edge that keeps things very interesting.
Other things I love about this game:
. Drips with atmosphere. There's a lot of RPG-Maker games out there - and they can be fantastic too, story-wise, but the aesthetics...meh...Here, monsters are vile beyond belief (Inchoate Flesh, anyone?), everything is grimy and gothic, dungeon doors swing open with a shriek of hinges, altars are made out of human skin, deformed swine-people vomit on your heroes and send them into throes of panic, and if you let the lights go out, you might run into an Elder God's illegitimate spawn.
. The characters are a little interchangeable...yet somehow favorites emerge; Willoughby, that one steadfast crusader who seemed to hit an abnormal amount of stun crits even without help from trinkets, and who died in the line of duty facing the Hag ages ago (yet still remembered); a jester with the odd name of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥('brothel' in French) and odder lines occasionally dropped, especially when he went Irrational a couple of times; Aschuill, the vestal I had right from the start and who's still with me, level 6 and the heart of any serious endeavour...There's that odd moment when a group that's been adventuring through near a dozen dungeons together face disaster as someone clings to life, and one of his teammates yells "Hang in there, my friend!". At that moment, the words 'procedurally generated' just don't seem to do things justice.
. Though it may not seem so, you cannot actually really get stuck in this game (that I've found so far). I've had group wipe-outs, I've lost all my cash - twice! - and I've always pulled myself back into the game. YOu just have to be ready to sacrifice your second-string heroes like it's going out of style: sending them in without light or food and ignoring their whining and eventual screams of panic until they bring back enough dough to make the trip worthwhile, then firing their asses and hiring on new <strike>fresh meat</strike> volunteers and doing it again.
Incidentally, for new players: I heartily recommend going online to find some 'beginner's strategy' guides. Make things a lot easier to get past that first period which is a bit of a killer, and where it's so easy to make a mistake that'll make things a bit of a drag for awhile.
Things I'd want the devs to tweak:
Not much, really. But it'd be nice if the vestal wasn't the only one with a reliable heal. As it is, I've made all kinds of groups but she's always the first player I add to the roster. ONCE I tried running with a crusader, a houndmaster, an arbalest and an occultist - everyone with self-heals or small party heals, and of course the occultist with the only other major heal of the game. How did that work? Well, the occultist's bleed-effect didn't trigger all that often...only when it was THE WORST TIMING POSSIBLE. The arbalest's heal wasn't enough to do bubkiss, the crusader had to pick up the slack and then he wasn't stress healing, so then the occultist when MAAAAAAD and then things got really interesting.
THis is not a problem per se, but the fact that the occultist is not, IMO, a very reliable healer, and the fact that the grave robber's blight heal is only for herself, makes them party members that I cannot really justify substituting for a vestal and a plague doctor. But I guess that's part of the fun: finding a group where I can make them work.
So...when's the official release already? I want to send my A-team against the Chthulu Wanabe in the estate proper already :)

I once gave this game a bad review because I lost a team of adventurers to critical hits.
I've since erased that review. This game is an absolute triumph in graphics, gameplay, sound, music, narrative and everything else. It's not been fully released yet but it's massive in content and I personally have not come across 1 bug yet.
The game is nervewrecking and will keep you on the edge of your seat. It is desperate and sad, too, and you will lose much. But don't let it dissuade you, like it did me, back when I wrote a bad review - one time fortune will be on your side and you will manage to raise your heroes and have them defeat the bosses.
And if your best heroes fail... well, it hurts so much more to lose them. But when they stand at Death's Door and their resolve is tested, their allies dying around them, and they unexpectedly find the courage to push on, you will remember that moment for a long time. And that's why the game is so good. Everything is permanently saved and you can never go back in time, so any loss you endure is permanent, but so is every victory. And that really makes your actions feel incredibly invested and meaningful.
Go play it - this will be one of the best games in whichever year it releases.
Oh, and, by the looks of it, there's one more major content update coming - the unfinished Darkest Dungeon (yes, same name as the game) which I think will be the ultimate test.

Original review appears below:
I've been playing Darkest Dungeon since it was first released into early access, as I was one of the Kickstarter backers. I played it for probably 20 hours or so at that point, got a fair ways in, then stopped, not wanting to play too far before things got close to full release. Many patches and content additions later, and I was alarmed to see some Steam reviews lamenting that the game had become imbalanced and impossible, etc. I jumped back in to see for myself, starting a fresh play rather than picking up where I left off, so I could be sure how things had progressed.
A very considerable amount of time later, and I can say with absolute certainty that those people are, frankly, wrong. And when I say "wrong", I don't mean that their opinions aren't valid, as Darkest Dungeon is very much an unforgiving game which demands players learn its systems intimately in order to succeed. This is absolutely not a game for everyone. What I mean is that the game is not artificially or even substantially more difficult than it was before. New systems have been added, and thus there is a fair bit more to learn, and a new area has been added which certainly carries with it a higher difficulty than those that came before it, but those things make for a deeper game experience, not an artificially difficult one. The experience remains fluid, organic, and incredibly well-balanced for the most part. I have not had any particular trouble steadily advancing into further tiers of the game in my 2nd play, though I have had to learn a few new tricks to get there.
There are, of course, still some rough edges here and there. It can be a real drag grinding for deeds in order to unlock certain town upgrades, for instance, and some classes may not yet quite have achieved the perfect balance compared to others. The thing people seem to fail to remember here is that the game remains in early access. It is not yet tweaked for final balancing. It is not yet content complete. There is more work yet to be done, and these things are very likely to continue improving even after final release, as Red Hook is very much dedicated to improving and adding to their game. That said, the game is remarkably stable and balanced. If you take your time to observe and learn how to play well, you will be rewarded. If you don't, you may not get too far.
It can be a tough call whether to recommend this game to someone, or to tell right off if it's something you may like. I highly recommend watching some stuff on YouTube or catching Pythagotron, CallofCthulhu, or any other Twitch streamer currently playing the game. A little gameplay should show you pretty quickly whether this is the sort of thing for you.
Rather than leave a detailed explanation of game mechanics, which I'm sure have been well covered by others already, I'll simply say this: at twenty bucks, this game is an absolute steal. It's not even content complete yet and people have already wrung hundreds of hours out of it. The core gameplay loop is fairly simple, but the procedural nature of the maps means things are always a little different, and you'll find yourself in a wide variety of circumstances depending on the course things take. This game offers FANTASTIC bang for your buck, and is challenging, deep, and satisfying not just in gameplay, but in story and visual design as well. The devs are also adding even more stuff, such as another character class, prior to the full release, which will then see the final, titular Darkest Dungeon for us to explore. With plans for more to come, the future of this game is very, very bright, and it's definitely something worth considering getting in on.
Just remember that all these rewards do come at a cost. The game won't let you in so easily, and it can be a somewhat punishing learning process. There's a lot to take in, and while most of the basics are well documented, internalizing those lessons will sometimes require you to learn the hard way, and many of the game's nuances will require you to sit up and pay attention, or even think outside the box in order to discover the various ways in which you can manage your heroes and use the existing game systems to your advantage. There is definitely more to this game than just combat. You won't have to be an economist, but there are definitely both fiscal and logistical concerns to think through when you're outside the dungeons. You're a team manager as much as you are a dungeon-delver, and your ability to think ahead will often serve you in ways outside the tactical combat.
But no matter how you slice it, this game is well worth your time. If you're a fan of difficult games that reward player knowledge and skill (Dark Souls and its kin being the go-to examples, these days), give Darkest Dungeon a try. It's one of the most balanced and complete games of its type already, with only further growth to come, and there are very few other games like it on the market.

Thanks to the free weekend and 67% off, I gave this game a go. Even though most of the recent reviews were less than flattering of Fallout 4, I figured "hey what the heck".
I have actually enjoyed it so far (16hours gameplay as of right now). It feels an awful lot like FarCry 2-4 with a lot less game ruining monotony. Don’t get me wrong, there is a lot of doing the same kind of task over and over again but it's different enough to mean you don't want to put your head through the screen like FarCry 2-4.
The playable area is pretty impressive, as I have only hit one of the invisible walls once whilst getting completely lost finding my way back to Sanctuary.
I've got to say that the hardcore fanbois of Fallout really have painted this as the Deus Ex 2 or F1 2015 of the series. It simply isn't. What it is, is a little less gruesome rendition of the series. Which I personally appreciate. It has it's bugs eg. when you place an object on terrain that isn’t completely flat, it sits on one edge and floats in the air on the other 3. Or when the dog (Dogmeat) runs into a rusted up car body, the car body is pushed around, not the dog.
Do these detail glitches kill the game, no. Yes it is a little aesthetically displeasing, and in some cases humorous but not game killing at all.
The story is pretty vague, you get thrown into a world that has very little forward loading, but once you emerge from the vault there is very little story to follow. I could imagine that if you were actually cast into the role in reality there wouldn't be a narrator close by to fill you in with what's happened anyway. So again, not a deal breaker (and that's from a guy who LOVES a strong story line).
And finally to the often whinged about choices available in the game. Yes, there are limitations. There are things that Bethesda doesn't allow you to do; my favourite complaint from one fanboi was that "he couldn't shoot the children in the game, if he wanted"... seriously! If this is your biggest concern... maybe it's time to go and get professional help. You've got issues.
I like the game, its fun and with plenty to do, build and explore.
Would I have bought it at full price? Probably not, but this genre is not my most enjoyable, it's something I will play on and off when the desire strikes.

Spiral knights is one of the more addicitve games ive played, although most MMOs share that qaulity. The missions in the game aren't great, they all seem to be quite the same, although a few of them differ from all the others. In each mission you kill enemies, solve puzzles, and defeat the occasional boss. One of the bigger issues I find in the missions is the fact that enemies are re-used A LOT. The missions become increasingly more predictable and only slightly vary in diffuculty, most are easily done solo. On a scale of 1-10 I would give the missions a 4.5 they havee a lot of room for growth.
There is an aspect of PvP, consisting of 2 game types. One being very reminicent of bomberman, although it isn't as widely played as the other, which is a shame really. The second game mode is a team based domination tpye of game. A purple and green team compete to hold points, who ever has scored highest in the end wins. To be completely honest I feel PvP in this game is a waste of effort, the gear is unbalanced, everyone genrally will use the same gear. There aren't many people playing at any given time, about 200. The only benefit of doing PvP is some costume pieces and a couple items. But I still give it a 6, as it provides a nice break from the tedious missions
One of the strong points this game hass is its graphical style, this game in my opinion looks amazing. The cartoonish style, albeit very generic, seems quite fitting in this game. Character creation doesn't go too in-depth, you get a default armor set which can be later used as costume pieces. The costume pieces however are where you get a lot more customization options. Currently the only available costume slots are your helmet and armor, it would be nice for a sword and shield costume slot, although i doubt that it will ever be implemented. Giving the game a rating based on graphical style I would give it a 8, maybe an 8.5 although that is pushing it
The player roles are very basic, slow DPS (basically tank,) fast DPS, and gunner which also takes the role of DPS. All healing is done through sprites or health capsules or potions picked up throughout missions. The armor sets for these roles are quite basic, you can't really go your own way with your gear or you will not do very well in high end content. On this side id give the game a 5, its a little hard to avoid this, and a lot of other popular MMOs tend to lean this way, World of Warcraft for example.
To wrap this up, there is DLC I haven't looked to much at it yet (it always lags for me :/,) The game feels a bit pay to win, gear upgrades require matireals (which are obtainable with ingame currency or through drops, but they take quite a while,) the story isnt much, its quite generic.
Don't get me wrong I quite enjoy this game, it's very approachable and would be quite enjoyable as a shared experience, although it does have QUITE a bit of flaws. My final score is 6.5/10 the game has a lot of room to improve.

I can't stop playing this game!
After 60 hours, I still find new combinations of powers/characters to try out, or I find new monsters in the level 5+ dungeons, or I go back down to the lower level characters and level up and find out how to use a new class to its fullest...The challenge of the game is such that, if you prepare really well and are cautious, you are mostly going to be okay going through the dungeons - and feel like you're Indiana Jones on steroids - but you are never entirely safe from sudden disaster, and that adds an edge that keeps things very interesting.
Other things I love about this game:
. Drips with atmosphere. There's a lot of RPG-Maker games out there - and they can be fantastic too, story-wise, but the aesthetics...meh...Here, monsters are vile beyond belief (Inchoate Flesh, anyone?), everything is grimy and gothic, dungeon doors swing open with a shriek of hinges, altars are made out of human skin, deformed swine-people vomit on your heroes and send them into throes of panic, and if you let the lights go out, you might run into an Elder God's illegitimate spawn.
. The characters are a little interchangeable...yet somehow favorites emerge; Willoughby, that one steadfast crusader who seemed to hit an abnormal amount of stun crits even without help from trinkets, and who died in the line of duty facing the Hag ages ago (yet still remembered); a jester with the odd name of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥('brothel' in French) and odder lines occasionally dropped, especially when he went Irrational a couple of times; Aschuill, the vestal I had right from the start and who's still with me, level 6 and the heart of any serious endeavour...There's that odd moment when a group that's been adventuring through near a dozen dungeons together face disaster as someone clings to life, and one of his teammates yells "Hang in there, my friend!". At that moment, the words 'procedurally generated' just don't seem to do things justice.
. Though it may not seem so, you cannot actually really get stuck in this game (that I've found so far). I've had group wipe-outs, I've lost all my cash - twice! - and I've always pulled myself back into the game. YOu just have to be ready to sacrifice your second-string heroes like it's going out of style: sending them in without light or food and ignoring their whining and eventual screams of panic until they bring back enough dough to make the trip worthwhile, then firing their asses and hiring on new <strike>fresh meat</strike> volunteers and doing it again.
Incidentally, for new players: I heartily recommend going online to find some 'beginner's strategy' guides. Make things a lot easier to get past that first period which is a bit of a killer, and where it's so easy to make a mistake that'll make things a bit of a drag for awhile.
Things I'd want the devs to tweak:
Not much, really. But it'd be nice if the vestal wasn't the only one with a reliable heal. As it is, I've made all kinds of groups but she's always the first player I add to the roster. ONCE I tried running with a crusader, a houndmaster, an arbalest and an occultist - everyone with self-heals or small party heals, and of course the occultist with the only other major heal of the game. How did that work? Well, the occultist's bleed-effect didn't trigger all that often...only when it was THE WORST TIMING POSSIBLE. The arbalest's heal wasn't enough to do bubkiss, the crusader had to pick up the slack and then he wasn't stress healing, so then the occultist when MAAAAAAD and then things got really interesting.
THis is not a problem per se, but the fact that the occultist is not, IMO, a very reliable healer, and the fact that the grave robber's blight heal is only for herself, makes them party members that I cannot really justify substituting for a vestal and a plague doctor. But I guess that's part of the fun: finding a group where I can make them work.
So...when's the official release already? I want to send my A-team against the Chthulu Wanabe in the estate proper already :)

This game can be frustrating, and it's very hard to get your party "off the ground" so to speak.  That being said, it's easily one of my favorite games.
The whole premise is one I really like.  This is no ideal adventure, where your party is nigh on invincible as far as storyline goes and any pitfalls can be avoided by a simple restart.  This is realistic adventuring; where the stakes are high and your "heroes" are just simple men and women with their own obstacles to overcome, and their own quirks.  They can't keep just rushing headlong into battle willy nilly, with no signs of wear and tear.  It's a nice change from the whole "the world is in peril.  Here's a group of misfits, go show them what your made of" type of deal.  Rather than relying on restarts, you have to decide: "Is it worth it?"  Is the extra treasure worth the increased danger of exploring in the dark?  Is the reward worth trying to finish the mission when your heroes are all stressed or near to death.  Is it worth it to stay in the battle when one or more people may be at death's door, or have already crossed over?  You have to decide what's worth risking, and to me, that's an incredibly interesting premise, and enough to keep me coming back right there.

This game is easily the best game of 2016. It is a great ending to the souls series. Dark Souls 3 is my first souls game. From what I've heard it is the hardest. After 4 playthroughs, I think I have played enough of the game to give a good review. ( I have not yet played any of the DLC). I am going to be revealing minor spoilers so be wary. Lets start with a list of the features I liked and disliked.
+Difficulty Level
This is the first game that I have ever played that really challenged me. My first playthrough was basically an abusive relationship. The game would hit me, I would cry about it and quit, but eventually came back to it after an hour. The first few areas had me thinking, "This isn't so bad". Then came the Abyss Watchers my favorite boss in the game. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥that was a hard fight for me. And that is my favorite thing about this game. The fact that is excrutiatingly difficult.
+Music
I am a sucker for instrumental music, and this game extremly delivered. Walking into my first Gundyr fight, when the music kicked in, it was a moment that I would remember for a long time. When I was fighting the Abyss Watchers, and they combined together to put up one last fight, the violin solo made me feel pity for the curse of the Watchers. The music is really amazing in this game.
+/- Level Design
The level design for this game is really unique, and it really does not hold your hand. It is highly possible for you to miss entire areas of the game, and exploration is key. I do not know how I feel about this. I like the style the game is going for, but it sometimes is annoying to miss an item. The side quest are somewhat hidden, and it is best to double back on an area to make sure you did not miss something. On my first playthrough of the game, I missed a lot of the items, and ended up looking up some of the locations. Having to do that took some fun out of the game, and it was annoying. The world it self is highly detailed and looks amazing. The locations do make the game world seem a little small though.
+/- Story
It is possible to play through this game and not know anything about the story, other than you have to keep a fire from going out. It is sad that the game does not tell you more, because the story for the game is really intresting. Most of the story is hidden in item descriptions, and vague npc dialouge. I would suggest looking up a video explaining the lore for the game if you plan on playing it, though be wary of spoilers.
+/- Enemies and Bosses
The games Enemies and Bosses are pretty unique. Each area has a specific set of enemies that the player has to learn to defeat. They are designed well. The Bosses are really awesome. In the begining cutscence, the Lord of Cinder are displayed as these unique and badass super people who you have to kill. Almost all of their fights are challenging (ahem Yhorm) and are entertaining. I wish there was a feature that allowed you to fight the bosses again individually, but the closest thing we get is a new game plus system. I played a playthrough of new game plus on my strength build, and it was a joke. Having end game gear against enemies who are slightly buffed makes the game downright easy. It may just be easier with a strength build, but I would stay away from it.
+/- Weapon and Estus System
The game changed the system which Estus flask and weapon upgrading works. For Estus, you find shards which can grant you additional flask, and undead bone shards, which make your Estus heal more health. I really like this system. Your Estus flask sort of "level" with you. I like the weapon upgrading system. I like how there is different types of titanite for boos weapons and normal weapons, and also how you have to devote a titanite slab to get a weapon to +10, which there are only 8 of in the game.  My only gripe with the weapons are the weapon arts. I think they are a cool way to make every weapon feel unique, but some weapons have seriously underpowered weapon arts.
Meh -The Invasion system
The pvp in this game is okay. I personally found that it was an annoyance to be invaded while clearing areas that are hard enough without another player making things more difficult. Though it was really entertaining to be right at the bonfire and then a deadly duo including Aberdolf Lincler ruins your day. I do like the summon system. I used it to help other players defeat bosses that I really liked to play against and that they might be having a hard time with.
I have really enjoyed this game, and I feel that it has ended the series in the best way it could. It gave intresting enemies and bosses, beautiful levels, an intriguing but somewhat hidden story, and a good weapon and estus sytstem. I would highly reccommend getting this game, as it will be well worth your $60.

Be sure to have at least played or witnessed I and II for the most fluid ecperience in III; However, one can also play the game backwards to have a retroactive/archeological experience by starting with III. That is because there are hidden narratives for the player to unveil if they are willing to take the time to read various descriptions of the world, dialogue, and items.
Narrative: Robust and intermingled throughout the series, therefore one must slow down and read in order to decipher and understand.
Environment: Phenomenal level design that consists of various locales and seamlessly leads the player and rewards thorough exploration.
Combat: Initially seem rudimentary at first with simple movesets and attack types, but has advanced set of techniques and timing that follow as more weapons and spells are discovered.
Role-Play: the game's stats are not as heavily emphasized in number crunch due to diminishing returns and finite item selections, but there are basically 3 types of play styles depending on the level bracket a players' characers decide to stay on: Physical, Magical, or Hybrid (higher lvl req).
Multiplayer: Dedicated servers and allows cross region play, while matchmaking allows a level range/bracket based on the players' choosing. A lot of arguments were made about 120 being the meta level bur it is ultimately up to the player to decide what kind of role and experience they want.
One greatest weakness is the replayability of this game, usually after about 100th hour. Most players would be exhausted by the time they've cleared the first play-through and sadly this game does not alter enemy placement and variants as much as its predecessors (I and II). The only late game reason to come back, would either be joining/invading to help or hinder the journey of newcomers. DLC will add about 15 hours ea depending on how much you want to digest.

Tl;Dr: It's an excellent game but is dumbed down in comparison to both DS1 and DS2. Is the most linear in terms of exploration and simple in terms of combat. Loved it but made me want more.
So for the record, on PS3 I played Dark Souls 1 for roughly 250 hours, it's a close game to my heart since it helped me deal with a lot of personal issues and taught me how to look at things differently. And I have 290 hours in DS2 which I think is the most fun of all three in the series and took risks that I respect. That being said, over the years I have become a lot more critical of the series, not because of some kind of growing cynicism of sequels, but because of how much I loved the series. So everything I'm saying may sound negative, but I do
this game, I say this because I know a lot of people will disagre with what I'm about to say:
Maps and where to go:
Dark souls 3 is the most linear of the 3, you literally only have one way to go, area to area, there may be verticality within those areas, but the overall exploration of the world as a whole is linear. It's no suprise that the most layerd and intricate levels were my favorite like the Cathedral of the Deep, and the Ashes dlc gave me the closest experience to DS1's explorative design. I know people criticised DS2 for it's world being too easy to explore and linear, and it was in comparison to DS1, but DS3 is a literal walk down the path, since there's 4 branch points and all those branches are dead ends. The complaints DS2 recieved for having too many bonfires gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on in comparison to the amount of bonfires DS3 has, it feels like areas were designed individually then stitched together, leading to you getting a bonfire at the end of one area then to walk 10m only to get another one for a new area, the best example I can think of is the Grand Archives bonfire where you can LITERALLY SEE the previous bonfire behind you. This doesn't ruin gameplay, but if the bonfire consistency was a factor to how easy the game is (which it isn't) then DS3 would be the easiest of the series.
This linearity isn't me calling the game bad though, since it does make the game "better" in the sense of a "game", by having clear sections it allows for better pacing and a more active feeling of progression.
Mechanics and the cogs that grind:
I love the weapon arts system, I love the faster paced combat and I love the way enemies fight now as well in tandem with the changes. But it's a dumbed down system, DS1 had buggy as heck combat when compared to DS3, but there was a lot of depth in the systems it placed with stamina management and such. DS2 built off this, it added agility and other things such as power stancing and more equip load brackets. DS3 got rid of stamina's many restrictions, there is now only
for equip loads, while DS2 had 7 and DS1 had 5 (according to fextralife it may have more). Also REGARDLESS of your equip load and amount of stamina, YOU WILL ALWAYS HAVE 6 ROLLS. On top of that, some daggers and light weapons take the same amount or more stamina to swing as ultra great swords, what seems to be the case is there's a greater emphasis on stamina recovery but they seem to have stripped away A LOT of the depth and complexity DS2 introduced, my best example is dual wielding; dual wield weapons now count as a single weapon, so rather than DS2's mix and match make your own styled system, they removed the thought of using two weapons completely and have done it for you, you can still use whatever combo you want, but if you ever want to swing them both at the same time then too bad. This simplification of systems does mean everything is faster paced, there's no more waffle, it's get in the get out, it's just a shame, I really liked Power Stancing and the complexity of the stamina system.
Story and the end of an age (I'll try not to spoil):
The story comes to an end with a multitude of endings and even a hidden one (oh how exciting), and the ingrained story telling of all the souls games is there, the environmental story telling, the descriptions, the very designs of the enemies, just like the other two souls games. This is the aspect of the game that I fell in love with, I would stand in front of enemies and let them kill me just to get a better view of them and I was so happy that DS3 has crammed so much detail in, like I could see the engravings and trimmings in the armour of all the knights. It wraps up the game and with the DLC it's nice to see how things are being given much more depth, with aspects of both previous games being brought back to help tie up the end of the souls series. I originally thought DS3 would be far more spoon feedish in the way it tell its story but this was't the case, upon taking a step back and reflecting on the way everything told the story in DS3 I can safely say I found myself engrossed with the way everything contributed to the experience and world.
DS3 IS A GOOD GAME and as the end of the series it works, it may be simplified and linear but as a game it's well optimised and thoroughly designed. There's only so much you can do with a single IP, I'm excited to see where Fromsoft goes with the end of souls.

I don't think that Trove is a good game. In my opinion, Trove is too focused on grindig, and it's not even fun to do so in Trove. There aren't many classes in this game, and each of them only got 4 skills- and it gets quite boring after a short while. While grinding, there are no quests and there is no story (which is something I do like about MMO RPGs)- you just pointlessly waste your time grinding. In addition, this game has micro-transactions that affect the gameplay, which is something I dislike, that sadly many free to play video games (except Valve's ones, which have a really good cosmetic items' system that probably earns them more money than Trove's system does while not making the game pay to win) usually do in their games. Trove's servers are bloody awful- sometimes it takes even more than 30 minutes in order to log into the game, which is ridiculous. In my opinion, all the different places look pretty much the same but with different colors, unlike in games like MapleStory 2 (a very simillar and free to play game that I believed inspired the development of Trove) where, in my opinion, there's a huge difference between the look and feel of the different places. I find the dungeons quite boring and repetitive, with no story, NPCs, quests or anything else to keep exploring the dungeons interesting for players. The combat in this game isn't really fun either- you just spam the mouse keys. I also find this game quite too easy- I think that leveling is way too easy than it should be and that there are no fun ways to level up since there is no story, there are no quests and there are no NPCs. The lack of NPCs makes Trove's world feel very empty and boring to explore. In my opinion, the game is way too crafting's based, and crafting isn't my cup of tea- I like games where there is plot, where I have quests to do from different NPCs with different personalities and stories, where I feel like there's a challange, where there are many other things to do except from grinding (and not just crafting, which in Trove crafting is usually just reading information in Trove's wiki, grinding or searching to get stuff and then crafting), where the combat system feels fun and challnging, where each job feels unique and fun to play with- and Trove just isn't it. In my opinion, Trove is like an MMO RPG version of Minecraft (for 3 year olds, as it seems from the level of challange). If that's what you're into, feel free to give this a chance, but that's not what I'm into.

A fun little Free to Play game.
The game places you into a variety of maps as a survivor of the zombie apocalypse.  You gather clothing, supplies, weapons, ammunition, food, medicine.  You seek shelter and eventually build it yourself.  You can ultimately take control of your world and reasert yourself as the dominant species.
The game is in pixalated graphics, like Minecraft, but with rounded edges.  Weapons are common, but ammunition is not as common, so unlike many zombie survival games, you have to ration and choose melee or avoidance often enough.  Fuel is also very scarce, so motorized transportation is rare.  Basica shelter can be fairly easy to make, but advanced bases can take quite some time.  The perk system is fair and well balanced.  It can be played with friends.
Unturned is very fun and I would recommend it, especially if you're open to the idea of Minecraft with guns or a lightcore zombie survival game.

I have played and enjoyed all of the soulsborne games (yes, I even enjoyed DS2) and this is a great send-off.  It has its problems, sure...(PVP is not as fun as it used to be) but the game is great.  The tanky style movement from DS2 is gone, and in fact rolling in this game is probably a little too powerful.  The stamina costs on rolls is simply just too low, and the medium roll at 70% is too good.  Think about it, if the most you could carry while walking was 100 pounds, how agile would you be if you were carrying 70?  The encumbrance level for that style of roll should be something like 40 or 50.  And yes, I'm aware there's a better roll than 70% (you get more roll distance) but I still maintain the 70% roll is to good.
Magic builds are not really that great, there's really only one or two weapons that are worth using for magic users.  Most people will be using quality (dex+str) because that is by the far the best bang for your buck, especially if you like being able to use a wide variety of weapons.
Just like all other Souls games, the patches can really make or break your character.  A few times now they have patched things, but even their patch notes were wrong.  Infusions that were supposedly given a buff, were actually nerfed!
Parries are a little too easy to perform in PVP, but the number of weapons that CANNOT be parried is also too high.  Due to this, you'll see very few people using easily parriable weapons at the serious pvp levels.  This turns pvp mostly into a ranging game, where you try to bait your opponent into thinking you are in range of his weapon, but you move out of range so you can counter attack.  It's just not as fun.
If you want to invade people, one of two things usually happen:
You find yourself into a gank squad, with 3 people twinked out waiting to smash your face.
You realize you're invading someone who is so afraid of dying they will just hide and hope you can't find them, or they will disconnect
Honestly the only times I've thoroughly enjoyed PVP were when I was summoned as a blue sentinel or darkmoon blade.  However, this is only true if I was summoned by a sole player...lots of times I would be summoned into someone's world and that person also had 1 or 2 other phantoms.  So it would be 3 or 4v1.  I'm sorry, but that is NOT fun.  However, the times when I was summoned into someone's world who had no phantoms, and you could tell they were the scaredy-cat kind of player, and the red phantom summoned was a good pvper, it was great!  It's funny though, that when the game first launched, blue summons almost never worked.  I would really have enjoyed that more, if it was able to be done when the game was new, and the player base was larger.
Another problem with the game is how easy it is to be twinked.  Sure, you can't give out titanite, or upgraded weapons to someone who didn't have that rank of weapon yet, but since items can be dropped and the person who dropped them can just reload their save, there's a lot of people using equipment they CLEARLY have not even seen yet.  I readily admit that after I've beaten the game a couple of times I have abused this, but it is just so rampant across players that clearly have not that it is a little off-putting.
This may be a pro, or a con, but there are a lot of NPC interactions that you can miss, or mess up entirely.  If you start off a character type and want to make a fundamental change to your stats, the problem is you might find that you literally cannot get certain spells or equipment in that play through because you didn't follow the questlines appropriately.  It can be almost impossible to set yourself up for maximum versatility in NG or even NG+ without following guides.  I personally think this is a double edged sword.  I am not sure if I like that aspect of it.
The NG+ cycle is not as hard as I remember.  NG+ used to be a lot harder than NG, that's not really the case here.
I've not completed a Soul level 1 run, but for me it seems like the only way I'd really enjoy continuing to play the game once I've seen and done everything.

I love this game. A lot of the percieved difficulty I see others describe seems to be a combination of not understanding the game (or taking the time to learn it) and not being willing to use a variety of strategies and approaches.
The art is great. The characters are fun and interesting.
But its the tactical depth that really gives the game super high ratings from me. Yes its hard and sometimes the RNG will seem unfair (the nature of RNG). But thats a whole intentional element of the strategic depth of the game. The disclaimer at the start of the games tells you that DD is about making the best of a bad situation.
You will be on dungeon runs that are going great and quickly start going horribly wrong. You are forced on the fly to make strategic adaptations to survive and continue or risk/reward analysis about fleeing the combat or abandoning the dungeon run entirely. I love that. I want to be challenged. I want to sometimes be put it what some describe as "unfair situations" despite my best planning and preparation. Thats an opportunity strategically delicious decision making. Few games do this.
If you are into X-Com played on Ironman mode you will probably like this game as there is no save scumming allowed. X-com is by for the game whose RNG and its effect on your tactical decision making most closely mirrors DD of games I have played. I am like 80 hours or so in and am still learning different ways to combo the heros, their abilities, and the lineup.
For the first 20 hours or so I didnt even realize this game was in beta. Sure I have run into at least one odd bug but its remarkably polished for a beta, I am excited to see Redhooks take on endgame content once they release that with the actual release of the game.
Honestly while the game is on the challenging side, its not nearly as hard as some reviewers make it out to be. If you are willing to change/evaluate your tactics, run from fights/abandon quests when things go terribly RNG wrong, and use the info on forums and the wiki to make better tactical decisions in group composition for the dungeon you are tackling and curios you activate you are probably the type of gamer who will really enjoy this game.
Also, it captures the Call of Cthulhu feel very well, especially with all the insanity stuff and real risk of death of your heros.

This led to me trying to pick enemies off one shot at a time, hiding until they gave up looking between each shot which after 20 hours in is making combat feel tedious. Whenever I decide to tackle enemies at a closer range it's either a complete walkover or I get pummeled by enemies that are far too powerful for my meagre level and I can't tell which it's gonna be until I'm committed.
The settlement system is promising, I've had some fun playing around with it. The radio stations are fantastic, especially Diamond City Radio with its nervous wreck of a DJ. The stealth system is quite fun and quite intuitive.
I would have been perfectly willing to recommend the game even with the issues I mentioned above...until the Fire Support quest bugged out on me. After completing the combat scenario, the quest NPC was stuck in a loop and the quest refused to proceed. This had the effect of locking me out of the entire Brotherhood of Steel storyline. After searching for it, I found posts on the Bethesda community forums about the same bug from last year. I simply cannot recommend an RPG that can lock you out of an entire significant storyline with a relatively common bug that has gone unfixed for over a year.

This game is the fruit of snob, elitist, crude "there are not enough hard games out there" design philosophy. This game is not a challenge, it's skewed by design to make you fail all the time. The difficulty is insane simply because all the chances are stacked against you and all RNG is tilted to make sure you are _ALWAYS_ on the losing end.
The self-admitted intention from the designers is that you need to not care about your specific characters, you just need to send waves after waves of goons to try to defeat the (artificially) insanely difficult quests. Well, guess what, if that's the way the game is supposed to be played, it actually completely defeats its own purpose. What's the point of making something so incredibly difficult when overcoming the difficulty is actually completely unmeaningful? I can just hire four new random guys from the stagecoach and send them to a dungeon.
The graphical style is charming and excellent, the sound is great, I personally liked the voice over too. The atmosphere is great, it could be a great game.
Simply, it's a plain not fun experience because everything that you do as a player has no meaningful impact on what happens in the game.
...Thinking about it, that makes Darkest Dungeon probably not eligible for the definition of "being a game".
I know the developers have their adamant, obstinate, stubborn vision of how they want the game to play out, but when your difficult but playable and enjoyable game (one year ago, give or take a few months) starts raking in more than 1000 negative reviews because of how unplayable and unfun you have turned the game into, shouldn't you start asking yourselves if your vision is just plain WRONG?
If I could, I'd refund this. Strongly NOT recommended to anyone.

I got this game based on a Let's Play on Youtube. It's also my first contact with the series. Overall it's great. For me it's mostly about the mechanics, which are quite deep. Easy to begin, you learn to click left mouse button and roll with space. But if you want to learn all the mechanics, it takes a lot of practice. The game itself is an incredible exercise in patience, and also analysis, strategy, and timing. There are some areas that could be improved, but the overall product is already great. The world is interesting, but the lore delivery is maybe too cryptic, I think this is something that could be improved. Gameplay-wise the world offers plenty of rewarding exploration, even though I wouldn't call this an open-world game. Foreword: This review actually hurts me to write, because I truly believe this game has insane potential, it just needs some tweaking to be something damn near a masterpiece, and since its still early access, its likely we could see those tweaks in the near future, so keep that in mind
When most people think of Darkest Dungeon, certain words may spring to mind: Difficulty, Frustration, Stress. But if I had to sum up this game in just one word, that word would be "Stagnation." I had been following this game rather closely for some time and loved everything I saw, the game seemed PERFECT in my eyes, at least until recent updates to the game brought some "rebalancing." The latest updates saw rather drastic increases in the cost of... well... pretty much everything, heros cost more to train, town upgrades require more resources, and stress healing will bleed you dry. This, on its own, wouldnt have been too bad, had they not also considerably decreased the gold you'll get for going on expeditions. Many times ive completed a quest, only to spend most the gold i just recieved to lower my troop's stress levels from said quest, before saving what precious little is left to fund the next mission. Repeat this proccess about 5-6 times and congratulations, you now have enough to upgrade one of your heros' equipment or skills, and maybe a town building or two..... once. But if you're dedicated enough you can do this for long enough to have a fully equipped level 2 team, now you're ready to progress!
Oh, you got surprised by a horde of spiders who shuffled the order of your party and killed your healer and highwayman before you could do anything about it? Well, have fun starting over, see you in another 35 missions and we'll do this again.
So the point is this: Players who came into this new update with their towns half finished and their parties mostly set up will be fine, but if you're just starting out, the unforgiving gold deficit will keep you in crippling poverty and grind progress to such a slow and repetitive crawl that you'll actually forget why you're even playing, if you're unsure on whether to pick this one up, I'd hold off for now, wait for a few more updates and then check again.

Bugs, Bugs, Bugs (and I'm not talking about Radroaches)
Before I get to the main issue with the game (you can probably already guess from /\) I want to give my overall impression of the latest Fallout game. This game is definitly making it clear which direction Bethesda plans on taking the Fallout series and so far it appears as though the influence of the minecraft survival genre (not to mention it's fanbase) has not yet been satiated. Of course, this new survival aspect (in a game already focusing on openworld resource managment and general not dying..) has come in the form of 'base building' or as Fallout would call it: Settlement Building.
Naturally, I wouldn't complain about the idea of trying to create a thriving community once I've become established, a final goal in the game. BUT the game introduced me settlement building within the first hour or so of gameplay. Which means that intead of spending the first 10 hours or so scavenging for caps anywhere I could get them, I have an unlimited supply of Purified Water to sell and I'm forced to pick up every stray can so I can continue building even more water purifiers.
Even if the settlement building was implemented properly, it's honestly a complete mess. Building is a pain because half the pieces won't fit together, and if they do they more often than not will not go where you want them to. On top of that managing settlers (equipting them + assigning them roles) is mind numbing. There should have been an update long ago making it easier to accept (and hopefully enjoy) a key aspect of Fallout 4.
Now the game has become something far different from the classic kill what you must and scavenge what you can, into more of a building management sim. Now, this wouldn't be suck a bad thing if this wasn't ♥♥♥♥ing Fallout. It makes no sense, now maybe to keep the players from gaining unlimited wealth there would be an economy so that Purified Water ceases to become a good sell item but there isn't. There is nothing to keep the settlement building from clashing with what the game is supposed to be: Skyrim with guns. I mean.... a post-apocalyptic FPS with RPG elements.
The other major flaw was the story + choice aspect of the game. It seemed to turn it's back on the praise New Vegas received in favor of the more bland Fallout 3. Once again this wouldn't be a problem if the game even tried to keep me interested. Why is my character sexting up singers in Good Neighbor when my ♥♥♥♥ing son is missing? It's almost impossible to even try and role play in this game.
Now my biggest issue... the bugs. I'm the type of person who prefers the vanilla game to modding so I figure I should never have any serious issues with the game. I was so wrong... it felt like every 30 minutes or so I would have some game breaking bug that would cause me to have to reset my computer multiple times to get the game to play (not to mention how the game is tied to refresh rate so I had to manually limit my fps to 60 to prevent screwy audio).
Okay... on to why I'm still giving this a thumbs up. I think that the dev team responsible for Fallout 4 may have overreached themselves a bit but I think it's not a bad thing to experiment while trying to add as much as you can. And I think that (should they listen to the responses) this can be an amazing platform in which to build Fallout 5 off of.
In summary: Take feedback from the community, spend less time on gimmicks and more time on story/world, use a more modern engine, and please don't forget that this is a Fallout franchise, and it doesn't need to incorporate what every other game is already doing to be a good Fallout game.
Final Verdict: 6/10

This is something of a sad thing to say, but I can't really recommend this game at it's current Price, or it's DLCs, not unless they're less than $30 at least.
I'll try to describe in Detail why this game isn't very good, from both a PvP and a PvE aspect as best I can, so let's start with PvE.
In Dark Souls 3 PvE, the game at first, doesn't seem too different from many other games of an RPG Genre, very basic enemies staggered by your weapon, they don't have very powerful weapons or tools to defeat you with but you have to play careful or be overwhelmed, very fair and basic stuff, so it's not very much so worth getting into, what's really worth getting into is later-game, wherein enemies actually deal fair damage to you. In mid-game  enemies still try to overwhelm you, though now they move much faster and their weapon strikes are almost always faster than yours, this can lead to unfair fights wherein if you begin to get over-tasked, you may not be able to get away before getting killed in combat because you simply can't move or the enemies lash out at you far too quickly for you to heal, this can be frustrating to deal with at first if you're going through the game alone, however this problem can be solved if you simply bait them out one at a time. In late-game, though there is a mix of a few newer enemies, for some reason they simply re-use the exact same enemies you fought earlier, only harder hitting and maybe a new technique or 2, but otherwise pretty well the same, any tactic you used on the enemies at the beginning of the game, which makes it ridiculously easy to simply walk up to them and smash your Light-attack button because your swings will almost always knock them out of any of their attacks, the only reason you'd have to stop is to regain Stamina so you can repeatedly swing your weapon again. This truly baffles me, as in previous games, from the Souls Series, I have never seen re-use of enemies on this scale, and likely for good reason, so as to make you learn new tactics for each area and make them more memorable. It is also very apparent that the tactic you use to beat Beginning level enemies can also be used to beat almost every enemy up until Mid-Game where they begin to get faster than you.
TL/DR: Enemies are somewhat poorly made
The very coveted Dark Souls Bosses. The bosses for Dark Souls 3 are mostly well made, save for some exceptions, which can be quite the annoyance or completely disappointing. This shor bit is going to list off some poorly made Bosses, so skip reading this if you don't want to be spoiled, but know that it's roughly 45/55 on how I personally feel about Bosses.
This is just something of a detailed list of bosses that were poorly done but were mandatory, if they weren't mandatory they wouldn't be worth mentioning in my opinion.
TL/DR: 1/4 of bosses are bad

Discussing the bosses also makes it apparent there are less bosses than the previous two Souls series games, With Dark Souls 2 having a bare minimum of 20-16 bosses if you use Shortcuts and skips and Dark souls 1 having 14 bosses if you use every shortcut and skip device available to you. This is another point Dark Souls 3 has against it, considering 4 of it's 13 are unimpressionable bosses, which isn't neccesarily something I can say about about the others in the previous games. This can also considerably reduce the time to beat the game.
TL/DR: Less Bosses than previous games, thus making game quicker to beat
Another thing worth mentioning is that many weapons in PvE are unviable, the only things you'll usually every need are a Dark Sword or an Ultra-Great weapon, using anything else is usually more of a challenge, and you'll often see this is usually what people are using when playing Co-Operativley or during Invasions. This removes a lot of personality from characters, because not many people will sacrifice personal taste for damage, though every weapon should be reasonably good.
TL/DR: No good reason for PvE weapon variety
Lastly, Co-Operative play and Host Bonus's in Dark Souls 3 makes it ridiculously easy. In regards to summoning: Now, don't get me wrong, this is true in every Souls-Game, however in this one, every enemy except for some bosses can be VERY easily staggered, meaning that if you bring 2 or 3 extra players into your game, you can usually just carelessly swing your weapon with abandon, as any enemy that comes into contact with a hit will be unable to move until they recieve a second hit, letting your and your friends keep whacking it in an infinite cycle. If you haven't somehow managed to kill it and your summons haven't taken the aggresion from the enemy, you have a large plethora of Estus and lots of Rolls to be able to survive almost anything, along with a 25% health increase to help you survive more lethal attacks. This in totallity means you can simply mow down enemies with your pals and never think about attacking Human-Sized foes and makes you sloppy at fighting bosses because all you've likely had to do is spam light-attack and you'll likely beat most bosses by summoning too.
TL/DR: Summoning+Being a Host makes game no challenge at all

Dark Souls 3 Re-uses a LOT of Assets from previous games.
For some reason a some magics were added from previous games and others were not at all.
In Dark Souls, there is a mechanic unique to it that you likely won't find in many other games, the ability to invade and combat people during their PvE experience. This being said, Dark Souls 3 has pretty well ruined this mechanic, with the previously mentioned Host Benefits and Co-Operative play and the ability to also stagger Invading players like regular enemies, this allows the Host and his phantoms to have an overwhelming advantage against invaders unless an invader uses only combat builds designed to kill other players in a single hit (Also known as Glass Cannons). Also in Dark Souls 3 was the inclusion of moving while using the healing item Estus, making it nearly impossible to punish another player who has run away and is currently healing because they can just walk out of punishments. With all this, there is no good reason to Invade in Dark Souls 3, it's literally been ruined to an almost unrecognizable degree, especially if you've played the previous Dark Souls games.
TL/DR: They've Soiled It

Now, I know there are some people who might be wondering what some above average things are about this game, so let me give you a brief summary of those:
By Jove, the Soundtrack is amazing, even for some of the lesser Bosses, it really gives you a feel for what you're fighting and puts you in the moment.
This one is a bit generalized, but I mean things like the armors, the Backgrounds and some areas, which clearly have a goodly bit of detail put into them, some of these clearly have had a lot of work put into them.

I'd love to go into more detail about some of these things but reviews can only be so long, so I'll just tell you my final score for Dark Souls 3 is a 5/10 and with it's DLC it's a 6/10. Again, I recommend buying it when it's cheap on price, or if you just wanna say you beat Dark Souls
