I would also like to insert my 50 coins in this discussion. And regardless all the negative I would like to intercede for the game. I think that all the negative comments about the game being too hard or unfair are there simply because people didn't understand the whole point of the game.
I agree with all players that corpses were a
bad idea. I understand what developers wanted to achieve with it but it was just stupid in terms of realism. Imagine a dark epic battle for The Middle-Earth for example where armies are fighting with corpses instead of themselves. It IS really stupid. But the devs listened and made this option switchable off. Congrats.
The heart attacks. Well, honestly the idea is not so bad. It is very realistic when people go mad and completely insane because of the horrors the faced. But the problem here that stress from 100 to 200 develops significantly faster then from 0 to 100. So if one of your party gets afflicted the whole party soon will be. And then you know what's gonna happen. Maybe after 100 the stress points should be halfed of increase the threshold to 300. I don't know, but again it also can be switched off.
And in general, the game is not too hard. It is challenging. You have to take into account almost everything. The party setup, skills setup, location, predictable monsters, equipment and so on.
I disagree that heroes are just cannon fodder that you every time send to death. No, you have to focus on you characters, try to stay them alive, upgrade their equipment and skills. And i mean all skills! There are no useless ones exept for the corpses if you switch them off (and you should really do). Upgrade all skills, not just the starting ones and choose wisely from them when building a party. Same hero with different skills and other party members can play defferent roles. It is very important in the game. So when you are about to loose a lvl5 hero with upgraded skills and equipment you begin to think how to save him, maybe abandon quest  or sacrifice another hero. Think about it.
In conclusion I want to say that it is a
great game. I like strategic games with character placement mechanics since good old Disciples 2. And this game brings this genre to whole new level. I definitly recommend this game. Just try it and make your own conclusion. And waiting for the 5-th location Darkest Dungeon and the release of the game.

Most of the way this huge roleplaying-shooter game works is carried over from its excellent predecessors, Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas. It is the Skyrim to Fallout 3’s Oblivion, if you will – it iterates on the previous game’s already amazing systems, and it’s similarly dense with locations to explore, genuinely creepy monsters to fight, and superbly engrossing post-nuclear atmosphere that blends unsettling gore and death with dark comedy.
A story that begins as a basic search for your lost family evolves into something much more complex and morally nuanced. Like in Fallout: New Vegas, we’re drawn into a struggle between several groups competing for control of the region, and deciding which of their imperfect post-apocalyptic philosophies to align with made me pause to consider how I wanted events to play out. Even the highly questionable Institute has a tempting reason to side with them, and turning away from them in my playthrough wasn’t as clear-cut a choice as I’d expected. I was impressed by the sympathy shown toward the villains, too - even the most irredeemable murderer is explored and given a trace of humanity.
Of course, as is the tradition with developer Bethesda Game Studios’ open-world RPGs, the main story isn’t nearly as gripping an attraction as the huge number of well-written side quests you’ll come across just by wandering through the ruins of the Boston area, now known as The Commonwealth. I found it difficult to complete even the most basic point-A-to-point-B task without being sidetracked at least twice by enticing detours. An abandoned comic book publisher office? How can I not explore it? Boston’s famous Fenway Park? Gotta see what’s become of that. A crumbling high school with heads on pikes outside? I bet there’s great loot in there! Practically tripping over new discoveries like this, I feel like a kid on Easter whose parents are bad at hiding the candy.
Perhaps because this adventure is such a long haul, Fallout 4 is  a bit overeager to hook us in the beginning. After a brief glimpse of pre-war life in Fallout’s familiar-but-strange near-future and a retelling of the events on the day the bombs fell in 2077, we barely have time to get our hands dirty in the post-apocalyptic era before Fallout 4 throws us into a big action moment: You’re given a suit of the big, stompy power armor and a heavy weapon, and put into an intense brawl against the series’ most iconic monster.
It’s certainly not an unconventional idea for a game with a long progression arc to give us an early taste of the powerful toys we’ll gain access to later in order to motivate us to work for them, but with Fallout it’s a misstep that trods on the series’ beloved feeling of working our way up from almost nothing to become the dominant force in the wasteland. This bothered me less and less as I began to explore, but knowing that armor was available when I wanted it made me a little cockier than I wanted to be when setting out into a hostile, unforgiving world.
One of the first things a returning Fallout player will notice after creating a character with the intuitive push-and-pull face-sculpting tool is that the entire concepts of skill points and traits have been consumed by the perks system, unifying all character progression under one big, elaborately animated Vault Boy chart with so many unlockable options you have to scroll through them to see them all. While this streamlining does mean giving up a lot of minute control over where your character improves with each level, it also means the decision of what to do with the single point you get each level has a significant impact, and therefore those decisions represent a commitment and are tough to make: do you want to spend it on a new low-level perk, increase the level of an existing one, or pump it into a SPECIAL attribute like Luck to boost certain stats and also open up a new, more powerful perk, like the Mysterious Stranger, that you’ll be able to unlock with your next level?
As if I didn’t already have enough of a hoarding problem, Fallout 4’s crafting system gives even more motivation to compulsively collect everything that isn’t nailed down. It’s so easy, too - grabbing things out of containers happens quickly in window that pops up when you look over it. Every item in the world is made up of material components, most of which you can intuitively guess: bottles are needed for glass, a desk fan will provide you with steel and gears, and a roll of duct tape is worth its weight in gold. I once went on a desperate search for pencils so that I could extract the lead they contained to use for radiation shielding. (Apparently Fallout's alternate universe never switched to graphite.) Nothing is worthless junk, which means that managing the weight of your inventory is a constant series of agonizing decisions of what to take with you and what to leave behind.
The value of those materials comes from their use in the fantastic equipment upgrades, which give most guns you pick up extraordinary potential for flexibility and longevity. Stopping at a crafting bench with the right components in hand can turn a pistol into a short-range, pray-and-spray automatic or a scoped sniper with a long barrel for accuracy and a big stock to reduce recoil. A few tweaks to a standard-issue laser rifle can add burning damage over time, or split the beam into a shotgun-like spread. The best part is that those changes aren’t just tweaked numbers in the stats; nearly every modification you make is reflected in the look of your gun as well, creating an extremely varied selection of weapons both for you and for enemies.
Likewise, the new armor system lets you piece together six chunks of gear - helmet, chest plate, and each individual arm and leg - on top of your clothes to form cobbled-together, asymmetrical outfits that feel like exactly what someone who assembled their wardrobe by scavenging the wasteland should wear. The suit my character wears now has at least one piece from each major faction, reflecting both his allegiances and his victories over foes. And of course, armor can be upgraded using collected materials as well, though it sadly doesn’t have as dramatic a cosmetic effect as with weapons.
The armor system suffers from some inconsistency: several times I was a little bit heartbroken to find a new outfit like a tuxedo or a Halloween costume, but couldn’t use them as the foundation of a new custom-built look. Only certain jumpsuits can have pauldrons and shin guards strapped onto them, it seems, and no distinction is made in the item description. Another major change to personal protection is that Fallout’s distinctive power armor behaves almost like a walking tank that you climb into and out of (with a great Iron Man-style animation as it closes around you) instead of wearing like clothes, and its fuel is a limited resource you have to find in the world. It’s a bold design move that makes these hulks’ appearance on the battlefield feel like a big event. However, since it’s always just a fast-travel away, in practice, having to run and grab it when the going got tough became more of an inconvenience than anything - two loading screens between you and resuming the fight. It also forces you to use fast-travel to conserve fuel, which would mess with a no-fast-travel play style. But I do love how every piece of the armor can be individually damaged, repaired, upgraded, customized, or even swapped out for other models.
Even small changes to gun stats are important, because Fallout 4’s gunplay feels more like a typical good-quality first-person shooter than the series ever has before, so skilled aim is important to the point where you could comfortably avoid the pause-and-plan Vault-Tec-Assisted Targeting System (VATS) button if you wanted to.

Spiral Knights is a MMO that plays like Diablo on fast forward. But this hack-and-slash RPG action is tempered by a spiteful pricing system that seems determined to stop you playing just as you’re starting to have fun.
The story of this game is that members of the Spiral Knights stranded on an alien planet, it’s our mission to hunt for the materials needed to get the Order’s spacecraft up and running so we can return home. That means fighting through The Clockworks: a series of layered dungeons leading to the core of the planet.
The Clockworks are vast, and full of monsters that vary according to the theme of each level. Forest areas contain wolvers and other wild creatures, while electric zones will have more robotic foes. Of course levels can have combined family mosters and statuses. Each level is full of spike traps, turrets and "danger rooms"
Each Knight can carry two weapons at a time (you can buy extra weapon slots at the NPC market in exchange for energy), melee or ranged, and switch between them at will. Controlling your knight couldn’t be easier. A quick click will swipe or fire your weapon, you can hold down the button for a charged attack or press X to trow up a shield who will protect you for any damage on any side, but the shield can break and it has to recharge and you have to wait some time. From the safe city of Haven, you can form a party of up to four knights, dive into a clockworks and immediately start your hunt for items. Every reward feeds back into the complex levelling system.
Progression in Spiral Knights is all about crafting. The level of your armour determines the depth you are allowed to reach. Higher tier weapons can be bought at massive prices, but it’s much more sensible to make them. If you don't have the materials you need you have to go the to NPC who trades tokens for materials.
In the past In Spiral Knights, everyday actions such as pressing a button on an elevator, crafting new items and reviving your knight all cost you energy but this has changed and now every player doesn't need to wait 24 hours for energy to regenerate or buy more of it.
Spiral Knights is fast, accessible and fun until the spiteful pricing system pops up to punch you in the face.

Reading most reviews here, the difficulty of the game seems to be the major hinderance to most players. It is true that characters (even your godly characters) are pretty much expandable, and accidents (mostly unfortunate ones) that kill them are really frustrating and sometimes unforseen (thus unfair). Yet, with the wisdom of our great humanity, the guides about this game are very abundant online right now. I would seriouly recommand any players who dare to venture into the darkest dungeon do read about those works of other players' pain and lessons. They would make you evade a lot of traps (due to designs, I feel like some features of the game are simply DESIGNED to be that horrible to go through).
However, this is still a quite difficult and intricate games that require very meticulous planning and exceuting at every step. One misstep, especially at high levels, can mean the demise of your "powerful" characters.
The designers want this game to be dark, gloomy, and excrucitaing, and they succeed greatly, Mistakes are not tolerated, and odds are hardly in your favor. Do I recommend this game then? It is really not the question, I would still "recommend" simply because It is a greatly designed game that deserves some respect and applause. However, please think twice before deciding to launch your adventure into the darkest dungeon, it is not a game for lesiure fun. If you want to trully enjoy the experience the game offers, you need to treat this game seriously and with respect. Doing so, you will certainly be rewarded by this masterfully crafted work of art.

Apparently there was an update that significantly raised the overall difficulty of Darkest Dungeon that was released a short time before I decided to purchase this game. This means that I can only review the current state of the game and can't compare it to any earlier versions. This brings up my main problem with the game: its insane difficulty, especially during earlier stages of the game. It seemed that no matter what I did my party would always end up near death after the first encounter in many dungeons. The only instances where this didn't occur were when I had a healer non-stop compensating for the massive amounts of damage I was taking and even then they would still have about half health at the end of the encounter. This made healers absolutely necessary in many of the earlier quest and any attempt to try any unique combinations of heroes would end of getting completely destroyed by any enemies they encountered. These enemies also seemed to always occur in groups of 4, almost completely mirroring my party in damage output. The fact that some quests require you to kill every group of these enemies in a dungeon becomes completely ludicrous when your party loses so much health during every encounter. This, accompanied by the fact that there is almost no way to heal your party between encounters, makes every quest, even the shortest ones, massive risks for every one of your heroes. The game also discourages abandoning these difficult quests by raising every hero's stress level once they leave. Despite these many problems I faced, I loved the overall atmosphere and aesthetics of the game, which drew me into buying it in the first place. Unfortunately the flaws are too glaring to continue risking my characters' lives until they release a new update fixing the difficulty issues. This review is coming from someone who has put countless hours into all of the Fallout games, over many different devices.
Pros:
+Graphics (The previous games had a better atmosphere, but Fallout 4's graphics are still great)
+Gunplay (My favorite thing about Fallout 4, the gunplay feels much more natural)
+Character customization (Only the customization of the physical appeareance of the character, the rest is terrible)
+Companions (Well thought out companions, not as good as the previous games, but still good)
+Engine (The reason I have so much time on Fallout 4, the engine is much more stable, and allows for more modding)
Cons:
-Absolutely horrid Dialogue system (One of my main problems with Fallout 4)
-Voiced Protagonist (This one is more subjective, but it makes it harder for modders)
-Lack of player freedom (The player is forced into the role of either a male veteran or a female law graduate)
-Lack of player choice (The only real choice you have, is on how the game ends, the rest is almost the same)
-Perk and leveling system (The "perks" are a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of the previous games' perk system)
-World is too packed (This is a nuclear wasteland, wide open spaces help push the narrative)
-Lack of humor (Bethesda failed attempts at humor were only delivered through "press x to sarcastically say yes")
-Factions (The factions were good, but nothing when compared to the New Vegas)
-Very little replay value (There are only four endings, three of which are exactly the same)
-No karma system (Again, another more subjective one, I really like the karma system from the previous games)
-Story is lacking (The story isn't bad, it's just not very good)
Conclusion:
It is a good game, but a terrible Fallout game. It feels like a dumbed down version of Fallout 3, which is really saying something. It doesn't have a story on par with that of any of the previous games, it doesn't have the player freedom that the older games had, and most of all, It doesnt have the dark humor that is synonymous with the Fallout games.
Overall, Fallout 4 is disappointing
I would only reccomend this game if you plan to heavily mod it.

Heavily RNG based game.  It's not a roguelike and it's more frustrating than fun.  There is very little editability to heroes, you can upgrade their abilities but all this does is lower the RNG essentially--they hit more frequently and do more damage or heal more/apply an effect more often.  Because of this, there is a massive illusion of customizibility but it's guised in the idea that a level 0 hero is different than a level 1 hero.
The really not fun part about this game is that skillful play is not rewarded and the signal to the player that what they're doing is effective or not is clouded by a serious roll of the dice in every fight.  Every fight you risk 1 member in your party screwing over everyone else, in every fight if the AI all decide to screw over 1 key person they die.  All it takes is one unlucky crit roll (crits do 3x damage)--note that's unavoidable.
And that's the real problem--anytime someone dies you're punished for it.  It costs around 5-6 missions in gold rewards just to fully upgrade / unlock the key things you want a hero to have.  So 1 small error, possibly one you have absolutely no idea exists yet, is punished to the maximum.  I find this incredibly poor game design.  The game would be signfiicantly more fun if characters were injured.
Even more troubling is that killing hours of your time in a hero, how about those trinkets you equip that are vital as you move onward through the game?  Well if you get wiped or have to run from combat--you lose everything that was dropped as people die or you simply don't have inventory space to hold.
Here is the massive kicker though.  The poorest feature of this game's design is the lack of rewarding good risk taking.  Going into a harder dungeon results in you not having enough inventory space to carry back the loot or the dungeon rewarding about the same amount of loot as something that is easy.  That's a huge failing of this game--the carrot and stick of why you're even going to harder areas has no logic behind it.  And by doing so, you're typically beat over the head.  Hardcore style games like this of the past ALWAYS reward the player appropriately for taking risks and succeeding, all you end up with here is an inventory full of loot faster.
I really want to like this game, but I'm a stickler for good game design.  I am a huge fan of zangband/angband and actual roguelike titles.  It irritates me when developers slap the 'roguelike' title on firstly a game that is not actually a roguelike and then use permadeath as a means to feign difficulty when the difficulty is that all of the game's mechanics remove skill and your only real strategy is to move the goalposts of high/low RNG far enough away from people dying so you can progress--but there's always a chance of just losing everything.  It's bad design and shouldn't be given the acclaim it is getting.
I greatly enjoy massively difficult games--xcom is a difficult game (both the new and old), you can wipe and lose in a fight but there is a wide variety of what skillful play can achieve over non-skillful play and that is what Darkest Dungeon massively lacks.  Grinding back for hours to retry the dungeon boss that has a mechanic you simply must bring certain protection/strategy/units for...that's just idiotic, manufactured difficulty.
If you play this game I highly recommend save scumming--if you could restart your hour long dungeon that ends in failure, I'd take away my negative review.  I really like the idea of permadeath though, just the execution of it is flawed.

I'm writing this as part of my review, after some 100+ hours, 3 or so into release:
The game is bent on making the player uncomfortable as it says so. Do not expect the typical RPG. The design and the graphics might look cute at first, but all those guys will die and here won't be any loading.
There are times you feel everything is under control, everything is going according to plan and there are times you actually think you are good at it. You spend a lot of time to progress in the game and then you have one bad experience which is enough to ruin it for you because it tells you that all it takes is one bad decision. Contrary to what people say, you can actually never get good in this game. It is not a state that you can reach. It rather takes a constant effort to be able grind through it. You lose heroes and you need to recruit new ones (better ones?), retrain them. You always have to be alert and assess every aspect of the expedition at every stage or lose your characters which makes it rather exhausting for a "game". The game always finds something to make you upset with. It is almost like an experiment on "What can we do today to drive the player crazy?" and you are there trying to plug as many holes as possible before the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits fan. It is Sisyphean by design, so do not expect a welcoming game. Underneath its nice and polished graphic design lies a random number generator battle which has no winners or losers. You and the AI are doomed to roll dice until you learn the mechanics and get lucky to eventually finish the game.
Although characters are expendable, this is advertised as an RPG where the characters are customised and progress into the game as you progress through levels. It is not advertised as an HBG (Hamlet Building Game).
So while you are getting prepared for the stress and horrors, also get ready for the randomness and grind.
This is a game people hate to love, so heed the ancestor but get ready for "grindy fun?" More balance, fun, and rewards when they are due and this game is one step behind being a legend.
P.S. I have sugar-coated the fact that this game is unrecommendable with words. How do you like that, huh?!

Is Fallout 4 a good game? Yes. Personally, I find it to be a very enjoyable game.
Is it a good FALLOUT game? ...no, as others have said. It feels like one, but does it play like one? No.
I like Fallout 4, I really do, but I'd be lying if I said it doesn't frustrate the HELL out of me...
First thing first, let me talk about the good things...
- The open world in Fallout 4 is wonderful. It's littered with TONS of locations and things to do (Although I do like Fallout: New Vegas' better).
- Both gunplay and melee combat is VASTLY better than that of Fallout 3 and Fallout NV.
- It looks very polished; nice.
- Soundtrack is good.
- Great variety of customization and weapons.
- Neat enemies; creatures.
Now for the bad thing...
- RPG elements are absolute trash and practically don't exist.
- Some areas on the world map are so poorly optimized that it takes away the full experience of walking through and admiring certain areas of the game's world, many of which, are truly spectacular. One minute I'll be walking around with a solid 60 FPS, then suddenly, it'll drop to a 40-30 FPS.

I hesitate to write this review simply because it's an Early Access game. Also, might be worth mentioning that this is my first Early Access title.
I'll start by saying that, yes, everything you've heard about the difficulty and unfairness is true...to a point. If you have already looked over other reviews, you've probably read about the unfair RNG, corpses, heart attacks, increased critical hits and the list goes on. I'll rundown the pros and cons and then address the popular pain points just mentioned.
PROS:
INCREDIBLE storyline - The writers have crafted a downright creepy tale that would make Robert Chambers or Lovecraft proud. The story is also told in a very creative way. As you hunt down the various bosses, the story unfolds and you get a clearer view into the background of the estate in which the game takes place. It should also be pointed out the overall feel of the game is very much like reading an interactive graphic novel.
Amazing voice acting - The narrator of the story, presumably the ghost of the man that gets you involved in the estate, is very talented. The choice of language and parlance really make the setting believable. He is just really enjoyable to listen to. It seals the deal on the story’s authenticity.
Easy to learn UI - The user interface is well explained in the tutorial tips and I found the entire experience easy to learn. I'd say I had the basics down within a few hours. I'd firmly classify this as an easy game to learn but hard to master.
Auto-save like a champ - Darkest Dungeon offers instant saving pretty much with every click of the mouse. Any time you do something, no matter how seemingly insignificant it is, the game saves. This does 2 things ultimately for the experience. First, and most obvious, is it prevents the player from loading the game until he/she gets the result desired. This was something exploited often in X-Com, among other games. I really like this feature because it makes everything feel legit and final, increasing the excitement of the experience. You really have to commit to a course of action because you won't be able to go back and load. It also has the added effect of allowing the player to just turn the game off at any time and come back later, picking up right where they left off. A nice feature for working folk like myself.
Great soundtrack – The music fits the theme perfectly while at the same time really completing the experience. Incidentally, you can purchase the game soundtrack separately. I’d recommend it for all you role-players out there.
Well balanced classes – All of the hero classes are well balanced and well thought out; on both a mechanics level and story level. Your team typically winds up being something that resembles the dirty dozen or Kelly’s heros but certainly not the Fellowship of the Ring. There’s evidently going to be two more classes in the final game. Looking forward to that.
Solid combat and home base mechanic – Both systems are incredibly simple and quick to pick up. I only hope that upon final release, the village hub that functions as home base, gets beefed up a bit. It would be nice if you could do more in town; side quests, building, random events, something like that. Combat is tough. At the end of the day, it really is a random number generator. But, then again, what video game isn’t? And besides; the quirks, relics and camping skills give you ways to tilt the odds in your favor.
The stress system – A very smart and creative system of hero mental health and wellbeing. Things can happen that cause lasting mental damage and even negative disabilities or illness. Most of the time, stress damage can be viewed as worse than damage to health. Stress is much tougher to bounce back from.
The dev team – Red Hook seems to be very involved in the community of players. They regularly post in the forums and have addressed several issues that have been brought to them by normal, everyday people.
Now, the CONS:
The emotional learning curve – You really have to let go of looking at your heros as people. They are simply a means to an end. If someone isn’t pulling their weight, they “gots to go”, as the kids say. If it is going to take more money and time than it’s worth to get a hero up and on his feet again, show him the door. This might not be an issue for all gamers, but I’m not wired like that. So, it took me some time to embrace that viewpoint. I also started to think of the whole game as a business exercise; looking at everything in SWOT reports, gap analyses, sustainable systems, all that jazz. I kid, of course, but you get the idea. And it is just a game.
Repetitive, dare I say it…grind – It really is a grind at times. That’s why I mentioned the ideas for the village. If I’m going to dump more hours into this game, I need to see some more content. Another thought is monsters can sack the town and you have to rally to defend the homestead. Who knows what they have in store…I just hope it’s something.
The hunger system – I like the fact that the party has to eat while in the dungeon. However, determining when they eat needs a lot more work. Right now, it is completely random AND it doesn’t seem to be based at all on the last time the heros ate something. You will be traveling in hallways, the area between main rooms, and a hunger alert will pop up. If you have food, feed them and all is well. If not, they take damage and get stressed out. I once burned through 24 rations in the first 5 minutes of a dungeon. In game time, that’s like clearing out the Golden Corral hot bar during your lunch break at work. Red Hook, if you are listening, all I ask is put some more thought into this. It’s a good start.
And just a word regarding the overall difficulty. This game requires patients, forethought, number management, a thick skin and, I’ll just say it, luck. You’re going to take casualties along the way; that’s unavoidable. Another bit of advice; don’t be afraid to run away from a fight. Final Fantasy this is not. I do wish that the developers would stop listening to the minority of players clamoring on for the game difficulty to be kicked up. Isn’t that what mods are for?
Oh yeah and something I’m not going to go on about is heart attacks and monster corpses. They are optional. You don’t like those features, you simply turn them off. End of story. Please stop talking about it.
All in all it’s a fun and engaging experience. As I mentioned above, more content is needed. If you are having trouble getting started and need a point in the right direction, there are some really well done beginner guides out there. All I can leave you with is this advice: sometimes failure is actually success and sometimes success turns out to be failure.

When I fist got this game I found it amazingly fun. I would summerize the game as a rogue like party based dungeon crawl with some city building aspects. This game introduces a stress system that acts as a second bar of life. As the bar raises party memeber resolve is tested and can lead to some nasty effects. When the bar mexes out the character dies from a heart attack. Characters gain stress from going to dungeons and relieve stress through services in the city. Services take take time and force you to leave them behind to recover. I started enjoying this mechanic as it forced me to diversify my party, level up multiple people, and continually experience different class combinations. The dungeons are difficult and various mob and boss fights can easily get our of hand. A lot of the game turn into managment of city service slots, money for services, money for upgrades, money for dungeon supplies (these are important), and character stress.
I did really enjoy all the management aspects of the game until I finally was able to start leveling my pary members to level 3. Once a character reaches level 3 they can no longer run level the starter dungeons to help raise other party memebers. This ruined the game for me. The game is difficult and stress can kill characters of any level fairly easily if things get our of hand in an ambush. I did not ming struggling to unlock new tiers of content in the game but being forced to struggle in the lower level dungeons to attempt to level a new party memener to replace a higher level party memeber that died in the higher tier dungeon ruined all the fun I had in the game. Gaining levels in this game did not make a large difference in survival and allowing higher levels characters to shepherd lower level party members through dungeons for no XP gain would not be game breaking. It would not have been much easier but it would at least make the catchup process muchless stressful. The highest unlocked content would have been no easier by allowing this. This restriction just turned the game into an annoyingly grindy and unfun game in what appears to have been an attempt to make the game continually difficult and stressful. I am ok with diffiuclty but I think that it is ok for lower tier content to become easier as you progess the game.

I've been thinking about reviewing Starbound for a while, but the huge amount of content packed into this software is so good i've almost been forced to play non-stop until now. I'm a fan of survival games and i've also played some Terraria, even if i didn't enjoy it that much. The comparison between Terraria and Starbound is inevitable - both games share some basic mechanics and have 2D pixelated graphics - but in my opinion that is where the similiarities end. Starbound actually manages to push the survival concept further, by giving it a simple, yet effective context that will justify your actions and drive you through your game sessions. You're alone, temporarily stranded on an alien planet and your only objective is to survive while trying to establish a new home among the stars. Suddenly I felt like the usual "dig dig dig" action this genre requires had a precise goal, and the mining became a funny activity cause it's strictly tied to exploration; especially at the beginning, this is not a game who's going to throw ridicolous amounts of minerals at you, and the sheer quantity of content always gives out new motivations for your character to mine minerals and scavenge resources and food.
You'll never know what's lurking around the corner, wheter it's a friendly NPC, a bunch of weird pokemon-like monsters or an aggressive ancient cult of egyptian-like aliens. You usually set out to gather resources, and then end up exploring caves and building an unexpected sense of wonder and discovery. This is how i ended up wandering around a very deep cave, hidden under an ancient alien dungeon; a situation who made me feel like a character jumped out of a Jules Verne book, and everything happened while a perfectly-executed soundtrack covered my steps with a melancholic dream-like tune.
Starbound clearly cares about the story, the context, the environment, the mechanics and the graphics, and it also tries to give you varied emotions while you play; this is something other survival games fail to deliver.
In the end this is also a game where you can build your own pickaxe, break into an alien hut, kill the NPC in the process by sticking the tool in his head and sleep on his religious altar while you're half-naked. Just buy it :)

Okay, let me break it down for you. This game is, in my honest opinion, amazing. Never before have I been sucked into such an addictive (but simple in essence) gameplay loop. Most of the negative reviews you have seen revolve around the game's difficulty. The game tells you when you launch it up that you're going to have bad situations and party wipes but it's all about making the best out of it. Once you understand the basic stats and skills of combat (ACC, positioning, etc.) You become a pro at building sturdy parties in no time. Hence the gameplay loop. You go questing in the dungeon to collect gold and heirlooms to upgrade your heroes and buildings. There's just something so satisfying of getting that critical hit to end a long fought battle, or camping around the fire to reduce stress and buff your heroes. The difficulty over all is fair but punishing. The games narrator says it best, "Overconfidence is a slow and insedious killer." The stress system is one of the most unique additions to the RPG genre that I've seen in years. If you have been curious about this game and are into hardcore, elegant, and unforgiving dungeon crawls, then do not hesitate to buy this game and support the people who make it.

Darkest Dungeon is best summed up as an old school rogue style dungeon crawler mixed in with the lovecraftian horror and losing your sanity. It's not too difficult, per se, provided if you understand the mechanics of the game but enough difficulty that you would enjoy the game....or die frustrating (which it happens very little for me). The game content updates are slow in pace so brace yourself. The good thing about Darkest Dungeon, is the voice acting for the narrator, it is simply the best. Sound effects and music score is also very well done, making combat intense.
The game has a random dungeon generator with different loot and monsters to deal with. Colorful playable characters with each unique to its own use and abilities to fight, support or heal your own party. Plentiful of magical items, but not all of them are useful, only a handful out of the many dozens or hundreds that you find during your dungeon crawl. You'll either get afflicted with a disorder (or a severe one) or get a disease or worst, get both. You can level up your characters, provided the town's baracks and smithy has the proper upgrades to give you. It doesn't hurt that the artstyle for the game resembles to Mike Mignola's artstyle (if you're familiar to the Hellboy comics)
This game, as i said, is not too difficult, but enough difficulty to keep you in pace. You have think and plan, before making your move to dungeon crawl. And even then, you need to think and plan your move and attacks.
Its dark Gothic settings, its ominous narration, accompanied by its dark music scores, this is not a carebear RPG game.
This....is the Darkest Dungeon. And you will lose your sanity one way or another.

This game has a lot of pros, and a lot of cons.
Let me start with the notable issues that I had with this game in my 500 hours of play:
-The story is very forced. You do not have an option as to who you play, just how you play them.
-Though the world is large, the cells are barren and un-interesting.
-There are a lot of bugs. A lot.
-The workshop mode is extremely restrictive for very little reason.
-Most of the quests you come across will, essentially, be the same thing in a different location. Go get me a thing from the bad guys, or go kill the bad guys. In the wise words of memes; "Another settlement needs your help"
That said, I don't dislike this game. The very opposite. It's one of the few games that's held my attention for more than a few hours. Here are some of the reasons that I didn't give up on it.
-The world is beautifully crafted and designed.
-There are endless things to discover. The cells may be barren of debris, but there's always at least one interesting thing in each of them. I've spent an absurd amount of time playing this game, and I highly doubt I've found everything neat yet.
-It has a very high replay value. Sure, the beginning of the game will always be the same, and you'll always be a soldier or a lawyer, but whatever. Aside from the four different faction lines to go through, there are numorous other roleplaying oppurtunities that allow for an interesting playthrough no matter what number you're on.
-Most of the NPC Companionss are interesting and fairly developed (excluding Piper and Codsworth, the most basic and easy to come by NPCs).
-And of course, the most impressive thing about this game, the modding community. If you plan on getting this game, or already own it, make sure you keep an opened mind to the gifts that are modders. Dark Souls 3, por fim com seu final definitivo posso fazer uma análise completa. Então vamos lá...
Dark Souls 3 fecha a famosa franquia de jogos Dark Souls assim como pretendido pela sua desenvolvedora From Software e seu presidente Hidetaka Myazaki (Pai da franquia), com ele temos diversas novidades referente a jogabilidade e história, seguindo com fidelidade o estilo de jogo difícil proposto desde seu primeiro game.
Sobre as informações técnicas, Dark Souls 3 traz consigo belos gráficos, o motor gráfico é o mesmo usado em outro jogo da desenvolvedora (Bloodborne exclusivo de PS4). A taxa de quadros hoje está otimizada e fixa, funciona em computadores com configurações mais baixas como o meu (GTX 760) e temos mais recursos gráficos se comparados com seus antecessores.
Já a história em si, nos possibilita três finais diferentes, onde se tem como um conceito aquilo que melhor fecha o final para você, em toda a franquia temos a terrível escolha entre continuar ou não com a era do fogo, porém neste terceiro game temos mais uma escolha (da qual não darei muitos spoilers), a premissa é basicamente essa: “Terras se modificaram através das eras, com reinos, reis e lordes, inúmeros coisas poderosas que se ergueram e decaíram, se renovando ou se transformando a cada geração. Mas em algum momento isso parece ter chegado ao seu limite, pois as lacunas que mantém esse decurso desvanecem. A Era do fogo enfrenta, mais uma vez, o seu fim, mas talvez, apenas talvez, um fim diferente de todos os outros”. (Blog Mil). Particularmente, não posso dizer que a história é ruim, ela carrega um conceito que se constrói desde o primeiro jogo, onde um ciclo infinito sempre vai existir, apesar de nada ser muito claro ou explicito, a forma como tudo é contado em Dark Souls beirando o mistério, realmente é fantástico e nos possibilita imaginar diversas coisas.
As novidades que temos neste jogo no geral são as novas armas (Onde o jogo adaptou novos movimentos próprios ou habilidades especiais para cada tipo de arma, as chamadas “weapon arts”), novas armaduras, novos anéis, novas magias, milagres e piromancias (sendo que sortilégios agora são devidamente integrados nas outras três opções), novos npcs que podemos interagir para conseguir quests adicionais. Com as DLCs abrimos áreas opcionais que dão acesso a parte da historia, chefes (Alguns extremamente difíceis), armaduras e magias. O sistema de level continua basicamente o mesmo, com algumas diferenças entre tipos de skill, o sistema de upgrade das armas também não mudou tanto, porém agora não é nos permitido dar upgrade nas nossas armaduras (Elas vem com suas defesas base), e claro mas não menos importante o sistema de pvp/coop está mais liso e bem balanceado com a nova opção de jogo em arena contra amigos ou adversários seja cooperativo ou não.
Se recomendo comprar Dark Souls 3?, recomendo muito, para quem é fã e para quem não é, é diversão garantida com horas e horas de jogatina, a dificuldade é a marca do jogo então não se desanime com isso. E para você vai começar a jogar agora a série souls, recomendo pegar desde o primeiro pra sentir na pele toda a dificuldade e sadomasoquismo que esse jogo pode proporcionar a você.

Right off the bat I'm gonna tell you to try this game if you haven't. It isn't everyones type of game but if you like rpgs, sanbox games, voxel games, adventure games, or inovative games then atleast give the game a shot. Now, onto my full review.
Pros:
-Great dev team. They listen and even joke around with players
-Game's dungeons and armor is 99% player made
-A new class almost every month (11 at the moment)
-Each class plays quite differntly even if the use the same type of weapon
-Many unique biomes to run around in
-A completly player run economy
-You play the game to earn new classes
-It takes a while to get to max level so you won't get done super quick and get bored
-There are tons of decorations and building blocks
-You have a portable house called a cornerstone
-You can make your own club pretty easily (basically a guild)
-Each club gets it's own world were you can build anything you want
-You can be in up to 5 clubs at once each with their own world
-So many new people swarmed in at release they had to quadruple the servers to fit them all
-Controller support. They are still working on it so you can only change the controls from default in the files
-BIGGEST PRO! Not pay to win completly (see con #5). You can earn or trade with other players to get almost any item in the entire game. Some stuff is only buyable with real money but can be traded so non paying players can get them.
Cons
-Camera isn't very good at the moment
-Grinding for some levels can be tiring playing solo
-Can get very laggy in crowded worlds like some clubs
-Some things aren't explained very well and can be confusing
-New patron membership system. You can now pay monthly to get boosts like double cp, more likely to get good loot, and other things. It doesn't make people completly over powered but it does make it quite a bit easier for them.
-Challenges. When you get to mastery rank 30 you unlock challenges. They start at the start of every hour and go for 20 mins. You have to go do dungeons in a certain biome with your choice out of the 2 randomlly picked classes. They can let you get cool dragon mounts but can also get you an extreme amount of flux (the trade currency) which completly threw off the economy. Stuff that costed 5k flux might now cost 50k.
All in all it is a great game. I have played since last August so don't be fooled by my play time on here. I have actually played hundreds of hours on here. I have seen this game grow into what it is today. It has it's flaws but they are out weighed by the great parts. They're adding plenty of new features all the time too! They have a pvp system, an auction house, and plenty more in store for us! Won't you please come join us in this great big voxelly world of ours?
If you want to get ahold of me in game my ign is TheGamingReaver. I would love to help you guys get into to this great game!

I saw a lot of negative reviews here about this game being 'impossible' for new players so I thought I'd set the record straight.  The game is very easily playable you just need to understands its primitive character mechanics: Are the characters of this game heroes? Not at all, they're expendable fools whose only purpose is to do your bidding.  So yes they're going to die, a lot, that's afterall what they're there for.
So when you first start out it may be very hard to adapt to this game, it's relentless and unforgiving, but it's not 'unfair'.  Know that your little dungeon explorers are expendable and just adapt a 'do your best' attitude.  Build up your resources by sending ill equiped parties into dungeons and having them fight to the last!  If you're a new player concentrate on the wagon upgrades so that you get at least an influx of 4 characters per week/level.
Follow the above concept for upgrading your town and instead of relieving stress, until you have a good roster just dismiss them back to their lives.  The biggest mistakes you may become guilty of is becoming attached to somne of your party members, but by that time you should understand the game well enough to know how to keep them all alive.
So try to have fun and remember: Even in the darkest dungeons, there will be those that will seek out and become the beacon of light known as hope.

If you enjoyed Terraria, you will love Starbound. Starbound breaks the boundaries of your average sandbox mining/survival game by largely eliminating the need to tunnel your way across the map, replacing it instead with incentives to travel to, and explore, the surface of as many of the thousands of planets as possible. You will encounter both friendly and hostile NPCs of various races, whether in villages or dungeons, coordinating the whole adventure from your own personal starship - where you can either set up a makeshift mobile home, or teleport at will to your home planet of choice.
The game is currently in beta, meaning that there may still be upcoming wipes, as well as a slew of bugs, but even if it were a finished product, it would be worth the buy. Starbound is a very well-thought-out and well-designed game.

Great game and addition to the series. Though, it's fairly visible that Bethesda are trying to do more or just as much, for a lot less. They clearly spent a great deal of time conceptualizing and creating the mechanics of the game. The same cannot be said for the AI, which I've heard many others complain about and now I've also witnessed the gomey nature of the NPCs. They tend to not be able to find their own paths very well, get stuck on things, teleport around in a very un-immersive way, and somehow find themselves on top of buildings for no reason.
There are other un-immersive things that kind of irk me. Like things where the developers never actually finished what they were doing. For reference, there are occasionally "traps" like mines on the ground. Where you can see floating "pill bottles" with no texture, clearly used by one part of the team to mark where they thought the traps should be, but then were never pulled out of the visual map before the game release.
I want to continue playing this game. Though, based on quite a bit of deliberation I sincerely believe this product is not worth the "premium" pricing. $30 for an unfinished game like this is reasonable, $60 is not, whatsoever. Thus I base my negative recommendation on this.
Thank for offering the free weekend for us, Bethesda and Steam. I really think this will be the only way I'll ever play this game, though. Unless it's offered for a price much more reasonable during the Summer Sale 2017 or the Cyber Monday / Black Friday sales.

The game was enjoyable at first. Mostly because of unlockables and trying new abilities and character types. Once the initial discoveries have been made only a semi-insane completionist like myself would consider continuing to play. The battles are not really anything special or different from an old super nintendo turn based jrpg and the quests your characters go on don't actually vary much.
I got to the point where I had four level 5 characters and took them on a veteran mission (level 6 is the max, veteran level missions are the hardest). I took a few risks because my armor and weapons weren't at max level. It was tough but no one was dying. Then I faced a fat ectoplasm with 70 health and 2 of the smaller ones. I killed the big one. A smaller one spawned another big one with 70 more health. I killed that one. More small ectoplasms were spawned since I couldn't one hit them or stun them. I also couldn't run away from the battle. After killing 3 fat ectoplasms and about 7 small ones my characters were given death blows and all died by about round 20. I suppose I should have known better and played it safe by taking other characters on another 3 - 6 quests to get the money and artifacts to max out my armor, levels, and skills.
It may seem like I am giving the game a negative review out of frustration, I had done well up to that point, but losing my highest level characters and having no money left made me realize that a game that will set you back 4 - 6 hours while asking you to continue the same repetitive tasks over and over just to level is just poorly designed. Unfortunately I compulsively play games and want to see them through even if they aren't offering anything new. I thank the game for breaking its hold on me but would not recommend playing it for more than 5 - 10 hours. Why do so many games nowadays want you to keep playing them long after they have stopped being enjoyable? Is it a requirement that every game have 30 – 60 hours of playtime to create the illusion that you’re getting your money’s worth?

This game has recived some thumbs down and unfortunately I think it has been for the wrong reasons. The disclaimer at during the opening sequence is very precise and expressive in stating that it is not a game for the faint of heart. To quote almost directly "Be prepared to find it difficult. To die a lot. To get stressed a lot. To get annoyed a lot"
As long as you are able to embrace the frustrating you feel when playing this game then you will find it very rewarding. Yes the gameplay is kind of difficult to start with. The tutorial system does not really delve too much into the finer points of gameplay. I think, however, this was probably intentional as holding your hand throughout all the gameplay would really ruin what this game is about.
The reason the fighting is turn based is because it's supposed to be hard. It's meant to make you sit there and think long and hard about each turn. The stress system is incredibly difficult to manage and certainly relentless. Alongside that you also have the random hunger needs and also enemies, and numerous traps to deal with. As well as running out of provisions before the dungeon run is over.
I think its well worth remembering that this game is in early access. And it does offer a lot for being still in development. It IS a difficult game, but not impossible, which I think is what makes it enjoyable. It can also boast of an amazing soundtrack and a lovely gothic feel and beautiful art design. I was also very impressed with the varying classes that you could choose from and that their skillsets were nicely balanced.
If I were to say anythign bad about it it would be that it doesn't run very smoothly on my computer. However I cant really give it a thumbs down for that as it could be my tech! I also think that the randomness of the hunger and traps can sometimes seem a little overly unfair. However I am willing to accept that this game is unfair and you cant really complain about that. Other than that I don't think it has that many flaws at all. It is in early access and always has room for improvement but its not a bad little game from the offset.

Spiral Knights is free to play cooperative dungeon crawler fantasy MMORPG.
The player begins as a simple knight, and jump into action with an ever-changing, randomized world known as the Clockworks. Players can influence the areas they enter by depositing different minerals into the gates before they open. As players level up, they can upgrade their equipment or craft new items.
Every Spiral Knight has two attacks: one primary attack with a melee weapon and one special attack. You start with a gun but can later gain access to bombs, and your arsenal is constantly changing as you defeat new enemies and learn to manufacture new weapons.
One of Spiral Knights' greatest strengths is its art direction. Enemies are somehow a combination of threatening and adorable, armor upgrades make your Knight look both tough and huggable, and every environment you visit has tons of cool elements that make it interesting and distinct from the others in the game.
Spiral Knights is a wonderful game. It is beautifully designed and fun to play and offers hours of interesting combat in a variety of environments.
But there's one enormous catch: You have to pay real-life money to play Spiral Knights if you plan to play it for more than an hour at a time. Almost everything you do in Spiral Knights costs Energy. If you want to run a mission it costs 10 Energy, if you want to go to the second level of the dungeon it will be again 10 Energy. You start every day with 100 Energy, which you will quickly consume through normal gameplay.
Overall, Spiral Knights is a fun, engaging, pretty game. So if you have nothing else to do, you can check it out.

Where to begin.  If you want to something like Fallout 3 and New Vegas story-wise then this is not for you.  The story is shallow, there are no meaningful choices when making decisions and boils down to being railroaded into questlines that have little to no impact on the storyline.  If you want immersive story-telling and meaningful decisions then FO3 or NV are the better options for that.
What FO4 does offer is a much more reliable platform to run mods on, a major graphics overhaul, spamming sarcastic responses to everything, and not looking like burnt plastic while you run around doing whatever you want with actual likeable companions.  FO4 also allows you to run around the Commonwealth once the main story is over, allowing you to run around to improve settlements, finish side quests, defend checkpoints, and kill things over and over.  Since there is no level-cap you can hypothetically run around with a full skill tree, just have fun grinding to somewhere in the neighborhood of level 200.  With some mobs that level with the player, some of the deadliest enemies in the late-late-late game will probably be Bloated Charred Feral Ghouls.
If you want a little box to run around and goof off with mods, micromanage settlements and murder-hobo your way to self-satisfaction then FO4 is a fine game to fool around with, but it is still a shallow story game that only redeems itself with mods, DLC stories and being a walking demi-god.

I saw a lot of negative reviews here about this game being 'impossible' for new players so I thought I'd set the record straight.  The game is very easily playable you just need to understands its primitive character mechanics: Are the characters of this game heroes? Not at all, they're expendable fools whose only purpose is to do your bidding.  So yes they're going to die, a lot, that's afterall what they're there for.
So when you first start out it may be very hard to adapt to this game, it's relentless and unforgiving, but it's not 'unfair'.  Know that your little dungeon explorers are expendable and just adapt a 'do your best' attitude.  Build up your resources by sending ill equiped parties into dungeons and having them fight to the last!  If you're a new player concentrate on the wagon upgrades so that you get at least an influx of 4 characters per week/level.
Follow the above concept for upgrading your town and instead of relieving stress, until you have a good roster just dismiss them back to their lives.  The biggest mistakes you may become guilty of is becoming attached to somne of your party members, but by that time you should understand the game well enough to know how to keep them all alive.
So try to have fun and remember: Even in the darkest dungeons, there will be those that will seek out and become the beacon of light known as hope.

I've been thinking about reviewing Starbound for a while, but the huge amount of content packed into this software is so good i've almost been forced to play non-stop until now. I'm a fan of survival games and i've also played some Terraria, even if i didn't enjoy it that much. The comparison between Terraria and Starbound is inevitable - both games share some basic mechanics and have 2D pixelated graphics - but in my opinion that is where the similiarities end. Starbound actually manages to push the survival concept further, by giving it a simple, yet effective context that will justify your actions and drive you through your game sessions. You're alone, temporarily stranded on an alien planet and your only objective is to survive while trying to establish a new home among the stars. Suddenly I felt like the usual "dig dig dig" action this genre requires had a precise goal, and the mining became a funny activity cause it's strictly tied to exploration; especially at the beginning, this is not a game who's going to throw ridicolous amounts of minerals at you, and the sheer quantity of content always gives out new motivations for your character to mine minerals and scavenge resources and food.
You'll never know what's lurking around the corner, wheter it's a friendly NPC, a bunch of weird pokemon-like monsters or an aggressive ancient cult of egyptian-like aliens. You usually set out to gather resources, and then end up exploring caves and building an unexpected sense of wonder and discovery. This is how i ended up wandering around a very deep cave, hidden under an ancient alien dungeon; a situation who made me feel like a character jumped out of a Jules Verne book, and everything happened while a perfectly-executed soundtrack covered my steps with a melancholic dream-like tune.
Starbound clearly cares about the story, the context, the environment, the mechanics and the graphics, and it also tries to give you varied emotions while you play; this is something other survival games fail to deliver.
In the end this is also a game where you can build your own pickaxe, break into an alien hut, kill the NPC in the process by sticking the tool in his head and sleep on his religious altar while you're half-naked. Just buy it :)

Fallout 4 is actually a pretty good shooter and if that were the only question on the table I'd have no problem recommending it. But the game really ought to have been much more than just that. The frustrating thing is that most of the elements for a great game are there but they never come together.
It is supposed to be a RPG but it cuts the character creation mechanics down to the absolute bone. Skill points, traits, karma & reputation are all gone. All you get is a single perk for each level and since perks now replace skill points you have to use those to get the talents (weapon proficiency, lockpicking, crafting, etc.) that skill points previously provided. Not that this matters much -- The fun, quirky perks that were available in the previous games are mostly gone, squeezed out by the ones that replace skill points. This takes all of the fun out of leveling up and creating a unique character.
Regarding the addition of voiced protagonists, Fallout 4 is practically a demonstration reel in why this doesn't work for games like this. No matter what the player character looks like that character will always have the same voice actor -- an actor whose performance is really, really bland by necessity, since their acting needs to be as generic and nonspecific as possible. The game's dialogue interface is famously terrible too.
Fallout 4's main storyline is simply too linear and therefore unsuited to an open-world rpg. It initially tries to create a sense of urgency by having the player start off with the goal of rescuing their character’s kidnapped newborn child. What could possibly be more urgent then that?  Nevermind that this scenario runs completely contrary to the random exploration that open world games are all about — exploration that Fallout 4 actively encourages the player to engage in by immediately distracting them with sidequests. This creates a weird cognitive dissonance that runs throughout the first half of the game. Fallout 4 had the bizarre effect of making me feel like a negligent parent -- surely a first in a major AAA release.
The story supposedly has four main questlines but in reality there's just two: Join the mysterious organization called the Institute or help another group destroy it. It doesn't help that the game never makes it clear what precisely the Institute is up to -- or even if it truly is a threat. The big revelation regarding the Institute's leader (I won't spoil it here) was clearly meant to major shock along the lines of Bioshock's big plot twist but it just doesn't pay off that way and instead makes the question of what faction the player joins really unpleasant.
The sidequests are almost exclusively kill and/or fetch missions. The writing for them is subpar and almost never give the player an option other than "kill everything in your path."
One of the game's supposed innovations is the inclusion of random, procedurally-generated sidequests which give it a literally infinite amount of content. In theory, this sounds pretty cool. In practice, it means the player can easily find themselves stuck in an endless cycle of tedious grinding. After a short while the words “General, another settlement needs our help...” will fill you with absolute dread.
The game does have its good points. The survival mode is cool. Some of the companions are cleverly written and acted. Power armor suits are now functionally one-man tanks, a neat innovation. If you just want a game where after a long day at school or work you can blow off steam by mowing down some bad guys, then Fallout 4 is a good option. But that is as deep as this game gets.

This is one of the rare few times I will write a serious review so read carefully.
Trove is a ver addicting game with countless hours of gameplay. Even though I only have 30+ hours into Trove, I highly recommend it if you like adventure multiplayer/singleplayer games. Now lets move to Pros and cons show we?
-A very fun and addicting game that is actually Free to play!
-Item gear rankings, The higher the gear the better,
-Very smooth frames and fun gameplay mechanics
-Each class is something new not just a recycled concept which can lead to hours of fun gameplay
-No PvP, which means no overpowered uber 5 players kick new players arses in combat
-Club worlds! Create a club and a club world where only you and your friends can hang and build together
-Each dungeon is equal, meaning that a Pirate biome dungeon isn't harder then a cursed vale dungeon biome
-Shadow levels! Increase you level from the max of 20
-The game can get very tedious grinding for flux
-The game can also be very tedious trying to get a legendary or higher if you dont improve your magic find
-You must pay attention to the tutorial or you will get very lost mid game
-Although they are fixing this, Queue times are very long on weekends due to "weekend traffic"
-If you run out of potions mid battle with a dungeon boss, your screwed
-Corner stones can be hard to find at times
-You have to mine for materials to make new portals to uber 1 and above
-Mushrooms
-I find that challenging dungeons at uber 3 and bove can prove to be very difficult at times
-wings dont come to you early and are quite hard to obtain
-You are stuck to one class and cannot change unless you collect cubits daily or spend in game currency
Trove is a very fun game and I highly recommend it. While it may seem that some of my cons are a bit bias or even very true, the game has a lot of pros that will make up for them.
If you like singleplayer open world adventure games, or even a multiplayer play with your friends game, then trove is the game for you! Also I personally recomend the Neon Ninja and the Shadow Hunter for beginners, but mostly Neon Ninja if you like to be up in the front lines, Shadow Hunter is a ranged class requires more brainpower and strategy.

Warning: This will essentially just be a rant. Skip to the end if you want my conclusion.
After 14 hours of play, the game corrupts my exit save and crashes any time I attempt to load a different save. Even before then the game has frequently been unstable, with framerate drops, random crashes, etc. Bethesda, if you can't make a stable game, that's free from game-breaking bugs, after 31 YEARS in this business, I don't know what to say.
The Story
Garbage. Don't even bother. Only a handful of actually interesting characters. The new factions are just boring. Generic good guys, generic villains with no goals, mislead good guys, BoS, etc. The main character, despite now being voiced, has less personality than any previous Fallout protagonist. Every reaction is a dull surprise, every line is delivered as a short, halting sentence.
The Combat
Shallow. Why use anything except VATS, where you can gain a guaranteed hit on the torso at nearly any range, as long as your enemy isn't behind cover. Oh, the enemy needs to be shot in the head? As long as you have decent dexterity and the laser pistol you can plink away a dozen shots at a time until they die. VATS hasn't been improved either, it's essentially the same as the last two games. Melee combat is worthless. Run up and hit them with a stick until they die, while they shoot you in the head with a pipe rifle at point-blank range. Nothing feels like it has any impact.
The Roleplaying
NONEXISTENT. This game should not be considered an RPG. It is a shooter, first and foremost. Think about it: Boring story, mostly unlikeable characters, and, as I will get on to, the illusion of choice. Sounds just like a lot of yearly shooter franchises. To go on a tangent, the main reason I liked New Vegas more than Fallout 3 was because it felt like a good hybrid of tense shooting and roleplaying. Choices had consequences, there was a likeable cast, and so on. In this game, you have no choices. Dialogue-based skill checks are reduced to speech only, since there are NO SKILLS. No skills in an RPG. What. Since the only way to improve skills is to max out your SPECIAL scores, you'll do just that. The game "streamlines" the system by REMOVING IT. So now you just pump into every stat so every character is the same. Ironically, the SPECIAL scores you choose at the beginning have no impact on the long run, making your character less special. Dialogue is abysmal. Remember in 3 and New Vegas when you had a variety of options? Now you have four! "Yes.", "Not right now.", "Maybe.", and "Sarcastic". Notice how ALL OF THOSE ARE YES. The sarcastic option is essentially a wild card; being anything from "Oh, sure." to "I WILL GUT YOUR ENTIRE FAMILY, SUBHUMAN". And the karam system is gone.
CONCLUSION
A step back for the Fallout series. We took a major step forward with 3, and were on possibly the best track possible with New Vegas, but this... Jesus. It's just not good enough, Bethesda. It's the Final Fantasy: Mystic Quest of the Fallout series. If you're wondering, FF:MQ was intended as a "beginner" JPRG game, but just ended up gutting out everything that made Final Fantasy good in the first place. That's what Fallout 4 is, but it's not even intended to be a "Beginner's Fallout game", at least not to my knowledge. I hope Bethesda does better next time, but I'm just tired of reviewers sucking them off and letting them get away with murder because "THEY MADE FALLOUT 3 AND SKYRIM THEY ARE THE BEST COMPANY EVER". If you really love something, you have to admit when it does something wrong.
Final Score: 3.5/10

I started playing Darkest Dungeon without knowing how it was balanced and designed on release.
A few reviews for this game relate to the changes that have been made over time and the state it now is in.
There seem to be many complaints about the fun factor having changed and the game beeing unfair and frustrating.
Well I had now a good 30 hours of fun with the game. So far it demanded a lot from me in terms of:
1. Ressource Management
2. Party Setup
3. Battle tactics
4. My own greed and will to finish a run
1. Ressource Management
Money is short and at best I accumulated 20000 Gold. I had to get inventive with my party setup and made sure I healed as much stress as even possible with the jester, houndmaster, crusader or via camp before leaving the quest. I had to pass on healing quirks which were either not relevant to be healed (like ranged malus on a pure melee character) or not that grave.
2. Party Setup
Befor every run I spend about 5 to 10 minutes deciding which item i take along and which characters will do the job. Taking to account which enemies I will encounter and what my battle tactics will be for this run. There are tons of nice combinations and some that are just not a good option :D
3. Battle tactics
Goes hand in hand with the Setup. Once you are in battle and your party is for example not equiped with a stress healer like the hound master or jester you put hard focus on any enemy that inflicts pure stress damage.
4. My own greed
Is key...
Letting low level characters die in a dungeon is not a big deal and pushin forward is only rewarding. But well trained and equipped characters.. when all vanquished.. is just the worst.
Summa summarum:
The game is super fun. Good atmosphere. Graphics do their job and fit the game and the narrator is just epic. At some point I wished for even more variation in the narration just because you heard it all at some point but nevertheless genius.
I recommend this game to:
- Indie and Fantasy-RPG genre game fans
- Round-based, dungeon crawling and Build-up simulation gametype fans
- People with a taste for uncommon audio and visual setting
After all everyone will make his/her own experience with the game and this is just a very very small view into how I experienced the game.

If you look at this as a Fallout game or an RPG it’s a dismal failure. If you look at it as ‘Power Armored ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Simulator 2015’ it’s alright for $20.
Most of the actual roleplay elements have been ripped out of the game. Really, there’s no other way to put it. Skills are gone, skill and stat checks in dialogue are gone except the occasional Charisma “give me more money” check and you will never have more than four dialogue options to choose from. Character growth is almost entirely handled by perks, and even they are watered down. Every time I chose a perk, it wasn’t to define character growth, it was because some (like lockpicking or science) are virtually required. Weapon-specific perks just give a percentage increase in damage. Even without taking any, the fact you get power armor within the first hour of the game ensures you’re almost never in any actual danger. Yes, you get power armor in the first hour of the game.
Oh God I have to talk about the writing now. Bethesda doesn’t ruin everything (I liked Piper and some other companions, and individual areas can have clever backstories) but the same problems from Fallout 3 are even worse in Fallout 4. No one really has clear motivations or backstory. Who are the Gunners and why do they shoot on sight? Do the super mutants have any goals or are they just there because blarg evil badguy? Why is the Institute sending armies of weak Synths to attack the surface when they could build an army of sentry bots and just flatten everything? Toss in an overreliance on radiant quests and the game feels less like an RPG and more like a shoot-and-loot.
Frankly, they did improve the shooting mechanics in Fallout 4. The guns feel more responsive and are fun to use. The problem is that most enemies are bullet sponges. That might make the game difficult, but you get power armor in the first hour of the game. Power armor was improved too, it’s now something you step into like a vehicle and can customize. It’s not only tough as nails, but now feels like a proper walking tank, letting you breathe underwater and drop from great heights with no damage. With that power armor letting you shrug off damn near everything, the result is a boring war of attrition where you’re in no danger of dying, but the enemy isn’t going down quickly either. Power armor needs fuel, but fusion cores are so plentiful I’ve never needed to worry or actively seek them out.
Ultimately, Fallout 4 provides a lot of content to explore, but little of it is memorable. If it’s on sale and you want a brainless open-world shoot-and-loot it’s an ok buy, but it’s not an RPG anymore.

Quite a nifty f2p survival game.
The community is varied, you'll get killed on sight and beaten to death right as you spawn (most of the time in my case), you'll get followed around awkwardly (happens more oftenly than you'd expect) and you'll come across some pretty cool people.
Maps are around medium in size imo, with obvious hot spots and a decent amount of locations to explore. There are about 7 maps (excluding the festive and halloween variations, arena maps and the tutorial).
The shaders make this game look surprisingly visually appealing.
Food and weapons aren't particularly difficult to come by, but if you do have trouble finding them, you can always resort to just crafting as the recipes aren't that demanding.
Base building is pretty simple and not too time consuming.
Doesn't have any pay-to-win features, gold upgrade only introduces some cosmetic options and the skins don't really serve much of a purpose.
It has come a long way since the old Roblox days (coming from someone who has played all of the versions during their prime time, on a different account, mind you) and I'd say it's aged pretty well, as there's still quite a chunk of people still playing it (24 hour peak: 32k). I urge everyone who plays this game to get the gold upgrade, not for the things it offers, but to support the dev who has clearly put a lot of time and effort into a game that just about anyone can get.
