So you're probably looking at this game for the first time and thinking something along the lines of this.
"Okay, this looks a lot like Terraria." Or, perhaps, "This looks a lot like Minecraft." Maybe if you're tired of those sort of games, something like, "Oh my god, another Minecraft clone? Not buying."
Well, I can assure you that all of those are legitimate first thoughts-- but you don't need a review to tell you that, of course. What I can really assure is thatm regardless of any passing likeness to certain mine-built-fight sorts of games, Starbound has something unique to offer.
My first impression of the game was the soundtrack. The soundtrack of this game never failed to invoke that spark of exploration for me, and it serves as an excellent accoutrement to the rest of the experience. The next was character creation-- which, I will admit, I am biased in. I just like the idea of having my bird-man explore the universe!
The next is the gameplay. If you've played Terraria, you probably have a basic familiarity of the controls. What sets the game apart here is the ship system, for me. Basically, since you're a spacefarer, you have a spaceship you can beam back to, sort of like a persistent base between worlds. Maybe you'll keep it neat and tidy inside of that ship, but most likely you'll end up with a ship like mine-- an absolute mess, full of various supply chests and crafting workshops. It's clutter, but it's your clutter.
So yeah, if you're a packrat, you will like this game. (And become aware of it.)
The next major point is exploration. This is no one-world game like Minecraft, that extends forever and ever-- worlds are typically small enough to circumnavigate on foot, though it'll take you a while to get all the way around. But it's what you find that makes the game. Even just exploring the surface, you'll battle the procedurally generated monsters, wailing in terror as you realize the adorable-looking deer thing can BREATHE FIRE and it kills you almost insttantly. You'll find other sentient creatures, hostile or no-- from bandits to fortresses to little homes that sell you clothes. And once you're done exploring the surface, you'll find more under the surface, with new beasts deeper below and some strange cavern setups (I'd name some, but I think it would be a spoiler of sorts.).
And if you're tired of the planet you're on, gather enough fuel and fly somewhere else. While the game makes you record coordinates other than your "home" planet and where you are at the time (which will hopefully pass, as the Early Access continues), there are tons of planets to explore, and weird setups like asteroid belts and moons mixing up the game.
And that isn't the full release yet. With such a solid beta, I would fully suggest, at the very least, watching this game. Maybe try it out. Maybe buy it! I've definitely enjoyed the game, maybe you will too.
Caveats: If you don't like minecraft lookalikes, you won't like this game. It can get repetitive if you play it for a full weekend, with little else (but honestly, what doesn't?). The game is a bit hard to stick with without friends that play it too (multiplayer is super fun).

[Re-Review] Okay, the big thing they changed here is that ELEVATORS, and CRAFTING items no longer require ENERGY. That's a WHOLE lot better. It made the game truly free to play. However, they changed their business model under the hood, and the way items level up in order to get people to 'push' on rushing their upgrades with their real-life wallet. They truly went F2P (80%-ish, I'd say). Swords, Guns, and Bombs are still there.
ENERGY (the premium currency used for real-life cash transaction that can be bought with in-game currency as well) is still usable to buy stuff in the Cash Shop place via the 'Supply Depot'. It's mostly for convenience (Ex: to craft your gear faster with ALCHEMY STONES [in the old game, it requires ENERGY to craft items]. You can normally find ALCHEMY STONES in dungeons).
In addition, they added pets that fight alongside with you, each having their own skills and leveling up mechanics. The way you level up gear has changed. It is both a gift and a curse. You can individually level up an item however you like, but when it reaches it's MAX exp required to level up, you need to get FORGE STONES to level up. You can either find them normally in dungeons (OR CASH SHOP! See a pattern there?).
There is DLC that costs 5.95 called the Crimson Hammer to get more exclusive items just for that DLC, and there are these 'cosmetic grab bags' they charge for 2k energy or so (equivalent to 10~15 dollars give or take).
They even went as far as to give this game a story and a mission system. Previously, gear was dependant on how much you've equipped. But if you're an old character with Tier 3 equipment already (5-star stuff), then you're omittted from these restrictions. New characters, however, will have to go through the MISSIONS in order to have clearance on equipping higher level gear.
There's even PVP modes as well between deathmatch and territory points.
This is at least how Spiral Knights should of been to maintain a high crowd status quo. The game is still great in terms of gameplay if you're into a Zelda-esque style. I really recommend this game now that the business model is fair.
For weapons, Bombs are the most time investing items to level up, as they show their usefulness by 4* star and it takes 5* to really bring out their generous AOE potential. Guns and Swords are useable at any time, and their specialties grow stronger. Leveling pets? Very time consuming. Their potential does not show until spending 40+ hours leveling them up.
I give it a hard recommendation if you enjoy dungeon crawling Zelda style, and aren't turned off on the video that you see.

I have loved the Fallout franchise from the very first game.  Fallout 4 is the first one that I give a big thumbs down.
It isn't a terrible game -- the problem for me is that the gameplay doesn't have any of the DNA of its predecessors.  This is essentially a world exploration FPS game, not a turn-based (or pausable, action-point-based) strategic combat game. You're heavily rewarded for not playing it in VATS mode (you can essentially dump Perception, and SPECIAL points are very hard to come by), combat in VATS mode doesn't feel natural, and by far the most powerful way to play is to be a stealthy sniper.
The change from skill points to just perks is a good change, but it dumbs down the system a lot, and takes away a lot of the fun of levelling, in my opinion -- especially since you can't ever add to SPECIAL through levelling, either.  Basically, you just pick through a tree of perks that is predetermined base don your initial SPECIAL + bobbleheads and 1 book.
As an FPS, well, it's just not as fun as other FPS's; it takes out pretty much everything that's fun about an FPS, and turns combat into a terrible grind, where you strive to rush to the midgame and then basically have the ability to murder everything you come across.   The game is a lot like Skyrim, but without as compelling a story (though the beginning is very cool) and without the visuals.
The biggest problem for me, I guess,  is that I really didn't want another FPS in a market where a huge chunk of new games are FPS.
Long story short Terraria is you backyard and Starbound is the whole world and your ship is still being build and once your spaceship is finished. Starbound is born and full release.

Let's do a quick rundown of the pros and cons...
PROS:
-Beautiful block filled world
-All models (classes, mobs, items) made brilliantly
-easy fast paced gameplay which can be learned extremely quickly
-friendly community often willing to help others
-content available for purchase, but not required to progress in game (pay to win)
-cornerstone claiming allows to have a safe and teleporting stronghold
-style system allows players to look how they want, without suffering loss of stats
-crafting system gives exploration more of a meaning
-vast biomes and many dungeons
-class system allows players choice in what play style they want
CONS:
-class selection limits you to your armour style, only changing when purchased or achieved through level advancement
-mounts and allies are pretty limited as to free choices
-advancing in level for certain crafting areas takes quite a while, and a waste of materials
-finding recipes is quite hard until level 10 (Uber1 portal unlocked)
-random spawning of 'shadow' can destroy your cornerstone (it has happened to me before)
That's pretty much all I can say about this game. While it has its downsides, it is still a fun game to play, and I would definetely reccommend it to players with a lot of experience, or with little to no experience.

Fallout 4 is actually a pretty good shooter and if that were the only question on the table I'd have no problem recommending it. But the game really ought to have been much more than just that. The frustrating thing is that most of the elements for a great game are there but they never come together.
It is supposed to be a RPG but it cuts the character creation mechanics down to the absolute bone. Skill points, traits, karma & reputation are all gone. All you get is a single perk for each level and since perks now replace skill points you have to use those to get the talents (weapon proficiency, lockpicking, crafting, etc.) that skill points previously provided. Not that this matters much -- The fun, quirky perks that were available in the previous games are mostly gone, squeezed out by the ones that replace skill points. This takes all of the fun out of leveling up and creating a unique character.
Regarding the addition of voiced protagonists, Fallout 4 is practically a demonstration reel in why this doesn't work for games like this. No matter what the player character looks like that character will always have the same voice actor -- an actor whose performance is really, really bland by necessity, since their acting needs to be as generic and nonspecific as possible. The game's dialogue interface is famously terrible too.
Fallout 4's main storyline is simply too linear and therefore unsuited to an open-world rpg. It initially tries to create a sense of urgency by having the player start off with the goal of rescuing their character’s kidnapped newborn child. What could possibly be more urgent then that?  Nevermind that this scenario runs completely contrary to the random exploration that open world games are all about — exploration that Fallout 4 actively encourages the player to engage in by immediately distracting them with sidequests. This creates a weird cognitive dissonance that runs throughout the first half of the game. Fallout 4 had the bizarre effect of making me feel like a negligent parent -- surely a first in a major AAA release.
The story supposedly has four main questlines but in reality there's just two: Join the mysterious organization called the Institute or help another group destroy it. It doesn't help that the game never makes it clear what precisely the Institute is up to -- or even if it truly is a threat. The big revelation regarding the Institute's leader (I won't spoil it here) was clearly meant to major shock along the lines of Bioshock's big plot twist but it just doesn't pay off that way and instead makes the question of what faction the player joins really unpleasant.
The sidequests are almost exclusively kill and/or fetch missions. The writing for them is subpar and almost never give the player an option other than "kill everything in your path."
One of the game's supposed innovations is the inclusion of random, procedurally-generated sidequests which give it a literally infinite amount of content. In theory, this sounds pretty cool. In practice, it means the player can easily find themselves stuck in an endless cycle of tedious grinding. After a short while the words “General, another settlement needs our help...” will fill you with absolute dread.
The game does have its good points. The survival mode is cool. Some of the companions are cleverly written and acted. Power armor suits are now functionally one-man tanks, a neat innovation. If you just want a game where after a long day at school or work you can blow off steam by mowing down some bad guys, then Fallout 4 is a good option. But that is as deep as this game gets.

I wanted to make a simple positive recommendation after reading a few of the top "not recommended" reviews.  This game is hard, this game is sometimes unfair and resources are difficult to accumulate early on.  Despite this, I have only suffered 5 deceased heroes, 2 of them early on when I hadn't yet learned the limits of the risks I should take and the other 3 when I brought in a weaker party composition (once against a boss) for the sake of trying out different comps.
All 5 deaths were ENTIRELY my fault and I do not blame the game at all.  I took risks and paid for it.  The addition of corpses and heart attacks have not caused any further difficulty or deaths.  I learned to play with them in mind and have not suffered because of them.  In fact, the corpses often aid you by positioning enemies favorably for your ranged attackers (Arbalest/Grave Robber/Highway Man) and I haven't gone above ~130 stress on any character, even in my worst dungeon runs.
Basically I'm complaining and recommending this game because of the people whining that it's too hard or unfair.  It's not, you have more control than you realize.  Don't build a triple vestal party with a jester and expect to come out alive....that might actually be a viable comp.
Also...the narrator is amazing.  I got a little tired of his initial release commentary after 35 hours, but the additional cove lines are superb.  Furthermore, un-nerf the highwayman, he's the weakest damage oriented class in the game now.
TL;DR - game is extremely fun and moderately hard but not unfair, get good and win with no casualties/shortage of resources.

I've been playing this game since 2011, before I even used Steam. I'm actually kinda proud to say that even with microtransactions and some corporate shenanigans, the game still holds up.

Maybe it's worse in the higher levels (though I'm at the endgame I've never actually entered a shadow lair) but you can easily get through the whole game without needing to pay at all.

The people who are still around generally do runs of the final boss anyway (and really that's what everyone does in the endgame) and you can easily solo most missions. On top of that, it's 100% free, so you could easily get a group of friends together if you needed help.
As a long-time veteran of this game, I still reccomend you play it 6 years later.

This game is the reason my insomnia isn't getting treated properly.
Starbound should technically be classified as a 2D Action/Adventure/RPG/Simulation/Casual game, because it has elements of each of these, and it executes them brilliantly.
- The Action comes in through the sidescrolling, sword-swinging, monster-hunting elements, which do get a little old after a while, but once you get a gun or laser rifle, it all picks up tremendously. The choice of weapons increases as you gain more materials to make them with, or locate them in chests, which are scattered randomly across each planet.
- The Adventure is introduced through the procedurally-generated planets, of which there are a near-infinite number thanks to a 32-digit seed for each planet, each one different from the last. You can explore multiple biomes and sub-biomes, and even discover entire civilizations which will either like you, be cautious of you, or kill you on sight. The races are uniquely-textured and have deep lore for each of them, which is the biggest draw in this category.
- The RPG happens through the starship and weapons/armor upgrades, which are available through crafting stations, which are crafted with things you find in the world. In order to move on to the next tier, you must defeat a boss, which is summoned through certain crafting items. It also has a story behind each race, but leaves your individual character up for your interpretation, which I really appreciate.
- The Simulation is a small part of the game, but still fun. You collect or create materials and blocks to build your own home out of, both background and foreground. Multiple things are available to build with, including wood, stone, iron, steel, titanium, moonstone, even meteorite rock! You can even set traps for enemies or put up defense drones. Plus, you can spawn others of your race using a crafted item, so you can make your own little village!
- The Casual part is the best part, in my opinion: MODS. Starbound is 100% completely moddable, and you can make literally anything. You can make your ship customizable and build it yourself, you can add in new weapons and armor, you can even visit new biomes with new enemies and new liquids! There's no limit to what can be done. And the best part is that it's really easy to do! I'm a total idiot, and even I managed to mod this game!
I would recommend this game to absolutely anyone who enjoys a 2D space adventure with various elements to it. There's something here for everyone to enjoy. Plus, for 15 bucks, you can get just as much enjoyment out of it as an MMO subscription if you enjoy adding mods.

Fallout 4 is actually a pretty good shooter and if that were the only question on the table I'd have no problem recommending it. But the game really ought to have been much more than just that. The frustrating thing is that most of the elements for a great game are there but they never come together.
It is supposed to be a RPG but it cuts the character creation mechanics down to the absolute bone. Skill points, traits, karma & reputation are all gone. All you get is a single perk for each level and since perks now replace skill points you have to use those to get the talents (weapon proficiency, lockpicking, crafting, etc.) that skill points previously provided. Not that this matters much -- The fun, quirky perks that were available in the previous games are mostly gone, squeezed out by the ones that replace skill points. This takes all of the fun out of leveling up and creating a unique character.
Regarding the addition of voiced protagonists, Fallout 4 is practically a demonstration reel in why this doesn't work for games like this. No matter what the player character looks like that character will always have the same voice actor -- an actor whose performance is really, really bland by necessity, since their acting needs to be as generic and nonspecific as possible. The game's dialogue interface is famously terrible too.
Fallout 4's main storyline is simply too linear and therefore unsuited to an open-world rpg. It initially tries to create a sense of urgency by having the player start off with the goal of rescuing their character’s kidnapped newborn child. What could possibly be more urgent then that?  Nevermind that this scenario runs completely contrary to the random exploration that open world games are all about — exploration that Fallout 4 actively encourages the player to engage in by immediately distracting them with sidequests. This creates a weird cognitive dissonance that runs throughout the first half of the game. Fallout 4 had the bizarre effect of making me feel like a negligent parent -- surely a first in a major AAA release.
The story supposedly has four main questlines but in reality there's just two: Join the mysterious organization called the Institute or help another group destroy it. It doesn't help that the game never makes it clear what precisely the Institute is up to -- or even if it truly is a threat. The big revelation regarding the Institute's leader (I won't spoil it here) was clearly meant to major shock along the lines of Bioshock's big plot twist but it just doesn't pay off that way and instead makes the question of what faction the player joins really unpleasant.
The sidequests are almost exclusively kill and/or fetch missions. The writing for them is subpar and almost never give the player an option other than "kill everything in your path."
One of the game's supposed innovations is the inclusion of random, procedurally-generated sidequests which give it a literally infinite amount of content. In theory, this sounds pretty cool. In practice, it means the player can easily find themselves stuck in an endless cycle of tedious grinding. After a short while the words “General, another settlement needs our help...” will fill you with absolute dread.
The game does have its good points. The survival mode is cool. Some of the companions are cleverly written and acted. Power armor suits are now functionally one-man tanks, a neat innovation. If you just want a game where after a long day at school or work you can blow off steam by mowing down some bad guys, then Fallout 4 is a good option. But that is as deep as this game gets.

I started playing DD on this last patch and I for one like the game. I cannot recommend it unfortunately. Echoing many of the other reviews that have been written recently, DD has a myriad of wonderful features, including excellent voice acting and mechanical rpg enhancements, the concept of stress, the artwork, and the music all serve to make Darkest Dungeon a joy to play to a point. That point is reached fairly quickly in the game due to the compounding effects of stress and the costs to combat stress and improve your crew. None of the provisions like torches and food you purchase for a given expedition that you don't use are lost upon return. Oversupply yourself and you lose a significant amount of coin. Underprovision yourself and you risk failing the expedition and really getting behind on your coffers. With the high costs of stress reduction and improvement opportunities, and expedition costs, I am starting to see a challenge in making any progress to the higher levels in this game. Recruiting newer characters that are too weak to explore your only choice of dungeons and being unable to use your higher level characters much due to the effects of stress or the many negative quirks they aquire that cost too much to remove means you end up playing only the very beginning portions of a given dungeon and make barely any progress.
Bottom line, a really great game ruined by too high of a challenge level. You will find yourself getting frustrated playing it now so I would wait until another patch comes through that addresses the difficulty issues.

Warning: This will essentially just be a rant. Skip to the end if you want my conclusion.
After 14 hours of play, the game corrupts my exit save and crashes any time I attempt to load a different save. Even before then the game has frequently been unstable, with framerate drops, random crashes, etc. Bethesda, if you can't make a stable game, that's free from game-breaking bugs, after 31 YEARS in this business, I don't know what to say.
The Story
Garbage. Don't even bother. Only a handful of actually interesting characters. The new factions are just boring. Generic good guys, generic villains with no goals, mislead good guys, BoS, etc. The main character, despite now being voiced, has less personality than any previous Fallout protagonist. Every reaction is a dull surprise, every line is delivered as a short, halting sentence.
The Combat
Shallow. Why use anything except VATS, where you can gain a guaranteed hit on the torso at nearly any range, as long as your enemy isn't behind cover. Oh, the enemy needs to be shot in the head? As long as you have decent dexterity and the laser pistol you can plink away a dozen shots at a time until they die. VATS hasn't been improved either, it's essentially the same as the last two games. Melee combat is worthless. Run up and hit them with a stick until they die, while they shoot you in the head with a pipe rifle at point-blank range. Nothing feels like it has any impact.
The Roleplaying
NONEXISTENT. This game should not be considered an RPG. It is a shooter, first and foremost. Think about it: Boring story, mostly unlikeable characters, and, as I will get on to, the illusion of choice. Sounds just like a lot of yearly shooter franchises. To go on a tangent, the main reason I liked New Vegas more than Fallout 3 was because it felt like a good hybrid of tense shooting and roleplaying. Choices had consequences, there was a likeable cast, and so on. In this game, you have no choices. Dialogue-based skill checks are reduced to speech only, since there are NO SKILLS. No skills in an RPG. What. Since the only way to improve skills is to max out your SPECIAL scores, you'll do just that. The game "streamlines" the system by REMOVING IT. So now you just pump into every stat so every character is the same. Ironically, the SPECIAL scores you choose at the beginning have no impact on the long run, making your character less special. Dialogue is abysmal. Remember in 3 and New Vegas when you had a variety of options? Now you have four! "Yes.", "Not right now.", "Maybe.", and "Sarcastic". Notice how ALL OF THOSE ARE YES. The sarcastic option is essentially a wild card; being anything from "Oh, sure." to "I WILL GUT YOUR ENTIRE FAMILY, SUBHUMAN". And the karam system is gone.
CONCLUSION
A step back for the Fallout series. We took a major step forward with 3, and were on possibly the best track possible with New Vegas, but this... Jesus. It's just not good enough, Bethesda. It's the Final Fantasy: Mystic Quest of the Fallout series. If you're wondering, FF:MQ was intended as a "beginner" JPRG game, but just ended up gutting out everything that made Final Fantasy good in the first place. That's what Fallout 4 is, but it's not even intended to be a "Beginner's Fallout game", at least not to my knowledge. I hope Bethesda does better next time, but I'm just tired of reviewers sucking them off and letting them get away with murder because "THEY MADE FALLOUT 3 AND SKYRIM THEY ARE THE BEST COMPANY EVER". If you really love something, you have to admit when it does something wrong.
Final Score: 3.5/10

I debated picking this game up for quite some time, until I finally saw it on sale and decided to give it a shot.
I'm glad I did. Hell, I would've paid full price if I had known the extent of what Darkest Dungeon had to offer.

Darkest Dungeon is a very interesting experience, and although I'd like to heartily reccommend it, the game is probably not for everyone. In order to answer the question of "Should I purchase this or not?", ask yourself first how well you cope with failure and loss. How well do you function in a bleak situation? Do you thrive under pressure, or do you crumble? Those who answer negatively may still enjoy the game, but I'd recommend waiting for it to go on sale.
However; if you answered positively, I think you'll find something quite interesting with Red Hook's roguelike RPG. For the crafty and intelligent gamer, Darkest Dungeon offers a plethora of benefits ranging from interesting and invetive gameplay, wonderful sound, art, and voice direction, and a genuinely engaging world with a rich, albeit dark lore.
I'm immensely pleased with the game, especially seeing how the theme works wonderfully with the month of halloween, and I whole-heartedly recommend the game to any brave soul who habors a love for dark fantasy... And maybe a small masochistic streak.

A great game in terms of FPS, but a horrible contribution to the fallout series. Because every gun is unique, none of them are. The settlement building is just a gimmick, not a real mechanic, and replaces playerhomes (one is still present, but its just an indoor settlement, no upgrades or themes). Class builds dont matter, and the dialogue mechanic is so basic a toddler could beat the role playing element to the game (just always select up to speech check or down to confirm/good morality speech(morality does NOT make a return, and faction standing are practically non-existent). The map is large, but a huge portion (literally around 40%, but it feels like 80%, is completely unused. There are a few good and memerable quests, but few and far between. The main story line is horrendously gimmicky, and not a single person i've discussed the game with liked it.
This is an FPS, not an RPG. If you loved fallout 3 or new vegas, dont get this game. This feels like when a developer rushes a well loved franchise into being more "accessible"  to mainstream videogame audiences, alienating previous fans.
TL;DR? Fallout fans, save your money, Call of duty fans, this is more your style

I debated picking this game up for quite some time, until I finally saw it on sale and decided to give it a shot.
I'm glad I did. Hell, I would've paid full price if I had known the extent of what Darkest Dungeon had to offer.

Darkest Dungeon is a very interesting experience, and although I'd like to heartily reccommend it, the game is probably not for everyone. In order to answer the question of "Should I purchase this or not?", ask yourself first how well you cope with failure and loss. How well do you function in a bleak situation? Do you thrive under pressure, or do you crumble? Those who answer negatively may still enjoy the game, but I'd recommend waiting for it to go on sale.
However; if you answered positively, I think you'll find something quite interesting with Red Hook's roguelike RPG. For the crafty and intelligent gamer, Darkest Dungeon offers a plethora of benefits ranging from interesting and invetive gameplay, wonderful sound, art, and voice direction, and a genuinely engaging world with a rich, albeit dark lore.
I'm immensely pleased with the game, especially seeing how the theme works wonderfully with the month of halloween, and I whole-heartedly recommend the game to any brave soul who habors a love for dark fantasy... And maybe a small masochistic streak.

On a positive note, I love the concept of this game, I like the art, the rogue-like elements, and in large part the execution is fantastic. It hooks you in with the progression of the town and your heroes and I genuinely felt excitement and nervousness at attempting a quest because you never know whats going to happen!
Now on the more neutral side of things, but ultimately the downfall of the game, is the difficulty, which is ridiculously hard... and believe me when I say I enjoy really hard games.
It took me about 2 dead heroes and 4 failed attempts at runs before I even finished my first run at the first basic quest. While I personally didn't mind this, I don't think this is a good way to bring new players into the game and it is going to turn a lot of people away very quickly.
Despite the tough learning curve I began to piece together how things worked, I began developing my town and upgrading and recruiting a variety of heroes to put strategic compositions together to take town tough quests.
It felt good.
I was absolutely loving it... then, I attempted the Wisened Hag quest for the first time... with obviously no idea of what she did or what I needed to prepare for. Fortunately, everything was going swimmingly. I breezed my way through the dungeon and headed into the boss room on full health with practically no stress... Perfect!
At which point, the boss randomly captured and reordered my units, with basically no way to stop it because they were all permanently moved into the one position they could not attack. If I tried to move one into the position it needed to be in, she just moved it back. So I completely helplessly lost my 4 best heroes at once, with no way to retreat or counter what was happening...
Frustrating... to say the least.
Don't get me wrong, I understand you're going to lose heroes, it's part of the game. And, as bad as it was, that wasn't the real issue.
The zero option and severity of that fight just felt hollow. I could have done nothing about what happened because I had no idea what I was in for, I just clicked that button to enter the room and lost everything.
But the really aggravating and ultimately insurmountable problem was that I now had nothing. No money, and therefore zero way to buy provisions for another quest; or de-stress heroes; or upgrade heroes; or in fact actually attempt to get back into the game at all.
That was it: 9-10 hours of gameplay down the toilet.
So lesson learnt, I suppose? All I need to do now is make sure I keep a buffer of gold in case things go bad right?
Sure, but  do I want to start over and build my town up from scratch?
Nope, do I heck. I'm done.
I had a great time with it, but it just ended all my motivation to keep playing right there and then and I can't bring myself to spend the time starting over, only to hit the next boss I haven't seen before and I get set back another 10 hours.
I'm confused why they thought this was sensible game design and what outcome something like this would have with anyone other than just feeling like you've been duped into wasting your time.
So just like the heroes in the game, my resolve was tested:
Did I become Focused? Stalwart? Courageous?
No.
At best, they might hope that someone becomes Masochistic and starts over. But, frankly, it just left me feeling Hopeless.

I have been waiting for a long time to test out this game and the Weekend Trial gave me the opportunity to get through the entire story(I sided with the institute) with time left to explore and side quest.
Here is what I can say about the game:
1) It is by far graphicly superior to Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas.
2) The Power Armor sytem in this game is much more practical and in depth than previous games.
3) The story sort of has similar aspects of the Fallout 3 and New Vegas stories, it also allows you to briefly see the Fallout world just before the bombs drop, which is something I wanted for a long time. My only real problem with it is that I wish it was longer and more complex than it is.
4) The Settlement Building feature feels limited and incomplete, but I hope to see it fully realized in future games as I feel it has potential.
5) Since your Wanderer/Survivor is someone who lived before the US became the Wasteland I feel that they should have been more of a coveted ally to the factions of the game but for some reason they all seem to shrug it off like it is nothing or are disinterested in the Survivor's life before the Wasteland entirly. When brought up in conversations it barely lasts more than a couple lines of diologue which I find disapointing since it is the secondary driving force behind the character.
6) Play in survial mode if you want to REALLY have a "Your life is in constant danger" feel.
7) The Legendary creatures are plentiful no matter what difficulty you play on.
8) Death Claws are still scary af demons from hell
9) Don't go out into the Glowing Sea without a lot of stimpacks, ammo, some rad away and power armor, YOU.WILL.DIE
10) By exploring Vaults you uncover evidence of their REAL purpose and Vault-Tech's morally questionable plans for their residents is further expanded upon through various terminal entries and recordings found throughout the game.(This may not seem like much but it is integral to the entire story and you should definitely read through them since they are very telling)
All in all I think that if you love Fallout or even if you are new to the series, ask a friend if you can borrow their copy of the game to try it out, play through the story and some sidequests. I don't think there is really any one type of player this game will appeal to specifically, personally I loved my time playing this game. So if you end up enjoying it, buy it for your self, if not then try one of the previous games or wait for the next one and give the series a second chance because it really is great.

Dark Souls III is an action role-playing game set in a third-person perspective. According to director Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game's gameplay design "follows closely from Dark Souls II". Players are equipped with a variety of weapons including shortbows, explosives like fire bombs, greatswords and dual-wielding swords to fight against enemies, and shields that can be used to deflect an enemies' attack and protect the player from suffering damage. In addition, attacks can be evaded through dodge-rolling. Bonfires, which serve as checkpoints, also return from previous installments.
Ashes, according to Miyazaki, will play an important role in the game. Magic is also featured in the game. Each attack has two different styles. One of them is standard attack, while another provides power-ups to players, and is slightly more powerful. When performing miracles and spells, the players' magic points are consumed and decreased. In order to refilled these points, they need to consume Ash Estus Flask. There are two different Estus Flasks in the game. One of them can help refill magic points, while another refill hit points. Combat and movements were made faster and more fluid in Dark Souls III. Several players' movements, such as backstepping and swinging heavy weapons, can be performed more rapidly, allowing players to deal more damage in a short period of time.
Throughout the game, players encounter different types of enemies, each with different behaviors. Some of them change their combat pattern during battles. New combat features are introduced in Dark Souls III, including "Ready Stance", which are special abilities for players that allow them to deal much more damage to enemies than ordinary attacks are capable of. Small gravestones are also introduced. These gravestones light up when interacted with and not only serve as players' torches, but also provide additional lore to the game.
The game puts more focus on role-playing, in which the character builder is expanded and weapons are improved to provide more tactical options to players. The game features fewer maps than its predecessor Dark Souls II, but levels were interconnected and were made larger, which encourages exploration. The agility stat from Dark Souls II was removed from Dark Souls III. The game also features multiplayer elements, like the previous games in the series

My new favourite game of all time.
After finishing the second DLC it motivated me to go and 100% this game achievement wise, something I haven't felt the want to do in years. This game is a masterpiece. As a lover of boss battles this game fills all my needs, Mega Man, Castlevania, Ninja Gaiden, nothing else really gives me as long lasting memories as this game. The combat is refined and PVP to this day is still getting balance patches for weapons and such. Playing with friends left me with tonnes of memories and fun videos that will stay with me forever. The DLC bosses Sister Friede and Slave Knight Gael give you lasting boss fight memories as much as Dracula in Symphony of the Night and Artorias in Dark Souls 1. The final boss fight of the main game is incredible. Nameless King is the best optional boss in the main game, not to forget Midir the optional monster hunter like boss fight in the second DLC. If you only have time to play 1 playthrough, get all the DLC look up on the wiki and fight every boss, and go for the usurption ending, don't summon friends unless absolutely necessary as everyones first playthrough should ideally be experienced solo - Trust me, you won't regret giving this game a go. It's never too late to play through it, however PVP wise I'd get on as soon as possible as it may not be as lively as it is now. You don't have to play previous games to get into this one, in fact DS2 is barely mentioned, however if you are committed do play through Dark Souls 1, there are so many nods and references and pieces of lore relating to 1. Do give this game a go, do try and 'Git Gud' you won't ever regret it.

I want to give this game a good recommendation, the beginning and middle is so much fun, but by the end...
The enemies level up more than your heroes, Apprentice Dungeons are only challenging as you learn the mechanics. Veteran Dungeons are fairly challenging, but as you find great party combinations and learn the best abilities and synergies you will start winning fairly consistently. The next step up is Champion dungeons. They aren't fun. At this point the enemies have levelled up past your heroes. Maxed heroes with maxed weapons and maxed abilities will die in 3 hits if the RNG decides to focus fire him.
Even if you pick an awesome party, with maxed abilities, you are at best going to come out of a Champion dungeon with massive stress and clinging to life. If you do it with a fun party that isn't optimal you will die or lose.
This is especially bad because the game up to this point is a ton of fun, but after you reach this point it just becomes work to slog through completing all the bosses and grinding to level up replacements for the heroes who will die through RNG and overpowered enemies ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

I'm not the type to write reviews for games. Most of the time, the games i enjoy most or play the most, i dont even think of writing a review for, but this game is MUCH different from those.
Like most reviews, im going to do a "Pro's and Con's" type review.
Pro's:
- This game is free! this game is absolutley free to play, with little, unimportant, unemphasized micro transactions, now i know, i know "Microtransactions?? UGHHH im completley apphaled!! 0/10" but no, its not like that. unlike in CS:GO where micro transactions are shoved in your face with pressure to make your AK47 look like a chandelier, or like TF2 where you are pressured to make your character look like the next lady gaga concert outfit, you simply every once in a very very rare (and i mean RARE) blue moon you might get something like a loot box? i have one and you can buy a key to open it and get a skin for a gun or a t-shirt or something, but LIKE TF2, these skins/shirts are usless, and unlike shirts you find and put on In-Game, they can't give you any extra storage room to hold your weapons/bandages/meds e.t.c. All in all the micro transactions are really not pushed and the only thing you can really buy other than a key that is not free is the gold upgrade. Please please PLEASE do NOT get confused and think that this game is Pay-to-Play. It is not. The gold upgrade (which i myself do not even own) merley adds more character customization to the game (you can add more faces and make your character like green or red). I reccomend just playing free, but its up to you!
- This game has an active, competent Dev team. Yes people, free to play games that valve didnt create with GOOD devs DO exist, your on the page of one right now. The Dev team for unturned has put a lot of effort into making this game fun and enjoyable for everyone, with bug patches and more always being added to make sure the game stays fresh and fun.
- The game has little to no bugs. Most survival games are riddled with bugs the Dev team doesn't care to do anything about, which can make the game VERY unenjoyable. Unturned has NO major bugs that i myslef have witnessed in game, except for one, but im pretty sure that was a server-only bug that only existed on that server i was on (i kept fallling through the map then being teleported back to where i was).  All-in-All this game runs cleanley and smoothley, with minimal game-altering bugs.
- This game looks and runs BEUTIFULY. Yes, the fact that i think it looks really good for a free to play game is MY opinion, but what ISN'T my opinion ia the fact that the game runs very smoothley, with little lag. Sure, depending on your PC, there will be some lag here and there, but because of this games blockey, simple look, it plays very well, meaning that people who don't have an Alienware Area-51 custom GTX-1080 Ti water cooling, can play this game, making it fun if you cant run games like DayZ. (PS: this game STRONGLEY resembles DayZ in the way it plays, game mechanics wise, but in my opinion this game is better than DayZ)
- Finally, this game has A LOT of content with so much to do. From starting naked, looking for clothes and weapons, to gunning down hoards of the undead as well as the occasional surviver you see, this game has hours of content and replayablity. Got killed? Heres your chance for a fresh start! go find some clothes, a weapon, maybe even a gun if you're lucky enough, either way you won't get bored quickly with this game.
Con's:
- The playerbase on some servers can be toxic, with abusive admins, toxic, mean players and sometimes, hackers!
Obviously this isn't EXACTLY a Con, but more of a communtity issue. I thought i still might put it in, just as a warning. (PS: DO NOT get the idea from the trailer of the game that you will just meet randoms with gear and become friends. most of the time you will end up getting yourself killed if you aproach a geared person, even as a naked, fresh spawn. my advice to you is shoot first, ask questions later, or just avoid that person/run away.)
- This game lacks a reliable way to get needed items. Since this game is a survival game (and i love it!) you will rely mostly on scavenging, early and late game, and this WOULDN'T be a bad thing IF the drop system was a little more reliable. From experience, if you need something. (let it be meds, food, water, e.t.c.) you will have to FIND it. This can be INFURIATING and ver unenjoyable if everything has been looted. Imagine this, you are fully geared. Full armor, big guns, lots of ammo. You run the server, then, you realize, your at 20% radiation! well naturaly, you would just take some meds. BUT WAIT!! you're all out of meds! you used them all while fighting a hoard of zombies at the military base! oh well, guess i will just have to find them.... so where is the closest....town.....hospital?...ANYTHING?!?!?! you run down a road for seemingly forever, until you come across a town. you search around EVERYWHERE for meds, but find nothing. you die of radiation and some naked comes and takes all your hard earned lot. THE END. you see, the drop sytem in my lacks any real structure, but then again, it is a drop system.... so what can you really expect. this sytem can also make it hard to find goot gear early-game.
- finally, most servers are not vanilla. If you dont know what "vanilla" means, it basicaly means the server has only what the original version of the game had in it (no thing like teleporting or loot+, kits, e.t.c.) If you like vanilla, great! you found something you enjoy and should enjoy it to its fullest extent! but for me, i like vanilla because i like the challenge. sure, its cool if every zombie you kille drops a gun (loot+ servers) and sure, maybe it is cool to type something in chat and get a bunch of end-game gear (kits) but, like the challenge of finding your gear fair and square. This way, the game stays intersting, and is MUCH MUCH more satisfying to get it legitly, however, servers that ARE vavilla, are usually unpopulated, or on maps that your not looking to play on, or are like russian server (not that i have a problem with russian servers, i just dont speak russian xD). This means you are forced to play on servers that have all those extra, non-vanilla aspects that i previusly mentioned. i think there should be some official servers like in rust. just plain, vanilla, survival fun!
And that's it for ya! that was "Sirphantom's Unturned review" I hope it was helpful! now get out there and slay some zombies! -Sirphantom :D

A spaceship crashes on an alien world. Gears turn below the planet’s thin surface, moving subterranean continents borrowed from other lands. In the center, the Core hums with power—power the player and his allies need to return home.
Welcome to Spiral Knights! The hack-n’-slash gameplay is based around completing missions set in various areas of the clockwork labyrinth below, as well as exploring it on your own initiative. After acquiring a handful of starting weapons and armor, the player must periodically upgrade his arsenal to survive the lower levels. Other aspects of the game include guilds, bosses, PvP, holiday events and interactive pets.
Though it has always been a worthy time sink, SK was once something I could not recommend. This was because of its Energy system, which often made playing for free a difficult task. However, as of July 30th players can explore to their hearts’ content, and creating equipment is mostly Energy-independent. I’m still unsure of the merits of the crafting change, but that doesn't change the fact that Spiral Knights is better than ever... and that's saying something. Give it a try, but be warned – I will “back in my day” you at the slightest provocation.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this review so I could get it over with and get back to playing. Darkest Dungeon is a dark fantasy, turn-based RPG from Red Hook Studios. Also, I’m totally obsessed with it.
The Good
Even though Darkest Dungeon is still in early access, it has quickly become one of my most favorite games that I have ever played. It’s unforgiving. There’s zero hand-holding for new players. You do or you die. Once your characters begin to go up in level, there’s no going back. You must continually do harder and harder quests.
For starters, the art style is phenomenal. I don’t remember the last time I loved the art in a game this much. It’s dark, moody, and a perfect fit.
The classes of characters you can recruit transcend the age old monikers of “Warrior” or “Wizard” and, instead, have things like “Leper”, “Occultist”, or “Plague Doctor”. This alone is a breath of fresh air in a genre that I consider myself very steeped in.
The enemy designs are spectacular. Everything has a distinctly Lovecraftian feel to it. You can do battle with hideous fish men in the Cove or go to the Ruins and take on bloodthirsty cultists and hordes of the undead. Some enemies can be found in multiple areas, while others are exclusive to one area.
On the topic of the Cove and the Ruins, the various areas in the game in which you can quest are all fantastic. Currently, there are four: The Cove (the newest area), the Ruins, the Warrens, and the Weald.
The Torch mechanic is something that I find very cool and original. Depending on the level of light that you maintain by burning torches during quests, enemies that you encounter can be stronger or weaker. The risk/reward ratio comes into play as well. the darker it is, the better loot you’ll find. However, the darker it is, the more likely it is that your whole party will get eviscerated in a dark corner.
The Stress and Disease mechanics are pretty cool as well. Your character’s begin to get stressed while questing. This can lead to debilitating afflictions. You have to give them time off in town for their stress level to go down and for them to get back to being fighting fit. The same with diseases. If you contract a disease (I’m looking at you pigmen), you’ll need to get it fixed or your character’s stats will suffer.
The Bad
I have nothing bad at all to say about Darkest Dungeon. You know what is bad? The fact that you’re reading this review and not buying/playing it right the hell now.

I -love- this game's atmostphere, setting, character design, and theming. Truly a masterpiece. And I love the turn-based combat, and the large variety of character classes.
So why don't I recommend this game? Simply put, it is way too difficult to for your average gamer (in the beginning). The game suffers overall because of its difficulty balancing. All but hardcore gamers will quickly become frustrated and quit after losing their first few heroes and feeling like they've barely accomplished anything. It's a very, very slow start and a slow burn, until a point. After you jump this massive hurdle, the game becomes too easy quite quickly. I'm not sure -exactly- how devs could fix that, but there it is.
Because of this game's harsh early trials (and the fact that grinding is impossible once your hero outlevels a dungeon, OMG I wanted to kill someone when I found that out), the scope of the audience becomes severely limited.
My suggestion would be to introduce difficulty settings so that the game can be more accessible to a larger scope of players. If you go to the official forums, topics discussing difficulty settings quickly degrade to people flaming "filthy casuals" and how they're glad there's finally a game that appeals to their desire for hard as nails games. I can't even begin to understand the sort of elitism it takes for someone to say that the OPTION for a more casual experience shouldn't be permitted. Sigh.
Anyway, the game looks great and plays great, but the difficulty needs some severe tuning.

The main story is quite short which is disappointing. Due to the fact that bond between player and the main quest characters are weak, I couldn't get vicarious pleasure in the game. As a RGP game, it is unsatisfying, but as a story, the content is quite astonishing and enjoyable.

Furthermore, dialogues and interactions for players and NPCs are remarkable, every companions have their own attuitudes and relationship statues with you, which make the game more lively. In the conversation, there are sarcastic dialogues for you to pick which makes the game more entertaining. Being a jerk is part of our life right?
I would like to conclude my review of the game in short under my observation. This game's approach is trying to make you feel like you are living in the Commonwealth by using some small missions or you may say side missions and communicate with each other, NPCs are no longer a person for you to get missions but living together. Ironically, bond with player and side quest character are stronger and more enjoyable than main quest line.

Pros:
- Environment, especially in the wild as well as in all the destroyed areas are very impressive and immersive.
- Ambient Music, the OST sounds very good and fits the atmosphere, though the Radio Station's music and overall quality is low because the good music repeats after 30 minutes or even earlier and the radio man repeats the same crap over and over in a very short time.
- I really liked the idea of having companions and how you choose them/they choose you.
- Some things are well designed, like for example the Pip-Boy.
- I didn't really see many bugs.
- Allowed me to write a review that will be flamed and attacked by fanboys and franchise♥♥♥♥♥kissers.
Cons:
- Lore, the main story is BORING, UTTERLY BORING.
- Characters, or should I say lack of character? There is barely anyone that I could possibly remember. In the beginning Codsworth was funny. Piper also had character. That's it. Nobody else really had anything rememberworthy. Even the most important characters, according to the lore, had little to no character and just felt like they were placed there to fullfil a single role. Like the mayor of Diamond City, he is just a mayor. That's it.
- Additional Lore, side stories and remnants from the pre-war past are BORING, sure some are funny or interesting at first glance, but overall none really stunned me or were impressive.
- THIS IS NOT AN RPG, this game is a shooter game "with RPG elements" (R).
- V.A.T.S. IS A JOKE, it adds 0 to strategy. It is nice too look at, if you don't know how it works, but other than that it doesn't add any strategy or RPG-like depth into combat. None.
- Everything is kind of... expansive, extensive, quantified, but the quality is on a low level. You can have so many weapon, apparel mods. You can customize your own homes, etc. But either it is boring and repetetive or it doesn't really have any depth into it. Regarding the Weapon/Armor mods, you can change it to your liking while seeming in depth but overall all the weapons don't really have a huge difference between each other. Sure, you can adjust some minor things, but it doesn't really allow you to make anything innovative. Also the house customization is a joke. You can make it look to your liking but it doesn't really have any function or bonus, except the couple crafting tables of different kind and the Power Armor stand. That's it. All the other junk is just for looks.
- DIALOGUE IS A JOKE, it is terrible. Not credible, when seeing/reading/listening to it. No matter what you "choose" the result of the "dialogue" will always be what the game wants you to do. I literally even had situations, where my character answered one generic and very general answer instead of the one I chose. There is no real "choice" it's purely an illusion. Of course games do that frequently, but this game does this even more annoyingly and hardcore while pretending to be open-world, extremely extensive and fantastic, etc. Also you can only talk to certain types of people.
- Engine, the graphics etc. are terrible. It's obsolete.
- Load times, Witcher 3 looks 10 times more gorgeous and it has only a single loading time, which is when loading a save game. In this game you face a loading screen every time you change an area. And the game's graphics and overall visual quality is low, according to what is expected from an overpriced game on release.
- REALLY BAD DOCUMENTATION, a tutorial is basically non-existent. You have to find out how 90% of the game works by yourself and sometimes you simply have to look it up on Google. Imagining that someone who isn't too familiar with games would try to play this game, I wouldn't wonder at all if they would stop playing shortly after and then be attacked by fan boys, because they simply don't understand how the game works.
- PRETENDING TO BE A SURVIVAL GAME, it has many survival mechanics on the one hand, but on the other hand it tries to suppress them again, so in the end it doesn't make sense and just makes the game crappier. For example I put almost all my SPECIAL points into strength right in the beginning of the game. But the maximum weight you can carry was STILL an utter joke. So apparently this was one of the "we make this game more survivey" thing. On the other hand you get tons of random loot and crap you don't even need which diminishes the "survival" aspect on the game. Mixing both sided mechanics together just makes it annoying and unnecessary.
I probably could add more points, but that's all for now. If you want to play an RPG game, get Divinity: Original Sin or the newest Torment. If you want to play a Fallout game, then go get Fallout 2 or something.
But if you want to play a shooter game with some extra lore (compared to other shooter games) and an impressive environment, then this game is for you. Not for me and not for many people who would expect a typical "Fallout" game. Because this one is not.
This game is not a "Fallout" game.

Dark Souls III is an action role-playing game set in a third-person perspective. According to director Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game's gameplay design "follows closely from Dark Souls II". Players are equipped with a variety of weapons including shortbows, explosives like fire bombs, greatswords and dual-wielding swords to fight against enemies, and shields that can be used to deflect an enemies' attack and protect the player from suffering damage. In addition, attacks can be evaded through dodge-rolling. Bonfires, which serve as checkpoints, also return from previous installments.
Ashes, according to Miyazaki, will play an important role in the game. Magic is also featured in the game. Each attack has two different styles. One of them is standard attack, while another provides power-ups to players, and is slightly more powerful. When performing miracles and spells, the players' magic points are consumed and decreased. In order to refilled these points, they need to consume Ash Estus Flask. There are two different Estus Flasks in the game. One of them can help refill magic points, while another refill hit points. Combat and movements were made faster and more fluid in Dark Souls III. Several players' movements, such as backstepping and swinging heavy weapons, can be performed more rapidly, allowing players to deal more damage in a short period of time.
Throughout the game, players encounter different types of enemies, each with different behaviors. Some of them change their combat pattern during battles. New combat features are introduced in Dark Souls III, including "Ready Stance", which are special abilities for players that allow them to deal much more damage to enemies than ordinary attacks are capable of. Small gravestones are also introduced. These gravestones light up when interacted with and not only serve as players' torches, but also provide additional lore to the game.
The game puts more focus on role-playing, in which the character builder is expanded and weapons are improved to provide more tactical options to players. The game features fewer maps than its predecessor Dark Souls II, but levels were interconnected and were made larger, which encourages exploration. The agility stat from Dark Souls II was removed from Dark Souls III. The game also features multiplayer elements, like the previous games in the series

Due to the removal of the game's energy system, everyone who completed the main storyline grinded the exact same boss level in order to grind for ingame currency. What do players do with the currency? There are three possible things:
~Get stronger gear in order to more efficiently grind the same level, or to duke it out in a PvP where a select few weapons and armor pieces are clearly superior to the others. Hint: they are the Achereon, Polaris, Combuster, and Chaos armor.
~Trade ingame currency with other players for Steam games. Working for minimum wage is significantly faster at acquiring money than grinding in this game.
~Spend ingame currency (and now REAL MONEY) for overpriced recolors of cosmetic armor pieces and accessories. This would be useful if the gameplay was satisfying.
A few select weapons broke the metagame, and due to no incentive to spend money (other than cosmetics), OOO had some layoffs from SEGA. There hasn't been any meaningful updates with actual gameplay-like content for many years, which would cripple any MMO. There used to be a reason to go to the weaker levels in order to actually explore; however, the somewhat new Mission system removed any need to explore. The cutesy art style, unfortunately, does not make up for this.
There are many other MMOs out there to enjoy. This game ran its course; it was fun, charming, innovative, and creative while I was active. Now, I would recommend for those who currently play the game to find something new to enjoy, and for those who are interested in joining to reconsider.

I'm not the type to write reviews for games. Most of the time, the games i enjoy most or play the most, i dont even think of writing a review for, but this game is MUCH different from those.
Like most reviews, im going to do a "Pro's and Con's" type review.
Pro's:
- This game is free! this game is absolutley free to play, with little, unimportant, unemphasized micro transactions, now i know, i know "Microtransactions?? UGHHH im completley apphaled!! 0/10" but no, its not like that. unlike in CS:GO where micro transactions are shoved in your face with pressure to make your AK47 look like a chandelier, or like TF2 where you are pressured to make your character look like the next lady gaga concert outfit, you simply every once in a very very rare (and i mean RARE) blue moon you might get something like a loot box? i have one and you can buy a key to open it and get a skin for a gun or a t-shirt or something, but LIKE TF2, these skins/shirts are usless, and unlike shirts you find and put on In-Game, they can't give you any extra storage room to hold your weapons/bandages/meds e.t.c. All in all the micro transactions are really not pushed and the only thing you can really buy other than a key that is not free is the gold upgrade. Please please PLEASE do NOT get confused and think that this game is Pay-to-Play. It is not. The gold upgrade (which i myself do not even own) merley adds more character customization to the game (you can add more faces and make your character like green or red). I reccomend just playing free, but its up to you!
- This game has an active, competent Dev team. Yes people, free to play games that valve didnt create with GOOD devs DO exist, your on the page of one right now. The Dev team for unturned has put a lot of effort into making this game fun and enjoyable for everyone, with bug patches and more always being added to make sure the game stays fresh and fun.
- The game has little to no bugs. Most survival games are riddled with bugs the Dev team doesn't care to do anything about, which can make the game VERY unenjoyable. Unturned has NO major bugs that i myslef have witnessed in game, except for one, but im pretty sure that was a server-only bug that only existed on that server i was on (i kept fallling through the map then being teleported back to where i was).  All-in-All this game runs cleanley and smoothley, with minimal game-altering bugs.
- This game looks and runs BEUTIFULY. Yes, the fact that i think it looks really good for a free to play game is MY opinion, but what ISN'T my opinion ia the fact that the game runs very smoothley, with little lag. Sure, depending on your PC, there will be some lag here and there, but because of this games blockey, simple look, it plays very well, meaning that people who don't have an Alienware Area-51 custom GTX-1080 Ti water cooling, can play this game, making it fun if you cant run games like DayZ. (PS: this game STRONGLEY resembles DayZ in the way it plays, game mechanics wise, but in my opinion this game is better than DayZ)
- Finally, this game has A LOT of content with so much to do. From starting naked, looking for clothes and weapons, to gunning down hoards of the undead as well as the occasional surviver you see, this game has hours of content and replayablity. Got killed? Heres your chance for a fresh start! go find some clothes, a weapon, maybe even a gun if you're lucky enough, either way you won't get bored quickly with this game.
Con's:
- The playerbase on some servers can be toxic, with abusive admins, toxic, mean players and sometimes, hackers!
Obviously this isn't EXACTLY a Con, but more of a communtity issue. I thought i still might put it in, just as a warning. (PS: DO NOT get the idea from the trailer of the game that you will just meet randoms with gear and become friends. most of the time you will end up getting yourself killed if you aproach a geared person, even as a naked, fresh spawn. my advice to you is shoot first, ask questions later, or just avoid that person/run away.)
- This game lacks a reliable way to get needed items. Since this game is a survival game (and i love it!) you will rely mostly on scavenging, early and late game, and this WOULDN'T be a bad thing IF the drop system was a little more reliable. From experience, if you need something. (let it be meds, food, water, e.t.c.) you will have to FIND it. This can be INFURIATING and ver unenjoyable if everything has been looted. Imagine this, you are fully geared. Full armor, big guns, lots of ammo. You run the server, then, you realize, your at 20% radiation! well naturaly, you would just take some meds. BUT WAIT!! you're all out of meds! you used them all while fighting a hoard of zombies at the military base! oh well, guess i will just have to find them.... so where is the closest....town.....hospital?...ANYTHING?!?!?! you run down a road for seemingly forever, until you come across a town. you search around EVERYWHERE for meds, but find nothing. you die of radiation and some naked comes and takes all your hard earned lot. THE END. you see, the drop sytem in my lacks any real structure, but then again, it is a drop system.... so what can you really expect. this sytem can also make it hard to find goot gear early-game.
- finally, most servers are not vanilla. If you dont know what "vanilla" means, it basicaly means the server has only what the original version of the game had in it (no thing like teleporting or loot+, kits, e.t.c.) If you like vanilla, great! you found something you enjoy and should enjoy it to its fullest extent! but for me, i like vanilla because i like the challenge. sure, its cool if every zombie you kille drops a gun (loot+ servers) and sure, maybe it is cool to type something in chat and get a bunch of end-game gear (kits) but, like the challenge of finding your gear fair and square. This way, the game stays intersting, and is MUCH MUCH more satisfying to get it legitly, however, servers that ARE vavilla, are usually unpopulated, or on maps that your not looking to play on, or are like russian server (not that i have a problem with russian servers, i just dont speak russian xD). This means you are forced to play on servers that have all those extra, non-vanilla aspects that i previusly mentioned. i think there should be some official servers like in rust. just plain, vanilla, survival fun!
And that's it for ya! that was "Sirphantom's Unturned review" I hope it was helpful! now get out there and slay some zombies! -Sirphantom :D

A fan of lovecraft, roguelikes, and rpgs I was really excited for this game.  I was sold on the solid art style and the neat idea that mental stress is a serious factor from all the crazy-scary lovecraftian stuff your party is putting up with.  Unfortunately, how it plays out has major flaws that are just killing any existing fun for me.
First off, the stress thing just becomes a random feeling annoyance most of the time.  It is like playing a turn based RPG where you are managing all the usual stuff, health, upgrades, gear, spells etc, BUT additonally someone is slapping your head often and usually for an unknown reason.  When it works and it is clear why stress is happening it can be interesting and part of the fun -- like when your party gets critted hard, they all do an underwear check and the narrator says "witnessing a killing blow bends the mind," or when someone freaks the hell out because they reach 100 stress and they start doing panicy actions.   But those are the far minoriy reasons.  Sometimes they will all of a sudden have a huge stress bubble, when nothing happened at all.  75% of the time it seems totally arbitrary and you won't even know why they are gaining stress.
Second, not being able to heal (health or stress) outside of combat is terrible, horrible game design.  It makes no sense whatsoever -- "hey healer help me out,  I'm bleeding and blighted and low on health." says the warrior.  "NOPE, sorry, but that last enemy just died so ... you know, my hands are tied.  Wait until someone attacks us before I can heal you, you know... just like in real life."  Aside from how stupid that is, it creates the annoying but clearly best strategy where you have to whittle the enemies down to one, and then keep that enemy alive by using non-damaging attacks until you heal up and/or reduce-stress on your whole party.  This is just boring and tedious.  Incredibly, the game then tries to punish you for you know, being smart and managing your health and stress well within the system the designers made by adding B.S. stress... because? -- "OH no, that skeleton with 2 health that we've been kicking around for the last 5 min is SO SCARY... jeez, I'm getting stressed and scared now!"  That is just more lazy, bad design trying to mask a fatal flaw in the design.
Lastly, you will be flooded with characters.  At first it is kind of fun and interesting to learn about the different classes and their abilities, even though it is a lot of information at once.  But even after you learn, you see that this flood will be constant.  It is really hard to find your main party members in this river of characters.  The pacing just feels very off and it makes you not care about anyone eventually.
I will admit that I haven't gotten into the meat of the game, but those first two points are huge glaring issues that make it so that I can already see how tedious it will be to even keep playing at all.  Furthermore, after playing it I've been reading more about it and other reviews here confirm the grindfest that it is already feeling like.

Dark Souls III is an action role-playing game set in a third-person perspective. According to director Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game's gameplay design "follows closely from Dark Souls II". Players are equipped with a variety of weapons including shortbows, explosives like fire bombs, greatswords and dual-wielding swords to fight against enemies, and shields that can be used to deflect an enemies' attack and protect the player from suffering damage. In addition, attacks can be evaded through dodge-rolling. Bonfires, which serve as checkpoints, also return from previous installments.
Ashes, according to Miyazaki, will play an important role in the game. Magic is also featured in the game. Each attack has two different styles. One of them is standard attack, while another provides power-ups to players, and is slightly more powerful. When performing miracles and spells, the players' magic points are consumed and decreased. In order to refilled these points, they need to consume Ash Estus Flask. There are two different Estus Flasks in the game. One of them can help refill magic points, while another refill hit points. Combat and movements were made faster and more fluid in Dark Souls III. Several players' movements, such as backstepping and swinging heavy weapons, can be performed more rapidly, allowing players to deal more damage in a short period of time.
Throughout the game, players encounter different types of enemies, each with different behaviors. Some of them change their combat pattern during battles. New combat features are introduced in Dark Souls III, including "Ready Stance", which are special abilities for players that allow them to deal much more damage to enemies than ordinary attacks are capable of. Small gravestones are also introduced. These gravestones light up when interacted with and not only serve as players' torches, but also provide additional lore to the game.
The game puts more focus on role-playing, in which the character builder is expanded and weapons are improved to provide more tactical options to players. The game features fewer maps than its predecessor Dark Souls II, but levels were interconnected and were made larger, which encourages exploration. The agility stat from Dark Souls II was removed from Dark Souls III. The game also features multiplayer elements, like the previous games in the series

Okay, I made a recommendation in the past of this game; and since then, my opinion has changed.
Honestly, the economy in this game is a pretty good representation of what the real world's economy looks like. There are basically 3 stages to this game
1. You start out making just enough money to make the beginning tier weapons and armour. The game seems pretty appealing because the make it really easy to craft things at the beginning of the game. Things seem to work out pretty well, until you get to the second stage.
2. Armour begins to cost more than 100 CE (The amount of energy you regenerate in a day), and you have to begin grinding to get enough currency to buy more CE. You buy energy in packs of 100, costing about 2 days of grinding each at this point in the game. it gets even more frustrating, as the cost of armour increases even more as you improve it. The costs go like this
(Beginning game armour)
1* = 10 CE
2* = 50 CE
(Mid game armour)
3* = 200 CE
4* = 400 CE
(End game armour)
5* = 800 CE
On top of all this, it costs you 10 CE to explore a dungeon. So you can't even use all of your temporary energy for crafting.
3. After many grueling weeks of grinding (Not exagerating), you finally obtain a full set of 5* armour. This gets you access to the final boss dungeon; where you can earn up to 200 CE worth of currency per day. This allows you to grind continuously for more and more CE; as you're making more than you're spending. Eventually, you learn how to manipulate the game a little bit (selling things on the auction house, and dragging characters on seperate accounts through the final boss dungeon with you). You learn how to use the money you have, to make more money, and quickly.
However, most people don't play this game long enough to make it to the third stage. Because of this, everyone who has made it to the end game gets a lot of respect from other players; which is one of the reasons I still play this game.
Also, the PvP mode is very entertaining and addicting (Once you obtain decent gear at least). Occasionally , I find myself going on sometimes just to play against other players.
But overall, this is a pretty decent game. It would be a whole lot better if they did something about the grinding though. In the next update, they plan on adding difficulty settings (Higher difficulty = more money). Hopefully that helps the problem.

"Terraria in space" isn't really fair to this game. This game isn't even finished yet and I already feel that it's far more then Terraria managed to be. Starbound looks like a 2d side-scroller but it has a depth that I would even dare to compare to an Elderscrolls game. It may look like a simple space exploration game but I expect great things from this. As it stands now, there's no real story and only a few beginner quests. But if you get this Early Access version and get the better gear and do the few quests you get, you actually start getting around out there in the galaxy and coming accross worlds with villages of various races with quirky personalities for some of the towns folk... there's even sky-pirates! One of the things that impressed me a lot were the various books and manuscripts and diaries found in villages and other places. You find a Prisoners diary complaining about the food and the bad company and, "oh my god what is that!? AHhhh!!" you'll also find a military base with a soldier's log book talking about spoilery type stuff but also that he was getting stir-crazy being cooped up in his base, which probably explains why they're all crazy and shooting at me when I drop in to say hi.
Even un-finished this game has more spirit and personality then Terreria ever though of. I sincearly hope the people responsible for this thing take the real opptortunity that they have to create an epic game that could actually be on par with the likes of Skyrim. A a whole big main quest line with story and memorable NPC's and everything. The galaxy is so huge that you could probably have star-charts and manuals and log books hidden around that say things like, "There's cool stuff and/or things to do at these coordinates in this sector in that system on one of those planets!"
