Firstly I should say that I'm writing this review based on having played a limited amount of the game during the free weekend, having never played any previous Fallout games, but having played Skyrim. The first part of the game, set in the "past", is quite a treat. The visuals, such as the 1950s-esque setting, are all very cool. I only wish there was more to do/explore in this time setting. Perhaps too quickly, we get rushed into the future, and find a complete wasteland. There's something quite chilling about listening to cheery instrumental music on the "classical" radio station, while looking at a desolate world. However, once the novelty of everything wears off, I found that the game I was playing was so... familiar. Basically, it's Skyrim! Okay, it *looks* completely different, but underneath the surface, it feels like I'm playing the same...exact... game (even on the surface, you can tell it's the same dated graphics engine). This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but for me, I've been there and done that already. In Skyrim, there were dungeons, here, there are sewers. Yawn. I'm sick of having to browse through lists of hundreds of inventory items trying to find what I want. They say that the game has thousands of hours of voice acting, but to me most of it sounds like people just reading lines. And why is it always sunny? Aren't there are any overcast days? Rainy days? The game also runs rather sluggishly on my GTX660 (@1680x1050), despite it exceeding the minimum requirements and being less than 4 years old. Skyrim ran fine. However, a lot of people out there will probably have faster cards than this, so it's not a huge issue. In summary, I would recommend this game to someone who perhaps has not played Skyrim before, or someone obsessed with everything Fallout. For me, though, it just felt like much of the same.

Ok, now seriously, buy this game. You wont regret it. This game will take a lot of time and effort from you, but it is well worth it. I have more than 90 hrs on the game, and it still feels fresh. there is always stuff to do, and i havent even touched the NG+.
Pros:
- Great combat system. I have never seen a combat system that good. Every single weapon is unique in its own way, and there are definitely no weak or noob weapons in here. The system is easy to learn, but hard to master. The combat is entirely skill based, and does not depend on your level or weapon.
- the overall design of the game is amaizing. Almost every single bossfight was challenging enough, but even though some bosses are extremely hard, the game never made me wanna quit. The boss desighn is also great. The bosses are really different, unlike in some other games.
-As I already said, there is always stuff to do, and this game doesnt get boring. You can try NG+, you can start a new game as a different class, with a totally different gameplay, and there are also DLC's that extend the gameplay and make the game even longer.
Cons:
-This game has a weird coop system. Every single time you have to use an ember to see other peoples summoning signs, and getting an ember is not that easy, and really depends on your luck (random drops from enemies)
-I understand that this was supposed to be mostly a console game, but buying a controller for it feels a little too much. The game has the keyboard controls, but those are some of the worst controls i saw out there. You will have to buy a controller, or suffer on the first boss for like 3 hrs. The game also doesnt show the keyboard keys. Instead it shows you the controller controls. I managed to complete the first half of the game by using keyboard, but then i just couldnt proceed without using a controller.
Summary:
This game is definitely worth 60$ I spent on it. In my steam library, this is the only game i didnt really regret buying. The game has its own unique style that cant be compared to anything else. The game also has an amazing lore, which seems simple at first, but as you dig further into it, you realize that every single thing in this game has a meaning to it, and every NPC has a story.

Dark Souls III is an action role-playing game set in a third-person perspective. According to director Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game's gameplay design "follows closely from Dark Souls II". Players are equipped with a variety of weapons including shortbows, explosives like fire bombs, greatswords and dual-wielding swords to fight against enemies, and shields that can be used to deflect an enemies' attack and protect the player from suffering damage. In addition, attacks can be evaded through dodge-rolling. Bonfires, which serve as checkpoints, also return from previous installments.
Ashes, according to Miyazaki, will play an important role in the game. Magic is also featured in the game. Each attack has two different styles. One of them is standard attack, while another provides power-ups to players, and is slightly more powerful. When performing miracles and spells, the players' magic points are consumed and decreased. In order to refilled these points, they need to consume Ash Estus Flask. There are two different Estus Flasks in the game. One of them can help refill magic points, while another refill hit points. Combat and movements were made faster and more fluid in Dark Souls III. Several players' movements, such as backstepping and swinging heavy weapons, can be performed more rapidly, allowing players to deal more damage in a short period of time.
Throughout the game, players encounter different types of enemies, each with different behaviors. Some of them change their combat pattern during battles. New combat features are introduced in Dark Souls III, including "Ready Stance", which are special abilities for players that allow them to deal much more damage to enemies than ordinary attacks are capable of. Small gravestones are also introduced. These gravestones light up when interacted with and not only serve as players' torches, but also provide additional lore to the game.
The game puts more focus on role-playing, in which the character builder is expanded and weapons are improved to provide more tactical options to players. The game features fewer maps than its predecessor Dark Souls II, but levels were interconnected and were made larger, which encourages exploration. The agility stat from Dark Souls II was removed from Dark Souls III. The game also features multiplayer elements, like the previous games in the series

Gameplay-wise it´s a very solid, well designed, turn-based dungeon crawler with some unique mechanics,

Heroes come, heroes die, but your estate goes on, growing with the loot your adventurers manages to bring back.

The games´ only flaw, in my opinion, lies in it´s currently limited gameplay, the dungeon-crawling is brilliant, but the game offers little variety apart from this (and the estate building).
Still, there´s something to be said for doing one thing and doing it with style and competence!
Bottom line: fantastic, dark and gorgeous game that rewards patience and intelligence.

I've seen a lot of negative reviews from people lately and I thought I'd put this out. Those of you who may already be spoiled by the fallout franchise may be disappointed in this game based on the reviews from others who have played fallout games before. I can't know. This is my first fallout game I've played and I've enjoyed playing it quite a bit. I caught it on sale and was able to trial it before I purchased it during a free weekend. I'm not one to pay more than $40 for a game these days with many other games $20 and lower that are real good. I like to save money where possible.
The story in this game is a bit hard to follow but the base premise that I've seen is you're looking for your kid that was kidnapped while you were in cryo stasis after atomic bombs were dropped - No spoilers there, if you played 1 hour of the game you should know that. (There won't be any spoilers because I still have no idea where my kid is at this point so its safe to read on).
The game's intro is pretty immersive, you can play as a male or female and both story lines are identical however there are a few female specific items like "black widow" skill that will allow you to persuade men better than women, (I assume a male equivilant is there on the male side of things, but I don't know). The intro you get cryo frozen and then wake up at some point in the future where you witness your kid's kidnapping and in the process they kill your spouse who tried to protect the baby from kidnapping. There's a mention that "at least we have a backup" while they look at you. No idea what that means...but it sounds interesting.
After a while you wake up due to a power failure in your cryo tube and you have to find your way out of the fallout shelter. Once you reach the surface you must find your way around the destroyed landscape. The visuals in the game are amazing for a 2015 game in my book. Still looks great compared to other games.
After a short bit you find allies and then they help you setup a settlement which is almost a game in itself where you build up a small community of AI. You can build shelter walls and make your own structures. You setup everything from water supplies to defenses to electricity for lights. I haven't been attacked yet and I'm not sure you ever will get attacked, but having defenses, and food and water make your people happy which make them more productive.
The base building is a bit strange and cumbersome and needs a lot of work. For a game that's been out for nearly 2 years i'm very disappointed in the building system. I'd hope they would have fixed these things and made it more intiuitive but videos I've watched are from the release period are pretty much exactly as it is now and its upsetting they haven't improved on it at all. You're unable to rebuild standing structures or even repair them to their former glory prior to the nukes going off and that's also a big minus to me. Having to live in a hole filled building is annoying. Some people have gotten very creative and the videos show this on how to repair those buildings but I for one don't like their "solutions" of using glitches to have to patch holes. The lack of wall prefabs with windows (which you'd think that all the glass bottles laying around you'd be able to craft a window...) is upsetting. I have a base that basically is 4 walls, no windows and very ugly looking with salvaged up trailor roofing rolls as walls. It def keeps with the feeling of scraping up anything you can find, but it would be nice to be able to do something that would allow for better looking walls (maybe a building skill that would open up better looking more refined walls) ANYTHING would be nice. I hate living in shacks and busted up buildings. Just my opinion, clearly that's not what the game designers were going for so I live with it.
Combat in the game is intersting to say the least. You have two ways to fight, the V.A.T.S system where you can have the game do all your aiming for you based on your character's skills and situation targeting specific body parts such as arms or head or torso and then a roll determines if you hit or not and you have limited action points to spend each "round" of combat, however its mixed with the second type of combat which is more FPS where you aim and hit targets. I'm much better at playing the game without using the V.A.T.S system as I can aim better than my character's skills can. Also when your waiting for your action points to build to do another round of AI controlled aiming, you still have to move around and can't do anything like run or anything like that. You can shoot and move, but to me that seems crazy since you already shot. To me combat should be one or the other, the mix of combat with the V.A.T.S. system doesn't make sense. The V.A.T.S. system should be more tactical combat where you move certain distances and have aiming, and shooting kind of like an XCOM system, or you can be in FPS mode where you just do your own aiming and shooting, but not both. I'm not sure how they did in the other games but this system is a waste. I use it occationally just to see the action sequences but most of the time I just FPS my way into it.
The stealth system is pretty good as well where you can sneak around and pickpocket people if properly approached and with the appropriate skill however your companion will ALWAYS give you away so you must command them to stay put if you want to stealth into a situation. If your skill is high enough you can even walk up to someone and steal all their stuff and drop a live grenade in their pocket and watch the fun...:). The downside to their crime and punishment system is that if you decide to pick the pocket of a main city guard or something and they catch you, the whole city comes down on you like a bomb, and the biggest problem, you can't undo it without a reload. You can have 30 - 40 people on you instantly and it seems they have some level of omniscience where they can see you even inside someone's house in another instance. I broke into a house once in diamond city (the main city) and was in the middle of snooping around when every merchant from the main area came into my instance area and there were so many guards and merchants trying to kill me in this guys house there wasn't any room to even move. So if you want to stealth stuff, be sure you quicksave before doing it. Not sure if that's a bug or not, when I broke into this house, nobody was around and nobody had line of sight on me so i have no idea how that happened. Seemed to me if someone saw me, it should be me vs that guy and nobody else, but whatever...
Open World, def intesting. No worries if you want to get around quickly, there's no working vehicles in the game. IMO that's stupid. You should be given a bike or car or something or could fix one up and have that available to you. Instead you have a teleporting system where you can "fast travel" somewhere. In my book an open world should be that, open, huge, persistant, and always dangerous to travel on. The fast travel makes it small and safe traveling. Some people might like that, but not really me. Give me a horse or a car or a bike or something I can ride and let me see the world you all painstakingly made. The game makes you go to any location at least once in the open world, but after you get a few key points fast travel makes it easy to get somewhere pretty easily.
So I've ran out of available text so I'll cut the rest short:
TL;DR - The game is pretty fun. There's a lot of neat things you can do, it has some flaws but overall I've enjoyed the game. If you've played the franchise before you might be disapointed, thankfully I wasn't poisoned by the previous games and therefore enjoyed this one. If its your first jump into fallout, and you like open world adventure games, this one is for you. The $50 - $60 price tag is pretty steep in my book, wait for a sale and get it less than $30. Its worth at least that much.

I have been waiting for a long time to test out this game and the Weekend Trial gave me the opportunity to get through the entire story(I sided with the institute) with time left to explore and side quest.
Here is what I can say about the game:
1) It is by far graphicly superior to Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas.
2) The Power Armor sytem in this game is much more practical and in depth than previous games.
3) The story sort of has similar aspects of the Fallout 3 and New Vegas stories, it also allows you to briefly see the Fallout world just before the bombs drop, which is something I wanted for a long time. My only real problem with it is that I wish it was longer and more complex than it is.
4) The Settlement Building feature feels limited and incomplete, but I hope to see it fully realized in future games as I feel it has potential.
5) Since your Wanderer/Survivor is someone who lived before the US became the Wasteland I feel that they should have been more of a coveted ally to the factions of the game but for some reason they all seem to shrug it off like it is nothing or are disinterested in the Survivor's life before the Wasteland entirly. When brought up in conversations it barely lasts more than a couple lines of diologue which I find disapointing since it is the secondary driving force behind the character.
6) Play in survial mode if you want to REALLY have a "Your life is in constant danger" feel.
7) The Legendary creatures are plentiful no matter what difficulty you play on.
8) Death Claws are still scary af demons from hell
9) Don't go out into the Glowing Sea without a lot of stimpacks, ammo, some rad away and power armor, YOU.WILL.DIE
10) By exploring Vaults you uncover evidence of their REAL purpose and Vault-Tech's morally questionable plans for their residents is further expanded upon through various terminal entries and recordings found throughout the game.(This may not seem like much but it is integral to the entire story and you should definitely read through them since they are very telling)
All in all I think that if you love Fallout or even if you are new to the series, ask a friend if you can borrow their copy of the game to try it out, play through the story and some sidequests. I don't think there is really any one type of player this game will appeal to specifically, personally I loved my time playing this game. So if you end up enjoying it, buy it for your self, if not then try one of the previous games or wait for the next one and give the series a second chance because it really is great.

Quite magnificient!
It feels, looks and sounds wonderful, the design reminiscent of Games Workshops "Warhammer" universe with a touch of H.P. Lovecraft added for good measue.
In it´s own twisted way it is one of the most beautiful games I own.
Gameplay-wise it´s a very solid, well designed, turn-based dungeon crawler with some unique mechanics,
you do not actually play as the heroes, but rather the person who employ these heroes to try and destroy the evil plaguing the vast estate you have inherited.
Heroes come, heroes die, but your estate goes on, growing with the loot your adventurers manages to bring back.
It´s very chance based, which makes for very tense gameplay, but can be immensely frustrating when your well made plan falls to pieces because nothing you do hits and the enemies won´t stop landing critical hits.
Worth mentioning also is the difficulty, your plans will fail, you will face disaster,
but the game is designed around this and there´s always a way to bounce back.
The games´ only flaw, in my opinion, lies in it´s currently limited gameplay, the dungeon-crawling is brilliant, but the game offers little variety apart from this (and the estate building).
Still, there´s something to be said for doing one thing and doing it with style and competence!
Bottom line: fantastic, dark and gorgeous game that rewards patience and intelligence.
Limited gameplay but well worth the low pricetag for the gentleperson looking for a challenge.

The best sniff I played so far. Buy it if you are a masochist.
Ok, now seriously, buy this game. You wont regret it. This game will take a lot of time and effort from you, but it is well worth it. I have more than 90 hrs on the game, and it still feels fresh. there is always stuff to do, and i havent even touched the NG+.
Pros:
- Great combat system. I have never seen a combat system that good. Every single weapon is unique in its own way, and there are definitely no weak or noob weapons in here. The system is easy to learn, but hard to master. The combat is entirely skill based, and does not depend on your level or weapon.
- the overall design of the game is amaizing. Almost every single bossfight was challenging enough, but even though some bosses are extremely hard, the game never made me wanna quit. The boss desighn is also great. The bosses are really different, unlike in some other games.
-As I already said, there is always stuff to do, and this game doesnt get boring. You can try NG+, you can start a new game as a different class, with a totally different gameplay, and there are also DLC's that extend the gameplay and make the game even longer.
Cons:
-This game has a weird coop system. Every single time you have to use an ember to see other peoples summoning signs, and getting an ember is not that easy, and really depends on your luck (random drops from enemies)
-I understand that this was supposed to be mostly a console game, but buying a controller for it feels a little too much. The game has the keyboard controls, but those are some of the worst controls i saw out there. You will have to buy a controller, or suffer on the first boss for like 3 hrs. The game also doesnt show the keyboard keys. Instead it shows you the controller controls. I managed to complete the first half of the game by using keyboard, but then i just couldnt proceed without using a controller.
Summary:
This game is definitely worth 60$ I spent on it. In my steam library, this is the only game i didnt really regret buying. The game has its own unique style that cant be compared to anything else. The game also has an amazing lore, which seems simple at first, but as you dig further into it, you realize that every single thing in this game has a meaning to it, and every NPC has a story.

I've seen a lot of negative reviews from people lately and I thought I'd put this out. Those of you who may already be spoiled by the fallout franchise may be disappointed in this game based on the reviews from others who have played fallout games before. I can't know. This is my first fallout game I've played and I've enjoyed playing it quite a bit. I caught it on sale and was able to trial it before I purchased it during a free weekend. I'm not one to pay more than $40 for a game these days with many other games $20 and lower that are real good. I like to save money where possible.
The story in this game is a bit hard to follow but the base premise that I've seen is you're looking for your kid that was kidnapped while you were in cryo stasis after atomic bombs were dropped - No spoilers there, if you played 1 hour of the game you should know that. (There won't be any spoilers because I still have no idea where my kid is at this point so its safe to read on).
The game's intro is pretty immersive, you can play as a male or female and both story lines are identical however there are a few female specific items like "black widow" skill that will allow you to persuade men better than women, (I assume a male equivilant is there on the male side of things, but I don't know). The intro you get cryo frozen and then wake up at some point in the future where you witness your kid's kidnapping and in the process they kill your spouse who tried to protect the baby from kidnapping. There's a mention that "at least we have a backup" while they look at you. No idea what that means...but it sounds interesting.
After a while you wake up due to a power failure in your cryo tube and you have to find your way out of the fallout shelter. Once you reach the surface you must find your way around the destroyed landscape. The visuals in the game are amazing for a 2015 game in my book. Still looks great compared to other games.
After a short bit you find allies and then they help you setup a settlement which is almost a game in itself where you build up a small community of AI. You can build shelter walls and make your own structures. You setup everything from water supplies to defenses to electricity for lights. I haven't been attacked yet and I'm not sure you ever will get attacked, but having defenses, and food and water make your people happy which make them more productive.
The base building is a bit strange and cumbersome and needs a lot of work. For a game that's been out for nearly 2 years i'm very disappointed in the building system. I'd hope they would have fixed these things and made it more intiuitive but videos I've watched are from the release period are pretty much exactly as it is now and its upsetting they haven't improved on it at all. You're unable to rebuild standing structures or even repair them to their former glory prior to the nukes going off and that's also a big minus to me. Having to live in a hole filled building is annoying. Some people have gotten very creative and the videos show this on how to repair those buildings but I for one don't like their "solutions" of using glitches to have to patch holes. The lack of wall prefabs with windows (which you'd think that all the glass bottles laying around you'd be able to craft a window...) is upsetting. I have a base that basically is 4 walls, no windows and very ugly looking with salvaged up trailor roofing rolls as walls. It def keeps with the feeling of scraping up anything you can find, but it would be nice to be able to do something that would allow for better looking walls (maybe a building skill that would open up better looking more refined walls) ANYTHING would be nice. I hate living in shacks and busted up buildings. Just my opinion, clearly that's not what the game designers were going for so I live with it.
Combat in the game is intersting to say the least. You have two ways to fight, the V.A.T.S system where you can have the game do all your aiming for you based on your character's skills and situation targeting specific body parts such as arms or head or torso and then a roll determines if you hit or not and you have limited action points to spend each "round" of combat, however its mixed with the second type of combat which is more FPS where you aim and hit targets. I'm much better at playing the game without using the V.A.T.S system as I can aim better than my character's skills can. Also when your waiting for your action points to build to do another round of AI controlled aiming, you still have to move around and can't do anything like run or anything like that. You can shoot and move, but to me that seems crazy since you already shot. To me combat should be one or the other, the mix of combat with the V.A.T.S. system doesn't make sense. The V.A.T.S. system should be more tactical combat where you move certain distances and have aiming, and shooting kind of like an XCOM system, or you can be in FPS mode where you just do your own aiming and shooting, but not both. I'm not sure how they did in the other games but this system is a waste. I use it occationally just to see the action sequences but most of the time I just FPS my way into it.
The stealth system is pretty good as well where you can sneak around and pickpocket people if properly approached and with the appropriate skill however your companion will ALWAYS give you away so you must command them to stay put if you want to stealth into a situation. If your skill is high enough you can even walk up to someone and steal all their stuff and drop a live grenade in their pocket and watch the fun...:). The downside to their crime and punishment system is that if you decide to pick the pocket of a main city guard or something and they catch you, the whole city comes down on you like a bomb, and the biggest problem, you can't undo it without a reload. You can have 30 - 40 people on you instantly and it seems they have some level of omniscience where they can see you even inside someone's house in another instance. I broke into a house once in diamond city (the main city) and was in the middle of snooping around when every merchant from the main area came into my instance area and there were so many guards and merchants trying to kill me in this guys house there wasn't any room to even move. So if you want to stealth stuff, be sure you quicksave before doing it. Not sure if that's a bug or not, when I broke into this house, nobody was around and nobody had line of sight on me so i have no idea how that happened. Seemed to me if someone saw me, it should be me vs that guy and nobody else, but whatever...
Open World, def intesting. No worries if you want to get around quickly, there's no working vehicles in the game. IMO that's stupid. You should be given a bike or car or something or could fix one up and have that available to you. Instead you have a teleporting system where you can "fast travel" somewhere. In my book an open world should be that, open, huge, persistant, and always dangerous to travel on. The fast travel makes it small and safe traveling. Some people might like that, but not really me. Give me a horse or a car or a bike or something I can ride and let me see the world you all painstakingly made. The game makes you go to any location at least once in the open world, but after you get a few key points fast travel makes it easy to get somewhere pretty easily.
So I've ran out of available text so I'll cut the rest short:
TL;DR - The game is pretty fun. There's a lot of neat things you can do, it has some flaws but overall I've enjoyed the game. If you've played the franchise before you might be disapointed, thankfully I wasn't poisoned by the previous games and therefore enjoyed this one. If its your first jump into fallout, and you like open world adventure games, this one is for you. The $50 - $60 price tag is pretty steep in my book, wait for a sale and get it less than $30. Its worth at least that much.

All in all, I decided to amend this review, and give the game a reccomandation despite its flaws, as it keeps me coming back. Unless you're really nearly certain, I'd wait for it to go out of early access though.
If you're here, you're probably going to alreadly know the many strengths of this game from trailers and LPs. Darkest Dungeon has phenomenal art (reminds me a lot of Argentinian comic genius Enrique Breccia). It has an interesting premise, simple and fun mechanics. It avoids tedium by keeping you changing your party, and throwing very difficult stuff at you, forcing to think strategically. What spoils it for me is the grinding.
Ok, a mistake can cost me dearly. I'm fine with that.
Sometimes, a particularly screwy RNG can also cost me dearly, ok.
Sometimes, you'll enter a dungeon and discover a new monster that has unique mechanics and will do 150% of your character's hp in bleeding damage, so you're screwed unless you know it was coming.
I'm not mad I lost my carefully raised adventurers, I'm mad I have to grind them back.
I have not had a chance to check the old versions of this game, but the reviews saying it got worse ring true.
Leveling heroes and rising resources is a bloody chore. It's made worse by the fact you can't take higher-level heroes in low-level runs (it makes sense, but it could be implemented better), level-0 heroes go down with a breeze, and money is absurdly hard to get considering a colossal chunk of it will be required to prepare for missions and to heal your adventurers from stress and disease. Game basically encourages you to make multiple "meat grinder" expeditions with sacrificeable level 0 adventurers, trying to scrounge all you can get before discarding them. It's annoying as hell.
I'm a fan of hard games, but this one occasionally gets the frustrating kind of hard.
However, it keeps me coming back. So, it's doing something right.
It has the potential to be very good — unless you're really eager for it, though, I'd wait until after it's out of early access.

"Terraria in space" isn't really fair to this game. This game isn't even finished yet and I already feel that it's far more then Terraria managed to be. Starbound looks like a 2d side-scroller but it has a depth that I would even dare to compare to an Elderscrolls game. It may look like a simple space exploration game but I expect great things from this. As it stands now, there's no real story and only a few beginner quests. But if you get this Early Access version and get the better gear and do the few quests you get, you actually start getting around out there in the galaxy and coming accross worlds with villages of various races with quirky personalities for some of the towns folk... there's even sky-pirates! One of the things that impressed me a lot were the various books and manuscripts and diaries found in villages and other places. You find a Prisoners diary complaining about the food and the bad company and, "oh my god what is that!? AHhhh!!" you'll also find a military base with a soldier's log book talking about spoilery type stuff but also that he was getting stir-crazy being cooped up in his base, which probably explains why they're all crazy and shooting at me when I drop in to say hi.
Even un-finished this game has more spirit and personality then Terreria ever though of. I sincearly hope the people responsible for this thing take the real opptortunity that they have to create an epic game that could actually be on par with the likes of Skyrim. A a whole big main quest line with story and memorable NPC's and everything. The galaxy is so huge that you could probably have star-charts and manuals and log books hidden around that say things like, "There's cool stuff and/or things to do at these coordinates in this sector in that system on one of those planets!"

Very interesting and unique take on dungeon crawling. Combines the atmosphere of Diablo 1 with the essentials of table-top turn-based gaming and a variation of the sanity mechanic from Amnesia: the Dark Descent. Superb visual aesthetics and narration. Despite being roundly criticized as a tribute to the RNG gods, Darkest Dungeon at its core simply demands dispassionate decision making: whether and when to abandon a quest; how long to let an adventurer languish with some combination of stress, afflictions, and disease; or whether and when to dismiss him/her altogether. Recommended for those with a certain mindset and an appreciation for learning about game mechanics.

Obsidian's stellar New Vegas set a gold standard for the Fallout franchise that is sadly not met here. Quests are simplistic murder simulators with little deviation from the "go here, shoot this" approach, shaping your character is practically non-existant as you're relegated to a cliched "GIVE ME BACK MY SON!" role, and the writing is woefully dry. Bethesda's idea of characterisation seems to amount to little more than making its characters have a churlish attiude, and many of the stories on display here feel bizarrely out of place within the Fallout universe, or have nothing meaningful to say. The Sims offshoot that forms the crux of the game is best left ignored. What the game does have in its favour is a rich and incredibly dense world to explore, though hindered by its increasingly creaky engine, and the combat can be enjoyable. This leads me to conclude that Bethesda's strengths lie as world-builders and gameplay designers, but any kind of depth and nuance, so expertly realised by New Vegas, is clearly not their forte. Whereas that wonderful game felt like a significant step forward, this feels like a huge step back and I hope the Fallout franchise can find its footing again next time.

As you've no doubt noticed, a lot of reviewers point out that the game can be punishing, if not frustrating. That may well be so—I haven't played it long enough to hit that particular wall. But if the only thing holding you back from giving Darkest Dungeon a try are the words "Early Access," I can tell you that you would never guess that this title is not yet in the full release stage, it's so polished and playable. Other developers would long have declared this the final version and released patch after patch with bug fixes. I usually stop reading as soon as I see the phrase "Early Access," and Darkest Dungeon is the first EA title I bought. I'm glad I did. Whatever balance fixes and other tweaks the game may still need, it's already hella fun, and a truly unique and novel concept to boot. I've paid twice as much (sale or no) for some titles that weren't half as fun as this.

There's quite a lot of controversey around whether or not Fallout 4 is worth buying, and many people argue over whether or not Fallout 4 was better than Fallout 3.
First of all, it takes a pretty decent computer to run this. It wouldn't run on my original computer, so when I got a new one I decided to play the game right away. Even though the game is mega optimized, it still takes a strong computer to run it (great graphics require a great computer I suppose).
In my opinion, this game is fantastic, and is definitely worth purchasing. I can spend hours on end venturing through the Wasteland and I never fail to uncover something I hadn't seen before. There are thousands of quests, and the character development of the companions, as while as the companion's unique looks and personalities, is astounding. The map is massive, and the detail put into it is miraculous.
On a side note, the game also touches on a lot of real issues, such as racism and sexism, which is a pretty great thing in itself. Most makers of video games don't take real world issues into account when making a fictitious game, so it's nice to see some good moral lessons in the game.
Another thrilling aspect of the game is that you are able to choose how your character responds to situations in order to pursue the kind of character that you, as an individual, want to see in the game. You can choose how you treat your companions, as well as how to respond to conversation and missions.
Overall, I'd give the game a 9/10. Being such a large game, there are some bugs that can be encountered, some of which alter and affect the gameplay. Bethesda has a history of putting out games with glitches, which makes it easy to laugh them off and keep playing. Definitely play this game.

So before I start, I want to make it clear I really want to like this game. I will continue playing because I believe it will be better at some point. This was not an impulse buy for me. I read through the forums and looked at videos before buying. I waited for a sale to make it easier for me to see value in the purchase. It has nice graphics and interesting mechanics. It has an RPG elements to add some depth to the basic rogue structure. There's a base building mechanic simialr to X-com, which is something I usually like. There's resource management which should lead to interesting decisions. All these things appealed to me and made me decide to buy it.
I expected to be greeted by difficult challenges that required me to closely monitor my resources and make difficult choices about my characters and their fates.
Ultimately, I'm just faced with a mindless grind over and over.
My current state of gaming after 14 hours is:
And the worst part is there are no shortcuts. You can't fire everyone at the end of an adventure. You can't recruit four characters from the adventure screen. It's like they're trying to convince me that these choices have meaning. They don't and they just add clicks until I get to the ones that do have meaning.
That meaning shows up every third week or so.
Every few weeks, you'll take your main party on an adventure and you'll try and push them to the end so they gain gain resolve to level up. You'll even equip them with shovels and food like a real party would want. If all goes well, they'll finish an adventure and you'll get some cool things.
Of course the party will also be a stressed out wreck and require several weeks of rest to recover enough to go on another adventure. This of course is ok, since you'll need several weeks to gather enough resources to pay for their stress recovery and any upgrades you may want to put on them.
This of course means you'll spend several more adventures going through the earlier cycle with a bunch of characters who's names you don't even bother to read. You'll even gloat a bit when the starvation screen comes up as that means you've had a better than average run and should get some decent money out of the adventure. The fact that you're technically starving four people to death in order to make your return on investment worthwhile should never be brought up.
Is any of this difficult? Does it make the game challenging?
Not really.
The monsters so far have posed little or no threat. Even if a character gets to zero health, it's unlikely you'll lose them. You can probably give them a health on the next combat round and they'll usually hang in there long enough for you to finish any really tough battles.
The base poses no difficulty once I figured out the grinding part. And since it's clear that in the long term I'll get enough resources to build up to maximum, there's no interesting choices to be made there.
What is difficult is stress, and only because the game doesn't give you the resources to deal with it if you keep pushing on. It won't matter most of the time because the throw away characters can get as stressed as they want as long as they don't all die before you abandon the adventure.
For your main party, stress is the real enemy. I would go as far as to say your only enemy. From the start of your adventure, you'll be wondering if they'll get to the end before they stress out. There is little chance the monsters will kill your characters, but once one of your characters goes over 100 stress the threat of heart attacks becomes a real and pressing problem. At that point, you're playing with fire while showering in gasoline. The characters will start talking and the stress levels will skyrocket. Then another character will go over 100 and they won't shut up and three turns later someone will fall over dead from a heart attack. Once one goes, it's belly up for all of them and you get to start over. Since you'll quickly learn this lesson, you're unlikely to ever face this problem more than once. At that point, stress then just becomes an annoyance instead of a difficulty. It will quickly come to represent extra weeks of tedious trips through the cycle of collecting resources.
What about the times where it really does go bad for your main party? It has happened once to me because I didn't want to go through a medium adventure a second time for two rooms. I pushed on even though I knew heart attacks were close.
I started raging against the fates and designers right?
No. Remember, you only play with these characters once every 3 weeks. You're not really attached to them. The entire party went belly up and the most I could manage was a tired sigh as I thought about the button presses of tedium while I started a new party to replace .... hmm .... what were their names???

And in case you think I'm exaggerating this point, I give you the following example of my total ambivalence for these characters. One time, I fired one of my main party members by mistake. I had forgotten their name and their stress was high. It was only when I started the next adventure with my main party that I realized what I had done.
In all the rogue games that I thought were good, I could remember the names of my characters. I cared what happened to them. I would go so far as to say that's the heart of a good rogue game. Make the player care about what's happening, and then put them in an impossible situation. Most of the times things will go badly and the player will hate the game and the developer.
Sometimes though, a miracle will happen. You'll get that perfect set of circumstances to overcome the impossible. And that character will be your hero. The game and developers will be brilliant. That story will be told to everyone who will listen. Of course the character will then be killed by a lowly slime moments later, but the memory of them overcoming the impossible will live on and make you believe you can win. You will honor that character by starting again. You will swear to defeat that game because of all the fallen heroes who did the impossible to get one more level further than you had ever seen before.
I wish that was happening in Darkest Dungeon. Unfortunately, the designers have forgotten to make me care.

After logging 480 hours in game. I definetly enjoyed this game. Gun play is tremendously better than previous games where I find myself rarely if ever using vats to assist me in battle. (fallout 3 and new vegas always had me building characters with lots of action points for vats because gunplay was pretty wonky for me). While the main storyline was a bit lacking, i spent hours upon hours scouring old buildings finding the hidden story in everything on terminals and notes left behind which is pretty much a staple of Bethesda open world games. I did find the map a bit small pretty quickly. The amount of things to find was great but i think it should have been spaced out more like the northern part of the fallout 3 map where there was vast open spaces to get lost in if it was your first time around. Fallout 4's map felt like everytihing was practically on top of each other. The downtown region IMO was near perfectly crafted. All one playable area unlike the separated areas of previous titles so that cut down the time spent on loading screens by a huge amount. Graphics were okay, they werent terrible but nothing to go crazy about (mods fixed that). The crafting in this game was a huge plus to me, being able to make weapons to be exactly what you want instead of the lacking gun mods of new vegas. While many grill this game for being to far from what fallout used to be I personaly think that this is the next step for the franchise. Many people thought (some still do) that fallout 3 strayed to far from what the older fallouts were so this just seems like another iteration to keep the franchise from being too much of a repeat of the last release.
All in all i very much enjoyed this game and look forward to whatever the Fallout VR turns out to be and also look forward to the next release whenever that happens to be.

I don't really know what happened. I guess the novelty just wore off over time, and I find myself thoroughly disinclined to play this game anymore. I'm mostly disappointed that I kept my faith in the developers for as long as I did.
This game falls short when it comes to it's mid-endgame 'challenges,' which are hourly events that reward players with an rng chest that mostly just spits out a bunch of flux, which is considered the main currency and is the primary material you use to upgrade your weapons. Challenges are not fun. Every hour on the hour you have twenty minutes to clear dungeons in a specified biome, with bonuses for playing as one of two specified classes, and a bonus for playing on one of the two highest 'difficulty' worlds.
People complain that this leads to zerging, which I only did once before deciding that I just wouldn't do it. Because it's not fun. I thought that I would instead spend my time mining for other materials and save up to be able to trade when a global market comes out. A few weeks later and I'm still waiting for that promised update.
And this is where my disappointment really kicks in. Devs put out a lot of new content every week. This would be great, but each round of new content comes with new and more bugs and issues. If you're like me and don't encounter these issues yourself, you get to experience the disappointment of seeing them brought up in the forums and realize that there's even more work to be done before they can even get to focusing on content updates that you actually care about, the ones that actually mean anything.
There's promises of upcoming changes to challenges, and promises of a global market being introduced, but I fear that by the time these things come out, there will be so many bugs and issues with every update between now and then that it'll take even more weeks before these updates will have their own bugs ironed out. And by that time there will be even more content with even more bugs to further perpetuate the issues.
It's a fun game, and it seemed like it was going in the right direction, but I fear that unless the devs pull back on adding new content and spend a few update cycles dedicated to bug fixes, this game will progressively get more and more difficult to enjoy, as it already has been.
My optimism for this game and it's developers has turned into disappointment, but as a free game, it may still be worth trying. Personally, I do plan to continue to keep an eye on the game's forum and log in once in a while, however, I can no longer say that I particularly recommend this game.
---Update 7/30/15:---
Due to the issues of a patch release causing downtime that lasted most of the day, players who log in this weekend should obtain free items. I'm not sure if completely brand new players will be able to get in on the free class token and cubits, but it might be a good time to join just in case.
Queues and wait times have been reduced considerably, but there's still some waiting once in a while. Last week there was a lot of lag issues to contend with as well, though I believe most of that should be fixed with the current state of the game. There was mention of a bug involving enemies walking out of the loaded area of a world causing the database to start to cave in on itself. These two days since the aformentioned patch downtime have been pretty smooth for playing, but I did have a five minute queue to wait one of the times I logged in yesterday.
The game is still definitely fun. Since my first review, I've leveled up one of my characters to 20 and have reached 30 mastery, getting me in on challenges. Essentially challenges are timed dungoen rush missions that grant bonus rewards for completing enough quests in the specified time.
There are also plans to add another class soon along with inventory expansions (though the inventory expansions may be restricted to being purchased with currency that can only be obtained through spending real money). This may be a bit of an issue, but one way around this is to utilize club worlds (you can be a member (or owner) of up to 5) and the storage space granted by creating and using specail 'club chests' there.
If you were turned away by the queues before, I'd say give it a try now. They're still around, but not nearly to the extent of half-hour wait times as they were before. Devs are continuing to strive for a game that's fun for everyone, including free players, thankfully not caving in to unreasonable demands made by "the ones that paid."
There's still plenty of kinks, but the game continues to be thoroughly enjoyable.
---Original 7/19/15 Review---
This is an amazing game and the Devs are working like mad to sort out the limited server space issues that cause long queues. This game is amazing and I love it. I have played the game since it was first realeased. When It first came out I was absolutley amazed by it, and quickley compleated all there was to do (which was a surprizing amount seeing as it had only just enterd early access) and then stopped playing it. I just got back into DD and, in my opinion, the game has only gotten better. Some people are saying that the game is getting grindy and repeditive, that it is to hard and unfair, and that corpses suck. I dissagree with all of this. Yes, there currently isn't much variety in quest types, but the difficulty of the game makes every adventuer, every battle, a horrifyingly exilerating expiriance. There are times when you yell at you screan barking: SERIOUSLEY! FOUR MISSES IN A ROW!!!! and you feel like you want to reach through the screen and strangle your party members, but often times when you fail misserably it is all your fault. The game is very much about risk vs reward and, in the case of the previous example, I probbably should of cured my parties rabies instead of leaving them with -10 acc and +15%dmg. Also, corpses arn't hard, they just make the game ballanced, making classes that target the back rows viable at the end of battles. Now you have to carefully construct your team while before corpses you could totally cheese the game with four hellions spamming break through (which still worked pretty well even after the nerf). I recently played through the game to the point at which I was taking on champion missions and, while I found the game to be horrifyingly difficult as always, I had a great time and at no point felt like I was forced into any one playstile, in fact, the difficulty of the game and fact you have to cycle through your roster to find the least stressed heros  often leads to some interesting ideas and neat party combos that usually fail hillariously (although instead of laughing you are crying) but sometimes wreck house. As for the new region, the cove, I really enjoy it. The new enemies are interesting to work around and the 8 bleed per turn from lobsters is horrifying and the bosses are clever and it is just a whole lot of fun.
To be fair, DD isn't the game for everyone. It is not a game you want to play after a stressful day and it is deffinitly not a game for casual gamers. I have tried to get some of my friend into it, but the game just isn't for most of them, which isn't a bad thing for them or a bad theing for DD. I think DD exists because it fills a niche in a gaming library that no other game fills and that no future game needs to try to fill. But for the times when life fells a bit to calm and you want to stress out about something with no actual impact on you life but you also want to play a dungeon crawler with a narrator who uses words you can't even pronounce, then DD is the game you should play
Also it is hillarious to name your adventurers after your friends and watch them get kikedout of a brothel because they were "making strange requests"

I started playing Darkest Dungeon just after the controversial update including corpses and heart attacks - I bought the game for its challenge, and these features only enhance that.  However, the great outcry of criticism stating this made the game 'too hard' was heard by the developers and is now an option to toggle within the settings.  Great job, Red Hook!
The game has a tagline about its challenge factor - quests will be abandoned/failed.  You will lose your favorite heroes to permadeath.  It does not lie.  Even in the most experienced parties, after over 100 hours of gameplay, I will still lose an occasional adventurer to crits, followed by a deathblow.
The depth and play strategy also keep me coming back.  There are so many ways to mix and match classes with each other that replayability based on that alone is excellent.  Red Hook has also seen fit to title some of the more synergistic parties, which is a nice Easter egg to be found (Stunrise sunset is a personal favorite).  I can only hope the title is not only for show and that there is some minor small skill increases, but that would probably unbalance the game and pigeon hole all your party choices.
Only one catch here - if you are not looking for a challenging dungeon crawler, stay away.  This is not your daddy's Diablo.
3-11-16 Addition:  Red Hook has since released this game in all its glory.  Despite being released, reviewed and easily left alone, what does the developer do?  They just released yet another new class and additional features/fixes to their game.  For this Indie title, I say everybody and their dog should buy this game.  AAA title developers need to take a page from Red Hook here and not only wait to release a game that is polished and enjoyable, but to go above and beyond to tweak it after release.

Darkest Dungeon is a good game.  It's a depressing game, but it's a good game.
If you have dreams of creating a team of characters that will go hacking their way through dangers and ridding the world of evil, you'd best move along.  You're "dream team" will become fodder, and their replacements will become fodder, until you discover that the hero's in this game are basically the currency you use to gain gold.  Gold is necessary to unlock the village buildings upper levels, to try and make keeping characters around somewhat affordable.
You'll build a roster of characters that you'll select from to go on dungeon raids.  The raids are somewhat 2 dimensional, and with basic tactics you'll be able to clear most of the dungeons, but most likely your characters will pick up negative traits from their brushes with death/fear/evil along the way, making them damaged goods.  Usually it's not worth the effort, time or money to recover them.  You'll begin to think of your characters like used cars.  If they pick up enough bad traits, they'll probably be totaled... so you'll ship them off on the next wagon and replace them with new fodder.
If you do this long enough, you'll be able to field a team of slightly higher level characters, but using them comes with greater risks.  These new higher level characters refuse to accompanying the noob fodders on lower level missions, so you won't be able to help your new folks with your experienced folks.  And if you lose these experienced characters, which will probably happen, you're back to slogging through the aforementioned fodder characters in attempt to rebuild your team.
All in all, after about 50 hours of play, it just seemed a little bit too much like a grind for me.  Some people will probably really dig the style of play, and the masochistic difficulty, but for my play time/dollar, it doesn't have enough diversity in the early stages to really make it a great game.
A well designed, crafted game though, in all other respects.  Kudos for trying to think up something outside the box to the developers.  All -in-all, I give it a thumbs up, even though it isn't a great game for me personally, I think others will find it enjoyable.  I will probably give it another go later.

People compare this game to Minecraft and Dayz, however I think this game is a lot more like Fallout 3 than either of those games.
First of all, I suppose they compare it to minecraft due to the inherent blockyness of the character in the game, however the game shares little to no similarities to minecraft beyond that, it's crafting system and building system is completely diffrent in every way.
Second of all, they compare it to DayZ because well, it's a multiplayer zombie game! However I think these people have completely forgotten that DayZ has been completely abandoned by its playerbase and developers, and will never leave early access hell.
I think this game is a lot like Fallout 3 due to it's interesting gunplay, scavenging mechanics and linear story, the NPC's in this game are extremely similar to those of Fallout 3, if you cut out the part that NPC's can actually shoot at you.
Also most of the locations in Unturned are very interesting and usually quite unique, yes you've got your forgettable farm, but who can forget Seattle or the tunnels in Moscow?
Unturned ofcourse also doesn't come without some lower qualities.
Like I mentioned before some locations in the maps are utterly forgettable.
The difficulty ramp is a little too steep, which easy being a stroll through the park and normal mode being death of thirst.
Zombies can be quite frustrating to deal with, especially if your connection to a server isn't the greatest, a runner zombie can completely drain half of your health with a small amount of lag, it would be better if the game was better optimized, so low-end computers could run it again, like they could in unturned 2.0
Player customisation is also limited in a way due to there only being one playermodel.
But also due to hairstyles instantly dissapearing by wearing any hat whatsoever.
Some of the weapons in the game are utterly garbage, such as the sportshot, which barely does any damage whatsoever, I suppose the upside is the low amount of sound it makes, however this can still easily be heard by other players.
Basebuilding could use an upgrade, due to all bases in the game looking like literal blocks, and it basically never being worth it to build a base at an existing location.
Maybe introduce an NPC mechanic where you can build houses for NPCs which will give you radiant quests or sell certain items to you.
Possibly increase the amount of chance you have for an NPC to move in when building in an existing location, encouraging growth in an amount of bases in such areas.
In the end Unturned is a very fun game with a lot of interesting mechanics that work really well with this sort of game.
-Also the graphics don't look like they were made by a child, they look like they were made by a programmer (which they were)-
-Also also when's the lever action coming back to the game?-

I started playing Darkest Dungeon just after the controversial update including corpses and heart attacks - I bought the game for its challenge, and these features only enhance that.  However, the great outcry of criticism stating this made the game 'too hard' was heard by the developers and is now an option to toggle within the settings.  Great job, Red Hook!
The game has a tagline about its challenge factor - quests will be abandoned/failed.  You will lose your favorite heroes to permadeath.  It does not lie.  Even in the most experienced parties, after over 100 hours of gameplay, I will still lose an occasional adventurer to crits, followed by a deathblow.

Darkest Dungeon is a good game.  It's a depressing game, but it's a good game.
If you have dreams of creating a team of characters that will go hacking their way through dangers and ridding the world of evil, you'd best move along.  You're "dream team" will become fodder, and their replacements will become fodder, until you discover that the hero's in this game are basically the currency you use to gain gold.  Gold is necessary to unlock the village buildings upper levels, to try and make keeping characters around somewhat affordable.
You'll build a roster of characters that you'll select from to go on dungeon raids.  The raids are somewhat 2 dimensional, and with basic tactics you'll be able to clear most of the dungeons, but most likely your characters will pick up negative traits from their brushes with death/fear/evil along the way, making them damaged goods.  Usually it's not worth the effort, time or money to recover them.  You'll begin to think of your characters like used cars.  If they pick up enough bad traits, they'll probably be totaled... so you'll ship them off on the next wagon and replace them with new fodder.
If you do this long enough, you'll be able to field a team of slightly higher level characters, but using them comes with greater risks.  These new higher level characters refuse to accompanying the noob fodders on lower level missions, so you won't be able to help your new folks with your experienced folks.  And if you lose these experienced characters, which will probably happen, you're back to slogging through the aforementioned fodder characters in attempt to rebuild your team.
All in all, after about 50 hours of play, it just seemed a little bit too much like a grind for me.  Some people will probably really dig the style of play, and the masochistic difficulty, but for my play time/dollar, it doesn't have enough diversity in the early stages to really make it a great game.
A well designed, crafted game though, in all other respects.  Kudos for trying to think up something outside the box to the developers.  All -in-all, I give it a thumbs up, even though it isn't a great game for me personally, I think others will find it enjoyable.  I will probably give it another go later.

People compare this game to Minecraft and Dayz, however I think this game is a lot more like Fallout 3 than either of those games.
First of all, I suppose they compare it to minecraft due to the inherent blockyness of the character in the game, however the game shares little to no similarities to minecraft beyond that, it's crafting system and building system is completely diffrent in every way.
Second of all, they compare it to DayZ because well, it's a multiplayer zombie game! However I think these people have completely forgotten that DayZ has been completely abandoned by its playerbase and developers, and will never leave early access hell.
I think this game is a lot like Fallout 3 due to it's interesting gunplay, scavenging mechanics and linear story, the NPC's in this game are extremely similar to those of Fallout 3, if you cut out the part that NPC's can actually shoot at you.
Also most of the locations in Unturned are very interesting and usually quite unique, yes you've got your forgettable farm, but who can forget Seattle or the tunnels in Moscow?
Unturned ofcourse also doesn't come without some lower qualities.
Like I mentioned before some locations in the maps are utterly forgettable.
The difficulty ramp is a little too steep, which easy being a stroll through the park and normal mode being death of thirst.
Zombies can be quite frustrating to deal with, especially if your connection to a server isn't the greatest, a runner zombie can completely drain half of your health with a small amount of lag, it would be better if the game was better optimized, so low-end computers could run it again, like they could in unturned 2.0
Player customisation is also limited in a way due to there only being one playermodel.
But also due to hairstyles instantly dissapearing by wearing any hat whatsoever.
Some of the weapons in the game are utterly garbage, such as the sportshot, which barely does any damage whatsoever, I suppose the upside is the low amount of sound it makes, however this can still easily be heard by other players.
Basebuilding could use an upgrade, due to all bases in the game looking like literal blocks, and it basically never being worth it to build a base at an existing location.
Maybe introduce an NPC mechanic where you can build houses for NPCs which will give you radiant quests or sell certain items to you.
Possibly increase the amount of chance you have for an NPC to move in when building in an existing location, encouraging growth in an amount of bases in such areas.
In the end Unturned is a very fun game with a lot of interesting mechanics that work really well with this sort of game.
-Also the graphics don't look like they were made by a child, they look like they were made by a programmer (which they were)-
-Also also when's the lever action coming back to the game?-

Trove is a unique game. It's a simplistic MMO with a heavy focus on the enviroment. One character able to use all the classes. That automatically puts it in my good books.
Pros: So many pros, so little time.
- Simplistic. (Any new MMO player can and most likely will feel comfortable playing this game)
- Heavy focus on the Enviroment. (The "Dungeons" found in this game are found throughout the world and never force you to party up just to beat them. The ability to blow up blocks in the world and use them to make your house is just so amazing.)
- Housing. (Housing. One of the best things in this game. Look at other MMO's that have housing. They make you select a pre-set home and just add pre-made things. Guess what, none of that in trove. You want a skull house? Make it! you want a castle? Build it! The options are endless)
-Loot. (Loot is also a heavy focus in this game. Getting loot is not hard and grinding doesn't feel like a burden.)
-One Character: All Classes. (Title speaks for itself.)
-No Pay2Win (The most "Pay2Win" ability in this game is membership which gives magic find. THAT'S IT! So more magic find. Do you need it? NO! do you want it? YES! Everything can be bought with in game money.)
Cons: There aren't that many cons.
- Servers. (Servers aren't that big so you may have to wait to be able to get into the game.)
-On and off lag (The average player will sit at about 100-200 Ping while playing.)
- Simplistic (This only goes into the cons if you enjoy MMO's with about 20 buttons that you need to press; while this one only has 5)
That's my short review of this game. Thanks for Reading and I hope to see you in Trove.

3 out of 5 Stars.
I always wanted this game to do well. It was cute and  fun, but without shying away from challenge, which was viciously emphasized if you tried to do anything alone. The biggest grievance I have with this game is one of the biggest taboos I find in the gaming genre as a whole. Your modern anti-marathon mechanic, where some tertiary energy supply inhibits constant play. This game is one of the few that foolishly includes such a feature and tries to cash in on the limitation. While this game is fun, that alone is an effective deal breaker. Rather than giving the game solid replay value , it only elongates the inital endeavor. Which is pretty tedious in the first place.
It's several different themes of instance dungeon crawling with block pushing and puzzle solving not unlike Zelda, and the venues themselves change rather often due to the player base having a small degree of influence on the inner mechanisms of the world. As they turn the metaphoric and literal gears, layers of hostility align as your character descends into the Core of the world. The bosses are the most static aspect of the trek, given the smaller pool of variance, but it isn't so diverse as to say one voyage will never look like another. To this game's benefit, the comparison to Zelda comes with a grim warning of the latters time tested simplicity being absent. There are some genuinely crafty enemies designed that require a fair level of familiarity to keep at bay as well as proper equipment loadouts, all the while only modestly equipped with hit points.
I'll happily recommend this game, with the hope that no one falls in love.
Because sadly, you're always playing on borrowed time. And you can't go alone, either.

Dark souls 3 is a action JRPG made by FromSoftware just for you to play, have fun, suffer, and cry.
The "have fun" part is not guaranteed to be present for everybody.
Anyway, the game's great. A solid 8/10 honestly, very good closing game for the souls series. Is it the end of souls? I dunno, companies these days would beat any dead horse
just to keep their capita's heart pumping.
STORY?:
So, the story, first thing I want to address, I have no idea what the hell is going on.
You have to kill some Abyss Watchers, a giant called Yhorm, Aldrich the snail guy and two cripples so you can start a new age of fire or bring upon the age of dark, as per
usual, nothing much has changed with the story as in the previous games.
For anybody that really gives a heck about lore I'd suggest you go watch VaatiVidya or whoever the heck is hogging the youtube views from making up theories that
Miyazaki later just <can't show this word on a christian gameing site!> on.
COMBAT:
So combat, pretty fun, pretty challenging, don't get hit, but hit back.
Two attack buttons, this time dual wielding is available, no power stance, boohoo what can you do.
Two attack buttons, a block, parry button, backstep and dodge. I know it sounds like "oh wow that's not that complex" yeah, it's not that complex until you get into PvP I
suppose, then you really need to think what to do.
From charged R2's, regular attack into a special with a finishing charged R2, you got plenty of ways to kill your enemies, just make sure you don't get killed of course.
The game is this time around way faster than DS1 and DS2, feels like Miyazaki liked Bloodborne so much he wanted to make another one but then remembered he was making a souls
game halfway through the development.
Shoutout to the parry kings out there though, you guys are killing it.
BOSSES IN THE BASE GAME:
Bosses are all cool and dandy, none of them do really feel unfair, at least in the base game. I got one complaint on the difficulty curve with Pontif of Sulyvahn, because
he is probably one of the hardest bosses in the game, and throwing him out there like that felt like a "casual filter" as some would say. Like I imagine that's a point where
a bunch of people just rage quitted, or is it just me? Might be me, I am still a casual.
THE DLC'S:
Anyway as I said, none of them feel unfair in the base game, but in the Ringed City DLC a lot of players have been complaining about Midir's massive health pool, so I guess
you could write that one down as an "unfair" boss, even though he's just more tedious than anything.
The two DLC's though? Ashes of Ariandel was a dang letdown and don't let anybody tell you otherwise. Two bosses? Yeah I regret getting a season pass just because of that
DLC. And no the arena was not worth it, the usual invasions are much more fun than that. But it's too late to cry about that now I suppose.
Ringed City though, boy oh boy, that one surprised me. Don't get me wrong I expected From to make a DLC to make up for their mistake with Ashes of Ariandel but the sheer size
and content of this DLC was amazing, it might even be better than the DLC from Dark Souls 1, simply glorious, honestly get Ringed City you will not be disappointed.
Amazing 4 boss fights and a lot of cool weapons and spells are just waiting for you to pick them up.
THE WEAPON AND ARMOR:
Armor in this game has no upgrades and poise is useless outside of hyper armor. If you're not using a slow weapon that hits hard, wearing havels really won't matter.
But if you're using a havels while you're wielding the Fume UGS then you can bet that you will out-trade anybody in PvP no matter who it is. Well unless you get outsmarted.
In which case if you're wearing Havels and are using the Fume and do get outsmarted I suggest you delete the game and never come back on steam you filthy casual.

Even in dark souls, a game known for its punishment - there is some degree of immediacy. This is quite literally - torture.
I admire that. I admire that some team of indie developers went out there, made a game so far departed from the norm. There is no game that quite feels like the darkest dungeon. And for that uniqueness, combined with the flawless presentation - This review is uniformly positive. However subjectively, I don't often want to actually play the damned thing. Starbound brings to life what games such as Minecraft and Terraria couldn't. The world presents itself as a magnanimous, peaceful haven with birds chirping and the wind blowing. Your character has the freedom to dig deep, deep down into the planet you've landed on, or search in either direction for goodies in caves and randomly-generated establishments. While the option for customization in terms of aesthetics isn't mind-bogglingly large, the game offers a wide array of materials, colors, and clothing options to choose from. Maybe not on the level that Minecraft has been famous for, but it's enough to complement the game's beautifully serene and awe-inspiring landscapes.
However, at nighttime, creatures of all kinds stalk the surface (and underbelly) of each planet. The game, too, gives you a selection of weapons to choose from, each with their own statistics and features.
There is enough here to purchase the game: from the jaw-dropping mountains, caverns, lakes, and forests, to (personally) one of the most relaxing and beautiful soundtracks to a game I've ever heard. I have literally felt my shoulders ease up tension and relax from listening to the title screen song.
Nevertheless, the game is still in development. Yes, you will come across useless items with no current purpose. Yes, you may encounter a character wipe as a result of a patch. And yes, you will grow tired of the redundant mining, chopping, and crafting necessary to get the momentum going in this game. But in the end, it is all worth it, because when your character lay there in the bed you've crafted under the warm glow of a finely perched torch in the dark of the night, your home will seem more than just pixels on a computer screen: you will feel a sense of impending happiness and accomplishment in your tangible self for having created something so unique from the recesses of your mind. You will feel part of a planet, of a solar system. This game could be argued as a metaphor for the insignificant-yet-significant impact humanity can and has made on this planet, and, heck, maybe the next one over.
Explorers, get this game. Thinkers and creators, pick it up ASAP. Adventurers, don some armor.
Starbound is not a revolutionary idea in any sense in terms of gaming, but it is a fresh start to the void of game development games have seldom crossed: limitlessness.
It is unlike any Minecraft or Terraria knockoff you will find on the gaming market. It is a personal, transcendent experience with the great beyond, right here on your computer.
It's an entire universe, and it's just begging for your attention.

Spiral knights is a game where you control a knight through 29 floors, defeating monsters and bosses in hope to find a mysterious power in the core to power your ships and return home. Along the way you'll meet other knights that you may grow accustom to and venture on your journeys together. Crafting weapons with different elements Is an essential part of the game due to the fact that different enemies are weak to different elements but not so weak to others (eg. A zombie being weak to elemental weapons but not so weak to shadow weapons).
This game heavily revolves around grinding to get what you want (like most mmos out there). This could lead to people getting bored of its repetitiveness, due to the fact that there are only a certain ammoumt of floors before you start to see a pattern (I found myself constantly taking a break then coming back after x ammoumt of months due to this). I guess (for me at least) it would have been completely fine before the energy revamp mainly because of the fact that every time I made a 5* weapon (the highest Tier of weapons that can be made) there was a sense of acomishment behind every weapon made. After the revamp, that feeling was no longer there as it felt more like a chore than an accomplishment (again for me at least).
This game, sadly is one of the few that suffered from slow-developer-syndrome (the game having little to no update). So far I have witnessed three games suffer from this (starbound, Lost saga EU, and Spiral Knights). From time to time we have been promised many large updates, but out of the many we have only received two after about two years of waiting each. Why it takes them so long to bring us updates, I don't know much. But coming from someone who has been playing since 2012 this has become a huge annoyance to me as well as many other players.
Prize boxes........don't get me started.....
While this game is what it is, there are some positive points to this. First of all, although grindy it would be a blast for new players making their way to endgame territory. The mission system added is great for people who didn't know what to do starting out. Plus the guild system and community was the main reason I still played. I have made many friends in this game that soon became one of my closest friends outside of this game too (you know who you are) as well as been apart of many guilds and even helped people on their quest to endgame. At the end I've only seen one other game with a community this friendly (Osu!).
So after all of this I will still recommend this to people who decide on giving it a go, mainly because it's fun up to a certain point. After that it's just a stand still. I do also recommend making as many friends and join a guild and there are many nice people out there that will help you out without hesitation....just....don't ask them for money....no one likes a begged xD
