The darkest dungeon is not fun and rewarding. Visually and Aurally it's flawless. - the dark reds and blacks perfectly complementing the endlessly grim atmosphere. As someone that collects rougelikes, I can handle random turn of events and sudden death - yet in this game there is a constant elongation of that death. You are slowly losing. Slowly being eaten away like a bunch of flies digesting a almost dead warrior with no eyes on a empty battlefield. Even in dark souls, a game known for its punishment - there is some degree of immediacy. This is quite literally - torture.
I admire that. I admire that some team of indie developers went out there, made a game so far departed from the norm. There is no game that quite feels like the darkest dungeon. And for that uniqueness, combined with the flawless presentation - This review is uniformly positive. However subjectively, I don't often want to actually play the damned thing. Because my time spent will involve slowly becoming as stressed as the protaganists as I am torn apart until there is nothing but an empty husk hobbling along a worn path of nothingness. While enemies point and laugh at my feeble attempts at carrying on. And in the end, that's what you do. Even if you win. You carry on. You don't come out powerful. Or even slightly enhanced. You survive another day of stress and hate.
Sounds a bit too much like my life.

Obviously from my hours played I enjoy this game a great deal.
A lot of the negative reviews mention the same things:
- there's too much RNG
- the game is unfair because of RNG
- the game is too hard because it's unfair.
I've seen a lot of people mention they save scummed because of this game's difficulty. If you're the type of person to save scum, this probably isn't the game for you.
The whole point of this game is predicated on RNG. It's about making the best of bad situations. Even if you do everything right, things will go wrong. Some people consider this arbitrary, and it is. What's not arbitrary is your decision making in those moments. The game will put you into those situations to force you to decide whether you want to risk complete failure or cut your losses. Yes, it feels arbitrarily punishing at times. Yes, it gets frustrating. That's the point.
DD is a game about what you do in the face of that frustration and adversity. It's about how you mitigate transactional risk and how you invest severely limited resources. If that sounds like a chore to you, look elsewhere. If it sounds like fun to put yourself through the wringer and see if you still come out on top, look no further.

Dark souls 3 is a action JRPG made by FromSoftware just for you to play, have fun, suffer, and cry.
The "have fun" part is not guaranteed to be present for everybody.
Anyway, the game's great. A solid 8/10 honestly, very good closing game for the souls series. Is it the end of souls? I dunno, companies these days would beat any dead horse
just to keep their capita's heart pumping.
STORY?:
So, the story, first thing I want to address, I have no idea what the hell is going on.
You have to kill some Abyss Watchers, a giant called Yhorm, Aldrich the snail guy and two cripples so you can start a new age of fire or bring upon the age of dark, as per
usual, nothing much has changed with the story as in the previous games.
For anybody that really gives a heck about lore I'd suggest you go watch VaatiVidya or whoever the heck is hogging the youtube views from making up theories that
Miyazaki later just <can't show this word on a christian gameing site!> on.
COMBAT:
So combat, pretty fun, pretty challenging, don't get hit, but hit back.
Two attack buttons, this time dual wielding is available, no power stance, boohoo what can you do.
Two attack buttons, a block, parry button, backstep and dodge. I know it sounds like "oh wow that's not that complex" yeah, it's not that complex until you get into PvP I
suppose, then you really need to think what to do.
From charged R2's, regular attack into a special with a finishing charged R2, you got plenty of ways to kill your enemies, just make sure you don't get killed of course.
The game is this time around way faster than DS1 and DS2, feels like Miyazaki liked Bloodborne so much he wanted to make another one but then remembered he was making a souls
game halfway through the development.
Shoutout to the parry kings out there though, you guys are killing it.
BOSSES IN THE BASE GAME:
Bosses are all cool and dandy, none of them do really feel unfair, at least in the base game. I got one complaint on the difficulty curve with Pontif of Sulyvahn, because
he is probably one of the hardest bosses in the game, and throwing him out there like that felt like a "casual filter" as some would say. Like I imagine that's a point where
a bunch of people just rage quitted, or is it just me? Might be me, I am still a casual.
THE DLC'S:
Anyway as I said, none of them feel unfair in the base game, but in the Ringed City DLC a lot of players have been complaining about Midir's massive health pool, so I guess
you could write that one down as an "unfair" boss, even though he's just more tedious than anything.
The two DLC's though? Ashes of Ariandel was a dang letdown and don't let anybody tell you otherwise. Two bosses? Yeah I regret getting a season pass just because of that
DLC. And no the arena was not worth it, the usual invasions are much more fun than that. But it's too late to cry about that now I suppose.
Ringed City though, boy oh boy, that one surprised me. Don't get me wrong I expected From to make a DLC to make up for their mistake with Ashes of Ariandel but the sheer size
and content of this DLC was amazing, it might even be better than the DLC from Dark Souls 1, simply glorious, honestly get Ringed City you will not be disappointed.
Amazing 4 boss fights and a lot of cool weapons and spells are just waiting for you to pick them up.
THE WEAPON AND ARMOR:
Armor in this game has no upgrades and poise is useless outside of hyper armor. If you're not using a slow weapon that hits hard, wearing havels really won't matter.
But if you're using a havels while you're wielding the Fume UGS then you can bet that you will out-trade anybody in PvP no matter who it is. Well unless you get outsmarted.
In which case if you're wearing Havels and are using the Fume and do get outsmarted I suggest you delete the game and never come back on steam you filthy casual.
Weapons are amazing as far as I'm concerned, sure From doesn't know how to balance them, but a lot of weapons are just amazing and I love the different weapon arts that each
of them have. Just today I found out the Man Serpent Hatchet had charge with the charged R2 after you use the warcry, 10/10 surprised me really.
The weapon upgrades might be some of the most detailed in the game, you have heavy, sharp, raw, chaos, fire, simple, refined, hollow, dark, deep, I'm sure I missed some,
but yeah a lot of upgrades to choose, so that was a very nice thing.
THE PVP:
Not sure what to think about it. On another hand I love killing people, but on the other hand the netcode makes it unbearable at times. Well, might have something to do with
my internet. Can't wait till I upgrade to a 4G internet from my 3 million BC slavic router. Do not go into PvP expecting everything to be peaches and cream honestly.
The magical universe of starbound is bursting with terrific content, to keep you interested for a long time, Despite having one less dimension, Starbound hides greater depth than its 3D cousins

I have over 6 months on this game and am 120 mastery rank
I would like to say before I start that I was a HUGE fan of this game, and was always on and happy to play. Sadly, it only takes a couple major things to bring a game down, and that is what happened here.
I understand many people will not share some of my opinions, but some of what I state are legitimate facts and issues that one should consider before investing too much time and or money into this game.
The GAME itself, is very fun. Its a simple, classic, enjoyable game. Refreshing and usually not stresful
The combat is simple but is also complex at the same time, do to the free form attacks and movement while attacking, unlike some games such as WoW.
Classes are pretty fun and unique, however a couple are either really boring or not good anymore (due to other classes replacing aspects of another in a better fashion)
Building is awesome! Seen alot of cool stuff and ive made a whole song string on my club world
Leveling is very easy, until level 18 or so then its a grind. (this i am on the fence on, on one end i like leveling, but also hate grinds, so at times i like it and at others i dont)
Gear is good, aquiring good gear now is more grind and resource based and less luck based
The amount of content is very nice, and its also not easy to get rare items (duh) but its not SUPER hard, so you can get some rare stuff within a few weeks to month of playing. So when you see something cool you like, you know its more working hard for it and not "oh wow ive been grinding this for hours and still didnt get the drop!" (Although some items are luck based)
Easy to remember and keep up to date on the content. By this i mean within a few days youll be really into this game and youll understand it very well
Art style is very fun
Now onto the heavy cons
Server lag, bugs, glitches, and ques (fixable)
The amount of older and more inteligent players is dropping, and more new players are joining, this means more new players that dont have rare items for trade, bascially makes trading alot harder these days
Trade system is trash, people only want a select few items these days, and also want VERY rare items, and wont pay the price for them (basically means trading is very difficult to do for ANY kind of player)
Lack of auction house
Chaos chests WERE good, until resources became EXTREMELY more common, now chaos chests arent worth the money, should they revamp them then we will see
Trion has left games in the past, this could be the case for Trove in years to come
Once you play this game for a few months or even more, youll get the sense that this game isnt going to last.
The game feels sort of left to rot in MY OPINION. lack of decent content being added, not much being done (that i can see) to the servers and que times. PvP is rumored to be added, which would suck. This game is NOT MEANT for PvP, anyone with 2 working eyes and a sense of gaming could understand this
Despite Trion SAYING they will NEVER DO PVP and the IMMENSE AMOUNT OF PLAYERS AGAINST PVP they are STILL ADDING IT. I have spent a decent amount of money, and am most likely going to begin a youtube channel. i would LIKE to do videos of this game, but with the current rate its going at, i dont see it happening. Many high level and older players have left (youll soon see why if you play this game)

Update (24-05-2016):
So it's been quite a long while since I last played this game. I really loved it back then, but with the inbalance issues and several bugs (plus the lack of content at the time) it was a severely distressing game and not worth it at the time..
I'm now VERY happy to say that this game has come a long way and is extremely satisfying to play now. Even when a few of my characters die if I have a bad dungeon adventure, it's okay - The game is still rewarding and when a character dies, it's more accepting than it used to be.
The game has more character classes, which adds more variety to the game + the different combinations of groups you can have, as well as more enemy types which again adds more variety to the combat.
Last time I played was for the patch were gold was modified massively and the game was near impossible as a result - I'm also very happy to say that I feel this has been very nicely balanced as well. You aren't rich, but assuming you don't wrack up disease and death you aren't poor either - Which is exactly what the game aims for so I think it's nailed that.
I originally gave this 8/10, but that was based on what the game COULD be. I think now I would give the game a 9/10 for what the game IS, and I definitely urge you to try this game. It is without doubt a unique dungeon crawler and an absolutely extravogant one at that! :)
Original:
If you are prone to smashing your screen after you get ROYALLY screwed over time after time after time... Don't even think about trying this game.
Cleared a level 1 dungeon, medium length, all the way to the room before the boss with max 47 stress and only 2 stress on my healer (somehow). I thought I was in the money (for once) at this point as I've just lost 8 characters across 2 consecutive runs so I REALLLLLYYYYY needed something. I thought ''Huh, might as well camp and reduce that stress to absolute minimal (just incase) and buff where I can!''. I could not be more wrong...
I proceeded to cast -10 Stress on All, to which my character seemed to determine the task pointless and didn't do it due to her previously attained paranoia. I then, somehow, accidentally skipped the rest of the camp and just woke up immediately, no idea how, and got ambushed.
A tad annoying, but meh.. I've got this far and barely been harmed at all (regardless of heals). So .. After several rounds of missing repeatedly and characters in wrong positions due to the surprise, my healer dies of a heart attack. Not too long after that my main damage dealer is on Deaths Row (though doesn't die) and I kill the ambushers soon after... I limp into the boss room determined to finish this off. But, the boss seems to be able to have 4 turns to my every 1. Stunning at least 1 character a round and seemingly bringing down the roof on my head (literally), fear is overwhleming my characters in moments and I doubt I will last very long.. Oh, yep, there goes the 'tank' with a heart attack..
So... 8/10 for the game from me. It truelly is a one of a kind and an amazing one at that. If you've ever thought ''I wish I lived back in the old days, I'd just roam around questing for peeps where ever I want''.. Yeah, this game is what that would really be like.. Not nice.. Stressful.. Full of disease if you aren't careful and no where NEAR as rich as some games allow you to become (which is a nice touch as you have to manage it more carefully).

At the time, I didn't like this game when I'd first played it on the Xbox One, but just when I got it on Steam when it was free for a few days and decided to buy it when it was on sale, I'm liking it. The PC port has a lot of issues when it comes to it's optimization, at times the framerate goes to 60 to 20 and this laptop I'd own should go through the game's specs just fine.
Anyway, the optimization isn't the real issue, the real issue is the game's plot and it's Role-Playing (or lack there of). The story is weak, most of the time it's just boring and the ending doesn't get any better, the dialouge system is dumbed down where it treats you like an idiot and doesn't belong to a Fallout game at all, the settlements while quite expansive of what you'd can do, doesn't belong in a Fallout game, and the Skill system is dumbed down to this S.P.E.C.I.A.L. Chart, which I don't mind much, but this is a issue from a lot of people who'd plays the previous Fallout games.
I've brought up quite an amount of negatives, but there's a lot of things I'd like. The combat feels and flows better than Fallout 3 and New Vegas, expanding the armor and weapon upgrading system is really nice, this new Survival mode the game has is pretty neat, collecting items is quicker, upgrading your own power armor and the way it's used in this game is pretty cool, some of the side-quests are really fun, some of the characters are likable, and even though the game doesn't look great, it has some well-done lighting and some areas look quite nice.
In conclussion, it's a bad Fallout game, but it's not a bad game in general. There's some fun to be had and I recommend this game because of that, but don't expect this to be a good Fallout game, but if you're a fan of shooting and looting, I definitely recommend it.

Magnificent, gorgeous, and surprisingly difficult (Survival Mode is not for anyone short of  determined & dedicated) .
But it has its flaws.
The story still lacks the inherent draw of Fallout 3 and falls into the same trap of Fallout New Vegas wherein the multi-branching plot becomes self-excluding.
Community building is tedious, irritatingly so.
The clothing/armor system is finally logical and las weapons are actually useful. But most other weapons in particular seem oddly conceived and/or executed such as the new 5.56 assault rifles which are now modeled on the Lewis LMG family. What was wrong with the PTR 91 Classic or retro AR-15 models? And why does it weigh nearly thirty pounds even when totally stripped down? Nitpicking, yes but every tenth of a pound really counts in Survival mode.
Finally there was never the same sense of "I wonder what that is?" or "Where does this go?" exploring complusion as was in Fallout 3 but New Vegas lacked this as well.
TL;DR version: Superb but with definite flaws.

A fantastic rogue-like. Absolutely captures the fear and dread of not knowing what is behind the next door or even what will happen if you take a single step forward. All the while driving you onward with the lure of gold, progress and a noble crusade to rid your home of ancestral evil.
It is still heavily in development AND some people might not like everything about it. I however love it. Everything in this game is fantastic. It all leads up to that clutch crit on the boss you sacrificed 3 parties on previous failed tries. That moment of heart pounding tenseness when 3/4ths of your party are at death's door. One hit away from oblivion. That crucial moment where your heroes shine or crumble under pressure turning the battle.
Is the game perfect? No. Allot of things just don't make sense. Why do all my provisions get sold? Why would I not stockpile non perishables? Why did this dungeon spawn 4 walls to block my path in a row? Why is this dungeon literally a cube? Why do my heroes pick up traits EVERY battle meaning 90% of them just get swapped around for no reason, doesn't this just mean they don't actually have a unique personality but just risk a random one every time they go into a dungeon? Why can't I get rid of this debuff despite it being 3 weeks later?
There are points of improvement and I would definitely like to see a better perk/flaw system than the absolute RNG currently in the game. The fact there is no actual way to lose the game is both why the difficulty is manageable but it also results in the game risking allot of grind if the RNG decides to give you crappy dice. Losing your top tier party essentially means little else than regrinding another party to that level.
Some bonus like special relics being left behind or some other mitigating factor like a page or apprentice of that hero showing up after their death could mitigate the grind to a few levels instead of grinding one up from 0.
In summary a game with amazing athmosphere that truly puts the dread of the dice roll into your soul. Tight strategic combat where prioritizing, status effects and synergy are the path to victory and not power leveling. It does however get very grindy and the game's logic is inconsistent or nonsensical at times.
Definitely recommended though. If you like TB-RPG combined with rogue-like gameplay this game will scratch that itch.

The GAME itself, is very fun. Its a simple, classic, enjoyable game. Refreshing and usually not stresful
The combat is simple but is also complex at the same time, do to the free form attacks and movement while attacking, unlike some games such as WoW.
Classes are pretty fun and unique, however a couple are either really boring or not good anymore (due to other classes replacing aspects of another in a better fashion)
Building is awesome! Seen alot of cool stuff and ive made a whole song string on my club world
Leveling is very easy, until level 18 or so then its a grind. (this i am on the fence on, on one end i like leveling, but also hate grinds, so at times i like it and at others i dont)
Gear is good, aquiring good gear now is more grind and resource based and less luck based
The amount of content is very nice, and its also not easy to get rare items (duh) but its not SUPER hard, so you can get some rare stuff within a few weeks to month of playing. So when you see something cool you like, you know its more working hard for it and not "oh wow ive been grinding this for hours and still didnt get the drop!" (Although some items are luck based)
Easy to remember and keep up to date on the content. By this i mean within a few days youll be really into this game and youll understand it very well
Art style is very fun
Now onto the heavy cons
Server lag, bugs, glitches, and ques (fixable)
The amount of older and more inteligent players is dropping, and more new players are joining, this means more new players that dont have rare items for trade, bascially makes trading alot harder these days

Chaos chests WERE good, until resources became EXTREMELY more common, now chaos chests arent worth the money, should they revamp them then we will see

Fallout 4 has an interesting story to begin with and the Fallout world (if you're a fan) is great to be within. But you'll slowly begin to see that wear away as you progress further into the game. This is a Fallout game front to back, but after awhile the combat, NPC interaction, and story start to get old or outright stale.
The combat is fun and the perk system is a great take on it. But after a time you will find yourself auto-piloting through most combat encounters. There isn't really anything that makes the combat interesting and nothing that you can use aside from your weapons to spice things up. After killing the Nth mutant with a long-range rifle, you get kind of bored and wish you had gone down another perk tree.
The most criticism I've seen is from the interaction system and how bare-bones it is. You get a chat wheel that shows you the IDEA behind what your character will say, not what they actually say to the NPC. So it'll show "sarcastic" or something akin to that and then you'll say something snarky back. But you never get to see what that whole response is before you select the 1 word on the wheel. The one saving grace is that you can download a mod that will pull the sentence onto the comm wheel so you can see what that option begins with as dialogue. But that doesn't save the game as much when the dialogue options don't really make a huge difference. There wasn't really a reason for me to play through a separate time because your decisions largely make no difference. So what you choose to say or do doesn't really do much. There is perhaps a small handful of events that actually change an outcome based on how you act or talk. But they are few and far between.
And finally the story was something I was interested in to begin with until it started unraveling further and I realised that it wasn't very well thought  out and felt kind of pasted together. Some of the story lines don't feel very connected and feel more like someone trying to find any connection to place them in a flow and sticking with that. The culmination of the story didn't feel like it had any weight and I wasn't attached to anyone or anything going through. Most of the NPCs didn't have much depth to them and I left the game really only enjoying the interactions with Nick Valentine. Aside from that, the game's story didn't connect me at all with anyone from the other factions or from the main story.
Overall, it's a Fallout game. If you enjoy the Fallout universe then I would say that you should pick this up if you ever see it on a steep sale. But I would never advise to buy this for full price unless you absolutely love the Fallout universe and want to throw the devs/prods your money.

A fantastic rogue-like. Absolutely captures the fear and dread of not knowing what is behind the next door or even what will happen if you take a single step forward. All the while driving you onward with the lure of gold, progress and a noble crusade to rid your home of ancestral evil.
It is still heavily in development AND some people might not like everything about it. I however love it. Everything in this game is fantastic. It all leads up to that clutch crit on the boss you sacrificed 3 parties on previous failed tries. That moment of heart pounding tenseness when 3/4ths of your party are at death's door. One hit away from oblivion. That crucial moment where your heroes shine or crumble under pressure turning the battle.
Is the game perfect? No. Allot of things just don't make sense. Why do all my provisions get sold? Why would I not stockpile non perishables? Why did this dungeon spawn 4 walls to block my path in a row? Why is this dungeon literally a cube? Why do my heroes pick up traits EVERY battle meaning 90% of them just get swapped around for no reason, doesn't this just mean they don't actually have a unique personality but just risk a random one every time they go into a dungeon? Why can't I get rid of this debuff despite it being 3 weeks later?
There are points of improvement and I would definitely like to see a better perk/flaw system than the absolute RNG currently in the game. The fact there is no actual way to lose the game is both why the difficulty is manageable but it also results in the game risking allot of grind if the RNG decides to give you crappy dice. Losing your top tier party essentially means little else than regrinding another party to that level.
Some bonus like special relics being left behind or some other mitigating factor like a page or apprentice of that hero showing up after their death could mitigate the grind to a few levels instead of grinding one up from 0.
In summary a game with amazing athmosphere that truly puts the dread of the dice roll into your soul. Tight strategic combat where prioritizing, status effects and synergy are the path to victory and not power leveling. It does however get very grindy and the game's logic is inconsistent or nonsensical at times.
Definitely recommended though. If you like TB-RPG combined with rogue-like gameplay this game will scratch that itch.

Dark Souls 3 is (probably) the final installment in a series long known for its interesting lore, unique combat system, and unrelenting-yet-rewarding difficulty. It took me 43 hours to complete my first playthrough, but I'll probably be diving back in considering the game has multiple NG+ cycles and a healthy amount of DLC.
DS3 is my favorite game in the series when it comes to mechanics. It's more fast paced than previous games in the series, but don't expect a hack n' slash title like Metal Gear Rising or Devil May Cry. You can perform various actions such as light/heavy attacks (heavy attacks can be charged), rolling/dodging, and blocking/parrying, to name a few (since I use a melee build, I'd actually advise against blocking in most cases; get used to rolling and two-handing your weapon for higher damage output. Blocking is useful for certain bosses and several sections of the game with projectile spam, but shouldn't be used as a crutch imo). This is governed by your stamina bar, and if you deplete it you'll be unable to perform any of these actions. Dark Souls 3 requires you to be patient and observant at all times, waiting for the right opportunity to strike. Skillful play is rewarded, while button mashing will quickly and justly get you killed. Yes, finding better equipment, using the right rings for your build, and leveling yourself and your weapons are all helpful, but your level of skill is easily the biggest factor that decides whether you succeed or fail. Killing enemies will net you souls, which pretty much functions as an in-game currency to level your character or purchase items. However, if and when you die, you will drop every last soul you are carrying at the time and respawn at your previous bonfire (basically a checkpoint). When this happens, your souls will be dropped at the location of your death and you have
to return to that spot and reclaim them. If you die before you reach your souls, they're gone forever. This instincively makes you want to be cautious and play it safe, but DS3 balances this by heavily rewarding exploration. Maybe you've travelled a long way, you have a ton of souls, and you're low on health. The next bonfire might be right around the corner, or you might walk right into a boss area and die immediately. Do you backtrack to safety or press on? Your first playthrough, before you memorize the game's locations, will be extremely tense and suspenseful. Always be on the lookout; shortcuts are not always obvious, but it's crucial to find them if you want to save yourself a lot of headache upon your many inevitable deaths. DS3 has some great level design, with areas seamlessly linking to one another and brimming with secrets and treasures for the observant. Coupled with a strong combat system and a way of making you always want to press on just a little bit further, Dark Souls 3 shines in its ability to make you want to keep playing.
Dark Souls 1, although it was a great game, will forever go down in my book as one of the worst PC ports of all time. With a 30fps lock and a disgustingly low internal resolution, it looked terrible without the use of DSfix and other 3rd party tools. However, subsequent games fix this. Dark Souls 3 looks great with its varied locations and improved lighting effects. Is it going to blow your socks off and become the game you use for benchmarking your dual 1080ti setup? Hell no. It's a console-focused title optimized to have a consistently high framerate. It still looks great though, and there's opportunities for lots of awesome-looking screenshots with gorgeous views. Going back to how all the areas link together, it's cool to find a high point and look around at all the places you've been. Visually, this really helps the game's world look and feel like a real place rather than just some map littered with game assets. Some of the animations aren't perfect and the smoke/fire effects aren't on par with what we'd see in something like MGS V, but that's getting nitpicky. While not a technical masterpiece, the game looks great as a whole with its absolutely fantastic artstyle...and that's good enough.
DS3 has the best sound design in the series in my opinion. Everything is punchy, impacful, and effective. Certain areas become much more atmospheric with the right ambient sound effects, and the lack of music outside of boss fights really draws attention to it. When you
encounter bosses...my god. DS3's sountrack is incredible. It's extremely dramatic and movie-like; the heart-pounding thrill of taking down an enemy much bigger than yourself is only amplified when it's accompanied by a full orchestra and choir. The theme for the Lorian & Lothric boss fight is my personal favorite.
With minimal cutscenes and dialogue, DS3 uses the game itself to explain story points and lore. It's very effective, and is one of the things that helps the series feel so unique. Due to the nature of the game's unique blend of singleplayer and multiplayer, it cannot be paused; some may find this to be an annoyance while others may find that it increases the game's tension and immersion. I'm somewhere in between those two opinions (if you go afk in a non-safe area while embered, you deserve anything that happens to you). There's not much to speak of here; the Souls games have always been minimalistic in a sense, and DS3 is no exception.
Dark Souls 3 is an action-oriented rpg with what can almost be described as Metroidvania-esque level design (it bills itself as an open world game, but it's awfully linear for better or for worse). It's challenging and rewarding, forcing you to think tactically instead of just rushing through it like any other game. It combines a lot of gameplay elements from previous games in the series, and as a result it's the most Souls-feeling game you can play imo. It looks good, it sounds good, and it feels good. If you're open to something new, want to get into the series, or want to see how far the series has come, Dark Souls 3 is a must-have in your library.

Games like this are the reason why I really wish Steam's "do you recommend" question had more than just two options. Here's why: because I would very, very highly recommend this game... to a certain breed of gamer. Let me explain.
First, the good.
is a masterfully crafted game. The artwork is beautifully grotesque and animation is smooth. The game is balanced fairly well, even if it is balanced towards the "hard" end of the spectrum. Even in early access there is nothing about this game that feels sloppy or poorly considered.
The stress mechanic, in which your characters accumulate stress which can affect them in various negative (and sometimes even positive) ways, is a really interesting idea and something that you don't really see a whole lot in video games. The only place I've seen anything like this before would be the
games, and I honestly feel like it's handled a lot better here.
Oh, and the fact that it's constantly auto-saving, while intended to prevent save-scumming, also has the effect of allowing you to quit and pick back up whenever you want without losing progress, great for people who don't have a lot of time to sit down and play a game.
The game wasn't my cup of tea (I'll get to why in a minute) but I can't honestly call it bad just because of that. It's not bad. In fact...
But wait, don't stop reading yet, because now it's time for the bad. As I said before,
is a hard game.
Well, no, that's not really accurate.
is hard. That's why I like that series, and it's why I thought I would like this game too.
is not hard, it's unfair.
See, you can be riding high one minute, dominating every encounter and getting a ton of good items from the various chests and cupboards (called "curios" in the game) that litter the dungeons. Then you get into that one battle. You know the one I mean. It's the one that doesn't even seem like it should be all that hard. It's the same enemies you've been wasting with ease this whole time. Except this time you do nothing but miss your attacks over and over, while they stack critical hit upon critical hit. Before you can even click the "retreat" button half your force is at Death's Door... or through it. It's a little like
in a way.
And the thing is, that's not an accident. I said this game was masterfully crafted and it honestly is. This isn't poor game balance, it's the entire point. It's the underlying design philosophy of the game.
The developers never intended this to be a game where you train up max level badasses and retake the estate.  There are no badasses in the
. There are no heroes.
No, this is a game where you recruit expendable idiots by the wagon-load (literally) and send them to die for the greater good. (This is also why there are so few levels of upgrades for your characters: so that restarting when your top character dies is easier.)
That's why I say, I really wish that Steam allowed more options than just "recommend" or "not recommend." Because, on the one hand, the game is very well made. It has become exactly what I feel the developers wanted it to be. It is a GREAT GAME.
But "great" and "universally enjoyable" are not the same thing. A lot of people don't like hard games. I do like hard games and even I was turned off by the unfairness and the inability to properly take care of my people.
If I really had to choose (and for the purposes of the Steam version of this review I kind of do) I would say that I don't recommend the game, if only because I think the number of people who would enjoy it are in the minority.
That said, if you're the type who thinks you might enjoy that then by all means buy the game right now. It's only $19.99 USD on Steam right now, and for that you get one Hell of a solid classic-style RPG with an interesting twist.
If you're more like me and you get attached to your characters and don't want to see them die (or if you just don't like hard games) then skip this one.

At the time, I didn't like this game when I'd first played it on the Xbox One, but just when I got it on Steam when it was free for a few days and decided to buy it when it was on sale, I'm liking it. The PC port has a lot of issues when it comes to it's optimization, at times the framerate goes to 60 to 20 and this laptop I'd own should go through the game's specs just fine.
Anyway, the optimization isn't the real issue, the real issue is the game's plot and it's Role-Playing (or lack there of). The story is weak, most of the time it's just boring and the ending doesn't get any better, the dialouge system is dumbed down where it treats you like an idiot and doesn't belong to a Fallout game at all, the settlements while quite expansive of what you'd can do, doesn't belong in a Fallout game, and the Skill system is dumbed down to this S.P.E.C.I.A.L. Chart, which I don't mind much, but this is a issue from a lot of people who'd plays the previous Fallout games.
I've brought up quite an amount of negatives, but there's a lot of things I'd like. The combat feels and flows better than Fallout 3 and New Vegas, expanding the armor and weapon upgrading system is really nice, this new Survival mode the game has is pretty neat, collecting items is quicker, upgrading your own power armor and the way it's used in this game is pretty cool, some of the side-quests are really fun, some of the characters are likable, and even though the game doesn't look great, it has some well-done lighting and some areas look quite nice.
In conclussion, it's a bad Fallout game, but it's not a bad game in general. There's some fun to be had and I recommend this game because of that, but don't expect this to be a good Fallout game, but if you're a fan of shooting and looting, I definitely recommend it.

It does get a bit tedious in a huge dose, such as a 4 hour stream, but in small doses, it has the enjoyment of all the raids in WOW combined. I often don't support MMO games, for the fact that they become addictive and each session is like a shot of heroin into your veins, but this game actually is much different than many other MMOs because of the fact that it doesnt encourage long play sessions due to the tediousness of that huge dose. This game gets a solid 8/10 from me.

EDIT:
Most of all the issues have been resolved by the devs. The dev team did something that I wish more games would by adding game play customization options. Basically if you dont like certain features (like the stressful stunning) you can disable them. This is really fantastic! every player can now customize the game play to their liking. Congrats to the devs for listening to the community on this one.
The good:
The game starts off extremely fun! It is difficult in the beginning and has many unique classes. The stress mechanic is interesting and could be fun if they tweaked it. Its fun to upgrade locations to reduce hero stress. The graphics are appealing. The positional strategy for your heroes is pretty good. Basically heroes have different abilities depending on whether they are in the front or back. The game's concept seems fresh and intriguing.
The bad:
So far the games fun factor wears off very quickly! The way they implemented stress is pretty frustrating. You can get hit with a normal attack from a monster that does 14 damage and your heroes are A OK. But by golly if a little♥♥♥♥♥♥ant creature crits you for 2 damage OMG SO SCARY! All your heroes stress increases dramatically. Also your heroes get stress by going backwards even when the hallway is fully lit and cleared. It is almost as if your heroes are children and scared of the dark. It costs so much to treat diseases, negative traits, and stress, that the game essentially becomes stress manager 2.0. The game's makers add in a bunch of irrational and frustrating game mechanics as well. You cant heal outside of combat and there are no healing items except for a “camp fire”. Some how your heroes forget how to heal as soon as they are out of combat. I understand that this is a game mechanic to make it more challenging but it is a bad one. Please increase the difficulty in other ways that don’t seem as dumb as your heroes just refusing to heal outside of combat. There is another frustrating mechanic they used to prevent stunning one enemy while your entire party heals up inside combat. Basically if you stun the last enemy alive all of your heroes increase stress dramatically and say stupid comments like “stop toying”. It is so scary to my heroes that I am stun locking an enemy to heal up because I cant do it outside of combat. Then there is the annoying voice of the narrator. He states the same obnoxious comments over and over. You can beat a fight with 100% health and 0% stress on heroes and he says “A trifling victory but a victory none the less”. Please explain to me how that is a trifling victory? It is like the narrator tries to make the game seem so hard and scary when in actuality it is easy and grindy. It feels as if there are basically 3 possible strategies to the game. 1 play the game how it is meant to be played, all of your heroes die, and you run out of money trying to manage their stress and never progress. 2 exploit the game and leave one enemy up while you heal all of your party's stress and health (very grindy). 3 stun stun stun and include part of number 2's strategy. The game just becomes a grind fest. Same quests over and over. Get in combat that you aren’t worried about losing and draw it out way to long to heal. Then rinse and repeat.
Conclusion:
This game shows a lot of potential. If they fix some of its annoyances it will be an awesome game!  Unfortunately, in its current state I would probably hold off to see how it turns out.

If you aren't familiar with Fallout, with Elder Scrolls and not a huge RPG fan, I'm going to venture to say that by now your missing out on some of the openning spats they had with bugs, the engine being pushed a lil past it's abilities and other matters. With all the mess we get with games when they are first released, what problems remain you can overlook. And while the modding community cant match Skyrim, there are plenty of people busy at work on fixing and adding content to the game. Casual gamers and some die hard fall out fanboys will still enjoy this game. Look into the Nexus website to explore the modding community though, or you will be missing out. Mods! Even ho hum games can be fun modded to your liking.However... This is as close as I can get to giving the game a 50/50. I'm not saying hands down don't buy it, I'm just saying think about it, and the message our sales send to the dev's and corps, if you actually care.
Pro: It's a decent lil game. Better than many that come out these days.
Con: It's not what I expect from Fall Out. It falls short in the degree of awesome I expect, and also just in the material seeming to fall short of what it could have been.
If you ARE going to get this game, get it NOW, while it's on sale! Or wait for the next time.
Yes, yet another mixed review. I'm of the mind that people not familiar with the in depth richness we have enjoyed in some earlier, less advanced games don't understand how people can play a game like this and go.."meh". It is the writing and thought going into multiple possible plot lines like a noveltist and an old school table top rpg gamemaster working hand in hand that made earlier games so intellectually stimulating and explosive within the confines of our own imaginations, and not just a quick explosion of adrenaline and pretty graphics. The entire industry seems pushed for flashy graphics and action, less thinking, grab quick bucks and kick a product out the door that just isn't finished or isn't polished in the way/to the degree most games used to be when they were released. Charge people to help develope, then drop the ball and say oh well, or toss out a product with bits missing and call it DLC for more quick bucks. Yet , now, in some cases it also seems like people even toss out games with limited amounts of content, even flaws in gameplay or plotlines, and expect modders in the gaming community to pick up their mess, and leave it to the players to polish the game off to their own tastes. And people at Steam see this like DLC, just another opportunity for them to slide in there and charge money in some fashion so they can get their extra, extra slice on yet more sales of the same games or what was left out of the product in the first place.
Just as much as I loved Skyrim, the weak magic system was tacked on at the end, apparently, and the lore messed up to explain the reasons why, perhaps out of rushing or from trying to force melee warrior and thief type play for whatever reason. Sure characters were to look rough and dirty, but the character and NPC's were not quality material. Some of the DLC actually wasnt that bad, but some of it should have been either free or there in the first place. On one hand I'm glad they have backed up and said it will be years before the next Elder Scrolls. I think they know if they botch it, the storm will be thick and fierce.  Yet, if the industry and the gaming community as a whole continue going down hill, it's not going to be what we really want anyway.

Dark Souls 3 quickly became one of my favorite games of all time. The graphics are amazing (even at low settings), it controls very smoothly and it's at a very good price for what it has to offer,  which is an amazing experience... that if you don't bail at The Abyss Watchers, hehe.
You play as "The Ashen One" and you have a quest to defeat the lords of cinder, in order to reignite The First Flame... while getting destroyed by fat ladies, skeleton dogs, Mr. Krabs, a giant hand with legs and much more. You travel through 24~ locations, filled with enemies, items, hidden walls and messages from players telling you to jump off a cliff, or to "Try Tongue But Whole". Almost all of them have a boss at the end. It depends on the player's skill, or to be more exact, timing his rolls and R1 spams, on how quickly it dies. While you might be stuck at one of them for around 50 deaths, when you actually defeat it, it is very rewarding and it gives you the feeling "OH MY GOD, FINALLY!".
When you defeat all the bosses, including the last one, you have the option to "Begin Journey 2", or to start New Game + (NG+), which lets you replay the game, with its difficulty raised up a little and with some items you find better than on your first playthrough.
If you played the previous games, you should definatly give this one a shot, and if you have never played them and DS3 takes your "Souls virginity", than be prepared to die a lot to the tutorial boss, or to die 80 times at the Abyss Watchers (like I did), until you finally "git gud".

Completed Fallout 4 over the steam free weekend, plays more like a shooter than an RPG, never once did I feel the need to use VATS, so it almost felt more like a Bioshock experiance.
They give you power armour right of the bat, whereas I remember in Fallout 3 and New vegas - power armour was something that had to be earned, and when you got it, it felt rewarding. None of that was here, drop you in and here you go, power armour - go get 'em slugger!
Well I ditched the power armour and went through the game without using it, story and writing is weak sauce compared to the other games, and I didn't get the same fallout universe feeling as in 3, the world didn't feel AS immersive, though after playing for a while the atmosphere did start to grow on me, and felt like I was playing a fallout game.. just not as good of a fallout game.
The main plot has a twist and branching point where you decide which faction you'll work for, and while I won't spoil the twist for anyone who hasn't played, it was predictable, shallow and didn't have the impact that they had clearly intended to get you invested, at least that was my take on it.
With all that said, game is game, you can still have fun with it, but it may not be the fallout you want. I'd reccomend 3 or New Vegas over this any day of the week.
Overall 6.5/10 - Average, not bad, but doesn't completly live up to the Fallout brand.

I will start off by saying that the narrator is AMAZING and really helps in the immersion.  The small hints of character interactions (mainly groundskeeper) outside of the narrator are great.  The writing is very well done and the gravitas of the narrator really sells the environment.  Unfortunately the narrator is more of a bonus feature than a main attraction as he is mostly there for brief one liners.
As for the mechanics.  I feel that they are mostly solid.  The light mechanics giving you advantages for paying for more torches or allowing you to skimp and risk stress and ambushes is well done.  Many of the characters give you multiple options for how you want to deal with things.  I found a few classes less than stellar, but I'm not sure that I had the opportunity to use them appropriately and/or they may just represent a class for a playstyle that isn't mine.  Also, the upgrades that I did do at my home town felt meaningful even if I didn't keep a session going long enough to always truly utilize them.
Okay now onto my complaints.  This game is extremely frustrating to me.   This game is an attrition based resource management/squad based tactical game. I  appreciate a very challenging attrition based game.  The best example of this I've played is the Long War MOD for XCOM.  If you make a mistake you are punished, you are punished VERY hard, but you also know that you made the mistake and therefore that you could have played better.  If you play well you're rewarded (more you're not punished), but if you play poorly you're punished.
Darkest Dungeon for me always just feels punishing.  I never feel like I've made a correct decision (and this I feel is the real problem). One culprit of this is the stress mechanic.  In principle I like the stress mechanic.  The more you deal with the dark and dangerous the more you're affected until a breaking point.  In actuality it just feels like a constnatly looming sword of Damacles waiting to fall and punish you.  Those breaking points come far too easily and when they do they can be very debilitating and not just for the character who had the breaking point, but the whole team.
All in all I can't say if the game is overtuned or I'm just bad.  Either way the idea is sound, but the execution is lacking.  I'll be honest they even found a way to make killing your enemy feel punishing (they turn into a corpse that can prevent you from hitting other targets).  If you can find a way to make killing your enemies feel unsatisfying because of the consequences... you're really doing something wrong.

When I installed this game for free I was expecting it to be some Cube World Minecraft piece of crap that I would play for 5 minutes and laugh at. I was very, VERY wrong.
From the moment you step foot into the world it's surprising how much detail went into it and how large it is. I know that sounds silly for a cube based game, but the devs put a lot of work into fleshing it out. There are lots of different classes which excel at different things. If you like melee, there are classes for that and they offer different flavors of melee fighting (for example Knights are sturdy, can charge, and be defensive while Neon Ninjas rely on stealth and being sneaky). The same goes for ranged combat. Shadow Hunters are like ranged assassins, whole Tomb Raisers attack with necromancy magic and raise skeletons from the ground to fight for you for a short time. That's just a small part of the variety.
There are TROVES (pun intended) of treasures to find and dungeons to explore and defeat either by yourself or with some buddies. Bosses aren't too difficult as far as mechanics, but they still can privide a challenge.
The world is almost fully destructible, and you can mine cubes and build practically wherever (however what you build is only permenant if you build it in your cornerstone, or player owned home that can be summoned at any plot of land with a sign in front of it, or if you build in a Club World. Club Worlds are basically a world for you and your "Club" (aka Guild, Clan, etc) to do whatever you'd like.
Trove CAN get repetitive and grindy if all you do is just burn through dungeons as fast as possible and sprint off to the next without any exploration or distractions, so I do not recommend following that sort of play-style. Take your time, do what you want, build what you want, and just have a good time!!!
There is also the issue of having to wait a LONG time to log in during high-traffic hours. The game just released and the devs were not expecting it to be such a smash success, so they are having to constantly fix bugs and add more server space. Just have some patience while they get used to so many people playing their game and offer some feedback. I believe this game can go to great places  with the right support :)

You will lose, and sometimes you will lose even when you have played as perfectly as you can. This is because the enemies are merciless, but not as much so as the arbitrary lord and master of this dark realm: RNG. If you can't handle playing with a combination of luck and skill, then avoid this game.

The good, the bad and the ugly:
Ill start with the ugly - bugs/glitches. Ive played FO:NV and FO3 so im used to bugs and glitches but i was hoping FO4 would have improved on that. In those previous 2, i remember having to reboot my system seemingly every hour or so due to freeze ups (New Vegas was far worse than 3 however) so i hope this isnt the case with FO4 as i get higher in level. So far its mainly minor stuff like clipping, occasional frame rate drops and not always getting a dialogue pop up when pointing at NPCs without a little work, but these are occasional and not too huge an issue. The one thing that does♥♥♥♥♥♥me off is that followers dont seem to listen when i send them to a settlement. Ive lost 2 followers already because of this so i hope they implement something like what NV had where you can see where they are on your map. To not have included this at release was dumb.
The bad - the ugly things are things that i feel are somewhat inexcusable. The bad is just stuff i dont really care for, but this is a lot more opinion than it is fact. Anyone who has played previous Fallouts will know what im talking about here - dialogue is really lacking the fun factor of past games. The voice acting is fine (more on that in the good). What im talking about is the limited options you have when talking to someone. Basically a yes, no, maybe and sarcastic option. Thats it. I miss the S.P.E.C.I.A.L or skill based options. Playing the game with 1 or 2 in intelligence was always funny. Sometimes when interrogating someone, if you had high intelligence or perception, you had unique choices. That went for most other attributes and skills. It made dialogue a lot more interesting and made each play through unique in that respect. I definitely miss that
The good - ok, this might be long, so bear with me. I just hope i can convince you to still play this game even with those negatives listed above (just trying to be unbiased and honest)
*The new leveling system - i freakin LOVE it. The skills from past games are still there, theyre just disguised as a much more advanced perk system. The past games made decisions too easy at level up in my opinion. Now, having everything available right from the start, you really have to plan out your build form the get go. If you want the Concentrated fire perk at level 2, you can do that (i think you got that at level 18 in previous games), BUT it requires you to max out perception right off the bat. Or maybe youre a sneaky sniper type and want the better criticals perk early on - possible if you have enough luck. That may or may not be a great idea. Its your CHOICE. Thats what i love about this new system, you can build your character how you want, even if it may not be the smartest choice :D. The character building was pretty meh in both FO3 & NV because by level 28-30 or so, you were maxed out in everything if you did it right. Choices didnt really feel that important like they do now. Im level 20 right now and have so many skills that im lacking in, but thats a good thing in my opinion.
*The story. For me, FO3's main story was just ok. Its not what made me fall in love with that game. It was the brilliant side quests and unmarked quests, the huge, strangely beautiful world filled with goodies to find and baddies to avoid, and the numerous buildings with interesting stories behind them if you took the time to fully explore. FO:NV did a better job i think, introducing multiple factions and ultimately making you pick one to support in the end so i felt that game had a better main storyline, but i felt like the side quests werent as diverse as FO3, and some were just downright annoying where you were just going back and fourth playing telephone between characters (add to that the fact that you sometimes had 3 load screens like at casinos or fort macarran) and it was an exercise in patience. FO4 to this point has been awesome, both in terms of main story and side quests. Nice variety and not too many annoying and unnecessary load screens.
*Dialogue - yes, the choices you have in dialogue is a bad for me, but what we DO have is a really well voice acted game. Gone are the days of what seemed to be like 5 voices for every character in the game. This is another area of major improvement for this series. The voice acting is wonderful and i cant remember hearing the same voice on 2 characters yet. Im sure theyre there, but it isnt obvious.
*Crafting - major improvements over New Vegas, and quite literally makes everything you pick up useful, and not just for selling for caps. The settlement stuff leaves much to be desired though. I dont see much use for it for as un-userfriendly as it is. If it proved more useful, i could see myself trying to work it out, or if it were more user friendly, i wouldnt really care that it wasnt helpful, id just do it for fun. But as it is now, i dont care for it much.
*The companions - much like New Vegas, interesting companions with fun quest lines of their own. Me *hearts* Piper. I cant wait to go through each of their quest lines.
*The world - ok, so i saved the best for last. Oh my goodness this world has so much to explore! Ive spent over 30 hours in this game so far and my map is probably 20% explored. Maybe not even that much actually. Im loving the new legendary enemies and the loot theyre dropping. Ive died many times just trying to beat these guys cuz the loot is almost always worth it. Originally being from the northeast, getting to explore a post apocalyptic Boston is so fun. Running into NPCs with that distinct accent makes me a little home sick :). When i first arrived at Diamond City, i was just in complete awe. Those folks sure are proud of their Green protector. I could go on about how awesome this world is, but ive been typing too long as it is.

If you only play one fantasy RPG in your life -- don't choose Darkest Dungeon.
That's not meant as a knock on the game. It's a great game with beautiful artwork and a dark sense of humor. The world of Darkest Dungeon also feels somewhat unique -- it's the typical, vaguely medieval European setting but with a decidedly Lovecraftian bent.
But to fully appreciate a game like this, it seems to me you must have some familiarity with the fantasy RPG genre and its tropes.
The game is absurdly difficult. Here are just a few examples...
I've played these games going back to Wizardry, and most feature a town where your characters can seek refuge, heal, sell trinkets, listen to gossip and so on. These places are usually safe. Not so in Darkest Dungeon, which is the first game of this type I've played where one of my characters was recuperating from a dungeon outing in a village brothel, where he suffered an injury that delayed his return to duty. The village is full of potential pitfalls.
In addition to traditional "hit points", you also have to monitor your characters' stress levels. As their stress levels mount, they can become dysfunctional and pick up all sorts of annoying habits. Sometimes this leads them to essentially disobey your commands -- refusing to fight in combat, inspecting chests you fear might be booby-trapped, keeping loot for themselves, and so on. They can become abusive and berate the other characters, thereby rendering their stress contagious to the rest of the party. If a character's stress level reaches the max, he or she keels over from a heart attack, regardless of how many hit points remain.
There are no unambiguously good magic relics either, like a "long sword +1". Every advantage conferred by an object is offset (or more than offset) by a serious disadvantage. I rarely equip any of the "treasures" I find.
In most games it is prudent to "buff up" your characters before tackling a dungeon where a previous party was slaughtered, right? In Darkest Dungeon your newly-buffed characters will refuse to participate in missions they deem insufficiently challenging.
Then there is the whole corpse controversy. I won't even get into that here, other than to recommend turning off the corpses option when you start up a campaign.
Sounds fun, right?

Like with most Early Access games on Steam, Starbound uses the convenient excuse of being an "unfinished version" to explain away the various and many design flaws present in its current state. Let's be fair here: most people got hyped about this game with the expectation that it would be like Terraria. After all, when Terraria's updates supposedly ended indefinitely, people were directed to Starbound as a work-in-progress to look out for, and perhaps creating an unrealistic expectation of the game in the process. And right now it just isn't as fun.
Just about everything in the game
is extremely boring. Mining is ploddingly boring, and even the best equipment you can find for that purpose still struggles to deal with cobblestone in a timely manner. Hunting monsters has little purpose beyond finding money and maybe leather; meat isn't even an issue because you can find fruits galore in chests or in the ground. Finding chests isn't interesting because all they contain are things you already have, or weapons - and the weapons aren't interesting. The variation between them right now is just numbers, and the enchantments (fire, poison, lightning) don't differ between items. Even finding rarer, "legendary" items is a banal experience because the enchantments do roughly the same thing as everything else and they're not even better than the greens you find.
Exploring is only interesting in the sense that you MIGHT just find something interesting like furniture, instruments, or vanity hats. Yet if you're doing so for anything useful like weapons or armor you're better off just digging mindlessly because the ore-based weapons and armor you make are superior to anything else you find. And there's nothing to be found in these "randomly-generated dungeons" as well, besides a certain tech piece that isn't even useful right now. PROTIP: for higher level monsters, make sure you have the high ground, or they'll stomp a mudhole in your♥♥♥♥♥
The interface has some interesting foibles as well. When opening the 3D printer, focus automatically goes to the search bar in the bottom left, preventing you from easily opening your inventory to deposit what you need to scan in the machine.
Stuff that isn't dirt goes into the "dirt" section of your backpack, but there's no way to sort your inventory so everything gets cluttered as hell unless you painstakingly take the time to do it yourself. You can't even delete characters without digging into the file structure of the game itself.
Suffice to say Starbound has got a long way to go before it can be truly compared to its predecessor. In Terraria, finding certain things or conquering bosses was an achievement. In Starbound I can literally build a wall around any threatening monster and just slap them with my boring 23 dps stick until they die. Oh and they don't drop anything besides the "thing" that you need to get to the next tier of ores.

Spiral Knights! A "F2P" (Free To Play) Game released by Three Rings and SEGA back in April 2010.
Plot: The mystery of the story unfolds as you follow your quests down into the depths of Cradle (The planet setting) to know why the Spiral Knights have crashed down onto this mysterious planet. To get out, they will have to harness the energy from "The Core" which lies in the deepest parts of the planet, but with the mysterious machine and world called the "Clockworks" that lies below, the dangers of delving into the planet and the knight's fate will remain unknown... In this ever-changing world. As the game's main storyline is still incomplete, the developers still keeps updating the game. We are surely all thrilled to see what will unfold when "The Core" patch finally releases in the upcoming future.
Gameplay and Multiplayer: Spiral Knights is a very interesting co-op dungeon crawler, as it is a face paced gameplay through many diverse environments in the clockworks. As the players will be able to play together to 4 player, it is also a drop-in/drop-out multiplayer which does not affect how you play but make the hostile enemies get a little tougher. It is a top-down third-person real-time action/adventure game which could be compared to some old games for example The Legend of Zelda and so. As for this style, some hardcore gamers that play games like Diablo and so might find this very boring and a little too "old school" for what they call "games" nowadays.
Visuals: The game runs with the Java engine, which restricted them to do anything much with higher-level graphics, however the game again really does resent old games as mentioned which could also be a reason why they kept the graphics the way it is, but compared to modern games and what you can really do with visuals, this would be medium rated. There are a few cut scenes in the game which still used fully the game mechanics, however with switched over and close-up angle directed camera, although with this being the visuals it is suitable for any age group of audiences.
Audio: The OST is made by Harry Mack, which did a truly amazing job of making the game sound really old-school, keeping the styles of 8-bit music from the time, but using newer technology and sound systems such as the strings, and so on. The soundtrack of this game is very diverse when comparing to any other RPG game, since this is a cartoon/fantasy type. With the game being free to play, Three Rings did not invest too much in putting 'voices' into the game, so therefore there was no voice acting, but even without it-- The game plays itself with all the dialogues coming up as comicified themed speech bubbles that do not disturb the player's gameplay. You probably wouldn't find any other game's soundtrack feeling "old school" style of the original 8-bit gaming music that sounds really modern as Spiral Knights'.
Reception: As the reception goes, there are many awards and positive comments on it from communities such as "Ars Technica", "Wired" and "PC Gamer". In 2011, the Game Developers Choice Online Awards has nominated Spiral Knights as "Best Visual Online Arts, Best Online Game Design, Best Audio for an Online Game, and Best New Online Game". It was awarded for the "Best" Online Game Design. Most of the reception and comments also really do find the game really addicting as far as the community goes, 2 year after its initial release-- Over 3 million accounts were registered and having near a million active per day.

This game is great, and I really like it. However, it isn't perfect, so I will break down my review below:
~The Biomes~
Rich and diverse, each populated with different foes which have different AI; very well made, but lacks any kind of linking between them. Where one biome suddenly stops, another just begins. You can go from a world of candy to a lava filled hellscape in under a second.
~Building~
The cornerstones let you take your home with you, and the clan system is well set up. Very well made.
~Levelling~
Pretty well balanced; I have to say it's nice. Level cap is a bit low, though. However, each class levels individually.
~Bosses~
A bit of a sore point for this game, unfortunetly. The bosses either die in a few seconds or hit you for all but 2 of your health, leaving the last of it to be instantly removed by their minions or arena traps. Frustrating, and seldom feels rewarding. They just aren't quite diverse enough yet.
~Items~
The items are very aethetically pleasing, and the cosmetic system is very nicely done. The teirs and such can be annoying when it takes hours of farming to improve gear, but beggars can't be choosers.
~Shadow Arenas~
Difficult, but not necessarily fun. Needs more variation and better drop rates, especially in Uber 4+.
~Sky Dimension~
I hate this place so much. It's just annoying to navigate and just a huge waste of time and potential.
~The Classes~
These are the classes I have played so far. These are based on my experiences.
Dracolite: Very strong, if a bit bland. You get to transform into a dragon, which is cool and all, but nothing spectacular.
Gunslinger: Pretty weak, all things considered. When you get the the higher levels, you can hardly notice each of you shots doing any damage at all; it's just sad really. And his kit is reall, reall bland. The only cool thing is you get to hover if you hit enemies constantly in the air... Which is much harder and doesn't make the reward seem worthwhile.
Neon Ninja: My personal favorite at the moment; very powerful, but also very squisjhy and dies eaisly. Has a large AoE snare and powerful crowd control, but requires a bit more skill and luck than other classes, but handles tight areas better.
Fey Trickster: Relies on a similar "hit and run" strategy as the Neon Ninja, but is almost entirely reliant on basic attacks, and has one attack (the "glitter bomb") which is completely useless; it has low damage, high cost and does pathetic AoE knockback. I find this class tedious and tends to struggle in the tight arenas against multiple enemies. Does OK at the Shadow Arenas though.
Shadow Hunter: Kind of cool, but it's all up to dumb luck whether your passive marks the boss or not, which means you can end up being almost useless for a good 10 seconds. You ult marks all enemies in an area, which is nice, but the AoE it adds is buggy right now. Pretty strong, though.
Pirate Captain: The most hopelessly bad class in my opinion; he has short range, slow attack speed, not real direct way of attacking and just two measly turrets he throws out. Boring.
Tomb Raiser: The Minion Minigame. Almost as boring as the Pirate Captain, but atleast the Tomb Raiser is useful... However, his minions die very quickly when mobbed.
~Pay To Win?~
No.
~PvP~
Maybe in the future.
~Pets and Mounts~
Very cool, and all mounts give the same speed boost (paid mounts are the same you can buy relatively early in the game with ingame currency). Pets give unique and powerful bonuses, but are not overpowered; they just give you a little hand.
~Music~
Pretty good.
~Aesthetics~
It's a voxel game; make your own judgement. Pretty nice style, though.
~Mastery Rank~
Universal levels which increase as you level classes or find new styles of weapons; gives buffs and new pets/mounts. Well made.
~The Worst of It~
The Neon Biome. Where to begin? It's BY FAR the worst part of this game. It has the Punchbot (a basic minion, let me remind you), which can nearly 1 shot you, annoying and absurdely tanky ranged enemies and bosses whcih, once again, can pretty much one shot you. Not to mention that the neon bosses are more mobile and have the ability to draw you in with a suction ability. To top mit all off, it's an eyesore, and monotonous. It's meant to look robotic, but it's just generally irritating.
Plus, the grind can get pretty annoying, and you can die simply because the game wanted to ♥♥♥♥ you over with the right combination of high damage enemies and moboility inhibiting bosses. The rewards are hardly every worth it... It takes so damn long to get a gear "improvement" of about 20 damage. Which doesn't amount to jack♥♥♥♥♥♥in the Uber levels.
~Finale~
So this sums up my review of Trove. It isn't Pay To Win, and is great fun and very addicting. The loot is pretty bad and you will seldom replace it near end game, and they all feel the same. The bosses can feel cheap and the ingame store has EXCEEDINGLY high prices for no reason. Still a great game.
7.5/10 would reccomend.

If you only play one fantasy RPG in your life -- don't choose Darkest Dungeon.
That's not meant as a knock on the game. It's a great game with beautiful artwork and a dark sense of humor. The world of Darkest Dungeon also feels somewhat unique -- it's the typical, vaguely medieval European setting but with a decidedly Lovecraftian bent.
But to fully appreciate a game like this, it seems to me you must have some familiarity with the fantasy RPG genre and its tropes.
The game is absurdly difficult. Here are just a few examples...
I've played these games going back to Wizardry, and most feature a town where your characters can seek refuge, heal, sell trinkets, listen to gossip and so on. These places are usually safe. Not so in Darkest Dungeon, which is the first game of this type I've played where one of my characters was recuperating from a dungeon outing in a village brothel, where he suffered an injury that delayed his return to duty. The village is full of potential pitfalls.
In addition to traditional "hit points", you also have to monitor your characters' stress levels. As their stress levels mount, they can become dysfunctional and pick up all sorts of annoying habits. Sometimes this leads them to essentially disobey your commands -- refusing to fight in combat, inspecting chests you fear might be booby-trapped, keeping loot for themselves, and so on. They can become abusive and berate the other characters, thereby rendering their stress contagious to the rest of the party. If a character's stress level reaches the max, he or she keels over from a heart attack, regardless of how many hit points remain.
There are no unambiguously good magic relics either, like a "long sword +1". Every advantage conferred by an object is offset (or more than offset) by a serious disadvantage. I rarely equip any of the "treasures" I find.
In most games it is prudent to "buff up" your characters before tackling a dungeon where a previous party was slaughtered, right? In Darkest Dungeon your newly-buffed characters will refuse to participate in missions they deem insufficiently challenging.
Then there is the whole corpse controversy. I won't even get into that here, other than to recommend turning off the corpses option when you start up a campaign.
Sounds fun, right?
It actually is very fun. It is also very difficult, and as I said I think it is meant for people who have played Bard's Tale or Baldur's Gate and maybe feel as though they've already seen everything the genre has to offer.
Nuclear war and survival afterwards are very serious things. How does this game expect to be taken seriously when it uses a smiling cartoon child as a logo when levelling up?

Great game. It may still be in early access, but it already is one of my favourite games of all time.
First of all is the atmosphere of darkness and depression which you slowly resolve. Step by step, deed by deed, building by building. The monsters, the bosses, the heroes. The story is awesome, one thing you see in the letter of your ancestor, but completely another when you start to investigate what he really did. The abominations he created and his memories about them.
The calm voice of narrator, the astonishing comments help even more. The game descriptions and art in this game are absolutely fabulous. The game itself is somewhat hard if you try to jump on it without planning. Unlike many games where you can just load last save or be reborn loosing some of your XP or cash, this game forgives no mistakes. You characters die forever, and there is no way to turn back time. Diseases and quirks need to be treated, wounds patched and supplies used. Otherwise expect heavy losses and bad performance. But with good planning you can cut through those abominations with relative ease. Relative, because sometimes things can go bad even for a well-prepared party. Random dungeons and events make this part even more exiting.
Another interesting thin is the stress system. forget your unbreakable and ever-brave characters of other games. Here you need to keep a close eye on your morals, since they are as important as physical good-being of your characters. If you get too much stress, you get negative quirks, if you leave them stressed for too long, prepare for a serious madness. You character become afflicted. Such  character becomes a serious problem for the party until treated. Push them even further and they reach the limit, a heart attack, which ensures his death.
I recommend this game for those who like good and atmospheric games, who like dark and gloomy style and a nice story. Remembers me of a good old Disciples 2 who had a similar style.

I've tried to play this game with the advise given on the opening screen. I'm aware that the game is designed to involve constant meat-grinding of the characters. That is not an issue I cannot overcome. There is a lot that, with enough polish, would make for an amazing game. Even meat-grinders have their place.
So what went wrong? You know that feeling where you're telling Windows to do something but Windows is ignoring you to do something else? This game has something even worse. In this game, that frustration is an intentional feature. As you play the characters you're controlling go insane, and they have a chance of ignoring your input to perform other, deliberately inconvenient, actions. The game's designers believe they are trying to model mental illnesses, but instead all that's happening is they refuse to do what's in their own best interests.
Reviewing a game like this is particularly gut-wrenching because the developers had a really good game. The earlier sections, where the characters are still usable, have definite promise. There is a lot of nuance and a lot of interesting stuff in those sections, but the developers lost sight of what appeals to the fans of strategy games. If they had simply placed limits that were somehow understandable so that the player could work around them in-the-moment then cope with the baggage later on, the game could have been amazing. Unfortunately, what starts out as an engrossing every-move-matters strategy game quickly degenerates into something unpredictable. No more strategy. When your planning doesn't matter anymore there's just a typical par-for-the-course "you have to have a healer" click-fest.
Hit points are all that matters in this game. Heal people. Damage people. Heal yourself more than they damage you. You can't account for the nuance anymore, so who cares about all of the flavor and the details. The game is just going to have disorganized shizophrenia anyway.
