This is an unpolished version of my review. The finished review will have a much more lengthy explaination of the game and what I like or dislike about it. Until then, please enjoy the TL;DR version below!
Graphics/Atmosphere: 2/2
Between Klei Entertainments beautiful animation and the narrator's- I only know him as Wayne- smexy voice, this game gets a perfect score in this category. I can't take my eyes off the screen and I wait on baited breath for the Ancestor's next line. I know that Wayne is also known for audio books, documentaries, and other video games, so if you know his last name, please share!
Gameplay/Controls: 1/2
The controls are pretty simple to master, so no problem there. The difficulty can be a bit of a turn off for some players, so I will take a point away from that, but I don't believe it should disway you from purchasing the game!
Story/Content: 2/2
Lots of content even in this stage of Early Access. The story is interesting as well: Your Ancestor disturbes an great evil while digging for a source of power benieth your family home. The estate is overrun by monsters, provoking the local villagefolk to form a mob and storm the keep. Your ancestor, twisted into madness by what he witnessed in the catacombs below, sends a letter to his last living relative- you- then kills himself before the mob reaches him. It's up to you to slay the evil that has overrun your family home and restore order... likely at the cost of many of your loyal servants' lives.
Immersion/Replayability: 2/2
You will lose. A lot. But that shouldn't stop you from playing. It might drive you to restart a few times before you get the hang of it, but that's okay! I did the same thing. Eventually what you'll find is that having a few of your best men die (because you made some horrible mistake *cough cough*) doesn't mean the end of your short reign as the lord of the family estate. Great game. It may still be in early access, but it already is one of my favourite games of all time.
First of all is the atmosphere of darkness and depression which you slowly resolve. Step by step, deed by deed, building by building. The monsters, the bosses, the heroes. The story is awesome, one thing you see in the letter of your ancestor, but completely another when you start to investigate what he really did. The abominations he created and his memories about them.
The calm voice of narrator, the astonishing comments help even more. The game descriptions and art in this game are absolutely fabulous. The game itself is somewhat hard if you try to jump on it without planning. Unlike many games where you can just load last save or be reborn loosing some of your XP or cash, this game forgives no mistakes. You characters die forever, and there is no way to turn back time. Diseases and quirks need to be treated, wounds patched and supplies used. Otherwise expect heavy losses and bad performance. But with good planning you can cut through those abominations with relative ease. Relative, because sometimes things can go bad even for a well-prepared party. Random dungeons and events make this part even more exiting.
Another interesting thin is the stress system. forget your unbreakable and ever-brave characters of other games. Here you need to keep a close eye on your morals, since they are as important as physical good-being of your characters. If you get too much stress, you get negative quirks, if you leave them stressed for too long, prepare for a serious madness. You character become afflicted. Such  character becomes a serious problem for the party until treated. Push them even further and they reach the limit, a heart attack, which ensures his death.
I recommend this game for those who like good and atmospheric games, who like dark and gloomy style and a nice story. Remembers me of a good old Disciples 2 who had a similar style.

I've tried to play this game with the advise given on the opening screen. I'm aware that the game is designed to involve constant meat-grinding of the characters. That is not an issue I cannot overcome. There is a lot that, with enough polish, would make for an amazing game. Even meat-grinders have their place.
So what went wrong? You know that feeling where you're telling Windows to do something but Windows is ignoring you to do something else? This game has something even worse. In this game, that frustration is an intentional feature. As you play the characters you're controlling go insane, and they have a chance of ignoring your input to perform other, deliberately inconvenient, actions. The game's designers believe they are trying to model mental illnesses, but instead all that's happening is they refuse to do what's in their own best interests.
Reviewing a game like this is particularly gut-wrenching because the developers had a really good game. The earlier sections, where the characters are still usable, have definite promise. There is a lot of nuance and a lot of interesting stuff in those sections, but the developers lost sight of what appeals to the fans of strategy games. If they had simply placed limits that were somehow understandable so that the player could work around them in-the-moment then cope with the baggage later on, the game could have been amazing. Unfortunately, what starts out as an engrossing every-move-matters strategy game quickly degenerates into something unpredictable. No more strategy. When your planning doesn't matter anymore there's just a typical par-for-the-course "you have to have a healer" click-fest.
Hit points are all that matters in this game. Heal people. Damage people. Heal yourself more than they damage you. You can't account for the nuance anymore, so who cares about all of the flavor and the details. The game is just going to have disorganized shizophrenia anyway.

when you start off you end up coming across little square plots of land within the worlds that when activated pops uo a tiny prebuilt starter house and a non craftable starting bench from which you build everything else except euipment, because equipment isn't craftable at all. from there anything within the tiny square plot will be permanent and wverything outside it will be erased along with the world when everyone has left it
all the ores and whatnot can be found along the surface or dropped by enemies. three most important ores in the game are a purple ore blocks called shapestone, blue ore blocks called formicite, and yellow ore blocks called infinium. these are used in everything so you will need large bulk quantities at all times when crafting. all fancy blocks are crafted from "primal" blocks and all the blocks in the workd drop as "primal" blocks.
basic equipemnt is randomly generated and dropped from enemies and dungeon rewards instead of crafted and consists of hats masks and whatever your primary weapon is for your class. there's also side equipment that is craftable and you can also improve equipment using the 4th most important ore called flux obtained only from recycling equipment and stuff you dont want.

I started playing Darkest Dungeon after the hoopla about corpses and heart attacks so I never experienced the game without the added difficulty. I found the game to be well-crafted with some great ideas that, once polished for release, will really shine. The game itself is quite hard in the early levels, and you definitely have to let go of any sort of affection or attachment to your heroes. Be ready to dismiss an ailing hero without regret and you'll be fine.  Once you get a few levels and town upgrades under your belt, however, the game becomes substantially easier which I have mixed feelings about. Not that I want to lose my leveled up heroes, but I think it's less fun to have a game with a reverse difficulty curve. I'm hoping this will be addressed in future releases.
I'm also interested to see some improvement in the trinkets. For the most part I found them to be useless, with the disadvantages essentially negating the advantages (or sometimes even outweighing). This seems like a flawed loot model, and maybe something can be tweaked or a mechanism added by which you can improve the trinkets.
Bottom line, it's kept me entertained enough to not regret my purchase, and I'm very much looking forward to future releases. The game is not for the faint of heart, however, and if you have more fun steam-rolling dungeons (not judging; those games are fun too), you might want to give this a pass.

This is a really great game.
First off, don't be hesitant about buying into Early Access with this one if it looks appealing to you. It is already extremely playable and I have run into no real bugs or issues
As for the game, the first thing that struck me is the wonderful ambience. The theme is dark and sombre throughout and does an excellent job of potraying a thoroughly sinister and foreboding atmosphere. The narrator is excellent and really helps set the mood and overall the game does a fantastic job of making the environments that you adventure through really quite unnerving.
The stress and quirks system is another great and unique addition to this type of game. I've never really encountered a similar system before and while it can be harsh at times, it adds a lot of appeal and individuality to your team of adventurers. It's impossible to avoid the psycological scarring that befalls them as they traverse the perilous dungeons, and before long you end up with an almost comically deranged bunch of lunatics manning your ranks. For example two of my regulars are an bloodthirsty alcoholic Vestal (Priest) who is afraid of the dark, and a kleptomaniac Crusader (Paladin) with a brothel addiction. What a combo :)
In terms of the difficulty, don't buy this if your'e looking for an easy ride. There's no reloading and if (when) you lose a party member, they're gone for good. A run of bad luck can turn the tide of battles very quickly, but bby the same token a few lucky rolls can swing the odds in your favour and make for a very satisfying victory out of the jaws of defeat.
So if you like RPG's and / or roguelikes, don't hesitate to give this a shot. It's already great fun and I'm looking forward to seeing even more additions once it's complete.
One final piece of advice - If you do try the game, my advice would be to turn off the enemy corpses mechanic. It's counterintuitive and adds unnecessary tedium to battles. Other reviews seem to suggest opinion is mixed on this, so it is to the developers credit that they recently added the ability to toggle it on or off according to your preference.

When I first saw this game, I thought it looked amazing, plus I loved the thought of the fair and balanced challenge it offered. I saw how it had very positive reviews, and then it happened I scrolled down to the review section and read the same thing over and over and over again.
"Game was great, but then they added corpses and heart attacks and PROT to enemies and now it is total garbage and I'd never recommend this to anyone until they fix it, cuz they just had to go and ruin and now it sucks."
This honestly made me debate whether to buy this or not, but it was on sale, so I decided to go ahead and try it. I can say without a doubt this is one of my favorite games in my library right next to Towerfall: Ascension and Borderlands 2.
What makes this game great?
Pros
1. The art, animation, and narration all phenomenally convey the atmosphere and story like nature of the game. Even though the narrator does not have a huge variety in what he says, just the way he speaks never grows old or redundant.
2. Though there isn't much music, all of it is mesmerizing and I could sit on that title screen all day just to listen to it.
3. The unique strategy that goes into this game. Do you have a plan? Good now throw it out the window, because chances are some unseen event is going to come along and completely screw with you. Maybe someone will run away or lock themselves in the brothel preventing you from using them that week. Maybe someone will randomly investigate the dark arts and grow bloodthirsty as a result. Maybe a small group of weak spiders will destroy you're near healthy team, while your weak team takes out a formation of brigands in two turns. The point is you can strategize all you want and you definitely should, but in the end chances are something is going to go wrong anyways.
4. Almost any team can work, as long as a hero can attack from where they're standing this allows you to mix and match heroes creating unique teams, so it helps keep the game fresh along with the randomly generated dungeons.
5. Very much risk vs reward based. Do you want more gold? Then you're going to have to risk more health and sanity in order to gain more money, by snuffing out your torch simple as that.
6. The town though very simple on the outside is very integral to the overall game and I actually enjoy spending my time in there.
7. The stress meter makes this game unique, because it affects how you play through each dungeon, and as long as you aren't doing a dark run, you are almost never at risk of a heart attack.
8. Corpses there I said it, I love them and I think the game without them would be as much fun.
Cons
1. The enemy formations are lacking to say the least, yeah they have a good amount, but chances are more often than not you'll be fighting the same battle two to three times in a dungeon.
2. Once buildings are done being upgraded the heirlooms are no longer necessary meaning dungeons become a lot easier, because you'll just be tossing out heirlooms every time you come across one.
3. The lack of easing the player into the game, which wouldn't be bad, but it makes the game seem more challenging than it actually is, because once you know how to play the game grows ten times easier, and chances are by dungeon 3 or 4 you'll see a huge drop in the difficulty.
4. Lack of description, it took me a long time to figure out what was going on with each hero when I started, but after a while I grew used to the screen, but most of the time I still don't know what I'm reading on the screen.
5. Repetitive and short, unfortunately all the dungeons feel the same, except with different enemies like most battle based rpgs, and there are only five, so you'll see everything there is to see fairly quickly.
6. The two opening videos are so cool and interesting, plus they provide excellent exposition, but they freeze on my computer everytime, meaning I had to either skip them or watch them one second on one second off.
7. This might just be a personal problem, but the game crashed the first three times I tried to play, before I even got to do anything, haven't faced that problem since though.
Finally, to address the 2 reasons why people hate this game
1.Corpses they make the game challenging and prevent you from just bashing the front enemy like in most other tactical rpgs, which I personally think is brilliant, plus there are a handful of moves that remove all corpses from the field, so they can be worked around.
2. Heart attacks are only a concern in three scenarios. a. You're taking a lower resolve hero into a higher resolve dungeon. b. You're fighting a boss. c. You're doing a dark run. Otherwise unless you're an idiot you should never come across a problem with them.
Also, you can turn both of them off, so if you don't like them you don't have to deal with it, so please disregard all reviews that say the game sucks because of those features.
Overall I think this game is very unique and atmospheric with some great music and narration with a few quirks that the devs can still work on. I'd easily give it a 9.5 out of 10, and highly recommend it to anyone, who enjoys Lovercraft, challenging games, dark atmosphere, or loves strategy games or any mix of that, because this is a grueling game filled with both fun and frustration hidden in a dark and beautiful lore. Plus it's not done yet, since chances are it will only grow better.

If you enjoyed Terraria then you'll probably get a kick out of this little jewel. Almost as simple to pick up as Terraria and just about as addicting too. This game shows so much promise for being an early access game. I love the idea behind the design and gameplay. This game is going to be a good hit when it is released.
However, with all this said, the game (in its current state) is not very well organized or optimized, pusing even high-end PCs to their limits. I have problems running the game at points due to mass amounts of lag, especially when their are many NPCs on the screen like towns and certain dungeons. The idea of infinite world possibilites that you can discover leads players to want to actually explore the universe that they spawned in, never knowing what to expect on the next planet you happen to travel too. The game also offers cameos to other games such as FTL and Minecraft, which some people seem to have an issue with, but I think they're right at home.
Probably the best aspect of the game right now, which many will disagree with me, is the ability to build mass structures very quickly and easily. You can literally just stand there and build walls 30 to 40 blocks up in the air, making creating large structures quickly and efficently. If the idea is there, you can make just about anything your little heart desires, in a realitively small amount of time. Of course, large structures will take much more time. The combat is fairly basic so far as the monsters do not have many emotions and attack strategies, either they ignore your presences or charge right for you. Which these behaviors can be improved with the large amount of mods already available to players created by other dedicated players.
As I stated before, exploration is the key element this game is trying to offer. The infinte worlds idea is beautiful. Every world has its own unique feel and environment to an extent (Which the developers are working to make every single world as diverse as possible). With that, you will see some worlds feel like others, but there will be vast differences if you explore the surface and see the art that went into the design of the worlds. At later points in the game, mining and exploring become somewhat stale as there isnt much end-game content as far as exploration, but the game seems to focus mainly on end-game content which makes you, as the player, want to immerse yourself into the Starbound universe just to see whats out there.
This game can be very addicting at times, (it has gotten me in trouble lol), but can give you want you've always wanted in a game, the freedom to do whatever you want when you want to. Tired of the world you're on? Fly to a different one. Tired of your house? Destroy it and build a new one. Tired of your home planet? Screw it, you'll find a better one. This game can offer so much and so much more. As I stated before, the modding behind this game can and will run deep as more and more creative players are intoduced to the Starbound environment. I say buy it now if you wish to support the development and test out the game for yourself. But if you can control that burning hole in your pocket, give it a time for the game currently experiences many character/universe wipes due to the mass amount of content the developers are putting into the game. Plus the current poor optimization and organization.
Inconclusion, this game is very very promising for the future and is only looking to get better. Bravo Chucklefish and keep up the good work! For $15, its worth every penny.

A combination of DayZ and Minecraft is what makes this game so brilliant.
The blocky texture of the game creates a unique atmosphere for the game. As well as the zombies and how they were designed.
The guns in the game are challenge to receive as they are found in gun shops or other locations and unless you have an actual weapon, the chances of getting one are slim, but unless you can track down a care package, all is good.
The crafting system of the game is a little complex but overall rewarding in the end.
The customization with the player and cosmetics found is also unique, as the player can find clothes and other items to help them out while surviving.
The player status creates a lifelike feel for the character, as he must find food, water, medicine, and other materials to help him survive.
The landscape is flawed but with improvement can create a lush landscape for the player to explore.
Multiplayer creates a unique feel for PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS, as the player struggles to survive with others and kills others as well.
One flaw I felt with the game was the lack of customization options with the character. You only have a few faces and beards and other items. The rest of the customization options can be unlocked by purchasing something for $4.99. This makes the game flawed but however great as a whole.
The game is free and it is worth waiting, so I recommend this game and I hope you get it too.

If you enjoyed Terraria then you'll probably get a kick out of this little jewel. Almost as simple to pick up as Terraria and just about as addicting too. This game shows so much promise for being an early access game. I love the idea behind the design and gameplay. This game is going to be a good hit when it is released.
However, with all this said, the game (in its current state) is not very well organized or optimized, pusing even high-end PCs to their limits. I have problems running the game at points due to mass amounts of lag, especially when their are many NPCs on the screen like towns and certain dungeons. The idea of infinite world possibilites that you can discover leads players to want to actually explore the universe that they spawned in, never knowing what to expect on the next planet you happen to travel too. The game also offers cameos to other games such as FTL and Minecraft, which some people seem to have an issue with, but I think they're right at home.
Probably the best aspect of the game right now, which many will disagree with me, is the ability to build mass structures very quickly and easily. You can literally just stand there and build walls 30 to 40 blocks up in the air, making creating large structures quickly and efficently. If the idea is there, you can make just about anything your little heart desires, in a realitively small amount of time. Of course, large structures will take much more time. The combat is fairly basic so far as the monsters do not have many emotions and attack strategies, either they ignore your presences or charge right for you. Which these behaviors can be improved with the large amount of mods already available to players created by other dedicated players.
As I stated before, exploration is the key element this game is trying to offer. The infinte worlds idea is beautiful. Every world has its own unique feel and environment to an extent (Which the developers are working to make every single world as diverse as possible). With that, you will see some worlds feel like others, but there will be vast differences if you explore the surface and see the art that went into the design of the worlds. At later points in the game, mining and exploring become somewhat stale as there isnt much end-game content as far as exploration, but the game seems to focus mainly on end-game content which makes you, as the player, want to immerse yourself into the Starbound universe just to see whats out there.
This game can be very addicting at times, (it has gotten me in trouble lol), but can give you want you've always wanted in a game, the freedom to do whatever you want when you want to. Tired of the world you're on? Fly to a different one. Tired of your house? Destroy it and build a new one. Tired of your home planet? Screw it, you'll find a better one. This game can offer so much and so much more. As I stated before, the modding behind this game can and will run deep as more and more creative players are intoduced to the Starbound environment. I say buy it now if you wish to support the development and test out the game for yourself. But if you can control that burning hole in your pocket, give it a time for the game currently experiences many character/universe wipes due to the mass amount of content the developers are putting into the game. Plus the current poor optimization and organization.
Inconclusion, this game is very very promising for the future and is only looking to get better. Bravo Chucklefish and keep up the good work! For $15, its worth every penny.

I reviewed this game when I had played about 10 hours of it. here's a do-over:
so dark souls III is a brilliant game
it is a brutal game. it is a very punishing and tormenting game.
but never will you feel that you have been cheated or exploited by the game
the game's brilliance and challenge is based on a mechanic of how you have to place your bets on your moves. if you're in a battle with an enemy, whether they are weak or strong, there is a chance that if you trip up, you might just fall and not get back up. and then all your exp. falls with you.
the game is quite difficult to adjust to if you are new
mostly, "hack and slash" games have a formula of "press attack, attack immediately happens". I'm thinking mostly of god of war and devil may cry here.
but in dark souls (III), every attack is a wind up and release. pressing attack doesn't attack. it initiates what will be an attack in about half a second. but that half second is how the game becomes so dangerous - you have no idea what might happen in that half-second window. you might beat the enemy, you might dodge and heal yourself just in time, or you might die.
that is why the challenge in this game is so fresh - such a window of gamble and faith gives you the fun of a hack and slash game but also the strategy of an RPG turn-taking game. you are rolling the dice when you are choosing to attack or dodge. and dodging itself is not just "dodging". dodging is matching a wave, or a pulse - a split second too late or too early and you've missed it. and it hurts.
the boss battles are mostly brilliant. I have just completed the game twice in a row and out of the 10+ major boss battles, I would say that about 90% of them are breathtaking. and the brilliance of the bosses is not simply the unique challenge each one poses, but the backstories of each one is alluring. and that point is emphatic when referring more so to later bosses like the nameless king who is shrouded in mystery and hidden within cryptic clues. his mere existence within the game is a secret in itself, as well.
dark souls 3 surprised me. when my friend recommended I play it, I had essentially forget about video games. but the lore intrigued me. and watching them play it and experiencing the difficulty sucked me in. on the surface, dark souls 3 might just appear to be a god of war style game. but dark souls 3 is a whole different beast. dark souls 3 (and its predecessors) will go down in games history as fresh, innovative and original masterpieces in the medium of its kind.
I would rate this game 9.5/10
and that's saying something, seeing as I don't believe in "perfect games".
(but in my opinion, the lock-on feature, clipping and camera work is rather flawed sometimes)

Trove is a massive multiplayer adventure game (mmorpg). Your character will live across a series of build-able, destructible, explore-able, and randomly created worlds. Each one will have its own objectives, monsters, buildings, and you'll live in it from the beginning until its end... whatever that may be. Things you might have created in one world, could wind up showing up in the next, as each world will pull from the hundreds or thousands of worlds that came before it. Even though a world might end, you'll carry pieces of it to keep forever in your own Cornerstone, which follows you from world to world and shares your past exploits with friends, strangers, and anyone in the next world. Trove is a game for exploration, creation, destruction, and adventure. It seeks to find that sense of "newness" you experience when you first discover a new world or MMO, and to never let it go by constantly giving you new worlds to explore and conquer.

At first glance, this game is very simplistic, but when you delve deeper into it's mechanics, you can see that this game is much more complex than you may think...
First I'd like to start by saying that for a Free to Play game, this is an absolute gem. Before playing Free games, many gamers will ask themselves a question, are there paywalls? And to that I have a very satisfying answer! The F2P model in this game almost couldn't be any better! Honestly, everyone is pretty much on the same level. You CAN buy resources for credits, and getting them without the in-game shop can become a bit tedious and repetitive, but ultimately, you do not need to spend a dime on this game.
At the beginning, the game will present you with a series of tasks, each of these tasks reward you with Cubits, a currency available in the in-game shop. It is the alternative of credits, but is easily earned in-game, unlike credits themselves. The best thing to buy for Cubits are alternative classes, that's about it. If you have any left over, there are cosmetics to buy aswell.
But what about the game itself? You excitedly scream towards the screen in suspence, well, the game is pretty good, and quite addictive. It's basically something like Minecraft, only it has much smoother combat, it's an MMO, and contains many RPG features. If you made Minecraft into a third-person MMORPG, this is probably what you'd get.
In the game, you can do anything from mining and creating your house on your "corner stone" (Small areas scattered throughout the multiple worlds, places which you can claim for free, and build without anyone getting in your way. If you decide to claim another corner stone, your entire building with all the stored items rebuilds in that location, so your progress carries over whereever you go.), to raiding dungeons with your friends. It also features a very nice system for going in and out of "build mode" with TAB.
The weapons... Oh boy, the weapons... So many weapons, so much variation. I wouldn't compare it to Borderlands, but it comes quite close! I'd even say that you get rare loot a bit too often, so often that after time, it becomes a bit underwhelming. I'd recommend the devs lower the drop rates of epic loot, to make it more exciting, and to keep players wanting more of this excitement, as right now, you get two high-quality items from every dungeon boss, and those are very easily defeated, even while soloing.
The game is great for both soloing and group play. There is probably only one downside I can think of right now, that being that after time, the game can become a bit repetitive if played for long periods of time, as the formula remains the same throughout most of the game. I believe this issue will be easily resolved through constant updating.
In conclusion, the game contains little to no shady microtransactions all of us hate so much, the gameplay is really nice and addictive, loot feels slightly underwhelming but is ultimately very fun to earn, game is very balanced, and constant updating and improvements are a guarantee.
For now, it's a nice 8/10, and I expect it to rise to at least a 9 after some more updates.

This is a really great game.
First off, don't be hesitant about buying into Early Access with this one if it looks appealing to you. It is already extremely playable and I have run into no real bugs or issues
As for the game, the first thing that struck me is the wonderful ambience. The theme is dark and sombre throughout and does an excellent job of potraying a thoroughly sinister and foreboding atmosphere. The narrator is excellent and really helps set the mood and overall the game does a fantastic job of making the environments that you adventure through really quite unnerving.
The stress and quirks system is another great and unique addition to this type of game. I've never really encountered a similar system before and while it can be harsh at times, it adds a lot of appeal and individuality to your team of adventurers. It's impossible to avoid the psycological scarring that befalls them as they traverse the perilous dungeons, and before long you end up with an almost comically deranged bunch of lunatics manning your ranks. For example two of my regulars are an bloodthirsty alcoholic Vestal (Priest) who is afraid of the dark, and a kleptomaniac Crusader (Paladin) with a brothel addiction. What a combo :)
In terms of the difficulty, don't buy this if your'e looking for an easy ride. There's no reloading and if (when) you lose a party member, they're gone for good. A run of bad luck can turn the tide of battles very quickly, but bby the same token a few lucky rolls can swing the odds in your favour and make for a very satisfying victory out of the jaws of defeat.
So if you like RPG's and / or roguelikes, don't hesitate to give this a shot. It's already great fun and I'm looking forward to seeing even more additions once it's complete.
One final piece of advice - If you do try the game, my advice would be to turn off the enemy corpses mechanic. It's counterintuitive and adds unnecessary tedium to battles. Other reviews seem to suggest opinion is mixed on this, so it is to the developers credit that they recently added the ability to toggle it on or off according to your preference.

If you enjoyed Terraria then you'll probably get a kick out of this little jewel. Almost as simple to pick up as Terraria and just about as addicting too. This game shows so much promise for being an early access game. I love the idea behind the design and gameplay. This game is going to be a good hit when it is released.
However, with all this said, the game (in its current state) is not very well organized or optimized, pusing even high-end PCs to their limits. I have problems running the game at points due to mass amounts of lag, especially when their are many NPCs on the screen like towns and certain dungeons. The idea of infinite world possibilites that you can discover leads players to want to actually explore the universe that they spawned in, never knowing what to expect on the next planet you happen to travel too. The game also offers cameos to other games such as FTL and Minecraft, which some people seem to have an issue with, but I think they're right at home.
Probably the best aspect of the game right now, which many will disagree with me, is the ability to build mass structures very quickly and easily. You can literally just stand there and build walls 30 to 40 blocks up in the air, making creating large structures quickly and efficently. If the idea is there, you can make just about anything your little heart desires, in a realitively small amount of time. Of course, large structures will take much more time. The combat is fairly basic so far as the monsters do not have many emotions and attack strategies, either they ignore your presences or charge right for you. Which these behaviors can be improved with the large amount of mods already available to players created by other dedicated players.
As I stated before, exploration is the key element this game is trying to offer. The infinte worlds idea is beautiful. Every world has its own unique feel and environment to an extent (Which the developers are working to make every single world as diverse as possible). With that, you will see some worlds feel like others, but there will be vast differences if you explore the surface and see the art that went into the design of the worlds. At later points in the game, mining and exploring become somewhat stale as there isnt much end-game content as far as exploration, but the game seems to focus mainly on end-game content which makes you, as the player, want to immerse yourself into the Starbound universe just to see whats out there.
This game can be very addicting at times, (it has gotten me in trouble lol), but can give you want you've always wanted in a game, the freedom to do whatever you want when you want to. Tired of the world you're on? Fly to a different one. Tired of your house? Destroy it and build a new one. Tired of your home planet? Screw it, you'll find a better one. This game can offer so much and so much more. As I stated before, the modding behind this game can and will run deep as more and more creative players are intoduced to the Starbound environment. I say buy it now if you wish to support the development and test out the game for yourself. But if you can control that burning hole in your pocket, give it a time for the game currently experiences many character/universe wipes due to the mass amount of content the developers are putting into the game. Plus the current poor optimization and organization.
Inconclusion, this game is very very promising for the future and is only looking to get better. Bravo Chucklefish and keep up the good work! For $15, its worth every penny.

You have to admire a few things about Unturned. Use of the Steam Workshop also lets you introduce creations made by yourself or other players, so what goes on in your adventure is ultimately up to you. By all means, survey the world flying about on a handglider, I won't stop you!
The game has just left Early Access and it is still free-to-play. Because of this, everybody is welcome to try it out. You might enjoy the experience more than I did, to the point where it becomes a regular thing with friends. With me, it just didn't seem to click. Unturned is not for me; The learning curve is just too steep and unforgiving.
My hour or so of playing Unturned was a delightfully cringey endevour. There was even a smile on my face as I failed to fight off the zombies that inevitably got me. In spite of my poor experience with Unturned, I suggest you play this game at least once, if just to be certain as to whether or not you enjoy it. Good luck out there!

When I first saw this game, I thought it looked amazing, plus I loved the thought of the fair and balanced challenge it offered. I saw how it had very positive reviews, and then it happened I scrolled down to the review section and read the same thing over and over and over again.
"Game was great, but then they added corpses and heart attacks and PROT to enemies and now it is total garbage and I'd never recommend this to anyone until they fix it, cuz they just had to go and ruin and now it sucks."
This honestly made me debate whether to buy this or not, but it was on sale, so I decided to go ahead and try it. I can say without a doubt this is one of my favorite games in my library right next to Towerfall: Ascension and Borderlands 2.
What makes this game great?
Pros
1. The art, animation, and narration all phenomenally convey the atmosphere and story like nature of the game. Even though the narrator does not have a huge variety in what he says, just the way he speaks never grows old or redundant.
2. Though there isn't much music, all of it is mesmerizing and I could sit on that title screen all day just to listen to it.
3. The unique strategy that goes into this game. Do you have a plan? Good now throw it out the window, because chances are some unseen event is going to come along and completely screw with you. Maybe someone will run away or lock themselves in the brothel preventing you from using them that week. Maybe someone will randomly investigate the dark arts and grow bloodthirsty as a result. Maybe a small group of weak spiders will destroy you're near healthy team, while your weak team takes out a formation of brigands in two turns. The point is you can strategize all you want and you definitely should, but in the end chances are something is going to go wrong anyways.
4. Almost any team can work, as long as a hero can attack from where they're standing this allows you to mix and match heroes creating unique teams, so it helps keep the game fresh along with the randomly generated dungeons.
5. Very much risk vs reward based. Do you want more gold? Then you're going to have to risk more health and sanity in order to gain more money, by snuffing out your torch simple as that.
6. The town though very simple on the outside is very integral to the overall game and I actually enjoy spending my time in there.
7. The stress meter makes this game unique, because it affects how you play through each dungeon, and as long as you aren't doing a dark run, you are almost never at risk of a heart attack.
8. Corpses there I said it, I love them and I think the game without them would be as much fun.
Cons
1. The enemy formations are lacking to say the least, yeah they have a good amount, but chances are more often than not you'll be fighting the same battle two to three times in a dungeon.
2. Once buildings are done being upgraded the heirlooms are no longer necessary meaning dungeons become a lot easier, because you'll just be tossing out heirlooms every time you come across one.
3. The lack of easing the player into the game, which wouldn't be bad, but it makes the game seem more challenging than it actually is, because once you know how to play the game grows ten times easier, and chances are by dungeon 3 or 4 you'll see a huge drop in the difficulty.
4. Lack of description, it took me a long time to figure out what was going on with each hero when I started, but after a while I grew used to the screen, but most of the time I still don't know what I'm reading on the screen.
5. Repetitive and short, unfortunately all the dungeons feel the same, except with different enemies like most battle based rpgs, and there are only five, so you'll see everything there is to see fairly quickly.
6. The two opening videos are so cool and interesting, plus they provide excellent exposition, but they freeze on my computer everytime, meaning I had to either skip them or watch them one second on one second off.
7. This might just be a personal problem, but the game crashed the first three times I tried to play, before I even got to do anything, haven't faced that problem since though.
Finally, to address the 2 reasons why people hate this game
1.Corpses they make the game challenging and prevent you from just bashing the front enemy like in most other tactical rpgs, which I personally think is brilliant, plus there are a handful of moves that remove all corpses from the field, so they can be worked around.
2. Heart attacks are only a concern in three scenarios. a. You're taking a lower resolve hero into a higher resolve dungeon. b. You're fighting a boss. c. You're doing a dark run. Otherwise unless you're an idiot you should never come across a problem with them.
Also, you can turn both of them off, so if you don't like them you don't have to deal with it, so please disregard all reviews that say the game sucks because of those features.
Overall I think this game is very unique and atmospheric with some great music and narration with a few quirks that the devs can still work on. I'd easily give it a 9.5 out of 10, and highly recommend it to anyone, who enjoys Lovercraft, challenging games, dark atmosphere, or loves strategy games or any mix of that, because this is a grueling game filled with both fun and frustration hidden in a dark and beautiful lore. Plus it's not done yet, since chances are it will only grow better.

I am a huge fan of Dark Souls, having done many challenge runs and delved into the lore behind that game. I only say this as a testiment to my love of difficult games, dark aesthetics (love this on Darkest Dungeon), and even a certain amount of Sadism/Masochism that comes with playing that series.
However, I cannot recommend Darkest Dungeon.
Where as Dark Souls gets away with incredible, kill-you-so-fast-you-say-hey-man-why-you-kill-me-so-fast deaths, this is due to the fact that any death you receive in that franchise (Except Bed of Chaos (♥♥♥♥ BED OF CHAOS))  is entirely based on how you as a player plan and act according to the situations you're in.
Darkest Dungeons' combat is based on a dice roll. Playing the tutorial several times, once I was able to soundly kill the "Boss" due to constant critical hits on my part. Another time, I limped into town with 5 health left on one character because I would go on 7 Miss streak for every hit I managed to land. Yet another both characters were reduced to 10 health.
I would say that Darkest Dungeon would absolutely be my favorite Turn Based RPG (Even more so than Pokemon or even my most loved Legend of Dragoon) if they turned down the random chance. Being party wiped (And death is permanent) because RNGesus decided to be a ♥♥♥♥♥ that encounter isn't fun, despite managing you're parties' Sanity, Training, Equipment and Health being everything I've ever wanted in a RPG. However, as it is you might as well flip a coin on if your characters survive or not.

As of December 4th, 2013, this game has changed enough to warrant a new review.
Spiral Knights, in one word, is "addicting." A moderate-paced RPG dungeon crawler with a light feel to it, it's embodies the idea of easy to pick up but difficult to master. The progression is slow to a free player, fast to a paying player, and yet nothing is completely out of reach if you don't cough up- not even the cosmetics (limited-time purchase deals excluded). The gameplay is both varied and entertaining, and the few bosses inside are creatively done.
Hell, even the community so far has proven to be excellent.
The only drawback is that for a free player, getting higher-powered gear takes a while. The economy is dual-currency (crowns free, energy paid) with an exchange, and with the price of some items necessary for it (rarely found in the Clockworks), it becomes somewhat grinding.
Overall a great game, which I'm disappointed that Metascore rewarded with such a low opinion. But if you believed Metascore, you wouldn't be reading this, would you?
Edit: Just a small note, as of the 30th of July, 2013, the game was significantly changed in numerous ways. Some reviews before then might not reflect the game as of now.

I wish I would have read somewhere amongst all the reviews and information about this game, that this game is written for gamepad users. My first obstacle was to save changes I made. I have an azerty keyboard, yet the game converted it to a qwerty one. So in order to not get all confused about keys, I reset the keybindings. I couldn't get them to save. Everytime I pressed ok (right click then choose "ok") it reset everything again. Till my friend told me I have to use "back" in order to save them (how logical is that eh?). Upon creation my character's features in the beginning I had the same issue (my changes wouldn't save; I have not tried the 'back' option there I was rather fed up with it all by that time).
The game itself. I didn't get past the first boss. You die, you restart, all the mobs respawn. You think by yourself, I'll play this smart, I'll go heal up at the bonfire before facing the boss ... guess what ... all the npc's respawned. So that deal didn't work either. I tried the boss countless times. By then I knew the location of all the npc's and how to strike fast.
In my case, I'm very unhappy to say I bought the game. It's wasted money. I wish there was a trial period for games, whereas you decide whether you want to play further and thus buy the game, or can decide "no this is not my thing" and uninstall it.
Perhaps for gamepad users this is a fun game, I don't own a gamepad, therefor never even tried that way of playing, nor am I planning to purchase one. I'm not very fond of games where you die or rest and have to start over. Nor of the part where you loose everything collected and might regain what you lost next round. Games are supposed to be entertaining and fun, not something you get all angry and upset about. I don't mind things to be tough where you have to figure out the way to tackle the problem(s) but this is over the top. So, keyboard/mouse users, be warned, this is not an easy game to play. Hard as hell, and fun as f....  flying?  Yeah.  Flying.  Let's go with that.
I enjoy a hard game, so long as it's fair.  Darkest Dungeon is hard, but fair.  Thus, I enjoy Darkest Dungeon.
Some people; however, think it's too hard.  Corpses and heart attacks are sometimes looked at as 'fake difficulty'.  For those of you who don't know about TVtropes, saying a that game has fake difficulty is a way of saying that it's unnecissarily hard, or unfair.  I am not among those people.
Heart attacks?  Gives me additional motivation to keep the stress level of my adventurers down.  If I pay attention, I'll be able to prevent it from happening very reliably.
Corpses?  Most people hate them, I actually like them.  Part of this probably has to do with the fact that I got the game recently, and they were already in the game at that point.  There's more to it than that, though.  Each character has 4 skills, and those skills can only hit enemies in certain places.  Corpses can get in the way of that, thus some people hate them.  However, the inverse can also be true.  Instead of getting in the way of being able to use the ability you want, they can also keep an enemy in the area you need them to be in in order to use that skill after you kill the guy in front of him.  In the rare occasion that they do get in the way, which for me has only happened like 2 or 3 times, it takes only 1 turn to get the normal ones out of the way for any combat class, such as the man-at-arms, hellion, crusader, etc...
Here's my experiance about it...  My favorite combat class is the hellion.   Of the 4 skills I take into battle for these characters, I use the standard attack, 'If it bleeds', 'adrenaline rush', and usually, 'iron swan'.  Iron swan covers the furthest slot, if it bleeds covers the middle two, and the standard attack covers the first two.  This means I can attack any of the enemies at any time I want.  I usually prefer to attack using 'if it bleeds' if the target isn't undead, for the extra bleeding damage.  This doesn't work in the front spot, so what do I do after I kill the first guy?  Leave his corpse there so I can still hit the 2nd guy with my preferred attack.  Maybe if I used characters with less flexible attack abilities, such as the man-at-arms, who, as far as I know, can't hit all 4 enemy slots with any combination of his abilities, with the exception of his battle cry, or whatever you call it, because that does minimalistic damage, and its main use is for debuffing the enemy.  Maybe then if I relied more heavily on these classes, corpses would be more annoying.  However, I like hellions, and I almost always have one, if not two, in my crew when I embark on a mission, and corpses aren't a problem for them.  In fact, nearly all the classes I use avoid this problem.  Plague doctors with the right skills can hit all enemy slots, as can vestials, houndmasters, and probably several of the classes I've never used, such as the grave digger, jester, mercenary, etc... can also likely hit all enemy slots with the right skill set.
Thus, I don't mind corpses.  If someone chooses character classes or skill sets that can only target a small amount of enemy spots, then yes, corpses would be a problem and would be very annoying.  My personal preference is to have my characters be more versatile, which makes corpses not a problem.  If someone like smore specialized characters, then corpses could really be a pain by 'cramping your style'.
I suppose it could be said that it comes down to planning and strategy, in order for corpses to not be a problem, but at the same time, the point of a game is to have fun, and it's most fun to play according to your own preference.  So all in all, I will steadfastly maintain that corpses are NOT fake difficulty, because with the right playstyle they aren't a problem, but they can be annoying and make the game harder with the wrong playstyle.  Please note that when I say 'right' and 'wrong' playstyle, I'm not asserting that my playstyle is superior to all the others, I'm refering it to being 'right' and 'wrong' in accordance to dealing with corpses.

Your characters will drop like flies.
This is not a "oh, you'll probably have a few deaths" or even "there could be a few adventurers that die".
No, no, by the time this game is over, your graveyard will be filled with the rotting maggot infested corpses of once brave heroes (“heroes” used very liberally in this case). Heroes, you will be able to see recorded down from your first mission where that Rouge had a heart attack, to that last mission where your party is eaten by…. Oh, gods… I can’t go on talking about it… It’s too awful and hideous to describe.
The game shines in it’s brutal but not punishing gameplay. This may sound like a contradiction at first but you will do reasonably well in the game as long as you continue to refresh your stock of victim… I mean “heroes” mission after mission and throw away the dying, insane and weak that cost more than they are worth.
It is difficult to rage quit at this game early on as even when your entire party is sent to oblivion, you know you can just scrap up more recruits later (feed the dungeon, feed it).
The gameplay in the dungeon (the most important part, hence the name) is tense and has moments that shift from hoplessness to pure ephoria. There is nothing more satisfying than watching a hero hit full stress and then, instead of going insane, flipping the bird at your enemies by going valiant, or watching one solitary hero resist death blow after death blow from a boss.
On the flip side nothing is more devastating than watching a fully equipped highly trained party go insane in the depths of some long forgotten crypt or panicking as the light… slowly goes… out.

Brilliant game that will leave you laughing victoriously one minute and crying out the name of a dead hero the next (for me it was Victor the leper).
Good luck, and bring lots of torches.

Hard as hell, and fun as f....  flying?  Yeah.  Flying.  Let's go with that.
I enjoy a hard game, so long as it's fair.  Darkest Dungeon is hard, but fair.  Thus, I enjoy Darkest Dungeon.
Some people; however, think it's too hard.  Corpses and heart attacks are sometimes looked at as 'fake difficulty'.  For those of you who don't know about TVtropes, saying a that game has fake difficulty is a way of saying that it's unnecissarily hard, or unfair.  I am not among those people.
Heart attacks?  Gives me additional motivation to keep the stress level of my adventurers down.  If I pay attention, I'll be able to prevent it from happening very reliably.
Corpses?  Most people hate them, I actually like them.  Part of this probably has to do with the fact that I got the game recently, and they were already in the game at that point.  There's more to it than that, though.  Each character has 4 skills, and those skills can only hit enemies in certain places.  Corpses can get in the way of that, thus some people hate them.  However, the inverse can also be true.  Instead of getting in the way of being able to use the ability you want, they can also keep an enemy in the area you need them to be in in order to use that skill after you kill the guy in front of him.  In the rare occasion that they do get in the way, which for me has only happened like 2 or 3 times, it takes only 1 turn to get the normal ones out of the way for any combat class, such as the man-at-arms, hellion, crusader, etc...
Here's my experiance about it...  My favorite combat class is the hellion.   Of the 4 skills I take into battle for these characters, I use the standard attack, 'If it bleeds', 'adrenaline rush', and usually, 'iron swan'.  Iron swan covers the furthest slot, if it bleeds covers the middle two, and the standard attack covers the first two.  This means I can attack any of the enemies at any time I want.  I usually prefer to attack using 'if it bleeds' if the target isn't undead, for the extra bleeding damage.  This doesn't work in the front spot, so what do I do after I kill the first guy?  Leave his corpse there so I can still hit the 2nd guy with my preferred attack.  Maybe if I used characters with less flexible attack abilities, such as the man-at-arms, who, as far as I know, can't hit all 4 enemy slots with any combination of his abilities, with the exception of his battle cry, or whatever you call it, because that does minimalistic damage, and its main use is for debuffing the enemy.  Maybe then if I relied more heavily on these classes, corpses would be more annoying.  However, I like hellions, and I almost always have one, if not two, in my crew when I embark on a mission, and corpses aren't a problem for them.  In fact, nearly all the classes I use avoid this problem.  Plague doctors with the right skills can hit all enemy slots, as can vestials, houndmasters, and probably several of the classes I've never used, such as the grave digger, jester, mercenary, etc... can also likely hit all enemy slots with the right skill set.
Thus, I don't mind corpses.  If someone chooses character classes or skill sets that can only target a small amount of enemy spots, then yes, corpses would be a problem and would be very annoying.  My personal preference is to have my characters be more versatile, which makes corpses not a problem.  If someone like smore specialized characters, then corpses could really be a pain by 'cramping your style'.
I suppose it could be said that it comes down to planning and strategy, in order for corpses to not be a problem, but at the same time, the point of a game is to have fun, and it's most fun to play according to your own preference.  So all in all, I will steadfastly maintain that corpses are NOT fake difficulty, because with the right playstyle they aren't a problem, but they can be annoying and make the game harder with the wrong playstyle.  Please note that when I say 'right' and 'wrong' playstyle, I'm not asserting that my playstyle is superior to all the others, I'm refering it to being 'right' and 'wrong' in accordance to dealing with corpses.

In all seriousness though, this game is great. Apart from the login-queue and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥-connection that the single server they have brings to european players (and i guess asian, australian and african players as well) - it is hosted in North America after all - this game brings forth a ton of fun content.
The combat grows a bit stale after a while, because you only have 3 skills and a basic attack, but it's still relatively fun. And, if you truly grow bored of it, you can always get a new class for a relatively cheap 5000 cubits (Which is equivelant of 8  consecutive days of daily quests). not only do the classes truly play very differently - which is sadly a bit of a commodity these days - they also break free from the "Warrior, Rogue, Wizard, Priest" basics that most RPGs tend to stick to too much. Early on the combat is pretty easy, but past level 10, things get really challenging and fun!
The building is slightly limited, because you can only truly build big structures in your club world (which is basically your club, or "guild's", private world) and only relatively small structures in your cornerstone (play the game to found out what exactly a cornerstone entails). However, the limited opportunities for building are compensated for by the sheer amount of variation in building materials. there are litterally 100s of possible blocks and decorations to place!
As for the concerns of the "Free to Play" aspect of the game: Yes, money can impact your characters quite a bit, but almost everything - except for cosmetics - can be acquired without pay-wall. You can buy wings, but you can also earn them. You can buy mounts, but you can also earn them. Only Costumes (skins) are largely money-only, but even some of those can be earned for free! That isn't to say you can't costumize your character's looks, on the contrary! every weapon, hat, or accesory you find can be "Collected"; you lose the item, but gain flux (which is the main trading currency in the game) and you save the item's "Style", meaning you can give your character the look of that equipment piece regardless of what you have equipped.
You earn 500 cubits per day if you do your daily quest, which is very easily done in just 15 minutes, and this increases to 1000 on weekends. a class costs 5000 cubits, and most other things purchased with cubits are either around that same price, or extremely expensive but can ONLY be purchased with cubits (like a mount for 20000 cubits, which is really only in the game for people who want to show off how long they've played the game)
The community is also really awesome, i have not seen a single person be mean to someone yet, and i have played since beta. Generally people are either nice to each other or outright ignore each other, which is not a bad thing.
All in all, this game is definitely worth at least a few hours of your time, especially if you are a fan of RPG's or creative sandboxes, because this game blends the two very well! I therefore give it a solid 7.5/10 try it out with a friend or two, i bet you'll like it.

I reviewed this game when I had played about 10 hours of it. here's a do-over:
so dark souls III is a brilliant game
it is a brutal game. it is a very punishing and tormenting game.
but never will you feel that you have been cheated or exploited by the game
the game's brilliance and challenge is based on a mechanic of how you have to place your bets on your moves. if you're in a battle with an enemy, whether they are weak or strong, there is a chance that if you trip up, you might just fall and not get back up. and then all your exp. falls with you.
the game is quite difficult to adjust to if you are new
mostly, "hack and slash" games have a formula of "press attack, attack immediately happens". I'm thinking mostly of god of war and devil may cry here.
but in dark souls (III), every attack is a wind up and release. pressing attack doesn't attack. it initiates what will be an attack in about half a second. but that half second is how the game becomes so dangerous - you have no idea what might happen in that half-second window. you might beat the enemy, you might dodge and heal yourself just in time, or you might die.
that is why the challenge in this game is so fresh - such a window of gamble and faith gives you the fun of a hack and slash game but also the strategy of an RPG turn-taking game. you are rolling the dice when you are choosing to attack or dodge. and dodging itself is not just "dodging". dodging is matching a wave, or a pulse - a split second too late or too early and you've missed it. and it hurts.
the boss battles are mostly brilliant. I have just completed the game twice in a row and out of the 10+ major boss battles, I would say that about 90% of them are breathtaking. and the brilliance of the bosses is not simply the unique challenge each one poses, but the backstories of each one is alluring. and that point is emphatic when referring more so to later bosses like the nameless king who is shrouded in mystery and hidden within cryptic clues. his mere existence within the game is a secret in itself, as well.
dark souls 3 surprised me. when my friend recommended I play it, I had essentially forget about video games. but the lore intrigued me. and watching them play it and experiencing the difficulty sucked me in. on the surface, dark souls 3 might just appear to be a god of war style game. but dark souls 3 is a whole different beast. dark souls 3 (and its predecessors) will go down in games history as fresh, innovative and original masterpieces in the medium of its kind.

Pretty cool game, but it's one of those games where they have probably spend countless nights balancing the random. A "roguelike" in only the sense that it's randomly generated and replayable with severe consequences. It just goes too far into the severe consequences it gets rediculous. It's like it's set on a hardcore mode that only a few would enjoy. It's got a tone, that just oozes smugness, telling you in the start "Don't worry, we made this game to be no fun at all, because..."
Take provisions as an example. Apparently these spoil instantly as they enter a ruin, and cannot possibly be used afterwards, they loose all value and probably get thrown away even though at the end of the journey they eat into your carrying capactiy on what you can bring back. So you are constantly in need of balance for how much you might get out of a quest, how much stuff you might need to pass a dungeon, and how much you might find? Add to this the fact that dungeons "level up" for no reason, and you're running out of capable warriors, it's like your playing a game over and over again, just increasing the difficulty level but not really getting anywhere.
Another awkward balance to keep things "tense" is healing, you may have healers, but they can't heal out of battle. So instead of figuring out a system to balance having too much healing ability, the game designers chose to make an arbitrary descision on not being able to do something outside of lethal situations. This lack of strategy just leaves me bummed. This also makes it that there are tons of helaing abilties, and you just need to balance multiple party builds with enough healing, but not too much. Oh the fun.
Lastly the need for 4 people in your party is just contrary to how the game begins with 2 characters. So even if you'd be okay with your 3 fresh and sane adventurers, to maybe just take a half way excursion into the dungeon, you NEED to take gibbering jim who really should really be spending time in the asylum instead. I mean it just wouldn't be fun if the game couldn't force its stress mechanic onto you every step of the way, would it? The characters in this world are also by far the most fragile examples of humanity. Someone says something bad more then once, steals all valuable loot, refuses to help, and then DIES!? Well oh no, why don't you all just slip on into eternal hopelessness. This is a game that was obviously designed by people who think getting "triggered" is as serious as social science wants you to belive. I suppose the real answer was to just let gibbering jim go, not get him help and maybe then the game would let me just play with 3 characters- ah who am I kidding, probably would have shown a kill screen and ended it all if I was that sick.
I havn't really gotten too far into this game, and my above examples probably makes that clear. Its just one of those games where you need a community forum to go read over, to learn the basic concepts, ammounts and progression just to have fun. Although this is apparently what "ruined" the original game (before the hound and whatnot update)  because there was a strategy which could be applied, to far too great an effect. This broken game from the past apparently got all glowing reviews, and now tha game is just completely different, but some people are happy about it I guess?
There is no amateur mode. The game also does such a poor job at teaching you anything I have the feeling the game creators just thought Deamons Souls was the greatest game in the world because who knows what the heck that game wanted, was really more of a community puzzle then a game. Those outside of the community aspects just had to try and fail countless times. However that game got one thing right which this didn't, you failed a lot but this was the "normal" state of things and it kept going. In this game you fail a lot and you just start over and over again, doing that same tedious fight, see the same tired cut scenes, progress the same 3 missions before you get everything in the game... Ugh. This games "normal state" is to fail, and get nowhere and start over again, so if that sounds like fun by all means, sign up to the closest darkest dungeon community forum, load up a ton of reading and pull an all nighter. Its got charm, it's got variety, it's just too much "raw" for my taste.

"Darkest Dungeon is about making the most of a bad situation. Quests will fail or must be abandoned. Heroes will die. And when they die, they stay dead. Progress autosaves constantly, so actions are permanent.
The game expects a lot out of you. How far will you push your adventurers? How much are you willing to risk in you quest to restore the Hamlet? What will you sacrifice to save thfe life of your favorite hero?" - Excerpt from the Darkest Dungeons' warning screen.
It doesn't lie ether. Failure is often, and death is final.
>I've lost countless heroes.
>90% of my heroes are under equiped and under trained.
>We barely find enough gold to cover the next expedition, let alone pay for stress relief, training, equipment, and medicine.
>I have had to send out expeditions with no supplies what-so-ever.
>I've had entire teams die of heart attacks. Othertimes someone dies in the very first fight, forcing the rest to retreat and waste all the supplies for that trip.
But it's not all bad. Victories are small, but we must hold on to them.
>Many bosses lie dead.
>The Hamlet is recovering.
>Heroes have stood on Death's Door only to rally and crush all that stand before them.
>We've scored flawless victories on strong enemies.
>For every understocked expedition, there is one well equiped for the coming trials.
The gameplay is a mixture of resource managment, and stratigic combat. In town you manage your heroes and equip them for the coming fights. In expeditions you combat the horrors of the Dungeons in hopes of finding enough gold to take care of your heroes. Stress is a real part of the game, for both you and your heroes, and effects every choice you make. Too much stress, and your heroes could suffer a major debuff. Worse still, they'll drag others down til they are cured.
In the game, everything matters. I find myself having the same reactions as my heroes to various things. When someone scores a crit, I'm emboldened and so are my heroes. Enemy crits cause us both to despair. Loot is needed just to keep things going. You have to squeeze all you can out of the town's facilites to have a fighting chance.
The game scales HARD. The green missions are fairly easy. Ment to give newbies a challenge but a experinced player should have little trouble so long as they stay sharp and luck doesn't turn against them. In yellow missions victory is not assured. You will be challanged to keep your team from falling apart. Red missions: Pray to whatever gods you believe in. They will not hear you.
That's the game in a nut shell. Here's some pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Challenging gameplay
+ Every choice matters
+ A fitting artstyle
+ Next to no bugs
+ Promising varity (More then dozen heroes types, a myriad of enemies, creative bosses, 5 dungeons and more of everything on the way)
+ Success is not assured and thus means something.
+ Interesting backstory with a Lovecraftian flavor.
+ Truely horrific enemies. (Look out for the mushroom guys... See what they really are... And don't even think about The Flesh. The Darkest Dungeon itself is filled with unending horrors.)
+ Dont' quote me on this, but I've heard the DLC is going to be free. Woot!
Neutral:
> The Darkest Dungeon isn't actually in the game yet... It's on it's way though. EDIT: It's a full game! All 5 Dungeons are playable, and you can actually beat the game now!
> Music is fitting, but forgetable.
Cons:
- Combat is % to hit. So it's possiable your entire team wiffs their attacks while the last enemy crits... Very frusterating.
- Very stressful at times.
In a phrase, this game is a masochist's dream.
I highly recommend this to anyone who wants a significant challange or just likes to get beaten every once in a while.

It's impossible to mimic the exact feel and wonder of the original Dark Souls, as everything after will be, by definition, reiterations of the same concept with improvements. That said, FromSoftware has honed the Souls formula to near perfection, retaining the excellent worldbuilding and lore that the series is known for, and streamlining some parts, like weapon upgrades, to help the player get back into the game faster. Boss battles in this installment are the best they've ever been, with music that accentuates every encounter and gives each battle a distinct tone and weight. The addition of Weapon Arts makes each weapon feel a little more unique, forcing the player to consider more than just type and damage output. The areas are a little more linear this time around, although they are beautifully designed, and the first DLC area is a bit of a letdown in terms of content added, but what's here is unforgettable. Definitely worth every penny.

If I had to describe Darkest Dungeon in a single word it would be "Chaotic". There are so many different things to manage during battles that you can often find yourself overwhelmed with the amount of crap that your poor characters are having to deal with. Your health points are being smashed, bled and blighted away and all the while their sanity is fading to nothing which just makes the fight that much more difficult. You finally reach the end of a dungeon and give a sigh of relief that somehow you managed to make it out the other end...except it feels a lot more like luck than your own skill and perseverance that got you there.
Darkest Dungeon presents itself as a game that is meant to be unfair, characters are supposed to die and become afflicted with various disorders and you're forced to find yourself in very difficult situations that there is no way out of other than to call it quits. Money is the main issue as no matter how many succesful dungeon runs you have you always seem to find yourself scrambling for cash and you spend a fortune getting your adventurers back into fighting shape, upgrading their skills and gear and providing enough provisions so that their run is not a complete failure. The game is difficult and challenging but not in a good way.
Blight and bleed effects work very well against your adventurers but are next to useless against the enemy. It's better to just hammer away at then with your most damaging skills as depending on bleed or blight effects will just end up getting you killed. Stunning is occasionaly useful but not enough. Simply put there isn't much variety in how to win a fight, keep your team healed whilst the hard hitters smash away at the opponent and keep a jester around to buff or a plague doctor to stun.
The game itself is very pretty and the presentation of the game is brilliant. It's succesful in creating a sense of impending doom and hopelesness that you will inevitably feel at many times. The main problem of the game is that it's difficult for all the wrong reasons, no matter how many provisions you take or how much time you spend organising the right team you will still be forced to abandon quests and say goodbye to adventurers simply because the chaos of the game is unmanageable. There is a challenge and then there is Darkest Dungeon, if you enjoy being a punching bag then by all means pick this up otherwise you should probably just give it a miss.

So first things first, the game is fun.
What is the problem? It didn't really gave me the Fallout experience I was looking for.
RPG Elements - These were basically thrown out the window. While in previous Fallout games you could build your character the way you wanted and go about solving problems the way you wanted, this has been watered down to basically a first person shooter. Narrative first person shooters are not a bad things, games such as Metro Last Light did a great job in immersing yourself on a post-apocalyptic world and telling you an interesting story. The problem with Fallout 4 is that the story really wasn't that interesting, and so taking those RPG elements in decision making hurt the game more than it actually helped.
Mechanics - They felt they were cut out of Fallout 3, simplified and pasted into Fallout 4. I was really expecting more from a new gen game.  No dodging/rolling or taking cover, or driving your own vehicles. I was hoping for at least that considering how heavy they rely in gameplay over roleplay.
Settlement building and management - Fun idea, building your own city and all, but in the end is very limiting as to what you can edit and thus breaks the immersion. Some houses cannot be scrapped, the level of craftiness is very poor, etc.
Power Armor - It definitively needs mention. I believe is one of the highlights of the game. Putting the power armor definitively made me feel powerful and a complete beast, and some of the editing options somewhat allow you to play different styles and not only the walking tank. This was done right.
Basically its a fun game, not a good Fallout game. I wouldn't recommend paying full price for it.
