I'll try to keep this review short and succinct, focussing on the most important game elements rather than boring you with my rose-tinted impressions. After all, half the fun is discovering the stuff on your own.
Darkest Dungeon is a squad-based dungeon crawler where you're constantly juggling your different resources (health, stress, supply items, light, gold, time) to make the most out of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation. You have thirteen distinct hero classes at your disposal each coming with a set of seven active skills and the possibility to carry two trinkets (ouf of what are probably 70+ available trinkets). You put together a group of four heroes and then send them on increasingly difficult missions into randomly generated dungeons, while at the same time trying to upgrade your home base to unlock better weapons, more powerful abilities and better ways to relief your heroes of stress. And you never have enough of anything.
It's not a traditional RPG. It doesn't really have a story except for little snippets here and there that hint at a bigger story going on in the background. There are no NPCs to talk to, no quests to do, no princesses to save. It's just you against the monsters. Except that the monsters are better armed, better geared and better prepared than you. And they brought their whole familiy.
It's hard. At times even unfair. But it's never unbeatable. Until you reach the late game, no matter what you do, the odds are stacked against you. Your heals are unable to keep up with the incoming damage, your supplies are limited because you need that gold for more important stuff and from time to time the randomness of the dungeons and encounters just kicks your teeth in. Even if you're perfectly prepared. For funsies. But over time you adapt. You learn to expect catastrophic failures and what to do to survive them. You
lose some of your heroes to an encounter which you haven't figured out yet, or to a boss which doesn't give a ♥♥♥♥ about your well planned group setup. It's a constant learning experience. And you get all the tools to make it right, just don't expect to get it right on the first attempt.
Holding your hand. There isn't really an in-game tutorial, or a lot of explanation. You have a glossar, which explains the basic workings of the game, but everything that goes beyond
you need to figure out for yourself. And there's a lot to figure out. And while you figure everything out, you'll probably shed a few tears for all the shiny loot you couldn't get and the heroes who didn't quiet make it.
Great, addictive fun. At first you're completely overwhelmed by all the different things you can do and all the different choices you have to make even though you have no clue what exactly they do or how they will interact with each other. But then you learn, you fail, you figure things out, you fail slightly less and eventually you succeed. And then you have an immensely robust game at your hands which offers you an abundance of possible ways to play it. The class mechanics are rock solid, the game mechanics are intricate and interact very well with each other. Once you've figured out the basics, you can put your thinking hat on and come up with whatever group composition you can dream up and make it work. And make it work you need to do. Because the enemy is doing the same.
Your regular, run-of-the-mill casual game that you can just play for an hour or two of relaxed entertainment every now and then. You really need to invest a bit of time and brains to get things rolling. Once you are accustomed with the inner workings of the game, you can casually play a couple of dungeons every now and then and have a good time, but until then you either need to be very patient and resistant to frustration, or you embrace the challenge and face the difficulties head on. If you hold on though, you will be rewarded with a game full of rewarding challenge and pure joy.

"Darkest Dungeon is about making the most of a bad situation. Quests will fail or must be abandoned. Heroes will die. And when they die, they stay dead. Progress autosaves constantly, so actions are permanent.
The game expects a lot out of you. How far will you push your adventurers? How much are you willing to risk in you quest to restore the Hamlet? What will you sacrifice to save thfe life of your favorite hero?" - Excerpt from the Darkest Dungeons' warning screen.
It doesn't lie ether. Failure is often, and death is final.
>I've lost countless heroes.
>90% of my heroes are under equiped and under trained.
>We barely find enough gold to cover the next expedition, let alone pay for stress relief, training, equipment, and medicine.
>I have had to send out expeditions with no supplies what-so-ever.
>I've had entire teams die of heart attacks. Othertimes someone dies in the very first fight, forcing the rest to retreat and waste all the supplies for that trip.
But it's not all bad. Victories are small, but we must hold on to them.
>Many bosses lie dead.
>The Hamlet is recovering.
>Heroes have stood on Death's Door only to rally and crush all that stand before them.
>We've scored flawless victories on strong enemies.
>For every understocked expedition, there is one well equiped for the coming trials.
The gameplay is a mixture of resource managment, and stratigic combat. In town you manage your heroes and equip them for the coming fights. In expeditions you combat the horrors of the Dungeons in hopes of finding enough gold to take care of your heroes. Stress is a real part of the game, for both you and your heroes, and effects every choice you make. Too much stress, and your heroes could suffer a major debuff. Worse still, they'll drag others down til they are cured.
In the game, everything matters. I find myself having the same reactions as my heroes to various things. When someone scores a crit, I'm emboldened and so are my heroes. Enemy crits cause us both to despair. Loot is needed just to keep things going. You have to squeeze all you can out of the town's facilites to have a fighting chance.
The game scales HARD. The green missions are fairly easy. Ment to give newbies a challenge but a experinced player should have little trouble so long as they stay sharp and luck doesn't turn against them. In yellow missions victory is not assured. You will be challanged to keep your team from falling apart. Red missions: Pray to whatever gods you believe in. They will not hear you.
That's the game in a nut shell. Here's some pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Challenging gameplay
+ Every choice matters
+ A fitting artstyle
+ Next to no bugs
+ Promising varity (More then dozen heroes types, a myriad of enemies, creative bosses, 5 dungeons and more of everything on the way)
+ Success is not assured and thus means something.
+ Interesting backstory with a Lovecraftian flavor.
+ Truely horrific enemies. (Look out for the mushroom guys... See what they really are... And don't even think about The Flesh. The Darkest Dungeon itself is filled with unending horrors.)
+ Dont' quote me on this, but I've heard the DLC is going to be free. Woot!
Neutral:
> The Darkest Dungeon isn't actually in the game yet... It's on it's way though. EDIT: It's a full game! All 5 Dungeons are playable, and you can actually beat the game now!
> Music is fitting, but forgetable.
Cons:
- Combat is % to hit. So it's possiable your entire team wiffs their attacks while the last enemy crits... Very frusterating.
- Very stressful at times.
In a phrase, this game is a masochist's dream.
I highly recommend this to anyone who wants a significant challange or just likes to get beaten every once in a while.

With the recent take over of Grey Havens I can assure myself and the community that this game will have a second light, a Second Chance as people put it. They have managed to put out new content not in the form of microtransactions but in the form of content. Something Three Rings have failed to do within recent years.
The game is a MMO topdown shooter with some elements of an RPG being able to upgrade your equipment and floating companions known as Sprites with the goal of finding an energy source to power your ship back home. Spoilers, this never happens as far as the story is implemented. The game's story is very much required for progression of the game, once you overcome some of these hurdles you may take a break from the story and explore what is known as the Clockworks whether it be for enjoyment, or grinding.
The Clockworks outside of the mission are procedurally generated along with a wide variety of themed levels. These levels are made of two combinations, Monster Type and Status Type. The only problem with this is that these "procedurally generated" aren't exactly that, there are specific setpieces that put into the map and are connected by linear pathways. This means you will most likely see a room more than once on your adventures. Though once in a while you'll get a few surprises.
Unlike the commom MMORPGs equipment such as weapons and armor don't have random stats whether it be the defense points of an item, or actual stats like critical damage bonus. Instead the stats of equipment are preset and do not fluctuate. With every Level up to level 10 the stats of the equipment go up the preset amount. This is a very unique approach on how equipment fairs agianest each other instead of just finding the one with the best stats. Allowing you to use different combinations of sets for different tasks. There are tons of different armor sets and weapons to try out and experiment with. Whether it be hard hitting and tanky, or an even mix of both ranged and melee.
Combat is divided into three different catagories: Melee, Ranged, and bombs. Combat with these weapons are pretty basic. Click for a 2-3 attack combo. hold the weapon and it'll charge for a stronger attack. these charge attacks are unique to the weapon type with adds to usability of a weapon.
Enemy combat is also pretty basic, they just mainly go up to you and attack. For the most part they're very predictable and can be easily avoided with the blocking of your shield. Some enemies are more unique into how they fight. Whether it be blocking your attacks or borrowing to go behind you it's still easy to out maneuver them.
Yes this game used to be transactions heavy when Three Rings still had ownership of the game putting out "new" content every two weeks. Though now toned down greatly there are still transactions to help progress through the game at a MUCH faster rate.
The game is very unique as a whole. Level generation is semiprocedurally generated as in you'll get new layouts but you'll see some rooms again. Equipment and how it's handled is very unique and different, greatly allowing you to experiement with other items for maximum efficiency on those levels. Combat in the game is basic and is quite bland. Enemies are very predictable and avoidable. Yes there are a lot of microtransactions to help progress through the game much faster, but it's not really needed if you're willing to grind.

Trove is a game that was recently released on Steam, but already existed prior to that. Kind of a bland start, but Trove is still in like 1.0, so it definitely has room to grow. Right now it's pretty good, so I'm going to go over what it does right and what it could because I'm definitely important sheesh
* Simple yet addicting gameplay. Find dungeon, hold down M1 on all enemies with occasional M2, and spam skills on dungeon boss until it crumbles. Rinse and repeat while occasionally finding ore veins to mine. Sounds pretty bland, but it's actually quite fun and the way the game handles smacking stuff around or crafting that next table is frankly satisfying and doesn't take too long to actually do.
* Progression is quick. As stated above, it doesn't take too much effort to craft the essential stations or upgrade your gear, and not much time either. If you can mine shiny things that are sticking out of the ground and beat up a lot of monsters, you're generally set for life. As of this posting, I have played Trove for literally 10 hours, and I'm at level 12 and 8 on two of my characters. The maximum level is 20, so I'm already a decent ways there.
* Truly free gameplay. You don't NEED to pay for that flaming, 5-pronged sword in the shop because you can find your own if you invest enough time into it. Cubits+ or whatever they're called only really buy costumes and neat mounts, and you can already find mounts of the same caliber off of monsters or craft them yourself like a big boy would. And should be able to. Dungeons always end in chests with 2 pieces of loot that hold class-respective gear inside them, no questions asked. You're a knight? Sword and hat/face mask. You're a gunslinger? Gun and hat/face mask. Simple, useful, efficient. And this isn't even counting in the monster drops.
* The queue system. Currently, you'll be waiting 10 minutes or more depending on your position in queue, which will usually be well over 1000. As the devs weren't too prepared with the sudden spike in new players, this could easily be fixed with hardware upgrades or the like.
* Constant maintenance. Again, the game is only in 1.0 and this is bound to slow down along with the wave of players, but right now it kinda sucks to get through a challenging dungeon or a shadow arena, beat it...and then get kicked out of the game due to emergency maintenance. All that loot and effort down the toilet.
VERDICT
Trove is a fun game for me and I don't mind playing it. Progression is smooth and doesn't take too long, completely free to play if you choose to make it that, and very easy to just pick up and start playing for the first time. Aside from server issues and maintenance that will inevitably improve with time, Trove is definitely worth the download.

I'll try to keep this review short and succinct, focussing on the most important game elements rather than boring you with my rose-tinted impressions. After all, half the fun is discovering the stuff on your own.
Darkest Dungeon is a squad-based dungeon crawler where you're constantly juggling your different resources (health, stress, supply items, light, gold, time) to make the most out of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation. You have thirteen distinct hero classes at your disposal each coming with a set of seven active skills and the possibility to carry two trinkets (ouf of what are probably 70+ available trinkets). You put together a group of four heroes and then send them on increasingly difficult missions into randomly generated dungeons, while at the same time trying to upgrade your home base to unlock better weapons, more powerful abilities and better ways to relief your heroes of stress. And you never have enough of anything.
It's not a traditional RPG. It doesn't really have a story except for little snippets here and there that hint at a bigger story going on in the background. There are no NPCs to talk to, no quests to do, no princesses to save. It's just you against the monsters. Except that the monsters are better armed, better geared and better prepared than you. And they brought their whole familiy.
It's hard. At times even unfair. But it's never unbeatable. Until you reach the late game, no matter what you do, the odds are stacked against you. Your heals are unable to keep up with the incoming damage, your supplies are limited because you need that gold for more important stuff and from time to time the randomness of the dungeons and encounters just kicks your teeth in. Even if you're perfectly prepared. For funsies. But over time you adapt. You learn to expect catastrophic failures and what to do to survive them. You
lose some of your heroes to an encounter which you haven't figured out yet, or to a boss which doesn't give a ♥♥♥♥ about your well planned group setup. It's a constant learning experience. And you get all the tools to make it right, just don't expect to get it right on the first attempt.
Holding your hand. There isn't really an in-game tutorial, or a lot of explanation. You have a glossar, which explains the basic workings of the game, but everything that goes beyond
you need to figure out for yourself. And there's a lot to figure out. And while you figure everything out, you'll probably shed a few tears for all the shiny loot you couldn't get and the heroes who didn't quiet make it.
Great, addictive fun. At first you're completely overwhelmed by all the different things you can do and all the different choices you have to make even though you have no clue what exactly they do or how they will interact with each other. But then you learn, you fail, you figure things out, you fail slightly less and eventually you succeed. And then you have an immensely robust game at your hands which offers you an abundance of possible ways to play it. The class mechanics are rock solid, the game mechanics are intricate and interact very well with each other. Once you've figured out the basics, you can put your thinking hat on and come up with whatever group composition you can dream up and make it work. And make it work you need to do. Because the enemy is doing the same.
Your regular, run-of-the-mill casual game that you can just play for an hour or two of relaxed entertainment every now and then. You really need to invest a bit of time and brains to get things rolling. Once you are accustomed with the inner workings of the game, you can casually play a couple of dungeons every now and then and have a good time, but until then you either need to be very patient and resistant to frustration, or you embrace the challenge and face the difficulties head on. If you hold on though, you will be rewarded with a game full of rewarding challenge and pure joy.

"Darkest Dungeon is about making the most of a bad situation. Quests will fail or must be abandoned. Heroes will die. And when they die, they stay dead. Progress autosaves constantly, so actions are permanent.
The game expects a lot out of you. How far will you push your adventurers? How much are you willing to risk in you quest to restore the Hamlet? What will you sacrifice to save thfe life of your favorite hero?" - Excerpt from the Darkest Dungeons' warning screen.
It doesn't lie ether. Failure is often, and death is final.
>I've lost countless heroes.
>90% of my heroes are under equiped and under trained.
>We barely find enough gold to cover the next expedition, let alone pay for stress relief, training, equipment, and medicine.
>I have had to send out expeditions with no supplies what-so-ever.
>I've had entire teams die of heart attacks. Othertimes someone dies in the very first fight, forcing the rest to retreat and waste all the supplies for that trip.
But it's not all bad. Victories are small, but we must hold on to them.
>Many bosses lie dead.
>The Hamlet is recovering.
>Heroes have stood on Death's Door only to rally and crush all that stand before them.
>We've scored flawless victories on strong enemies.
>For every understocked expedition, there is one well equiped for the coming trials.
The gameplay is a mixture of resource managment, and stratigic combat. In town you manage your heroes and equip them for the coming fights. In expeditions you combat the horrors of the Dungeons in hopes of finding enough gold to take care of your heroes. Stress is a real part of the game, for both you and your heroes, and effects every choice you make. Too much stress, and your heroes could suffer a major debuff. Worse still, they'll drag others down til they are cured.
In the game, everything matters. I find myself having the same reactions as my heroes to various things. When someone scores a crit, I'm emboldened and so are my heroes. Enemy crits cause us both to despair. Loot is needed just to keep things going. You have to squeeze all you can out of the town's facilites to have a fighting chance.
The game scales HARD. The green missions are fairly easy. Ment to give newbies a challenge but a experinced player should have little trouble so long as they stay sharp and luck doesn't turn against them. In yellow missions victory is not assured. You will be challanged to keep your team from falling apart. Red missions: Pray to whatever gods you believe in. They will not hear you.
That's the game in a nut shell. Here's some pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Challenging gameplay
+ Every choice matters
+ A fitting artstyle
+ Next to no bugs
+ Promising varity (More then dozen heroes types, a myriad of enemies, creative bosses, 5 dungeons and more of everything on the way)
+ Success is not assured and thus means something.
+ Interesting backstory with a Lovecraftian flavor.
+ Truely horrific enemies. (Look out for the mushroom guys... See what they really are... And don't even think about The Flesh. The Darkest Dungeon itself is filled with unending horrors.)
+ Dont' quote me on this, but I've heard the DLC is going to be free. Woot!
Neutral:
> The Darkest Dungeon isn't actually in the game yet... It's on it's way though. EDIT: It's a full game! All 5 Dungeons are playable, and you can actually beat the game now!
> Music is fitting, but forgetable.
Cons:
- Combat is % to hit. So it's possiable your entire team wiffs their attacks while the last enemy crits... Very frusterating.
- Very stressful at times.
In a phrase, this game is a masochist's dream.
I highly recommend this to anyone who wants a significant challange or just likes to get beaten every once in a while.
Overall not a really good game. Good for children but wouldn't really recommend for people above the age of 12. Easy controls but not so good graphics

Updating this review as of v1.3-
What began as a somewhat simple and directionless "Terraria in space", Starbound has come a long way and taken on its own identity in that time. I first reviewed this game in early alpha and while it was fun then, the game has been practically rebuilt from the ground up leaving only the core concepts the same. So here's the good and the ugly:
Good:
-Fleshed out and interesting lore for each race
-Well integrated main quest line with fun and challenging dungeons
-Fluid and varied combat (much improved since release)
-Rewarding progression in terms of manipulator upgrades, tech, and an ever increasing ship size
-Mech building and space combat
-Wide assortment of creatures as well as biomes
-A building system that provides 100s of furniture, decorations, and block types
-Many options for fashion (You can dress up as an alpaca)
-Side activities like space trade, being a landlord, fishing, farming, bug catching, pet taming
Ugly:
-Limited and mostly predictable planet types
-Linear progression up through the star system tiers
-Side quests are all very similar and get tedious
-Your crew and pets die quickly
-Content is limited. Eventually you realize that yes, while the weapons are random, and lots of different armor types exist, they all have tiers and every tier 2 helmet is the same, every tier 4 assault rifle does the same damage. You will end up keeping one armor set through the game and upgrading it as you raise up the tiers.
-The game requires modding toget maximum enjoyment
I definitely recommend the game more so than ever before. More content is always being planned and added to the base game. I do highly recommend Frackin Universe mod if you want to get hundreds of hours of gameplay as well as fix most of the ugly points listed above.

A long time ago I used to play DnD casually with some friends. Once my character died crit failing eating some strange fruit from a magical tree. Then my friends couldn't roll high enough to successfully give my character the Heimlich maneuver and I choked to death. It was just chain of bad luck and bad rolls all around. This is kind of how Darkest Dungeon feels sometimes, cept there is no local necromancers, churches or witches to bring your character back.
Normally I don't do reviews but I really feel like I'm experiencing something special here. I do like SOME tune based RPG's. Loved Disgaea DS and the Fire Emblem series. I started this game this week and I can't stop.  I'm aware I've been thrown into without prior experience before some of the infamous patches (that brought the game to my attention in the first place. Even bad press is still good press.) I could see why maggots with PROT can wreck your day, and I'm greatful I never had to deal with that. I've never known DD without corpses so I've built teams from the beginning to deal with them without much issue.
That being said I highly recommend this game to people who have not played it before with the risk that in the future, everything might change and all your in game investments might turn against you. If your a masochist like me or your mentally crippled character it is  worth the risk. Keep in mind this game is BRUTAL. Sinking time and money into a character alone will not save them. This is beyond Darksouls type risk (Crusader even looks like Oscar the Fateless!). Perma death is a the punishing reality of this game that must be accepted.
I can totally empathize with veteran players who have been already established a go to team and strategy. This is not a short game with near Disgaea lvls of micromanaging and spending time with disposable characters who sometimes need to be leveled just to be used as fodder later. It takes quite a while just to get your characters strong enough to medium and high level dungeons and losing a whole medium to maxed lvl team must be like a punch to the gut just because your entire strategy just broke to deal with stagnate meat piles. Its not just switching up team members either, it takes lots of time and resources just to buy and upgrade skills that work together with other classes. And yes, perma-death is a huge deal, like Fire Emblem but with the unforgiving auto save feature of Darksouls so restarting the game wont save your favorite character.
That being said as a new comer the corpses patch and enemies with massive PROT forced me to experiment with classes and class skills I would have never used (The Occultist, Bounty Hunter's Come Hither and Flash Bang skills, Plague Doctor's Disorienting Blast and Blinding Gas Skills) while not relying on just heavy hitters like The Leaper and Crusader. Due to the stress meter, stress spreading to other characters when one finally snaps and risk of heart attacks I have to constantly shuffle through party members each run while mentally treating ones that just came home, or firing them because the expenses of treating stress and disease is quite high. Darkest Dungeon will teach you the art adapting and letting go. Sometimes painfully.
I'll end this with a story of a typicl harrowing experiance of normal DD playthrough. I had an Arbalest who I later named Boomy (word of advice, don't name them... it just hurts more later). I reluctantly recruited her fully intending her to be a disposable character, needing a healer while one Vestal healer was being flagellated to treat her Paranoia (as one does) and the other went missing FOR DAYS on a bender (when she finally came home she swore off drinking so I forgive her now). Boomy was not the best healer (paired her with the Occultist who is a...unpredictable and problematic healer but they could proabably keep most of the team alive for a quick short scouting mission) but OMG did she blast mofos back to the abyss from whence they came like a pro. She soon became my baby, raising her from nothing to wrecking the first bosses like they were mere mortals, and saving her comrades from death's door like a champ. Her flexibility, her power, she was a GODDESS on the field. Then, her first medium dungeon...she was hit with bleed and blight (over time a build up of bad quirks and disease from her inability to stop touching things killed most of her resistances) and then she was slapped in the face with a tree... My Boomy, my baby girl. I lost her but learned and learned a valuable lesson. The Crusader is beyond awesome in your easy dungeons but he suddenly became more useful as a healer and tank in medium dungeons. There are TONS of enemies with massive PROT, he also cannot heal the back row where Boomy tended to be. Characters with mark abilities became my new heavy hitters. Debuffs and buffs are now VERY important. Stunning is a necessity to keep your party alive. You learn to adapt, and use other classes for stuff you didn't think you would use them for.  I fled that battle and that dungeon to keepy my lvl 3 characters alive. I had to learn to live without Boomy and my other Arbalest was only lvl 1. It's unfair but you move on, learn to love a new character and switch up your style constantly. I'm building up a new team and have sucessfully ran 2 medium dungeons...,barely but boy did it feel good.

****Early Access Review****
Has the appeal of Plants Vs. Zombies, the art style of a comi-cthulhu graphic novel, and the strategic depth of X-Com:EU. It's still in development, but already is money well spent. I have not personally encountered any bugs, plays smooth, and has hordes of content.
I love the atmosphere and art in this one. It comes off as playful almost, or south parky, but it's got more grit and atmosphere than many more 'advanced' games. The gameplay is nicely simple, but has a multitude of strategic elements that tie the game mechanics together in complex, and dangerous, ways. Much time can be spent just managing your roster of adventurers, making sure they are occupied, skilled, fitted, disease free, and making sure the kleptomaniacs in the group dont steal your stuff :0 Buildings in town can be upgraded with special loot found in the dungeons.
There is a disclamer at the begining of the game, telling the player that the game is difficult. Now I guess that can kinda seem pretentious, but it is indeed true. A lot of games will tell you how dangerous the world is, but they are mechanically geared to make your life stress free. This one refreshingly takes the opposite approach, and entertains you by making things go wrong for you. Even when you do everything right, and get the best luck, bad stuff will still happen. Your adventurers are hardly heroes, and will develop..... strange behaviors over the course of their likely short lifetimes. Sometimes they cross the line and start becoming a problem in a variety of mechanical ways. You can dismiss them at any time, but the investment in skills and gear, make that a difficult choice in many cases.
Pro Tip: Do not rename your adventurers after people you care about.
Adventuring itself seems to have quite a variety for what I was expecting. There are a handfull of tilesets, each highlighting a different locational environment in the world. Quest types are chosen from town, and then four of your adventurers set off to complete a task. Multiple quest types, variable rewards, dungeon layout changes, and encounter differences, all make for a deep exploration experience. There are bosses to hunt down, sewers to explore, chests to open, and traps to step on.
Death is permanent. Not an option. Trying to keep your people alive, and sane, is the meat of the gameplay. Yes you're trying to kill the bad guys and make money too still, but if your cleric panics and decides to curl up in a ball and cry, causing your fighter to become abusive and start yelling at him, the archer is going to become suicidal and stab himself in the face, giving your rogue a heart attack. Oh and that last worm encounter gave them rabies and stomach problems, so that isn't helping either.
Anyhow. Short version: If you like a dark atmosphere, turn based strategy, and a fun challenge....buy it.

I really enjoyed this game. I see a lot of people saying the story and npc's were lame, based building sucked and crafting was pointless. Which I disagree on all fronts. I had no issue with the story personally. If lame parts existed it was the side stuff I had less fun with and felt could of been improved. These games were all about discovery and learning about the world. It has that. I had a lot of fun seeing everything I could and reading everything I could.
-I enjoyed the combat. It had bigger groups of enemys. I liked going in guns blazing or sitting back being a bit sneaky and picking people off. If I was in a pinch I would use the vats system, which is how I used it in every fallout so far that had it. I keep seeing New Vegas being pointed out  over and over. I honestly wasn't as happy with that game. I'm not sure why people are saying that game had way more depth then this. I don't remember much from every faction in that game. If it was amazing I would hope it was memorable as well. I played New Vegas quite a bit. Enjoyed that game also. I just don't see it being this amazing game people are making it sound over Fallout 4.
-I enjoyed crafting. I always hated in older games that the guns really were set and you couldn't do much with them. It also has progression which every other Fallout was lacking with weapons. You found a weapon...and that was it. Hoping you would find another later on. All the crap in the world had purpose now. I would just toss most trash in other games away. It gave me a big reason to look around now everywher I could.
-Power Armor- I don't feel that the armor was a endall thing once you first got it. Not sure how people played the game but I liked the armor but after a bit I stayed away from it. Ruined my sneaking around. I did however like the carry capacity it had. Would make trips a bit easier when I went on resource runs. Less tedious. Later on when I started to be able to modify it and add things to it I had more fun with it.
-Npc's- So i'm seeing a lot of flack for the npcs you interact with. I liked most of them and had a lot of fun learning about what role they are playing in the world that went to s@#*. Seemed to be way more options to choose from perk wise from them. In Vegas I just used Boone. I didn't feel that any other npc was ever worthwhile. I did have fun with the factions though. I got the feeling like I had more purpose with them then any other game. Once you were done doing quests for npc's in other fallouts that was the end of it. This game at least I can signal for help and that faction with help me if i'm in trouble.
-Base Building- I'm surprised this upset people. This is what they wanted to see and they do it and people are saying it's terrible? I had no problem with it. The only problem with base building was that I wanted to spend hours doing it over the game. It did however feel good to build a base up over time as I progressed.  I know I spent a lot of time in starlight drive since it seemed to have a lot of deathclaws around. I surrounded that whole place with fence and put up a missile turret. Took quite of bit of time to do.
-DLC- This is my only gripe with the game. I enjoyed other fallouts dlc a lot. I liked the new stuff to explore and new story to go through. This games dlc was more for having fun in the world and tinkering with stuff. Gave more purpose to trash. It was cool but still wished it had more story driven dlc.
All in all I really enjoyed this game. It could also be that the games story was based around the players son being kidnapped. My son was born that year and it was a lot different for me then i'm sure other peoples experience. The story hit harder this time around.
At the end of the day if you like the fallout worlds you will like this one. All the things that they did this time around is a good step forward. I didn't expect base building. I didn't expect this much gun customization. I didn't expect power armor to have so many options. Could it be made better? Well yea, anything can be. It is also a big step in the right direction for them. Was it perfect? No. This was the first time we had it. I just hope at some point in the future you can play with one other person. For vats users im sure it would be a bit lame.

For those that are curious about the recent negative reviews this game has gotten I was prompted to write this next part after a number of my friends came to me, wanting to buy the game while it was on sale but turned off by the wave of recent negative reviews related to the latest update. So here goes:
I bought the game in early February and immediately fell in love with the brutal turn based combat and the thick Lovecraftian atmosphere, since then I have started a new game every time a new update was added and I loved all of them. Then came the latest update "The Corpse and Hound", this added 3 new mechanics and a new character. I for one, actually liked the new mechanics (they made non-melee character actually viable and made well rounded parties a better choice) however it was mishandled and brought with them some balance issues making a hard game almost impossible so I gave the devs some constructive feedback and stopped playing until the new update came out,
I assumed other had done the same. However this is the internet so people immediately  took to the forums and reviews screaming about how the games was dead now and how the devs were Satan or some such thing. Lo and behold a month later (which was faster then I expected given the soon to be released content update) the devs released a new patch which fixed almost all of the problems. Since then I have played the hell out of it again and loved every blood-soaked minute of it.
Ultimately the devs missteped when they released the Corpse and Hound update with good ideas poorly implemented, however they are obviously very passionate about the game and were very quick to remedy the mistake. A misstep, nothing more, nothing less and certainly nothing to crucify them over.

Alrighty, adding my opinion to the many already here!
DD does a great job of taking a classic set-up and giving it a good spin! You and your characters travel through an atmospheric world that perfectly captures the feeling of despondence felt by the towns folk and your long suffering party members. The upgrade system in the game is scaled very well and the enemies are also well suited to keep you and your characters in check as you go up in level. Balancing stress and health, especially when camping, is an important part of the game and really gets you invested as some enemies attack physically and others make your characters really feel the psychological strain of the quest. The enemy types are also quite varied so each new attack feels interesting as you plunge through the depressing landscapes.
On the other end of the spectrum it is sometimes hard to keep track of your characters. There were several times in the game where I tossed high stress individuals into my party because I didn't notice they were already at 100 but I do blame that more on my own inattention than the game itself. I also find myself getting angry at the characters when they fail a saving throw, again, it's an important part of the game and it does really well in making you think about human nature and all but the 3rd time your Hound Master becomes Selfish and steals 2500 worth of loot you're going to wish you could order your highwayman to shoot him. There are also a few bugs for me but it is in early access so I'm not worried, they go away when I restart the game(which takes about 1.5 minutes).
All in all I thought it was a great game! Sorry for my disjointed ramble, hope it helps you decide if you want to buy the game!

Fallout 4 is an engrossing game that lures you in with mystery and the promise of adventure. Its wretched wasteland can be captivating, and you never know what odd person or settlement lies around the next bend. Fallout 4 uses its dark world as a canvas for exciting combat and gripping stories, and when you dig deeper into its post-nuclear-apocalypse version of Boston--defending yourself from violent scavengers and using your wits to climb social ladders--you become attached to the new you, and ultimately invested in the fate of your new world.
You transform into an influential wasteland warrior over the course of a multitude of dangerous quests, but this is difficult to imagine at the start when you're a well-to-do citizen of 1950s-esque Boston. The game begins on a peaceful morning at home with your spouse and child; a robot butler provides upbeat banter and a glimpse at what America might have become if the World's Fair era of invention and optimism from the 1930s persisted into the 21st century. Life is pleasant, until a distressful television broadcast. Your family is quickly rushed underground. It's within Vault 111 that you spend the next 200 years, frozen in cryogenic-stasis until your eventual rude awakening in the year 2277.
Exploration has its own rewards, as this is the most diverse Fallout world yet, with dilapidated urban areas, ominous dead forests, eerie swamps, a desolate area mired in a hellish radioactive haze, and even some areas that look borderline hospitable like beaches and budding farms. The Commonwealth’s much more color-saturated than Fallout 3’s Capital Wasteland, though it has its fair share of grays and browns, and it shares New Vegas’ bright blue sky (as opposed to oppressive clouds) when it’s not night time or raining or green with a terrifying radiation storm. It’s often beautiful. Attention to detail is evident everywhere – Fallout 4 might not be a leader in all areas of graphics technology (character animations are still a weakness) but from the intricate Pip-Boy wrist-computer interface (which completely changes when you’re in power armor), to careful arrangement of skeletal remains that tell the tragically dark or tragically funny stories of long-dead characters, to tattered poster art on the walls, to even raindrops on your visor (if you’re wearing one) it’s consistently impressive.

As for the changes since my last review, they got rid of the whole derpy boss battle to progress mechanic, and instead added in a quest hub (Don't store items in the quest hub, its bugged for some reason and deletes them) where you have missions and instances. They also redid the armor mechanics, progression, and sprites. Most of the new armor looks amazing, but I actually preferred a couple of the old human armor sets (specifically the old red one with the 3 fins and the gold visor) to the newer versions. Also the Novakid race is very cool, but their armor all looks kind of vaguely the same to me.
All in all, I recommend this game even more now that they've added so much content! I'd def. pick it up on sale or even for full price! Don't forget to install mods!

A fantastic game overall. It is a top-down dungeon crawler with an amazing art style and music, with fitting audio for each creature, explosion, and weapon. It should be noted that this game is not without its bugs, but they are fairly rare, and even more rarely intrusive.
Everything, including DLC can be obtained by grinding, which this game is fairly infamous for. In my personal opinion, it is easy as hell to maximize profit simply through experience, without doing the same mission over and over.
At its core, it is a simple hack 'n' slash with little extra detail - if you don't look for it.
Each monster has its own weaknesses and resistances to damage types and status conditions that make each monster unique. That, and each monster has its own unique attack pattern.
Some weapons are nearly useless compared to others, and some armours have no point to them. However, they all arguably have a niche somewhere.
Also, this game is free to play. So go play, make some friends, and earn yourself the prestigious title of 'Vanguard'. Once you've done that, get better, and better gear.
Recommended for all ages.

I was sceptical when I first saw this game. Steam had suggusted it (for reasons I dunno) and it just seemed like another mindless MineCraft clone. After a few friends mentioned they were playing I decided to try it out and I was actually suprised. For a F2P game Trove is actually quite fun and different. Its not the typical MineCraft experience I though it was going to be. The gameplay is simple but involved, you dont have 20 spells like most MMOs, only about 4 total which means its easy to play. The maps are quite big and theres a lot of stuff to unlock and craft.
I wouldnt recommend playing in long sessions as the game can feel a bit tedious when you are grinding up resources to craft certain items but at the same time unlocking things feels rewarding because you know that you put the effort into making something.
The added aspect of clubs also takes away from the grind a bit. If you can find a few people to play with you can work together to make some of the harder to craft items and set them up for all club members to use on your own ClubWorld map.
All in all, if you are looking for a F2P MMO-ish game that is simple yet different, give this a try.

You get 100 free energy per day, which you use to go down the elevator to fight monsters and such, or you use to it craft new weapons/armor/items. I love Dark Souls. Ever since i played the first one on the 360 at release i've been in love with the series. This has been the reason for my review:
Dark Souls 3 is a lovely game that lost itself to "balancing" and catering to the broken meta that has been developed by the mass that plays Dark Souls nowadays. The more the merrier, but when developers start to cater to the majority that's playing your game, you start to lose focus on your game itself. And that's what happened here, not as similar as it did with dark souls2(where they destroyed the concept of builds by implementing the idea of soul memory) wich they later fixed, admitting to some guilt of it being a mistake. Not really fixing it by needing to replace something for it to work.
There are few efforts to balance out the gameplay and when there are actual patches they barely balance the game at all.
It comes down to a few weapons that only the current meta uses. And There's no real indication that they look at most of their own content when looking at balancing. It seems the don't care as much about the beautiful weapons they've designed in the game and instead focus on feeding the meta some more as you can clearly see from below. Heavy weapons and heavy armor has been the meta ever since there was a meta.
And with their latest patch they've shown what type of game they want to have and it isn't Dark Souls anymore. The new DLC is beautiful though!

A unique dungeon crawl experience with exceptional atmosphere and brutal, roguelike mechanics to ensure that every encounter is dangerous and meaningful.  The stress mechanics alone are enough to make the game stand out from its predecessors, but the game goes a step further with interesting line combat mechanics and customization options which serve to distinguish the game from any others like it.  The game drips with atmosphere from the outstanding artwork to the enriching, if at times sesquipedalian, narration.
I feel the game stands out for its emphasis on resourcefulness.  Due to the randomness of recruitment, character trait assignment and dungeon generation, it's extraordinarily rare to put together an optimal party for all situations.  There are times where your primary healer will be nursing her paranoia in a tavern, or you'll design a team to defeat a boss only to have it ripped apart by an unfortunate monster spawn.  Each class has 8 active abilities and 6 camping abilities, of which you can only take 4 and 3 with you respectively.  As a result, you often find yourself assembling teams and kits which aren't great for any situation, but are good enough for every situation, and therein lies the beauty as you tend to scrape by tough encounters more often than dominate them, making those encounters memorable and engaging.
My critique in its current form are tied with the volume of information you must keep track of.  Each character in your group may possess as many as 10 traits, both positive and negative (and might have some diseases on top of that) which can have various impacts on their abilities.  These traits will also change over time after each successful dungeon run.  Add onto that having to manage equipment, skill and camping skill layouts for numerous party members and it can be a bit daunting to remember what role each character plays in your group and which dungeons they would best serve in.  Consequently, at least for me, most of this information ends up being ignored.
There is some commotion over the new mechanics introduced by Red Hook, but I personally feel the game has continuously improved over the course of its time since its beta release.  To cover some of the more recent changes, corpses present another opportunity cost question to your party (should I scrap a more general purpose ability for one that's not as useful, but clears corpses) while heart attacks further test your risk/reward assessment abilities.  Increased PROT for monsters adds value to blight/bleed effects, which themselves require planning around as enemies might be more resistant to one or the other.  I do not endorse early access games by in large, but I will endorse this game.  If you are looking for a dark, unforgiving game that tests your resourcefulness and willingness to take dangerous risks for the promise of substancial rewards, purchase this game immediately.  For $19.99, you are getting an exceptional bargain for the entertainment you'll get with this title.
As a bonus, the game's narrator will also likely improve your vocabulary.

It's fun-ish, but there's too many things in this game that make it feel like a chore.  Here's a few to mention by name:
- You get them constantly, and seemingly at random as even when you complete a dungeon flawlessly, your character can just randomly contract a disease at the rewards screen.  They're very expensive to cure, and you can only cure 1/week from a hero.
- The same thing as diseases... but I guess they felt diseases weren't a big enough pain in the♥♥♥♥♥by themselves, so negative quirks are in a seperate category.  Again, expensive to cure, and can only cure 1/week.
- During fights... you kill something, and it's corpse remains on the ground, meaning that in order for many characters to be able to hit a monster behind the corpse, you have to first kill the corpse.  Useless and adds nothing but frustration to the game.
- Yup, normally these are a blast to find in almost any game, but in this one... they decided to add negative effects to every item, that are typically so debilitating that it's almost better to just not equip them at all.
- This is the all-time biggest pain in this entire game.  I would seriously give this game 2 or 3 points of a higher score, maybe even recomend it if stress was removed altogether.  What's stress you may ask - So when your characters fight, they accrue stress from getting critted, walking through dungons, and also monsters will have abilities that just do nothing by raise stress.  You can make stress go down with a lucky crit or an ability - but the problem is, normal mobs will have AOE abilities that raise stress of the entire group by 10-15, that they spam constantly.  If you manage to get a lucky crit (at low levels, maybe 5% of time) you can make your stress go down by a whopping 4-5.  Woohoo.  So once they reace 100 stress level, they typically get a debuff that does the following: makes them badger your other group members raising their stress and will sometimes skip their turn or act on their own accord.  At 200 stress, your character simply dies permanently.  To make things worse, once you finish a dungeon, you then have pay out the♥♥♥♥♥to lower everyone's stress levels.  I think it's honestly one of the biggest nuisances as a mechanic I've ever come across.  Devs... remove this please, it's simply ridiculous.
- You spend lots of hard work leveling up a character, and then... as soon as they hit level 3, they refuse to run level 1 dungeons, which is actually at the point where they can complete level 1 dungeons without your characters getting massively stressed out, which would be a great way to get money for all the bullsh*t you have to spend money that I've outlined above.  Maybe this wouldn't be so much of an issue, but there's seemingly no level 2 dungeons (not that I saw in all the time I played).  Only levels  1 and 3.  I tried a level 3 dungeon, with all level 3 characters, and you're fighting groups that can wipe your entire group in 1 encounter.

Fallout 4 is a well-made game, but it isn't a good Fallout game, nor is it a good Bethesda RPG.
RPG Mechanics:
Fallout 4 is the most simplified, streamlined, and casualized Bethesda RPG to date. You are forced to play a pre-determined  character with a general personality that is decided for you. You're either a war veteran or a law student, you're married with a middle-class life, and you have a baby that you care for and will traverse the wasteland to find. This is a huge departure from previous Fallout games where some minor aspects are decided for you, but by and large your character is your own. In Fallout 3, you grew up in Vault 101, your mother died in childbirth, and you have a father that escaped the vault. These details don't change the personality of your character, and you can build your character around these events. Fallout: New Vegas has even less predetermined backstory: You decided to take a courier job, and you delivered a package to the Divide, and you got shot in the head. Nothing about this determines your personality.
The lack of meaningful choices is a huge disappointment. None of your choices make any difference in the long run, except for maybe one choice regarding Diamond City. The faction that you join has no affect on the world at large except for some people from your faction appearing in areas (I sided with the Brotherhood and Brotherhood soldiers appeared in Diamond City). This is Fallout 4's biggest problem, in my opnion.
In addition, the perk chart is an even simpler version of Skyrim's perk trees. At least Skyrim's system had some interesting perks that gave you new abilities that influenced your playstyle. In Fallout 4, most of the perks are just basic damage upgrades or unlocking new tiers of weapon upgrades.
The World and Exploration:
This is arguably the most important part of a Bethesda RPG. Even if you hate the main quest, you can still explore the world and find cool locations and interesting sights. In Fallout 4, the interesting places are replaced with settlement locations. Empty, barren settlement locations with maybe a few bugs or ghouls to clear out before you can place your settlement down. This really kills my desire to explore the world because I know that every potentially interesting location has been hollowed out and made a canvas for "player freedom". Locations and structures hand-crafted by developers will always be better than whatever a player makes with the limited in-game systems.
A big part of exploring is to find cool loot and rare items. Fallout 4 subverts this by having annoying "legendary" enemies that replenish their health, making them huge damage sponges, and dropping a randomly generated "legendary" item. This is extremely boring. Gone are the days of finding a special item that has a feature or effect that no other similar item has. That is what made exploring worth it for some people and gave players an actual material gain from exploring, not just the experience of exploring, which can be rewarding in its own right.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is what Bethesda seems to have prioritized following citicisms of Fallout 3's average shooting mechanics. They work as well as any other first person shooter, with the usual Bethesda clunkiness of course. The combat is arguably the best part of the game. Everything feels nice to shoot and enemies are more reactive than ever. They'll even spam molotovs at you and take cover. My only gripe with the combat is the weapons sound a little weak.
Graphics:
Despite the fact that some people seem to hate Fallout 4's engine with a furious burning passion, I don't think it's all too bad. The fact that game speed is tied to framerate is a major problem, but everything else seems to be fine. The game looks nice, even on my outdated computer. I dont have any other complaints aside from the framerate thing.
Mods:
I haven't done any modding on Fallout 4 (in fact, I haven't even launched the game since I quit initially), but I've seen a bunch of mods for the game and they look promising. However, I don't think mods are going to be able to fix Fallout 4's fundamental problems. They can certainly enhance the experience, but not fix it.
Minor Gripes/ Nitpicks:
-I don't like the weapon design. The pipe weapons make no sense and look awful. The assault rifle looks like a Maxim machine gun and look really dumb. The left handed bolt on the hunting rifle annoys me. Automatic weapons are useless, just use semi-automatic if you want to do damage. The gatling laser is the best weapon in the game.
-Power Armor breaks comically fast. For something that was supposed to win America the war, it falls to pieces after the slightest bit of damage.
-Minor lore disrespects: Jet being mentioned in a pre-war vault terminal. The T-60 power armor retcon. More power armor retcons.
-Settlement system is boring. My only options to build are structures made from actual garbage. Scrapping large objects instantly feels very weird.
That's it. That's all I have to say.

I'm going to be completely honest. I'm having ton of fun playing this game. It takes time to get your heroes to a level where they can be useful in higher level dungeons and your town into good condition, but if you aren't adverse to spending some time building a strong team and tackling tough challenges, this game might be for you.
A lot of people are downvoting the game due to the addition of corpses as it "slows down gameplay" but that would mean that the game was even faster than it already is combat wise. Battles already take very little time to complete (unless a boss battle or some of the bigger monsters and that's not due to corpses).
Corpses require you to have a well-rounded team instead of the formula 2 supports in back and 2 heavy hitters upfront. Now you might want to invest in some ranged damage as well. That's a good thing. It means that your team has to be a bit diverse and might have to be tailored for the dungeon you are planning on descending into if it's a higher level dungeon.
And that's a good thing; more challenge and more variety are what set this game apart from other games. The creators may have added a way to turn off corpses and heart attacks, but I can't see myself playing this game any other way.
Not to say there aren't imbalances (Spoiler: Jester's Finale sucks major dong), but I'm looking forward to devs tackling those. They might not consider actual balance concerns however if people don't stop whining about balances that fix imbalances. It astounds me how the playerbase can so thoroughly miss the point of additions.
Corpses encourage extra ranged damage or specific corpse clearing support and discourage focusing all damage on frontline melee attackers. PROT encourages the use of DoT and discourages focusing on pure damage.
It's not "breaking the game" it's just requiring you to adapt and have a more thoughtful playstyle, but I guess a lot of people don't want a strategy challenge but a pandering cakewalk.
As the hip young ones say, "Haters gonna hate."
If you like this game (and are reading this review obviously), please leave a positive review to balance out all the hatred for the game becoming more well-rounded. Hoping the game doesn't get killed by spoiled brats who want things to remain exactly the way they had it before.

It's early access, but more fleshed out than most games, my experience was as follows:
0-10 hours, figuring out the mechanics and system: frustrating but really fun. I'll assume the finished product will have a better tutorial.
10-30 hours, leveling up my characters, exploring the different classes, having a lot of fun
30-50 hours, built my 'A-Team' maxing out a few character classes, figured out my playstyle
50-100 hours, just slogging through the rest of the boss fights and tasks.  Still okay, but became tedious at this point.  End game content is not there, and there's a giant amount of grinding that just becomes a chore.
Verdict:  I expect the endgame content to be added much later, but for ~15 bucks, I played this game for almost a 100 hours and had a fun during a large majority of it.
EDIT: thinking about it some more...I will say the battles take too long and the game is a massive timesink just to do a few dungeons, which do not change much and gets very tiresome fast.
I was expecting the negative traits to be something that adds to the experience to create unique characters, but they just become more stats on a page.
A large majority of the classes, houndmaster, grave robber, plaguebearer and just not useful.  I got through the entire game with this party combo that destroyed everything:  Hellion, Bounty Hunter, Occutist, Arbolist.
The difficulty is backwards - levels 1-2 will have you screaming at the screen, and a few wrong battles can leave you ready for a restart, while levels 3-5 (except boss battles) don't require much and are just tedious obstacles to get through a dungeon so you can have your other character recover from stress.
I still would recommed it because I had fun with it, but I will warn anyone to while they are getting addicted to it, that there will be a point ~30-50 hours that you'll start getting bored.  Just turn it off at that point, it won't change and will just get worse.

I loved Dark Souls. Even as I got spit-roasted by undead spearmen and pin-cushioned by undead archers. But the Dark Souls train has left the station for there is only so long you can invest in a game and after 4 years of time invested you have to take stock and things start to get a bit old hat way before that point. So I needed a new Gothic Fantasy RPG and I'd never really given the elusive 'Dungeon Crawler' genre a go (bear this in mind for later). So I perused the Steam Store, searching for an antidote to my lack-of-Gothic-RPG-itus and boy did Darkest Dungeon deliver!
Right off the bat Darkest Dungeon hits a home run regarding its unique aesthetic value, being a game with minimalistic animation surrounded by a dark and gritty colour palette. Definately one of the more unique looking games on the Early Access shelf, Darkest Dungeon is able to balance cartoonish and exaggerated imagery complimented well by many engrossing and immersive gameplay features which are split into two core sections both with their good aspects and bad aspects. Darkest Dungeon places you in the familiar 'invisible general on the sideline' seat where you direct, manage and provision parties of four to raid dungeons, find loot and of course slay the baddies. The loot that you gain in these raids assist with the refurbishment of your estate, which acts as your party's respite as another party is sent into another dungeon. It's a simple formula to understand and is easy to pick up however the problem lies within this formula. It's always cool to complete a dungeon sure but by the later dungeons you get into the grooves like alcohol induced vomit on a stone pavement, the stench of repetiton sets in.
The Estate mechanics seem to be completely useless other than to keep party members sane with no real worthwhile items to purchase  when you could just as easily loot something equally as good if not better. The sanity and disease system, for what it's worth, is a great addition to the status quo of RPGs. It helps to create those water cooler moments where you tell Bob IV about Bonnel the Hopeless Plauge Doctor and how an attack from a vicious maggot gave him syphilis and the runs. This again though, leads to some annoying moments where Bonnel The Plauge Doctor goes insane thanks to Toby The Hound Master criticising poor Bonnel's critical strikes. But, call me a nutter and paint me pink, I think this is where the game truley shines. I referenced Dark Souls earlier for a reason, reader, and I'm about to do so again. I like the brutality and high difficulty curve of the game. It's definately something that will ruffle some feathers as the fat bandits with rusty shivs manage to score four consecutive critical strikes on your healer but somewhere deep down in the shriveled hearts of all gamers is the desire for challenge.
Combat is turnbased therefore I have a few issues, in fact let's just skip a bunch of unnecessary padding and say that ALL of my problems with this game comes from the combat system. For starters the game doesn't make much of an effort to explain what each skill does and what some creatures are immune to. For example, in my fourth dungeon I ran accross some madatory undead blokes who seemed to be making a great time of being both dead and in a dungeon and to iniciate my first strike I tried an attack that does bleeding damage (small amounts of damage before enemies take their turn) but my target seemed to resist with a struggle. It was only a few dungeons later when a loading screen popped up 'reminding' me that undead creatures were immune to bleeding damage. Ah well, that was good to know game, kind of a rookie error on my part I mean- skelletons don't seem to be prone to bleeding in real life either but neither do they seem to contract many illnesses in real life which made me scratch my head at the fact that poison seems to be quite effective against them.
Combat also suffers from the typical turn based combat gripes and also some bizzare atypical ones as well. One of my least favourite is the lack of knowledge of who's going next. Maybe you can help me here, reader, but it either seems to be clogged up in menus like everything else in the game or completely missing which is fine if that was a design choice but I'd like to know if my stun attack is needed to buy me another attack and I'd also like to know who's going to attack after Sir Kill-Machine because if it's Derpy Dave who only does like four damage per hit then I'll execute my biggest attack now. Combat seems to be a bit off regarding strategy like a lot of turn based combat systems these days. Pokemon is a prime example and something that can be easily compared to this game's combat. The only real strategy seems to be to use the attack with the biggest number in response to the enemy's attack with a big number it's all kind of one big sarcastic circle to be honest, much like this review.
However, if you're reading this developer, know that I only say what I say (or write what I write, whatever) because I care- and that a helluva lot more than I can say about most games these days. Core concepts are good touching on great however I just wish that this game gets the support and attention it needs to reach that level of greatness. Games like this are the reason why Early Access exists. If I have to leave words of advice I would leave these: 'remove the bloody corpses!'- Honestly, if I have to kill a monster twice then what's the point in killing it the first time?!
7/10- A promising project that I can reccomend to casual fans of RPGs and Dungeon Crawlers. Reccomended for gamers with that little streak of stalwart defiance in the face of a brutal, dark and insane challenge.

Fallout 4 is a well-made game, but it isn't a good Fallout game, nor is it a good Bethesda RPG.
RPG Mechanics:
Fallout 4 is the most simplified, streamlined, and casualized Bethesda RPG to date. You are forced to play a pre-determined  character with a general personality that is decided for you. You're either a war veteran or a law student, you're married with a middle-class life, and you have a baby that you care for and will traverse the wasteland to find. This is a huge departure from previous Fallout games where some minor aspects are decided for you, but by and large your character is your own. In Fallout 3, you grew up in Vault 101, your mother died in childbirth, and you have a father that escaped the vault. These details don't change the personality of your character, and you can build your character around these events. Fallout: New Vegas has even less predetermined backstory: You decided to take a courier job, and you delivered a package to the Divide, and you got shot in the head. Nothing about this determines your personality.
The lack of meaningful choices is a huge disappointment. None of your choices make any difference in the long run, except for maybe one choice regarding Diamond City. The faction that you join has no affect on the world at large except for some people from your faction appearing in areas (I sided with the Brotherhood and Brotherhood soldiers appeared in Diamond City). This is Fallout 4's biggest problem, in my opnion.
In addition, the perk chart is an even simpler version of Skyrim's perk trees. At least Skyrim's system had some interesting perks that gave you new abilities that influenced your playstyle. In Fallout 4, most of the perks are just basic damage upgrades or unlocking new tiers of weapon upgrades.
The World and Exploration:
This is arguably the most important part of a Bethesda RPG. Even if you hate the main quest, you can still explore the world and find cool locations and interesting sights. In Fallout 4, the interesting places are replaced with settlement locations. Empty, barren settlement locations with maybe a few bugs or ghouls to clear out before you can place your settlement down. This really kills my desire to explore the world because I know that every potentially interesting location has been hollowed out and made a canvas for "player freedom". Locations and structures hand-crafted by developers will always be better than whatever a player makes with the limited in-game systems.
A big part of exploring is to find cool loot and rare items. Fallout 4 subverts this by having annoying "legendary" enemies that replenish their health, making them huge damage sponges, and dropping a randomly generated "legendary" item. This is extremely boring. Gone are the days of finding a special item that has a feature or effect that no other similar item has. That is what made exploring worth it for some people and gave players an actual material gain from exploring, not just the experience of exploring, which can be rewarding in its own right.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is what Bethesda seems to have prioritized following citicisms of Fallout 3's average shooting mechanics. They work as well as any other first person shooter, with the usual Bethesda clunkiness of course. The combat is arguably the best part of the game. Everything feels nice to shoot and enemies are more reactive than ever. They'll even spam molotovs at you and take cover. My only gripe with the combat is the weapons sound a little weak.
Graphics:
Despite the fact that some people seem to hate Fallout 4's engine with a furious burning passion, I don't think it's all too bad. The fact that game speed is tied to framerate is a major problem, but everything else seems to be fine. The game looks nice, even on my outdated computer. I dont have any other complaints aside from the framerate thing.
Mods:
I haven't done any modding on Fallout 4 (in fact, I haven't even launched the game since I quit initially), but I've seen a bunch of mods for the game and they look promising. However, I don't think mods are going to be able to fix Fallout 4's fundamental problems. They can certainly enhance the experience, but not fix it.
Minor Gripes/ Nitpicks:
-I don't like the weapon design. The pipe weapons make no sense and look awful. The assault rifle looks like a Maxim machine gun and look really dumb. The left handed bolt on the hunting rifle annoys me. Automatic weapons are useless, just use semi-automatic if you want to do damage. The gatling laser is the best weapon in the game.
-Power Armor breaks comically fast. For something that was supposed to win America the war, it falls to pieces after the slightest bit of damage.
-Minor lore disrespects: Jet being mentioned in a pre-war vault terminal. The T-60 power armor retcon. More power armor retcons.
-Settlement system is boring. My only options to build are structures made from actual garbage. Scrapping large objects instantly feels very weird.
That's it. That's all I have to say.

Really great game. Grafics, sounds, visuals and most other things really proof how hard they are working on DD.
If english isnt your native language its a little challenging here and there to understand everything since some advanced stuff is spoken by the characters or told by the narrator, but bascially you wont miss THAT much.
Getting into everything takes an hour or two, for example how the skills work (active skills, passive skills, changing skills, increasing skill levels...) or how to keep your group up (eating food to regenerate is quite useless if you dont find tons of it while walking through the dungeon). The lighting system took me three or four missions to understand too. Same for the madnesses and deceasses.
Killed monsters (as long as not killed by "Damage Over Time" effects) leave corpse piles, which strongly affect your ability to attack enemys since your melee adventurers usually cant hit beyond the second row. There exist skills to get rid of all corpses at once, pull enemys towards you or change enemy row order to meet your whises more, but that requires the related heroes with these abilitys. But those who dont want to deal with corpses can deactivate this mechanic in the options menu since a recent patch.
The missions are pretty challenging at the beginning, but thats the smallest problem. You need to aquire enough profit on each run to fix your payments for food, light, mental & decease treatment and to remove negativ traits. If bought also for tools like bandages, antidotes, tools or others. Usually a successful mission rewards some gold additional to your claimed loot. Adding up, every run where you gained a total of less than 4000 gold is a failure and usually creates more costs then you got out of it. It may feels like a deathtimer to your savegame, but since you can recruit unlimit heroes you can sacrafice them if necessary.
About dead heroes there are also some things. Sooner or later there will be deaths. Loosing a heroe with increased gear and  skills will be an absolute horror, so retreating in the right moment is the best choise. But with heroes in your group suffering from madness this will become more harder, so take care.
All in all a great game and yet I didnt played pretty far. I am really looking forward to upcoming patches!

This is a game full of what I like to think of as "artificial difficulty," where the devs couldn't actually make something challenging, so they made something that passes for it by lacking internal consistency.
All the abilities of your party members only work while in a limit number of positions in the marching order, then only target a few specific positions in the enemy marching order. Many classes, enemy and ally, have the ability to try and force their opponents to change position. This can be devastating for you, but the enemies seem to use the same abilities regardless of position. There's no internal consistency to that. It isn't challenging, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Heart attacks were another problem, wherein the stress of a party member could climb so high that your characters simply die, while things that can lower stress are few and far between. There are one or two good abilities for this, but abilities can't be used outside of combat. Not even non combat abilities, like healing—so, if you end combat on death's door (a literal status wherein the party member is out of HP and could be killed by his or her next blow), then you'd better hope your healers get to go first. Except, of course, they aren't known for their speed, so expect to just lose that character. The heart attack problem was so obviously bad that the community turned against the devs pretty hard, so it can be disabled, but the truth is it never should have been added to begin with. It's artificial difficulty, not challenging, and it makes for an overall bad game experience.
Don't buy this. If you absolutely have to have it, wait a year after its official release, get it for the inevitable 90% off that all halfhearted attempts at a greenlight game eventually get.

What a satisfying change of pace.
Darkest Dungeon takes the standard dungeon crawler concept and puts a sobering, Lovecraftian twist on things.  There are serious dangers and mental stresses that come from adventuring that no other game I've played brings to light.
The game opens with a warning that much will be demanded of you.  That quests can be failed or need to be abandoned. Heroes will be diseased, mentally scarred, and killed.  In the midst of this, you need to know how to make the best out of a bad situation.
I didn't take the warning as seriously as I thought.  It wasn't long before I experienced my first total party wipeout.  My four adventurers didn't die to grave wounds or enemy steel, but by heart attacks.  All four were killed by thier own hearts.  Later, one of my favorite heroes was struck by a string of diseases, misfortune, and critical hits.  In a bout of frustration, I shut the game off in an attempt to save him.  After restarting, I was back in the exact same spot as I left, with my hero teetering on the edge of life.  There was no easy escape from this, I had to make the best of the situation for him to survive.  I did, he lived, and it was immensely satisfying.
While there are a few issues I have with the game, like the inability to heal between fights, I understand they're there to make a statement: nothing is certain, victory won't be easy, and sacrifices will have to be made.  No save points or massive stockpiles of potions will save you here.
In closing, I highly recommend this game to anyone not afraid of a challenge, who is tired of feeling like the almighty hero who stands head and shoulders above the foes he fights.  This is a game that is immensely rewarding not because you saved the world, but because you merely survived.
