Unlike many, I did not buy this game at the beginning. A friend of mine did. He ranted and raved to me about how awesome it was and how much I would like it, since I liked dungeon crawlers, rogue-likes, and Lovecraftian horror. Still, I did not check it out and buy it for some time. In fact, I only started playing it when he bought it for me for my birthday just this past year.
When I started playing, I instantly regretted not just breaking down, spending the money, and getting the game for myself way earlier. It was a fantastic concept. Amazing art, stellar writing and voice acting, interesting and unique mechanics and classes. I don't get much time to game, but I have played it as much as I could since. I loved each update as it came it, slowly shaping the game into it's final form, which it, of course has yet to reach.
Unlike a lot of players, I actually love the addition of heart attacks and corpses. Corpses keep many classes' skills relevant and with the addition of corpse clearing skills (also pulling enemies across corpses also clears them), they aren't the huge unwieldy road blocks other reviewers make them out to be. They also make sense to me, I actually wondered why a game with such a huge emphasis on position did not have corpses. Before heart attacks, stress wasn't that big a deal. You could easily get to the end of a dungeon and complete it with all of your heroes insane, completely ignoring the stress mechanic and only getting a few annoyances in exchange. Heart Attacks make stress a mechanic you cannot ignore and that's great since stress is one of the awesome unique mechanics that I fell in love with. I also appreciate the difficulty heart attacks add.
Of course, if people still have issues with these mechanics, the problem is no longer there, because they can both be toggled off. That is a nice this Red Hook did, but I'm not sure if it was the right decision to make. They could have just made difficulty levels, adding toggleable difficulty features is basically the same thing. Either way, it is a good method of pleasing all the hard core players and the casual players at the same time. I must give Red Hook credit there. They really care about their community, which is why I feel so badly about all the flak they are suddenly getting.
Anyway, I love this game and recommend it to everyone I can. Buy it and love it like I do!

As other reviews have said, this game is Terraria in space. The functionality is practically identical (foreground and background walls, inventory system where you collect everything you find, etc). The TL:DR version of this review is that the game is solid and fun to play. The combat can get a bit samey, but if you like games where you have a sandbox exploration and crafting function then this game is for you.
The soundtrack is quite relaxing, and there is separate music for when you are in combat. Usually I watch TV when I'm playing a game like this, but when I do listen to the music it is still good to hear.
Combat
The combat is quite basic, again like terraria. you swing weapons in an arc in front of you, or else straight forward, depending on weapon type. If you watch the video above you can see how the swinging works. There are differences from Terraria though. Instead of having descriptions like 'fast swing/slow swing' you are told a DPS, swings per second and base damage figure. So for example you may have a fast weapon that does 20 DPS due to having 2.00 swings per second and 10 damage on hit. One thing to consider is the knockback that your attacks create - unless you back an enemy up to a wall, you're unlikely to USE both of those swings to hurt it. However, knowing that fact allows you to consider using slower, more powerful weapons. There is also a 1h/2h system in place, so you can not only choose to dual wield, but also have one weapon out whilst holding food/bandages which makes for greater survivability. Finally, the actionbar is set out from 1-0 so you can have 10 items hotkeyed for use. There is also a left/right hand section. This allows you to place a weapon in your hands and freely swap between your actionbar 1-0 and your hands by pressing (default) the 'x' key. This means you can be mining, suddenly get attacked and press x to get your weapon out. Press x again, or any other number, and you can swap to your actionbar once more.
Enemy combat is an area that is a little hit-and-miss for me. Generally when you are underground you will find walking enemies, and outside you will find a lot of flying enemies. All enemies are spawned with default attacks, and when colonising a planet it will help you to work out by sight which enemies use what attacks. Unfortunately, most land enemies just use a basic charge or body slam, which means combat is invariably an enemy running straight at you and jumping around. Flying enemies offer a greater range of attacks - flamethrowing, dropping rocks, ice clouds, and the most powerful - ACTUALLY STAYING OUT OF YOUR MELEE RANGE. In order to melee a flying enemy, you usually have to go further underground to make them chase you, then quickly climb back up before they get the chance to fly away. Failing this, there is a bow weapon easily craftable - but I often don't want to use it because of the loot generated.
Loot
In Terraria (apologies if you haven't played it and don't understand the comparisons) enemies were created with a large loot table - mostly coins, but random items like torches and bombs could be dropped.
In Starbound, enemies are limited to very basic drops apart from some rare chances. The currency in Starbound is 'pixels' - and these are required for most of the important crafting recipes. An enemy will either drop pixels, meat or 'holiday spirit' (which I am hoping is removed very soon because it is too common to drop and prevents access to actual useful drops). In order to obtain pixels you either need to kill enemies, build a machine to convert ore to pixels, or find them in a variety of underground smashable machines and boxes. Whilst this system does allow for balancing - you will generally find yourself hitting a wall for an hour or so, then rushing to the next stage when you've spent a lot of time mining - it can sometimes feel that there is a burden on players to use melee weapons. The reason for this is that the craftable bow will only cause an enemy to drop meat or leather - NOT PIXELS.
Whilst the intention behind this is to allow players to farm meat for the hunger system to prevent starvation, it imposes a harsh learning curve for melee combat. As I have said, melee combat against flying enemies can be difficult without tricking them into coming lower then jumping at them, and with ground enemies you have to contend with them bouncing around the room. This can be difficult if your computer lags (particularly when playing multiplayer games) and can result in a quick and painful death. I have been told that you can acquire guns later in the game which will allow you to kill enemies at range and collect pixels, but I haven't seen any in the early stages of the game, and it is likely that by the time you have found a gun you will already have a refinery to convert your ore, so pixel farming won't be an issue.
In terms of loot items, these are usually found in chests in an existing cave or a random settlement. These can be a huge bonus or a waste of time, depending on how far you have progressed with your own gear before you find them. The best feature of these items is the random stats that can occur on them - for example a weapon with a lightning bolt icon in its description will fire a projectile forward - and this can be extremely useful in a pinch.
Progression
One of my favourite features of Starbound is that there is a genuine sense of progressing from one stage to another because your crafting is deliberately limited. Your basic crafting tools start with one set of built-in recipes, and then in order to create better items you will need to upgrade the crafting table with a component item that is only dropped by a certain boss. In addition, upgrading items like tier armour or pickaxes will require you to sacrifice your existing item (for example, a copper pickaxe requires pixels, copper bars and a stone pickaxe to create). This may sounds like a restriction when you first come to it, but it does allow for the game to be balanced. Although it is technically possible to come to a new game and go mining until you can afford to upgrade everything in one go, the time this would take (especially with just a stone pickaxe) means that it actually makes more sense to steadily improve your equipment over time.
<><><>POTENTIAL SPOILER<><><>
The game's bosses are created by you - the initial quests lead you up to creating a distress beacon which spawns the first boss. This boss drops the component part that upgrades your anvil and therefore unlocks the next stage of your equipment. Because this is the only source of the component, you will need to spawn the boss multiple times if you want to colonise other planets, unless you bring your original crafting table with you.
<><><>POTENTIAL SPOILER<><><>
Exploration
The first thing you see with exploration on this game is that it NEVER ENDS! There are thousands of planets over several sectors of space, and each of them will be unique in some way. Most aspects of the planet will be the same - you still collect dirt and ores and build on them - but there is always a variety of different plants and creatures, random settlements of NPCs and even varying levels of gravity. The only real way to get a feel for how big this aspect of the game is would be to go exploring yourself. However I would strongly advise setting your starter planet as a home planet since you can then use your ship's teleport to return there from anywhere in the universe.

So I’ve been a big fan of this game right from the get go. Great meta, great choice its all their. Yet, I feel once they added these new changes it completely broke the game.
Hears why.
You could maybe add a corpus to larger enemies but smaller ones like maggots, not only does this not make sense. It completely breaks the game play and thematic suspension of disbelief. How can one miss 3 times on a corpus...  of a maggot? Seriously!!!!!!, In the middle of a heated sword fight!!!? The Answer? You shouldn’t. Thus a BROKEN GAME. The game is now broken in terms of battle pacing, you now have to slow down your attack style and account for dead bodies. Where as before you could time your kills and move on, it was streamlined, it was paced. Granted, I understand ‘bring a guy that can clear dead bodies’. To counter. That removes player choice from the composition. Where as before I could pick and choose the load out of classes and felt I was not hurting in any particular area. Now I have to bring a body clearer NO MATTER WHAT or its slog city.

One of the first things I tried to do was blast the dog you meet in the face.  It soaked the bullets up and didn't even react.
A small thing, but emblematic of the problem with Fallout 4.  It strips away the freedom the previous games allowed.  It doesn't want you to play your way, Bethesda has a neat little script that you have to follow.  This problem translates to many quests too; the majority of them are extremely linear in how you can complete them.  Yeah there's still some choice, but it's a far cry from the open ended nature of the other games.
Dialogue choices have the same problem.  Your choices are; sarcastic jerk, or persuasive sarcastic jerk.  Bethesda has forgotten about the "RP" in RPG.
The pacing is off.  Power armor in the first hour and a minigun, and the game seems largely balanced under the assumption that you'll use them.  And why wouldn't you?  I found 3 fusion cores just while exploring on my way to Diamond City.
The graphics are nice and it runs smoothly.  The combat is refined, the crafting is robust, but none of that matters.  Who honestly picked up Fallout for its combat?  Even at its best, it's ultimately a mediocre shooter compared to titles that focus on that.  That was never the point of the game.  It's a welcome change, but it's one step forwards for three steps back.
Game is as large as a lake but shallow as a puddle.  Bethesda has lost sight of why this franchise was great.  We all know why, of course; they're streamlining their games, appealing to a broader audience and marketing to a console playerbase that has a shorter attention span.  It's a damn shame, really.

This is a game full of what I like to think of as "artificial difficulty," where the devs couldn't actually make something challenging, so they made something that passes for it by lacking internal consistency.
All the abilities of your party members only work while in a limit number of positions in the marching order, then only target a few specific positions in the enemy marching order. Many classes, enemy and ally, have the ability to try and force their opponents to change position. This can be devastating for you, but the enemies seem to use the same abilities regardless of position. There's no internal consistency to that. It isn't challenging, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Heart attacks were another problem, wherein the stress of a party member could climb so high that your characters simply die, while things that can lower stress are few and far between. There are one or two good abilities for this, but abilities can't be used outside of combat. Not even non combat abilities, like healing—so, if you end combat on death's door (a literal status wherein the party member is out of HP and could be killed by his or her next blow), then you'd better hope your healers get to go first. Except, of course, they aren't known for their speed, so expect to just lose that character. The heart attack problem was so obviously bad that the community turned against the devs pretty hard, so it can be disabled, but the truth is it never should have been added to begin with. It's artificial difficulty, not challenging, and it makes for an overall bad game experience.
Don't buy this. If you absolutely have to have it, wait a year after its official release, get it for the inevitable 90% off that all halfhearted attempts at a greenlight game eventually get.

What a satisfying change of pace.
Darkest Dungeon takes the standard dungeon crawler concept and puts a sobering, Lovecraftian twist on things.  There are serious dangers and mental stresses that come from adventuring that no other game I've played brings to light.
The game opens with a warning that much will be demanded of you.  That quests can be failed or need to be abandoned. Heroes will be diseased, mentally scarred, and killed.  In the midst of this, you need to know how to make the best out of a bad situation.
I didn't take the warning as seriously as I thought.  It wasn't long before I experienced my first total party wipeout.  My four adventurers didn't die to grave wounds or enemy steel, but by heart attacks.  All four were killed by thier own hearts.  Later, one of my favorite heroes was struck by a string of diseases, misfortune, and critical hits.  In a bout of frustration, I shut the game off in an attempt to save him.  After restarting, I was back in the exact same spot as I left, with my hero teetering on the edge of life.  There was no easy escape from this, I had to make the best of the situation for him to survive.  I did, he lived, and it was immensely satisfying.
While there are a few issues I have with the game, like the inability to heal between fights, I understand they're there to make a statement: nothing is certain, victory won't be easy, and sacrifices will have to be made.  No save points or massive stockpiles of potions will save you here.
In closing, I highly recommend this game to anyone not afraid of a challenge, who is tired of feeling like the almighty hero who stands head and shoulders above the foes he fights.  This is a game that is immensely rewarding not because you saved the world, but because you merely survived.

Unlike many, I did not buy this game at the beginning. A friend of mine did. He ranted and raved to me about how awesome it was and how much I would like it, since I liked dungeon crawlers, rogue-likes, and Lovecraftian horror. Still, I did not check it out and buy it for some time. In fact, I only started playing it when he bought it for me for my birthday just this past year.
When I started playing, I instantly regretted not just breaking down, spending the money, and getting the game for myself way earlier. It was a fantastic concept. Amazing art, stellar writing and voice acting, interesting and unique mechanics and classes. I don't get much time to game, but I have played it as much as I could since. I loved each update as it came it, slowly shaping the game into it's final form, which it, of course has yet to reach.
Unlike a lot of players, I actually love the addition of heart attacks and corpses. Corpses keep many classes' skills relevant and with the addition of corpse clearing skills (also pulling enemies across corpses also clears them), they aren't the huge unwieldy road blocks other reviewers make them out to be. They also make sense to me, I actually wondered why a game with such a huge emphasis on position did not have corpses. Before heart attacks, stress wasn't that big a deal. You could easily get to the end of a dungeon and complete it with all of your heroes insane, completely ignoring the stress mechanic and only getting a few annoyances in exchange. Heart Attacks make stress a mechanic you cannot ignore and that's great since stress is one of the awesome unique mechanics that I fell in love with. I also appreciate the difficulty heart attacks add.
Of course, if people still have issues with these mechanics, the problem is no longer there, because they can both be toggled off. That is a nice this Red Hook did, but I'm not sure if it was the right decision to make. They could have just made difficulty levels, adding toggleable difficulty features is basically the same thing. Either way, it is a good method of pleasing all the hard core players and the casual players at the same time. I must give Red Hook credit there. They really care about their community, which is why I feel so badly about all the flak they are suddenly getting.
Anyway, I love this game and recommend it to everyone I can. Buy it and love it like I do!

It is borderline grind-to-win, but I won't call it that since the dungeons are fast and kinda fun and it doesn't take 2 weeks of hard grinding to get a simple item. (COUGH COUGH DIRTY BOMB COUGH COUGH.) However, buying new classes does pretty much require paying.
The gameplay is simple and fun, but there is a lot to be improved upon. Throughout the levels, (novice, adept, elite, master, and all the ubers,) the enemies get harder but the worlds do not change, and I think the should. I played this on the free weekend. It's definitely not worth even the 20 bucks for me. Any feel of an actual Role-Playing Game, like the first two Fallouts or Fallout: New Vegas, is completely gone. Most of the time, you will be doing annoying repetitive quests for people you don't care about in a world that is intricately placed together, one quirky skeleton at a time, but ultimately shallow and lifeless.
Story telling and pacing is awful. This game is not more than a shooter with a clumsy inventory and a quick "Fallout" veneer slapped over the generic Bethesda product, to kinda hide the fact that it's basically Skyrim. It also has scavenging and general Minecraft-style mechanics, to get the kids going. You get everything in the beginning - the home base, the dog, the robot, the Power Armor, the source of infinite ("radiant") quests for XP... all you have to do is get out there and find more junk to scrap. I don't know how long I can really be with this. Many people have hashed over this game multiple times, listing out pros, cons, all that good stuff. There's been a fair amount of complaint about recent issues regarding Corpses (which, for those who haven't played, are literally just corpses. Piles of meaty bits that occupy an enemy's spot after you've killed them, which either means your ranged characters deal with the enemies behind them, or you quick 'kill' the corpses a second time) and Heart Attacks (basically if a character goes crazy enough, they'll have a Heart Attack and die on the spot. This game is brutal. This is not surprising.)
Given Red Hook's solution to these issues (giving you the option to turn those features on or off, one or both), I see no reason not to recommend. Are there balance issues? Probably. But most games require tweaking and we're still in Early Access here, not to mention that if you're getting stomped, the game's delivering what it promised on. Good devs, crafting a good game, listening to players and finding good solutions to problems. What more do you want here?

So I’ve been a big fan of this game right from the get go. Great meta, great choice its all their. Yet, I feel once they added these new changes it completely broke the game.
Hears why.
You could maybe add a corpus to larger enemies but smaller ones like maggots, not only does this not make sense. It completely breaks the game play and thematic suspension of disbelief. How can one miss 3 times on a corpus...  of a maggot? Seriously!!!!!!, In the middle of a heated sword fight!!!? The Answer? You shouldn’t. Thus a BROKEN GAME. The game is now broken in terms of battle pacing, you now have to slow down your attack style and account for dead bodies. Where as before you could time your kills and move on, it was streamlined, it was paced. Granted, I understand ‘bring a guy that can clear dead bodies’. To counter. That removes player choice from the composition. Where as before I could pick and choose the load out of classes and felt I was not hurting in any particular area. Now I have to bring a body clearer NO MATTER WHAT or its slog city.
So game play wise you have taken choice away and created less player meta. Ok, I guess that’s their artistic choice. Yet I don’t see how that ‘adds’ anything. You had a system that was fine. Granted the status procs needed a buff and a little armor protection on some super baddies was needed. Yet I don’t see how corpus’s adds a strategic element to the range of tactics. Your limited in scope and time already, so I don’t know where the devs thought it was a superior idea to force a priority on range or back targets when the mechanism to allow one to attack them is not fully in place. You only have so many men with abilities that can reach or do enough damage to them!! Duh!!! Game design 101.
So, in short I think these changes are short sighted and improperly implemented. This is compounded by a stubborn and talented developer, who recently has shown it will sacrifice its meta and depth for pure difficulty and the pursuit of longevity. I hope they change course. This was such a fun game.

Decided to give this a shot during a free weekend.
Very disappointed by both the story and the gameplay mechanics:
- The game has been optimized for controller play at the expense of mouse + keyboard to the point it's unwiedly to play without a controller.
- The story is highly linear and the morality system has become non-existant. Instead you can only make mildly snarky remarks against "the good guys" which goes against the idea of previous and similar games about morality being grey in a post-apocaliptic world
- The game is still buggy almost a year after release and there is not GotY bundle to acquire it with the DLC instead having to buy a season pass separately to get the full experience.
Sure, you can mod all of this to improve it but why bother? You can get much better done mods for Fallout 3 and New Vegas or play Skyrim if what you want pretty graphics with a story that is at least serviceable.
At barely 3-4 hours played I had enough. I wanted to give the game a fair chance despite negative reviews but it is clear that the critique voiced against the game is well earned.
Don't get it unless it's at a very low bargain price and even then make sure to research if the mods have been able to fix the mess that is the game's menus for mouse and keyboard.

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic game. I played it an absolute butt-ton in Early Access and while I haven't played it much recently, it's still wonderful and totally worth your money.
There have been a ton of complaints about it lately, though:
I think Red Hook has been in a really difficult position recently - they're trying to cater to a bunch of different groups of people, some of whom have vastly different expectations about what's appropriate difficulty-wise in their game.
Personally? I think corpses are incredibly stupid. Prot is really stupid. Heart attacks are awful. BUT, I know that some people out there will love them, and I think Red Hook has been trying to please everyone, which is hard.
The saving grace here is that Red Hook is, simply put, the most responsive group of developers I've ever seen. Giving people the option to turn these features off is *exactly* the right solution here, and I really appreciate their continued responsiveness and willingness to try new things.
Give 'em your money.

Dark Souls in my opinion is difficult to describe to someone. Its like rubbing your♥♥♥♥♥♥on a cheesegrater for an hour or so but then having the best sex ever. Its a really weird comparison to make, but it fits in my mind.
The game never fails to build an atmosphere. You enter the undead settlement and see the corpses hanging from the rooves and the locals have fallen victim to some sort of dark forces. Then theres the Irithyll Of The Boreal Valley, more of a maze than a city, with knights wanting to put you on the end of whatever weapon they are weilding. However its also oddly peaceful with silence and the spectres simply walking down the streets not paying attention to what is happening in reality.
Then there are the bosses.... Oh boy they are the star of the show. The games beautiful animations really shine through with interesting movesets that define the whole "feel" of a boss. For example some are elegant doing wild flips and pirouets to confuse the ♥♥♥♥ out of you whilst others will literally beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.... No IFS no BUTS. Each boss has their own themes that fit in well with the soundtrack that again add to the "feel" of a boss fight.
And finally there is the difficulty curve. I'm going to be honest as a newby to the SoulsBorne series, the game feels perfectly balanced as your deaths are YOUR fault. This leads to the game a bit like a learning experience in which the game shines as it is incredibly satisfying when you finally kill a boss after so many failed attempts.
In conclusion, this is one of the most atmospheric and satisfying games i have ever played and would highly recommend.
So do your self a favor, praise the sun and buy this game when you can, because i believe that everyone needs to play a SoulsBorne game and finish it.

Forget what you've learned from previous games. Rethink your views on party management. Accept the fact that you will abandon a quest or run away from battle.
This game is hard, maybe a little unfair (as of writing, this game is only in Early Access and doesn't have a final release date) but only to those who bite over more than they can chew.
Forget about bonding with your mercenaries, they are replacable should they prove too expensive to keep sane. Stress, supplies and torches are more important than your pride.
This is one of the most fun games I've played in quite a while and unlike Demon's Souls, this game is a lot more fair despite not holding your hand. The tutorial is short, shorter than short to be honest, compared to many other modern games and this could be seen as a weakness, but I see it as a strength. It weeds out the weak, like the rest of the game, culling you mercilessly if you forget yourself.
The tools to success is money, knowing how to spend your resources and knowing when to run rather than fighting to the last man.
Red Hook studios have created a gothic, enticing, cartoony horror-esque game with clever and punishing mechanics, should you fail to take into account your resources, your heroes and your stress levels.
The art style is cute, but still manages to be grotesque to the point of giving me the chills, as some monsters makes me FridgeHorror about their fate.
Despite being Early Access, this is a must for any RPG fan with a masochistic streak.
The few dislikes that I have so far are insignificant, as I have faith in the developers that they will have fixed them before release.

I absolutely love the multiplayer mechanics in these games. Such a feeling of companionship when you summon a sunbro to help you out. Always loved having the weapon flailing and emote spamming party before and after a really challenging boss fight. That "oh ♥♥♥♥ off" feeling you get when you get invaded right in the middle of a new, unknown area. And DS3 improved upon it even more with the chaotic, several-man battles. Loads of different covenants to suit your playstyle.
And there is no greater feeling in the video game universe than defeating a hard Souls boss that you have been stuck on for hours. Your heart beats out of your chest and you have this overwelming sense of euphoria. The boss design in these games is always top-notch, both gameplay mechanic wise and aesthetically. Always challenging, sometimes frustrating, never impossible.
It's always been a love-hate relationship with Souls. Dealing with annoying enemies, getting stuck for hours on hard bosses, but we always overcame, and in the end it has turned out to be one of the most magical gaming experiences we've ever experienced.

TLDR: 10/10 would gruesomely die in tutorial again.
- Flagellate your priestess girl for 2 weeks in a row in order to relieve her stress from fighting malformed man-fungus-plant beasts and being cooked in a pot alive.
- Find some chunks of meat on the carcass of unknown animal the moment before your team starves to death.
- Lit a strange altar with a torch and have one of your team members escape after others are brutally murdered by a horrific H.P. Lovecraft-style demon that you summoned.
- Meet that altar again after several weeks and squash the demon like a worm with your much smarter composed and a bit more developed team, taking almost no damage.
- Watch your team miserably fail to insanity as one of your guys turns into abusive jerk after taking hits from several traps, clearing the path from debris for hours and getting poured with soured wine by some undead noble or whatever: watch him insult every teammate that gets hit, misses or hits not well enough; watch as other guys turn paranoid, refuse to accept healing and take orders from you, start to act on their own and think the team is plotting against them, become selfish and take all the loot for themselves, etc.
- Watch your team come back from the brink of failure as one your guys refuses to accept miserable fate, finds inner strength in a most tense situation and inspires all others to not give up, until you win.
Emotions aside. I've purchased the game just recently and don't have the experience of playing before the infamous Corpse Update, so I'd like to provide a perspective from a new player's point of view. And my point is: the game is awesome and works like a charm in it's current design state.
In those almost 25 hours I've played to date I didn't experience a single situation where I needed to destroy a corpse in order to finish the fight. I run balanced parties of heroes that can handle any enemy position and composition. Most my heroes are multi-purpose, switching to healing hp or stress when they are not demanded in dispatching any terrihying, abysmal, maddening things we encounter.
After some time I even find the game a bit too easy, as I am able to effectively finish dungeons with full health and close to 0 stress,
One of the most beautiful things of the game design is that you almost never feel punished unfairly. While most roguelike games tend to destroy you with unfavourable RNG, in this game something bad happens 90% of the time only when you either have not enough understanding and don't know what you're doing or overextend and go too greedy or self-confident. You chose the measure of your punishment yourself, you have to actually put some effort to get even one of your guys killed and you almost never are put into irreversible situation, where you can't take a step back, lick your wounds and try again without actually losing any progress. I guess, devs pulled some strings so there are no more unfair demises which you cannot control, or at least I didin't encounter them yet.
Still, there definitely are some negative things about the game in its current state, like:
- Some classes are obviously underwhelming and sometimes very boring to play, for me - best example is the default Highwayman, which is currently a gimp in every part of his design, having average health, low damage, zero control or team support with the only choise you can make while playing him is hitting one guys or hitting 3 guys - not a single interesting mechanic, choise or tactical possibility. While new things are constantly added to the game, it's possibly hard to balance all existing content and as in the past Highwayman hero probably was a prime damage dealer, now he is simply nothing, outshined by other classes.
- Overall hero design is pretty weak and very immature, with most heroes having several skills that you use all the time and other worthless skills that you will never use in any hero composition. However, compositions may greatly vary so some tactical depth persists, yet very basic, compared to what is possible.
- Currently the game kinda dictates the playstyle, being very control-oriented. You have to focus considerable effort not letting enemies attack at all, or you perish. At least this is what I play and I haven't found any other viable options. I may think of some burst-damage rush builds, but they are definitely going to be less stable and sometimes lead you to sad situations. There are also a lot of skills for sustaining damage in the game, a lot of tanking skills, and all of them are 100% worthless and have not a slight option to run. Buffing your defence is the only option when you want to pass a turn, in all situations it is totally worse than any most basic attack.
Hope this is all fixed when the game is finished.
Nevertheless, I've had a great fun with Darkest Dungeon. When you go YOLO with your weakest party composition and summon an additional boss on a mission where your task is to kill another boss, and then you destroy both of them, winning the turn before one of your guys is cooked alive, you get an awesome dark souls style accomplishment feeling.
The game is a struggle in every aspect from finishing missions to developing your heroes in a way you want, and this struggle is very interesting and invigorating. It also seems to be constantly and intensely improving so I can't recommend it more.

I don't write reviews, but for a game as overall spectacular as Darkest Dungeon I will. I picked this game up because of positive reviews, and even after the most recent patch I have a ton of fun with it and am glad I did. I hope that others will see this review and be able to make their decisions on purchasing or not purchasing based on both sides of the coin.
This game is not for people who insist on shoving square pegs into circular holes. It is a strategy game, first and foremost, and everything from your quest inventory spaces to your characters' health points to your characters themselves are tools and pawns in this grand game of chess. You will lose characters, and you will miss them. You will throw away torches, which light the path in the dungeons, in favor of loot and regret that decision when you come upon enemies that reduce your torchlight and stress out your team. You will have to balance your teams appropriately based on the dungeon you're doing and the threats you will face there. And sometimes you will be beaten by RNG beyond your control in spite of having made every decision flawlessly. You will have to balance DOT classes with direct-damage classes so that you're not destroyed by high defense or high HP monsters. You will have to be willing to run away from both combat that's going bad and quests that are going worse.That's the name of the game, and that's what you should expect.
Despite all of those challenges, you can never truly lose the game. Everyone in your party dies and you can regroup in town, your hamlet undiminished, and continue with others, now humbled by your experiences. If this kind of adversity is the kind of thing you like, then you should buy this game. If you're easily frustrated by irreversible death, high difficulty, and challenging strategy, then spare yourself and don't buy it. It's as simple as that.
This game has fantastic narration, haunting melodies, uncompromising difficulty, gorgeous gothic art, and harrowing RNG both in your favor and against it. There will be moments when you want to scream at your monitor, and there will be moments when you'll fistpump at getting the pivotal critical hit that wins the battle. It is for these reasons I've played it over 100 hours, and will continue to play it in the future.
For those interested, a lot of negative reviews are hinging on corpses, PROT (monster protection), and stress management. The game recently got a lot tougher because RedHook felt it was too easy for people to shove square pegs into circular holes, and in my opinion it was for the better. Prior to the patch, certain classes would never get used because why bother when you can just smash everything with massive critical hits every round? Now you have to come to terms with the fact that your characters will be stressed, and you can't stop it forever. You have to deal with enemies who can resist direct-damage attacks all day, and you will have to adapt. You now have to deal with enemies that leave behind corpses, and either manage the corpses effectively or take advantage of them to get the upper hand, which is easy with smart team compositions.
Let this review temper the negative reviews you've read so far, and with it hopefully you'll be able to make a more educated decision as to whether this game is for you or not. For me, I have no regrets, have played the game a lot and will continue to do so. That's the best recommendation I can possibly give.

I'm really glad Grey Havens took over - everything runs much more smoothly. Before Grey Havens took charge, players were experiencing a lot of performance issues, bugs, and other issues. Most, if not all, of those problems have been solved.
GAMEPLAY
Controls are fine. You can adjust to a high degree to find your perfect setup. Works with Steam Controller (never tried it). Weapons, mobs, etc don't cause any problems. The gameplay is perfectly fine. Nothing for me to say.
PERFORMANCE
As I said. Grey Havens have sorted most of those out. There's still the occasional lag spike that many players experience, but no major issue for me. The biggest cause of lag in this game will probably be your internet connection - if it's poor, your experience may be too.
GRAPHICS
Good. Very creative visuals, nice design... Looks great with high settings and some extra settings cranked up. IPS screens with help ;)
COMMUNITY
Not as many players as there used to be, but I see a lot more people starting to play now that Grey Havens have taken over and the game's not a wreck anymore. Still a lot of veterans around. Lots of guilds (mine has 290 members). Community is fun, enjoyable and friendly.
CONS
Just some... My main disagreement is with SK's new leveling system. They have these stupid Rarities that you need to forage to level up your gear. Getting anything up to 5 star is insanely difficult compared to before. The previous leveling system was far better (level up gear with Heat, something acquired through use of the item).
FINAL words...
I've been playing this game for years and will probably be playing it a while longer (while I have the time!). Do give it a go, it's a great free game and you certainly don't need to pay to win. Sure, the leveling system is a bit of a joke, but I still enjoy the game and I'm sure you will too, if you're into this type of game.
However, I'm really hoping for some new missions or endgame content to be created. I've basically completed the game and don't see and active point to playing anymore, which is a shame. New players will have fun with it though. Maybe you'll see me around in-game (username: Bulbus).

Dark Souls in my opinion is difficult to describe to someone. Its like rubbing your♥♥♥♥♥♥on a cheesegrater for an hour or so but then having the best sex ever. Its a really weird comparison to make, but it fits in my mind.
The game never fails to build an atmosphere. You enter the undead settlement and see the corpses hanging from the rooves and the locals have fallen victim to some sort of dark forces. Then theres the Irithyll Of The Boreal Valley, more of a maze than a city, with knights wanting to put you on the end of whatever weapon they are weilding. However its also oddly peaceful with silence and the spectres simply walking down the streets not paying attention to what is happening in reality.
Then there are the bosses.... Oh boy they are the star of the show. The games beautiful animations really shine through with interesting movesets that define the whole "feel" of a boss. For example some are elegant doing wild flips and pirouets to confuse the ♥♥♥♥ out of you whilst others will literally beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.... No IFS no BUTS. Each boss has their own themes that fit in well with the soundtrack that again add to the "feel" of a boss fight.
And finally there is the difficulty curve. I'm going to be honest as a newby to the SoulsBorne series, the game feels perfectly balanced as your deaths are YOUR fault. This leads to the game a bit like a learning experience in which the game shines as it is incredibly satisfying when you finally kill a boss after so many failed attempts.
In conclusion, this is one of the most atmospheric and satisfying games i have ever played and would highly recommend.
So do your self a favor, praise the sun and buy this game when you can, because i believe that everyone needs to play a SoulsBorne game and finish it.

Forget what you've learned from previous games. Rethink your views on party management. Accept the fact that you will abandon a quest or run away from battle.
This game is hard, maybe a little unfair (as of writing, this game is only in Early Access and doesn't have a final release date) but only to those who bite over more than they can chew.
Forget about bonding with your mercenaries, they are replacable should they prove too expensive to keep sane. Stress, supplies and torches are more important than your pride.
This is one of the most fun games I've played in quite a while and unlike Demon's Souls, this game is a lot more fair despite not holding your hand. The tutorial is short, shorter than short to be honest, compared to many other modern games and this could be seen as a weakness, but I see it as a strength. It weeds out the weak, like the rest of the game, culling you mercilessly if you forget yourself.
The tools to success is money, knowing how to spend your resources and knowing when to run rather than fighting to the last man.
Red Hook studios have created a gothic, enticing, cartoony horror-esque game with clever and punishing mechanics, should you fail to take into account your resources, your heroes and your stress levels.
The art style is cute, but still manages to be grotesque to the point of giving me the chills, as some monsters makes me FridgeHorror about their fate.
Despite being Early Access, this is a must for any RPG fan with a masochistic streak.
The few dislikes that I have so far are insignificant, as I have faith in the developers that they will have fixed them before release.

TLDR: 10/10 would gruesomely die in tutorial again.
- Flagellate your priestess girl for 2 weeks in a row in order to relieve her stress from fighting malformed man-fungus-plant beasts and being cooked in a pot alive.
- Find some chunks of meat on the carcass of unknown animal the moment before your team starves to death.
- Lit a strange altar with a torch and have one of your team members escape after others are brutally murdered by a horrific H.P. Lovecraft-style demon that you summoned.
- Meet that altar again after several weeks and squash the demon like a worm with your much smarter composed and a bit more developed team, taking almost no damage.
- Watch your team miserably fail to insanity as one of your guys turns into abusive jerk after taking hits from several traps, clearing the path from debris for hours and getting poured with soured wine by some undead noble or whatever: watch him insult every teammate that gets hit, misses or hits not well enough; watch as other guys turn paranoid, refuse to accept healing and take orders from you, start to act on their own and think the team is plotting against them, become selfish and take all the loot for themselves, etc.
- Watch your team come back from the brink of failure as one your guys refuses to accept miserable fate, finds inner strength in a most tense situation and inspires all others to not give up, until you win.
Emotions aside. I've purchased the game just recently and don't have the experience of playing before the infamous Corpse Update, so I'd like to provide a perspective from a new player's point of view. And my point is: the game is awesome and works like a charm in it's current design state.
In those almost 25 hours I've played to date I didn't experience a single situation where I needed to destroy a corpse in order to finish the fight. I run balanced parties of heroes that can handle any enemy position and composition. Most my heroes are multi-purpose, switching to healing hp or stress when they are not demanded in dispatching any terrihying, abysmal, maddening things we encounter.
After some time I even find the game a bit too easy, as I am able to effectively finish dungeons with full health and close to 0 stress,
One of the most beautiful things of the game design is that you almost never feel punished unfairly. While most roguelike games tend to destroy you with unfavourable RNG, in this game something bad happens 90% of the time only when you either have not enough understanding and don't know what you're doing or overextend and go too greedy or self-confident. You chose the measure of your punishment yourself, you have to actually put some effort to get even one of your guys killed and you almost never are put into irreversible situation, where you can't take a step back, lick your wounds and try again without actually losing any progress. I guess, devs pulled some strings so there are no more unfair demises which you cannot control, or at least I didin't encounter them yet.
Still, there definitely are some negative things about the game in its current state, like:
- Some classes are obviously underwhelming and sometimes very boring to play, for me - best example is the default Highwayman, which is currently a gimp in every part of his design, having average health, low damage, zero control or team support with the only choise you can make while playing him is hitting one guys or hitting 3 guys - not a single interesting mechanic, choise or tactical possibility. While new things are constantly added to the game, it's possibly hard to balance all existing content and as in the past Highwayman hero probably was a prime damage dealer, now he is simply nothing, outshined by other classes.
- Overall hero design is pretty weak and very immature, with most heroes having several skills that you use all the time and other worthless skills that you will never use in any hero composition. However, compositions may greatly vary so some tactical depth persists, yet very basic, compared to what is possible.
- Currently the game kinda dictates the playstyle, being very control-oriented. You have to focus considerable effort not letting enemies attack at all, or you perish. At least this is what I play and I haven't found any other viable options. I may think of some burst-damage rush builds, but they are definitely going to be less stable and sometimes lead you to sad situations. There are also a lot of skills for sustaining damage in the game, a lot of tanking skills, and all of them are 100% worthless and have not a slight option to run. Buffing your defence is the only option when you want to pass a turn, in all situations it is totally worse than any most basic attack.
Hope this is all fixed when the game is finished.
Nevertheless, I've had a great fun with Darkest Dungeon. When you go YOLO with your weakest party composition and summon an additional boss on a mission where your task is to kill another boss, and then you destroy both of them, winning the turn before one of your guys is cooked alive, you get an awesome dark souls style accomplishment feeling.
The game is a struggle in every aspect from finishing missions to developing your heroes in a way you want, and this struggle is very interesting and invigorating. It also seems to be constantly and intensely improving so I can't recommend it more.

Before I begin, please keep in mind I haven't been writing reviews for a long time.
This'll be short and sweet (and focused on gameplay) and to the point, so read on.
Trove is a MMO dungeon delver game with the simple goal of raiding dungeons, killing monsters, finishing quests, and getting loot/leveling up. I easily blew 24 hours of seamless gameplay on the game while I was leveling up, getting better equipment, following the objectives given by the game (Which felt out of place toward the end).  But then I found my issue. What had been "fun" quickly became repetitive with the same character, as the same dungeons did nothing but "rotate" (randomly spawn biome related) bosses and these fun items in game quickly turned into grinds for experience/ resources of some sort.
Another issue is that each of the "proffesions" (Gardening, Fishing, Ring Crafting) seemed to be under-nurtured. (Such as having little "build up", just beginning and end tier items) and to get one item you wanted you'd have to throw in 3-4 hours of work depending on how hard that item is to acquire.
The final thing I'll point out is getting something can be a grind as well, such as my first ally (Small things that follow you around like pets and give some sort of stat bonus and rarely a passive boost.) took me probably 12 hours to get. Items such as wepons being upgraded can take ~4 hours of grinding to upgrade, depending on the level of that item.
Lastly at first the game had some queing issues (Waiting for ~1 hour to get in) But last time I logged in that was fixed, however I'm not sure if it'll be completely fixed or if it may come back with the expanding playerbase.
tl;dr: Closer to end tier you got the less of a game and the more of a grind the whole thing became.
For the pros/cons people:
Pros:
The game can be fun for a while
Lots of things to do with your time on trove
You can get a good play through with or without paying $$$
One of the few games that has a "mid-game" progression in place
Developers seem to work to fix the game, not just release it and expect players to suffer
Cons:
Ques which may or may not come back
After a while everything you do becomes a grind
Mid game seems confused, lack of objectives causes lost guidance around Uber 2-3 worlds
Upgrading gear becomes a pain
Eventually you feel like you have to become a patron (Essentially someone who gives money for benefits) to get anywhere in game.
I'd give this game a 8/10 considering it's only in 1.0 and I'm sure the developers are trying to please the fan base.

I don't write reviews, but for a game as overall spectacular as Darkest Dungeon I will. I picked this game up because of positive reviews, and even after the most recent patch I have a ton of fun with it and am glad I did. I hope that others will see this review and be able to make their decisions on purchasing or not purchasing based on both sides of the coin.
This game is not for people who insist on shoving square pegs into circular holes. It is a strategy game, first and foremost, and everything from your quest inventory spaces to your characters' health points to your characters themselves are tools and pawns in this grand game of chess. You will lose characters, and you will miss them. You will throw away torches, which light the path in the dungeons, in favor of loot and regret that decision when you come upon enemies that reduce your torchlight and stress out your team. You will have to balance your teams appropriately based on the dungeon you're doing and the threats you will face there. And sometimes you will be beaten by RNG beyond your control in spite of having made every decision flawlessly. You will have to balance DOT classes with direct-damage classes so that you're not destroyed by high defense or high HP monsters. You will have to be willing to run away from both combat that's going bad and quests that are going worse.That's the name of the game, and that's what you should expect.
Despite all of those challenges, you can never truly lose the game. Everyone in your party dies and you can regroup in town, your hamlet undiminished, and continue with others, now humbled by your experiences. If this kind of adversity is the kind of thing you like, then you should buy this game. If you're easily frustrated by irreversible death, high difficulty, and challenging strategy, then spare yourself and don't buy it. It's as simple as that.
This game has fantastic narration, haunting melodies, uncompromising difficulty, gorgeous gothic art, and harrowing RNG both in your favor and against it. There will be moments when you want to scream at your monitor, and there will be moments when you'll fistpump at getting the pivotal critical hit that wins the battle. It is for these reasons I've played it over 100 hours, and will continue to play it in the future.
For those interested, a lot of negative reviews are hinging on corpses, PROT (monster protection), and stress management. The game recently got a lot tougher because RedHook felt it was too easy for people to shove square pegs into circular holes, and in my opinion it was for the better. Prior to the patch, certain classes would never get used because why bother when you can just smash everything with massive critical hits every round? Now you have to come to terms with the fact that your characters will be stressed, and you can't stop it forever. You have to deal with enemies who can resist direct-damage attacks all day, and you will have to adapt. You now have to deal with enemies that leave behind corpses, and either manage the corpses effectively or take advantage of them to get the upper hand, which is easy with smart team compositions.
Let this review temper the negative reviews you've read so far, and with it hopefully you'll be able to make a more educated decision as to whether this game is for you or not. For me, I have no regrets, have played the game a lot and will continue to do so. That's the best recommendation I can possibly give.

To go from three star to four star, you need a lot of elite orbs. People complain about this part in particular for the grind. If you just keep playing boss levels for a few hours you already have pretty much half of the orbs you need, or the money needed to buy half. It does not take very long at all. Going from four to five star does take a little longer cause the crystals needed are very high, however by this time, you are pretty much good to be able to clear most levels by yourself so you can easily get the crystals by just playing the game for fun.
EVERYTHING in the game can essentially be obtained for free. Let me elaborate on this:
the only items that "cost real money", are the promotional prize boxes every two weeks. HOWEVER, there are always people buying them and selling them on the auction house for a very reasonable price. I have gotten every item in this game buy using the currency I eanred ingame. I have spent some money on here, but only for "cosmetic" items I was a little short of. I happily spend money for energy every now and then to support the game but I usually just use them for guild hall items.
I understand many will disagree and argue with my post, however, if you enjoy the combat of the game, then you will not have any problem with the grind. I love trying to gain crowns from arcade and boss levels everyday. It is enjoyable in my opinion. Hope you all have fun and if you need help on missions let me know or ask for help in haven! I like that you don't need as much energy for crafting and progressing as before, but ultimately the game feels too grindy and limited. When there are enemies with different types of resistances and you only have 2 weapons in your arsenal, you can get overwhelmed rather easily.
Using a rank 3 bomb with normal damage requires a full, long charge and only deals 52 damage when enemies in tier 2 arcade seem to have around 500hp or more if they are a mini-boss.
Using a rank 4 piercing melee weapon does up to 140 damage vs beast-type enemies, but it's hard to use against things like slimes or melee fighters, especially if you have 15+ enemies on screen along with traps around the room. You will simply take too much damage or get overwhelmed if you go near these too much.
For optimal performance you need a handgun to go along with the melee weapon, but when you can only shoot around 1.5 shots per second (burst of 3 in 2 seconds + 1 sec reload or so), it's rather tedious to kill many enemies at higher levels.
Traps stay up for long, but reset quickly. Some rooms have a lot of traps and so many enemies that you can' t even evade them all alone or kill them fast enough to be able to evade properly.
Because of slow killing and only being able to choose between 2 weapons, the gameplay starts to feel tedious. It is made even more tedious with the RNG in getting orbs of alchemy and the bad market economy - there are not many players playing and as a result you don't know what price to sell items at, getting almost no sales until much later when you see what other players are selling at.
I was going to farm those orbs of alchemy, but when I got overwhelmed because of my lack of firepower once more, I decided to stop playing.

I'm guessing this review will be slapped down by a much more active part of this community, but enough is enough I must speak.
Darkest Dungeon is a great game. I've found myself coming back to this game more than I expected to. Sure I haven't logged 50+ hours, but damn me if it isn't fun. Recent changes have caused quite the uproar from the more dedicated fanbase and while I won't argue the changes are troublesome I will argue that the devs don't deserve the response that has come about. I'm here to set the record straight, from a casual players prespective.
There has been a growing divide between this games player base since the beginning. A small minority of extremely hardcore fans and the majority of, we'll call them invested, fans. Regardless of the size of these groups, they are pretty equal in voice. The hardcore minority were finding the experience a little to easy toward the later stages of the game. Parties could be formed that basically annihilated the front line of the enemy group, thus bumping up the fragile backline. Sure things were always brutal and your party members died, but for someone who was TRYING to play the game the SUPER efficient way it became rather boring in a "HULK SMASH" kind of way.
Then some changes came that really made things difficult, but instead of creating cool new AI or developing new challenging enemy parties the devs added corpses, prot, and heart attacks. Basically these changes didn't increase the difficulty in a fun manner, only in a numbers way. Suddenly regular enemies had the equivalent of elite variants that take a lot less damage from basic attacks. Enemies killed started spawning corpses where they died, now blocking the enemy backline from moving forward. Adventurers stress even became an instant death chance once raised above a certain threashold.
All these changes sure made the game harder, but don't you find them a little to simple? Lazy even? I know I do, but that doesn't mean Darkest Dungeon isn't worth buying. If you compare the game, even in its current form, to the ocean of♥♥♥♥♥♥early acess titles it STILL stands above a vast majority of them. The ocean of survival horror, zombie, crafting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that we so quickily forgive because "the devs are working on it/updates are coming/it is an early access game."
So I stand here, among what seems to be an ever increasing flood of thumbs down reviews, to recommend that you buy Darkest Dungeon. The game is great, even better than great in my opinion. Sure there have been bumps and potholes along the way, and there are sure to be some more, but this is one of the few early access titles that actually deserves your money.

Starbound is essentially the successor to Terraria, which blew up relatively quickly and had a series of free udpates past its release date. There are many similarities as well as differences between the two games that work together to create a different experience between the two games.
Starbound allows players to pick from (as of this review) 6 races; Humans, Apex (monkey men), Avians (Birdmen), Floran (Plant People), Glitch (Robots), and Hylotl (Fish people). When you begin, rather than start off on a large plot of land you are on a space ship hovering above a planet; awaiting to explore its ins and outs. From there, you mine resources craft, build, fight bosses and the denizens of the planet whether beastly or civilized to a certain manner. This is the spirit of the game. Of course, rushing through killing each boss and making the proper tiered armor and weapons will make you tire of it relatively quickly. I believe the charm of the game matters on your pace. Taking your time to explore what you've never seen is exciting. Being able to build your own towns and cities and even colonizing them is another thing.
Starbound allows for a lot more creativity that was partially limited in Terraria. Each race comes with a story, and as the developers themselves work on the game; their will no doubt be a long lifeline that Terraria had also experienced. Would recommend to play with a friend or more! And just don't be that guy that rushes to defeat the last boss. There's plenty to explore!

Okay. So here's what's up.
There is a great game hidden in here somewhere, but the thing is, they've overstepped on making it challenging and stumbled into a faceplant.
There are a TON of features and mechanics in the game, it's very very fleshed out and polished for an Early Access. But the design choices make you want to pull your hair out.
It's supposed to be difficult. Yes, Devs, we get that. The problem is, the stress system, RNG events, and inconsistent battles make the game well.... Inconsistent.
Listen, you're talking to a Dark Souls/Bloodborne fanatic. Hardcore modes in Diablo 2 and 3.  I love difficult and challenging games -
. And it pisses me off that I have an addiction with this game, but the design choices make me want to throw my laptop against the wall. I'm not some carebear that cries when things get the slightest bit difficult, but this game... It's BS.
Lets get the pros/cons outta the way.
Pros
Cons:
The design of the graphics and sound, and the base model of the combat and exploration.  At the game's core it has an outstanding heart to its design. If the devs would balance things out, they would have a truly addictive game that would have players begging to explore more of its world and get the satisfaction of fleshing out their party members.
How horribly unbalanced the game is, in it's effort to "be challenging" or "difficult." Darkest Dungeon trips over its own feet, and bars the players from reaching its finer points. There's no lesson to learn, its not like Dark Souls where you can study an enemy and learn the weaknesses.  Other challenging games still have plenty of ways to keep the player honest and test his/her skills, without cheating them.
The devs behind Darkest Dungeon have a great thing, but they need to figure out a way to make the game an honest challenge, while still leaving players available to explore the games deep and enthralling features.  As of right now, the game is far too frustrating to recommend, even as I bought it for $13 on sale. You're basically paying to be insulted and trolled.

Darkest Dungeon was never meant to be a game where you never fail and complete every dungeon flawlessly.

I am a huge fan of Dark Souls the original due to its sound mechanics and deep, interesting plot for each and every character in the game. Dark Souls is like a huge canvas painting that has been pain-stakingly completed with a fine brush.
Dark Souls 3 is that same canvas with paint loosely daubed across it, with the name "Ariandel" scrawled in the bottom corner.
Where item placement and character developments were a well thought out puzzle in the first game, Dark Souls 3 has maps sprawling with seemingly randomly placed items and many characters fall by the wayside. Some npcs in this game are well developed to be fair.
PvP.
Poise doesn't work, armour is useless (just equip any piece in a slot) and there are a few weapons which are just broken. This is especially true for DLC weapons. There is a definite hierarchy.
Invaders are really challenged, given that the host can summon 3 phantoms and a blue sentinel/blade of the dark moon. Very often, these power groups just gank you. I would argue black phantoms are a fun and integral part of the gameplay. Whenever a phantom invades, excitement and fear levels rise. It is wrong that they are so punished. Also, black phantoms invade for free but drop their souls when they die as a phantom. Just bizarre.
People use estus in duels. I know there are lloyd's talismans which stop estus use but it is very annoying the way people just chug estus flasks all the time. Instead of a duel lasting a minute or so, it is a drawn out affair, with even phantoms healing while you duel. No honour.
I am a massive fanboy of this series but Dark Souls 3 does just feel lazy in a lot of places. Artificial difficulty is implemented by simply making many enemies and bosses damage sponges.
Hit boxes are also waaaaay off with some bosses. This was true of the original also (here's looking at you, Gaping Dragon tail swipe!) but they really should of improved it.
The DLCs are both dissapointing. The stories introduced in both are weak and poorly set up. It all feels rushed.
We all knew we were in for a rough time when poise was broken from the start and they are yet to fix it and yet we perservered with the hope of fixes. They are not coming.

Great game when I first bought it, but a recent patch having introduced a frankly inconvenient and unfun mechanic (corpses) in a game that's already dangerously RNG and frustration prone makes me have to change my review. If you hate yourself or play nothing but difficult and frustrating games that function off high risk low reward, you'll still love this game, but if you're a casual gamer or generally don't enjoy RNG-driven difficulty spikes then avoid this for now.
This IS a fun game, but it could really use a difficulty toggle that doesn't penalize your gains so much that playing on easy actually makes you suck more in the long run, since you gain less loot and gold, for only a small decrease in difficulty.
The game would greatly benefit from letting you play on easy for the first few dungeons you run and clear, and then gradually ramping up the reward curve for playing on hard so as to incite you to get comfortable and increase difficulty at your own pace. But also, it would benefit from easy being easier. As it is right now it really is just a self-imposed penalty on gains for only a tiny decrease in difficulty, and RNG can still totally screw you over anyway.
TL;DR: Easy mode not easy enough, imposes huge penalty for almost no gain, especially combined with RNG. Latest patches have been pandering to the vocal minority asking for a harder more tedious game, alienating casual players. Game desperately in need of a game mode to separate players.

Pros:
-Absolutely gorgeous, the amount of time and care that went into crafting the world is amazing.
-Gameplay was (and to a lesser extent, still is...but more about that in Con) a blast. Managing your party in the middle of a dungeon and fighting through nearly impossible odds is a blast.
-The RNG God is a cruel master, and you'll pay for it. Your best squad may die or maybe a survivor will limp back to safety, aflicted with all sorts of horrible insanities. I personally like this. The idea that your party is nearly always vulnerable is amazing.
- The gameplay does reward tactical thinking in ways that even other hardcore roguelikes don't.
-The combination of darkness, sanity, and enemy debuffs keeps you constantly on edge. It's a unique combination of gameplay that really does work and is incredibly rewarding
-The dialogue: it doesn't happen much but its great when your occultist speaks to Cthullu and translates it as code.
-The classes are a blast. You won't see any noble knights or good hearted theives. You'll see Lepers, Highwaymen, Battle hardened crusaders, and grave robbers. They're flawed, they have fears, those fears might very well kill them.
-DAT ANCESTOR THO. He can narrate my life, he can narrate your life, he can narrate life itself.
Ok so the negatives
-First off the combination of gameplay. This is a rather new issue (and hopefully it'll get changed soon) but a variety of patches have essentially made the game both more difficult and somehow more tedious. To give a better explanation, the game penalizes you for dragging out fights via a constant increase in stress (this was done because players would leave one mob alive, stun lock it, then heal their entire party). This wasn't so bad, as core gameplay remained. Then they introduced corpses. This is the patch you'll see everyone complaining about. Essentially when you kill an enemy, it now leaves a body behind... which in turn needs to be destroyed before that slot frees up. This is a big deal because typically your melee troops can only hit the front two rows, which means that you killing an enemy twice. It's incredibly tedious and frustrating when you lose because your leper couldn't actually reach the 4th enemy because corpses were blocking you. The same is true to the introduction of protection on enemies (damage is reduced and only DOT can effect them). Meaning you have to drag along a DOT heavy party member even if he doesn't work well with your group. This, in combination with corpses drags fights out longer (which the game penalizes you for) without adding much tactical depth.
EDIT: The recent patch changed a lot of this, corpses can now be disabled if you want them to be. They also patched a lot of the more tedious corpse aspects (your heavily well armed and trained soldiers could miss hitting a dead body with swords) and made it so it's easier to destroy them (a DOTed monster will pass on his DOT to the corpse if he dies).
-Building off the previous point: two of the bosses don't feel unique any more. Prior to the patches they both had unique abilities (one had walls that acted similarly to corpses and the other had protection) a lot of that feel is gone.
-The game gets super repetative. There are 6 bosses, each with 3 levels of difficulty. Your heroes won't enter dungeons beneath a certain level, which means you'll spend a lot of time training new parties to kill bosses that other parties are too strong for.
-Bosses don't actually change tactics, they just get more health/damage. Meaning when you've beaten them once you've done it all three times.
-You can't actually lose DD, because its free to recruit more soldiers and you can send them adventuring without any supplies have them come back with as much money as they can, then dismiss their paranoid asses. You can keep doing this till your rich enough  to send out a party you actually care about.
TLDR: Game is good, used to be great- a variety of patches that don't synthesize well creates an ultimately tedious and frustrating combat gameplay. World is beautiful, characters are great. It is certainly roguelike, but like many roguelikes, expect it to become repetative.

The gameplay, atmosphere, and art are wonderfully executed. The theme of the game is well thought out and original (For more about that, check the reviews by kotaku or other professional game sites).
Furthermore, the Dev's are constantly rolling out new updates, and the mechanics and gameplay are constantly being tweaked and balanced.
The main problem with that though, is that, sometimes an update would make a game too easy, and an update meant to address that makes the game too hard.
Most negative reviews basically state that "The game was good until they updated and ruined it!!! DO NOT BUY!". More often than not, it's followed by a rant about how the Dev's have been deaf to the outcry from the community.
Well, guess what, they haven't. Just a few days ago a new patch was released, that continued to rebalance the gameplay mechanics. Although they haven't erased the mechanic that caused the huge outcry from part of the community, it has been tweaked to be much more managable.
The main reasons for these tweaks and rebalancing comes from the fact that Darkest Dungeon stives to be a hard, harrowing, but ultimately rewarding game. It forces players to constantly pick between risk and caution, when to press on or when to call it quits. The patches that the devs release are meant to make sure you cannot 'cheese' yourself through challenges that are supposed to be difficult.
In the end, my positive recommendation stems from the fact that the Dev's have shown themselves time and time again willing to listen to the community whilst also being committed to the vision of what the final game should be. Some of their patches might be great, others might leave something to be desired, but this game would NOT be an abandoned game. Nor would it be a game that is artificially difficult or have its difficulty diluted. Any real problems with the game have always been fixed in a timely manner.
Since the game is on sale right now, BUY IT!

Starbound is essentially the successor to Terraria, which blew up relatively quickly and had a series of free udpates past its release date. There are many similarities as well as differences between the two games that work together to create a different experience between the two games.
Starbound allows players to pick from (as of this review) 6 races; Humans, Apex (monkey men), Avians (Birdmen), Floran (Plant People), Glitch (Robots), and Hylotl (Fish people). When you begin, rather than start off on a large plot of land you are on a space ship hovering above a planet; awaiting to explore its ins and outs. From there, you mine resources craft, build, fight bosses and the denizens of the planet whether beastly or civilized to a certain manner. This is the spirit of the game. Of course, rushing through killing each boss and making the proper tiered armor and weapons will make you tire of it relatively quickly. I believe the charm of the game matters on your pace. Taking your time to explore what you've never seen is exciting. Being able to build your own towns and cities and even colonizing them is another thing.
Starbound allows for a lot more creativity that was partially limited in Terraria. Each race comes with a story, and as the developers themselves work on the game; their will no doubt be a long lifeline that Terraria had also experienced. Would recommend to play with a friend or more! And just don't be that guy that rushes to defeat the last boss. There's plenty to explore!

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
After reading tons of positive reviews when Darkest Dungeon was released to Steam as Early Access, I was very exited when I this game entered Midweek Sale.
However, after spending a few hours in the game I have become pretty frustated.
Do not get me wrong. I totally did expect a hard game. I did not, however, expect a game with unfairness so grave that the RNG LITERALLY kills you in the tutorial. And if it does not, then it will in the first or second dungeon, at which point you can delete your save and restart, because you will not be able to recover.
Overall, this is way too unbalanced in several means:
- Monsters crit and dodge like mad where your heroes crit and dodge LITERALLY once in their lifetime
- After finishing a dungeon, you get about 2 negative feats for every positive. Also, the positive feats only make a character slightly better, where the negative feats LITERALLY render the character useless
- Since stress can LITERALLY kill, it is dealt way too abundant. And if one character freaks out in the middle of a dungeon run, not only is this character more or less rendered useless, it will also kill the whole party because stress is contagious in this game
I strongly believed that this was a game that I would enjoy. However, the great presentation (beautifully grotesque heroes and monsters, terrifying music and sound and a fantastic narrator) is overshadowed by the broken game mechanic.
Since this is still early access, there might be the chance that the devs will do more rebalancing. Which could be good, but seeing the direction the development took, I am not very optimistic.

I played this pre-Steam, but I dumped my old account which didn't do much when it got thrown on here. Either way, I had an idea of what this was about.
What I do have to say though is it's one of a fairly short list of F2Ps on Steam which I'd genuinely recommend trying out.
The presentation is fairly unique, and while there's an element of pay to do more, at least it's not pay to win. The 100 daily mist energy generally gets you through places (10 energy to descend a level, and you're unlikely to spelunk long distances), and energy can be bought on the market for okay prices when the market isn't exploding.
The only time you need to buy energy is upgrading weapons, but that can be done with crowns or real cash. It's all choice, and that's what I like about this. It doesn't say "you should only buy everything with real world cash", it offers a good, albeit longer, alternative.
Combat is fun, but a little repetitive. You can't really ask for more in a F2P than to have fun.
