This game will NOT hold your hand.
Granted there are some tweaks that need to be made. For example: Every successful dodge or attack (however minute) should bestow a portion of relief. Hypothetically, if I throw a large rock at your head and you dodged it, you would be ecstatic right?
Regarding Monster and Player Damage output:
Players and monsters should not hit below or above their damage range unless they roll a crit 20.  To elaborate: if a crusader's damage is 7-18, even while the defending monster has protection, the damage should not be under 7. The maximum damage should be reduced at least 15% of protection of the defending monster and or player regarding what multiples of protection that unit has. For example: 15% less damage if the monster has 10%  30% at 20 protection and so forth. Or if I hit a monster without a crit, it shouldn’t be 35 dmg. Granted this is without trinkets.
Let's take the Grave robber for example: Highest dodge capacity out of all the units in the game. She should not be hit 5 times in a row if each shadow fade boosts her dodge. Or let’s look at the Leper, the leper has an accuracy rating of 65, granted it's rare for him to hit someone, but when he does it should feel powerful. Then again, all he has to do is stand there and take a beating. Which is pointless when each attack has the possibility of critting and annihilating a party member.
Overall Costs:
Keep in mind, we have to scavenge for our lost relics. However, during the first month of in game time, stress recovery should be reduced to help ease the player into the oncoming horrors. I would go as far as to suggest that since the town hasn't seen anyone in ages, they would be eager to sell their wares at a discount. Or insert a druid or shaman to give buffs before venturing.
In game Totems: (Curios)
The only complaint I have here are some shrines give out "protection" for only a couple of rounds. The Downside to this is that you have to beat the current room to activate the shrine. There could be a better way to incorporate this. Either let a player take a turn to activate the shrine while in battle, have the buffs last until camp or remove those 4 round buffs all together.  Also, more hints are needed for effective curios investigation. Such as Bandages can protect your hands from cobwebs, mummies and knives. Or something along those lines, the only one available at the moment is Holy water on once powerful idols.
Virtue & Affliction System:
Beautiful, I get ecstatic when a couple of my units get virtuous. The stress and backtalk that the units give to each other can be drawn out, but it does what it's supposed to do: build stress. Even with diseases and quirks preventing the possibility of virtue are detrimental, however; if my units have irrepressible and other buffs that lead to virtue, stress should not negatively afflict them right away. It should be along the lines as the Death Blow resist. Then again, the check should be done at stress 100, if it's over by 30 or so then immediately afflict the unit.
Trinkets: Are they worth it?
No. The trinkets are so detrimental to the gameplay. It's a bait and switch mechanic that lures you into getting a moderately effective trinket only to lose it if you have to escape. As I pointed out earlier, you need all the cash you can get just to keep your parties stress down and other dastardly illnesses at bay. If the trinket system actually promoted more beneficial ratios, I would see the usefulness of actually equipping them. Instead it goes 1:1 1:2 2:2 3:2 from left to right and left being positive and the right being negative.
Benefits of No duplicate members and Single Target skills.
Meaning, that you don't have two hellions in one party. There are a lot of combinations you can play as and each one brings their own set of skills with them. Everyone should walk out with a buff when camping, if they can't save some of the shrines and buff the non-buffed member.
New game modes:
Rescue System: When adventuring one has the possibility of rescuing a "shaman" or another npc that will add value to your town. They can only be saved on successful completion of the quest. Or Escort missions or mini games. If one of the units is relieving stress at the bar, have them play darts or quarters with other units that are occupying the same stress relief.
Unused Rations and inventory:
There should be a storage unit that could help ease the stress and give more incentive on being a minimalist as possible. For instance, the recovery of relics or medicine bags or foods take up your inventory space and there will be instances when you have to back out of a room or dungeon. Maybe inset an xp penalty for having to take out from storage or you can use Rogue legacy as an example and go back into the same dungeon at a cost.
I’m pretty sure there’s a possibility of slaughtering your own cattle and raising a farm, this would go well for storage and crafting your own supplies. Think about it, the Plague doctor is constantly drinking.
Artwork:
Phenomenal, however; there should be more variation. Such as, if a unit is on death's door, have them kneel and actually show that they are hurting instead of just flashing red, or if bleeding, have like a pool of blood underneath them. If they are blighted, have their hands or face show some sign of erosion. Do not take away from the artwork!
Having to release Units early from stress relief:
Granted I understand that these are non-refundable. Which makes mini-games more of an incentive if most of your party is out of whack. And the mini-games could take a “day” instead of a “week”. This also can go back to buffing the town and having a parade of some sort and reliving your entire roster’s stress, yet take a week and some cash to do so. Only after certain intervals, once after a boss to let the town know you mean business.
Unit Names:
Thank you for allowing us to rename our heroes, but there should be some file that separates the male and female names accordingly. I don’t know how many times that a received a Hellion named Cornelius.
Soundtrack:
Gothic Adventure awaits. The intensity during the battles is well placed with the dimming of the torch!
The Torch System:
Love the idea of that darkness reaps death and riches. Fantastic.
This game expects a lot out of you, and I expect a lot out of this game. I paid for it, I played it, it’s not perfect, but it’s better than a lot of triple A titles.

Do you like:

b) Borderlands

For every "Yes", add 5% to the score, starting at 65%.
As others have mentioned, this is a great game, but has not much to do with Fallout. If I scored this as a Fallout game, I would say it's a disaster.
However- if you don't look at it as a Fallout game, it's actually quite awesome.
I'm saying that as someone whose first memorable game on a CD was Fallout 1 demo with Junktown back in the day... and who has played Fallout 2 approximately 20 times.
It is a refreshing change. This game is more like a shooter. Don't expect a strong story or role playing aspects. Look at it like a post-apocalyptic shooter with some fun crafting. That's all it is.
The gun play is amazing. One of the best I've ever seen. The guns feel great, they just feel "right", there's a lot of customization going on and you'll be checking every corpse to see if there's a better item.
On the other side, you might have a problem enjoying this due to the p*ss poor optimization. On my PC, it doesn't really matter if I play on the lowest, or the ultra settings. So I just play on ultra and have the same performance as if the game looked like a piece of horse turd.
The story and overall writing is quite bland at times and doesn't really drive you forward. I found myself just sprinting to the next city to see what happens there, ignoring the sidequests thrown at me.
When I first opened the PipBoy radio and tuned in to it, I found that they added some of the old songs from previous games- and quite frankly, it felt really weird- like it didn't belong. That's how different this game feels.
In conclusion- don't buy this if you expect a true Fallout game. Although, it has been quite obvious since Fallout 3 that Bethesda isn't planning to reproduce the Interplay/Black Isle formula. If you're up for some shooting and crafting, with some Fallout feeling sprinkled on top- I think it's well worth it on sale. But it's even less Fallout than Fallout 3- honestly, it feels a bit more like Borderlands to me, just a tad more realistic and added crafting- and unfortunately, missing a lot of the famous Fallout humour.
As for me- after the free weekend, I have decided to buy it. I realized that I just wanted more Fallout. And I'm glad that I did it. Maybe it's just nostalgia- but it feels good to be back.

Dark Souls 1 was good because of the combat, the art style, the lore, the characters, the questlines, the map design, and the challenge.
Dark Souls 3 has the same combat, more or less. Decent art style but nothing special. The lore, characters, questlines, map design and challenge are all quite lacking however.
IMO, get Dark Souls 1 instead and use DSFix, a HD texture pack, and a sweetfx pack (legacy from NexusMods imo).
If you're into pvp: imo, play an actual pvp game like a moba, an rts, or a fighting game. You can't invade w/o ending up in a 2v1 in this game, and the netcode is hilariously bad.
But if you're new to the series, and just want to hack stuff up as a knight or a thief in a visually appealing game with really solid combat, and want to PvP in this type of game, this is stil a good game and has an active community behind it.

I do not play MMORPGs, so it's special when I say I play Spiral Knights. It's kept extremely simple, which makes it a great casual game that I can pick up and drop off without intense involvement. This is a good pizza-and-mouse game, meaning you can play one-handed due to the simplicity of the controls. It's a nice, calm, relaxing game, with stretches of tension and frustration. It's FtP, so there's limits on how much you can do in a 24 hour span, which kind of helps keeps me from seeing the limitations of the campaign missions. The skirmish missions are always different, but to clear a campaign, you must fight the same enemies on the same map. It has a difficulty spike in some areas. I love the visual design, and the music is an awesome combination of eight-bit and chill. Some of the collecting and trading aspects are difficult, as it isn't always easy to find someone who will buy what you want, even though it is extremely easy to buy items from others at the sub-ten tiers.  8.5/10.

From the equipment system, to the weapon system that has been improved on(for better or worse is up for debate). The Miracles, Spells, and Hexs that can be used on their own, or in conjunction to one's weapons, or with a primable spell make a diverse mix of content leaving room for a player to discover different challenges, and methods of attack. Though the game itself offers little room for straying from the path, the journey through a vaguely doomed kingdom, or once forgotten land, or a cursed residence is an adventure. Much of the game centers itself around the online, and very active community, where players can fight each other, or help each other meet a common goal (advance further), all while having diverse ways of approaching a fight. This installment of the series is supposedly the last entry. Dark Souls may be done, but much is expected from the creators after this.

So I've played this for quite a while, and I still recommend it. However, I do still have some reservations about it.
1) The combat is very basic. There's not much to it. It gets repetitive pretty fast.
2) The characters, while diverse lore wise and story wise, lack action variety. For example, the Leper and Crusader generally do the same thing, their stats are just different. Because of this, party variety isn't as deep as it could be. You can generally get away with any party and play just about the same way.
3) The dungeons are mechanically walking simulators. Once you know how to interact with certain objects, they lose their charm. I spend so much time looking at the map instead of the artwork and background, simply because there's no reason to look at the background; there are no "secrets". Dungeon variety is limited to different pathways and different curio/enemy spawns. All maps essentially play the same regardless.
4) Mission variety is lacking. You can visit 90% of rooms in a dungeon, complete 100% of room battles, or pick up/drop off items in dungeons. They all generally end up with the player visiting nearly all the rooms anyways.
5) It is not actually a difficult game. I sit back and play this when I want to chill out and just get lost in the atmosphere. It's not hard to set up parties for the respective dungeons, as most dungeons have a certain quirk that can be countered and exploited with trinkets (eg the "Ruins" has a lot of Unholy enemies, so you can stack unholy specific troops and trinkets). RNG plays a role, but your chances to hit are rarely ever ridiculous (they generally stay above 70+, disregarding the Leper), leading to generally successful hits and very few strings of misses, if any.
All this being said, I still like the game. I understand why people are disappointed with the game and all of its failings. If any of the above is a deal breaker for you, feel free to disagree with my recommendation.

This game will force you to make difficult choices. The game drops you in an estate with a ruined town, very little money, and only a few glory hungry fools at your command.  Every step will be paid for in blood and you have no choice but to move forward regardless.  You will need to see everything in context and pick what is worth preserving and what resource is the most important at the time.
I won’t go deep into exactly how the game and all its mechanics work because,
1: it’s early access and might change
2: half the fun is figuring those things out and mastering them
This game pulls no punches, there is no easy mode here and you will lose adventurers but with each quest done you learn more and get better at the game.  You figure out what the cultists moves are, how to build a strong party, how to respond to finding an iron madden, etc.  Sometimes, even the most prepared party gets messed up by the random factor but that just make every win feel real, significant and earned.  The entire appeal of this game for me is plucking victories from the gaping maw of crushing defeat no matter the cost and making the best of a bad situation.  To push an adventure gone bad just a little bit farther, to get through just one more room and somehow eek out that victory after losing your healer in the 3rd fight feels so satisfying.
This game will challenge you.  This game will most likely frustrate you at some points.  But I think that this game is defiantly worth the time to play if you enjoy dark and unique worlds, easy to understand yet deep mechanics, and being challenged in a way few other games do.

For every "Yes", add 5% to the score, starting at 65%.
As others have mentioned, this is a great game, but has not much to do with Fallout. If I scored this as a Fallout game, I would say it's a disaster.
However- if you don't look at it as a Fallout game, it's actually quite awesome.
I'm saying that as someone whose first memorable game on a CD was Fallout 1 demo with Junktown back in the day... and who has played Fallout 2 approximately 20 times.
It is a refreshing change. This game is more like a shooter. Don't expect a strong story or role playing aspects. Look at it like a post-apocalyptic shooter with some fun crafting. That's all it is.
The gun play is amazing. One of the best I've ever seen. The guns feel great, they just feel "right", there's a lot of customization going on and you'll be checking every corpse to see if there's a better item.
On the other side, you might have a problem enjoying this due to the p*ss poor optimization. On my PC, it doesn't really matter if I play on the lowest, or the ultra settings. So I just play on ultra and have the same performance as if the game looked like a piece of horse turd.
The story and overall writing is quite bland at times and doesn't really drive you forward. I found myself just sprinting to the next city to see what happens there, ignoring the sidequests thrown at me.
When I first opened the PipBoy radio and tuned in to it, I found that they added some of the old songs from previous games- and quite frankly, it felt really weird- like it didn't belong. That's how different this game feels.
In conclusion- don't buy this if you expect a true Fallout game. Although, it has been quite obvious since Fallout 3 that Bethesda isn't planning to reproduce the Interplay/Black Isle formula. If you're up for some shooting and crafting, with some Fallout feeling sprinkled on top- I think it's well worth it on sale. But it's even less Fallout than Fallout 3- honestly, it feels a bit more like Borderlands to me, just a tad more realistic and added crafting- and unfortunately, missing a lot of the famous Fallout humour.
As for me- after the free weekend, I have decided to buy it. I realized that I just wanted more Fallout. And I'm glad that I did it. Maybe it's just nostalgia- but it feels good to be back.

Pretty much exactly as underwhelming as I expected this to be. If you didn't like Fallout 3, this game is actually worse in most respects. If you did like Fallout 3, this game is still worse. Fortunately, the free weekend permitted me to waste only my time on this and not my money.
Gunplay is unsatisfying and tedious. Over-the-top gore doesn't make up for poor enemy scaling and weapons that have no real impact. Shooting things is what you're doing about 90% of the time, so this isn't something that can really be ignored. Stealth is utter garbage, as I have come to expect, so it's basically a non-factor. You run into fights, try to hide behind cover in the environment, and fire your little pea shooter at the usual cast of Fallout enemies. Or you can use VATS, the still uninteresting nod to the actually good combat of the first two Fallout games.
The move to a voiced protagonist adds nothing to the game but limitations. Another change at the expense of depth to appeal to the lowest common denominator.
The writing is awful. Bad plot, bad dialogue (and often mediocre VO as well). I'm getting pretty tired of player character-centered narratives that come up with contrived excuse to make you the distinguished leader of something or another, despite having done nothing and being a nobody. Role-playing and meaningful choice are similarly absent, but at least they voiced a bunch of common player names! Innovation!
The enemy scaling is trash. I'm not a fan of this practice in general, but this game does not do it well. It's not Oblivion levels of bad, but it is a detriment to the game.

And to top it off, this is a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor PC port with forced Vertical Sync and hacked together console menus, complete with using enter to confirm menu selections. If you force VSync off externally, you get to experience the reality that their physics simulation is tied to framerate. This is particularly noticeable because, as usual for BGS games, this game is horrendously optimized, so framerates for me have gone from the 30s to 200 (with the lockpicking screen going over 800 before I capped the framerate), with my character's movement speed varying all the while.  And because they're still hacking together their games on yet another modification of the Gambryo engine, the game doesn't look good anyway, particularly the animations which are the usual stilted, awkward mediocrity one would expect from the once respectable developers of the good Elder Scrolls games.
Sorry, Todd, but this kind of mediocrity doesn't cut it anymore with companies like CD Projekt RED doing everything better. I will not be purchasing this game.

Spiral knights is an ARPG with a third person viewpoint locked on your character. The player character has various choices of equipment that are aquired through crafting, trading, purchasing or sometimes rarely through random drops. Various types of equipment change the way you play the game and approach and deal with enemies.
Grinding is a very large part of the game, whether it be for resources or experiance(heat), which eventually decreases in enjoyment the longer you play due to the insanely long leveling process on rank 5 equipment.
The development time taken between meaningful content updates is, and I cannot emphasise this enough, VERY long. The update schedule is so infrequent that it would not surprise me to see if there are no content updates that werent purely cosmetic or repeats for over 6 months.
Although the game has a fantastic aesthetic style, I cannot recommend this game.

This game will force you to make difficult choices. The game drops you in an estate with a ruined town, very little money, and only a few glory hungry fools at your command.  Every step will be paid for in blood and you have no choice but to move forward regardless.  You will need to see everything in context and pick what is worth preserving and what resource is the most important at the time.
I won’t go deep into exactly how the game and all its mechanics work because,
1: it’s early access and might change
2: half the fun is figuring those things out and mastering them
This game pulls no punches, there is no easy mode here and you will lose adventurers but with each quest done you learn more and get better at the game.  You figure out what the cultists moves are, how to build a strong party, how to respond to finding an iron madden, etc.  Sometimes, even the most prepared party gets messed up by the random factor but that just make every win feel real, significant and earned.  The entire appeal of this game for me is plucking victories from the gaping maw of crushing defeat no matter the cost and making the best of a bad situation.  To push an adventure gone bad just a little bit farther, to get through just one more room and somehow eek out that victory after losing your healer in the 3rd fight feels so satisfying.
This game will challenge you.  This game will most likely frustrate you at some points.  But I think that this game is defiantly worth the time to play if you enjoy dark and unique worlds, easy to understand yet deep mechanics, and being challenged in a way few other games do.

Dark Souls III is a challenging game series. Not because it's hard, but because of it's design that makes it's approach difficult, and it's gameplay varied. From the equipment system, to the weapon system that has been improved on(for better or worse is up for debate). The Miracles, Spells, and Hexs that can be used on their own, or in conjunction to one's weapons, or with a primable spell make a diverse mix of content leaving room for a player to discover different challenges, and methods of attack. Though the game itself offers little room for straying from the path, the journey through a vaguely doomed kingdom, or once forgotten land, or a cursed residence is an adventure. Much of the game centers itself around the online, and very active community, where players can fight each other, or help each other meet a common goal (advance further), all while having diverse ways of approaching a fight. This installment of the series is supposedly the last entry. Dark Souls may be done, but much is expected from the creators after this.

, and yes I still say it post Corpse and Hound. I picked this game up right after its release and unlike most people I like it now more than I did before, allow me to explain why this game is easily worth the $20.

Pros:
-Free

-Constant Updates
-Haven't come across hacker in months
-Cant see game dying for a considerable amount of time
-Can do bootleg CS:GO style unboxings
-Easy to make private/public server to play with friends

Cons:

-If you look to start server know that getting traffic is difficult with the endless amounts on some maps.
-Shooting mechanics involve bullet drop but very small amount of recoil on most guns.
-Ingame group system results in safe teamups which reduces that instability or anxiety usually had in survival games between players.
Overall I do enjoy the game but dont see it as anything more than an arcadey shooter in either arena or modded server. However, the options to play it as a (free) game similar to Dayz or Miscreated. The game has simplified versions of farming, vehicle repair, and weapon attachments, Rust style building. I would actually go as far to bet that this FREE game has more features than any person would expect. Does it execute them all well is another bet. As I said before most systems in place are very simple. With the right group of players on a good server you can surely lose yourself and overcome the small learning curve in an openworld zombie survival game. Or go into the arena mode duke it out in maps of varying sizes. At the end of the day the game is free. Which means a review isn't really necessary since you can just check it out for yourself ;)

Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based RPG game about psychological stresses of adventuring, recuritting, trainning, and leading a team in dark and horrifying dungeons to defeat death and horror face to face.
The game is beautiful of it's oldschool and legendary atmosphere of castles, where you get throwed deep into the game and it's introduction of unimaginable horror. Currently you have 13 heros to choose between to fight the enemies. The 3 dungeon envireoments will give you plenty of  time to explore and fight the dozens of monsters with more than 130 items, that either are bought, found or sold by vendors, If you have gold and items in your inventory and die with your team, they will be gorn. If you leave a quests, it will effect your heroes and current progress.
You fight to protect the good and restore humanity in the forgotten worlds. Every fight agens evil will give you points/actions you can do to either stun, kill, debuff, heal etc, friendly or deadly while passing traps. The town you support has . Stage coach, where you recruit new heroes, Tavern/Abby, to stress relief, Sanitarium, that treat quirks and diseases, Guild, too upgrade combat skills, Blacksmith, too upgrade weapons and armor, and a nomad wagon, where you complete quests to unlock.
Overall, a interesting and well looking turn-based game. So If you like turn-based games, with a oldschool environment with deadly enemies and special abilitys between 13+ and more heroes to comes. Then this game is for you.

-Shooting mechanics involve bullet drop but very small amount of recoil on most guns.
-Ingame group system results in safe teamups which reduces that instability or anxiety usually had in survival games between players.
Overall I do enjoy the game but dont see it as anything more than an arcadey shooter in either arena or modded server. However, the options to play it as a (free) game similar to Dayz or Miscreated. The game has simplified versions of farming, vehicle repair, and weapon attachments, Rust style building. I would actually go as far to bet that this FREE game has more features than any person would expect. Does it execute them all well is another bet. As I said before most systems in place are very simple. With the right group of players on a good server you can surely lose yourself and overcome the small learning curve in an openworld zombie survival game. There isnt any game that will make me feel as connected to my character as much as the Soulsborne Series has. But specifically, Dark souls 1-3.
Now dont let my play time decieve you, ive easily played this 3-4x more than the playtime suggests (I also own it on PS4)
As such is has a special place in my heart, it might not be the best game the bosses not as hard as some but i made a character and that character i have never had a better representation of my self in any game and ill explain why.
In August 2012 i bought a copy of Dark Souls "Prepare to die" Edition. i was going through a hump and honestly retreated further back into video games than i did previously, I remember putting the game on my PC and dealing with the buggy Microsoft Windows Platform but i kept going, I made my character look like me like i always do after the back tingling sensation the opening cut scene gave me. The witches of izalith with thier chaotic flame, Gwyn smiting the dragons, Nito moving with his wrathful stance.
And the Pygmy, With his Dark Soul. Sharing it with others. Humanity.
From that moment i knew i was in for a hell of a good time. I was wrong obviously dark souls stomped me into the ground but eventually i got the hang of it, Buggy controls or not i had fun, Not just playing the game but reading desciptions of items trying to scrounge up what the lore ment and filling in the gaps that i missed. I wanted more and more, the story was great even if it wasnt offered up straight to you and you had to look for it, and i think thats probably why it was great.
Miyazaki once said in an interview that he made dark souls in a similar way to what he experienced as a child, Growing up he had a lot of time alone and he spent it reading, He loved it but his favorite books were those about the knight who goes on daring quests to save a princess or slay a dragon and find treasure, However these books were in english and so he didnt understand them completely, a lot of the information was missing and he filled in the blanks with his day dreams of how HE wanted the story to go. imagining the hardships the knight must have gone through to get to where he was, and he couldnt have done it in a better way than what he did with dark souls, He made a community of people who feverishly try to fill in the blanks of the story even so complex that it makes your head spin.
Then there was Dark Souls 2. I continued the fantasy and made my character look like me again, Making it a continuation of my characters story -
SPOILERS
To be fair Dark souls 2's story was lacking more than everyone expected but it was still a great game, the controls were more optimized so the game itself didnt seem as hard and the opening cutscene was great, i got goosebumps when the old firekeeper said "And like a moth to the flame your wings will burn in anguish, Time and Time again" and that was very true to the game we kept going for more even though you would get that angry sensation to just put it down and not pick it up. but you always do.
Then theres Dark Souls 3. To me the true Dark Souls 2 is the third, a perfect continuation of the story from the first, probably due to Miyazaki having more influence on this game and not being distracted with a different project (Bloodborne if i recall) and it continued the story for me perfectly, from beginning to end Dark Souls 3 has made me feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ I always ALWAYS start Deprived (recommend it to everyone even if you're just starting) because i enjoy the feeling of starting from scratch and tearing my way through challenges to distract me from my challenges in life, i enjoy the struggle and Dark souls 3 Gave me a good fight but like every challenge its there to be completed. and with the release of The Ringed City and Dark Souls 3 : The Fire Fades  Edition the series will sadly be put to rest and to me it will go down in my history as the game that pulled me through depression because even though its hard when i felt like i couldnt accomplish anything in my life the Dark Souls franchise showed me that if i kept trying eventually i could pull through.
SPOILERS
Thank you Miyazaki And FromSoftware as a whole. For this trilogy, For the DLC. For the adventures and the times i spent jolly co-operating. For helping me pull through. For the Fantasy of Struggle. Thank you.

Not so Ambitious a game, as Bethesda would have you believe.
Bear with me - I've been inside this franchise since the time it was the pre-Fallout Wasteland game, have played all versions of Fallout since the beginning, and admittedly am biased toward the "dark" presentation experienced when Fallout series first went to an FPS format, in Fallout 3.
This Fallout 4 - in my opinion has many flaws in its artistic presentation, storyline, and technical aspects of gameplay.  Where to begin to unravel the so-called ambitiousness of Bethesda and F4:
- Too cartoony.  Bethesda, you had a great thing going with the dark aspects of F3, and instead you've tuned up the game to become a colorful mess.  From an artistic standpoint, you made too much attempt to put color into this game.  The darkness, bleakness of F3 should be reverted to, for any/all future version of Fallout games.  Get out of the cities, make the game somewhere you don't live and work, somewhere you don't know much about, because that's another issue I have with it (too many Dev's apparently wanted to get their personal/pet project of local area into this F4 game...).
- Too much gifting of everything up front.  No effort to find the dog, find first Power Armor, and companions in general.  Almost too many choices.  It's one thing to attempt a sandbox - it's another thing to shove all possible toys into the sandbox when you start playing.  Doesn't come off well.
- Storyline.  Pathetic.  This guy was military, but then you have him ask basic questions like a doofus who can't do basic math.  You should have offered varying starting backgrounds, left it neutral, or -- if you do make him military background, then give him dialogue that matches such.  Instead, you portray him as prior military hero but he has dialogue options that look like a pencil-pushing, passive geek in a cubicle (oh I forgot, that's where you do coding from...).
- Power Armor.  Not powerful.  You get Power Armor right away, yet it really doesn't protect you.  I modded my suit up to 45C (2 upgrades w/Armor 1 and Science 1) soon as I could, didn't use Power Armor until fully repaired and upgraded, to spare it for a trip to the city.  Very disappointed - couldn't make it halfway to the city without dogs and mosquitos biting through the suit - really?  So, this suit of armor that helped fight in all-out conventional war, could not possible stop the bite of a dog or the small stinger of a mosquito??  You really needed to work on basic Damage Reduction (DR) coding on this one.  It's not about reducing damage - you should have had the Power Armors have minimum DR thresholds so no damage is received if the source is from below a certain damage point.  You should be able to stand in the middle of a pack of dogs in Power Armor, and laugh at them.  Instead, you've coded in DR so you slowly die in Power Armor.  Silly.
- Crafting.  What bugs me the most about this crafting system, is that it appears to be so detailed, that it obviously took much of your available manhours for coding the game.  As result, it's nothing but a technical distraction that probably pacifies the average gamer out there who likes crafting only, and helps to alleviate all the flaws in my prior comments (storyline, cartoonish appearance, and technical gameplay flaws).  So, I build a Spotlight, that gives 2 Defense to my new town -- and it's on a pathetically short 4 foot high stand, instead of being on a pole like normal defensive lighting is.  Defensive guns - articulate all of about 30-45 degrees left and right, hardly useful and no way to open them up.  What's most odd about the crafting system, is that you can make just about anything that you can also deconstruct.  But why/how can I make Aircraft seating at my crafting station, from raw materials?  Really?  I can smelt aluminum and forge/cast it into aluminum aircraft seating??  And not a single extra bit of time involved, either.    So, Bethesda, what you introduced here, in this non-magic game, is -- magic.  I can magically create junk in an instant, as long as I have the materials.  Oh, and I can magically deconstruct things in an instant also.
- Social themes/memes and biases embedded in the game.  So, you went there, Bethesda.  You just had to get as much additional environmentalist propaganda, social propaganda, and anti-business propaganda, all packaged into this game.  War never changes?  Howabout a new phrase, given that you seem to have changed the "theme" of Fallout series into your own pedestal to spew your worldview on your customers.  Who comes up with this drivel that they think is sacrosanct?  You just had to put the Vault-Tec company in a bad light for this one also, eh?  We can't have any survivalist types shown as caring people, they always have to be money-grubbing and up to something?
- Nuclear physics issues.  Without going into great detail, I must simply say, that you clearly did not have knowledgeable nuclear physicists advising you on this game.  200 years later, and you still have residual radiation? Really?  Ever heard of half-lives of nuclear material, and what happens over a 200 year period?  If you wanted to be ambitious, then you should have had more detail and accuracy for nuclear effects and residual material affects within this game.
- Inner City is not a Sandbox.  Probably my biggest disappointment.  I get to the "big city" and think - Bethesda will have made it a huge sandbox.  Here's what you forgot, Bethesda - to make each and every building accessible!!!  Over half of the buildings have boards over the doors and windows.  For once, I thought we were about to get a true urban sandbox, but no - mostly just quest buildings sprinkled about a mostly inaccessible city scape.  Maybe some of the manhours spent on the detailed crafting system could have been better applied to the city sandbox aspect.
- DJ. Pathetic.  We went from the coolness of 3-Dog to a lame, cubicle bound IT professional who comes off as a make-shift voice actor, subbing as a video game's DJ.  Poor entry for the game, doesn't set the tone well.  So annoying, I actually had to off tune the radio channel after a while.  Useless info, mostly same songs as prior games, and with some annoying commentary about the songs.  You could have quadrupled the library of songs, but instead you have only a handful of new songs in addition to many of the same from prior games.
- Not dirty enough.  What I mean by that, you have people that could only wash themselves rarely, if your version of radiated water were the norm (not irradiated, btw, you use incorrect terminology to describe radiation).  The people - aren't dirty enough, such as we saw in F3.  A news reporter that is all glammed up, wearing a leather coat, well-trimmed hair, makeup, carrying just a pistol, and can waltz around outside the city gathering information in a literal war-zone filled with super-mutants, Raider sects, ghouls, etc.?  Really?  A bit pro-media, are we?  Let's get more real characters into the Fallout series, and less of this mythical, illogical stuff you're pushing.
- Drugs and ESP/Magic beyond reason.  The Fallout series has been a bit pro-drug use for a while now, and if you were to become more socially conscious, it could be to whittle down the interaction of drugs with progression in the game.  The Mama Murphy pro-drug story arc is flat out dumb.  You're insinuating several things in that arc: that drugs can be justified, that ESP could be real and could be assisted by drugs.  As a freedom loving American, I'm against warning labels and such, but I'd make a rare exception for this game - it encourages virtual drug use and drug involvement for the story arc(s).
I will update this again, if I get more time and I actually play this game more, but as of now - I probably won't spend much time in this game.

Short Review:  7/10.  Buy if one sale.
Long version:  Darkest dungeon is a roguelike dungeon crawler.  You recruit heros and try to level them up (with varying degrees of sucess) in the various dungeons.  Completing a quest will give your guys some loot.  All pretty standard stuff.
Like pretty much all RPG's, you will spend a lot of time grinding through dungeons, trying to level up characters.  These characters take a lot of money to upgrade.  Bad quirks have to be removed.  Good quirks locked in.  Deseases need to be cured.  Weapons need to be upgraded.  Abilities need to be upgraded.  You can easily drop a large fortune in gold on an individual character, especially your level 6 'high end' champions, who you pamper and give only the best.  Be warned though, RNG is a cold hard mistress who isn't afraid to kill your characters.  Sometimes she'll slap you and you deserve it.  Sometimes you'll be doing everything right, playing it safe, and you'll still get dicked.  We all get greedy sometimes, it happens.  We all occassionally set out without the proper equipment, or go on 'dark runs' with all damage characters and no healers.  My point is, there are times when RNG is genuinely justified in obliterating your team.  But then there are those other times.  Let me give you an example.  I'm fighting a brigand 16 pounder with a team of all lvl 6's.  I've got 2 damage dealers, a tank, and a healer.  Plenty of supplies, best trinkets equipped.  Each round, my two damages take out the match stick man.  Healer keeps people well healed.  Extra damage goes to the boss itself, ignoring the small fries.  This is the safest way to kill this boss.  Well both my damage dealers miss the match man.  Match man lights fuse.  I dodge buff my crew in anticipation for shot.  Shot misses everyone but my healer who goes from full health to death's door.  I have 2 characters with healing skills 1 with a guard skill, so next time i get the chance, i'm pulling her back from the edge.  Well wouldn't you know it, before I get the chance, she gets hit with a scattershot for 1 damage and dies.  My point is this, even if you 'learn the game' and take precautions, every now and then, the odds still won't break in your favor and you'll loose someone.  And if that someone represents a significant gold investment, tough tiddies.
Other points to note: There is a definite muffin top to the game.  Once you get your guys get strong enough to do high level missions, collect the right trinkets, and upgraded all the buildings, you can really start crushing the game and building a fortune.  You start getting fat (stacks).  Personally I enjoy this.  What's the point of grinding it out if the rewards don’t help?  In all fairness some of your currency does become useless, (all non-gold currency is worthless when you've upgraded all buildings)
Unfortunately the pendulum of updates has swung a little too hard on on the side or nurfed trinkets. That comfortable muffin top has just shrunk a whole bunch, and a lot of people are butt hurt over the whole thing.  That being said, the DD developers have been very receptive (on the whole) to the community, and I for one have faith they will fix it eventually.  Right now I'm just waiting around for the tide to turn so I can get my Level 6's off the bench again and into the game.
If certain things get fixed or added, i would change to a buy at full price.  As it is though, pick up this game at 50% off.  It's worth the price at $10. $20 seems a bit much unless you are a REALLY big fan of Dungeon Crawling RPG's.
Some big pros:
-Stylistic game, cool looking characters, dungeons, etc.
-some diversity between characters.
-receptive Devs who appear to genuinely care what the community say/think.  (they haven't grown large♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out of their forheads just yet at least)
-interesting story line,
-narrator’s voice is chocolate fun times.
Some big Cons:
-Recent updates put a damper on things. (protection is the devil, new trinks are useless)
-RN-Jesus is not your friend.
-Some lack of characters/enemies.  Characters of the same class are exactly the same.  (i expect enemies at least to be added slowly over time to an acceptable number)
- There is little mission variety.  Regions are slightly different (different enemies), but with the exception of boss battles, every mission either is the same or feels the exact same.
Things I want added:
-Customizable towns.  (gives me something to do with my hard earned seals, crests, etc.)
-Heros that feel more like individuals rather than being defined so much by their class.  (I'm not lying, class IS hero, there is no difference between 2 same level, same class characters)
-More enemies, more champs, etc.
-More narrator voice, because it's awesome.
-Balanced Classes.  Some are useless, some are situational, others are auto drafts for almost every party.
-different gendered characters?

If you've read the reviews recently, you may be deterred from buying this game due to one recent feature: corpses. This is the one feature that has split the community. Do they add more strategic elements, or are they just there to waste time while you take more damage? As someone that came in AFTER corpses were added, I'd go with the former.
For those that are thinking of buying this game, let me give you a bit of info. Enemies can leave behind corpses as of recently, which will then take their place. They are completely harmless, but their presence can prevent you from using certain abilities until they are destroyed due to the placement battle system. However, it only takes a bit of pre-planning before embarking to create a balanced party, and some strategic thinking while in battle to render them practically non-existent. Going with brute force will only get you so far, but thinking clearly about your actions will win you the battle. Even better, some characters have abilities that can instantly remove all corpses on the field.
The only thing that I felt was a real issue was that you could actually miss corpses. Thankfully, the most recent patch removed this.
In conclusion, if you're still having second thoughts about this game, I recommend giving it a go. This game is still in Early Access but has dedicated developers, so simply leaving feedback about a feature you don't like can go a long way.

There are much better, more in depth reviews on here, so I'll keep mine brief-ish.
Playing Darkest Dungeon, at least at the moment, is like going to the casino; the house always wins.
In the patch notes, the developers mention players breaking the game to the point that it's insanely easy. I'd like to know how many people this includes, because it, again, feels much like a visit to the casino: a handful of people win. Everyone else loses.
I've reached a point where I'm not sure the game takes much skill, but rather getting on your knees, praying, and then realizing it does nothing.
I still like the game. I like the corpses, even--it was frustrating working a monster to the front only for ranged characters to have nothing to do. It can be good. At the moment, however, it's kinda not. And that's my review as it stands. Lots of design decisions that could be good, but just aren't really.
Also: while I understand most of the new classes, when first introduced, were OP, the houndmaster strikes me as the absolute worst. I could be missing something, but a group, 1 bleed attack is just worthless. Yes, he can lower protection--another questionable  recently impelentated mechanic--but on the whole he feels like a waste of a slot, and only helps to drag battles on longer. And, given that time and chance are your two biggest obstacles every step of the way, you're better off bringing along someone stronger, who can take enemies out faster.
So much for keeping it short. But, if you're interested in the game, ask yourself: how salty do I get? If you get very salty at games, move along. It's not worth the frustration. And that's my real complaint. The developers need to find a balance between their vision and something that's actually fun to play. Unless you like losing money at the casino, find something cheaper, and more rewarding. Something that you feel like you've earned through skill, perhaps, and not just dumb luck.
But also know that while I'm not recommending the game, I kinda am. This game could be amazing. Maybe it even was, at one point. Hopefully it will at least be somewhat fun again.

Quick and to-the-point review:
Pros:
- Hard but fair system. It's easy to understand why your terrible decisions led to the extermination of your whole party.
- Great pacing and timing.
- The random dungeons are quite good.
- "Just one more time....". Dungeoneering is quite addictive
- Music is quite Good and moody
- The way autosave works - you can stop at any moment of the game and this system is nearly exploit-proof, so it still feels really scary to go bad on an expedition AND you don't need to wait one hour to save the game.
Borderline:
- Narration is good but you'll get really tired of it after 20+ hours
- It might be really frustrating at start. But it's quite sactisfatory to look at your own progress.
Cons:
- Some aspects of battle are quite annoying. Such as the lack of Initiative order (wich forces some rather arbitrary decisions) and the often weird AI Behaviour (it seems more random than a state machine behaviour). Also, it's filled with tiny exploits such as retreating after your party is ambushed.
- When you go down, it takes a long time to get back up. Loosing a party at the beggining of the game is a problem that might take you more than two hours to solve.
- [early access only] it kinda halts too soon, but it's ok as long as the full game doesn't take way too long to come by.
That said, full thumbs up for this game! I'm craving for the full version

I started playing Darkest Dungeon about a month ago, soon after the Houndmaster update.  The gameplay and narration are excellent and I think the graphics/battle animations are superb, as well.  The storyline reminds me of H.P. Lovecraft's "The Rats In The Walls" and that's a great thing!  Kudos to Red Hook on capturing the same dark, dreary feel.
I found the game to be very difficult early on because I was trying to save all of the party members after each mission and didn't have enough gold to fix all of their problems.  Once I accepted that the level 0-1 characters were simply cannon fodder to use for the greater good of the Hamlet (sending out on no provision runs to gather gold/resources and then dismissing the entire party afterwards), the game became easier.  Using the gold to fund real mission and item/ability upgrades for my main characters, I slowly built up my roster and continued doing no provision runs when my core teams required rest.
Now, I have a full roster of upgraded (though not max level) characters.  The days of no provision runs with new recruits is over but they served their purpose.  My "A-Team" (Grave Robber/Vestal/Crusader/Man-at-Arms) is level 5 and has completed several Champion runs; the remaining heroes are level 3-4 and are capable of completing the Veteran runs in various party combinations.
In my opinion, the best classes are the Man-at-Arms and the Vestal; I haven't had any success with the Occultist or the Plague Doctor.  It seems like the Occultist's heal fails at a critical time and isn't worth the risk, the Vestal has proven to be a more reliable healer.  The Plague Doctor hasn't been a strong enough healer or damage dealer in my expeience; I'd take the Vestal/Crusader for healing or just about anything else (Arbalest/Bountry Hunter/Grave Robber/Highway Man) for damage dealing, over the Plague Doctor.
Would I recommend this game to others?  Absolutely!  For only $20 (about the same price as a movie or two at the theater), I've had over 70 hours of enjoyment and I am looking forward to the next 70+ hours of gameplay.

Being a M@$$hole myself, I was excited when I found out that Fallout 4 was going to be set in and around post-apocalyptic Boston. Unfortunately, my excitement quickly turned to disappointment. That isn't to say this game is terrible. But comparing New Vegas to Fallout 4 is like comparing a filet mignon steak to Dinty Moore beef. There is some fun to be had with it. However, I am in no rush to purchase this game as I already own the far superior New Vegas.  In short, I do not recommend this game at full price and suggest that you do as I am and wait for the Game of the Year edition to go on sale in a couple years or so. If you haven't played New Vegas, get that instead for now.
Just so I don't appear to be a pessimist, and because (as I've stated) I do enjoy some aspects of this game, let's start with what I think is good:
VATS are now executed in slowed down action mode rather than stopping time altogether. I think this makes the fights more fun/challenging. IMO weapons are handled better overall and the fights are sometimes more fun this time around. The crafting system is also much improved over what was available in Skyrim.
Now what I don't like:
The biggest problem I have with this game is it doesn't seem to know what it wants to be. Each game Bethesda makes seems to slip further away from their roleplaying roots. This is more like a mediocre Adventure/FPS hybrid game with some rudimentary RPG elements and weird Minecraft stuff thrown in for some reason. In New Vegas, you can play pretty much however you want. But in this, you have the "Play how we want you to while we give you the illusion of choice" approach that Bethesda has unfortunately become known for in their recent offerings. There are also a couple of things from previous games that are annoyingly missing, such as the Karma system and the wait button (you now have to find a chair or something similar that you do NOT own).
Another user review stated that the world in New Vegas was more exciting (and it was a desert). I remember laughing when I read that, but now that I have played this I absolutely agree. This world just seems pretty empty and half@$$ed. A lot of the buildings I've seen are just for show, and there is no way to enter them.
Another issue (as others pointed out) is Bethesda's poorly ripped version of the Bioware dialogue system. Sometimes you only get 1 word that is too vague to understand what the character is going to say (or even what might happen if you pick that choice). Before, you had full lines of dialogue to read and conversations just made more sense.
Oh, and I want to kill that nerdy DJ on the radio. Definitely not as good as previous Fallout radio hosts.

This game is very, very good. It started out as a rogue-like with heavy Lovecraftian influences. Great artwork, soundtrack, and very cool and novel concepts such as "stress", "light levels", and encouraging team work. Sometimes you had to sacrifice a beloved character in order for the rest of the team to finish and level up. No problem there, it actually gave the game personality and added depth to the story. All of these great things are still in the game, but...
The game went really off-balance in the July 15 Build Update. Enemies get major boosts in crit damage and frequency, so most of your turns you will be healing. I get the idea behind having a corpse in the way after defeating an enemy, but when 2-3 hits to get rid of it, it gets annoying. Also, I like the fact that you can now die from stress. But, in a dungeon, stress builds up WAY faster than you can get rid of it. And you can only do so in:
a) Battle- Some characters can heal stress. During battle is when stress builds up the most, and the amount of stress healed is mostly insignificant.
b) Camps- A lot of stress can be relieved here, but you can camp only so many times, and it can feel like a waste of resources if your HP are still high with a long road ahead of you.
So good luck with not dying of a heart attack during long dungeons. Please, add a stress relieving item if you are going to have stress be such a major issue.
I know this is still Early Access, but hopefully developers pay more attention to negative reviews and actually do something about these issues. Avoid raging at your monitor and come back when these things are fixed.

With the final DLC pack finally out, I feel now is the most appropriate time to write my review for this game.
Dark Souls III is the 3rd and final game in the critically acclaimed Dark Souls franchise. Taking place in the Kingdom of Lothric, the Age of Fire is once again at a close. However, the one chosen to link the flame refuses to do so, and previous Lords of Cinder are resurrected from their graves to rekindle the fire once again. All of these Lords refuse to do so, and for the first time in the history of Dark Souls, undead who attempted and failed to link the fire are ressurected as a last ditch effort to save the flame. This is where you come in.
Lothric is known as the Transitory Land, where space and time converge into a single area. This causes the landscape to be vastly different from area to area. For example, one second you're in a swamp, and the next you're in a beautiful city of frost. The time distortion also allows areas from previous games to show up, and it's a real trip to see areas from before.
There are 19 bosses in the base game, 3 or 4 mini-bosses, 2 bosses in the first DLC, and 4 in the second. These bosses are more often than not quite difficult, but about 4 or 5 are extremely easy or gimmicky and end up leaving a sour taste in your mouth. This still leaves about 15 bosses that will give even veteran players trouble, as the learning curve for this game is steeper than the previous games, with bosses getting significantly harder at the first Lord of Cinder. The first boss is also the most difficult first boss in any game previous. This can turn some players away, but veterans and new players who beat this boss are in for the game of their life.
The pacing of this game is obviously very influenced by Bloodborne, and is much quicker paced than the previous 2 games. Rolling is the best option for avoiding attacks, as most bosses and enemies have multiple swings in a single attack cycle, and will deplete your stamina if using a shield.
Speaking of Bloodborne, weapons now have what is known as "Weapon Arts", which use the newly re-implemented Mana (FP) system to do a special, hard hitting attack, or buff the player.
The NPCs are memorable as always, and there is even the return of some friendly (and not so friendly) faces from previous games. Each questline is long and takes most of the game to complete, with some questlines starting during a stage of another NPC's quest. The voice acting is phenominal, and you will end up liking all of the NPCs based solely on this fact.
The lore for this game is extensive, and convoluted, as ever. So much has been added, and is connected to the first game, unlike Dark Souls II. It's interesting to see legacies of previous characters continued in this game, as many stories from past games are continued one way or another in this game. This is just the base game as well, and the DLC adds even more to decipher and speculate on.
TL;DR: This game is a great send off to the series. The pacing has changed and the learning curve is much steeper than the other 2 games, but all in all it's an amazing experience. The lore, the bosses, the NPCs, and the weapons are all amazing and memorable. This game is a must buy.

I love the souls series. I've played 'em all for hours on end. Even this one, you'll find, i've sunk 300 hours into. But 299 of those hours were spent lying to myself. I was happy that soul memory was gone, and that the password system had made it in. But the password system wasn't the only thing they took from Bloodborne. The combat system functions more like Bloodborne than Dark Souls. Dark Souls was about being caution, timed blocking and stamina management. Now it's about being fast, and agressive. That worked in Bloodborne, but Dark Souls 3 gives you the tools to play cautiously, like other souls entries, but encourages that you play fast and agressive. There are many risks to playing slowly and carefully such as being guard broken or being overwhelmed, but all these risks can be negated by abusing the powerful dodge roll. It costs little stamina and has incredible frames, which can be further buffed by rings.
The plot is a mess. "Time is convoluted in Lordran" is what we're told, but that statement can be used to answer most lore questions. There are a few interesting character questlines, and these really shine. When the game isnt appealing to your nostalgia by directly and unironically refrencing the previous games is where Dark Souls 3 perks up. But then they recycle a theme, location or straight up character and the game shrugs its shoulders and says "time is convoluted but isnt it cool they're here?" The DLC does little to bring anything new, content to wallow in nostalgia. They even go as far as to make a certain boss painfully similar to a Bloodborne boss. Anything new is shoved aside and concluded poorly to focus on refrences.
One of the most praised elements of Dark Souls 3 is its level design, but even there the laziness shows. The world isn't interconnected, like Dark Souls 1. There are 3 branching paths that are available later in the game; a secret area acessed pretty cleverly, a second secret area accessed by going left in a fork in a road, and the DLC. The rest of the levels are in sequence. The level themselves are pretty boring, however. They do look good and are visually pleasing, but very often rely on "find a bonfire and then unlock shortcuts back to that bonfire." There are very few options for alternate ways to progress, as most levels are incredibly linear. Some areas either have a shortcut available that just needs some clever dropping/jumping, or are simply huge open forested areas. Exploring these areas yields very little, as equipment is very limited. There are plently of weapons available, but each weapon class has its clear best choice, while the other weapons in its category are largely worse.
There is no replayability in Dark Souls 3. Once you've beaten the game, you'll find that NG+ has nothing new to offer except some stronger versions of already exsisting rings. The only point to NG+ aside from the rings is resetting your respec currency and respawning the bosses. The bosses are where the game really shines, sometimes. There are very few unique and original ideas for bosses here. They tried to step away from armored humanoids that Dark Souls 2 continued to throw at us, but ended up relying on that trope too much again. So many bosses are praised to be the best in the series, when they're painfully generic. The soundtrack sounds good, but all the songs are interchangable. "An orchestra has a fit while a woman goes "ahhhhhhhhhhh" sums up most tracks in the game. A lot of bosses are just more nostalgia pandering as well, as they all have some tie to a previous souls game. It wouldn't be so bad if they expanded on the refrence, but they dont. The refrences are there just to refrence. That's it. The bosses can be defeated by rolling through their attack, then pressing your attack button as fast as you can. Rinse, repeat, dead. There are very few bosses that deviate from this, but the ones that do either die in one hit after jumping through some hoops or are defeated using a special weapon that directly refrences Demons Souls.
I tried to tell myself that all the obvious pandering, poor gameplay and horrible multiplayer was ok. It was more Dark Souls, that's not a bad thing. But it is. From Software designed Dark Souls 3 to be a trip down memory lane, to be experience once and then shelved. It might be the closest thing we get to Bloodborne on the PC, but that doesn't mean i'm supposed to ignore the issues and praise it because it's the last entry in the series. It's unfortunate that Dark Souls had to end this way. If you're looking to pick up Dark Souls 3, don't. Play the other entries in the series and don't spoil your love for the series with this lazy attempt to appeal to it.

There are much better, more in depth reviews on here, so I'll keep mine brief-ish.
Playing Darkest Dungeon, at least at the moment, is like going to the casino; the house always wins.
In the patch notes, the developers mention players breaking the game to the point that it's insanely easy. I'd like to know how many people this includes, because it, again, feels much like a visit to the casino: a handful of people win. Everyone else loses.
I've reached a point where I'm not sure the game takes much skill, but rather getting on your knees, praying, and then realizing it does nothing.
I still like the game. I like the corpses, even--it was frustrating working a monster to the front only for ranged characters to have nothing to do. It can be good. At the moment, however, it's kinda not. And that's my review as it stands. Lots of design decisions that could be good, but just aren't really.
Also: while I understand most of the new classes, when first introduced, were OP, the houndmaster strikes me as the absolute worst. I could be missing something, but a group, 1 bleed attack is just worthless. Yes, he can lower protection--another questionable  recently impelentated mechanic--but on the whole he feels like a waste of a slot, and only helps to drag battles on longer. And, given that time and chance are your two biggest obstacles every step of the way, you're better off bringing along someone stronger, who can take enemies out faster.
So much for keeping it short. But, if you're interested in the game, ask yourself: how salty do I get? If you get very salty at games, move along. It's not worth the frustration. And that's my real complaint. The developers need to find a balance between their vision and something that's actually fun to play. Unless you like losing money at the casino, find something cheaper, and more rewarding. Something that you feel like you've earned through skill, perhaps, and not just dumb luck.
But also know that while I'm not recommending the game, I kinda am. This game could be amazing. Maybe it even was, at one point. Hopefully it will at least be somewhat fun again.

Quick and to-the-point review:
Pros:
- Hard but fair system. It's easy to understand why your terrible decisions led to the extermination of your whole party.
- Great pacing and timing.
- The random dungeons are quite good.
- "Just one more time....". Dungeoneering is quite addictive
- Music is quite Good and moody
- The way autosave works - you can stop at any moment of the game and this system is nearly exploit-proof, so it still feels really scary to go bad on an expedition AND you don't need to wait one hour to save the game.
Borderline:
- Narration is good but you'll get really tired of it after 20+ hours
- It might be really frustrating at start. But it's quite sactisfatory to look at your own progress.
Cons:
- Some aspects of battle are quite annoying. Such as the lack of Initiative order (wich forces some rather arbitrary decisions) and the often weird AI Behaviour (it seems more random than a state machine behaviour). Also, it's filled with tiny exploits such as retreating after your party is ambushed.
- When you go down, it takes a long time to get back up. Loosing a party at the beggining of the game is a problem that might take you more than two hours to solve.
- [early access only] it kinda halts too soon, but it's ok as long as the full game doesn't take way too long to come by.
That said, full thumbs up for this game! I'm craving for the full version

I started playing Darkest Dungeon about a month ago, soon after the Houndmaster update.  The gameplay and narration are excellent and I think the graphics/battle animations are superb, as well.  The storyline reminds me of H.P. Lovecraft's "The Rats In The Walls" and that's a great thing!  Kudos to Red Hook on capturing the same dark, dreary feel.
I found the game to be very difficult early on because I was trying to save all of the party members after each mission and didn't have enough gold to fix all of their problems.  Once I accepted that the level 0-1 characters were simply cannon fodder to use for the greater good of the Hamlet (sending out on no provision runs to gather gold/resources and then dismissing the entire party afterwards), the game became easier.  Using the gold to fund real mission and item/ability upgrades for my main characters, I slowly built up my roster and continued doing no provision runs when my core teams required rest.
Now, I have a full roster of upgraded (though not max level) characters.  The days of no provision runs with new recruits is over but they served their purpose.  My "A-Team" (Grave Robber/Vestal/Crusader/Man-at-Arms) is level 5 and has completed several Champion runs; the remaining heroes are level 3-4 and are capable of completing the Veteran runs in various party combinations.
In my opinion, the best classes are the Man-at-Arms and the Vestal; I haven't had any success with the Occultist or the Plague Doctor.  It seems like the Occultist's heal fails at a critical time and isn't worth the risk, the Vestal has proven to be a more reliable healer.  The Plague Doctor hasn't been a strong enough healer or damage dealer in my expeience; I'd take the Vestal/Crusader for healing or just about anything else (Arbalest/Bountry Hunter/Grave Robber/Highway Man) for damage dealing, over the Plague Doctor.
Would I recommend this game to others?  Absolutely!  For only $20 (about the same price as a movie or two at the theater), I've had over 70 hours of enjoyment and I am looking forward to the next 70+ hours of gameplay.

Ah, Spiral Knights. How can I keep this recommendation within the character limit. Well, it's a free-to-play action-based MMO, but it remains free-to-play due to a mechanic that allows only so much playtime each day. And if you get addicted, which you will, you need to at least buy a monthly pass, that's basically required to enjoy the game anyway, unless you only have an hour or two to play each day anyway, in which case this is a perfect system for you. The game starts out easy, the controls are very simple, and they recently added an optional tutorial/questing system, which makes it even easier to start playing. However, things get insanely challenging later on. Bullet hells, spike hells, fiery helly hells. There are even special areas made just to be cruel hells. Admittedly it gets easier once you become experienced and know what to expect, but there are still areas that are basically impossible to progress through solo. This game will teach you how to use a shield, I'll say that.
UPDATE:
I'm changing this recommendation from positive to negative. This game is dying. A year ago, this was an underappreciated gem of an MMO. There was new content being regularly released for free that drew you in, and then while you were here there were cosmetics and boosts that you could pay for if you wanted to. This is how the free-to-play model should work, content that draws you in and keeps you playing while simultaneously not being locked behind a paywall and being open to anyone, whether they pay or not. And for the most part, this model still applies to new players who haven't experienced all the content yet.
But the new content updates that comprise the backbone of this model have long since died off. Promises were made and never kept, the lead developer upped and left, and a noticeably large chunk of the playerbase has died off due to boredom. It feels like a lot of drive and inspiration has been lost and Three Rings thinks it can fill this void with shiny "new" reskins and repeating event content and hope that no one notices while they try to piece everything back together behind the scenes, IF they're trying to piece everything back together behind the scenes, maybe they aren't. It's been over a year now and there are STILL a bunch of unfixed problems and bugs related to the sprites update that was released just before everything fell apart.
Examples: Some minerals have no purpose and get stuck in your inventory; sprites have a level numbering system that makes no sense, the "true" max level is some number over 100 that the game doesn't tell you; the only way of knowing that you've reached this "true" max level is that your sprite glitches out and stops accepting levelup food; and there are quite a few balance issues with pet abilties and ultimates, some are even outright bugs themselves.
(Seraphynx's Violent Heart Attack ultimate causes targets enchanted with Heart Attack to explode. Sounds cool, right? It does until you realize that the explosion does almost zero damage even in tier three and is really only good for breaking blocks. And the alternative ultimate, Iron Heart Attack, has a chance to drop defense orbs that maybe cushion half a pip's worth of damage, also in tier three. Take your pick between useless and more useless. In fact, just stay away from Seraphynx in general, its first ability has a deceptively large hitbox combined with a maximum hit limit per enemy that makes no sense, its second ability is very unreliable and might not even have an effect at all, and its third ability has too small of a radius to be useful in the team setting that it's meant to be useful in and has only enough health for one, maaaaaaybe two hits for everyone and not per person, it's mostly just for running over traps that you're too impatient to wait for. Hell, the other non-defense-oriented sprites have BETTER individual defensive abilities than the defense-oriented sprite, because the defense sprite is meant for providing defense for the whole team, yet the balance just isn't there to actually provide reliable and worthwhile defensive abilities for multiple people simultaneously, it's better if everyone just brought their own Flame Barrier and Shadow Cloak buffs and went from there. Unless you just like shiny cosmetic kittens, of course.)
Phew.
My point is, these things are acceptable for a month or two after a big update, not a year, and the fact that so little has changed to make the game better in that time tells me that they've probably stopped caring about Spiral Knights altogether. If you're new to the game you will have all sorts of fun in everything that's been established already, but don't invest too much into your future here, at the rate things are going you won't have much of one.

There are much better, more in depth reviews on here, so I'll keep mine brief-ish.
Playing Darkest Dungeon, at least at the moment, is like going to the casino; the house always wins.
In the patch notes, the developers mention players breaking the game to the point that it's insanely easy. I'd like to know how many people this includes, because it, again, feels much like a visit to the casino: a handful of people win. Everyone else loses.
I've reached a point where I'm not sure the game takes much skill, but rather getting on your knees, praying, and then realizing it does nothing.
I still like the game. I like the corpses, even--it was frustrating working a monster to the front only for ranged characters to have nothing to do. It can be good. At the moment, however, it's kinda not. And that's my review as it stands. Lots of design decisions that could be good, but just aren't really.
Also: while I understand most of the new classes, when first introduced, were OP, the houndmaster strikes me as the absolute worst. I could be missing something, but a group, 1 bleed attack is just worthless. Yes, he can lower protection--another questionable  recently impelentated mechanic--but on the whole he feels like a waste of a slot, and only helps to drag battles on longer. And, given that time and chance are your two biggest obstacles every step of the way, you're better off bringing along someone stronger, who can take enemies out faster.
So much for keeping it short. But, if you're interested in the game, ask yourself: how salty do I get? If you get very salty at games, move along. It's not worth the frustration. And that's my real complaint. The developers need to find a balance between their vision and something that's actually fun to play. Unless you like losing money at the casino, find something cheaper, and more rewarding. Something that you feel like you've earned through skill, perhaps, and not just dumb luck.
But also know that while I'm not recommending the game, I kinda am. This game could be amazing. Maybe it even was, at one point. Hopefully it will at least be somewhat fun again.

Quick and to-the-point review:
Pros:
- Hard but fair system. It's easy to understand why your terrible decisions led to the extermination of your whole party.
- Great pacing and timing.
- The random dungeons are quite good.
- "Just one more time....". Dungeoneering is quite addictive
- Music is quite Good and moody
- The way autosave works - you can stop at any moment of the game and this system is nearly exploit-proof, so it still feels really scary to go bad on an expedition AND you don't need to wait one hour to save the game.
Borderline:
- Narration is good but you'll get really tired of it after 20+ hours
- It might be really frustrating at start. But it's quite sactisfatory to look at your own progress.
Cons:
- Some aspects of battle are quite annoying. Such as the lack of Initiative order (wich forces some rather arbitrary decisions) and the often weird AI Behaviour (it seems more random than a state machine behaviour). Also, it's filled with tiny exploits such as retreating after your party is ambushed.
- When you go down, it takes a long time to get back up. Loosing a party at the beggining of the game is a problem that might take you more than two hours to solve.
- [early access only] it kinda halts too soon, but it's ok as long as the full game doesn't take way too long to come by.
That said, full thumbs up for this game! I'm craving for the full version
