Darkest Dungeon is in a couple of words: Fresh, Thoughtful, and Punishing.
This game really stands out from other games genres you could try to pitch it into. It has roguelike elements in that the dungeons are randomized, but the adventure isn't over when you die. It's a dungeon crawler, but not a Skinner's Box. It's a football manager but instead your players are fighting shrieking pigs and terminal disease. I find it a wonderful combination of many different styles of games, all of those styles blend really well together to form the end product, and none feel forced.
That said, this game can be brutal. The game even tells you before you begin that your characters will die and missions will fail and that the player needs to understand that it's supposed to happen. It adds a new level to the idea that game over is not a fail-state. I found myself when I first started this game restarting over and over, since my first couple of dungeon runs wound up with bad luck. This was frustrating, so I decided instead to roll with the punches and then my experience felt much more bleak but also more rewarding. Tenacity is what this game rewards you for. Understanding when to cut your losses is critical. I digress.
Great game! Highly reccomend sitting down and playing with it and taking the hand you are dealt, as you are in the end going to grow from the trials of the Darkest Dungeon.

Up until just recently I would have reccomended this game to everyone. However, not long ago they implimented a new patch that seems to effect a great deal of game balance (in the monster's favour). The game, which was already incredibly challenging and unforgiving, became nearly impossibly challenging. My team is surprised more often (even in bright torchlight), critted (what seems like constantly), already debilitative mental conditions have been separated into mental and physical ailments (and then allow those to compound and get harder to remove), and even the damage of the monsters seems to have increased. Some characters (like the occultist) have had their debuffs nerfed and have become an almost useless class compared to others now.
What used to be a game that made you strategize your supplies and fight a war of attrition now kills off your (well prepared and equipped) characters before you're even through a second room sometimes. Bosses aren't the only major threat now, a group of mini-bosses seems to be able to wipe you out at any time. It's now nearly impossible to keep a skilled team, and thus you're frequently forced to train up low level characters to replace the ones you've lost. Then, only to lose them again without being able to explore the deeper levels. The difficulty curve ramps up way too much, way too fast.
Also, it's hard to raise character levels because you only seem to get advancement experience if you complete a dungeon (which is often VERY difficult now), so even if you complete 90% of the dungeon and are forced to abandon it because most of your characters have been wiped out, the remaining characters recieve ... nothing, no experience at all. You only get more trinkets and money (and lots of it, but it doesn't really help you out much).
They've also added this strange corpse mechanic, which seems kind of interesting, but doesn't really function logically. Sometimes you have to "kill" the corpses of the enemy that you've already killed just to get at the back row of enemies, yet your own characters never leave corpses, and most enemies can hit all ranks of your characters anyway.
All that said, I have hope that this patch will be modified to make the game playable again. It was honestly one of my favourite games that I've ever played before, but I'm going to bench it for now in the hopes that it will become a more balanced game in the updates (and release) still to come.
Fingers crossed!!!

This review is going to be more PvP oriented than PvE
Ashes of Ariendal is mediocore coming from a dark souls vet, I wish it was longer. Tbh It has its moments and don't get me wrong its a good dlc, just too short.
Ring City is REALLY GOOD. Its akin to the Artorias of The Abyss DLC. Good map design, bosses, balanced difficulty, and the boss music is amazing. The new weapons are all viable, and might actually bring salvation to the bullsh*t that is the PvP meta right now.
The singleplayer in the base game itself is well, more dark souls. It takes a lot from Bloodborne and Dark souls 1 so its a mix between the two and you can definetly see the elements of BB and DkS1 mashed in it. The boss's OST's are hot af per usual of a souls game, and there is only 1 or 2 gimick bosses that I didnt like out of them all.
The PvP is another story, Its still flipptiy floppity since the new DLC came out and its made the meta wayy different, which I love, I still cant say for sure if its good or not besides my personal experience. Its better than DkS1's now but still sadly not as good as DkS2's
The reason I say this is because, Dark souls 1 had a poise system that was broken af and the insta backstabs with latency were aids, thought it still had a variety of weapons to use that were viable. Magic was also pretty busted in DkS1.
Dark souls 2 on the other hand had had still, a broken backstab and latency compensation, but not nearly as bad as 1's. Its hitboxes weren't very good, but the thing that made it amazing was because literally every single weapon in the game barring 1 ( a ♥♥♥♥in' wooden cooking spoon ) were good. Even the broken straight sword had a meta of its own (seriously go look up Limit Breaker's "HERE COMES THE PAIN TRAIN!") The magic was good but not super op broken like in 1, and it was a really ♥♥♥♥ing good game for pvp, while lacking a bit in PvE, (besides the DLC which was ♥♥♥♥ing god like, like DkS1's)
Now we come to Dark Souls 3, which has definetly improved over the course of the second dlc. I cant say much about sorceries since I dont use them, but pyros have devinetly become WAYY more viable, with the addition to a new pyro weapon and the new spells, you can become a pressure got if you use it right, and its actually really fun to use AND TO FIGHT. The DLC Great / Ultra Great weapons are actually good and balanced.
TL;DR: PvP is 50/50 since meta isnt solid yet, may be good may not be good. Single player is pretty solid with the addition of The Ringed City. 8/10 I'd still like poise tho

A friend got me into this series in 2013-2014 I believe.  I got my copy of Dark Souls I for PS3 originally and we beat it together.  Ever since, Dark Souls has been one of my favorite franchises, and I'm sad to see it come to an end.  But, it's definitely going out with a bang!
Dark Souls III did an amazing job of taking everything I loved about the series and making it better, while taking most of the things I didn't like and fixing them.  Gameplay is fluid, environments are gorgeous, character customization is good (there's hair physics!), and the replay value is high.
If you've played Dark Souls II but not Dark Souls I, Dark Souls III might feel a little foreign as Dark Souls II was a very different game from the rest in the series.  However, I believe that if you enjoy the overall ideas behind the souls series (risk, reward, difficulty, loss) then you'll like this entry all the same.
People say that this is the easiest game in the series, but those words should be analyzed carefully.  The game is still not 'easy', trust me.  I've played every souls game so far, and this one was still a good challenge for me.
Also, for those who enjoy co-op, this game has an easy to use password matchmaking system so you'll only be connected to people using the same password as you.  So, all you and friends have to do is use the same unique password and you're all set to enjoy some Jolly Co-operation! Praise the Sun!
Dark Souls III is another fantastic, quality experience from FromSoft & Hidetaka Miyazaki, and I can't wait to see what they come up with next!
P.S: I personally play with a controller and I recommend that, but this entry in the series is definitely the most Keyboard + Mouse friendly out of all of them, so that's a plus!

This game really feels like it SHOULD be good, but it's just too grindy and there just is not enough real content. Once you play for about a half-hour you have played the entire game.
It's got some really cool ideas that I haven't seen before, don't get me wrong, but it really needs just more to it. For example, there's spots in all the worlds where you can claim them as your home. Basically you build your home and take it with you into worlds. It can't be widened, but you can build it up extremely high or extremely low.
The game is also really easily accessible which is nice. It's about a GB in size and there's no party system. You just teleport to your friends and everyone auto shares loot and everything you pick up, even with other randoms that are roaming around.
That's about all the good parts tho. The combat is just too overly simple to really enjoy after a while. I'd say it's a bit more involved than most MMOs honestly, but with only 3 abilities there's only so much you can do.
The game really just needs to be less of a grind and give me more reason to have fun and build. I noticed there are "community-dungeons" but there's no way for someone like me to make one. (There is a way, but it's a lottery if yours gets in and not a simple in game option.) In a game like this, everyone should be able to. Have people rate your dungeon and the better the rating the more chance it has to show up.
Anyway, tldr; game is almost good but not enough it needs more to do and more fun to be had. Also the music is really boring and uninspired. It's decent for a free to play game though

It makes me very sad to give this game a thumbs down - there is so much potential. The gorgeous hand-drawn aesthetic and comically overwrought prose of the story really stand out as unique. Big, smart-sounding words will be misused (swarthy means dark-skinned, you guys), the low-low-low gamma will make you squint at your screen, and the 'heroes' will dodder around on-screen like children playing dress-up. The hamfistedness really works out favorably overall, though you may tire of the rasping narrator after the 50th time he tells you about the “dancing steps of war”.
The heroes themselves are diverse and unique, and the sheer number of classes (10 and counting), skills, and personality quirks mean that no two are ever quite alike. Your nymphomaniac  Plague Doctor will save you cash by being… efficient at the brothel, but his Fear of Beasts will make him pretty damned worthless in the Weald (where he probably acquired the Fear in the first place after contracting rabies from a dog). Luckily, you can forcibly remove his phobia (for a steep fee) at the Sanitarium, where you can also cure the rabies.
In addition, there is also a really great gameplay mechanic called ‘Stress’. As they’re subjected to more and more horrors in the dungeons, each heroes’ stress level increases until a critical point at which they crumble, becoming an abusive, cowardly, selfish, or (extremely rarely) more heroic version of themselves. In between dungeon runs, the heroes can spend a week or two blowing off steam at the Tavern or Church (though I’m still not sure how self-flagellation can possibly be as effective as a visit to the brothel).  Thus, even though you can only use 4 heroes at any given time, you’ll want a sizable roster to rotate them in and out of your lineup. This also forces you to use vastly different combinations; sometimes you’re  just stuck with three healers and a mage with the red plague on a given week and you have to make a dungeon run anyway.
All of this sounds great, doesn’t it? Why am I giving this a thumbs down? Unfortunately, the gameplay is entirely dominated by compounding randomness. The damage ranges are wide as a barn, critical hit and dodge percentages are huge; even aoe’s can be completely dodged or be complete critical hits. Blight, bleeding, and disease resistances similarly operate on an all-or-nothing percentage basis. The net result is that your careful strategic choices, character development plans, and painstaking expenditures have very little bearing on success or failure. Your awesome high-hp crusader could be killed from full health by the very first group of enemies you encounter on a dungeon run before you even get a turn. This is true of *any* group of enemies you encounter, whether the first or the 20th, whether you’ve been dominating all of them or not, whether you’ve made wise choices or simply clicked on whatever skill seemed cool at the time. I don’t mind punishing difficulty when it can be circumvented by skill and strategy (e.g., Dark Souls; XCOM), but neither of those traits need apply here.
Because of this, it feels less like a game and more like a spectator sport. You’re on a rollercoaster, watching various heroes die. There isn’t any significant progression in strength, and micromanaging the various traits becomes a chore because really, what does it all matter? The repetitive runs through the dark dungeons yield nothing permanent or tangible. Worse, there is never any doubt that you’ll prevail eventually; throw enough heroes at it and eventually the dungeon will divulge its secrets through sheer numerical luck. The feelings of difficulty and danger *aren’t even real*.  Perhaps this will change through development, but I doubt it. The game designers seem to have embraced randomness as difficulty instead of more complex gameplay mechanics. But, that’s life – sometimes your lead programmer is fearless but flatulent, your head designer has photomania and misanthropy, while your story writer is lazy-eyed, a clutch hitter, and a known cheat. If only they could have assembled the perfect team… but life just doesn’t work that way. Maybe video games should, though.

I think i have played a hefty amount of hours, enough to give it a review. This game i have played in alpha and beta, and it has exceeded my expectations on full release. In "early access" outside steam you have this game with a great idea and to show Picroma (the cube world dev team) To show how to do it correctly. Now as much as i would have loved cube world to be developed, Trove filled in that empty hole not to mention it is also very f2p not once have i been forced to spend a penny. Although, the currency system isn't quite the best it could have been. Basically you have a chance to earn a crap ton of "cubits" (the in-game currency) by doing these tasks in the beginning And that could buy you a few classes out of the plethora of classes you can choose. Now after that, You can only earn 500 cubits daily through dungeons on week days, and weekends 1000, but something about it is just not my style. If I were to create it i would do maybe 50 cubits every smaller dungeon, Or the 1 star tasks, and 100 for 3 star tasks. But enough with the currency issue, time to get to my list of pros and cons.
Pros = +    Cons = -
+ Very exciting gameplay with a new feel in the gaming world
+Many different and creative classes with more to come soon
+MANY different weapons and styles to choose from.
+ A good amount of biomes with different style dungeons in each biome.
-+ A little too easy in the beginning, but gets way better around level 6
+ Many different side skills, F.E, Runecrafting, ring crafting, gardening, etc
+ Very f2p, the only money you can spend on is classes and cosmetics, nothing gamebreaking or OP
-+Login queue was a bit shotty, but the very active devs got right on the case, and i give props to them.
+New Content Every week, made by the players as well!
+Great community, no spams in chat about money selling websites
+Mounts! SO MANY MOUNTS!!!!!!!!!!!
-Could use a better way to earn cubits but its nothing too serious
+In later levels help from friends is a great thing since it gets very challenging
-The Music is okay, but it could use something better, with more taste. When Fighting bosses i want Super Epic  dramatic adventure music, or when exploring to hear something like the lord of the rings main theme song. Biome music should have even more spunk to them, but still have the retro voxel feel.

I have read a lot of reviews by people who are frustrated with this game. I remind you all that when you first load the game it gives a pretty candid disclaimer about the challenges ahead. It's a different kind of grind than what people are used to today. Saying with all due respect to darkest dungeon (for real I love it) if you're looking for a game that's rewarding, ground breaking, and relaxing, this is not the game for you.
My first impressions were of the art the art and narration. The grimdark medieval and classic horror fantasy depictions remind me of of what first drew me to Diablo 1 and 2. From the trailer it appears they've resurrected H.P. Lovecraft to write their narration. Truly is one of the most glorious aspects of this entire project.
Secondly I analyzed the game play. Once I read the disclaimer and played my first few failed saves, it was obvious that this game isn't your typical run and slice, grab the chest and move on. With all the various and numerous aspects in play, it becomes less about success and more about damage control and your your on the spot choices coupled with a random number generator. Much like poker, it invokes equal parts luck, skill and the ability to hedge your bets.
Ultimately, the game play flow reminds me of Diablo 2, path of exile, or any game where you have the option to do just about whatever you want, but it will not be apparent where your mistakes are being made. It honestly makes for a throw back and refreshing grind.

UPDATED AND REVISED FOR RADIANT UPDATE:
My original review for Darkest Dungeon was long, rambling and basically ended with me comparing it to being an ex girlfriend: it was a game you loved, but she wouldn't communicate with you and would punish you without warning or explanation-  no matter how much effort you put into it, it wouldn't love you back.
Well just like with my ex who dumped me for calling her a ♥♥♥♥♥demon in a drunken fit on Valentines Day, I've come crawling back for more!
Looking past the constant fluctuations in gameplay and difficulty that came during Early Access, Darkest Dungeon's biggest problem had always been the grind: grinding to level up your characters, Grinding to fight all of the higher level boss recolors, grinding to get your Vestal free of the black plague....And the Yips....And getting her to unwind at the bar only to have her wander off and not show up again for 3 weeks...You get the idea- it was a great and simple game at it's core that was bloated by a lot of busywork
Well thankfully, it seems someone noticed with the release of Radiant Mode, which promised to cut down on the tedium. And so far, I'd say it has cut down a bit of it!
The keyphrase here is " a bit" . It's definitely still there, but a couple of important bits like allowing high level adventurers to travel with low level guys and vice versa means you're no longer having to spend several hours running a squad of level 0 ♥♥♥♥♥ around a beginner dungeon just so your high level guys can all recover and go stomp that Necromancer in the Ruins.
So it's still on the repetitious side, but I've definitely enjoyed playing it again.
With that, I'll get to the straight facts:
PROS:
+ Simple and addicting turn based combat belies a large amount of depth and strategy in party loadouts and positioning.
+ Fantastic art style
+Wayne June, perhaps the most acclaimed Lovecraft audiobook narrator (is that really all that common?) does so much for the game with his brooding, wonderful voice.
+ Great music combines fantasy, grunge and horror.
+ This game and Bloodborne are probably the best representations of the Lovecraftian genre in gaming
+Easy to learn, incredibly hard to master
+Radiant mode does a fair bit to counter some of the problems plaguing it''s earlier incarnations
CONS:
- Still got some grind to it; Radiant mode breaks it down to taking 'just' 40 hours instead of upwards of 80. I'm not sure the game really has enough content to justify 40 hours. You know if you're the kind of person who can get behind that kind of time comittiment, so I'll leave that to you.
- Not all classes are created equally, and knowing what classes to keep and who to dump is going to make a big difference. Ideally they should all be viable, but this can be dealt with if nothing else.
-Despite the time and effort you'll have put into it, your legendary heroes will not feel as competent or as powerful as they really ought to be the end. The feeling of powerlessness is inherent to Lovecraftian entertainment and I of all people understand that, but for the amount of time you put into this, I do think you should get some degree of well earned value in return.
VERDICT:
It's a good game, but one of diminishing returns.
Truthfully, I think the game's got some deep flaws in the grinding, and WILL waste some of of your time on it. The final dungeon is punishing for all the wrong reasons and the looming fact will always be there that the house of cards you've spent 40+ hours building can tumble down in only a few moments, all at the capricious mercy of circumstance. I am of the opinion that this sort of ever present fragility is fine, but would be best in a game inherently shorter, like 15 hours maybe.
But you know what? ♥♥♥♥ it. Go get it on sale, you'll get your money's worth and entertainment out of it by the time you become fed up with it.

So I've come back to change my review
Pros:
-Voxel based terrain, can destroy basically anything
-Crafting, unique crafting system
-Level system, Cap is 20 but you obtain shadow gear and that expands on your max level (Similar to Destiny)
-Massive loot system, tons of mounts to choose from, materials to collect, gear to obtain
-Gear upgrade system, wait until you get shadow gear to upgrade!!! It is awesome to improve!
-Scaling difficulties based on realms, I.E. Uber 1-6 etc.
-Multiple characters to choose from, each character contributes to your mastery level
-Ships, instead of mounts in areas with water you can mount your ship and have pirate battles! Yarr!
-Guild/Club system, can join multiple clubs/guilds
-Club worlds, design your own world for your club however you want!
-Boosting, you can invite low level players to join you in high level areas and help them level and get lots of compliments
-Benefits for joining clubs, such as sky realm portals and finding people to play with
-Shared loot, no need to worry about fighting amongst yourselves to get the best loot, everyone gets their own
-Teamwork and community oriented gameplay, it's best to play with friends!
-Unique graphics
-Socially active developer team, livestreams all the time, Q&A's, they make frequent in-game announcements
-Not super pay to win, you can get most content just playing the game
-Always entertaining and always goals to attain
-Mastery and trophy system allow for plenty of end-game content
-Shadow Arenas for high level players to run through and try to get epic loot!
-Gardening, craft materials with gardening to be able to farm high level materials
-Runecrafting, craft runes with materials harvested from the sky realm to obtain materials to craft tomes which give you rare items
-Bombs, bombs are awesome and allow you to harvest materials or do dungeon runs quickly, seriously, bomb everything
There are so many more good things I have to say, but you really need to play the game to experience them all! Very social game and great community!
Cons:
-The club based system is very weak in my opinion, you don't have controls over the permissions system, I made the mistake of trusting an individual with the rank of 'Officer' in my club, they stole everything from our club World; to be honest I was unaware they had the permissions to do that and it would be awesome if we could have control over what our ranks can and can't do. Ultimately it's my fault but it sucks to start from square 1, I wish it were a bannable offense, but meh.
-Queue, this game is so great that right now there's constantly thousands of people waiting to play, sometimes you have to sit there about an hour waiting, but I understand, it's a great game, who wouldn't want to play
Other than that I really have nothing to complain about, it's a great game. Given my hours played you can imagine how much I respect this game, the community, and its developers. Watch out for Farkyasu; he's the one who griefed me! Lol :P much love!

so this is the game that made me realise that gaming is a waste of time. That horrible realisation came to me when I had yet another one of my characters die because the game's mechanics are so utterly arbitrary, convoluted and befuddling that I can have my most skilled warriors miss attacks time after time and there is literally no way to anticipate or counter the sheer randomness of the game's rules. Accomplishments in this game are treated as insults, I have never seen another game be so utterly meanspirited when it comes to making progress; high level characters suddenly refuse to go on missions and become so "stressed" that they actually become a liability, wasting time and money trying to heal them. I lost two of my best characters killing a boss and when the mission was completed I got almost no reward, no new areas, no special equipment, buffs or any sign of progress. The game just went "♥♥♥♥ you for killing our boss. Now do it again. And again. And again." Combat in this game only gives the vague illusion of strategy; so much of the game is based on chance, which would be fine but the parts that are based on skill are almost impossible to work out and are governed by random factors which basically make it poinltess to even try. To top it off the enemies are just overpowered to the point of idiocy; the very few rules that actually govern combat just don't apply to your opponents, character positioning, buffs and targetting just get left by the wayside while they continue to rain hell on your characters with no indication that you're going part way to killling them. Meanwhile your characters get subjected to all sorts of pointless and petty rules and factors which just limit the entire game experience completely. The turn timer is a particular favourite; I once had two enemeis have four turns one after the other before my characters had even had their first go and there is literally nothing that can be done about it, apparently speed is a governing factor but its nigh on impossible to find your character's speed nor is it possible to actually understand what is considered good speed or find out how it compares to the speed of your enemies.
The thing is I like a challenging game and turn based combat is good fun but this game makes challenge and combat frustrating and utterly boring. Xcom is one of my favourite games but in that game you can understand the limitations and rules governing the game, similarly with darksouls the game is unbelievably hard but you can work strategy into your game and when you make progress you actually make progress, the game rewards you in ways Darkest Dungeon just refuses to. I will say that this is one of the most beautifully designed and atmospheric games I've ever played, for several hours the game can fully immerse you in its world delightfully and then you just find yourself fighting stupidly frustrating and drawn out battles and while initially the sense of triumph after completing a level will keep you going for a while there comes a point where it just stops being fun.
I know that responses to this post are going to be the same standard of "lol git gud" or "you just need to keep going" but at this point I have to
Why should I keep going with a game where combat is so ridiculous and frustrating and there is just no real reward. Every mission is just the same basic nightmarish grind and when they're completed the game gives you nothing new except more grind. No new characters get unlocked (characters appear randomly and don't really bring anything new) and after the first handful of missions you'll have unlocked all the buildings and after that progress becomes meaningless. There's no benefit to completing missions apart from "do it more" and after a while even the analysis of the stress mechanic becomes boring, when the only interesting part of the game is "what random negative effect has my character received now" then I just can't see the point of the game. With combat this frustrating and such little reward even the great atmosphere starts to pall, not lest because the game kinda stops world building and just drops you into the same basic locations with the same basic enemies with no real sense of anything changing. I will say that this game is great to play with friends, not least because you can get someone else to do the grinding while you do something else for a bit
tl;dr this game is like great foreplay that results in terrible sex...and instead of getting to♥♥♥♥♥at the end you're told you have to have even more terrible sex again and again with only the vaguest hint of a payoff at the end, except at the end you're told you need to keep doing it over and over again. After a while you just want to stop and walk away, although if you can get more people involved it can improve somewhat. I do want to say that this is by no means a bad game, its just not fun in the end.

I love this game.  It is wonderfully creepy, HARD, and requires a lot of strategy skills.  That said, I have had wonderful parties built up over long periods of time killed by minor monsters getting a string of crits.  I have also lost over 90% of all my characters to stress (bleeping heart attacks).  I find that there aren't enough ways to mitigate stress compared to the stress load of the average dungeon.  Even when camping, I can only get rid of maybe two boxes worth of stress if I am lucky.  Too bad I suffer 5+ boxes of stress per fight.  The bosses really cause massive amounts of stress and there is nothing you can really do about it.  A few character types can get rid of a little bit of stress each turn (instead of attacking), but the monsters trigger more stress than you could possibly heal to all your characters.
Either the amount of stress you can remove while camping needs to be much greater, the single turn stress removal for some characters needs to be better, the monsters need to generate less stress, or the characters when getting irrational/selfish need to stop mass spawning stress upon each other in a circle jerk.

To a person considering purchasing this game, I will illuminate a currently mis-used aspect of game play, the invisible timer that is stress:  Imagine that there is a timer over the head of each of your group reading four minutes, when the clock runs out you die.  As you walk forward the clock ticks down.  If you loot something, there is a good chance you will lose 15 seconds.  If you don't have enough torches the clock ticks down even faster as you move.  If you get into a fight and take too long trying to survive, you lose additional time.
If you are critically hit, EVERY party member loses fifteen seconds.  If you critically hit someone, one or two of your party members may gain a few seconds back on the clock.
One player class has the beneficial ability to sit in the back row and give one team member three more seconds to an individual timer.  In comparison there are common enemy special abilities you will constantly encounter, that deal a small amount of damage , while taking another 15 to 20 seconds off of one party members timer.
Enemies have group attacks that hit every party member and removes another 20 seconds from your play timer.  There is no friendly equivalent, not even something small that gives everyone 2 or 3 seconds back.
If one character hit's the halfway mark and is down to only two minutes remaining, roll a ten sided dice. If you roll a one through nine, that character instantly loses an additional 30 seconds, and each other group member loses 30 seconds as well.  That character will then randomly take away another 10 seconds from each player while walking, and in combat will continue to drain time away from the entire group about every two rounds.  If this triggers a second group member hitting the 2 minute mark, that person will then have a %90 chance of suffering something similar, and draining even more time from your play.  There is hope though, if you get that slim one-in-ten victory at the halfway point, you will gain a minute and a half back on your timer, and once every six to eight rounds of combat you will give out a party buff.  This experience will feel like winning a five dollar scratcher.  Sure, you won, but now you have to go back to the gas station.  Hooray.
This game has a lot going for it, a lot.  Great sound effects, incredible voice-over work, and perfectly moody and atmospheric soundtrack.  The game play is fun and interesting, unique leveling system and very cool buffs and debuff's that can arrive quickly and randomly.  Sadly, if the stress system doesn't get a whole lot more attention, this game will be doomed to bear the ultimate video game sin of being boring.  The stress meter has a lot of potential to create exciting or scary swings towards victory or defeat, akin to the random elements you normally expect from critical hits.  Unfortunately, the only thing the stress meter actually adds to the game, is redundant timer.  Regardless of preparation, or player choice, the stress bar is essentially a one way trip towards character heart attack, and that stress meter can suffer random spikes towards maximum from every single action you take or enemy you face.  There are methods in-game for reducing stress for party or characters, but those are comparitively small when measured against the steady swell of incoming stress.  Initially this feature is quirky and interesting, but when you realize how it works, and that it steadily and reliably defeats you with no recourse, the game becomes boring.  It's similar to knowing that tax season is around the corner, and you are going to owe again.  This game is not as difficult as some make it out to be. There is simply a pre-lit fuse over every action you take and that you can't put out, only slow down, poorly.

I want to be kind to this game, as it has a good deal of originality and fun gameplay (when you are not swearing at the screen), but some of the recent changes have been going in the wrong direction, and as a whole, probably tipped the scale to "don't buy at this time."
There are a lot of things in the game that are good: the art and visuals are striking, the choice of characters is quite varied, and there is a lot of dark humor running through the game. The game is unapologetically difficult, with things like an automatic up to the second autosave to prevent "favorable reloads" when you get in a jam, and it was made that way intentionally. People seem to like the challenge. Even the sound is good. The price is reasonable as well.
So this isn't a terrible game, and it is still early access so things might get even better as it nears "completion" (only 3 of 5 dungeons are playable at this time).
But recently there have been several game design choices that have pushed the game from "hard but enjoyable" to "too many things that make the game tiresome", which I have been sorry to see.
They recently introduced a "corpse" mechanic, that drops when you kill a creature without using a damage-over-time attack. This was a step back for gameplay and a change not alot of people like, as it makes combat more of a chore to have to "kill things twice" in order to get at the remaining creatures. This change has made several character types less effective (those that have no DOT attacks and can only attack the closest enemies) and really made combat less fun. It also makes several character types "necessary" even if you don't want to play them. This is compounded by the fact the computer opponents for the most part can attack any of your characters from whichever position without penalty.
In addition to this, there were recent reductions to player damage, which again changed a lot of things that were "hard but fun" into a a boring slog. Damage on critical hits was reduced, making fights take longer. Creatures were given "protections" running up to 80%, making fights run a LOT longer, especially at the higher levels. Even to the point that the game "penalizes" you, for thinking you are dragging the fights out on purpose.  For some creatures, the combinations of increased protection, lower player damage, and corpses getting in the way of the flow of combat, has taken the fun out of things to a large extent. Add to that the fact that a lot of creatures will spam AOE attacks that hit your entire party, turn after turn, and again, the fun factor really takes a dive.
There are also the usual number of growing pains with an alpha title, but those will likely get worked out.
And there is certainly time for this game to "recover" before launch. And I hope it does.
But right now it is over the line "hard but fun" into "a slog that I no longer feel like playing much".
I would hold off buying at this time.

Spiral Knights differs from most MMOs I've played in that it is more closer to the Legend of Zelda than anything else. It was this gameplay style that got me hooked. You can play as swordfighter, gunner or bomber for a variety of playing styles. Switching styles isn't exactly straightforward though, as the crafting system forms the main part of the game's revenue system and is what keeps players that don't pay in slow progress without locking the game off.
The fighting is pretty responsive and you face a variety of enemies. Fiends will present the biggest challenge with fast tricky monsters while beasts provide a more laidback experience. All of them prove to be very interesting.
Levels are partly random as most are made up of smaller chunks for a slightly different experience each time. That said, each level is still running to a specific theme with enough for you to experience a lot before the grind sets in.
It's fairly easy to find a party using the party finder or jumping in and hoping for the best, but the game's difficulty is also at a level where most challenges are possible fighting alone if you're good enough.
That's more or less going to be the main thing of note. Spiral Knights grind tends to go up and down as the game's paid currency is needed for some things but can be purchased using the game's non-paid currency. As this market is controlled by the players the price can fluctuate greatly. Fortunately, the introduction of crafting orbs as rare drops has helped to combat this slightly.

I want to be kind to this game, as it has a good deal of originality and fun gameplay (when you are not swearing at the screen), but some of the recent changes have been going in the wrong direction, and as a whole, probably tipped the scale to "don't buy at this time."
There are a lot of things in the game that are good: the art and visuals are striking, the choice of characters is quite varied, and there is a lot of dark humor running through the game. The game is unapologetically difficult, with things like an automatic up to the second autosave to prevent "favorable reloads" when you get in a jam, and it was made that way intentionally. People seem to like the challenge. Even the sound is good. The price is reasonable as well.
So this isn't a terrible game, and it is still early access so things might get even better as it nears "completion" (only 3 of 5 dungeons are playable at this time).
But recently there have been several game design choices that have pushed the game from "hard but enjoyable" to "too many things that make the game tiresome", which I have been sorry to see.
They recently introduced a "corpse" mechanic, that drops when you kill a creature without using a damage-over-time attack. This was a step back for gameplay and a change not alot of people like, as it makes combat more of a chore to have to "kill things twice" in order to get at the remaining creatures. This change has made several character types less effective (those that have no DOT attacks and can only attack the closest enemies) and really made combat less fun. It also makes several character types "necessary" even if you don't want to play them. This is compounded by the fact the computer opponents for the most part can attack any of your characters from whichever position without penalty.
In addition to this, there were recent reductions to player damage, which again changed a lot of things that were "hard but fun" into a a boring slog. Damage on critical hits was reduced, making fights take longer. Creatures were given "protections" running up to 80%, making fights run a LOT longer, especially at the higher levels. Even to the point that the game "penalizes" you, for thinking you are dragging the fights out on purpose.  For some creatures, the combinations of increased protection, lower player damage, and corpses getting in the way of the flow of combat, has taken the fun out of things to a large extent. Add to that the fact that a lot of creatures will spam AOE attacks that hit your entire party, turn after turn, and again, the fun factor really takes a dive.
There are also the usual number of growing pains with an alpha title, but those will likely get worked out.
And there is certainly time for this game to "recover" before launch. And I hope it does.
But right now it is over the line "hard but fun" into "a slog that I no longer feel like playing much".
I would hold off buying at this time.

Spiral Knights differs from most MMOs I've played in that it is more closer to the Legend of Zelda than anything else. It was this gameplay style that got me hooked. You can play as swordfighter, gunner or bomber for a variety of playing styles. Switching styles isn't exactly straightforward though, as the crafting system forms the main part of the game's revenue system and is what keeps players that don't pay in slow progress without locking the game off.
The fighting is pretty responsive and you face a variety of enemies. Fiends will present the biggest challenge with fast tricky monsters while beasts provide a more laidback experience. All of them prove to be very interesting.
Levels are partly random as most are made up of smaller chunks for a slightly different experience each time. That said, each level is still running to a specific theme with enough for you to experience a lot before the grind sets in.
It's fairly easy to find a party using the party finder or jumping in and hoping for the best, but the game's difficulty is also at a level where most challenges are possible fighting alone if you're good enough.
That's more or less going to be the main thing of note. Spiral Knights grind tends to go up and down as the game's paid currency is needed for some things but can be purchased using the game's non-paid currency. As this market is controlled by the players the price can fluctuate greatly. Fortunately, the introduction of crafting orbs as rare drops has helped to combat this slightly.
Has you on all fours, bleeding, blighted, driven insane and crawling back for more.

By now you've either researched or witnessed for yourself just how unforgiving this game is. It's rather unlike what our mainstream fantasy media would lead us to believe; Heroes dying? Guffaw! Maybe at the very end of a story, in a blaze of glory. Sure, that's dignified.
But something closer to reality doesn't lend very much dignity. I've had a hero die from a maggot bite. I've had several heroes bleed out while trying to fight the good fight. I've had a hero die from a heart attack because another hero shouted at him for stealing HIS kill. The nerve.
After giving up on a rocky first game, I started anew and have been doing much better. Almost the polar opposite in fortune, in fact. So is there a middle ground in how the pendulum swings?
Funnily enough, I had just an expedition. With most of my heroes at Level 3 and unwilling to do an Apprentice quest to kill a boss, I had to line up two Level 2 heroes, a Vester and Crusader (really hoping there'd be a lineup named "Holier Than Thou"), and two raw recruits, an Arbalist and Plague Doctor. Only two hall tiles into the quest, I found a Shambler's shrine and thought, "What the hell? I can just stack attacks and DOTs like I always do." Except not, and it happened to be the first time I realized that a Shambler can summon allies. Bugger.
So everyone survives after 9 grueling rounds, but my Arbalist goes batty and becomes Selfish. Immediately I weigh whether to pull back and let everyone unwind (stress was high all around) or push as far as I can and potentially let the new recruits die. Especially the Arbalist, because seriously, f**k that selfish swine. "Oh yes, grab that unburned torch for us, you totally deserve looting rights." Give me a break...
At least my Crusader snapped and went heroic, what a buffer that was. Later, the Plague Doctor dies, two battles before the boss, the Inchoate Flesh, who we press on to fight. That battle yo-yo'd so terribly that I thought my Level 2 heroes doomed - but at least that Arbalist was dead! As my Vester and Crusader were down to their last 3 or 4 life each, I commited to finish instead of backing out and made a harrowing victory.
It was the most fun I've had with the game so far, and simply because it FELT like a hard-won victory worthy of retelling. The busts I reclaimed quickly went to upgrading the Sanitarium, naturally.

One of the few early acess games that has provided exactly what it promised at the get-go, Darkest Dungeon acomplishes what it set out to do, and it does it damn well.
This game is set in a lovecraftian world where insanity and despair are perhaps the greatest threat to dungeoneers. The stress mechanic causes your heroes to slowly lose their minds as they witness the horrors that reside in the dark (and when pigs vomit on them). This leads to the player having to make very careful decisions, both within the dungeons and in the township you make your home.
Do I cure one hero of a crippiling illness, or do I bolster the strength of another?
Do I send one hero to releive his stress, or do I save the money to ensure the next party has what they need to survive?
Do I abandon a failing expedition, or press on, sacraficing my heroes' sanity to receive my rewards?
These are some of the situations you will face in Darkest Dungeon.
As for the story, it is told through memoirs found before fighting bosses. The different classes of heroes have a little backstory, but the game leaves most of their character for the player to interpret. You may remember a hero for being th e stalwart light of hope that the party needs, or the manic lunatic who got their allies killed. The characters write themselves.
This game is most certainly worrth a purchase in it's current state, and the developers update it on a regular basis. When it is released, it will be one of the greatest games that year, guaranteed.

By now you've either researched or witnessed for yourself just how unforgiving this game is. It's rather unlike what our mainstream fantasy media would lead us to believe; Heroes dying? Guffaw! Maybe at the very end of a story, in a blaze of glory. Sure, that's dignified.
But something closer to reality doesn't lend very much dignity. I've had a hero die from a maggot bite. I've had several heroes bleed out while trying to fight the good fight. I've had a hero die from a heart attack because another hero shouted at him for stealing HIS kill. The nerve.
After giving up on a rocky first game, I started anew and have been doing much better. Almost the polar opposite in fortune, in fact. So is there a middle ground in how the pendulum swings?
Funnily enough, I had just an expedition. With most of my heroes at Level 3 and unwilling to do an Apprentice quest to kill a boss, I had to line up two Level 2 heroes, a Vester and Crusader (really hoping there'd be a lineup named "Holier Than Thou"), and two raw recruits, an Arbalist and Plague Doctor. Only two hall tiles into the quest, I found a Shambler's shrine and thought, "What the hell? I can just stack attacks and DOTs like I always do." Except not, and it happened to be the first time I realized that a Shambler can summon allies. Bugger.
So everyone survives after 9 grueling rounds, but my Arbalist goes batty and becomes Selfish. Immediately I weigh whether to pull back and let everyone unwind (stress was high all around) or push as far as I can and potentially let the new recruits die. Especially the Arbalist, because seriously, f**k that selfish swine. "Oh yes, grab that unburned torch for us, you totally deserve looting rights." Give me a break...
At least my Crusader snapped and went heroic, what a buffer that was. Later, the Plague Doctor dies, two battles before the boss, the Inchoate Flesh, who we press on to fight. That battle yo-yo'd so terribly that I thought my Level 2 heroes doomed - but at least that Arbalist was dead! As my Vester and Crusader were down to their last 3 or 4 life each, I commited to finish instead of backing out and made a harrowing victory.
It was the most fun I've had with the game so far, and simply because it FELT like a hard-won victory worthy of retelling. The busts I reclaimed quickly went to upgrading the Sanitarium, naturally.

One of the few early acess games that has provided exactly what it promised at the get-go, Darkest Dungeon acomplishes what it set out to do, and it does it damn well.
This game is set in a lovecraftian world where insanity and despair are perhaps the greatest threat to dungeoneers. The stress mechanic causes your heroes to slowly lose their minds as they witness the horrors that reside in the dark (and when pigs vomit on them). This leads to the player having to make very careful decisions, both within the dungeons and in the township you make your home.
Do I cure one hero of a crippiling illness, or do I bolster the strength of another?
Do I send one hero to releive his stress, or do I save the money to ensure the next party has what they need to survive?
Do I abandon a failing expedition, or press on, sacraficing my heroes' sanity to receive my rewards?
These are some of the situations you will face in Darkest Dungeon.
As for the story, it is told through memoirs found before fighting bosses. The different classes of heroes have a little backstory, but the game leaves most of their character for the player to interpret. You may remember a hero for being th e stalwart light of hope that the party needs, or the manic lunatic who got their allies killed. The characters write themselves.
This game is most certainly worrth a purchase in it's current state, and the developers update it on a regular basis. When it is released, it will be one of the greatest games that year, guaranteed.

Reall this game is all around fun. It's very versatile in what you can do.
Want to survive alone? Singleplayer.
Want to roleplay as a bandit or a cop? Roleplay servers.
Want to mess around with the range of weapons this game has to offer? Creative servers.
Want to fight others in hunger games style arenas? Arena mode.
Want to survive against other players? Survival servers.
With the great customization this game has, from graphics, maps, weapon skins, workshop items, server settings, etc, you can get almost any experience on here. And all for free. All things you pay for are not game changing. You can't buy gold to get special items that stay on your body when you die, you can't sell your soul for a gun that's completly overpowered, or a vehicle that can't be destroyed. Nope, just cosmetics to make you look badass, but they aren't nesacary, and have no real upside besides being badass.
The only problem I have for this game, is optimization. The game for lower end computers is very taxing and doesn't run too well, thankfully there are maps and stuff that can run better for the lower end computers. Also Nelson, the single dev, is constantly updating every Friday, from stuff like bug fixes and level editor addtions (Yes you can make your own maps for the game), to new guns, cars, and items. Nelson puts his heart and soul into this game and has made it amazing.
My overall rating, 9/10.

If you are used to the sprawling maps, diverse and interesting characters and endless quests and tasks of the elder scrolls franchise and Fallout 3 and NV, then this is not the game for you.
The new game engine is an amazing improvement, however, it seems as though Bethesda spent all their money on the game engine development rather than depth and interactions.
One example: I picked up a distress radio signal and followed it to a trap door hidden under a bush. I thought that I may have an exciting quest exploring a vault or some creepy underground hideout.... It was a room with some bones and a 10mm pistol. There are countless opportunities for Bethesda to add content with this game but it just falls flat.
And then we come to the DLC. Adding items for building bases should not count as paid DLC. What happened to DLC like the shivering isles and knights of the nine? Far harbour is the only reasonable additional content and it is far too expensive.
In summary, this game was a swing and a miss for bethesda. Although, with the newly developed game engine, I cannot wait to see what they can do with content in the next game. I have recommended this game based on the game engine and because I haven't given up oin Bethesda yet... I am a huge fan of the series and they are truly epic games. With The Ringed City DLC right around the corner, From Software claiming it to be the last addition to the souls series, I thought I'd let curious people know what they're getting into.
Everyone else can review how awesome souls games are, Im just going to talk about performance.
DS3 does not perform well.
Go on over to the Technical Support page and you will see over 5000 unanswered comments in regards to performance issues and other problems. Dating from release to today (March 25th). In response, the Developer posted the minimum and recommended system specs. You can submit additional information to the customer support team. However that was posted nearly a year ago now at launch and the performance issues have not been improved on.
Additionally, the patch for the upcoming dlc has created a random bug that will generate a text pop up and boot you to the main menu.
My specs are i5-4590 3.30GHz 8GB RAM GTX 970 Windows 10 64 bit.
I cannot run this at 1080p/60fps ANYWHERE in game. If you have similar specs, expect to play between 40-60fps in the more optimized areas. Inb4 the nay-sayers, Believe me, I have tried it all to improve my experience.
I hope this helps you make an informed decision on whether or not this game will run to your expectations. I love it, but I cannot recommend it based on the performance. Thanks for reading.

This is a nice little action MMO; it's centered around exploring randomly-generated dungeons in groups of up to 4 players, employing a combat system similar to the 2D Zelda games (striking at enemies and parrying their attacks with your shield).  The combat is simple to pick up, but there's enough variety in weapon types and equipment to allow you to diversify and find a particular fighting style you like.
Of course, this is a cash shop MMO, and you're limited in what you can do by the stock of Energy you have -- you get 100 Energy over the course of a day, but it costs energy to descend to new dungeon floors, make your own equipment, unlock more than two weapon slots, or unlock the treasure boxes you occasionally find.  However, the cash shop is well-balanced; there's no cash shop only items that severely unbalance the game, like in many other games, and since there's an active currency exchange, you can convert your Crowns (the money dropped by enemies) into Energy at a fair rate.

WHAT STORY? DUN DUN DUN !

F*ck you, Bethesda, honestly. Just f*ck you.

Reall this game is all around fun. It's very versatile in what you can do.
Want to survive alone? Singleplayer.
Want to roleplay as a bandit or a cop? Roleplay servers.
Want to mess around with the range of weapons this game has to offer? Creative servers.
Want to fight others in hunger games style arenas? Arena mode.
Want to survive against other players? Survival servers.
With the great customization this game has, from graphics, maps, weapon skins, workshop items, server settings, etc, you can get almost any experience on here. And all for free. All things you pay for are not game changing. You can't buy gold to get special items that stay on your body when you die, you can't sell your soul for a gun that's completly overpowered, or a vehicle that can't be destroyed. Nope, just cosmetics to make you look badass, but they aren't nesacary, and have no real upside besides being badass.
The only problem I have for this game, is optimization. The game for lower end computers is very taxing and doesn't run too well, thankfully there are maps and stuff that can run better for the lower end computers. Also Nelson, the single dev, is constantly updating every Friday, from stuff like bug fixes and level editor addtions (Yes you can make your own maps for the game), to new guns, cars, and items. Nelson puts his heart and soul into this game and has made it amazing.
My overall rating, 9/10.

So much potential. Spiral Knights, in its early days, was a great MMORPG-ish thing with sensical mechanics and easy-to-learn gameplay. It was a great time-burner, trying to get all 5 star gear, running the Firestorm Citadel over and over. Unfortunately, as time passed, things took a turn for the worse. As OOO (or sega or whoever makes updates for this thing now) became more and more ambitious, the updates spiraled off and off into a sense of bleh. Missions were cool. Crimson Hammer was cool. Battle Sprites were cool. Mist energy being removed was passable. Being forced most of the time to spend $20 to upgrade a single piece of gear is not cool. At the advent of the Forge update, the game, while always being sort of a cash grab, became impossible to play. To get decently tiered gear now, you must slave away in T3, because the drops needed almost never actually drop. This has caused many of my friends who I knew to be seasoned veterans of the game to quit. The guild I was in, which had over 50 active players, went inactive a month after the update. Before the update with the Forge, pretty cool. After, not so much.

Okay, I want to say that this game is amazing, the concept and the play style, despite my desire to never lose a man in a fight, is pretty amazing.  I'd recommend the hell out of this game, but recently, there was a huge update, and while I thought it was just a class addition, it was total chaos.  I had read a review suggesting that the game had became unplayable, and I can safely agree with this, I felt the need to write an actual review for this game because of it in the hope that it'll at least get someone to tell the devs that they ♥♥♥♥ed up.  It's a damn fine game, it really is, but the new update added protection to basic level enemies, yes I understand that they can't take full damage from EVERY blow you dish out, but basic enemies, with wooden shields, hooks, and metal cans on their heads shouldn't be able to stop 3/4's of the damage that is coming at them, it makes sense in cases like the Brigand Cannons or large enemies but not for regular opponents, it was made to a point that maggots are actually a team kill, having armor, debuffs, AND stuns, as well as above average speed.  Yes, you're making the game more difficult, but you're also making the ability to clear any of the dungeons a horrible thought, you'll only complete a dungeon on rare cases now, considering enemy crit seems so increased that where you'll score a total of three crits in one dungeon they'll score a grand total of 12.  Added protection, and adding the fact that the buffs that are actually good can now be replaced with things you don't even want, as well as having to pay gold up to fix a characters "disease" of being worried, all of this is new, unwanted, and really, really not needed.  This is turning into a factor where you'll lose to a hallway encounter before getting through a room, I've only done short dungeons with the new update and I tell you I cannot imagine one winning in the longer runs, given while you may never have your health dented, the balance of health loss and stress is overdone, you'll walk out of a fight, untouched, with minimal injuries, but everyone of them seem to leave an etching on your men's souls that makes them panic extremely easily, and overall succumb to heart attacks at an intense rate, there's no getting lucky with heart attacks, you panic, become weaker, and if you don't get away before they stress you further, you get a 100% chance to lose your man simply because they thought it was a good idea to make your fighters the biggest weaklings out there.  Overall, you deal less total damage as fighters, they made a lot of the good abilities completely not usable, they made stress your worst nightmare, they made the perks your fighters have nearly uncontrollable since you can only save so many from so many problems at once no matter the money, enemies with weak hides and pathetic armor are oddly stronger than they should be allowed to be, you'll find fighting larger monsters is easier than fighting the peons, and finally, CRITS ARE NEVER GOING TO BE IN YOUR FAVOR REGARDLESS OF THE CHARACTER OR MOVE YOU USE, No, it doesn't seem like they bumped down your crit chance, but when it's compared to that of the enemies, it's generally 25% of their total crit chance as an estimation, I wouldn't buy this game unless you either pound the idea into the developers heads that they're making the game terrible, or they fix their mistakes on their own, but if the game goes on sale for half off and you have the money to spend I don't see why one wouldn't try it out to say in the least.

This game has many things right with it, and some things wrong with it. I'm just going to give a little story about my experience with the game so far.
Dark Souls 3 is my first introduction to the Souls/Borne games. I started playing the game, died to Iudex Gundyr, felt extremely accomplished, and then made a terrible mistake. I went inside Firelink Shrine with the notion that everybody is out to get you; so the first thing I did when I saw the guy sitting on the stairs was try and backstab him. This went wrong, as I didn't know what would happen, and didn't expect him to be nearly impossible to kill before you put the coiled sword in the fire pit at Firelink. I died, respawned, went to Firelink, and got killed. Repeatedly, I was killed by one of the least threatening characters in the game. I started a new game, and found that Firelink was my safehaven. Since I knew it was the fifth game in the Souls/Borne series (after Demon Souls, Dark Souls 1 and 2, and BloodBorne), I thought I'd watch a lore video or two (at the time I was looking for brief summaries) about Dark Souls. Many days worth of lore videos later, I was baffled at how detailed the lore was, even though it wasn't shoved in your face. You had to look for it; in the world, by talking to people, and--most importantly--reading item descriptions. The world is so beautiful, everything has a backstory and a meaning. Obviously, I have many hours on this game, now (174.4). My current profile I have named "[My Real Name Here] of Astora". I came up with a whole backstory for the character, and made decisions in the game as if I was my character. It has helped me emerse myself in the world for a fun experience. A lot of the time I play with theme builds and just have fun. The game has endless replayability.
My pros and cons of this game would be
Pros:
Graphics are great
Lore is extremely deep
Great game for a challenge
Lots of places to explore
PvP is well balanced (mostly)
Cons:
Some people play weird builds that just make it difficult (don't know if this is really a con though)
If you're not too interested in lore, then you won't get any of it in any playthrough
Game isn't too linear (if you're looking for that type of game)
Some of these cons aren't really cons, and honestly, it's a game you have to experience it to love it. I bought it knowing it was a hard game, and wanted to test my skills at it. While it's very unforgiving and will punish every misstep you take, it's not so bad when you learn about attacks, and how to defend against them. You have to learn how to play against each opponent. I am biased, I love this game, and love the lore of the Souls/Borne even more than the gameplay and beautiful art direction. If you already love this game and took the time to read this, then I hope you enjoyed reading my first, pitiful, experience with Dark Souls.
EDIT: All of those Cons and Pros are biased, and I couldn't think of cons. Don't pay attention to that section, and just enjoy the review.

Honestly I held off on buying Fallout 4 until a good sale. I bought the game plus the season pass for less than $50. For the content and the flexibility with mods I think it's more than worth it even with all the issues that have surrounded the game. It may not be as good story-wise as some of the previous titles, heck I even use a mod to negate fusion core use on power armor because it's never been a thing before and it's an unnecessary function. Sure power armor is more powerful but you still have to repair it every time you turn around which means using materials and finding a crafting station.
Still despite the bugs that Bethseda has ignored like: floating grass or massively long load screens, I still find the game fun-especially with all the dlc included. The modding community has shored up many of the issues with the game as well as added a number of cool features or even whole adventures. I mean there aren't many story-driven rpg games out there anymore since everyone else seems to have gone with microtransaction and/or 'mmorpgs'-which aren't even true rpgs-but Bethseda is still cranking out a decent story. People are really much too critical when it comes to FO4. To be fair though... I wouldn't have paid full price for the game simply because of the cost of the dlc/season pass at full price. Grab the game when it's on sale and you probably won't find much to complain about. Just don't go into FO4 thinking it's a better New Vegas. It's not, it's a different game and that's okay too.

Played this for a few hours during the free-play period thinking "hmm, I'll give it a shot, and it's $19 now. If I like it, I'll definitely get it for this price."  Now, I've never played any Fallout games, so I have nothing to compare this to except maybe Skyrim since it's from the same developers and I LOVE Skyrim. Even with Skyrim's sh! tty main story, the side quests and immersion of that f*cking game makes it so replayable. I'm all for role-playing games. I love playing a character, traveling with people with backstories, making choices, changing the story, and games that have fighting as the very last priority. Now, THIS game...
The intro got me super excited. The character creation got me excited. The voice acting is freaking ah-mazing (the voice acting is really about the only plus for this game when it comes to immersion)... so I was like "this might not be as bad as people are saying." I was originally put off from playing this game due to the sh! tty graphics I saw on console. One of my console peasant friends was playing it, and I walked in on him going at it -- get your mind out of the gutter -- and my immediate reaction was "this looks so ugly". So, I was right away put off from ever touching this game. But, the intro of the game was so good (story narration, character creation, and then right before you start to exit the vault) it was so good that I was willing to look over the plastic looking graphics and try to get into the story. But wait...
WHAT STORY? DUN DUN DUN !
That's right. Where the f*ck is the story?
Even my very first encounter with people was as bland as a wet piece of paper. I could have cared more for the sh!t that I took this morning floating in my toilet water than for these freaking people I supposedly saved at my first encounter with humans. And a f*cking gypsy? A gypsy who senses the energy of my missing child? Are you f*cking kidding me right now? I mean really? You couldn't have made me do a little more research, some CSI type sh!t... nope! A F*CKING GYPSY. "We don't really feel like actually putting any effort into problem solving or character connections for this game, so we're just going to place this magical being here to already tell you where you need to go to find your kid."  F*ck you, Bethesda, honestly. Just f*ck you.
Anyway, I used my power of "suspension of disbelief" to ignore that bit, and I went ahead to the city. But really, traveling there was boring. Sh!t just pops out of nowhere and attacks you, you don't even know from where or what until your character flails for several seconds. And nothing -- I mean --  NOTHING is nice to look at it. Mind you, I have everything on ultra, locked it myself on a perfect 60 FPS, and for what? So, because of the sh! tty story, I unfortunately was not able to get into this sh!t. I thought:
Sh! tty graphics but good story, I can do this.
Instead, I get sh! tty graphics AND sh! tty story. At least if the graphics were top-notch, I'd be able to create my own story in my head due to the immersion but I can't even do that.
I just don't understand how something as amazing as The Witcher 3 can be released EARLY 2015, and Fallout 4 is released LATE 2015 and look the way that it does. There is literally NO EXCUSE. And maybe if there were some cut-scenes? Sometimes the dialogue cut-scenes would happen but if I moved, they'd go away. Or there will be a dialogue cut-scene in an area I am nowhere near, it bugs out weirdly. I don't know, man. The game is just weird. And it sucks because when I met Piper, I was like "I really love the voice acting, and her personality, but..."  it's kind of like they just stuffed tiny little pieces of diamonds into a giant, deep, thick and unbreachable pile of sh!t. That is the only way to describe it.  As I was getting to the City of Diamond, all I kept asking myself was "am I really enjoying this? do I like this game?" -- it's so confusing... due to the 'tiny diamonds in sh!t' phenomenon I just described. I do not want to mindlessly walk around getting attacked by raiders that I can't even interact with at all other than by just shooting at them. I want to f*cking feel something, god damn it. I want to care for my character, care about the situation, and feel like what I'm saying to someone is actually going to change something.
"Well, what about that encounter with the mom and her drug addict kid?"  BLAND. WET PAPER BLAND. Didn't care. at. all.
Anyway, glad I played this sh!t for free and didn't buy it. Definitely not a role-playing game. Honestly, Bethesda needs to change its engine or some sh!t and stop trying to cater to mindless COD fanboys. I don't know, but they need to change SOMETHING and keep up with this next-gen sh!t. Cringey as f*ck for all of the hype.

Dark Souls III like previous installments in the series offers an experience few games come close to delivering. This game offers no hand outs.
My first play through had me die to the very first boss in the game, which is approximately 5 - 10 minutes into the experience atleast 5 times until I finally beat him. The feeling when you accomplish something in this game is incredible.
If you decide to go back for seconds like I did, you will immediately see how much you've improved! Dark souls is difficult as is known for but offers a rewarding gameplay experience through to the end. I will admit I played through this game almost entirely in Co-op which, Is always to preference for me to play through a game with a friend if possible. Only it doesn't necessarily mean it will be easier (atleast until you arrive at the boss) due to the fact that when you use the item that allows you to bring a friend into your world, will also open the door for bloodthirsty gankers to try and stop you. Invading players will come for you and very often! Pvp is a part of the experience. If you decide to take part in the muliplayer there is no co-op without pvp.
If you enjoy a challenge and games with a lot of depth into character creation as well as story, level design and fighting mechanics this is a must! The learning curve is a steep one but well worth it!

One of the harder games I've played in a while. Requires a good bit of strategy if you want to make any real progress. Extremely punishing:
Your heroes are not allowed to do missions below their skill range, meaning you can't just keep playing the easy missions with a high-ranked hero in order to amass money and upgrade materials. Additionally, having to manage your heroes' stress, not to mention having to sometimes cure them of serious character flaws ("quirks" as the game calls them) will force you to have several additional party members to swap out during these activities, and it also means making sure they're on par with the rest of your team.
Hero death is permanent, meaning you lose all the money and time spent upgrading a hero if they die.
Stress is equally lethal compared to damage, as it rises quickly and then drags down your entire party once someone becomes afflicted.
There is currently no "standard" way to adjust the game's difficulty other than opening the game's files in a text editor and then changing data values such as damage or resistance to better suit your personal skill level.
With all that being said, the game provides a considerable amount of fun. Completing a mission is always satisfying, the lore (albeing it somewhat restricted as of yet) is intriguing and will have you begging for more of the game's backstory, and the atmosphere is perfectly dark and suspenseful.
