OVERALL:
Spectacular, wellcrafted, balanced, engaging, and of course enraging; this is what a Dark Souls game is supposed to feel and play like. I purchased this game about a month after initial release and played the game for a solid 4 months as much as I could. The only drawback I have found is sparked when comparring this game to the initial DS game and that is difficulty. I have logged hundreds of hours into the first souls game on both pc and xbox yet the game is still difficult. You may argue that its simply bugs that make the first harder but I believe the overall difficulty to be much higher,. Another reason this may be is because I played the first game without any help due to the fact that I played the game around 2 years after release. This however does NOT make this game worse and especilly doesn't make it easy and is simply me addressing a common argument amongst the community. This is why I urge you to play this game on your own. Resist the strong temptation of summoning a friendly white or gold spirit and walk through the fog wall alone. When you're lost, embrace the fear of losing all progress and press onwards without the help of a guide. Feel the pain of traveling for over an hour without finding a bonfire. Feel the hopelessness that is running out of estus flasks so you can cherish the feelings of ecstacy when you finally find the bonfire. I urge you to do this not to bring pain onto yourself, but to feel the joy flow through your veins as you lay your final blow into a boss, to feel the curiosity race within your mind as you roll through an illusionary wall by simple mistake or educated guess, and to feel the comfort and safety of a bonfire after the long uphill battle that is this games learning curve. Moreover, I believe the issue many people including myself faced with this game was using the skills we had learned from the first game to rush through the interesting worlds we found ourselves in to play the pvp. Although fun I believe the pvp takes away from what the game could truly be. I am yet to play the first dlc (second dlc is soon to release) however I recently looked at this game within my steam library, smiled at the 100% achievement completion and over 250 hours logged, added the season pass to my wishlist (bought it a week later), and launched the game. To conclude, theres no reason why you should not play this game as long as you are prepared to die, and die, and die, and die, and when all hope is lost; succeed. Avoid the temptations caused by the cooperative function of this game and focus on your own journey. Don't seek help, carve your own path and the victory you are destined to achieve will feel much more rewarding.
OPINION AFTER DLC:
Holy hell was I wrong! This game is tough as nails! I just recently realized the reason why I was having such an easy time in this game and such a hard time in the first darksouls game. It's because I frequently play on ng7+ (new game 7 and beyond) in ds1 where I had only made it to ng3 in this game. After a few or so hours grinding bosses for souls and trying to git gud in preperation for both dlc's (I didn't decide to purchase the season pass until I read a few reviews on The Ringed City) I slowly made my way up to ng6 and started to feel a dramatic shift in the difficulty. Before I was able to withstand 5, maybe 6-8 hits from most bosses. Ng6, nearly every boss had the ability to 2-shot me with 40 vigor and full armor of favor. This increase in difficulty amazed me and got me even more excited for the dlc. To say the least without spoiling anything, if you are on ng5+ going into this dlc, you will get ravaged. You will get 2-shotted by bosses that seem to have well over 100,000 health. In short, this is the true prepare to die edition and I recommend the season pass with 100% confidence.
IN DEPTH REVIEW OF ONLINE PLAY:
I love the PvP and Co-op systems within this game. The weapon mechanics are spectacular, the summoning system has been almost perfected, and so have the invading mechanics (impossible to be perfect when you can get quad ganked by people weilding 3-shot weapons that can stun lock you if you don't have enough poise or roll at the perfect time). However like I said above I warn you not to make the same mistake I made which is prioritize the PvP or rely on the cooperative gameplay to get you through the game. To quote a common meme within the Dark Souls community: Git Gud. The same goes for PvP. Of course you're going to invade someone and get parried within your first attack and get hornet ring smough's great-hammer-ed and die instantly, and yeah you may invade some other person and get r1'd to death in a matter of seconds by a +10 dark sword, but thats the price you have to be willing to pay to git gud. I've owned this game since 1 month after initial release. I've seen "metas" (idk why they call them metas that makes no damn since, I blame iron pinapple) come and go. I suffered through the estoc bestoc crisis and the Fume Ultra-Greatsword 1-shots, and I can personnally say that this game's PvP is comfortably balanced. The only difficulty I believe any new-commer will face within the PvP is the same problem within the PvE, which is the learning curve. I personally do not know how hard this game's learning curve is because I entered the game with well over 500 hours in the first dark souls game. All I can say is if you rely on someone to guide you through this game you aren't getting the true experience.
CONCLUSION:
To conclude I'd like to restate one of my main arguments. You need to die over and over and over and over again. You need to stay up 3 hours later than you should because you have to give it "one more try". You need to be parried over and over, and fail parry after parry to become a parry god. Finally, to get the true dark souls experience you need to punch your table, throw your controller, talk to yourself like a madman, scream at the boss because "thats so f***ing stupid! He shouldn't be able to do that!", and furthermore, die, die, die, die, die, die, die, get close, die, die, die, change weapons, die, die, die, die, die, respec your build entirely, die, respec back to your old build, die, get really f***ing close, die, die, die, and of course... die, before you can truly call yourself a dark souls player.

Let's get one thing straight: You're not the main character. You might have a favorite hero, but you're more of a Caretaker, you lead these guys on their quests, but you're not fighting. You keep the town up, you keep provisions up, and you stock treasure and trinketss, but you're not physically handling these eldtrich abominations.
That being said, this isn't a bad game by no means, just because you're taking more of a "SimCity Mayor" role, doesn't mean you'll be a bystander, because this game projects what the heroes are feeling onto you, when you're wandering through these dark dungeons, you feel the dread that those heroes are feeling, scared that you'd run up on a trap, or in the case of the Warrens, run up on some sort of sickness.
I'd most definitely reccommend this game for anyone who wants a different kind of RPG experience.

"A mile wide, but an inch deep."
I love RPG's more than anything. I also love shooters, so an RPG shooter in a open post-apocalyptic world is MY JAM. This game calls itself an RPG, but it is ABSOLUTELY not in any real fashion. Perks and stats have no real impact on gameplay. They are an illusion. There are literally no consequences for the vast majority of actions (you can count the number of major plot choices on one hand, maybe two if you stretch it). The characters are shallow and cliche, the locations lack a sense of true vibrancy, and after a little while the world begins to feel hollow. I repeat again, there are almost NO real decisions you can make, and no consequences.
There are so few interesting quests, and the main story railroads you in a fashion that utterly destroys any semblence of free will (You are forced to join every faction, and as such you cannot truly roleplay). If you say "♥♥♥♥ you" to a characters face, they do not react in any way. I wanted to roleplay an evil aligned character, but cannot (there is no "karma", like in Fallout 3, nor any "reputation" like in New Vegas). A member of a good-aligned faction asked me to join them, and I chose to say "♥♥♥♥ no, how about I just shoot you instead". Her response was along the lines of "But we need you, so let us know when you are ready to get serious about helping people". I was forced to join, and then was given all of their secrets and tasked with being their #1 guy. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T. Another time, I attempted to persuade a character to join a faction, FAILED the persuasion check, and she still decided to join the faction. This was the moment I realized that Fallout 4 was utterly shallow and without substance.
There are some amazing details that truly make exploration satisfying and rewarding. Combat is well fleshed out, for instance. The world looks good, and there are some golden moments with certain characters and plot events. I really did have a blast with my first playthrough. However, after my first 50-60 hours of play I had to start making up excuses for a lack of cohesive lore, or for why characters acted the way they did (I love it when I leave Diamond City and a guard says "Head on in!", it breaks immersion almost as fast as a crash to desktop).
This game is not an RPG, and it does not have any real depth or character. The world is hollow, and none of your choices matter. This game is a fun open-world, explorative shooter. It is absolutely not an RPG, and as a long-time Fallout fan, I am deeply saddened to see Bethesda choose the wrong priorities in making this game. I know they put in a lot of work, and I respect the scope of the project they undertook, but they focused on the wrong things. This game is a console shooter thats been cleverly disguised as a Fallout brand RPG.
There are some awesome things about this game, and it is worth playing if you can pick it up for CHEAP; knowing what I know now I would buy it for $20. And dont even bother with Nuka World. I couldnt stomach finishing it even once, with three different characters. I really tried to love this game, but now I cannot unsee what I've experienced.
Play Fallout New Vegas instead, that game is truly one of the best modern RPG's to be made, and it showcases what the Fallout universe is really about.

There doesn't have to be excitement in every single building or small hamlet for it to be a great game.  Humanity was pretty much wiped out, so it's pretty realistic that some areas might be inhabited more than others.
Of course the normal "Suspension of Disbelief" applies to this game as much as any other.  Yes, the Fusion Cores don't last as long as they should, especially in light of entire buildings being powered by the same cores for over 200 years.  The developers did a great job of creating the atmosphere of a post-apocalyptic world and have included some inredicble detail as well.  There are hidden Easter Eggs throughout this game if you only take the time to explore a llittle.  I don't peersonally need an all-out excitement experience 100% of the time for a game to be enjoyable.  Onnce the primary quests lines are complete, the normal prograssion is to transition to managing your settlements and rescuing them from raiders, ghhouls, and remnants of the forces you defeated depending on your choices in the main quest line.
In my opinion, this game has a great first-time playability as well as a solid second and third-time run through capability.  You can choose to act totally differently (empathetic, rude, sarcastic, or noble, etc) in your interactions with the NPCs in the game and they will react differently based on what you do.
I did not receive any incentives or anything for my reivew, but I did receive this game as a gift from my son for Christmas.  It is reasonably priced on Steam as are the add-ons.
In conclusion, I highly recommend this game as I have had a great time playing it.  I do not find it to be shallow or lacking in storyline as other reviwers have mentioned.  I find it to be a world rich in locations and activities.

Do you like Terraria? Then this game could be for you.
The game plays smoothly with good hit detection, and there is plenty to explore. You feel like you don't like the planet you are on anymore? Just get some fuel and leave, and if you wrote down the co-ordinates of your previous world you can go back there when ever you want. Each world has can have a variety of NPC buildings ranging from towns to dungeons, and not only that they also have randomly generated trees, mobs, and color schemes. Depending on your luck you might find multiple planets with similar trees and mobs in a row.
Some nice little things it has:
Each race has unique weapons from the crafting system, and some unique armor sets. Currently this is only a visual change.
There is a vast variety of crops and food you can make with them.
You can dual weild 1-handed weapons.
And there are musical instruments that you can use to play ABC music files, and people playing in multiplayer can actually hear the song. (even if they don't have the music file)
Alien meat is somewhat commonly dropped from mobs, and you can cook it to make food.
I would list more, but it would start to be things that are almost a standard for this type of game.
Some annoyences:
Currently the game is in an early beta state, so there may be character or universe wipes.
Since it is in beta there are bugs that may crash the game or require a server to restart.
There are lots of times when you just feel way too strong, or way too weak.
Currently there is no point to farming or crafting foods with the alien meat drop rate.
Well those are my thoughts on the game for now.

OVERALL:
Spectacular, wellcrafted, balanced, engaging, and of course enraging; this is what a Dark Souls game is supposed to feel and play like. I purchased this game about a month after initial release and played the game for a solid 4 months as much as I could. The only drawback I have found is sparked when comparring this game to the initial DS game and that is difficulty. I have logged hundreds of hours into the first souls game on both pc and xbox yet the game is still difficult. You may argue that its simply bugs that make the first harder but I believe the overall difficulty to be much higher,. Another reason this may be is because I played the first game without any help due to the fact that I played the game around 2 years after release. This however does NOT make this game worse and especilly doesn't make it easy and is simply me addressing a common argument amongst the community. This is why I urge you to play this game on your own. Resist the strong temptation of summoning a friendly white or gold spirit and walk through the fog wall alone. When you're lost, embrace the fear of losing all progress and press onwards without the help of a guide. Feel the pain of traveling for over an hour without finding a bonfire. Feel the hopelessness that is running out of estus flasks so you can cherish the feelings of ecstacy when you finally find the bonfire. I urge you to do this not to bring pain onto yourself, but to feel the joy flow through your veins as you lay your final blow into a boss, to feel the curiosity race within your mind as you roll through an illusionary wall by simple mistake or educated guess, and to feel the comfort and safety of a bonfire after the long uphill battle that is this games learning curve. Moreover, I believe the issue many people including myself faced with this game was using the skills we had learned from the first game to rush through the interesting worlds we found ourselves in to play the pvp. Although fun I believe the pvp takes away from what the game could truly be. I am yet to play the first dlc (second dlc is soon to release) however I recently looked at this game within my steam library, smiled at the 100% achievement completion and over 250 hours logged, added the season pass to my wishlist (bought it a week later), and launched the game. To conclude, theres no reason why you should not play this game as long as you are prepared to die, and die, and die, and die, and when all hope is lost; succeed. Avoid the temptations caused by the cooperative function of this game and focus on your own journey. Don't seek help, carve your own path and the victory you are destined to achieve will feel much more rewarding.
OPINION AFTER DLC:
Holy hell was I wrong! This game is tough as nails! I just recently realized the reason why I was having such an easy time in this game and such a hard time in the first darksouls game. It's because I frequently play on ng7+ (new game 7 and beyond) in ds1 where I had only made it to ng3 in this game. After a few or so hours grinding bosses for souls and trying to git gud in preperation for both dlc's (I didn't decide to purchase the season pass until I read a few reviews on The Ringed City) I slowly made my way up to ng6 and started to feel a dramatic shift in the difficulty. Before I was able to withstand 5, maybe 6-8 hits from most bosses. Ng6, nearly every boss had the ability to 2-shot me with 40 vigor and full armor of favor. This increase in difficulty amazed me and got me even more excited for the dlc. To say the least without spoiling anything, if you are on ng5+ going into this dlc, you will get ravaged. You will get 2-shotted by bosses that seem to have well over 100,000 health. In short, this is the true prepare to die edition and I recommend the season pass with 100% confidence.
IN DEPTH REVIEW OF ONLINE PLAY:
I love the PvP and Co-op systems within this game. The weapon mechanics are spectacular, the summoning system has been almost perfected, and so have the invading mechanics (impossible to be perfect when you can get quad ganked by people weilding 3-shot weapons that can stun lock you if you don't have enough poise or roll at the perfect time). However like I said above I warn you not to make the same mistake I made which is prioritize the PvP or rely on the cooperative gameplay to get you through the game. To quote a common meme within the Dark Souls community: Git Gud. The same goes for PvP. Of course you're going to invade someone and get parried within your first attack and get hornet ring smough's great-hammer-ed and die instantly, and yeah you may invade some other person and get r1'd to death in a matter of seconds by a +10 dark sword, but thats the price you have to be willing to pay to git gud. I've owned this game since 1 month after initial release. I've seen "metas" (idk why they call them metas that makes no damn since, I blame iron pinapple) come and go. I suffered through the estoc bestoc crisis and the Fume Ultra-Greatsword 1-shots, and I can personnally say that this game's PvP is comfortably balanced. The only difficulty I believe any new-commer will face within the PvP is the same problem within the PvE, which is the learning curve. I personally do not know how hard this game's learning curve is because I entered the game with well over 500 hours in the first dark souls game. All I can say is if you rely on someone to guide you through this game you aren't getting the true experience.
CONCLUSION:
To conclude I'd like to restate one of my main arguments. You need to die over and over and over and over again. You need to stay up 3 hours later than you should because you have to give it "one more try". You need to be parried over and over, and fail parry after parry to become a parry god. Finally, to get the true dark souls experience you need to punch your table, throw your controller, talk to yourself like a madman, scream at the boss because "thats so f***ing stupid! He shouldn't be able to do that!", and furthermore, die, die, die, die, die, die, die, get close, die, die, die, change weapons, die, die, die, die, die, respec your build entirely, die, respec back to your old build, die, get really f***ing close, die, die, die, and of course... die, before you can truly call yourself a dark souls player.

This is the best game in the series, though it has a strange balance of simultaneously being easier to get into for new players but also managing to keep returning players on their toes with extremely aggressive enemy/boss behaviours. The level design has also shifted from the small and extremely dense style of the original to a much more grandiose layout. Levels no longer connect to each-other in the same twisting and branching manner, instead connecting in a much more linear fashion, though individual levels are still open and full of shortcuts. The layout of each level is now gigantic, often reaching what feels like several square kilometers in size and that's sort of a running theme with Dark Souls III. Everything is bigger, the music, the world and even some of the bosses. It's also to my knowledge the only game in the series that lets you yell "HEY!" and also the only one I've been able to win a match in PVP (probably my internet more than the game) so that's something.
Technical:

- 60 fps locked but it's fluid enough for now, graphics in general look fantastic except for some areas they don't think you'll look at
Side note: In terms of Japanese PC ports, From Software has only created 3 PC ports, ever. Each one significantly improved over the last. Sandlot did a good job with the EDF 4.1 port last year and that's their only PC port. Omega Force has 2 that were released within the last 2 months, out of several and the most recent one doesn't even recognise a mouse.

This game is odd. It offers standard RPG combat with a few refreshing new twists that make it more tactical. The game's atmoshpere is dark (obviously) and is very well done in a pseudo Lovecraftian style. The art is fantastic. The mechanics are fun to toy with, especially the light mechanic. The afflictions your mercs come down with are always entertaining and devastating.
However, little is done to draw you into the game. It doesn't have an engrosing story (or any story, really), no characters to get attached to and no real plot of any kind. While the gameplay is good, it is not enough to make the game a real game. Without a story to tie things together and keep it interesting, it gets stale very fast. After clearing out one or two missions (20-40 minutes) you get bored of the repetition and stop playing. Basically, you side scroll though a level until you find an object to interact with or enemies to fight. It gets a little deeper than that with scouting, camping skills, equipment upgrades, etc. There's an imbalance of an incredibly deep and complex micromanagement system for the town/your mercs' training and incredibly dull exploration/dungeon clearing.
To me, this feels like a mobile game, something you pick up for maybe half an hour a day to do a dungeon or two and put it down. The controls are reminiscent of a mobile game, even down to the purchase of supplies seems like it is optimized for a microtransaction laden mobile game (forget to buy or already run out of torches, shovels, food, etc? Buy some now for 99¢! Need to upgrade the forge? But a pack of relics now for $1.99!). While I am glad that this is NOT like that, it feels halfway there already. While there was obviously some good work put into this, it's not enough to make it worth $20. It seems like I could easily find something on the App Store that closely approximates this style of gameplay for free.
TL:DR
Wait until this comes out of early access and see where it ends up. Needs significant improvement before I would recommend spending $20 on it. I think it's a fantastic start but it lacks any real meat.

I have thoroughly enjoyed this game.  With 445 hours invested, so far, I have completed the main quest lne and many of the add-on content.  I disagree with other reviewers that have called this game "shallow" and have enjoyed the many locations throughout the Commonwealth, the Island, and Nuka World.   There doesn't have to be excitement in every single building or small hamlet for it to be a great game.  Humanity was pretty much wiped out, so it's pretty realistic that some areas might be inhabited more than others.
Of course the normal "Suspension of Disbelief" applies to this game as much as any other.  Yes, the Fusion Cores don't last as long as they should, especially in light of entire buildings being powered by the same cores for over 200 years.  The developers did a great job of creating the atmosphere of a post-apocalyptic world and have included some inredicble detail as well.  There are hidden Easter Eggs throughout this game if you only take the time to explore a llittle.  I don't peersonally need an all-out excitement experience 100% of the time for a game to be enjoyable.  Onnce the primary quests lines are complete, the normal prograssion is to transition to managing your settlements and rescuing them from raiders, ghhouls, and remnants of the forces you defeated depending on your choices in the main quest line.
In my opinion, this game has a great first-time playability as well as a solid second and third-time run through capability.  You can choose to act totally differently (empathetic, rude, sarcastic, or noble, etc) in your interactions with the NPCs in the game and they will react differently based on what you do.
I did not receive any incentives or anything for my reivew, but I did receive this game as a gift from my son for Christmas.  It is reasonably priced on Steam as are the add-ons.
In conclusion, I highly recommend this game as I have had a great time playing it.  I do not find it to be shallow or lacking in storyline as other reviwers have mentioned.  I find it to be a world rich in locations and activities.

5 second review. Like challenge? Get it. Hate getting salty. Move on.
Now onto the real review.
What do you get when you throw an old-timey novella, Edgar Allen Poe, Lovecraft, and Dark Souls into a blender? A catastrophic mess, right? Now if you form it into a rogue-styled strategy game it becomes a totally new type of beast. That beast is Darkest Dungeon.
Darkest Dungeon takes the best elements of both roguelike and strategy video games. It pits you and your not-so-merry band of adventurers against the horrors of the night in seemingly endless dungeons. You must journey into the proceduraly generated corridors and fight through hoards of baddies searching for loot, glory, and the answer to everyones question. What was behind that barrier? But horrific monsters are not the worst you will face. You must manage and properly care for each individual character in your gang, making sure they are both capable of the quest AND sane enough to not have a mental breakdown. The stress and insanity mechanics in the game are fresh and new, making you bite your nails and cheer in joy within the same battle. The game has many different character classes to choose from and will most likely get many more with future updates. A mainstay on both Twitch and YouTube for several weeks due to the difficult challenge the game presents to the players and the harsh choices the player must make. The popularity died down however due to one of the games biggest deteriorators. Darkest Dungeon was in the Early Access program, which may have ended up hurting the game in the end. Like most games in the program, by the time release came around, people had already played it so much that even new features weren't enough to draw a huge crowd back in. So, is the game good or bad? I cannot answer that question. You must decide for yourself if the game is worth buying. All I can do is tell you the good and bad.
Pro's:
+ Gorgeous Artstyle
+Engaging combat system
+Deep character customization
+Nail-biting challenge
Con's:
-Early Access killed hype
-Lack of "real" story
-Numerous launch bugs and issues
-Grindy character building

If you were a fan of Terraria, but wanted more exploration, a need to survive, and maybe even throw in a Sci-Fi twist into it; this is the game for you. Starbound is a 2D-Platformer that immediately throws you in the loop of Space Survival when you, as one of six races, leave your civilization to explore the Universe.
Graphics: It's a 2D-Platformer, I'm not expecting the game to look realistic, in fact, I'm looking for it to look like a game. Starbound delivers that feeling and look spectacularly. The world still looks alive, but with the creative touch and look that retro style games had. Tens of hundreds of different types in appearance for the same item, (such as dirt, trees, water, etc.) so you always have the "space-feel" of wanting to figure out what this new colored dirt could be. Monsters are randomly generated with what seems to be a "part-generator", where there are 3-5 different catagories that the monster needs to have a look and the system randomly picks in those catagories!     (9/10 for the sheer fact that graphics are always availible to be improved)
Sound: Great Soundtrack. Period. Exploration on the surface, deep in the planet, in space, on an asteroid - all have their own unique feel in terms of sound through music and SFX. You can even find instruments in the game and play classical hits, holiday songs, or even upload your own music into the game and play on the instrument - sounding like the instrument (haven't tried using with songs that have lyrics).  (9.2/10 Love the quality of the music and the ability to upload my own)
Gameplay: It has the feel of the generic sandbox-game, so you won't be lost on "what to do", you know what to do: Upgrade your stuff, build a home, explore, and SLAY EVERYTHING! ( -insert evil smiley- ) Even in Beta the gameplay feels unique, but still familiar to Terraria, assuming you've played it of course. Travel many planets on a ship (so the resources never run out), explore different terrains, and build yourself up a home on a planet that you decide to call "home". Even if you find a "home" though, make sure to take care of yourself! In this game you also have to keep an eye on your Hunger and Temperature. Farming and Hunting are both availible to keep you fed, and clothes/campfire to keep you warm. I've never been so excited to mine a dirt block just to find out what it was, "in the name of SCIENCE". Replayability is extremely high, very addictive.    (9.5/10 Be sure to look at it's list of incoming features as well as what the game has listed, you'll have plenty to keep you entertained and excited for more!)
Final Review (Beta): Overall, wonderful game. Can't get enough. Even in beta I find this game to be picking up where others lack. Fun, innovative in it's genre, funny (look for sooo many Easter Eggs), a challenge, and most likely the most addictive game that wasn't a MMO.   (9.3/10)

I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys sandbox titles, and not afraid of retro pixelized graphics. In a nutshell it's Terraria in space, but already has much more potential! If you enjoyed Terraria, I promise you are going to leave it for this game, and never look back. (Oh my poor old, Terraria world, farewell! :-( ) Starbound has a very huuuuuuuge, I mean VERY HUUUUUGEEEE world. You choose a race, customize it (Cute, and funny details!) and name your character. Then you end up on your very own starship. You get your first quest. Currently there is only a tutorial quest line, but more will come later! You travel around the galaxy with the ship. You need to mine (or inv edit, like I do haha) fuel to travel from planet to planet, and you need to destroy bosses to unlock new sectors with harder enemies and better loot. You can set a home planet and teleport there freely anytime you want, even though you are not even in the sector. You can add your own furniture to your ship as it pleases you. In multiplayer it also serves as a hub, where your friends can teleport/beam to. And steel your stuff if you invite complete strangers on a regular basis. :-) The game's currency is called pixel. It's a pain to get right now, but the whole system is still being balanced. If you die, your hunger, coldness level, breath and hp are filled, you are teleported back to your ship and loose many of your pixels. You can buy schematics (recipes for crafting), weapons, clothes and food from NPCs you find on planets. Also some crafting recipes need pixels, and your ship has a 3d printer. You can put inside any item, destroy it, and afterwards you'll be able to "3d print" that item in exchange for pixels. There are countless amounts of biomes, each one has their own trees, colors of dirt, endless amount of monsters and minibosses. Some will attack you, some are passive. There are only a few bosses yet. NPCs can be spawned by you trough special spawners, so you can build your own village, or even shops! (NPC traders can be spawned as well.) You can get skills via loot. Dashing, superjumps, your own controllable mech, etc. There are playable instruments. You can sit down on couches, fountains, chairs, and you can sleep on many objects (carts, pile of hay, dozens of beds, altars, tents, etc.). While sleeping you gain hp, the speed depends on how good is your bed. You can farm many fruits, vegetables, hunt for leather and meet, collect eyeballs from eyeball plants (yes, from plants, no, don't ask, lol :D) and cook them for buffs and fill your hunger meter. Else you'll die. You also need to have warm clothes or fire nearby if the weather gets cold, or you'll also die. Different planets have different biomes, weather and gravity.
In other terms, it's just like Minecraft and Terraria: you mine stuff. You loot stuff. You steel stuff if you're that kind of guy (shame on you :D). You get stuff, you build stuff. For fun, for aesthetic reasons, for shelter and (hopefully) for safety. You try to survive. You kill monsters. You get the idea.
There are so much more in this game, and content is constatly updated. I hope I gave you a basic insight of the gameplay. Give it a go if it comes out. Seriously. Worth every single dollar/euro/pixel/whatever.

Great game for RPG fans… IF it’s on sale. Mediocre game for a mediocre price.
I like to base reviews on what they game sets out to be instead of what we think it should be. That doesn’t mean we can’t bash the game if the developer proved they knew better.
For starters the graphics are well polished for the engine’s age but why even use such an old engine for such a big title to begin with? The pictures and videos on the steam page speak for themselves, this isn’t pushing next level by any stretch but beauty is in the eye of the beholder… the graphics are serviceable and don’t suck, but they aren’t great either, just good.
The lack of quest especially considering this has the name Fallout and made by Bethesda on it. While Skyrim had the main quest, side quest, and quests pertaining the different major organizations, Fallout 4 has the main quest, side quests…. And that’s about it. Once I finished the game I felt like “That’s it?!” and yup, there aren’t many quality quest lines to follow. Now that doesn’t mean there is nothing to do, because there is, just a lot less than previous Bethesda RPGS.
You know what’s next, that pathetic dialogue wheel. KotOR, an RPG from 2003, had better and more varied dialogue options. Here in Fallout 4 you get the generic nice response, the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥response (which will result in you denying most quests), and the snarky response. While yes, it is serviceable and could be worse, that shouldn’t excuse how predictable every conversation would be. Some depth would have been nice.
And lastly, crashes. You may not experience crashes as much as me. But, oh. My. Word. No one should boot up a game with the mindset “Gee, I hope I don’t crash before I can do something cool.” You would think they would patch these crashes out, but nah. I hope that if you already played this game that you didn’t experience the amount of crashes this game gave me.
The main story line is among the better ones I’ve played (I know I know, I actually liked it though). The combat isn’t stellar but feels solid both in and out of first person. The sound and music is absolutely gorgeous! Have you heard that main theme??? (but the radio wasn’t too innovated from the previous version). The exploration is decent. The power suits make you feel like total badass. And for such an old engine, some of the locations do look rather good. Oh, and the settlement building… you either like it or don’t. It can be totally ignored though (for the most part). The survival mode is pretty cool too, give it shot to spice up that gameplay.
Overall, Fallout 4 is a very solid game. But its praise ends there… solid. Its not great, or fantastic, but its not bad either. It’s a mixed bag, but I did enjoy my time here. I feel like if it didn’t have the name Fallout that it would have been received better; you’ll just have to manage expectations, as it doesn’t shine like Bethesda’s previous titles. If you’re a fan of RPGS, need a new one, and can cop it on sale then it’s a good game. Otherwise… pass.

I haven't put to much time in this game, but I will say that as of its current state, I can't recommend it.
Movement is very strange feeling, when you jump you hang in the air for far to long.  When you try to make jumps to perhaps a block or two (say in the middle of a poison puddle that you want to cross) it can be very hard to accurately land on it as you kind of float about as if you were on ice constantly.  While in the air and on the ground attempting to make minor adjustments in your position.
The games poison water is a complete nuisance as you tend to find single blocks of it quite often or at least from what I've experienced, and stepping over them causes you to get poisoned which is a serious pain to a new player.
Combat feels extremely clunky.  It is fairly slow paced.  The knockback on weapons is ridiculous.  The lack of health regeneration, while dificult to get used to, is okay.  I know it was a big turn off for me at first, but that portion of it really isn't as bad as it sounds.
The real deciding factor that made me choose to give this a negative review is due to the crafting system.
Currently the crafting system feels very odd.  You start off with an extremely slow multitool and have to craft stone tools which are significantly faster.  From there you must upgrade these existing tools to their next tier.  Should you get lucky and find enough ore for, say, the Gold Pickaxe, you would first need to upgrade your stone pickaxe to copper, iron, and silver first as one of the items required to craft each pickaxe is the former in the chain.  The same goes for all armor and weapons it seems as well.  It feels very poorly done.  I see no reasoning what so ever why I should be stopped from making a tool which I have materials for until I find materials for all of the previous tiers.
I am also including the games currency (Pixels) as part of the crafting system as it really seems to have no other function.  You can not store Pixels without losing a large chunk of it(40%) and on death you lose 20% of all Pixels you have on you at the time and they simply disappear.  I feel as though on multiplayer servers this would make PvP extremely undesirable in almost all situations.
I know I did not include any positives in my review, but there are quite a few.  For the positives just check some of the top recommended reviews, they pretty much cover it.
All in all I would give this game a 7.5/10.  It's a solid game, enjoyable to an extent, and most likely worth 15$.  However I simply am not satisfied enough to give it a recommended review yet.  As they release updates I will attempt to keep this updated as well, and should these various problems get addressed I will absolutely change my review as aside from these issues I do find the game rather enjoyable.  But in its current state I find it rather bothersome to play at times, and think I will take some time to let the game develop more fully before attempting to play again.

Dark Souls 3 is the third entry into the Souls franchise, and it comes in as a good way to close the series. Never before have I put so many hours into a game in such little time. With a great soundtrack and stylish boss fights, the game has high replayability, leaving you noticing different things each and every playthrough. The sense of immersion you feel is amazing, when you start understanding how your interactions with characters and bosses in the game affect the universe around you, whether it be positively or negatively. Overall, I give the game a solid 10/10, for it is easily one of the best, if not the best game I have played in a long time.

5 second review. Like challenge? Get it. Hate getting salty. Move on.
Now onto the real review.
What do you get when you throw an old-timey novella, Edgar Allen Poe, Lovecraft, and Dark Souls into a blender? A catastrophic mess, right? Now if you form it into a rogue-styled strategy game it becomes a totally new type of beast. That beast is Darkest Dungeon.
Darkest Dungeon takes the best elements of both roguelike and strategy video games. It pits you and your not-so-merry band of adventurers against the horrors of the night in seemingly endless dungeons. You must journey into the proceduraly generated corridors and fight through hoards of baddies searching for loot, glory, and the answer to everyones question. What was behind that barrier? But horrific monsters are not the worst you will face. You must manage and properly care for each individual character in your gang, making sure they are both capable of the quest AND sane enough to not have a mental breakdown. The stress and insanity mechanics in the game are fresh and new, making you bite your nails and cheer in joy within the same battle. The game has many different character classes to choose from and will most likely get many more with future updates. A mainstay on both Twitch and YouTube for several weeks due to the difficult challenge the game presents to the players and the harsh choices the player must make. The popularity died down however due to one of the games biggest deteriorators. Darkest Dungeon was in the Early Access program, which may have ended up hurting the game in the end. Like most games in the program, by the time release came around, people had already played it so much that even new features weren't enough to draw a huge crowd back in. So, is the game good or bad? I cannot answer that question. You must decide for yourself if the game is worth buying. All I can do is tell you the good and bad.
Pro's:
+ Gorgeous Artstyle
+Engaging combat system
+Deep character customization
+Nail-biting challenge
Con's:
-Early Access killed hype
-Lack of "real" story
-Numerous launch bugs and issues
-Grindy character building

"A mile wide, but an inch deep."
I love RPG's more than anything. I also love shooters, so an RPG shooter in a open post-apocalyptic world is MY JAM. This game calls itself an RPG, but it is ABSOLUTELY not in any real fashion. Perks and stats have no real impact on gameplay. They are an illusion. There are literally no consequences for the vast majority of actions (you can count the number of major plot choices on one hand, maybe two if you stretch it). The characters are shallow and cliche, the locations lack a sense of true vibrancy, and after a little while the world begins to feel hollow. I repeat again, there are almost NO real decisions you can make, and no consequences.
There are so few interesting quests, and the main story railroads you in a fashion that utterly destroys any semblence of free will (You are forced to join every faction, and as such you cannot truly roleplay). If you say "♥♥♥♥ you" to a characters face, they do not react in any way. I wanted to roleplay an evil aligned character, but cannot (there is no "karma", like in Fallout 3, nor any "reputation" like in New Vegas). A member of a good-aligned faction asked me to join them, and I chose to say "♥♥♥♥ no, how about I just shoot you instead". Her response was along the lines of "But we need you, so let us know when you are ready to get serious about helping people". I was forced to join, and then was given all of their secrets and tasked with being their #1 guy. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T. Another time, I attempted to persuade a character to join a faction, FAILED the persuasion check, and she still decided to join the faction. This was the moment I realized that Fallout 4 was utterly shallow and without substance.
There are some amazing details that truly make exploration satisfying and rewarding. Combat is well fleshed out, for instance. The world looks good, and there are some golden moments with certain characters and plot events. I really did have a blast with my first playthrough. However, after my first 50-60 hours of play I had to start making up excuses for a lack of cohesive lore, or for why characters acted the way they did (I love it when I leave Diamond City and a guard says "Head on in!", it breaks immersion almost as fast as a crash to desktop).
This game is not an RPG, and it does not have any real depth or character. The world is hollow, and none of your choices matter. This game is a fun open-world, explorative shooter. It is absolutely not an RPG, and as a long-time Fallout fan, I am deeply saddened to see Bethesda choose the wrong priorities in making this game. I know they put in a lot of work, and I respect the scope of the project they undertook, but they focused on the wrong things. This game is a console shooter thats been cleverly disguised as a Fallout brand RPG.
There are some awesome things about this game, and it is worth playing if you can pick it up for CHEAP; knowing what I know now I would buy it for $20. And dont even bother with Nuka World. I couldnt stomach finishing it even once, with three different characters. I really tried to love this game, but now I cannot unsee what I've experienced.
Play Fallout New Vegas instead, that game is truly one of the best modern RPG's to be made, and it showcases what the Fallout universe is really about.

The best of the 3 Dark Souls games, however you may argue it's not the hardest.
I'd highly recommend people who are new to the series to start at Dark Souls 3. This game is more smooth for new players, easier to get into. The mechanics and gameplay is more fine tuned in this game, so it's best for new players to start with this. You do not miss any major lore, although some things might make a lot more sense lore wise if you played the others, but you don't have to. I recommend that you start here, if you complete it and want more, I recommend you play the other 2 games as well. Then if you are into exploring the lore, then replay this one after you played the others. Then some messages and stuff might make more sense.
The difficulty in this game is Dark Souls level, not that much harder imo. You might find some bosses to be in X game to be easier than Y game, but remember what YOU find to be the hardest boss is very subjective. Some people fly through some boss while you might struggle, vice-versa.
I spend 725 hours on Dark Souls: Prepare to Die. (Dark Souls 1)
770 hours on Dark Souls 2. (Dark Souls 2 + Scholar Edition)

I cannot recommend this game.
1) Poisoned water - Putting pixel-sized pockets of poison water underground especially in a newbie planet is nothing but malicious. It generates frustration, slows exploration and punishes new players. Why does a planet have more poisoned water than normal ones? Terrible design decision.
2) Gear crafting - If you're going to put copper pants as prerequisite to iron pants, at least make copper more abundant than iron. Devs need to review the prereqs.
3) Floaty jumps - Jumps are too floaty and imprecise, taking a lot of midair adjustments.
4) Imprecise movement - Same for moving, if you try to inch towards the edge you will likely walk off it and fall to the poisoned water below.
5) Combat - Much slower and less feedback than Terraria, also too much knockback. Floaty movement and jumps don't help.
6) Pixels - Right now it's just forcing me to repeatedly kill mobs for pixels. It's a grinding mechanism that's more at home in a MMO.

The mechanics and gameplay is more fine tuned in this game, so it's best for new players to start with this. You do not miss any major lore, although some things might make a lot more sense lore wise if you played the others, but you don't have to. I recommend that you start here, if you complete it and want more, I recommend you play the other 2 games as well. Then if you are into exploring the lore, then replay this one after you played the others. Then some messages and stuff might make more sense.
The difficulty in this game is Dark Souls level, not that much harder imo. You might find some bosses to be in X game to be easier than Y game, but remember what YOU find to be the hardest boss is very subjective. Some people fly through some boss while you might struggle, vice-versa.

Im not very good at creating game reviews however Ill try my best in this case. So I bought Fallout 4 one or two days after release and everyone had that feeling of hype and excitment for the game (I still play it time to time but only for the mods) However after doing four seperate playthroughs of the quest all I have to say is this: Game had better combat (kind of) however everything else is worse.
The combat compared from 3 and New Vegas is much improved. However there is also a downside to the combat, no more random crtical hits and much less weaponry. Now Im pretty sure someone out there is going to say "What do you mean less weaponry are you stupid?" Lets face it, in my opinion a pipe rifle is no different from a pipe pistol. Also when they removed weapon and armor conditioning it felt less like a fallout game from time to time. Power armor in my opinion is useless since it requires regular repairs and it losses health almost as fast as the sniper rifle in Fallout New Vegas. Also the armor cores can be a pain. My favorite weapon to use, the minigun, is now completely useless, even when fully modded and has heavy gunner maxed the accuracy on the gun is horrible. I wanted to use the gatling laser because of the minigun issue however it used armor cores as ammunition and armor cores are more expensive than 5MM ammo. I also feel like melee combat overshadows ranged combat by a long shot.
Going away from combat related issues the quests in general are just stupid. Now I know this is a meme however it needs to be said "General, theres another settlement that needs your help." I literally had a hostage situation where I gave one of my settlers a gauss rifle, and fully upgraded combat armor along side with the settlement having 3 missile turrets 2 heavy laser turrets and 5 heavy machine gun turrets, and that one settler with the gauss rifle gets captured. I feel like the more defence your settlements have, the less and less chance of these types of situations. Honestly I dont want to go in the problems I have with settlements. Speaking of Preston, the companion I traveled the most with was Dogmeat. I'd rather have a dog that constantly gets in my way than have a companion judge me on every action. I hated the companion like and dislike system, It sometimes forces the player have to play in a way they dont want to.
Moving on from that the whole system of quests. First of all theres only 2 real endings.
In my opinion the only changes they have is one or more than one less faction. I'm going to keep DLCS out of this review just as a heads up.
Now Character creating does have more options and can be in more detail however that is another plus per say. However I mean the face of character creation not everything else. Skills in general have been removed, no more guns skill, no more unarmed skill, no more science skill, no more survival you get the point. Now its all perks and SPECIAL. Now you need perks to pick locks, hack computers, increase how much you heal.
Im pretty sure no one is going to take the time to read this but if you do, I recommend to not spend money on this game. If you still want to, that is your choice, I have no control over your money. I also recommend that you play Fallout 3 or New vegas if you are going to buy a fallout game for the first time, or even one or two if you want to. Just don't buy this one it will leave a bad taste in your mouth. If there is one thing a regret other than buying this game, its that I told my friends that the game was amazing when I got back to school the next day after I bought it.

Although challenging from the start, the difficulty curves stupendously to give you enough challenge to get ecstasy from satisfaction when you kill a boss. Never before have I put so many hours into a game in such little time. With a great soundtrack and stylish boss fights, the game has high replayability, leaving you noticing different things each and every playthrough. The sense of immersion you feel is amazing, when you start understanding how your interactions with characters and bosses in the game affect the universe around you, whether it be positively or negatively. Overall, I give the game a solid 10/10, for it is easily one of the best, if not the best game I have played in a long time.

I recommend this game for the visuals, music, gameplay, character progression (through leveling and upgrading gear) and the ARPG-esque style of the Clockworks.
Major updates to the game in the last several years include changes to the energy system (which previously restricted how much you could adventure in 1 day w/o spending $$), the crafting system and an added rank system. Going deeper in the Clockworks no longer takes energy. They added a nice pet/companion system. There are now ranks that, once reaching specific ranks, allow you to directly purchase recipes for gear from vendors (no more RNG at the end of maps... thanks).
If you have friends to play with, there are many hours of fun to be had in this game. And for free... Did I mention that you can play this game for free?
Note that there is a significant advantage to those who spend money, in terms of progression speed. This is due to a change in how crafting works (not recent, but a change since I made my last review). All of the top-tier (5-star) gear needs to be crafted with items that are very difficult to acquire. Unless you spend $$ of course, then it's fairly simple to upgrade your 4-star gear. You still need to acquire the heat (leveling your gear through completing levels/maps) to upgrade the gear, but I felt there were advantages to spending real $$.
I was able to get a full set of 5-star gear by normally playing the game for ~100 hours prior to the changes described above. This may or may not be possible now, and could require more time spent to fully gear your knight. Whether that is a negative or positive (it comes down to perspective: more grinding necessary vs. more gameplay before you reach endgame) is up to you.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone interested in a beautiful, dungeon-crawl ARPG game.

This game has decent combat and cool loot but that's it. This game doesn't go beyond that. The quests are shallow and usually come down to going to a settlement or a building to retrieve some screw or piece of machinery. You might through a  hoard of bad guys and you reach a chest with the tool....that's it. Previously, in other Fallout games that is, a quest would start in a similar way, go there and get that but it doesn't end there. You find people in those places who don't instantly try to kill you, you can use your perks and skills to outsmart them and not fight at all. You can talk to them, see what problem they have and why they are the way they are. Maybe a bar owner sent you to retrieve a piece for a water pump so he can fix it but you see that the people in that abandoned factory need it for a machine that could keep them warm for months. So you have to choose, help the bar tender and get some caps or help the people and feel good. Fallout 4 has none of that. The quests are shallow and boring except a few. Like helping robots get a ship to fly or helping vault dwellers in vault eighty something. The loot is the best part about this game, every legendary has special stats and looks different making the grind somewhat enjoyable. The combat is much much better that other Fallouts, its not stale, you don't need VATS all the time and it's just fun. Would I recommend this game no, not for $60 but for $10 maybe. It's a decent game but not a good Fallout.

Spiral Knights is a simple and easy-to-play hack-and-slash MMO (did I mention it's free?). Similar in some ways to games like Zelda: Four Sword Adventures, you can slash, detonate, or shoot your way through dungeons with up to 3 friends (or none, if you're the solitary type) at a time, or play PvP mini-games reminiscent of Bomberman or Unreal Tournament's old domination mode. While the actual amount of game content is somewhat small, it dodges one of the biggest bullets that free MMO's tend to get hit by: The entirety of the game's content is accessible to ALL players.
There is almost no reason for you not to at least give it a shot.

The addtion of the weapon skills is an extremely nice touch and adds a lot of addtional combat depth not found in the previous games. Despite having a rough inital launch this game runs flawless on PC, provided you've got the rig to supplement that kind of performance. Easily the flagship version of the title. If you're not quite able to pull 60FPS constant on PC stick /w the PS4 version of the title. 30FPS rock solid. XB1 can't hold a stable framerate (Dancer fight dropping into the single digits, awful.)
// Pros //
- Fastest pace combat of the Souls Series.
- Weapon Skills adds depth and variety in combat and how you approach enemies.
- Fantastic art direction/design.
- Best looking of the Souls Series games.
- Best controlling of the Souls Series games.
- Fantastic music. (Dancer theme in particular and the final boss sequence is something special.)
- Still awaiting the next DLC! More content on the way. AoA was fantastic and has probably the most difficult boss fight in the game thus far. Very rewarding.
// Cons //
- Isn't Bloodborne on PC @ 60FPS. (Seriously FROMSOFTWARE, come on.)
And if anyone bothers reading to the bottom - do yourself a solid and play Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2. The entire franchise is easily worth your time.
(And Bloodborne, if you own a PS4/PS4Pro)
(Seriously FROMSOFTWARE - PC@60FPS. Please. God.)

I finished the single-player "part" and I was satisfied, but playing online is just another world. The horrible netcode and the lack of poise completely ruined the game for me. If I had only played DS1 and the problem was just the lack of poise, I think I could live with that, after all, poise was abused in DS1. Spiral Knights is a simple and easy-to-play hack-and-slash MMO (did I mention it's free?). Similar in some ways to games like Zelda: Four Sword Adventures, you can slash, detonate, or shoot your way through dungeons with up to 3 friends (or none, if you're the solitary type) at a time, or play PvP mini-games reminiscent of Bomberman or Unreal Tournament's old domination mode. While the actual amount of game content is somewhat small, it dodges one of the biggest bullets that free MMO's tend to get hit by: The entirety of the game's content is accessible to ALL players.
There is almost no reason for you not to at least give it a shot.

A few years ago, I thought this game, despite the obvious lean towards premium currency and mist energy (which can only be described as energy points seen in games like Farmville), was incredibly fun. I wasn't nearly as invested in it as some of my other friends, but as you see by my playtime, I had enjoyed enough of it to keep playing. However, as the years went by, this game has unfortunately slided downhill in turns of quality and just overall enjoyment.
Anymore, the game doesn't have any actual story (it never really did, but you'd think they'd make reaching the core more exciting or rewarding) or even new dungeons since the release of the first DLC (which really wasn't all that exciting to begin with) aside from the Shadow Dungeons, which is hidden behind an outrageously expensive paywall with premium currency with the use of Shadow Keys (and even then, to get any of the new armors, you had to make repeated trips to get materials, and Shadow Keys as far as I know are ONE TIME USE.)
Mist Energy is gone, thus removing the fee for advancing in dungeons and removing the Zynga like energy system from the game. All though this is good, it now solely focuses on obtaining Crystal Energy, which is the premium currency of the game. And oh boy, does this game focus on this A LOT. In order to really advance in ranking and go further (as well as to create higher level gear), you need crystal energy, and/or materials that can be purchased with Crystal Energy (and chances are, you'll be using Crystal Energy for this because everything has an EXTREMELY RARE chance of dropping.) It is possible to obtain Crystal Energy with in game currency, and thus allow you to do this all for free. However, not only is Community Market so outrageously broken, the amount of time you're going to spend grinding for crowns make it not worth the effort, especially when the dungeons already give you a low amount of crowns to begin with.
Any of the new "updates" consist of outrageously priced cosmetic gear that don't do anything except make you look nice and cool. Back in the day, the market system run by players wasn't as busted as it is now. To get some of the higher armor and weapons, you have spend almost damn near $100 dollars for it. Three Rings doesn't really care about the playerbase anymore. They just want offer the least amount of content, to provide you with the least amount of entertainment, for the most amount possible.
Finally, being a newbie in this game anymore is GOD AWFUL. Unless you have friends with you, this game is going to be a nightmare for you. Very rarely will you find nice players. Avoid PvP like the plague, as you'll just be met with elistist, rude players who have outrageously powerful gear compared to yours. I never made the mistake of spending money on this game, and unfortunately, that's what made me hit a wall and eventually give up.
All in all, it was fun a few years back, but it is now a hollow husk of what it used to be. Avoid.

When I first saw this game I figured it was just another side-scrolling dungeon crawl, and to be honest, I haven't really been big on the dungeon crawl genre in the past. I bought it following a recommendation from a friend. I've barely touched any of the other games I bought during the steam sale. I ended up playing about 24 hours in the first week. I think it's the challenge. The fact that knowing that at any moment, everything could just go to♥♥♥♥♥♥
- "Bugs, huh? I gotta fight bugs? I think I'm a little old for Spider Stompin' (TM?), but ya gotta love those arcade classics!"
[mark - crit - crit - blight - ded]
- "The boss is a hag? And she doesn't summon? Pfffft. Cake walk."
[I recovered the remains of my best Man-At-Arms in a Campbell's soup can.]
- "Place a torch on the alter? This looks ominous. But there's *no way* it could be *that* tough."
[Death was swift]
- I burst out laughing when I first saw a "swinetaur".
[Still have not played a veteran level dungeon since that terrible, terrible night...]
I'll admit, I can see how mistakes could be made due to naivete of game mechanics. Like when all my characters died of heart attacks all at the same time. Who knew the Apprentice Necromancer was also a Krispy Kreme vendor? (also registered trademark) It may require some patience to endure the painful "learning experiences" of the game (although from what little I've seen of the most recent update, it looks like they're working to make the game less mysterious), but I never really considered the momentary confusion or unpleasant sudden realizations to ever outweigh the fun of playing. Honestly I rather enjoyed discovering the mechanics for myself.
All in all, the game is very challenging, highly addictive, pleasing to the eye and the sanity mechanics add an extra dynamic both in terms of game mechanic and in developing an emotional attachment to your cannon fodder (I mean...when you're one Obdurous Advancement away from a party wipe and your sexy booty ♥♥♥♥♥ hellion becomes Heroic and lets loose a raucous war cry as she cleaves a shamblers head off with one well placed justice crit it's kinda hard NOT to buy her a drink afterwards and offer to bear her children, yano?)
Highly Recommended/10

+Good art design. Cool lore.
+Polished combat. More forgiving than previous ones but harder to catch up with it because it is faster.
+There are many ways to make the game easier for you, from usable items to different builds, magic and weapons.
+Good item, armor and weapon variety.
+Smart level design, which encourages you to try different things gameplay-wise. It also uses visual story-telling, so most of the things don't look out of place. (unless it is designed to be)
+Good enemy variety.
+Pretty graphics and animations.
o The story is kinda obscure like older games. Which certainly gives it a charm.
o It is easy to miss some NPC interactions. But they add replayability.
o PVP and Co-op is a little too disconnected to the main game. Covenant rewards are pretty hard to get and not that cool. Some enemies and bosses are too easy with co-op even though some of them react accordingly with more AoE attacks. But they're still features and it's fun to play with people.
o The dodge is powerful so it helps with faster builds while making slower builds relatively worse.
o Shields are not good.
- Dodge is too powerful for the PVP. It is mostly a♥♥♥♥♥♥show. It becomes too chaotic and invasions can take forever.
- Armor is mostly fashion. Heavy armor only helps with poise(sometimes) and the damage reduction is bad. Especially worse when you could dodge out of the way in the first place. Shields are bad too so some builds are not good anymore. There was some gameplay value in the previous games which is not here anymore.
- There are places where the game feels inconsistent. A weak looking enemy not staggering when hit while a big guy can't stand against you, a mob spamming his best move, AI pathfinding freaking out. To be fair the game is about observing the enemy before acting so it does not affect the gameplay horribly.
- Some bosses are either too weak and/or don't feel special.
- Mouse support is not that good but they tried.
This game is not perfect but it is perfect with its flaws. It is aware of itself and does not pretend to be something it is not. The PVP and Co-op are not that good but you have to go out of your way to use them anyway. The armors are bad, but it is not like you can upgrade them like in DS1, they don't make you feel like armor is that important. Those bosses who don't feel special are not really special anyway. They're dudes who happened to be in your way.
This game is a complete experience, this game is difficult, it does not hold your hand but it becomes way easier when you figure it out like every game should be. It is never unfair, it is either you or your character not suited for that part of the game. Use your items, upgrade your items and abuse the systems of the game. The game will not feel cheated if you abuse it as it tries to abuse you constantly. Play it at your pace, don't hit your head against the wall, try to go around it. And if you feel like you don't want to find another way, you can still do it your way but it might be way harder. It is okay to be upset if that does not work, but if you don't like to get upset at times, there won't be any relief when you beat the challenge. So get ready for that.
DLC REVIEWS:
-Ashes Of Ariandel:
Short but fun. It is worth it but does not cut it when it comes to surprising you. It has 2 nice bosses, but nothing really new. Mostly some generic enemies and a beautiful map. The painting has its own story, but it is not as interesting as the rest of the game because it feels disconnected.
-The Ringed City:
This DLC would be really good if it was not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t level hard. High HP and DMG enemies all around. One of the bosses (the optional one) is like something from WoW or a JRPG. It takes a while to bring him down as he can pretty much one shot kill you instantly.
Other than that, it is pretty cool because it keeps on giving. It surprises you with traps that you have never seen in Souls series before. It shows you bits of unseen lore about the order of the Dark Souls universe.
The Dark Souls series end. But these games are never about "when you get there" anyway. It's always the climb.

Ok, so, it's been 2 years since my review of Darkest Dungeon, and I have shoved plenty of hours into it as of now, before i only had roughly 30 or 40, but this past month i've been plugging away at the game and have come to a similar conclusion. This is just not fun. I had killed almost every boss including the bosses in the DLC, which I had started my new save with (except for the 16 pounder, the countess and another boss I forget) and figured I could at least attempt the darkest dungeon.
nah, that ♥♥♥♥♥ dark, much darker than anything else in the game. I came at it full force and ultimately it didn't matter. There was simply no way to manage the stress well enough, deal with bleeds, deal with ridiculous targeting systems in place and still pump out damage (especially with enemies that have 30+ % dodge.)
In total, I have lost 8 members of my party to the darkest dungeon and after dealing with the crimson court dlc for the past 50 or so hours I have no drive to start grinding again to make up what I have lost. The game had become sort of fun, with triller moments (deaths door during particular boss fights for example and killing the boss) but ultimately the small joy you experience is simply not worth the trouble, especially when much of it revovles entirely around rng.
This is a shame, because the narration and the sound and artistic assets are really REALLY good.
Anyway, if you enjoy frustrating experiences that are frustrating due to things beyond your control, buy darkest dungeon.
If you want to experience harder enemies that completely take over the game and push out the old enemies that you're used to, in which 80 to 90% of encounters are things that are far too fast, and deal far too much damage, while infecting you with a plague that introduces even more rng to your already existing rng fest? Buy the dlc.
Otherwise, stay clear.

Takes everything fantastic about the Souls series and cranks it to 11. This game is an absolute masterpiece. The combat is faster and while not quite Bloodborne, it's as close as it's going to get. The addtion of the weapon skills is an extremely nice touch and adds a lot of addtional combat depth not found in the previous games. Despite having a rough inital launch this game runs flawless on PC, provided you've got the rig to supplement that kind of performance. Easily the flagship version of the title. If you're not quite able to pull 60FPS constant on PC stick /w the PS4 version of the title. 30FPS rock solid. XB1 can't hold a stable framerate (Dancer fight dropping into the single digits, awful.)
// Pros //
- Fastest pace combat of the Souls Series.
- Weapon Skills adds depth and variety in combat and how you approach enemies.
- Fantastic art direction/design.
- Best looking of the Souls Series games.
- Best controlling of the Souls Series games.
- Fantastic music. (Dancer theme in particular and the final boss sequence is something special.)
- Still awaiting the next DLC! More content on the way. AoA was fantastic and has probably the most difficult boss fight in the game thus far. Very rewarding.
// Cons //
- Isn't Bloodborne on PC @ 60FPS. (Seriously FROMSOFTWARE, come on.)
And if anyone bothers reading to the bottom - do yourself a solid and play Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2. The entire franchise is easily worth your time.

I'll make this short and to the point:
Pros:
-Fun
-Free
-Unique
-Flexible
Cons:
-Every update seems to be for the cash shop
-No new Single Player content for a very long time
-Everything outside the base game costs real cash
-You can buy gold with cash
The game is a lot of fun and you can play it start to finish for free, but everything that would make the game more fun costs money. Guilds cost real money. Revival items cost real money. Fashion items cost real money. You can buy advanced weapon sets from the start with real money. You get 1 pet. The others cost real money. They eventually released more single player content... as an expansion pack that costs real money.
This isn't a simple case of "Game is free, nonessential items for comfort or utility cost cash". This is more "Bare-bones game is free. Expanded content, community aspects, advanced gameplay features, and character resurrection cost cash".
Despite its many cash-related flaws, the game itself is very good and very fun.

It is so damn hard and repetitive to level up items, get mastery, and aquire empowered gems. Servers are laggy - surprise, surprise - but it's more of a hinderance than an actual problem, your character gets pulled back to random spots as you try to fly, and auto-attacks sometimes won't register which can result in your character's death, but for most situations it's not really that bad.
Aside from everything I listed above, the game is pretty addicting, and gives the player options on how to aquire items (that being either grind or buy your way up), and it rewards the player for spending long, repetitive hours grinding for items. There is a boat load of content to grind for to the point where it can almost feel overwhelming, especially to new players, thankfully, a lot of the content is grindable but like how I mentioned before, the grind is boring and it gets old very fast. Comparing the grind to now and back in early access, things are definitely better, with the introduction of Gems, it's now easier to get power rank because empowered gems are accessible to everyone.
Overall, the game isn't perfect, it has a couple bugs here and there, some I might not have covered in this review but the Devs are definitely trying to improve the game unlike before. I like the direction the game is going so I'll have to give the game - in its current state - a 7.5/10.

Trove is a MMO blockish game, which contains basic RPG elements inside gameplay, which is very enjoyable.
PROS+
-Smooth Combat Mechanics
-Loot System and currency isn't hard to earn
-Good, interesting dungeons
-Fun Boss Fights
-Friend system allows you to warp to your friend's location, anytime. Useful if you want to adventure with friends.
-Good amount of classes
-Customizable house that you can bring to any marked area and place down, while keeping everything inside your house
CONS-
-Ridiculous queue wait times
Biggest problem in the whole game, if not, the only problem with the game. Every time you play, you must wait in a queue. Wouldn't be so much of a problem if the queue took only a few minutes,  but I have to wait 30-60 minutes in order to get out of the queue and start playing. There is only one server in the game, so everyone who plays has to connect to just one server, not multiple ones, which wastes a great deal of time. This is ridiculous, and almost all of the negative reviews are about the queue wait times. I don't want to wait 30-60 minutes everytime I load the game up to play.
Overall, I would still reccommend the game, despite it's ridiculously long queue wait times. The gameplay is VERY fun and addicting, especially if you play with friends. The only problem would be the queue. If it weren't for the queue, I'd give the game a 9/10, but currently, I'd give the game a 8/10.
EDIT:
Now, the queue wait times have decreased, since they added more servers. The queue wait times are now about 3-5 minutes, which is a big improvement. So, my final rating is 9/10.

This is easily the worst game in the Souls series by far. Instead of taking the good parts of DS2 and improving upon them, it completely abandons all of them and tries to be Bloodborne 2 when it comes to gameplay, but fails horribly at it.
There are too many things gone wrong with the game to name them all, I'm just going to name those things that I hated the most:
1. Armor is completely useless and offers barely any protection, you can no longer upgrade it as well. This results in everyone running around in rags and pretty much treating VIT as a dump stat.
2. The overwhelming majority of weapons in the game scale exceptionally well with a "quality" built character, which eliminates any build variety in both pvp and pve. If you don't have 40STR+40DEX, you're playing the game wrong.
3. Instachugging, it's absolutely horrendous.
4. Rollspam is pretty much a necessity to beat most bosses, shields are a joke and aren't worth their weight and the needed VIT investment to use them.
5. Absolutely linear world deisgn, the absolute worst in the series. It is mind-boggling how bad it is compared to DS2 world.
6. Absolutely horrible pvp due to lack of build variety since any sort of magic is completely non-viable and everyone uses a "quality" build. Punishing chuggers is near-impossible and invasions are utterly horrible with everyone running around with 2 gold phantoms even before you actually enter their world.
7. Complete lack of any sort of incentive to play through NG+ and onward, this is a massive step back compared to DS2, which added new enemies and phantoms as well as added new enemies to boss fights. The only things that change in DS3 on NG+ and onward is the addition of +1/2/3 ring variants, which exist mostly to artificially inflate your playtime if you want to get all of the achievements.
8. Complete lack of any sort of interesting phantom invasions. Massive step back compared to DS2.
I could continue listing the things I hate about the game, but, personally, this is already enough for me to name DS3 the absolute weakest game in the series and a total letdown.
