I haven't played a whole lot of Trove.  From what I have played, it's a really fun game.  It's definitely a one-of-a-kind type and really holds onto that well.  I feel like a lot of people could dive into this world and really have a good time.  I do recommend the game to anyone, to at least try.
The big problem.  I would have more hours in this game, but I can never find the time to get in.  There is a waiting list because the server maxes out with people.  Even if I try to hop on at 6 or 7 in the morning, the waiting list is usually around 30 minutes.  I'm not going to sit around for 30 minutes trying to get some playing time in before work.  In the evenings, forget about it.  I've seen it up to 3,000 minutes.  The waiting system is a total joke, and has no type of preference or anything.  It just sticks you in a still-frame and makes you wait for eternity just for the chance to jump in.
This is also a problem, because now that you've finally gotten in - you never want to leave.  God forbid you need to leave and you turn your game off.  Uh oh, now you're going to be waiting another three hours to jump back in and play.  They seem to be constantly updating and creating more space in the server.  I don't think they realize this is a redundant strategy.
There is a tunnel to the entrance of the game.  It's overloaded.  You expand the walls a little more, and more people will just crowd the tunnel.  What they need to do, is create more servers.  Create more servers for different regions, all with their own caps.  It's necessary.  I know it isn't easy, but it is necessary.  Or Trove is going to be very limited in its use.

Starbound is the next Terraria or Minecraft. A big jump up in the genre, and wonderfully interactive developers clearly working hard to add a ton of new content.
The biggest accomplishment of Starbound is the feeling of exploration. You can pilot to an infinite number of planets, and keep finding new places to explore, new weapons, and new NPC villages of various degree of hostility. You can build a palace, a temple, a spaceship, or a city, and the game gives you a wonderful variety of tools and textures to work with.
There is also an extremely active mod community, which is fully supported and encouraged by the developers, meaning new tweaks and content are constantly being made available. This is not a game that will get old fast.

Why DARK SOULS 3 is my favourite game (tied with OW)
I don't really know why I'm writing this, enough people have already talked about how great this game is and why everyone should play it, so I don't know why I'm writing this. I guess that I got inspired by a great Dark Souls review that one of my friends wrote and I just felt like writing something anyway.
To begin with this game is f***n great and I know that I won't do it justice in this review, so I will just try to write about some things that I personally love about the game.
The first things that comes to mind when I think of Dark Souls is the combat and the bosses. The combat is simply amazing and there are so many reasons why. You can play your own character however you want, you can focus on strength and be a badass wielding a "huge" sword (or any other big weapon for that matter like a f***ng dragon tooth), you can also be quick with smaller weapons but do less damage and look less cool by picking anything else then a pure strength-build, or you can be a magic user that looks awesome when you see it on YouTube, but when you try it yourself you realise that it's sucks and complicated and that you've made a horrible mistake because you didn't pick strength.
Okay I'm a little biased when it comes to strength, but whatever! Just because my character wields a heavy sword the size of bodybuilder and has two equally huge dual wielded swords on his back doesn't mean that I can't appreciate other play styles as well! Pyromancy is pretty good... Pffffffftttt no f**k pyromancers, they hide like b****es in pvp and rely too much on their spells, f***n worthless s***s.

Okay moving on, the best part about the combat according to me is that every weapon is unique (except for those tiny swords with s*** scaling). Some swords will gain buffs and look cool and deal extra damage, others will do great AOE damage, and one katana will get stronger if you stab yourself in the stomach before fighting. It's really stupid but I love watching my enemies stab them selves before we fight, it's the best. Whatever weapon you choose is entirely up to you and when you find a weapon that you like, then you will feel awesome fighting countless of enemies and bosses with it.
I believe that my favourite boss is the "Name Less King" boss. He is this badass dude riding on a dragon (more specifically a "wyvern" but dragon sounds a loot f***ng cooler to me). He has a golden-looking spear with an edge shaped like a sword that also shoots lightning and you have to fight in the sky walking on storm clouds, so f***ng awesome. The first part of the boss is kinda dull, you have to chase him down while he's riding the dragon by killing the dragon, but the second part is much more awesome. The second part starts with a cutscene of the Name Less King putting the dragon out of its misery with a single strike, disintegrating the entire dragon. Now it's a one on one fight, you the protagonist who by this point should have finished the game VS this gigantic (not really gigantic but pretty large, I just don't felt, like writing huge anymore) skeletal warrior who is the son of the last boss from the first boss Gwyn, and now looking at this guy you start to feel very small.
Then the battle is on, it's warrior vs electric f***ng war GOD, the biggest difference is that he can kill you in two hits and that he tanks you hits like tank. This is known to be the hardest boss in all of Dark Souls 3 (without including dlc) and it feels so epic fighting him, his power against my power, his strength against my strength, and that's all because I play the way I play, like a goddamn badass swing around a sword large enough to rival his spear in size and power. He is simply my favourite boss and I believe that everyone has this sort of experience with at least one boss in the game, and that's one of the biggest reasons why I love Dark Souls.
If there is one thing that I believe every Dark Souls 3 player enjoys then it's the co-op. You might believe that Dark Souls is a single player game and you are right, but my greatest time playing Dark Souls has been with my friends, weather its fighting epic bosses together, fighting each other with random weapons, or yelling at my failed student because he can't time a simple dodge.
When you are fighting a boss then you feel tense, you are consenting and giving it your all, but it can be so demoralising to lose knowing that you have to fight boss over and over again, but it's different when you are playing with friends. Then you can take it easy and enjoy yourself a loot more because you know that they got you back. It's not like the boss is easier because there are more people the boss's stats will scale accordingly to amount of people playing against it but you can still feel a bit more relaxed and you can take it a bit less serious. For example I like to bring out my bow, the only strength bow in the game (as far as I know) and use it primarily instead of my 3 ultra great swords. Whenever I shoot an arrow (which is like every 5 seconds, the drawback is enormous) I like to yell out "ARROW!!!" in the voice chat even though the arrow can't hurt or affect them in anyway. It's just funnier than playing alone.
As I said before I don't really know why I'm writing this, I have been writing for about an hour and a half and it's 2:00 am, but I hope you liked reading my review and that you play more Dark Souls.

Overall, this game deserves 10/10 for being that great in open beta. This game is more than what I anticipated, and I recommend getting it.

Dark Souls 3 was my first souls game ever, and I spent about 3 hours on the first boss in the tutorial-area learning the game mechanics. Despite its soul-crushing difficulty, the game never feels unfair. It just makes you want to improve, you learn the game by doing, dying and failing. To some its off-putting, but to me when  it makes the game so much more amazing.
The world of Dark Souls is enticing and doesnt hand-feed you the story of the game in a way that other AAA games does, its subtle, and you can ignore it entirely and just slash undead down in droves if thats what you want to do. If you do however want the story of Dark Souls, you will have to find it yourself, by going off the main path of the game, and explore additional areas, read item descriptions, and do crazy un-intuitive things to initiate hidden quest-lines. The wonder of the Darks souls universe never fails to amaze me. If you want to find out more about the Dark Souls franchise story i highly recommend googling "VaatiVidya" for some amazing in-depth videos.
Overall the game took me about 40 hours to complete, without the DLC which i am SO going to play through. And then i can go back and play DSII and DS.  And thats not even counting the fact that you can restart the game from scratch after completing it all, (Newgame+), you keep all your gear and things, but loose all progression items and enemies become stronger.
The game also does multiplayer in the best way i have ever seen an RPG do, its not intrusive in any way, and you can completely turn it off. But it adds so much to the experience to do so.

I held off from posting a review in order to give myself time to consider what I thought of the game.
After a great deal of thought and musing,
+ The game is VERY pretty, and they paid a lot of attention to how terrain looks and erodes in the real world. I was honestly impressed by it, and the locations were really rather nice looking.
- The main character has no room for the player to create their own life and personality to much extent. The protagonist's life has already been given a shape and design.
- The story is... problematic, and requires that the protagonist be a little bit of an idiot.
- Non Player Characters are about as interesting on the whole as a gram of bleached flour.
- The games movement speeds have been significantly increased compared to previous games. While this may not be a negative for some people, it DOES slant the game very heavily toward reaction-based twitch gamers and people who like high-speed, frantic melee. For anyone who likes to take things at a realistic speed, have time to think, or has any sort of nerve disorder, combat in this game will probably be hell.
.
- Limited options: You get very few types of any given thing unless you start picking up DLC, or rely entirely on the modding community to actually give you a good variety of equipment to find.
- Skills have been... pretty much nerfed down to a few lines of things you pick up in a set progression with the stats, while the combat-centric nature of the game makes some of the stats fairly useless for much of the game.
Overall opinion: Not likely to ever bother installing it again.

Early Access games are always a potential risk. They could be terrible. They could never actually be finished. They could be full of bugs and crashes.
Darkest Dungeon is none of those things. It runs great, it's fun, and it is brutal. There is something really enjoyable about naming characters after friends or viewers on your stream only to have them slowly go insane and die in terrible ways. It makes you glad that despite occasional dreams of "Man if getting money for killing monsters was real I'd be rich" never include the darker side of "I might also go insane fighting unknown creatures in dark and dangerous environments".
I won't even get into all the amusing and yet still terrible traits characters can get but there are many of them! Some are good to get and some are decidedly terrible to get. Adventure beckons your party of 4 heroes (You can have more on the roster but only 4 per dungeon can be sent in at a time). Will you answer adventure's call? I think you should. This is one Early Access game well worth getting - it only gets better with each update (more content, more characters, items, etc). Great stuff.

This game is just amazing. The atmosphere is great, the art style is great, and the narrator puts a chill in my spine. That's not to say there isn't at least a few grips, but they are minor.
The music actually surprised me. When I was lead a pack of hardy adventurers into dark and certain doom, I noticed that the battle music changed when the torch got low. A drum line was added, and the music changed just a little to make everything feel more grim.
The battle animations are a joy to watch, while barebones, they bring a meaty, satisfying impact to attacks. They don't slow down the fights, and vary enough between actions to stay interesting. There is a single problem I've found with these. Attacks that hit all four enemy positions, such as the Man At Arms' shout, have some trouble showing the farthest back enemy.
The unpredictable nature of combat means that fights stay fresh. Occasionally you will surprise enemies and streamroll over them, and occasionally enemies will surprise you and everything starts to go wrong. A wry critical strike here or there can change the flow of a fight, turning a loss into a shocking victory, or showing just how mortal your adventurers are. Sometimes, things just get a little weird. For example: a dog once bit my crusader, dealt no damage, and made him bleed.
For a moment I sat there, thinking "But you have to break the skin to do that..."
Sometimes, one of my adventures will take a crit for some two damage, less that five percent of their health, and the narrator will tell me "Dazed, reeling, on the brink." It also seems curious that adventurers can't use any of their skills outside of combat. Shouts and warcrys I can understand, but the Vestals keeping healing from their commrades is just rude on their part.
Aside from those oddities, I just think that bonus relaxtion should be awarded for doing really well in a fight. Either from winning quickly or not taking damage. Athough, that's just wishful thinking.
This is a great game, buy it for a great time.

I think I'll write a short review telling people what to expect at this point in the Beta. To tell you the truth, it feels like a game in Alpha, with occasional character/world wipes and absolutely HUGE updates. So, this information can change very quickly. If this is a few months old, look for a more recent review. The devs recently said that they are working to prevent wipes in future updates.
---SINGLE PLAYER---
Starting the game is simple, but you probably want to look up the controls. The early game quests help you get started, and I had no problem playing from there without any guide whatsoever. After finishing the starting questline, there are no more quests, which I found strange. (They weren't very necessary) I'm sure they'll add more quests in future updates.
The game allows you to leave the starting planet rather quickly
. The main way to advance in the game to get stronger weapons, tools, and armor, is to travel to harder and harder planets. You don't just get new gear though - you find recipes, decorations, and vanity items along the way. To me, settling down was not an option. I simply set a home planet that I'd return to once I unlocked everything, and set out for adventure.
Throughout the "storyline" (the story is a skeleton at this point, I KNOW they will add so mucn more), a procedure develops. Get materials, get fuel, beat the boss, go to a harder planet. Advancing requires travel, and you won't be building houses everywhere you go.
After unlocking all armors, etc, I went back home and built a bit. At this point, singe player didn't cut it for me anymore. There wasn't much to do. This changes every time there's an update - I usually play through the whole game again because it can be radically different. However, the late game is like the late game of Minecraft in singleplayer. There are no more goals, and nothing to do.
---MULTIPLAYER---
I recommend playing multiplayer after you have played singleplayer at least once, so you don't run around dazed and confused.
Dungeons and exploration are much more fun with others. You can travel to a random world and just run around gather resources and killing things, or just sit around at your home planet.
The universe is absolutely massive. It's possible to never run into another person if you fly far away (I don't recommend this, you should play with others). A big problem for public servers is that people put giant saw blades at the spawn. Like any other game where creation is a theme, griefers exist to destroy it. Of course, you can always find a nice server with moderators to help you out.
You probably remember from singleplayer that when you die, you lose a large percentage of the currency you are carrying with you. Thus, dying in multiplayer is not the end of the world. Someone won't take all of your stuff leaving you at ground zero.
Personally, I recommend playing on a private server with friends. I don't know why, but people are generally meaner on public servers. I assume it's the mask of anonymity. For whatever reason,  playing with a few friends on a server is very fun. You can teleport to their ship (and thus their world, if they are in orbit of their home). Building competitions can be fun, and parties with musical instruments are a nice way to waste time. Once you all reach max tier, you can go colonize a planet, turning a jungle into a civilization. Just tell them the coordinates of where to fly, and you'll meet them.
Indeed, playing with others will multiply the fun. I like singleplayer as a way to get a player to become a master of the game and its mechanics, as well as the feeling of survival that comes with it. But singleplayer can never compare to multiplayer. Killing other players isn't really worth it when you can make a friend.
---SERVER SETUP---
I found it extremely simple to set up a server. I'll tell you how it goes.
First, identify the ports that the game uses (there are tutorials).
Then, forward those ports to your computer.  (again, see a tutorial)
Run the server executable.
It opens in a black-and-white command prompt window. You're done. People time in your internet IP address, you they connect using a password that you set (Default is "swordfish" and a couple of others. There can be multiple passwords that work!).
I really had no issues with running a server. The devs say that they want to add a simpler interface and many more commands, which I'm sure they'll get to. They always do.
I've heard that it is almost impossible to run a server and a client of Starbound at hte same time. I cannot confirm this, as I have not tried it on a decent PC. But if you can barely run Starbound, don't try both at once.
---SUMMARY---
Overall, it reminds me of Terraria back in the days when it received constant updates, and everything was new. It has an element of infinite adventure that is astoundingly better with others. Try the singleplayer first so you know what to do, then have some fun online. The constant updates, while a little annoying, will add new elements to the game all the time. If you get bored in multiplayer, find a crew to play with. You can create a party and quickly travel to each other's ships. Have fun building your own things, or killing aliens.
I would in no way like to imply that this game is a finished product. While it's already amazing, you can expect a lot more. I can tell from the updates that the devs will keep going until there's nothing to add. They even have a suggestions page on their website where you can share your ideas. I'm really amazed by how I can play what
like a complete game, yet it is still in Beta. If you want a game that you can play for years, I know you won't get let down.
Thanks for reading.
-Zatharis

So, where do we start? Fallout 4 is a great, and I mean great action game. Shootings fun, crafting's decent, and the settlement system is a way to get lost in the game. After 200.7 hours though, I can tell you that the story is pretty much garbage. I've been playing this on and off for the past two years, and I was honestly excited for it. After doing two playthroughs, playing the first dlc twice, and being unable to even get through the second DLC because it didn't connect with me. The story is the classic "Find your son" which is basically the opposite of Fallout 3. That's not bad though, what ruins the games are three things:
1. The factions that you can side with
2. The weapons
3. The Lore
Let's start with the problems with the factions [spoilers]
1. The brotherhood are genocidal maniacs, who basically turned into the enclave from Fallout 3 and want to destroy all mutation.
2. The Railroad don't have a long term goal, other than "Free the ♥♥♥♥ing synths, ♥♥♥♥ everyone else."
3. The Institute seem to want to replace everyone with a synthetic copy of themselves, and kill the original person.
4. The minutemen are literally children, and you have to keep helping them or they're going to die, resulting in the preston meme every 5 minutes.
Moving on to the weapons. Simply, at a certain point it feels like everything but top teir guns like the gauss rifle, fat man, and a select few other weapons are useless, even when they're fully upgraded.
Finally the lore. They changed what seemed to be the direction of the East Coast BoS to the opposite of where they seemed to be going at the end of 3. At the end of 3 they seemed to want to help everyone -- regardless of if they were a little mutated. Yeah they wanted to kill all the super mutants, but they seem to want to wipe out all mutation now. They're basically who they fought at the end of 3, the enclave, however with a human dictator, rather than a computer. Then they added a Power armor (T-60) that hasn't been in any other game, that is stronger than T51-B, and seems to have been standard issue at some point. I would've expected to see documentation of it in other games, but it's absent, and breaks the lore that T51-B is supposed to be the strongest Power Armor. On top of that it's pretty ♥♥♥♥ing ugly. Finally, the super mutants. In 1, 2, 3, and NV, you were able to find intelligent super mutants, that didn't want to kill everyone. In FO4, there was one -- Strong. Strong still wanted to kill everyone though, which doesn't really reflect well on the Super Mutant population.
All in all, I don't reccommend this game, however if you have 200 hours to kill, it's not the worst way to spend that.

Core Traits:
- Round-Based RPG with some strategy components
- Groups of up to four heroes are sent onto missions in different dungeons
- Hero Roster can be filled with many different classes
- Every class has a number of skills, from which only four can be chosen for a mission
- Iron-Man-Mode (only one savegame, every action is permanent)
- Sinister Lovecraft-Setting
Pros:
- Insanely awesome graphics. "Just" 2D-sprited but their are so beautiful and reflect the setting perfectly
- Also fitting and great music
- Unforgiving gameplay forces to think twice and plan somewhat ahead (see also negative point)
- Most hero classes can fulfill several roles due to their versatile skill sets (definitely not Bounty Hunter :P)
- Items as well as missions have downsides: Careful considering, whether it's worth it is important.
- Tactical combat involves positioning of enemies and allies and "stress management"
Cons:
-
- Even careful planning can be completely negated by the
. It is very frustrating to see your group decimated by to AOE-crits in a row. Note that this point is only a contra-point from a classical RPG-point-of-view. I think it's a core element of the game, that bad things happen and you just have to make the best out of it. You have to open your mind for a different approach or you will sometimes be VERY frustrated.
- Order of combat actions is also random and not clarified. Influence of the Speed attribute is not clear
- Boss-Battles: You either look up, how they work our you will probably lose one hero group into your first attempt. Due to the nature of the game there is no learning by doing. If you are lucky you can maybe make it even first-try, but it's difficult.
Summary:
Great but unforgiving game. Play it if you want to experience a new kind of challenge. Do not play it if you are easily frustrated by being helpless against the RNG.
It is Early Access but already pretty finished in terms of playability and is updated frequently. New content is released there and then (new classes and bosses were added recently). Nontheless the total goal of the game seems still provisorily just to have something (it's just: Kill all Bosses, get all Hero classes to max level).
In my opinion it is definitely worth its price!

I think I'll write a short review telling people what to expect at this point in the Beta. To tell you the truth, it feels like a game in Alpha, with occasional character/world wipes and absolutely HUGE updates. So, this information can change very quickly. If this is a few months old, look for a more recent review. The devs recently said that they are working to prevent wipes in future updates.
---SINGLE PLAYER---
Starting the game is simple, but you probably want to look up the controls. The early game quests help you get started, and I had no problem playing from there without any guide whatsoever. After finishing the starting questline, there are no more quests, which I found strange. (They weren't very necessary) I'm sure they'll add more quests in future updates.
The game allows you to leave the starting planet rather quickly
. The main way to advance in the game to get stronger weapons, tools, and armor, is to travel to harder and harder planets. You don't just get new gear though - you find recipes, decorations, and vanity items along the way. To me, settling down was not an option. I simply set a home planet that I'd return to once I unlocked everything, and set out for adventure.
Throughout the "storyline" (the story is a skeleton at this point, I KNOW they will add so mucn more), a procedure develops. Get materials, get fuel, beat the boss, go to a harder planet. Advancing requires travel, and you won't be building houses everywhere you go.
After unlocking all armors, etc, I went back home and built a bit. At this point, singe player didn't cut it for me anymore. There wasn't much to do. This changes every time there's an update - I usually play through the whole game again because it can be radically different. However, the late game is like the late game of Minecraft in singleplayer. There are no more goals, and nothing to do.
---MULTIPLAYER---
I recommend playing multiplayer after you have played singleplayer at least once, so you don't run around dazed and confused.
Dungeons and exploration are much more fun with others. You can travel to a random world and just run around gather resources and killing things, or just sit around at your home planet.
The universe is absolutely massive. It's possible to never run into another person if you fly far away (I don't recommend this, you should play with others). A big problem for public servers is that people put giant saw blades at the spawn. Like any other game where creation is a theme, griefers exist to destroy it. Of course, you can always find a nice server with moderators to help you out.
You probably remember from singleplayer that when you die, you lose a large percentage of the currency you are carrying with you. Thus, dying in multiplayer is not the end of the world. Someone won't take all of your stuff leaving you at ground zero.
Personally, I recommend playing on a private server with friends. I don't know why, but people are generally meaner on public servers. I assume it's the mask of anonymity. For whatever reason,  playing with a few friends on a server is very fun. You can teleport to their ship (and thus their world, if they are in orbit of their home). Building competitions can be fun, and parties with musical instruments are a nice way to waste time. Once you all reach max tier, you can go colonize a planet, turning a jungle into a civilization. Just tell them the coordinates of where to fly, and you'll meet them.
Indeed, playing with others will multiply the fun. I like singleplayer as a way to get a player to become a master of the game and its mechanics, as well as the feeling of survival that comes with it. But singleplayer can never compare to multiplayer. Killing other players isn't really worth it when you can make a friend.
---SERVER SETUP---
I found it extremely simple to set up a server. I'll tell you how it goes.
First, identify the ports that the game uses (there are tutorials).
Then, forward those ports to your computer.  (again, see a tutorial)
Run the server executable.
It opens in a black-and-white command prompt window. You're done. People time in your internet IP address, you they connect using a password that you set (Default is "swordfish" and a couple of others. There can be multiple passwords that work!).
I really had no issues with running a server. The devs say that they want to add a simpler interface and many more commands, which I'm sure they'll get to. They always do.
I've heard that it is almost impossible to run a server and a client of Starbound at hte same time. I cannot confirm this, as I have not tried it on a decent PC. But if you can barely run Starbound, don't try both at once.
---SUMMARY---
Overall, it reminds me of Terraria back in the days when it received constant updates, and everything was new. It has an element of infinite adventure that is astoundingly better with others. Try the singleplayer first so you know what to do, then have some fun online. The constant updates, while a little annoying, will add new elements to the game all the time. If you get bored in multiplayer, find a crew to play with. You can create a party and quickly travel to each other's ships. Have fun building your own things, or killing aliens.
I would in no way like to imply that this game is a finished product. While it's already amazing, you can expect a lot more. I can tell from the updates that the devs will keep going until there's nothing to add. They even have a suggestions page on their website where you can share your ideas. I'm really amazed by how I can play what
like a complete game, yet it is still in Beta. If you want a game that you can play for years, I know you won't get let down.
Thanks for reading.
-Zatharis

UPDATE. (I had wrote a very simple Biased review as I was younger so this is a complete rework)
Spiral Knights, It's a very visually colourful and cheerful "Entry Level" Action RPG MMO, you could say it's Entry Level but some of the later Endgame content can make you tear your hair out.
This game has changed so much throughout the years and I've been there the entire way to see it in it's prime and decline to what it is now.
This game used to be fair to the player, you could grind to earn practically everything without spending a cent, but it changed over time and the Devs focus on things you could spend your IRL Currency on grew.
Many good things were added to this like the Quest/Storymode missions, the Capture the Flag and Battle Arena modes. The combat in this game is actually pretty satisfying, as different monsters are affected by different element or attack types it just makes the combat that bit more detailed, it also requires you to look ahead at what is coming and you can prepare your loadout for it.
SUMMARY:
Pros:
+ Awesome Visuals, Very Colourful.
+ Combat is Satisfying and Fair, alot more indepth than it looks.
+ Friendly Community (Back when I played)
+ Fun Boss fights and the Story is pretty neat (Could do with more)
+ So many Variations of Armour and Weapons from Guns, Swords, Bombs. Along with Costume Slots to further customize your Knights look.
Cons:
- Devs are only adding Cash Grab Cosmetics and not actual game content
- If you play outside of the server Region you are going to have a hard time with the combat (Trust me, being Australian on a Constant red bar was hell in late game levels but I still maxed my character out during my time)
- Crafting is better than what it used to bed, but it's still trying to lure you into the temptation of spending IRL money.
I could never hate this game, so I will recommend it. It's definetly not what it used too be as much as I wish this game got updates and content with an active community, but it seems it's past it's time now. It is still very fun playing with a friend from the beginning, it holds a very special place in my heart.

This is the proverbial "game with a niche audience" game.
For me, this game is great. It's got the art, the darkness, the turn-based combat, the RPG, the rough-like, the toughness, the nerves, the atmosphere.
RNG is a big part of this game. To be honest, sometimes it can be quite rage-inducing. But having that RNG is what makes this game so damn fun. Challenges, Management, death, monsters, and a mysterious plot, all the righteous traits for something called the Darkest Dungeon.
There is something among the negative reviews that I must address for those thinking about getting the game. A lot of people complain about the difficulty of this game, which is warranted (this game is really hard and sometimes frustrating in a good way). BUT I CANNOT ACCEPT THE STATEMENT THAT THE GAME IS "BROKEN" BECAUSE YOU LOST SOME CHARACTERS, OR PARTY WIPED, OR SOMETHING LIKE THAT.
Grow up.
1) Once you know this game, know the mechanics, and play safely, smartly, and conservatively, those situations where bad things happen will very very very rarely happen.
2) The game isn't broken. It can be a bad game to you, but it is not broken. Most likely you took a big risk and lost or you didn't know how to play the game well enough yet.
3) When those things DO happen (and they do sometimes rarely happen even with the most careful planning), like, so what? Rage quit, fine (I've done that a few times). Cry, fine (I've also done that). The game isn't broken. It just is. It is the Darkest Dungeon.
The Devs have worked hard on this game, fixing a lot of issues constantly, and balancing the game while keeping true to its nature.
In summary:
If you don't like RNG, this game is not for you.
If you don't like hard games, this game is not for you.
If you don't like the tags on this game, this game is probably not for you.
And that's okay. But don't call this game broken.
For the rest,
Welcome, to the Darkest Dungeon.

I think I'll write a short review telling people what to expect at this point in the Beta. To tell you the truth, it feels like a game in Alpha, with occasional character/world wipes and absolutely HUGE updates. So, this information can change very quickly. If this is a few months old, look for a more recent review. The devs recently said that they are working to prevent wipes in future updates.
---SINGLE PLAYER---
Starting the game is simple, but you probably want to look up the controls. The early game quests help you get started, and I had no problem playing from there without any guide whatsoever. After finishing the starting questline, there are no more quests, which I found strange. (They weren't very necessary) I'm sure they'll add more quests in future updates.
The game allows you to leave the starting planet rather quickly
. The main way to advance in the game to get stronger weapons, tools, and armor, is to travel to harder and harder planets. You don't just get new gear though - you find recipes, decorations, and vanity items along the way. To me, settling down was not an option. I simply set a home planet that I'd return to once I unlocked everything, and set out for adventure.
Throughout the "storyline" (the story is a skeleton at this point, I KNOW they will add so mucn more), a procedure develops. Get materials, get fuel, beat the boss, go to a harder planet. Advancing requires travel, and you won't be building houses everywhere you go.
After unlocking all armors, etc, I went back home and built a bit. At this point, singe player didn't cut it for me anymore. There wasn't much to do. This changes every time there's an update - I usually play through the whole game again because it can be radically different. However, the late game is like the late game of Minecraft in singleplayer. There are no more goals, and nothing to do.
---MULTIPLAYER---
I recommend playing multiplayer after you have played singleplayer at least once, so you don't run around dazed and confused.
Dungeons and exploration are much more fun with others. You can travel to a random world and just run around gather resources and killing things, or just sit around at your home planet.
The universe is absolutely massive. It's possible to never run into another person if you fly far away (I don't recommend this, you should play with others). A big problem for public servers is that people put giant saw blades at the spawn. Like any other game where creation is a theme, griefers exist to destroy it. Of course, you can always find a nice server with moderators to help you out.
You probably remember from singleplayer that when you die, you lose a large percentage of the currency you are carrying with you. Thus, dying in multiplayer is not the end of the world. Someone won't take all of your stuff leaving you at ground zero.
Personally, I recommend playing on a private server with friends. I don't know why, but people are generally meaner on public servers. I assume it's the mask of anonymity. For whatever reason,  playing with a few friends on a server is very fun. You can teleport to their ship (and thus their world, if they are in orbit of their home). Building competitions can be fun, and parties with musical instruments are a nice way to waste time. Once you all reach max tier, you can go colonize a planet, turning a jungle into a civilization. Just tell them the coordinates of where to fly, and you'll meet them.
Indeed, playing with others will multiply the fun. I like singleplayer as a way to get a player to become a master of the game and its mechanics, as well as the feeling of survival that comes with it. But singleplayer can never compare to multiplayer. Killing other players isn't really worth it when you can make a friend.
---SERVER SETUP---
I found it extremely simple to set up a server. I'll tell you how it goes.
First, identify the ports that the game uses (there are tutorials).
Then, forward those ports to your computer.  (again, see a tutorial)
Run the server executable.
It opens in a black-and-white command prompt window. You're done. People time in your internet IP address, you they connect using a password that you set (Default is "swordfish" and a couple of others. There can be multiple passwords that work!).
I really had no issues with running a server. The devs say that they want to add a simpler interface and many more commands, which I'm sure they'll get to. They always do.
I've heard that it is almost impossible to run a server and a client of Starbound at hte same time. I cannot confirm this, as I have not tried it on a decent PC. But if you can barely run Starbound, don't try both at once.
---SUMMARY---
Overall, it reminds me of Terraria back in the days when it received constant updates, and everything was new. It has an element of infinite adventure that is astoundingly better with others. Try the singleplayer first so you know what to do, then have some fun online. The constant updates, while a little annoying, will add new elements to the game all the time. If you get bored in multiplayer, find a crew to play with. You can create a party and quickly travel to each other's ships. Have fun building your own things, or killing aliens.
I would in no way like to imply that this game is a finished product. While it's already amazing, you can expect a lot more. I can tell from the updates that the devs will keep going until there's nothing to add. They even have a suggestions page on their website where you can share your ideas. I'm really amazed by how I can play what
like a complete game, yet it is still in Beta. If you want a game that you can play for years, I know you won't get let down.
Thanks for reading.
-Zatharis

I have been following this game for several years now, playing it on and off single player.
is a labor of love by a single developer who started this as a teenager; that is to be comended in this day and age of asset flips and Unity demos. It's come a long way since I first started playing.
What keeps me coming back to this game is a surprising level of detail. Animations for putting on clothing or applying bandages to injuries, getting mauled by a zombie because,
, my new gun had the safety on.
I'm also amused by the fact that you start buck naked, even on the wintery Yukon map. It's the survival game cliche of suddenly spawning with nothing in the middle of nowhere taken to a comical extreme. I wanted so badly to like this game.  I love the idea of it, but the execution is pretty poor.  The balance of this game is bad.  I have restarted my campaign quite a few times, but this game is so unforgiving that I am pretty certain that I will not be playing this game anymore.  Here are the main problems I see:  There are a limited number of short dungeons that you can send adventurers into.  This means that there are times where you are forced to send an underexperienced and ill-equipped party into a more difficult dungeon.  Second, there is so much randomness tied into every system of this game, that balancing a player experience is probably very difficult.  I can say that in my opinion, they do not have the balance right yet.  After at least five times of restarting the campaign, I can tell you that the first part of the campaing seems fairly easy, but then the difficulty ramps up too quickly.  Right around the time I start to get a few level 3 adventurers, the game seems to suddenly get very difficult and I start to fail pretty regularly at the medium length dungeons.  This has caused me to restart the campaign at least five times.  Not again.  I think I'm done with this game.  Don't waste your time or money on this mediocre failure of a game.  In a nutshell, I don't want to spend 100+ hours making careful tactical and strategic decisions only to have it all ruined bya fe bad RNG results.  Great idea, poor execution= not worth the time or frustration.

A very nice game, enjoyed it a lot. There is a lot of RNG, but it all bases around concrete numbers you can work with. You have enough ways to take the RNG to your advantage. The game is not just play and slam enemies, you gotta think about which enemy you attack, what gear you go out, and so on. Lots of decisions have to be made, like do you want more crit, but less accuracy, or the other way around, or rather more stun chance and so on. It's nice to learn about the game mechanics and take more and more the right decisions (e.g. go crit, you crit, you win).
The only minus I have is that the game is harder in the beginning, than in the end. Without any gear, and especially without  knowledge about the mechanics, you are getting crushed when you start to play. After you understand more and more how things work, the game feels easier and easier. Alhtough you play "hard mode", it feels way easier than "easy mode" you played in the beginning. It should be the other way around, so that the hardest bosses should actually be harder than these on easy mode ;) In other words, easy mode is too hard for new players. This is demotivating and I may stop playing this game after 1h playtime, which is sad. But if you get beyond that point, it's really fun game, really nice one.

It's like Four Swords multiplayer, but an mmo PC game... and much more difficult in some parts!
The biggest complaint for the game is the energy system, in which you have to use to do ANYTHING in the game. You recharge 100 mist energy over 22 hours and then it caps there. After that, you will have to purchase crystal energy through the in-game currency- crowns, or with $$$. Basically, you can get about an hour of gameplay with the free mist energy (100). Eventually you can become self sufficient and earn enough in the terminal dungeons to purchase energy with the crowns you earned in order to play continuously without paying a dime- so it's not too big of a deal. You just can't expect to play this for more than 2-3 hours a day and then HAVE to be done with it.
That system aside, everything else about this game is really polished, and provides a fun addicting (which makes the energy system painful- you just want to keep playing) multiplayer experience. A must try, Play with friends!

A very nice game, enjoyed it a lot. There is a lot of RNG, but it all bases around concrete numbers you can work with. You have enough ways to take the RNG to your advantage. The game is not just play and slam enemies, you gotta think about which enemy you attack, what gear you go out, and so on. Lots of decisions have to be made, like do you want more crit, but less accuracy, or the other way around, or rather more stun chance and so on. It's nice to learn about the game mechanics and take more and more the right decisions (e.g. go crit, you crit, you win).
The only minus I have is that the game is harder in the beginning, than in the end. Without any gear, and especially without  knowledge about the mechanics, you are getting crushed when you start to play. After you understand more and more how things work, the game feels easier and easier. Alhtough you play "hard mode", it feels way easier than "easy mode" you played in the beginning. It should be the other way around, so that the hardest bosses should actually be harder than these on easy mode ;) In other words, easy mode is too hard for new players. This is demotivating and I may stop playing this game after 1h playtime, which is sad. But if you get beyond that point, it's really fun game, really nice one.

The ridiculous RNG.
That's quite literally it. Only thing I hate about it.
My bad luck in this game made me quit in the middle just because I stopped caring and got bored/tired of getting screwed over. But when you seemingly are 100% prepared for what's in front of you, I think it makes no sense for you to get wiped. I would be fine with it being difficult, and MAYBE a wipe even though you were prepared; if you didn't handle it right. But being wary of being unlucky throughout every single dungeon just doesn't seem fun to me.
I do not like reviewing games before playing them for a few hours. But I couldn't handle this one. Let me explain...
First off; it's luck-based. Not a big deal, right? If you've played games like Fire Emblem, Pokemon etc, you know what it is to deal with hit %. Sometimes it lands, sometimes it doesn't. Except in games like those; skill is also very important. Is you use a lot of debuffs against an enemy or hide in a forest or something in case things go wrong, it can turn out well.
Well... I've had HORRIBLE luck in games all my life. I'm a gamer, I play games all the time, some of them are luck-based and I never fare well in those areas. But I can still enjoy them. But in a game like Darkest Dungeon; where if your character dies, it dies for good... Bad luck WILL abuse, molest you and make you miserable.
I haven't even played the game for 2 hours, and yet I've tried several different setups. And that is because I kept losing my entire team. Not because I wasn't trying to kill them/keep my team alive etc. Whenever I attacked, I would miss. If I landed the skill that would stun, the mobs would resist. I seriously lost the first fight of a dungeon because I couldn't land any of my hits, even if I only used the high hit % ones. Full party, 3 mobs, I get wiped and I -might- have landed 2 hits.
I've got ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ luck, but if it was more skill-reliant at least I could balance it out or make up for it.
I seriously LOVE the setting, the art, the game itself. I really do. What I despise is the lack of control over the RNG.

After my first 100 hours of this game, I think I'm allowed to say this game is really addictive and fun (especially with dried finger clownfiesta with friends) once you get the whole "hardest game on the market" idea through your head. It may be tough to overcome the frustration of hard bosses and annoying peasent enemies at first, but once you beat a few bosses it gets pretty easy to know what to do. Constantly summoning phantoms to carry you through bosses kills the purpose of the game forcing you the learn the mechanics of the game.

This is not one of those games for perfectionists. Your monument to success here is built atop a mountain of failures. And that mountain will be staggering. Your characters will die, either going down swinging valiantly or from something extremely stupid because the entire world was out to get them at that particular moment. Learn to cut and run and use the resources you gained to upgrade your various systems in town to better maintain the next batch of troops. Sometimes you're just using recruits as stepping stones to get more upgrades to maintain your main fighting force, who are still traumatized from their last incursion or who are getting their negative traits tortured out of them in a medieval sanitarium. The game is designed around this, it expects you to do this, and it will passive-aggressively chide you for doing it. You burn through more recruits than a standard game of XCOM: UFO Defense, and that's an accomplishment.
So despite all the suffering, is the game good? Extremely. It is remarkably complex, difficult and addicting. You will almost never have an ideal scenario, so you have to learn to adapt to every scenario, learn who or what is worth investing in, and work towards that as your goal. Another body in the ground is another cobblestone on your road to success, and expect the ground to be littered with more corpses of adventurers than you will remember. To you it was the most important day in your life when you saw your companions die from a heart attack, bleed to death, and get mangled by a buzzsaw, but for me, it was Tuesday, and soon enough, it will be Tuesday for you as well.

Spiral Knights is one of several new MMOs that have adopted a system of "energy", where one has a certain amount of energy alotted to them each day with which to make things, explore dungeons, etc, but Spiral Knights brings it a step further.
They allow players to, on a player controlled market, purchase and sell energy in real time, as well as purchasing it directly using real money. This leads to all sorts of "Crystal Market Speculation" and is generally fun to be a part of.
As for the game itself, I praise them for their creative use of 2D and 3D, making a game that's very asthetically pleasing, but also quite fun to play.
An important thing to note is that, unlike a lot of the new free MMORPGs, Spiral Knights requires you to buy absolutely nothing to gain the full benefits of playing the game. There is no special treatment for anyone who has purchased energy nor are there features stripped from the game for those who haven't.
All in all, this is a fun, if not somewhat simple, MMO.

A wonderful, lovely designed game that can be very time consuming if you want it to.
It's Early Access but very playable. The developers are fast with updates and deliver many new features and changes per week. I am happy that they truly listen to the community and consider the wishes. The devs also posted a huge list with great coming features and already implemented some of these.
To the game itself: Your whole universe is random generated with numberless different planets. Planets can vary in biome, weather, gravitation, monster strength and some other things. Since everything is random, you never know what you'll find on a new planet.
During your exploration you will find LOTS of stuff (besides equipment) that you can use for building, so the more you explore, the more possibilities you get to customize your buildings. Once you found a nice sweet home planet where you want to build your homebase, it can be set as home so you can return easily.
Well, even if everything's random, if you hop from planet to planet you'll notice that after a while every planet feels the same. You land on a planet, run around to find chests and dungeons, dig into the earth for getting some materials, leave the planet and hop onto another. This may be only my opinion, because they did a few character/world resets and I had to start all over, so it felt quite repetitive. Soon, the beta will be in a state where no future resets will happen, so this problem may solve itself. But if you can't live with losing your progress, don't touch this game yet and wait a bit.
Multiplayer is possible and playable. There are already a few good starbound servers out there, you may find one that suits you. Alternatively, you can host your very own server by launching the server tool. Sadly, public multiplayer is not enjoyable without a few problems yet. If you party up with another player, he could beam to your ship and plunder all what's within. There is not chest protection yet as far is i know, so be careful. Anyway, I think this will change soon.
To sum up, this game is worth it, even it's not complete yet. Future updates will make the game even better, but the game may get more expensive, so consider buying it now even if you plan to wait.

this game is like terraria, 2D voxel based exploration and building thing, BUT ITS SO MUCH MORE!!! trust me, if you play terraria you wont after playing this as this is terraria on sterroids!
first of all its in beta and game wipes are expected at this early stage so dont go expecting to keep your saves....that held my review back a bit as i couldnt get to play it as much and at the start place it doesnt stand out much from terraria.
then once i decided to do stuff and power my spaceship (which is orbiting above the planet your on) i fueled it and decided to explore space.... what i found was a MASSIVE star chart of BILLIONS of systems with a multitude of planets in each and each planet you can go to and explore and build on and do stuff. and this was only the alpha quadrant....so many star systems that no matter how much i scroll i couldnt find any beta quadrant as alpha was massive! so the game is beyond any scope of HUGE!
then i decided to explore a asteroid field above a planet and as im on i notice  oxygen running out and my character getting cold... so there are survival aspects on this, you need to cook and eat food to prevent starving, it goes cold at night on most planets so you need to keep near a fire source after a while to prevent freezing to death, and on ice planets its quite hard as its always cold. you see dynamic changing weather effects that affect the game, meteor strikes from space that smash lots of the planet up if it happens.
also, to my surprise, as exploring a forest planet i noticed the entire planet was populated with freindly NPCs and they had most of the planet built up with houses and inns and shops....so there are populated words aswell. with many millions of planets to explore this game will keep you entertained and probably throw more surprises my way too!
i think theres also a option to upgrade you ship, fire planet devasting weapons at planets, terraform planets/moons and do other stuff like that. also the dev stated his interest in making ship vs ship combat too. so the game is already great and will get better (and probably more expensive) over time, so buy now while its still in cheap dev phase :)

Above is what I wrote in 2011. Seeing as I still occasionally check on this game from time to time I would like to present a newer conclusion that I have now come to seeing as my opinion has changed.
This is a very unique game that does a lot of things right, but equally so - it does many things wrong. Redeeming features this game has are articulated very nicely and are evident in it's composure, the art style if very appealing to the eye to look at, controller support is nice, combat is unique but still fitting, f2p is possible, etc...
However this game does some particular things very badly that seem to hit it hard when you look at the game itself in depth. I am going to talk about the one that bugs me most, and honestly stirs me from really every coming back to this game (provided I have time to play it). This is my cumulative opinion based on my experineces with this game throughout it's existence.
THIS GAME DOES RARES WRONG : Spiral Knights literally takes every step that it can take to prevent players from being rewarded from obtaining rare p2p items. If you are going to release rare p2p items in your game with the premise that they will truly be "rares" (or rare items) and gain value throughout time, you CANNOT re-release these items that your p2p players either paid a lot for or worked VERY HARD to get and make them easier to get the second time around.
This game dissolves rare items by making items that were promised to be "rares" merely common items by re-releasing them over and over, and then just create new rare items that they expect the p2p players to work for or spend more money on - effectively creating a sink for virtually every rare item they put into the game via the system they have set-up for buying/earning them.
Old rares become un-rare due to re-releasing them-> These items are no longer rare yet many players worked hard for them or paid a lot of money -> So, Three Rings release new rare items for p2p -> New items become old -> Old items re-released -> They are no longer rares -> Three Rings releases new items again because they want $$$ -> Ongoing process...
Good

This game is, supposedly, in a very early stage of beta. Don't listen to this; this game feels complete. With a gigantic diversity between solar systems, planets, alien fauna and flora, and a variety of races to meet, it feels as if you are scrounging the galaxy. It's also filled to the brim with obscure science fiction references, and an arsenal that shocked me coming out of the 600+ items in Terraria. With each update, even more is added, and the old becomes improved upon. The customization is, let's be honest, not as good as Terraria's, but still quite amazing. Each race has their own culture and backstory, although some of them are more hospitable than others. If you buy this game as it is, though, I recommend looking up coordinates for gun shops, they're a must have in the brutal universe.
Did I mention there are five sectors of infinitely generating star systems that go into the millions?
Explore. Dream. Discover.

Darkest Dungeon has a tendancy to pull you in HARD when you first start playing. The atmosphere, the incredible narrative voice acting.. etc. All of that will make you want more and more from the game. You'll probably spend about 10 hours in and the intensity will fall off some. There is a lull in gameplay once you get over this and you might find yourself bored for a little, but things start to pick up again once you upgrade your blacksmith/guild/sanitarium. Once you can upgrade a fighter and wipe away those negative attributes you start to feel like there is advancement. Up until that point you're kind of stuck playing beginner levels and getting your rear handed to you. There are odd mechanics to learn through trial and error and you'll end up losing relics/heros you REALLY didn't want to lose.
But there is a really interesting and engaging style play here. You aren't exactly investing everything into 1 or 2 heroes, you're working towards bettering all of them as they come and go. Inevitably, your town is the one thing you start to cherish as it allows you to advance more than the heros themselves.
As an early access game this is BEYOND polished. Especially when I look at the other early access games in my library, this one feels really close to done. But it also feels like a really polished flash game, which isn't necessarily an insult.. it just is what it is. Like all of myearly access games I'll play this for a while then put it down until release. Unlike the rest of the ones in my library, this one looks like it will actually see release fairly soon.
It's worth picking up if you like difficult RPGs.

Well at almost 20 hours in, I think it's time I write a review.
I wasn't a backer for this game when it was making waves on Kickstarter. Probably because I foolishly believed I didn't care for roguelikes earlier this year. But since some of my most played games of the year have been roguelikes, and since I missed out on the Minecraft boom, I decided to give this one a go.
First let me get the Early Access bit out of the way -- For a beta, there is an absolute TON of content available. I can easily see getting 100 hours into it right now and not making much of a dent. There's just so much to see and do. Every planet is different. No, really. I was skeptical, trust me. I expected one forest biome to be the same as the next, reusing assets that were just recolored and calling that "new," but when you hop from planet to planet--and especially from system to system--it's different. What was once massive, skinny birch trees is now thorny rose trees. Clear pools are now poison. An underground frog sanctuary is now a hostile avian temple.
It's a beautiful game, and you can already tell there's some wit in the writing from the item descriptions. I only expect more of this as time goes on. Honestly, it's just good, expansive fun. If you like exploring and you're a goal-oriented person, give it a try!

So as you can see, I have many hours logged on Trove now and here is my quick review of what to expect...
Pros:
- The combat is very fast-paced and fun
- The amount of character customization is insane!
- The cornerstone system (basically a moving house you design) is both brilliant and fun to build
- Tons of unique biomes, dungeons, enemies, and bosses
- Way too many props and block types to possibly get bored building
- Good social system with friends lists and clubs
- Not PAY-TO-WIN
Cons:
- Difficult to solo some of the higher level areas (but way fun with a group)
- Sometimes gets a little repetitive
- Difficult to find some of the needed crafting materials
- Currently no PvP (will be added in future according to devs)
- Some shop items take A TON of in-game currency to purchase
Also a note: Currently they have bad queue times to log into the server, which is full of new players from Steam. The devs have already released server patches to help with the issue, and are constatly adding new hardware, but until the flow of new players settles down a bit, expect to be waiting a while to log in (sometimes half an hour). Once you are on though, the servers are smooth and stable.
Overall I highly recommend this game. It is fun, especially with a group, and it has loads of content to use with more coming all the time. Feel free to add me on Trove (player name: jackobuddy) and happy building!!!

Simply put this is a very shallow, very simple game that doesn't feel finished.
I decided to check out Trove mostly out of boredom.  I've played my fair share of games that can fall into the same sorto f genre(MMO-y action RPG), and I've seen a lot of games that were bad.
Trove has to be one of the few that really struck me as a game that was clearly unfinished but shipped as a finalized product.
There are a lot of classes in the game...and they all have four moves.  For the most part the classes don't have a strong sense of identity, when you swap from one to the other you'll barely notice a difference.  The main changes are durability and damage.
The combat is mostly holding down the mouse button and watching things die.  You can bob and dodge and weave if you want, but until you get further into the game that won't be necessary in the slightest.
The quests are the same no matter what level you are.  You find a "Dungeon" and then go in and kill the boss of said "Dungeon".  At the lower levels that tends to mean climbing a staircase and punching the guy at the top.  The complexity of the dungeons and their overall difficulty to navigate doesn't ever really feel high.
Allow me to sum up your experience with this game:
You will wander around entering dungeons.
You will kill everything in your path, then kill the boss.
You will get "EPIC" and "LEGENDARY" and "OMG WHOALS HAX" drops that are actually heavily common and useless.
You will take all of those drops and toss them into an item grinder to get stuff out of them.
You will realize you just spent the last 4 hours repeating this and that there is NOTHING ELSE TO DO.
And that it takes thirty minutes(Currently) or longer to just join the game thanks to the queue.
Then you click uninstall.
As for the good:
The building portion is nice.  I like how you collect blocks from the environment.
The game is very shallow and empty, the game developers obviously put in the minimal amount of work to make the game and then released it.  Do not play it unless you heavily enjoy mindless grinding for almost no reward.

I remember in an issue of Game Informer mag an article about this game. From the time of the interview, it was nothing more then ideas, a very basic test dungeon, and art. Already, it had me interested. I've heard nothing about this game for at least a few years, then i saw it on steam on early access. I'd be dammed if I didn't support such an interesting concept of a game. Now I've been bitten in the♥♥♥♥♥♥once by early access, with me thinking H1Z1 would be the next step in multiplayer survival (it isn't). However, even for being simplistic gameplay with tons of exploits, it didn't disappoint. Here is why this early access is accually good.
1.the exploits, part 1. This game is ment to be hard as balls, and unforgiving. However, we are human beings, known for adapting to adversity. Some of the exploits I have learned about are as follows. The crusader tank and stress heal tatic, where you drag a fight out healling stress. The abusive tatic, where you get 4 abuseive teammates to do eco runs without stress problems, and protection, which could be abused to make one character invincible to direct damage entirely. (looking at you man at arms)
2. exploits, part 2. Now exploiting a game is generally not cool, and the devs didn't want an easy game. However, they took a smart route and added in new flavor to fix said exploits; to keep the game interesting, and still hard as balls. They added in heart attack mechanic, so you can't go abusive runs. They added in anti stalling mechanics, forcing you to end a fight, and not use them to get free heals. Finally, they changed protection, so it's still useful, but not utterly broken.
3. Rng is good for me. Now as much as all of us pray to RNGesus to not have Madder Bomber wreck us, rng can be a major letdown at times. however, for being a game thats still lacking some gameplay elements, rng makes it fun. It keeps it fresh by making it different, and rarely the same.
4. Darkest Dungeon, prepare to cry. This game is hard as balls, and this needs to be said at least 4 times. But that's what keeps it interesting for a  small game atm. If you look back at Nes titles, most were really hard, and had to be, because the game would end in 30 minutes if it was not. The difficulty lets this game, while it's in early access, keep it fresh, because its hard as balls. (told you it needed saying 4 times:P)
5. No Micro Transactions. Just 20 bucks, and think no more. Besides, micro transactions would ruin number 6.
6. The devs know what they are doing. They have a clear idea on what they want the game to be like, and know what to do to make it that way. They remove any exploit that makes the game easy and dull. They don't micro transaction because it would make it easy, which is not the goal. They do update, and I have found myself surprized when I took a break from the game for 3 weeks, just to find loads of new things, including Captain Hardhead, my favorate man at arms, and unoffical leader of the 1st brigade of the Hamlet of Swag. (he is still alive and kicking, dispite taking a 42 damage crit one time, and getting 2% away from heart failure another time)
Overall, if you are looking for a game with unique mechanics, good art direction, multilayered statigic thinking and planing, feels for characters, a great voice actor, regular updates, a small amount of horror, and you are a video game masochist, i'd recomend throwing down an abe. going on 40 hours, id say id gotten 50 cents of enjoyment per hour, and that will just get cheaper;)

My Experience: I beat the game and DLC with a strength build, and the re-played through most of the game with a faith build.
Difficulty: Bosses were too easy compared to previous games in the series.  With a basic strength build, I beat many of the bosses on my first try with no summons.  There is no fight even close to Ornstein and Smough, Manus, or even an early game challenge like Gargoyles.  Some of this is made up for by difficulty in the rest of the level – being forced to fight larger groups of enemies, or tough enemies (ex. Dogs guarding Deacon McDonald).
Design: The graphics are a huge upgrade over previous games in the series, and the scenery is beautiful.  My complaint is that the enemies seem uninspired.  In Dark Souls, you were fighting pigs with helmets, golems, trees, mushrooms, hydras, etc.  In this game, I find I’m fighting many iterations of crazed dead guy.  On the plus side, there is a huge variety of weapons, spells and special moves which make it fun to kill crazed dead guys.
PVP: The “arena” was a great idea.
Balance: Much better than previous games – especially Dark Souls I.  Still wish Poise were a thing though…
In terms of my ranking: Dark Souls > Dark Souls III > Bloodborne > Demon’s Souls > Dark Souls II.

Now that a needed price drop has hit Fallout 4, I feel better in recommending it, and as such, will be doing exactly that.
To justify this positive rating, I'll open this review with a brief description of what I felt Fallout 4 did well (which will seem small compared to what I hated about it, but I want the reason for my positive raiting to be apparent, and starting with the negatives would only obfuscate it).
Firstly, the gunplay, though not earth-shattering, was a massive step forward for the series. Every weapon feels good, with smooth and responsive animations, impressive models with decent texture work, good particle effects, especially for an engine of this age, and a smoothness which was sorely lacking in the previous fps fallout games, even the great one (New Vegas). That being said, almost every enemy, especially in the early game, are bullet sponges, which is probably my only major complaint with the gunplay, which is by far the biggest positive I can levy at the game, as every other positive is still a step back from the previous games (or rather game, that being New Vegas, which I'll be mentioning quite a bit in this review, as I feel its, for the most part, a fantastic example of what to do when making a fps fallout game).
The next positive worth mentioning would be the world, specifically the surprising depth and variation in atmosphere which fills this rather impressively large world map, filled with plenty of detail, though not quite The Witcher 3 levels. The world itself is also quite breathtaking to look at in certain areas, and even in the more uglier regions was never an eyesore, which has been a major problem for the fps fallout games since the very beginning. Outside of that, the world is still less interesting than New Vegas, but is certainly a massive improvment over Bethesda's last attempt, Fallout 3.
Now with all those positives out of the way, we can get to the overwhelmingly noticable negatives, which had previously had me marking the game with a negative rating before the price drop. To open this section, I'll mention the most damning of these problems, and the one which single handedly ruined the experience for me: The story, and the way the game handles role-playing.
From the very start of the game, you're given the impression there is something wrong: You're not given a blank slate character for you to role play with, you're given an all-but-named protagonist with set motives, goals and a personality, though worst of all they have a set history, which creates a massive disconnect between the player and the game itself. This problem exists throughout the entire experience, never allowing me to feel like the character I was playing, but rather I was something akin to the god-figure in the sims, a watchful eye who occasionally controlled the actions of someone else, a fact which is made clear by the fact that the protagonist is voiced, which attaches intention and motive to extremely limited lines, where before you could be whomever you wanted to.
The next aspect of the story which is terrible is the story itself, but this review is getting long enough, and I don't want to spoil anything for anyone who might want to play the game (not that the story is worth it), so I'll just say that it makes no sense, is completely insulting, and reads like an 8th grader's fallout fanfiction.
Following story and player-interaction with said story, the next most damning sin this game commits is to the RPG systems (ie leveling), which is to say they completely broke it. In previous games, you were limited in your options, forcing you to pick a certain play style and to stick with it, further sucking you into the role of the character you were playing, as you felt like a real person, instead of a vessel to enact chaos in a virtual world (which may be fun in action games like Far Cry, but  isn't in an RPG like Fallout, where immersing yourself in the role you play is the entire object of the game). In Fallout 4, much like the previous work Bethesda made with Skyrim, it was entirely possible and viable to be a jack-of-all-trades, good at absolutely everything, allowing you to become an unstoppable super soldier, while never truly feeling like a specific role to project yourself into. In New Vegas, you could be a lunatic in the desert, running around beating people to death with your bare hands, and the game and story would facilitate this, but you could just as easily be a brilliant but socially awkward scientist and master with computers who would rather avoid combat than enter it, and the game and story also would allow this. No matter what path you went down, the game never stopped you from going down it, rather it encouraged you to explore your options, and become who you want to in the wastelands, a fact which is made clear to you right from the start, when the tutorial area of goodsprings gives you not one but two options in progressing through the side quest. Either you A) side with the town of goodsprings in defeating the powder gangers, or B) side with the powder gangers to destory goodsprings. An option like this can start you off on either a path of good karma benevolence, or bad karma evil, truly shaping you into the person you want to be. In Fallout 4, you're either an ex-soldier searching for his lost son whom he loves after losing his wife whom he also loved, or you're a lawyer searching for her lost son, whom she loves, after losing her husband, whom she also loved. This great limits your ability to be who you want to be, and as I mentioned before in previous sections, ruins the game.
There are many, many other problems, like the return of the game and immersion breaking bugs, the terrible dialogue tree from mass effect, or the aging engine bottlenecking the whole experience, but this review is way too long as-is, and I'd like to wrap it up.
Despite all of these major problems, I would still recommend the game for people who enjoy the Bethesda style open world exploration, as this game does give you that, at least.
My rating would be a 6/10, above average, but not what I would call good.

It's a gem: small and well-crafted. It's simple but with depth (no complexity for the sake of it), and builds on the heritage of roguelikes and Diablo.
Three things that I think it does well:
The combat is enduringly fun and replayable, and the rest of the game is built on that. Good foundation!
The player economy is really cool: most loot that drops is crafting materials, and most equipment you could ever want is crafted from these (or bought at auction from other people who've done it).
The payment system is even-handed. You need "energy" to delve into the dungeons and to craft stuff. You get 100 energy per day for free (capped at 100). If you want more energy, spend cash (in fact, energy is the only thing you can buy for cash). Or, you can also buy it for in-game gold, which you got by questing or selling crafted stuff. So you don't need to spend a cent.
Anyway, it's a good game. It may not hold my interest for too long (it's not a huge game), but it's a fine time.

Quick Take:
Good: Turn-based, Rogue-like, Challenging (in the begining gets easier once you understand that people are going to die), Gritty, Campy.
Bad: Slow-paced at times, Grindy, Balancing,
The narration is awesome. Clearly that is just my opinion but it has greatly increased my enjoyment of this game. So much that it made the quick take.
Long Take:
Rejection of EA status: Technically in "Steam Early Access" this title has been there for many months and has been on sale several times. I personally take it upon myself to kick the label and the excuses away at some point because consumers have been purchasing the title at full price and while the game may improve the current state of the game is suitable for judgment. The Early Access-Completeness (term coined here trademark pending) of this game is not really an issue for me. There is plenty of content here versus other completed games available purchase.
I personally find the narration to be my favorite part. The verbose and ominous tone of the narrator is the pinnacle of campy over-the-top hilarity. This aspect is probably not going to be as enjoyable for everyone as it has been for me but if you like what you here from the video previews and intro there's much more fun inside.
The rest of the game is pretty solid adding some fresh stuff to the old-timey 4 character dungeon crawler rpg.
Big points for creativity on both the artwork and mechanics of the many diverse characters. One of the most atmospheric games I can ever remember playing in that if every ounce of it oozes with gothic doom.
On the downside this game is a little grindy after awhile.  In the begining its a tough affair to get started with. Later once you understand how to manage human loss with some Corporate America next drone up mentatlity the difficulty curve flattens out a good bit and the game starts to get a little too easy. The balancing issues seem to be a focus of the developers based on the last few updates so this could improve over time. The frustation and grindyness will likely turn some people off so maybe avoid if you get frustrated or bored easily.
